Part A · Object-oriented programming · Chapter 2

Inheritance and polymorphism

How C++ decides which function runs: inheritance access, static and dynamic binding, the vtable and vptr, and the rules around destructors, slicing, construction, name hiding and multiple inheritance. Interviewers love it because every rule has a sharp edge that compiles cleanly and then misbehaves, and "draw the object layout" separates memorised keywords from understanding.

TheoryDrillsCoding· about 6 hours· prerequisites: Ch 1 (constructors, destructors, rule of 3/5/0)

Inheritance, is-a and access

Theory

Mental model. A derived class object contains a complete base class object (the base subobject) followed by the derived class's own members. Public inheritance promises is-a: anywhere code expects a Base&, a Derived must work and keep every promise the base makes. If that promise does not hold, use composition (see Ch 3 for the Liskov substitution principle and the square/rectangle trap).

Public, protected and private inheritance

The inheritance access specifier caps the access of inherited members as seen through the derived class, and it controls who may convert Derived* to Base*. It never changes what the derived class itself can see: a derived class can always use the base's public and protected members, and never its private ones.

Base member: public Base: protected Base: private Base
publicpublicprotectedprivate
protectedprotectedprotectedprivate
privatenot accessiblenot accessiblenot accessible
Derived* → Base* allowed foreveryoneDerived, its friends and its derived classesDerived and its friends only

The default is private for class and public for struct, so class D : B {} is private inheritance. That catches people out when the upcast suddenly fails to compile.

Private inheritance means is-implemented-in-terms-of. It is composition with three extras: the derived class can override the base's virtual functions, can reach its protected members, and gets the empty base optimisation (an empty base takes no space, while an empty member takes at least one byte). C++20's [[no_unique_address]] gives the space saving to members too, so private inheritance is now rarely needed for that reason alone.

The protected access rule

A derived class may access a protected member of its base only through an object of its own type (or a type derived from it). It may not reach into an arbitrary Base:

class Account {
protected:
    long balance_ = 0;
};
class Savings : public Account {
public:
    void ok(Savings& other) { other.balance_ = 0; }   // fine: other is a Savings
    void bad(Account& other) { other.balance_ = 0; }  // error: other may be a Current account
};

The rule exists so that one derived class cannot break the invariants of a sibling class by going through the shared base. ([class.protected])

Construction order with bases

Virtual bases first, then direct bases in base-specifier order (never initialiser-list order), then members in declaration order, then the body; destruction is the exact reverse (Ch 1). -Wreorder warns when the initialiser list disagrees.

Static and dynamic binding

Theory

Mental model. Every expression that names an object has a static type (what the compiler sees in the declaration) and the object it refers to has a dynamic type (what was actually constructed). A call to a non-virtual function is bound at compile time using the static type. A call to a virtual function through a pointer or reference is bound at run time using the dynamic type.

#include <iostream>

struct Base {
    void hello() const { std::cout << "Base::hello\n"; }
    virtual void speak() const { std::cout << "Base::speak\n"; }
    virtual ~Base() = default;
};
struct Derived : Base {
    void hello() const { std::cout << "Derived::hello\n"; }
    void speak() const override { std::cout << "Derived::speak\n"; }
};

int main() {
    Derived d;
    Base& r = d;
    Base* p = &d;
    r.hello();         // non-virtual: static type Base
    r.speak();         // virtual: dynamic type Derived
    p->Base::speak();  // qualified name: dispatch is suppressed
    Base b = d;        // copy: b is a brand new Base object
    b.speak();
}
Base::hello
Derived::speak
Base::speak
Base::speak

Three conditions must hold for a virtual call: the function is virtual in the static type, the call goes through a pointer or reference (or this, implicitly), and the name is not qualified. A call on an object by value (b.speak()) always knows the exact type, so the compiler binds it statically.

What counts as an override

A function in a derived class overrides a base virtual function when it has the same name, the same parameter types, the same cv-qualifiers and the same ref-qualifier. The return type must be the same or covariant (see covariant returns below). If any of these differ, you get a new, unrelated function that hides the base one, and nothing warns you unless you wrote override.

struct Base { virtual void f(int) const; };
struct D1 : Base { void f(int); };                  // missing const: hides, does not override
struct D2 : Base { void f(long) const; };           // different parameter: hides
struct D3 : Base { void f(int) const override; };   // overrides
struct D4 : Base { void f(int) override; };         // error: marks the bug at compile time
  • virtual is implied on an override; repeating it is legal but adds nothing.
  • override changes no behaviour. It only asks the compiler to check that the function really overrides something. Clang's -Winconsistent-missing-override and GCC's -Wsuggest-override help enforce it.
  • final on a function forbids further overriding. On a class it forbids deriving from it. Both let the compiler devirtualise calls (see the cost of a virtual call).
  • override and final are contextual keywords, so old code with a variable called final still compiles.

The vtable and vptr

Theory

Mental model. The standard does not mention vtables, but every mainstream compiler implements virtual functions the same way. Each polymorphic class has one table of function pointers (the vtable), stored once in read-only data. Each object of that class carries a hidden pointer to its class's table (the vptr). A virtual call loads the vptr, indexes the table at a fixed slot chosen at compile time, and calls through the pointer it finds.

What the Itanium ABI puts in a vtable

  • Virtual function slots in declaration order, base class slots first. A derived class appends slots for its new virtual functions after the inherited ones, so a Base* call to slot 2 works on every derived class.
  • Two destructor slots for a virtual destructor: the complete object destructor (runs the destructor chain) and the deleting destructor (runs it and then calls operator delete with the right size). delete p on a Base* calls the deleting destructor of the dynamic type, which is why it frees the right number of bytes.
  • RTTI pointer to the std::type_info object, used by typeid and dynamic_cast.
  • Offset-to-top: how far this subobject is from the start of the complete object. It is zero except in multiple inheritance, and dynamic_cast<void*> uses it.
  • Virtual base offsets when the class has virtual bases (see multiple inheritance).

Where is the vtable emitted? In the translation unit that defines the class's key function: the first virtual function that is not pure and not defined inline. If you never define the key function, the linker reports undefined reference to `vtable for X', which confuses people because the missing thing is a function, not the table. A class whose virtual functions are all inline gets a copy of the vtable in every TU that needs it, merged by the linker.

#include <iostream>

struct Empty {};
struct EmptyVirtual { virtual ~EmptyVirtual() = default; };
struct Plain { int x; };
struct OneVirtual { int x; virtual void f() {} };
struct ManyVirtual { int x; virtual void f() {} virtual void g() {} virtual void h() {} };

int main() {
    std::cout << sizeof(Empty) << ' ' << sizeof(EmptyVirtual) << ' '
              << sizeof(Plain) << ' ' << sizeof(OneVirtual) << ' '
              << sizeof(ManyVirtual) << '\n';
}
1 8 4 16 16

On a 64-bit target, the first virtual function adds an 8-byte vptr, and padding rounds OneVirtual up to 16 for alignment. More virtual functions make the shared vtable longer but leave every object the same size.

The cost of a virtual call

A virtual call is two dependent loads (the vptr, then the slot) and an indirect call. When the branch predictor has seen the target before and the vtable is in cache, that is a few cycles more than a direct call. The real costs are elsewhere:

  • No inlining. The compiler cannot inline a function it cannot name, so it also loses everything inlining enables: constant propagation, vectorisation of the loop around the call, and dead code removal. For a tiny function such as area() in a hot loop, this dominates.
  • Misprediction. If a loop over a mixed container calls a different target each time, the indirect branch mispredicts, costing about 15 to 20 cycles on a modern core. Sorting objects by type, or keeping one container per type, restores predictability.
  • Size and cache. Every object grows by 8 bytes, and objects usually live behind pointers, which costs a cache miss per element. This is often worse than the call itself (see Ch 19).

Devirtualisation. The compiler turns a virtual call into a direct call when it can prove the dynamic type: the object is a local by value, the class or function is final, or link-time optimisation sees the whole hierarchy. GCC also devirtualises speculatively: it compares the loaded function pointer with the likely target and, if they match, runs an inlined copy of that target. Low-latency code often prefers compile-time polymorphism (templates, CRTP in Ch 3, std::variant) on the hot path for these reasons.

Key factValue or rule
vptr location (Itanium ABI)offset 0 of each polymorphic subobject
vtables per classone, shared by all objects, in read-only data
Object size costone pointer per polymorphic base subobject, independent of the number of virtual functions
Virtual callload vptr, load slot, indirect call; blocks inlining unless devirtualised
Dispatch needsvirtual function, pointer or reference (or this), unqualified name
Inside constructors and destructorsdispatch uses the class currently being built or destroyed
Default argumentstaken from the static type, never the dynamic type
Cannot be virtualconstructors, static member functions, member function templates
Can be virtualdestructors (including pure), operators, private functions, inline functions

Pure virtual functions and abstract classes

Theory

A pure virtual function (= 0) says "every concrete derived class must provide this". A class with at least one pure virtual function, declared or inherited and not overridden, is abstract: you cannot create an object of it, but you can have pointers and references to it, and it can have constructors, data members and non-virtual functions.

Two facts people miss:

  • A pure virtual function can have a definition. Derived classes can call it with a qualified name, for example to share default behaviour while still forcing every class to opt in. The definition must be outside the class.
  • A pure virtual destructor must have a definition, because every derived destructor calls the base destructor. Declaring the destructor pure is a way to make a class abstract when it has no other natural pure function.
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>

struct Shape {
    virtual double area() const = 0;
    virtual ~Shape() = 0;
};
Shape::~Shape() {}                          // required: derived destructors call it
double Shape::area() const { return 0.0; }  // optional default, reachable by name

struct Square : Shape {
    explicit Square(double s) : side(s) {}
    double area() const override { return side * side; }
    double side;
};
struct Dot : Shape {
    double area() const override { return Shape::area(); }  // opt in to the default
};

int main() {
    std::unique_ptr<Shape> shapes[] = {std::make_unique<Square>(3), std::make_unique<Dot>()};
    for (const auto& s : shapes) std::cout << s->area() << '\n';
    // Shape s;  // error: Shape is abstract
}
9
0

Pure virtual call. If a pure virtual function is called through dispatch while the object's dynamic type is still the abstract class (in practice: indirectly from the abstract class's constructor or destructor), behaviour is undefined ([class.abstract]). GCC and Clang put __cxa_pure_virtual in the slot, which prints pure virtual method called and calls std::terminate. A reading drill below shows it.

Virtual destructors and object slicing

Theory

Why delete through a base pointer needs a virtual destructor

delete p where p is a Base* but the object is a Derived is undefined behaviour unless Base has a virtual destructor ([expr.delete]/3). In practice, without the virtual destructor the compiler calls Base::~Base directly: Derived's destructor never runs (its members leak, its locks stay held), and operator delete receives the wrong size. With a virtual destructor, delete calls the deleting destructor through the vtable, which runs the whole chain and frees the right size.

#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <string>

struct Base {
    virtual ~Base() { std::cout << "~Base\n"; }
};
struct Derived : Base {
    std::string name = "a string long enough to live on the heap";
    ~Derived() override { std::cout << "~Derived\n"; }
};

int main() {
    std::unique_ptr<Base> p = std::make_unique<Derived>();
    p.reset();  // calls Derived's deleting destructor through the vtable
}
~Derived
~Base

The guideline (C++ Core Guidelines C.35): a base class destructor should be either public and virtual (you may delete through a base pointer) or protected and non-virtual (you may not, so the compiler rejects delete base_ptr outside the hierarchy). A class marked final, or a class never used polymorphically, needs neither.

Interview trap

"shared_ptr<Base> works without a virtual destructor, so virtual destructors are not needed with smart pointers." Half true. std::shared_ptr<Base> p = std::make_shared<Derived>() (and shared_ptr<Base>(new Derived)) records a deleter for Derived in the control block when it is created, so the right destructor runs. std::unique_ptr<Base> uses default_delete<Base>, which is a plain delete on a Base*, so it needs the virtual destructor. See Ch 11.

Arrays are the second exception people miss: Base* p = new Derived[4]; delete[] p; is undefined behaviour even with a virtual destructor, because delete[] needs the static and dynamic types to match. Indexing such an array through a Base* is also broken, because p[1] steps by sizeof(Base).

Object slicing

Slicing happens when a derived object is copied into a base object by value. The base copy constructor copies only the base subobject, and the new object is a genuine Base with Base's vptr. Nothing derived survives, and later virtual calls go to Base.

How to prevent it. Pass and store polymorphic objects by reference or (smart) pointer, catch exceptions by const&, and make polymorphic bases non-copyable (delete or protect the copy operations) so the compiler rejects accidental slicing. When you genuinely need a copy of an unknown dynamic type, add a virtual clone() (the "virtual constructor" idiom, drilled in Write the code).

Virtual calls in constructors and destructors

Theory

Mental model. While Base's constructor runs, the Derived part does not exist yet, so calling a Derived override would read uninitialised members. C++ prevents that: during a constructor or destructor, the object's dynamic type is the class whose constructor or destructor is running ([class.cdtor]). Under the hood, each constructor writes its own class's vptr into the object before running its body, and each destructor writes it back before running its body.

#include <iostream>

struct Base {
    Base() { std::cout << "Base(): "; who(); }
    virtual ~Base() { std::cout << "~Base(): "; who(); }
    virtual void who() const { std::cout << "Base\n"; }
    void call() const { who(); }
};
struct Derived : Base {
    Derived() { std::cout << "Derived(): "; who(); }
    ~Derived() override { std::cout << "~Derived(): "; who(); }
    void who() const override { std::cout << "Derived\n"; }
};

int main() {
    Derived d;
    std::cout << "main: ";
    d.call();
}
Base(): Base
Derived(): Derived
main: Derived
~Derived(): Derived
~Base(): Base

Fixes when the base needs derived-specific data at construction time: pass the data up as a constructor argument, use a factory function that constructs and then calls an init(), or make the base a template on the derived type (CRTP, Ch 3). Java and C# dispatch to the derived override from a base constructor, so candidates with that background often give the wrong answer here.

Name hiding, using-declarations and default arguments

Theory

Name hiding

Name lookup happens before overload resolution, and it stops at the first scope that contains the name. If a derived class declares any member named f, every base member named f is hidden, whatever their parameters and whether or not they are virtual. Overload resolution then picks among the derived fs only, using conversions if it must.

#include <iostream>

struct Base {
    void f(int) { std::cout << "Base::f(int)\n"; }
    void f(const char*) { std::cout << "Base::f(const char*)\n"; }
};
struct Hides : Base {
    void f(double) { std::cout << "Hides::f(double)\n"; }
};
struct Unhides : Base {
    using Base::f;  // brings every Base::f overload into this scope
    void f(double) { std::cout << "Unhides::f(double)\n"; }
};

int main() {
    Hides h;
    h.f(1);       // finds only Hides::f, converts 1 to double
    // h.f("x");  // error: no Hides::f takes a const char*
    h.Base::f(1); // qualified lookup still reaches the base
    Unhides u;
    u.f(1);
    u.f("x");
    u.f(2.5);
}
Hides::f(double)
Base::f(int)
Base::f(int)
Base::f(const char*)
Unhides::f(double)

A using-declaration brings all overloads of the name and can also change their access (a public: using Base::f; in a privately derived class re-exposes f). If the derived class declares a function with the same signature as one brought in by using, the derived one wins. using Base::Base; is the related C++11 feature for inheriting constructors.

Interview trap

Overriding one overload of a virtual function hides the other overloads. If Base has virtual void draw(int) and virtual void draw(double) and Derived overrides only draw(int), then derived.draw(2.5) calls draw(int) with a truncated argument. Calls through a Base& still see both. Add using Base::draw;. GCC's -Woverloaded-virtual warns about this.

Default arguments are statically bound

The function body is chosen at run time, but default arguments are pasted in at compile time from the declaration the compiler sees, which is the one in the static type ([dcl.fct.default]/10). So an override with a different default produces a call that mixes the derived body with the base default.

struct Base    { virtual void draw(int width = 1) const; };
struct Derived : Base { void draw(int width = 5) const override; };
Derived d; Base& b = d;
b.draw();   // Derived::draw(1): derived body, base default
d.draw();   // Derived::draw(5)

The rule: never redefine a default argument in an override (Scott Meyers, Effective C++ item 37). If defaults are needed, use the non-virtual interface idiom: a public non-virtual function with the default calls a private virtual one without.

Access and virtual functions

Access is checked at the call site using the static type, while the function that runs comes from the dynamic type ([class.access.virt]). So a private override is reachable through a public base function, which is what makes the non-virtual interface (NVI) idiom work: public non-virtual functions fix the policy and call private virtual hooks.

class Logger {
public:
    void log(std::string_view msg) { if (!msg.empty()) write(msg); }  // fixed policy
    virtual ~Logger() = default;
private:
    virtual void write(std::string_view msg) = 0;  // derived classes override a private hook
};

Multiple inheritance, the diamond and virtual inheritance

Theory

Layout and pointer adjustment

With struct File : Readable, Writable, a File object contains a complete Readable subobject, then a complete Writable subobject, then File's own members. Each polymorphic subobject has its own vptr. Converting a File* to a Writable* therefore changes the address: the compiler adds the offset of the Writable subobject (and checks for null first). A virtual call through the Writable* to a function that File overrides goes through a small thunk that subtracts the offset again before jumping to File's function.

#include <iostream>

struct Readable { virtual ~Readable() = default; virtual int read() { return 1; } int r = 0; };
struct Writable { virtual ~Writable() = default; virtual int write() { return 2; } int w = 0; };
struct File : Readable, Writable { int f = 0; };

int main() {
    File file;
    const char* base = reinterpret_cast<const char*>(&file);
    Readable* rp = &file;
    Writable* wp = &file;  // implicit upcast adjusts the pointer
    std::cout << "Readable at +" << reinterpret_cast<const char*>(rp) - base << '\n';
    std::cout << "Writable at +" << reinterpret_cast<const char*>(wp) - base << '\n';
    std::cout << "wp == &file: " << (wp == &file) << '\n';           // compares after converting &file
    std::cout << "most derived: " << (dynamic_cast<void*>(wp) == static_cast<void*>(&file)) << '\n';
    std::cout << "sizeof(File) = " << sizeof(File) << '\n';
}
Readable at +0
Writable at +16
wp == &file: 1
most derived: 1
sizeof(File) = 32

This is also why casting a File* to void* and then to Writable* is wrong: void* erases the type, so no adjustment happens and the result points at the Readable subobject. Always cast back to exactly the type you converted from.

The diamond and virtual inheritance

If B and C both derive from A normally and D derives from both, a D holds two A subobjects. d.a and the conversion D* → A* are ambiguous and fail to compile; you must say d.B::a. Declaring the inheritance virtual (struct B : virtual A) makes all virtual A bases in a complete object share one subobject.

Rules that come with virtual inheritance:

  • The most derived class initialises the virtual base. D's constructor calls A's constructor directly, before any non-virtual base. The A(...) initialisers in B's and C's constructors are ignored when they run as part of a D. If D does not name A, A is default-constructed, which fails to compile if A has no default constructor.
  • Virtual bases are constructed first, in depth-first, left-to-right order of the class graph, and destroyed last.
  • Cost: access to a virtual base's members goes through a vbase offset in the vtable, and static_cast from a virtual base down to a derived class is ill-formed, because the offset is not a compile-time constant. Use dynamic_cast.
  • The standard library uses it in iostreams: std::iostream derives from std::istream and std::ostream, which both derive virtually from std::basic_ios.

In practice, keep multiple inheritance for interfaces: classes with only pure virtual functions and no data, where the diamond has nothing to duplicate. The design side of this is in Ch 3.

Covariant returns, dynamic_cast and RTTI

Theory

Covariant return types

An override may return a pointer or reference to a class derived from the base function's return type (with the same or fewer cv-qualifiers). The classic use is clone(): callers holding a Circle get a Circle* back without a cast, and callers holding a Shape get a Shape*. When the override is called through the base, the compiler adjusts the returned pointer if the base subobject is not at offset 0 (another thunk). Covariance works only for raw pointers and references, so std::unique_ptr<Circle> cannot override a function returning std::unique_ptr<Shape>; the usual workaround is a public non-virtual clone() that wraps a private virtual one returning a raw pointer.

#include <iostream>
#include <memory>

struct Shape {
    virtual ~Shape() = default;
    virtual Shape* clone() const = 0;
    virtual const char* name() const = 0;
};
struct Circle : Shape {
    double r = 2;
    Circle* clone() const override { return new Circle(*this); }  // covariant
    const char* name() const override { return "circle"; }
};

int main() {
    Circle c;
    std::unique_ptr<Circle> c2(c.clone());  // Circle*, no cast needed
    const Shape& s = c;
    std::unique_ptr<Shape> s2(s.clone());   // through the base: Shape*
    std::cout << c2->r << ' ' << s2->name() << '\n';
}
2 circle

dynamic_cast

dynamic_cast asks the run-time type information (RTTI) whether the object really has the requested type. It requires a polymorphic source type (at least one virtual function) for downcasts and cross-casts. Its results:

  • dynamic_cast<Dog*>(animal_ptr) returns nullptr on failure.
  • dynamic_cast<Dog&>(animal_ref) throws std::bad_cast on failure, because there is no null reference.
  • dynamic_cast<void*>(p) returns the address of the most derived object.
  • Cross-casts work: with File : Readable, Writable, a Readable* can be dynamic_cast to Writable* when the object is a File.
  • Upcasts need no RTTI and compile to the same code as static_cast.

Cost. With GCC and Clang, a downcast reads the type_info from the vtable and walks the class hierarchy description, comparing type names or pointers. That costs tens of nanoseconds for deep or multiple hierarchies, much more than a virtual call. When the target class is final, a compiler is allowed to replace the hierarchy walk with a single vtable-pointer comparison (recent Clang does this as an optimisation), but do not rely on it. Frequent dynamic_cast is usually a design smell: a virtual function or the visitor pattern expresses the same thing.

static_cast downcasts are unchecked. If the object is not really a Dog, using the result is undefined behaviour. They are fine when the type is known by construction (CRTP does exactly this).

typeid and type_info

typeid(expr) returns a const std::type_info&. For a glvalue of polymorphic type it evaluates the expression and reports the dynamic type; for anything else it reports the static type at compile time. typeid(*p) with a null polymorphic p throws std::bad_typeid. type_info::name() is implementation-defined (GCC and Clang return the mangled name such as 3Dog), so compare type_info objects or use std::type_index as a map key rather than printing names. -fno-rtti disables typeid and dynamic_cast (except upcasts) and is common in embedded and some game and trading codebases.

#include <iostream>
#include <typeinfo>

struct Animal { virtual ~Animal() = default; };
struct Dog : Animal { void bark() const { std::cout << "woof\n"; } };
struct Cat : Animal {};

static void poke(Animal& a) {
    if (auto* d = dynamic_cast<Dog*>(&a)) d->bark();
    else std::cout << "not a dog\n";
    try {
        (void)dynamic_cast<Cat&>(a);
        std::cout << "a cat\n";
    } catch (const std::bad_cast&) {
        std::cout << "bad_cast\n";
    }
    std::cout << (typeid(a) == typeid(Dog)) << '\n';  // dynamic type
}

int main() {
    Dog d;
    Cat c;
    poke(d);
    poke(c);
}
woof
bad_cast
1
not a dog
a cat
0

Concept and tricky questions

Drills

ConceptWalk through what the machine does for p->speak() when p is a Base* pointing at a Derived.

Answer

Answer. Load the vptr from offset 0 of *p, load the function pointer from the fixed slot for speak in that vtable, then make an indirect call with p (possibly adjusted) as this.

Why. The compiler knows from Base's definition which slot speak occupies, and every derived class keeps that slot at the same index, so the only run-time work is finding which table this object uses. Under multiple inheritance the slot may hold a thunk that adjusts this before jumping to the real override. A common wrong answer is "the runtime searches for the function by name": nothing is looked up by name, and the cost is constant regardless of hierarchy depth.

TrickyWhy can a constructor not be virtual, and how do you get the effect of one?

Answer

Answer. Virtual dispatch needs an existing object whose vptr names its dynamic type, and the constructor is what creates the object and writes the vptr. To create an object of a type known only at run time, use a factory function, or for copies, a virtual clone() (the "virtual constructor" idiom).

Why. new T requires the exact type at compile time so it knows the size and which constructor to call. A virtual function selects behaviour based on an object that already exists. clone() works because it is called on an existing object, which then constructs a copy of its own type. Candidates sometimes answer "because constructors have no name": that is a grammar detail, not the reason.

ConceptWhat is the difference between overloading, overriding and hiding? Which are decided at compile time?

Answer

Answer. Overloading is several functions with the same name and different parameter lists in the same scope; overload resolution picks one at compile time from the static types of the arguments. Overriding is a derived class redeclaring a base virtual function with the same parameter types, cv-qualifiers and ref-qualifier; the body is picked at run time from the dynamic type of the object. Hiding is what happens when a derived class declares any member with the same name that does not override: every base member of that name disappears from lookup in the derived scope, decided at compile time.

Why. The textbook line "overloading is compile-time polymorphism, overriding is run-time polymorphism" is right but incomplete, and interviewers probe the gap. Overloading never crosses scopes, so a Derived::f(double) does not add an overload to Base::f(int): it hides it, and d.f(1) converts 1 to double. Writing override turns an accidental hide into a compile error, and using Base::f; turns a deliberate one back into overloading. Return types play no part in overloading, and only covariant changes are allowed when overriding.

TrickyCan a pure virtual function have a body? Does a pure virtual destructor need one? Must a class derived from a base with a pure virtual destructor declare its own destructor to be concrete?

Answer

Answer. Yes, yes, and no. A pure virtual function may have a definition, written outside the class (virtual void f() = 0 {} is ill-formed), and derived classes can call it as Base::f(). A pure virtual destructor must be defined, or the link fails with undefined reference to Base::~Base(). A derived class is concrete without writing a destructor, because its implicit destructor overrides the pure one.

Why. = 0 means "derived classes must override this", not "this has no code". Every derived destructor calls the base destructor directly (not through the vtable), so that call needs a body. The pure virtual destructor is the idiom for making a class abstract when no other function is a natural candidate. The common wrong answer, from Java and C# abstract methods, is "pure means no implementation, so a body is a compile error".

TrickyCan a virtual function be inline? static? A member function template?

Answer

Answer. Inline: yes. Static: no. Template: no (although a virtual function inside a class template is fine).

Why. inline is about linkage (multiple definitions allowed); the compiler inlines the body wherever it can devirtualise the call, and still emits an out-of-line copy for the vtable slot. A static member function has no this and is called without an object, so there is no vptr to dispatch on. A member function template can be instantiated with any number of types in any translation unit, so the vtable size and slot numbers could not be fixed when the class is defined. A class template's virtual functions are fine because each instantiation is a separate class with a fixed set of functions.

TrickyA class has one char member and ten virtual functions. What is its sizeof on x86-64 Linux?

Answer

Answer. 16.

Why. The object holds one vptr (8 bytes) whatever the number of virtual functions; the ten function pointers live in the single shared vtable. The char sits at offset 8 and the size rounds up to the 8-byte alignment of the vptr. The common wrong answer is 88 (ten pointers plus a padded char), which confuses the per-class table with the per-object pointer. The answer changes with multiple inheritance, where each polymorphic base subobject brings its own vptr.

ConceptWhen does a base class not need a virtual destructor?

Answer

Answer. When no one deletes a derived object through a pointer to it. The standard way to enforce that is a protected non-virtual destructor. Classes that are never used polymorphically, and final classes, also do not need one.

Why. [expr.delete]/3 makes delete base_ptr undefined only when the dynamic type differs and the destructor is not virtual. A protected destructor turns that misuse into a compile error, so you save the vptr and keep the class trivially destructible where possible. This is C++ Core Guidelines C.35: "public and virtual, or protected and non-virtual". Saying "every class with inheritance needs one" is safe advice but wrong as a rule: mixins and CRTP bases (Ch 3) deliberately use protected non-virtual destructors.

TrickyBase has a virtual destructor. Is Base* p = new Derived[3]; delete[] p; correct?

Answer

Answer. No. It is undefined behaviour even with the virtual destructor.

Why. [expr.delete]/3: for delete[], the dynamic type must be the same as the static type. delete[] walks the array using sizeof of the static type to find each element, and sizeof(Base) is not sizeof(Derived), so it would call destructors at the wrong addresses. The same stride problem breaks p[1]. The virtual destructor fixes single-object delete only. Use std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Base>> for a polymorphic collection.

TrickyCan a derived class override a private virtual function of its base? Why would anyone do that?

Answer

Answer. Yes. Access controls who may call a name; overriding is not a call. It is the basis of the non-virtual interface (NVI) idiom.

Why. The base has a public non-virtual function that checks preconditions, takes locks, logs or times the operation, and then calls a private virtual hook. Derived classes customise the hook but cannot skip the fixed policy, and outside code cannot call the hook directly. Many candidates think private members are "not inherited": they are inherited and present in the object, just not accessible by name from the derived class. The C++ standard library uses this pattern in std::streambuf (public sputc, protected virtual overflow).

TrickyBase::run() is public and virtual. Derived overrides it in a private: section. Which calls compile: base_ref.run() or derived_ref.run()? Which function executes?

Answer

Answer. base_ref.run() compiles and runs Derived::run. derived_ref.run() does not compile.

Why. [class.access.virt]: access is checked at the call site using the static type of the object expression, while the function executed comes from the dynamic type. Through Base& the name is public. Through Derived& it is private. This surprises people who expect the override's access to "win" at run time; access is purely a compile-time property.

ConceptWhen would you choose private inheritance over a data member?

Answer

Answer. When you need to override a virtual function of the class you are using, access its protected members, or (before C++20) get the empty base optimisation. Otherwise prefer a member.

Why. Both model "implemented in terms of" without an is-a relationship, since outside code cannot convert to the private base. A member is simpler, has a name and allows several instances, while a private base's names enter your scope and can hide or clash. C++20 [[no_unique_address]] gives an empty member zero size, which removes the main historical reason (storing an empty deleter or allocator for free).

TrickyA constructor does std::memset(this, 0, sizeof(*this)); to clear all members. The class has a virtual function. What happens?

Answer

Answer. The vptr is overwritten with zero, so the next virtual call jumps through a null table and crashes. Formally it is undefined behaviour, because a polymorphic class is not trivially copyable.

Why. The vptr is written by the constructor before the body runs, so the memset in the body wipes it. The same applies to memcpy between polymorphic objects, calloc plus a cast instead of construction, and writing polymorphic objects to a file and reading them back (the stored vptr is meaningless in another run, especially with ASLR). The fix is to use member initialisers (int x = 0;) or value initialisation. std::is_trivially_copyable_v<T> tells you whether byte copies are allowed.

TrickyThe link fails with undefined reference to `vtable for Widget'. Every function you call is defined. What is the likely cause?

Answer

Answer. Some non-pure virtual function of Widget is declared but never defined, most often the first one out of line (the key function), or the .cpp that defines it is not linked in.

Why. GCC and Clang emit the vtable only in the translation unit that defines the key function: the first virtual function that is not pure and not inline. Every constructor references the vtable, so the error appears wherever an object is constructed, even if nobody calls the missing function. Common culprits: a declared but undefined virtual destructor, forgetting to add a file to the build, or (with Qt) a missing moc step. A pure virtual function does not cause this; the slot simply holds __cxa_pure_virtual.

TrickyDoes marking a class final make all virtual calls on it faster?

Answer

Answer. Only calls made through a pointer, reference or object whose static type is the final class (or that otherwise prove the type). Calls through a Base* still dispatch.

Why. If the static type is Leaf& and Leaf is final, the dynamic type must be exactly Leaf, so the compiler can call Leaf::f directly and inline it. A Base* could point at any class, so final on Leaf tells the compiler nothing at that call site (unless whole-program devirtualisation can see the entire hierarchy). final also lets dynamic_cast<Leaf*> become a vptr comparison.

ConceptCompare compile-time and run-time polymorphism in C++. What does each one cost, and when would you choose each?

Answer

Answer. Compile-time (static) polymorphism is overloading, templates constrained by concepts, and CRTP: the call target is fixed during compilation, so it is a direct, inlinable call with no per-object overhead. Run-time (dynamic) polymorphism is virtual functions called through a pointer or reference: one vptr per object, two dependent loads and an indirect call, usually no inlining. Choose static dispatch when the set of types is known at build time and the call is hot; choose virtual functions when the type is picked at run time, objects of different types share one container, or the implementation must stay behind a library boundary.

Why. Static polymorphism pays in other currencies: one instantiation per type (code size and instruction cache), longer compile times, implementation in headers, and no heterogeneous containers. std::variant with std::visit sits between the two: a closed set of types, value storage and a jump table instead of a vtable. The usual wrong answer is "virtual calls are slow because of the vtable lookup". The lookup costs a few cycles when predicted; the real costs are the lost inlining and mispredicted branches on mixed targets (see the cost of a virtual call).

ConceptWith a diamond using virtual inheritance, who constructs the shared base, and when?

Answer

Answer. The most derived class constructs it, first, before any non-virtual base. Initialisers for the virtual base written in intermediate classes are ignored when those classes are not the most derived.

Why. There is only one virtual base subobject, so exactly one constructor call must initialise it; letting either intermediate class do it would be arbitrary. If the most derived class does not name the virtual base in its initialiser list, the virtual base is default-constructed, which is a compile error if it has no default constructor. The reading drill on virtual bases below shows the order.

ConceptWhen must you use dynamic_cast for a downcast, and when is static_cast fine?

Answer

Answer. Use static_cast when you know the dynamic type by construction (it is free). Use dynamic_cast when you need to ask, when you cast across branches of a hierarchy, or when the base is virtual.

Why. static_cast<Derived*>(base_ptr) just subtracts a compile-time offset; if the object is not a Derived, using the result is undefined behaviour. dynamic_cast consults RTTI and returns null (or throws std::bad_cast for references). From a virtual base, static_cast is ill-formed because the offset depends on the most derived type and is known only at run time. Cross-casts (Readable* to Writable*) are only possible with dynamic_cast.

TrickyYou have void collide(const Shape&) and void collide(const Circle&). Given Shape& s that refers to a Circle, which one does collide(s) call? How would you make it choose by dynamic type?

Answer

Answer. collide(const Shape&). Overload resolution is done at compile time on static types. To select on the dynamic type, make the operation a virtual member, and for two dynamic types use double dispatch (the visitor pattern) or std::variant with std::visit.

Why. C++ virtual functions give single dispatch: only the object the function is called on is examined at run time. Arguments are never examined. The visitor pattern makes two virtual calls, one on each object, to recover both types; it is the coding drill on double dispatch below. Candidates coming from languages with multimethods sometimes expect the runtime to pick the more specific overload.

Predict the output and find the bug

Drills

OutputDefault arguments on a virtual function. What does this print?

#include <iostream>

struct Base {
    virtual void show(int n = 1) const { std::cout << "Base " << n << '\n'; }
    virtual ~Base() = default;
};
struct Derived : Base {
    void show(int n = 2) const override { std::cout << "Derived " << n << '\n'; }
};

int main() {
    Derived d;
    Base& b = d;
    Base* p = &d;
    b.show();
    p->show();
    d.show();
    static_cast<Base>(d).show();
}
Answer
Derived 1
Derived 1
Derived 2
Base 1

Why. The body is chosen by the dynamic type, the default argument by the static type ([dcl.fct.default]/10). Through Base& and Base* the compiler inserts 1, then dispatch runs Derived::show. Through d the static type is Derived, so the default is 2. The last line creates a temporary Base by slicing, so it is a real Base object. Rule: never change a default argument in an override.

OutputFour ways to hold a dog. What does this print?

#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct Animal {
    virtual std::string sound() const { return "..."; }
    virtual ~Animal() = default;
};
struct Dog : Animal {
    std::string sound() const override { return "woof"; }
};

int main() {
    std::vector<Animal> zoo;
    zoo.push_back(Dog{});
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Animal>> zoo2;
    zoo2.push_back(std::make_unique<Dog>());
    Dog rex;
    Animal& ref = rex;
    Animal copy = ref;
    std::cout << zoo[0].sound() << ' ' << zoo2[0]->sound() << ' '
              << ref.sound() << ' ' << copy.sound() << '\n';
}
Answer
... woof woof ...

Why. std::vector<Animal> stores Animal objects, so push_back(Dog{}) copies (moves) only the Animal part into a new Animal: slicing. Animal copy = ref; slices too, even though ref refers to a dog, because the copy is a fresh Animal whose constructor installs Animal's vptr. Only the reference and the pointer keep the dynamic type. Making Animal's copy operations protected or deleted would turn both slicing lines into compile errors.

Find the bugThis program prints one line and exits normally. What is wrong, and how would you catch it?

#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

struct Buffer {
    ~Buffer() { std::cout << "~Buffer\n"; }
    virtual void fill() {}
};
struct FileBuffer : Buffer {
    std::vector<char> data = std::vector<char>(4096);
    ~FileBuffer() { std::cout << "~FileBuffer\n"; }
};

int main() {
    Buffer* b = new FileBuffer;
    b->fill();
    delete b;
}
Answer

Answer. Buffer is polymorphic but its destructor is not virtual, so delete b is undefined behaviour. In practice it prints only ~Buffer: ~FileBuffer never runs and the 4 KB vector leaks. On Linux, LeakSanitizer reports the leaked 4096-byte buffer, and ASan can also report new-delete-type-mismatch, because the object was allocated with 32 bytes and sized deallocation frees it as an 8-byte Buffer. The compiler warning below is the most reliable detector.

Why. Without virtual, delete b is compiled as a direct call to Buffer::~Buffer followed by operator delete(b, sizeof(Buffer)). GCC also warns with -Wdelete-non-virtual-dtor, which is in -Wall. Fix: virtual ~Buffer(), or hold the object in a unique_ptr<FileBuffer>. The output is not compared here because the behaviour is undefined.

OutputOverriding one overload. What does this print?

#include <iostream>

struct Printer {
    virtual void print(int x) { std::cout << "int " << x << '\n'; }
    virtual void print(double x) { std::cout << "double " << x << '\n'; }
    virtual ~Printer() = default;
};
struct Fancy : Printer {
    void print(int x) override { std::cout << "fancy int " << x << '\n'; }
};

int main() {
    Fancy f;
    Printer& p = f;
    f.print(2.5);
    p.print(2.5);
    p.print(3);
}
Answer
fancy int 2
double 2.5
fancy int 3

Why. In Fancy's scope, the name print finds only Fancy::print(int); the base print(double) is hidden, so 2.5 is converted to 2. Through Printer&, lookup sees both base overloads, picks print(double) at compile time, and since Fancy does not override it, Printer::print(double) runs. p.print(3) picks print(int) and dispatches to the override. Fix: using Printer::print; in Fancy. GCC's -Woverloaded-virtual flags this.

Find the bugThe thermostat always reports 0. Why?

#include <iostream>

struct Sensor {
    virtual double read() const { return 0.0; }
    virtual ~Sensor() = default;
};
struct Thermo : Sensor {
    double read() { return 21.5; }  // meant to override
};

static void report(const Sensor& s) { std::cout << s.read() << '\n'; }

int main() {
    Thermo t;
    report(t);
    std::cout << t.read() << '\n';
}
Answer
0
21.5

Answer. Thermo::read is not const, so it does not override Sensor::read() const. It is a new function that hides the base one in Thermo's scope. Through const Sensor&, the base version runs.

Why. An override must match the cv-qualifiers and ref-qualifier exactly. Writing double read() const override fixes it, and writing override on the broken version would have turned the bug into a compile error ("marked override, but does not override"). This is the single best argument for always writing override.

OutputVirtual base initialisation. What does this print?

#include <iostream>

struct A {
    explicit A(int v) : v(v) { std::cout << "A(" << v << ")\n"; }
    int v;
};
struct B : virtual A { B() : A(1) { std::cout << "B\n"; } };
struct C : virtual A { C() : A(2) { std::cout << "C\n"; } };
struct D : B, C { D() : A(3) { std::cout << "D\n"; } };

int main() {
    D d;
    std::cout << "d.v = " << d.v << '\n';
    C c;
    std::cout << "c.v = " << c.v << '\n';
}
Answer
A(3)
B
C
D
d.v = 3
A(2)
C
c.v = 2

Why. When D is the most derived class, D's constructor initialises the virtual base A first, with A(3). The A(1) and A(2) initialisers in B and C are skipped because those constructors are not running for the most derived object. When a plain C is created, C is the most derived class, so its A(2) is used. Remove A(3) from D and the program fails to compile, because A has no default constructor: many candidates expect A(1) from the first base instead.

Find the bugWhy does this not compile, and what are the two ways to fix it?

struct Device { int id = 0; };
struct Scanner : Device {};
struct Printer : Device {};
struct Copier : Scanner, Printer {};

int main() {
    Copier c;
    c.id = 7;
    return c.id;
}
Answer

Answer. A Copier contains two Device subobjects (one in Scanner, one in Printer), so c.id is ambiguous. Converting Copier* to Device* is ambiguous for the same reason.

Why. Fix 1: say which one you mean, c.Scanner::id = 7;, if the copier really has two independent devices. Fix 2: if there should be one device, inherit virtually, struct Scanner : virtual Device and struct Printer : virtual Device, so both share a single subobject. Fix 2 costs a vbase offset per access and makes Copier responsible for constructing Device. Often the best fix is design: make Scanner and Printer data-free interfaces and keep the id in Copier.

Find the bugThis prints nothing on stdout and aborts. Why? (Output is not compared: the behaviour is undefined.)

#include <iostream>

struct Task {
    virtual ~Task() { finish(); }
    void finish() { cleanup(); }  // indirect, so the compiler cannot reject it
    virtual void cleanup() = 0;
};
struct Download : Task {
    void cleanup() override { std::cout << "closing socket\n"; }
};

int main() {
    { Download d; }
    std::cout << "done\n";
}
Answer

Answer. When d is destroyed, ~Download runs first, then ~Task sets the vptr back to Task's vtable. finish() then calls cleanup() through that table, whose slot is the pure virtual stub. With GCC and Clang the runtime prints pure virtual method called to stderr and calls std::terminate, so done never prints.

Why. [class.abstract]/6 makes a virtual call to a pure virtual function from the abstract class's constructor or destructor undefined. A direct call would usually be caught at compile or link time; going through a helper hides it. Fix: do the cleanup in ~Download (each class releases what it owns, RAII style), or make cleanup non-pure. Never rely on derived behaviour from a base destructor.

OutputOverloads and dynamic type. What does this print?

#include <iostream>

struct Shape { virtual ~Shape() = default; };
struct Circle : Shape {};

static void collide(const Shape&) { std::cout << "shape\n"; }
static void collide(const Circle&) { std::cout << "circle\n"; }

int main() {
    Circle c;
    Shape& s = c;
    collide(c);
    collide(s);
}
Answer
circle
shape

Why. Overload resolution uses the static type of each argument at compile time. s has static type Shape&, so collide(const Shape&) is chosen even though the object is a Circle. Virtual dispatch happens only on the object a member function is called on. The visitor pattern (coding drill below) is the standard way to dispatch on argument types.

OutputAssignment through a base reference. What does this print?

#include <iostream>

struct Point {
    int x = 0, y = 0;
    virtual ~Point() = default;
    virtual void print() const { std::cout << x << ',' << y << '\n'; }
};
struct Point3 : Point {
    int z = 0;
    void print() const override { std::cout << x << ',' << y << ',' << z << '\n'; }
};

int main() {
    Point3 a;
    a.x = 1; a.y = 2; a.z = 3;
    Point3 b;
    b.x = 7; b.y = 8; b.z = 9;
    Point& ra = a;
    ra = b;
    a.print();
}
Answer
7,8,3

Why. ra = b calls Point::operator=, chosen statically because assignment operators are not virtual here. It copies only the Point fields, leaving a.z at 3: a half-assigned object that matches neither original. This is the assignment form of slicing. Making operator= virtual does not really help, because the override would have to accept a const Point& and decide what to do with a plain Point. The usual fix is to make polymorphic bases non-assignable (protected or deleted copy assignment).

Outputtypeid with and without virtual functions. What does this print?

#include <iostream>
#include <typeinfo>

struct A {};
struct B : A {};
struct P { virtual ~P() = default; };
struct Q : P {};

int main() {
    B b;
    A& a = b;
    Q q;
    P& p = q;
    std::cout << (typeid(a) == typeid(B)) << (typeid(p) == typeid(Q)) << '\n';
    P* none = nullptr;
    try {
        std::cout << typeid(*none).name() << '\n';
    } catch (const std::bad_typeid&) {
        std::cout << "bad_typeid\n";
    }
}
Answer
01
bad_typeid

Why. A is not polymorphic, so typeid(a) is resolved at compile time from the static type A: there is no vptr to consult. P is polymorphic, so typeid(p) reads the dynamic type Q. For a polymorphic glvalue obtained by dereferencing a null pointer, typeid throws std::bad_typeid instead of crashing ([expr.typeid]/3); this is one of the few places where *nullptr has defined behaviour. The name string itself is implementation-defined, which is why the program never prints a successful one.

Write the code

Coding

CodePolymorphic deep copy. Write an abstract Shape with area(), name(), scale(double) and a clone() that returns std::unique_ptr<Shape>, plus two concrete shapes. Then write Drawing, which owns a std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Shape>> and is copyable with deep-copy semantics. Requirements: copying a Drawing must not share shapes; slicing a Shape by accident must not compile; moving must be noexcept.

Answer

Approach. Give Shape a public non-virtual clone() that wraps a private virtual do_clone() returning a raw pointer, so each override can use a covariant return type and the public interface still returns a smart pointer. Make Shape's copy operations protected: derived classes can still copy themselves inside do_clone, but outside code cannot slice. Drawing's copy constructor clones each element; assignment uses copy-and-swap so a single by-value operator= handles copy and move and gives the strong exception guarantee (rule of five from Ch 1).

#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class Shape {
public:
    virtual ~Shape() = default;
    virtual double area() const = 0;
    virtual std::string name() const = 0;
    virtual void scale(double k) = 0;
    std::unique_ptr<Shape> clone() const { return std::unique_ptr<Shape>(do_clone()); }
protected:
    Shape() = default;
    Shape(const Shape&) = default;             // derived classes may copy, outsiders may not
    Shape& operator=(const Shape&) = default;
private:
    virtual Shape* do_clone() const = 0;
};

class Rect final : public Shape {
public:
    Rect(double w, double h) : w_(w), h_(h) {}
    double area() const override { return w_ * h_; }
    std::string name() const override { return "rect"; }
    void scale(double k) override { w_ *= k; h_ *= k; }
private:
    Rect* do_clone() const override { return new Rect(*this); }  // covariant
    double w_, h_;
};

class Tri final : public Shape {
public:
    Tri(double b, double h) : b_(b), h_(h) {}
    double area() const override { return b_ * h_ / 2; }
    std::string name() const override { return "tri"; }
    void scale(double k) override { b_ *= k; h_ *= k; }
private:
    Tri* do_clone() const override { return new Tri(*this); }
    double b_, h_;
};

class Drawing {
public:
    Drawing() = default;
    Drawing(const Drawing& other) {
        shapes_.reserve(other.shapes_.size());
        for (const auto& s : other.shapes_) shapes_.push_back(s->clone());
    }
    Drawing(Drawing&&) noexcept = default;
    Drawing& operator=(Drawing other) noexcept {  // copy-and-swap: copy happens in the parameter
        shapes_.swap(other.shapes_);
        return *this;
    }
    ~Drawing() = default;

    void add(std::unique_ptr<Shape> s) { shapes_.push_back(std::move(s)); }
    Shape& at(std::size_t i) { return *shapes_.at(i); }
    double total_area() const {
        double total = 0;
        for (const auto& s : shapes_) total += s->area();
        return total;
    }
private:
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Shape>> shapes_;
};

int main() {
    Drawing a;
    a.add(std::make_unique<Rect>(2, 3));
    a.add(std::make_unique<Tri>(4, 5));
    Drawing b = a;  // deep copy
    b.at(0).scale(2);
    Drawing c;
    c = b;          // copy assignment
    c.at(1).scale(0.5);
    std::cout << a.total_area() << ' ' << b.total_area() << ' ' << c.total_area() << '\n';
    std::cout << c.at(0).name() << ' ' << c.at(1).name() << '\n';
    // Rect r = static_cast<Rect&>(a.at(0)); fine, but  Shape s = a.at(0);  does not compile
}
16 34 26.5
rect tri

Complexity and pitfalls. Copy is O(n) allocations; move is O(1). Pitfalls: forgetting to override do_clone in a further-derived class silently clones the parent type (marking leaf classes final prevents that class of bug, and some codebases add a CRTP helper that writes do_clone for you); returning std::unique_ptr<Rect> from an override does not compile because smart pointers are not covariant; and a defaulted copy constructor on Drawing would fail to compile (unique_ptr is move-only), which is the compiler telling you a decision is needed.

Estimated rating: ~1400 · standard idiom, but it needs covariance, protected copies and copy-and-swap together

CodeDynamic dispatch without virtual. Implement an Animal "class" in C-style C++: a struct holding a pointer to a table of function pointers (speak, destroy) and a name. Implement Dog (with a bark count) and Cat (grumpy or not) that embed Animal as their first member, factory functions returning Animal*, and free functions speak(const Animal*) and destroy(Animal*) that dispatch. This is how C codebases (the Linux kernel's file_operations, for example) do dispatch, and how C++ compilers implement virtual functions.

Answer

Approach. One constant table per "class" plays the vtable; the first field of every object plays the vptr. Because Animal is the first member of a standard-layout Dog, a Dog* and a pointer to its base member are pointer-interconvertible, so the "override" can reinterpret_cast back to Dog legally. The destroy slot plays the virtual deleting destructor: it frees the object as its real type.

#include <iostream>

struct Animal;
struct AnimalVTable {
    void (*speak)(const Animal*);
    void (*destroy)(Animal*);
};
struct Animal {
    const AnimalVTable* vptr;
    const char* name;
};

static void speak(const Animal* a) { a->vptr->speak(a); }  // the "virtual call"
static void destroy(Animal* a) { a->vptr->destroy(a); }

struct Dog { Animal base; int barks; };
static void dog_speak(const Animal* a) {
    const Dog* d = reinterpret_cast<const Dog*>(a);  // ok: base is the first member
    std::cout << a->name << ':';
    for (int i = 0; i < d->barks; ++i) std::cout << " woof";
    std::cout << '\n';
}
static void dog_destroy(Animal* a) { delete reinterpret_cast<Dog*>(a); }
static constexpr AnimalVTable dog_vtable{dog_speak, dog_destroy};

static Animal* make_dog(const char* name, int barks) {
    Dog* d = new Dog{{&dog_vtable, name}, barks};
    return &d->base;
}

struct Cat { Animal base; bool grumpy; };
static void cat_speak(const Animal* a) {
    const Cat* c = reinterpret_cast<const Cat*>(a);
    std::cout << a->name << ": " << (c->grumpy ? "hiss" : "meow") << '\n';
}
static void cat_destroy(Animal* a) { delete reinterpret_cast<Cat*>(a); }
static constexpr AnimalVTable cat_vtable{cat_speak, cat_destroy};

static Animal* make_cat(const char* name, bool grumpy) {
    Cat* c = new Cat{{&cat_vtable, name}, grumpy};
    return &c->base;
}

int main() {
    Animal* zoo[] = {make_dog("Rex", 2), make_cat("Tom", false), make_cat("Grim", true)};
    for (const Animal* a : zoo) speak(a);
    for (Animal* a : zoo) destroy(a);
}
Rex: woof woof
Tom: meow
Grim: hiss

Complexity and pitfalls. Each call is the same two loads and an indirect call as a real virtual call. Pitfalls: the cast back is only valid while the embedded base is the first member of a standard-layout struct (otherwise you need offsetof, the kernel's container_of); calling delete on the Animal* itself would be undefined, exactly like a missing virtual destructor; and nothing checks that a table's functions match its object type, which is what the compiler-generated version guarantees for you. Mention in the interview that real vtables also hold RTTI and offset-to-top, and that you have reimplemented single inheritance only.

Estimated rating: ~1600 · needs the vtable model and the pointer-interconvertibility rule, little code

CodeType erasure with value semantics. Write a class Drawable that can hold any type T for which a free function draw(const T&, std::ostream&, std::size_t indent) exists, with no common base class required. Drawable must be copyable (deep copy), movable and storable in a std::vector<Drawable>. Make a Document (a vector of Drawable) itself drawable, so a document can contain a copy of itself. Draw a document holding an int, a std::string, a user Circle and a nested copy of the document.

Answer

Approach. This is Sean Parent's "runtime polymorphism without inheritance". Keep the hierarchy private: a nested abstract Concept with virtual draw_ and clone, and a class template Model<T> that stores a T and forwards to the free draw found by argument-dependent lookup. Drawable owns a unique_ptr<Concept>, copies by cloning, and exposes draw as a hidden friend. Constrain the converting constructor so it never hijacks copying a Drawable. This is the same technique as std::function and std::any.

#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

static void draw(int x, std::ostream& out, std::size_t indent) {
    out << std::string(indent, ' ') << x << '\n';
}
static void draw(const std::string& s, std::ostream& out, std::size_t indent) {
    out << std::string(indent, ' ') << s << '\n';
}

class Drawable {
public:
    template <class T>
        requires(!std::is_same_v<std::remove_cvref_t<T>, Drawable>)
    Drawable(T x) : self_(std::make_unique<Model<T>>(std::move(x))) {}
    Drawable(const Drawable& other) : self_(other.self_->clone()) {}
    Drawable(Drawable&&) noexcept = default;
    Drawable& operator=(Drawable other) noexcept {
        self_ = std::move(other.self_);
        return *this;
    }
    ~Drawable() = default;

    friend void draw(const Drawable& d, std::ostream& out, std::size_t indent) {
        d.self_->draw_(out, indent);
    }

private:
    struct Concept {
        virtual ~Concept() = default;
        virtual void draw_(std::ostream& out, std::size_t indent) const = 0;
        virtual std::unique_ptr<Concept> clone() const = 0;
    };
    template <class T>
    struct Model final : Concept {
        explicit Model(T x) : data(std::move(x)) {}
        void draw_(std::ostream& out, std::size_t indent) const override { draw(data, out, indent); }
        std::unique_ptr<Concept> clone() const override { return std::make_unique<Model>(*this); }
        T data;
    };
    std::unique_ptr<Concept> self_;
};

using Document = std::vector<Drawable>;
static void draw(const Document& doc, std::ostream& out, std::size_t indent) {
    out << std::string(indent, ' ') << "<document>\n";
    for (const auto& d : doc) draw(d, out, indent + 2);
    out << std::string(indent, ' ') << "</document>\n";
}

struct Circle { double r; };
static void draw(const Circle& c, std::ostream& out, std::size_t indent) {
    out << std::string(indent, ' ') << "circle r=" << c.r << '\n';
}

int main() {
    Document doc;
    doc.emplace_back(0);
    doc.emplace_back(std::string("hello"));
    doc.emplace_back(Circle{2});
    Drawable snapshot = doc;  // a deep copy of the document so far
    doc.push_back(std::move(snapshot));
    draw(doc, std::cout, 0);
}
<document>
  0
  hello
  circle r=2
  <document>
    0
    hello
    circle r=2
  </document>
</document>

Complexity and pitfalls. One heap allocation per stored value (a production version adds a small-buffer optimisation, see Ch 18), and one virtual call per draw. Pitfalls: the requires clause is defensive here, because a by-value template is never used to copy its own class ([class.copy.ctor]/5), but if you change the parameter to a forwarding reference T&&, the template beats the copy constructor for a non-const Drawable lvalue and wraps a Drawable inside a Drawable; the free draw for user types must be findable by ADL at instantiation, so declare it in the type's namespace; and copying doc while pushing into it (doc.push_back(doc)) is safe only because the argument is converted to a Drawable before the vector changes, which is why the reference makes the snapshot explicit.

Estimated rating: ~1800 · combines templates, a hidden class hierarchy, ADL and value semantics; many candidates have never seen it

CodeDouble dispatch with the visitor pattern. Build an expression tree with node types Num, Add and Mul owned by std::unique_ptr. Add a Visitor interface and two visitors: one that evaluates the tree to a long and one that prints it fully parenthesised. Adding a new operation must not require editing the node classes.

Answer

Approach. Each node implements accept(Visitor&) by calling v.visit(*this). The first dispatch (virtual accept) recovers the node type; inside it, *this has a static type, so overload resolution picks the right visit overload, and the second dispatch (virtual visit) recovers the visitor type. Visitors keep their state as members. The trade-off: new operations are cheap, new node types require changing every visitor. std::variant plus std::visit is the closed-set, allocation-free alternative.

#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

struct Num;
struct Add;
struct Mul;

struct Visitor {
    virtual ~Visitor() = default;
    virtual void visit(const Num&) = 0;
    virtual void visit(const Add&) = 0;
    virtual void visit(const Mul&) = 0;
};

struct Expr {
    virtual ~Expr() = default;
    virtual void accept(Visitor& v) const = 0;
};
using ExprPtr = std::unique_ptr<Expr>;

struct Num final : Expr {
    explicit Num(long v) : value(v) {}
    void accept(Visitor& v) const override { v.visit(*this); }
    long value;
};
struct Add final : Expr {
    Add(ExprPtr l, ExprPtr r) : lhs(std::move(l)), rhs(std::move(r)) {}
    void accept(Visitor& v) const override { v.visit(*this); }
    ExprPtr lhs, rhs;
};
struct Mul final : Expr {
    Mul(ExprPtr l, ExprPtr r) : lhs(std::move(l)), rhs(std::move(r)) {}
    void accept(Visitor& v) const override { v.visit(*this); }
    ExprPtr lhs, rhs;
};

static ExprPtr num(long v) { return std::make_unique<Num>(v); }
static ExprPtr add(ExprPtr l, ExprPtr r) { return std::make_unique<Add>(std::move(l), std::move(r)); }
static ExprPtr mul(ExprPtr l, ExprPtr r) { return std::make_unique<Mul>(std::move(l), std::move(r)); }

class Evaluator final : public Visitor {
public:
    long eval(const Expr& e) { e.accept(*this); return result_; }
    void visit(const Num& n) override { result_ = n.value; }
    void visit(const Add& a) override { long l = eval(*a.lhs); result_ = l + eval(*a.rhs); }
    void visit(const Mul& m) override { long l = eval(*m.lhs); result_ = l * eval(*m.rhs); }
private:
    long result_ = 0;
};

class Printer final : public Visitor {
public:
    std::string print(const Expr& e) { out_.clear(); e.accept(*this); return out_; }
    void visit(const Num& n) override { out_ += std::to_string(n.value); }
    void visit(const Add& a) override { binary(*a.lhs, " + ", *a.rhs); }
    void visit(const Mul& m) override { binary(*m.lhs, " * ", *m.rhs); }
private:
    void binary(const Expr& l, const char* op, const Expr& r) {
        out_ += '(';
        l.accept(*this);
        out_ += op;
        r.accept(*this);
        out_ += ')';
    }
    std::string out_;
};

int main() {
    ExprPtr exprs[] = {mul(add(num(2), num(3)), num(4)), add(num(1), mul(num(2), num(-5)))};
    Printer printer;
    Evaluator evaluator;
    for (const auto& e : exprs) std::cout << printer.print(*e) << " = " << evaluator.eval(*e) << '\n';
}
((2 + 3) * 4) = 20
(1 + (2 * -5)) = -9

Complexity and pitfalls. O(n) per traversal, two virtual calls per node. Pitfalls: in Evaluator, storing the left result in a local before evaluating the right side matters, because both recursive calls overwrite result_; forward declarations of every node are needed before Visitor; and deep trees recurse, so a pathological input can overflow the stack (an explicit stack fixes that). Interviewers often follow up with "how would you add a Sub node?" (every visitor changes) and "how is this different from std::visit?" (closed set, no heap, no virtual calls).

Estimated rating: ~1500 · classic pattern; the subtle part is explaining why two dispatches recover two types

CodeHand-rolled RTTI. The codebase is built with -fno-rtti, so dynamic_cast is unavailable. Implement LLVM-style isa<T>, dyn_cast<T> and cast<T> for a hierarchy Shape → Polygon → {Square, Triangle} and Shape → Circle, including a check for the intermediate class Polygon. Use it to sum polygon sides and square side lengths.

Answer

Approach. Store a kind enum in the base, set by each constructor. Order the enumerators so that each intermediate class covers a contiguous range (all polygons between K_Square and K_LastPolygon); then each class's static classof is one or two comparisons. dyn_cast checks classof and then does a static_cast, which is safe because the check proved the type. cast asserts instead of checking. This is exactly how LLVM's llvm/Support/Casting.h works.

#include <cassert>
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <vector>

class Shape {
public:
    enum Kind { K_Square, K_Triangle, K_LastPolygon = K_Triangle, K_Circle };
    Kind kind() const { return kind_; }
    virtual ~Shape() = default;  // only so unique_ptr<Shape> deletes correctly
protected:
    explicit Shape(Kind k) : kind_(k) {}
private:
    const Kind kind_;
};

class Polygon : public Shape {
public:
    int sides() const { return sides_; }
    static bool classof(const Shape* s) { return s->kind() >= K_Square && s->kind() <= K_LastPolygon; }
protected:
    Polygon(Kind k, int n) : Shape(k), sides_(n) {}
private:
    int sides_;
};

class Square final : public Polygon {
public:
    explicit Square(double s) : Polygon(K_Square, 4), side(s) {}
    static bool classof(const Shape* s) { return s->kind() == K_Square; }
    double side;
};

class Triangle final : public Polygon {
public:
    Triangle() : Polygon(K_Triangle, 3) {}
    static bool classof(const Shape* s) { return s->kind() == K_Triangle; }
};

class Circle final : public Shape {
public:
    explicit Circle(double r) : Shape(K_Circle), radius(r) {}
    static bool classof(const Shape* s) { return s->kind() == K_Circle; }
    double radius;
};

template <class To, class From>
static bool isa(const From* p) { return To::classof(p); }

template <class To, class From>
static To* dyn_cast(From* p) { return p && To::classof(p) ? static_cast<To*>(p) : nullptr; }

template <class To, class From>
static To* cast(From* p) {
    assert(isa<To>(p) && "cast<> to the wrong type");
    return static_cast<To*>(p);
}

int main() {
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Shape>> shapes;
    shapes.push_back(std::make_unique<Square>(2));
    shapes.push_back(std::make_unique<Circle>(1));
    shapes.push_back(std::make_unique<Triangle>());
    shapes.push_back(std::make_unique<Square>(3));

    int polygons = 0, sides = 0;
    double square_sides = 0;
    for (const auto& s : shapes) {
        if (auto* p = dyn_cast<Polygon>(s.get())) { ++polygons; sides += p->sides(); }
        if (auto* sq = dyn_cast<Square>(s.get())) square_sides += sq->side;
    }
    std::cout << "polygons=" << polygons << " sides=" << sides << '\n';
    std::cout << "square side sum=" << square_sides << '\n';
    std::cout << "circle radius=" << cast<Circle>(shapes[1].get())->radius << '\n';
    std::cout << "isa<Circle>(square)=" << isa<Circle>(shapes[0].get()) << '\n';
}
polygons=3 sides=11
square side sum=5
circle radius=1
isa<Circle>(square)=0

Complexity and pitfalls. Each check is O(1) with no memory access beyond the kind field, much cheaper than dynamic_cast's hierarchy walk. Pitfalls: adding a new polygon after K_LastPolygon silently breaks Polygon::classof, so new kinds must go inside the range and the "last" marker must move; the hierarchy is closed (a plugin cannot add a kind without editing the enum); and cast becomes an unchecked static_cast in release builds where assert is compiled out.

Estimated rating: ~1600 · small code, but the range trick for intermediate classes and the safety argument are what interviewers probe

CodeSelf-registering plugin factory. Design a CodecRegistry that maps names to factories returning std::unique_ptr<Codec>, where each concrete codec registers itself from its own source file with one line, without editing a central list. Requirements: registration must work regardless of the order in which translation units are initialised; create of an unknown name returns nullptr; duplicate names are rejected; names() lists registered codecs in sorted order.

Answer

Approach. The registry is a function-local static ("Meyers singleton"), created on first use, so a static registration object in any translation unit can safely call into it during static initialisation: this sidesteps the static initialisation order fiasco covered in Ch 3. A small Register<T> helper turns registration into one line per codec. A std::map keeps names sorted and emplace reports duplicates.

#include <cctype>
#include <functional>
#include <iostream>
#include <map>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class Codec {
public:
    virtual ~Codec() = default;
    virtual std::string encode(const std::string& in) const = 0;
};

class CodecRegistry {
public:
    using Factory = std::function<std::unique_ptr<Codec>()>;
    static CodecRegistry& instance() {
        static CodecRegistry registry;  // constructed on first call, thread-safe since C++11
        return registry;
    }
    bool add(std::string name, Factory f) { return factories_.emplace(std::move(name), std::move(f)).second; }
    std::unique_ptr<Codec> create(const std::string& name) const {
        auto it = factories_.find(name);
        return it == factories_.end() ? nullptr : it->second();
    }
    std::vector<std::string> names() const {
        std::vector<std::string> out;
        for (const auto& [name, factory] : factories_) out.push_back(name);
        return out;
    }
private:
    CodecRegistry() = default;
    std::map<std::string, Factory> factories_;
};

template <class T>
struct Register {
    explicit Register(const char* name) {
        CodecRegistry::instance().add(name, [] { return std::make_unique<T>(); });
    }
};

// Each block below would normally live in its own .cpp file.
class Upper final : public Codec {
public:
    std::string encode(const std::string& in) const override {
        std::string out = in;
        for (char& c : out) c = static_cast<char>(std::toupper(static_cast<unsigned char>(c)));
        return out;
    }
};
static const Register<Upper> reg_upper("upper");

class Reverse final : public Codec {
public:
    std::string encode(const std::string& in) const override { return {in.rbegin(), in.rend()}; }
};
static const Register<Reverse> reg_reverse("reverse");

class Rot13 final : public Codec {
public:
    std::string encode(const std::string& in) const override {
        std::string out = in;
        for (char& c : out) {
            if (c >= 'a' && c <= 'z') c = static_cast<char>('a' + (c - 'a' + 13) % 26);
            else if (c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z') c = static_cast<char>('A' + (c - 'A' + 13) % 26);
        }
        return out;
    }
};
static const Register<Rot13> reg_rot13("rot13");

int main() {
    auto& registry = CodecRegistry::instance();
    const auto names = registry.names();
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < names.size(); ++i) std::cout << (i ? " " : "") << names[i];
    std::cout << '\n';
    for (const char* name : {"upper", "rot13", "reverse", "zip"}) {
        auto codec = registry.create(name);
        std::cout << name << ": " << (codec ? codec->encode("Hello") : "<unknown>") << '\n';
    }
    std::cout << "duplicate accepted: " << registry.add("upper", [] { return std::make_unique<Reverse>(); }) << '\n';
}
reverse rot13 upper
upper: HELLO
rot13: Uryyb
reverse: olleH
zip: <unknown>
duplicate accepted: 0

Complexity and pitfalls. Lookup is O(log n). Pitfalls worth raising: if codecs live in a static library, the linker drops object files that nothing references, so their registration objects never run (fix with --whole-archive or an explicit reference); registration during static initialisation is single-threaded, but adding codecs later from several threads needs a mutex; and the registry must not be a namespace-scope global, because another TU's registration could run before it is constructed.

Estimated rating: ~1500 · easy code; the static initialisation and linker questions are what make it senior-level

Cheat sheet

Theory
  • Dispatch happens only for a virtual function, called through a pointer or reference (or this), with an unqualified name. Overload resolution and default arguments always use the static type.
  • Layout (Itanium ABI): one vtable per class in read-only data; one vptr per polymorphic subobject at its offset 0. The vtable holds virtual base offsets, offset-to-top, the RTTI pointer, then function slots, including two destructor slots. A virtual call is two loads and an indirect call; the real cost is lost inlining and mispredicted branches.
  • Always write override; a missing const or a different parameter type silently creates a new function that hides the base one. Use using Base::f; to unhide overloads. final enables devirtualisation when the static type is the final class.
  • Destructors: public and virtual, or protected and non-virtual. unique_ptr<Base> needs the virtual destructor; shared_ptr<Base> created from a Derived does not. delete[] through a base pointer is undefined even with a virtual destructor.
  • Slicing happens on copy or assignment by value into a base; the copy gets the base vptr. Pass by reference, store smart pointers, catch by const&, protect base copy operations, add clone().
  • Constructors and destructors dispatch to the class currently being built or destroyed, never further down. An indirect call to a pure virtual function there aborts with "pure virtual method called".
  • Multiple inheritance adjusts pointers on conversion and uses thunks. Non-virtual diamonds duplicate the base and make access ambiguous; virtual inheritance shares one base, which the most derived class constructs first. static_cast down from a virtual base is ill-formed.
  • RTTI: dynamic_cast returns null for pointers and throws bad_cast for references; typeid sees the dynamic type only for polymorphic glvalues. Covariant returns work for raw pointers and references, not smart pointers.

Part A · Object-oriented programming · Chapter 3

Abstraction and class design

How to design classes that other people can use correctly: interfaces, operator overloading with the canonical signatures, static members, friends, const correctness and the this pointer, then the design rules (SOLID, composition over inheritance, PIMPL) and compile-time polymorphism with CRTP. Interviewers ask these to see whether you can write a type that behaves like a built-in type and a class hierarchy that survives change.

TheoryDrillsCoding· about 6 hours· prerequisites: Ch 1 (special members, rule of 3/5/0), Ch 2 (virtual functions)

Abstraction and encapsulation

Theory
