Mental model. Abstraction decides what a type offers: the smallest set of operations that lets callers think about the concept without the details. Encapsulation decides how that is protected: the representation is hidden behind access control so that only the class's own functions can break its invariants. Abstraction is a design activity (choosing the interface); encapsulation is a language mechanism (private, the PIMPL idiom, modules) that enforces it.

A std::vector abstracts "a resizable sequence" (push_back, size, indexing). It encapsulates three pointers whose relationship (begin <= end <= capacity_end) is an invariant that no caller can violate because the pointers are private. You could replace the representation with a pointer plus two sizes and no caller would notice: that is the test of a good abstraction.

  • You can have encapsulation without much abstraction: a class with private fields and a getter and setter for each one hides the representation in name only, because every caller is still coupled to it.
  • You can have abstraction without encapsulation: a struct of public fields with free functions that operate on it, as in C APIs. Nothing stops a caller from breaking the invariant.

Constructors establish the invariant and the destructor releases resources (Ch 1); every public member function may assume the invariant on entry and must restore it on exit, including when it throws.

Interfaces via pure virtual classes

Theory

C++ has no interface keyword. The idiom is a class with only pure virtual functions, a virtual (or protected) destructor and no data. Concrete classes inherit from one or more interfaces publicly and implement them. Because an interface has no data, multiple inheritance of interfaces has no diamond problem worth worrying about (Ch 2).

#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

class Clock {  // the interface: what the code needs, nothing more
public:
    virtual ~Clock() = default;
    virtual std::int64_t now_ms() const = 0;
protected:
    Clock() = default;
    Clock(const Clock&) = default;             // no slicing through the interface
    Clock& operator=(const Clock&) = default;
};

class FakeClock final : public Clock {
public:
    std::int64_t now_ms() const override { return t_; }
    void advance(std::int64_t ms) { t_ += ms; }
private:
    std::int64_t t_ = 0;
};

class Timeout {  // depends on the abstraction, not on a real clock
public:
    Timeout(const Clock& clock, std::int64_t ms) : clock_(clock), deadline_(clock.now_ms() + ms) {}
    bool expired() const { return clock_.now_ms() >= deadline_; }
private:
    const Clock& clock_;
    std::int64_t deadline_;
};

int main() {
    FakeClock clock;
    Timeout t(clock, 100);
    std::cout << t.expired();
    clock.advance(99);
    std::cout << t.expired();
    clock.advance(1);
    std::cout << t.expired() << '\n';
}
001

Design rules for an interface class:

  • Destructor: public virtual if owners delete through the interface, otherwise protected non-virtual (Core Guidelines C.35).
  • No data members and no constructors that take arguments. Data turns the interface into a base class with state, and then the diamond and slicing problems come back.
  • Small and focused: clients should not depend on functions they do not use (the interface segregation principle, below). Several small interfaces composed by multiple inheritance beat one large one.
  • Protected or deleted copy operations, so code cannot copy "a Clock" and slice it.

The alternative in modern C++ is a concept: a compile-time interface checked at template instantiation, with no vtable and no inheritance. Use a virtual interface when the implementation is chosen at run time or must be hidden behind a library boundary; use a concept (or CRTP, below) when the type is known at compile time and the call is on a hot path.

Operator overloading

Theory

Mental model. An overloaded operator is an ordinary function with a special name, picked by overload resolution. a + b looks for both a.operator+(b) and operator+(a, b). The rule for a good overload: it must do what the operator does for int, with the same arity, precedence (which you cannot change anyway) and expected semantics. If + would surprise a reader, use a named function.

Member or non-member?

  • Must be members: =, (), [], -> and conversion operators. (C++23 lets operator() and operator[] be static members, and lets operator[] take several arguments.)
  • Should be members: operators that modify the left operand: compound assignment (+=, -=) and ++/--.
  • Should be non-members: symmetric binary operators (+, ==, <), so that implicit conversions apply to both operands. With a member operator+, money + 5 compiles but 5 + money does not, because conversions are never applied to the object a member function is called on.
  • Must be non-members: operator<< and operator>> for streams, because the left operand is the stream, not your class.
  • Hidden friends: define the non-member inside the class as a friend. It can access private members, it is found only by argument-dependent lookup (so it does not pollute overload sets for unrelated types) and it is the standard modern style.

Canonical signatures

OperatorCanonical declaration (for a class T)Notes
copy =T& operator=(const T& other);member; returns *this for chaining; handle self-assignment (Ch 1)
move =T& operator=(T&& other) noexcept;member; noexcept so containers use it
+=T& operator+=(const T& rhs);member; does the real work
+friend T operator+(T lhs, const T& rhs) { lhs += rhs; return lhs; }non-member; returns a new value, not a reference and not const T
==friend bool operator==(const T&, const T&) = default;C++20: also gives != and the reversed order
<=>auto operator<=>(const T&) const = default;C++20: gives < > <= >=; defaulting it also declares a defaulted ==
[]V& operator[](std::size_t i); and const V& operator[](std::size_t i) const;member; provide both const overloads
()R operator()(Args...) const;member; makes a function object
<<friend std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const T& x);non-member; returns the stream for chaining
prefix ++T& operator++();member; increments and returns *this
postfix ++T operator++(int);member; the int is a dummy tag; returns the old value by copy
conversionexplicit operator bool() const;explicit still allows if (x) (contextual conversion) but blocks int n = x;

Arithmetic in terms of compound assignment

Write += as the member that does the work and + as a non-member that copies its left operand and calls +=. Taking lhs by value lets the caller's temporary be moved in, and returning the local enables NRVO (Ch 24). Do not return const T from operator+: that old advice (to block (a + b) = c) also blocks moving from the result. If you want to block assignment to temporaries, ref-qualify the assignment operator instead: T& operator=(const T&) &;.

#include <compare>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>

class Money {
public:
    constexpr Money(std::int64_t cents = 0) : cents_(cents) {}  // implicit on purpose: 5 means 5 cents
    Money& operator+=(const Money& rhs) { cents_ += rhs.cents_; return *this; }
    Money& operator-=(const Money& rhs) { cents_ -= rhs.cents_; return *this; }
    Money operator-() const { return Money(-cents_); }

    friend Money operator+(Money lhs, const Money& rhs) { lhs += rhs; return lhs; }
    friend Money operator-(Money lhs, const Money& rhs) { lhs -= rhs; return lhs; }
    friend auto operator<=>(const Money&, const Money&) = default;  // also declares ==
    friend std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const Money& m) {
        std::int64_t c = m.cents_ < 0 ? -m.cents_ : m.cents_;
        return os << (m.cents_ < 0 ? "-" : "") << c / 100 << '.' << std::setw(2) << std::setfill('0') << c % 100;
    }
private:
    std::int64_t cents_;
};

int main() {
    Money price = 1999;
    Money total = price + 5;    // Money + int: 5 converts
    Money more = 250 + price;   // int + Money: works because operator+ is a non-member
    std::cout << total << ' ' << more << ' ' << -(more - total) << '\n';
    std::cout << (total < more) << (total == 2004) << (2004 != total) << '\n';
}
20.04 22.49 -2.45
110

Prefix and postfix increment

The postfix form takes a dummy int parameter purely so the two can be overloaded. Prefix increments and returns a reference to the same object. Postfix must return the old value, so it makes a copy, increments, and returns the copy by value. Implement postfix in terms of prefix:

Iter& operator++()    { advance(); return *this; }
Iter  operator++(int) { Iter old = *this; ++*this; return old; }

That copy is why ++it is the habit for iterators; for int and simple iterators the optimiser removes it.

Stream operators

operator<< takes the stream by non-const reference and the object by const reference, writes only the object's representation (no trailing newline) and returns the stream so that os << a << b chains. operator>> takes the object by non-const reference and must set std::ios::failbit on malformed input rather than leaving the object half-written.

C++20 comparisons: <=> and ==

C++20 replaced writing six comparison operators with two primary ones. The compiler rewrites secondary operators in terms of them ([over.match.oper]):

  • a != b is rewritten as !(a == b), and a == b also tries the reversed b == a. So one operator==(const T&, int) handles t == 1, 1 == t, t != 1 and 1 != t.
  • a < b is rewritten as (a <=> b) < 0, also trying 0 < (b <=> a).
  • = default on <=> compares bases, then members in declaration order, lexicographically. Defaulting <=> implicitly declares a defaulted ==; a user-written <=> does not, because equality can often be checked faster (compare sizes first) than ordering.
  • The return type says what kind of ordering you have: std::strong_ordering (equal values are interchangeable: integers), std::weak_ordering (equivalent but distinguishable values: case-insensitive strings) or std::partial_ordering (some values are unordered: floating point with NaN). auto picks the weakest category among the members.
#include <cctype>
#include <compare>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

class Caseless {  // equal ignoring case, so the ordering is only weak
public:
    explicit Caseless(std::string s) : s_(std::move(s)) {}
    std::weak_ordering operator<=>(const Caseless& o) const {
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < s_.size() && i < o.s_.size(); ++i) {
            int a = std::tolower(static_cast<unsigned char>(s_[i]));
            int b = std::tolower(static_cast<unsigned char>(o.s_[i]));
            if (a != b) return a <=> b;
        }
        return s_.size() <=> o.s_.size();
    }
    bool operator==(const Caseless& o) const { return (*this <=> o) == 0; }  // not implied
private:
    std::string s_;
};

int main() {
    Caseless x("Hello"), y("hello"), z("help");
    std::cout << (x == y) << (x < z) << (z > y) << '\n';
}
111

Interview trap

Overloading &&, || or the comma operator is legal but loses the built-in behaviour: an overloaded && is a function call, so both operands are always evaluated and there is no short-circuit. (C++17 at least fixed the evaluation order of the overloaded forms to left to right.) Overloading unary & breaks code that takes addresses, which is why generic code uses std::addressof. Operators you cannot overload at all: ::, ., .*, ?:, sizeof, alignof, typeid.

Static members and the initialisation order fiasco

Theory

A static data member belongs to the class, not to any object: one instance for the whole program, stored outside every object, so it does not contribute to sizeof. A static member function has no this; it can be called as T::f() without an object, can access private members of any T passed to it, and cannot be virtual, const or ref-qualified.

Before C++17, a non-const static data member had to be defined in exactly one .cpp file (int Widget::count = 0;), otherwise the linker reported an undefined reference. C++17 inline variables remove that: inline static int count = 0; in the class is a definition, merged across translation units. static constexpr data members are implicitly inline since C++17.

#include <iostream>

class Connection {
public:
    Connection() : id_(next_id_++) { ++open_; }
    ~Connection() { --open_; }
    Connection(const Connection&) = delete;            // a counted resource: not copyable
    Connection& operator=(const Connection&) = delete;
    static int open() { return open_; }                // no this: callable as Connection::open()
    int id() const { return id_; }
    static constexpr int max_open = 64;                // implicitly inline since C++17
private:
    inline static int open_ = 0;                       // C++17: no out-of-class definition
    inline static int next_id_ = 1;
    int id_;
};

int main() {
    Connection a;
    {
        Connection b, c;
        std::cout << Connection::open() << " open, last id " << c.id() << '\n';
    }
    std::cout << Connection::open() << " open of max " << Connection::max_open << '\n';
    std::cout << "sizeof " << sizeof(Connection) << '\n';
}
3 open, last id 3
1 open of max 64
sizeof 4

The static initialisation order fiasco

Objects with static storage duration at namespace scope (globals, static members) are initialised in two phases. Constant initialisation happens at compile time when the initialiser is a constant expression. Dynamic initialisation runs code before main, in declaration order within one translation unit, but in an unspecified order across translation units. If a global in a.cpp uses a global in b.cpp during its own construction, it may see it unconstructed (zero-initialised memory). That bug is the fiasco, and it typically appears or disappears when the link order changes.

Fixes, from most to least preferred:

  • Make it constant: constexpr or C++20 constinit, which forces constant initialisation and fails to compile if the initialiser is not constant. A constinit variable can still be modified at run time.
  • Construct on first use: a function-local static, Registry& registry() { static Registry r; return r; }. It is built the first time the function is called, and since C++11 that initialisation is thread-safe (the compiler adds a guard variable and a lock). Ch 2's plugin registry depends on this.
  • Avoid the dependency: pass the object explicitly instead of reaching for a global.

The mirror problem exists at exit: statics are destroyed in reverse order of construction completion, so a static destructor that uses another static may find it already destroyed. The usual answers are to construct the dependency first (it is then destroyed last) or to deliberately leak it: static Registry& r = *new Registry;.

Friend

Theory

A friend declaration grants one function or class access to the private and protected members of the class that declares it. The class grants access; nobody can take it. The rules:

  • Not inherited: a friend of Base has no special access to Derived's own members, and a class derived from a friend is not a friend.
  • Not transitive: a friend of a friend is not a friend.
  • Not reciprocal: if A declares friend class B;, B can see into A but not the reverse.
  • Not affected by access specifiers: writing it under private: changes nothing.

Friendship does not break encapsulation when it is used for functions that are logically part of the class's interface but cannot be members, such as operator<< or a symmetric operator==. It extends the set of functions that can touch the representation by exactly the ones the class author listed. Overuse (befriending a whole unrelated class to save writing an accessor) is the smell.

Hidden friends. A friend function defined inside the class body is not visible to ordinary name lookup at namespace scope; it is found only by argument-dependent lookup when one of the arguments is the class. That keeps the overload set small (faster compiles, better error messages) and prevents surprising implicit conversions, since the function is considered only when a real T is involved.

namespace geo {
class Point {
public:
    Point(int x, int y) : x_(x), y_(y) {}
    friend bool operator==(const Point&, const Point&) = default;  // hidden friend
    friend std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const Point& p) {
        return os << '(' << p.x_ << ", " << p.y_ << ')';
    }
private:
    int x_, y_;
};
}  // std::cout << p finds operator<< through ADL on geo::Point

The attorney-client and passkey idioms give finer control: instead of befriending a whole class, a member function takes a parameter of a Key type whose constructor is private and befriends only the intended caller.

const member functions, mutable and the this pointer

Theory

The this pointer

Every non-static member function receives a hidden parameter: the address of the object it was called on. Inside a member function of T, this is a prvalue of type T*, or const T* in a const member function (volatile works the same way). Member names used inside the function implicitly mean this->name. You need this explicitly to return *this for chaining, to pass the object elsewhere, to check self-assignment and to name members of a dependent base class inside a template (this->x).

this is never null in a valid program: calling a member function through a null pointer is undefined behaviour even if the function does not touch members, and compilers delete if (this == nullptr) checks for that reason. delete this is legal under strict conditions (see the drill below).

const member functions

A trailing const makes this a pointer to const, so the function cannot modify non-static members or call non-const member functions. Only const member functions can be called on a const object or through a const reference, which is how most objects are passed. So the rule is simple: every member function that does not change the observable state must be const, or your class becomes unusable through const T&.

The compiler enforces bitwise constness of the object's own bytes, which is shallow: in a const member function, a member int* p becomes int* const p, not const int*, so *p = 1 compiles. The PIMPL section shows the consequence. What the class should promise is logical constness: callers cannot observe a change.

mutable

mutable on a data member lets const member functions modify it. Use it for state that is not part of the observable value: caches, memoisation, access statistics, and the mutex that protects the object. Since the standard library treats const member functions as safe to call concurrently ([res.on.data.races]), a const function that writes a mutable cache must synchronise that write, typically with a mutable std::mutex or an atomic.

#include <iostream>
#include <mutex>
#include <string>
#include <thread>

class Document {
public:
    explicit Document(std::string text) : text_(std::move(text)) {}
    std::size_t word_count() const {           // logically const
        std::lock_guard lock(m_);              // const functions may be called concurrently
        if (!cached_) {
            std::size_t n = 0;
            bool in_word = false;
            for (char c : text_) {
                bool space = (c == ' ');
                if (!space && !in_word) ++n;
                in_word = !space;
            }
            count_ = n;
            cached_ = true;
            ++computations_;
        }
        return count_;
    }
    int computations() const { std::lock_guard lock(m_); return computations_; }
private:
    std::string text_;
    mutable std::mutex m_;                     // mutable: locking is not a logical change
    mutable bool cached_ = false;
    mutable std::size_t count_ = 0;
    mutable int computations_ = 0;
};

int main() {
    const Document doc("the quick brown fox");
    std::thread t([&doc] { (void)doc.word_count(); });
    std::size_t n = doc.word_count();
    t.join();
    std::cout << n << " words, computed " << doc.computations() << " time\n";
}
4 words, computed 1 time

const overloads

Member functions can be overloaded on const: the const version is chosen for const objects, the non-const one otherwise. Accessors that return references need both, so v[i] = x works on a mutable container and v[i] still works on a const one. To avoid writing the body twice, the classic trick is to implement the non-const version by calling the const one and casting the result (Effective C++ item 3); casting away const from the result is safe here because the object is known to be non-const. C++23 "deducing this" removes the duplication properly with one template.

#include <iostream>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class Grid {
public:
    Grid(std::size_t w, std::size_t h) : w_(w), cells_(w * h) {}

    // C++20 style: two overloads, the non-const one reusing the const one
    const int& at(std::size_t x, std::size_t y) const { return cells_.at(y * w_ + x); }
    int& at(std::size_t x, std::size_t y) {
        return const_cast<int&>(std::as_const(*this).at(x, y));
    }

    // C++23 deducing this: one template, self is Grid& or const Grid&
    template <class Self>
    auto&& cell(this Self&& self, std::size_t x, std::size_t y) {
        return std::forward<Self>(self).cells_.at(y * self.w_ + x);
    }
private:
    std::size_t w_;
    std::vector<int> cells_;
};

int main() {
    Grid g(3, 2);
    g.at(1, 1) = 7;
    g.cell(2, 0) = 5;
    const Grid& cg = g;
    std::cout << cg.at(1, 1) << ' ' << cg.cell(2, 0) << '\n';
    // cg.cell(2, 0) = 1;  // error: returns const int&
}
7 5

Ref-qualifiers overload on the value category of *this: std::string name() const & returns a copy for lvalues, std::string name() && can move the member out of a temporary. A function cannot mix ref-qualified and unqualified overloads of the same name and parameters.

SOLID with small C++ examples

Theory

SOLID is five heuristics for classes that survive change. Interviewers want a one-line definition, a C++ example of the violation and the fix, not a recital.

PrincipleOne lineViolation in C++Fix
Single responsibilitya class has one reason to changeReport computes totals, formats HTML and writes filessplit into ReportData, HtmlFormatter, FileSink
Open/closedextend behaviour without editing working codea switch (shape.kind) repeated in ten functionsa virtual function, a strategy object, or std::variant with one visitor per operation
Liskov substitutiona derived object must keep every promise of the baseSquare : Rectangle whose set_width also changes the heightdo not inherit; share an immutable Shape interface instead
Interface segregationclients should not depend on functions they do not useone IDevice with print, scan, fax; a printer must stub faxPrinter, Scanner, Fax interfaces; a copier implements two
Dependency inversionhigh-level code and low-level code both depend on an abstractionOrderService constructs a PostgresDb membertake a Database& (or a template parameter) in the constructor

Liskov substitution and the square/rectangle problem

The Liskov substitution principle says: if code works with a Base&, it must keep working when given any derived object. That is about behaviour, not taxonomy. A mutable Rectangle promises that set_width leaves the height unchanged. A Square cannot keep that promise, so Square : Rectangle breaks any caller that sets width and height independently, even though "a square is a rectangle" in geometry. The reading drill below shows a function that computes 16 where it expected 20.

Formally, a derived class may weaken preconditions (accept more) and strengthen postconditions (promise more), and must preserve the base's invariants; it may not throw new kinds of exceptions the caller does not expect. Fixes for the square case: make shapes immutable (then a square really is a rectangle, because nobody can set the sides independently), or make Square and Rectangle siblings under an abstract Shape with only area(). Other classic violations: a ReadOnlyList derived from List whose add throws, and a derived class that requires a call to init() the base did not need.

Composition versus inheritance

Theory

Mental model. Inheritance says "is a, and shares the implementation"; composition says "has a, and uses it through its public interface". Composition couples less: the containing class depends only on the member's public interface, can swap it for another implementation, can hold several, and does not inherit functions it never wanted. Hence the rule from the Gang of Four: prefer composition over inheritance; inherit to be reused polymorphically, not to reuse code.

The fragile base class problem. A derived class that overrides virtual functions depends on how the base calls its own functions, which is an implementation detail. The classic example: a CountingSet that overrides both insert and insert_all to count insertions double-counts, because the base's insert_all happens to call insert. If the base author changes that detail in a later version, the derived class breaks without any change of its own. A reading drill below reproduces it. A wrapper that holds a set and forwards calls has no such dependency.

Strategy by composition. Behaviour that varies is a member, injected through the constructor: an interface pointer (run-time choice), a template parameter (compile-time choice, zero overhead) or a std::function (any callable, one allocation and an indirect call).

class Retrier {
public:
    explicit Retrier(std::function<std::chrono::milliseconds(int attempt)> backoff)
        : backoff_(std::move(backoff)) {}
    // ... uses backoff_(n) between attempts; no subclass per policy
private:
    std::function<std::chrono::milliseconds(int)> backoff_;
};

When inheritance is right: the derived type really is substitutable (Liskov holds), you need run-time polymorphism through a base pointer, or the base is an interface designed for extension (an abstract class with a documented contract for each virtual function, often in NVI style, Ch 2). Mark classes not designed for inheritance final.

PIMPL: the compilation firewall

Theory

Mental model. The header declares the class with one private member, a pointer to an incomplete Impl type. All real data members and private helpers live in Impl, defined only in the .cpp file. Clients see a class whose size and layout never change, so editing the implementation recompiles one file and keeps the binary interface (ABI) stable for shared libraries.

// widget.h
class Widget {
public:
    Widget();
    ~Widget();                              // declared here, defined in widget.cpp
    Widget(Widget&&) noexcept;              // likewise: these need the complete Impl
    Widget& operator=(Widget&&) noexcept;
    void draw() const;
private:
    struct Impl;
    std::unique_ptr<Impl> p_;
};

// widget.cpp
struct Widget::Impl { std::string name_; std::vector<int> data_; };
Widget::Widget() : p_(std::make_unique<Impl>()) {}
Widget::~Widget() = default;                // Impl is complete here
Widget::Widget(Widget&&) noexcept = default;
Widget& Widget::operator=(Widget&&) noexcept = default;

The rules that trip people up:

  • The destructor must be defined where Impl is complete. If you let the compiler generate ~Widget() in the header, it instantiates std::default_delete<Impl> in every client, where Impl is incomplete, and the library's static_assert(sizeof(Impl) > 0) fails ("invalid application of sizeof to an incomplete type"). Declaring ~Widget(); in the header and writing Widget::~Widget() = default; in the .cpp fixes it. The same applies to move assignment (it destroys the old Impl) and to the move constructor (the generated code must be able to destroy p_ if a later member's construction throws). Declaring the destructor also suppresses the implicit move operations, so you must declare them anyway.
  • Copying is not automatic: unique_ptr is move-only, so write a deep-copy constructor that does std::make_unique<Impl>(*other.p_), or leave the class move-only.
  • Shallow const: in a const member function, p_->name_ = "x" compiles, because constness does not propagate through the pointer. Discipline (or std::experimental::propagate_const) restores it.
  • Moved-from state: after a move, p_ is null, so every member function must either tolerate that or document that a moved-from object may only be assigned or destroyed.

std::shared_ptr<Impl> does not have the incomplete-destructor problem (its deleter is captured at construction, Ch 12) but gives shared, not value, semantics, which is rarely what you want.

CRTP: static polymorphism

Theory

Mental model. In the Curiously Recurring Template Pattern a class derives from a base template instantiated with itself: class Square : public Shape<Square>. Inside the base, the derived type is a template parameter, so the base can call derived functions with static_cast<Derived&>(*this).impl(). The call is resolved at compile time and can be inlined: polymorphism without a vptr or an indirect call.

#include <iostream>

template <class Derived>
class Shape {
public:
    double area() const { return self().area_impl(); }               // no virtual
    void describe() const { std::cout << self().name() << " area " << area() << '\n'; }
private:
    const Derived& self() const { return static_cast<const Derived&>(*this); }
    Shape() = default;
    friend Derived;  // only Derived can construct Shape<Derived>: catches Circle : Shape<Square>
};

class Square : public Shape<Square> {
public:
    explicit Square(double s) : s_(s) {}
    double area_impl() const { return s_ * s_; }
    const char* name() const { return "square"; }
private:
    double s_;
};

class Rect : public Shape<Rect> {
public:
    Rect(double w, double h) : w_(w), h_(h) {}
    double area_impl() const { return w_ * h_; }
    const char* name() const { return "rect"; }
private:
    double w_, h_;
};

template <class D>
static double doubled(const Shape<D>& s) { return 2 * s.area(); }  // generic over every Shape<D>

int main() {
    Square sq(3);
    Rect r(2, 5);
    sq.describe();
    r.describe();
    std::cout << doubled(sq) + doubled(r) << ' ' << sizeof(Square) << '\n';
}
square area 9
rect area 10
38 8

Common uses: mixins that add operations to a class (std::enable_shared_from_this<T>, an instance counter per type, comparison or printing helpers); static interfaces in hot loops (expression templates in Eigen, HFT order book handlers); and clone helpers that write do_clone for every derived class.

Virtual functionsCRTP
Bindingrun timecompile time
Per-object costvptr (8 bytes)none
Call costindirect call, usually not inlineddirect, inlinable
Heterogeneous containeryes: vector<unique_ptr<Base>>no: each Base<D> is a different type (wrap in std::variant)
Code in headersnoyes, and one instantiation per derived type (code size)
Missing implementationabstract class, error at instantiation of the objecterror at the call inside the base template, often a long message; or infinite recursion if the base and derived functions share a name

C++23 "deducing this" (template <class Self> void f(this const Self& self)) gives the base access to the derived type without the class being a template, and removes the static_cast. CRTP remains common because a great deal of existing code and C++20 codebases use it.

Concept and tricky questions

Drills

ConceptWhat is the difference between abstraction and encapsulation? Give a C++ example where you have one without the other.

Answer

Answer. Abstraction chooses the operations a type exposes so callers can ignore the details. Encapsulation hides the representation behind access control so only the class can break its invariants. A C struct plus free functions (like FILE used through fopen/fread but with public fields) is an abstraction without enforced encapsulation; a class with a private field and a getter and setter for each one is encapsulated in syntax but offers no abstraction.

Why. Interviewers want to hear that the two are related but different levels: abstraction is the design decision, encapsulation the enforcement mechanism. The test of both together is whether you could change the representation (three pointers in std::vector versus a pointer and two sizes) without any caller noticing. Answering "encapsulation is data hiding and abstraction is hiding complexity" without an example sounds memorised.

ConceptName the four pillars of object-oriented programming and the C++ feature behind each. Does polymorphism need inheritance?

Answer

Answer. Encapsulation: access control (private, protected) so that only member functions can break an invariant. Abstraction: choosing a small public interface, expressed as a class's public members, an abstract class or a concept. Inheritance: derivation, with public, protected or private access and optional virtual bases. Polymorphism: one interface, many types, either at compile time (overloading, templates, CRTP) or at run time (virtual functions). Polymorphism does not need inheritance.

Why. Interviewers want each pillar tied to a mechanism and a caveat, not four definitions recited. Templates, std::function and std::variant give polymorphism with no common base class, and a non-virtual or private base gives inheritance with no polymorphism. C++ is multi-paradigm, so a design can use only some of the pillars. A frequent weak answer treats abstraction and encapsulation as synonyms; the previous drill separates them.

TrickyWhat is the difference between an abstract class and an interface in C++? Can an abstract class have a constructor, data members and non-virtual functions?

Answer

Answer. An abstract class is any class with at least one pure virtual function, declared or inherited and not overridden. An "interface" is only a convention: an abstract class with nothing but pure virtual functions, a virtual (or protected) destructor and no data. So yes, an abstract class can have constructors, data members, non-virtual functions and implemented virtual functions. You just cannot create an object of it, or pass or return one by value.

Why. Derived constructors call the abstract base's constructor to initialise its part, so the constructor is useful (make it protected, since only derived classes can call it anyway). The common wrong answer is "an abstract class cannot have a constructor because it cannot be instantiated". Use pure interfaces at module boundaries and for multiple inheritance, because without data there is nothing to duplicate in a diamond. Use an abstract class with state for shared implementation, as in the template method and NVI idioms (Ch 2).

TrickyWhich operators must be member functions? Why can operator<< for printing your class not usefully be a member?

Answer

Answer. operator=, operator(), operator[], operator-> and conversion operators must be members ([over.oper]). A member operator<< would make your object the left operand, so you would have to write obj << std::cout.

Why. For a member operator, the left operand is the object the function is called on. Streams put the stream on the left, and you cannot add members to std::ostream, so the printing operator must be a non-member, usually a hidden friend. The reason these five must be members is that the language wants them tied to the class (for example, a non-member operator= could change the meaning of assignment for a type from outside). Many candidates also list +=: it should be a member by convention, but a non-member operator+= is legal.

TrickyWhy does postfix operator++ take an unused int, why does it return by value, and should it return const T?

Answer

Answer. The int is a dummy tag that lets prefix and postfix overload each other. It returns by value because it must return the old value, which no longer exists in the object. It should not return const T in modern C++.

Why. Prefix returns T& to the incremented object. Postfix must copy the old state first, so it returns that copy. Older books recommended const T to make it++++ fail to compile, but a const return value cannot be moved from, which costs a copy wherever the result is used. Some style guides still say "return const for postfix", so be ready to explain the trade-off; the C++ Core Guidelines and the standard library return plain T. The copy is also why ++it is preferred for non-trivial iterators.

TrickyIn C++20 you define only bool operator==(const Id&, int). Do id != 5, 5 == id and 5 != id compile? If you write your own operator<=>, does == work?

Answer

Answer. All three compile in C++20: the compiler rewrites != as !(==) and also tries operands in reversed order. A user-written operator<=> does not provide ==; only a defaulted <=> implicitly declares a defaulted ==.

Why. [over.match.oper]/3 adds rewritten candidates: for x != y, x == y and y == x; for x < y, (x <=> y) < 0 and 0 < (y <=> x). Equality is deliberately separate from ordering because it can often be faster (two strings of different length are unequal without comparing characters). In C++17 you needed four functions for the four expressions above. A pitfall from the reversal: a member bool operator==(const T&) that forgot its const makes a == b formally ambiguous with its own reversed form in C++20; GCC and Clang accept it with a warning (Clang's -Wambiguous-reversed-operator), but code that was clean in C++17 starts warning. Make comparison operators const or hidden friends.

TrickyWhat can a const member function still modify?

Answer

Answer. mutable members, anything a member pointer or reference points to (constness is shallow), static members, globals, and other objects reached through parameters. It can also const_cast away const, which is defined only if the object itself was not created const.

Why. const on a member function only changes this to const T*, so the members of *this become const: a member int* p becomes int* const p, and *p = 1 still compiles. Modifying an object that was defined const (for example a global const Widget w;) through a const_cast is undefined behaviour, and the compiler may have placed it in read-only memory. The design rule is logical constness: callers must not observe a change, and a mutable cache written from a const function must be synchronised because const functions are assumed safe to call concurrently.

ConceptHow does a static member function differ from a non-static one? Can it access private members? Can it be const or virtual?

Answer

Answer. It has no this, so it can be called without an object (T::f()) and cannot use non-static members directly. It can access private members of any T object it is given. It cannot be const, volatile, ref-qualified or virtual.

Why. const and ref-qualifiers describe the implicit object, and virtual dispatches on it; without an object neither means anything. Access control is per class, so a static factory can call a private constructor. A pointer to a static member function is an ordinary function pointer (usable as a C callback), unlike a pointer to a non-static member function. People often wrongly say a static member function cannot touch private members.

TrickyWhat is the static initialisation order fiasco, and what are the fixes? Is a function-local static thread-safe?

Answer

Answer. Dynamic initialisation of namespace-scope statics in different translation units happens in an unspecified order, so a global constructor that uses a global from another file may see it before it is constructed. Fixes: make the dependency constexpr or constinit, construct it on first use with a function-local static, or remove the global. Function-local static initialisation is thread-safe since C++11 ([stmt.dcl]/4).

Why. Across units the order depends on the link order, so the bug comes and goes with build changes. A function-local static is initialised when control first passes through its declaration, behind a guard variable and a lock (__cxa_guard_acquire), so concurrent first calls block until one finishes. The often-forgotten half is destruction, in reverse order of construction completion, so one static's destructor can touch an already destroyed static. A common slip: constinit does not make the variable const; it only guarantees there is no dynamic initialisation to order.

ConceptIs friendship inherited, transitive or symmetric? Does friend break encapsulation?

Answer

Answer. None of the three: not inherited, not transitive, not symmetric. Used properly, it does not break encapsulation, because the class itself names exactly which functions may see its representation.

Why. A friend function such as operator<< is part of the class's interface that happens to need non-member syntax; making it a friend is no worse than making it a member. Stroustrup's phrasing: friendship is granted, not taken. It becomes a problem when a class befriends an unrelated class to avoid designing an interface, because then changes to the representation can break code far away. Hidden friends (defined inside the class) are the preferred form for operators.

TrickyIs deriving Square from Rectangle always a Liskov violation?

Answer

Answer. No. It is a violation when Rectangle is mutable with independent set_width and set_height. If rectangles are immutable values, a square satisfies every promise a rectangle makes, and the inheritance is fine.

Why. Liskov substitution is about behavioural contracts, not real-world taxonomy. The mutable rectangle's contract includes "setting the width leaves the height unchanged", which a square cannot honour. Remove the setters and the only promises left (it has a width, a height and area() == w * h) hold for squares. The common wrong answers are "always a violation because squares have one side" and "never, because a square is a rectangle in maths". Both miss that the answer depends on the operations.

ConceptWhen should you use composition, and when is inheritance the right tool?

Answer

Answer. Default to composition for reuse. Use public inheritance only when the derived type is truly substitutable for the base (Liskov holds) and you need run-time polymorphism through a base pointer or reference, typically from an interface or an abstract class designed for extension.

Why. Composition depends only on the member's public interface, so it survives changes to the member's implementation, lets you hold several or swap implementations, and exposes only what you forward. Inheriting for code reuse couples you to how the base calls its own virtual functions (the fragile base class problem in the reading drills) and exposes every public base member on your type. Private inheritance is the middle ground for "implemented in terms of" when you need to override a virtual function of the helper (Ch 2).

TrickyA PIMPL class holds std::unique_ptr<Impl>. Clients that create a Widget fail to compile with "invalid application of sizeof to an incomplete type". The header declares no destructor. Why, and what is the fix?

Answer

Answer. The implicitly defined destructor is generated inline in each client's translation unit, where Impl is incomplete, and it instantiates std::default_delete<Impl>::operator(), which static-asserts that the type is complete. Fix: declare ~Widget(); in the header and define Widget::~Widget() = default; in the .cpp after Impl is defined. Do the same for the move operations.

Why. delete on a pointer to an incomplete class type is undefined if the class has a non-trivial destructor, so std::unique_ptr turns that into a compile error. Defining the special members out of line moves the instantiation to the one file where Impl is complete. std::shared_ptr<Impl> would compile without this because it captures the deleter when constructed, which happens in the .cpp, but it also gives the class shared semantics, which is usually wrong.

TrickyWhat can CRTP not do that virtual functions can, and how do you stop someone writing class Circle : public Shape<Square> by mistake?

Answer

Answer. CRTP cannot choose the type at run time or store different derived types in one container, because Shape<Square> and Shape<Circle> are unrelated types. To catch the wrong template argument, make the base constructor private and declare friend Derived;, so only the named derived class can construct it.

Why. With the wrong argument, static_cast<const Square&>(*this) inside the base is applied to a Circle, which is undefined behaviour that usually reads garbage. With a private constructor, Circle's constructor cannot call Shape<Square>() and compilation fails. For a heterogeneous collection of CRTP types, combine them with std::variant and std::visit, or add a thin virtual interface on top. A third limitation: if the derived class forgets to implement the function and it has the same name as the base one, the base calls itself recursively for ever, which is why implementations often use a distinct name such as area_impl.

TrickyCan a member function execute delete this;? Under what conditions is it safe?

Answer

Answer. Yes. It is safe if the object was allocated with plain new (not new[], not on the stack, not as a member or inside a container), nothing in the function touches members or calls virtual functions after the delete, and no other code uses the object afterwards.

Why. After delete this, this is a dangling pointer, but the function's code is still valid and can return. Intrusive reference counting does exactly this: void release() { if (--refs_ == 0) delete this; }. To force heap allocation, make the destructor private or protected so stack objects fail to compile. Interviewers sometimes follow up with "can this be null?": not in a valid program, because calling a member function through a null pointer is already undefined behaviour.

ConceptWhich operators cannot be overloaded, and which can but usually should not be?

Answer

Answer. Cannot: ::, ., .*, ?:, sizeof, alignof, typeid and the cast keywords. Should not: &&, || and , (they lose short-circuiting and built-in sequencing semantics) and unary & (it breaks taking addresses).

Why. The non-overloadable ones either take a name rather than a value as an operand (., ::) or are needed to reason about any type (sizeof). An overloaded && is a function call, so both operands are evaluated before the call. Libraries that overload them (Boost.Spirit's ,, expression templates) do so for embedded languages, never for ordinary value types. Generic code uses std::addressof to be robust against overloaded &.

Predict the output and find the bug

Drills

OutputPrefix and postfix. What does this print?

#include <iostream>

struct Counter {
    int n = 0;
    Counter& operator++() { ++n; std::cout << "pre "; return *this; }
    Counter operator++(int) { Counter old = *this; ++*this; std::cout << "post "; return old; }
};

int main() {
    Counter c;
    Counter a = c++;
    Counter b = ++c;
    std::cout << '\n' << a.n << ' ' << b.n << ' ' << c.n << '\n';
    ++++c;
    std::cout << '\n' << c.n << '\n';
}
Answer
pre post pre
0 2 2
pre pre
4

Why. c++ runs the postfix operator, which saves the old value, calls the prefix operator (printing pre) and then prints post, returning the old n == 0. ++c prints pre and returns a reference to c, which is copied into b with n == 2. ++++c works because prefix returns a non-const reference, so the second increment applies to c itself, giving 4. With postfix, c++++ would increment a temporary and leave c unchanged by the second step.

Find the bugThis operator+ compiles (with a warning). What is wrong? (Output is not compared: the behaviour is undefined, and with GCC the program crashes.)

#include <iostream>

struct Vec { int x, y; };

static const Vec& operator+(const Vec& a, const Vec& b) {
    Vec r{a.x + b.x, a.y + b.y};
    return r;
}

int main() {
    Vec a{1, 2}, b{3, 4};
    const Vec& c = a + b;
    std::cout << c.x << ',' << c.y << '\n';
}
Answer

Answer. It returns a reference to a local variable that is destroyed when the function returns, so c dangles. Binding the result to const Vec& in main does not extend anything: lifetime extension applies only to temporaries bound directly, not to a reference returned from a function.

Why. GCC warns with -Wreturn-local-addr and, since the behaviour is undefined, compiles the function to return a null pointer, so the program crashes; Clang warns with -Wreturn-stack-address and may print garbage or the "right" answer by luck. Arithmetic operators produce new values, so the canonical signature returns by value: Vec operator+(Vec a, const Vec& b) { a.x += b.x; a.y += b.y; return a; }. Returning a value is cheap thanks to copy elision (Ch 23).

OutputWhich overload of operator[] runs? What does this print?

#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

class Row {
public:
    int& operator[](std::size_t i) { std::cout << "mutable "; return v_[i]; }
    const int& operator[](std::size_t i) const { std::cout << "const "; return v_[i]; }
private:
    std::vector<int> v_{1, 2, 3};
};

static int first(const Row& r) { return r[0]; }

int main() {
    Row r;
    const Row& cr = r;
    r[1] = 20;
    int a = cr[1];
    int b = first(r);
    std::cout << '\n' << a << ' ' << b << '\n';
}
Answer
mutable const const
20 1

Why. The overload is chosen by the constness of the object expression, not by whether the result is read or written. r is non-const, so r[1] uses the mutable overload. cr and the parameter r inside first are const references, so they use the const overload, even though they refer to the same non-const object. A common wrong answer is that "reading uses the const version": int x = r[0]; on a non-const r still calls the mutable one.

Find the bugA set of points silently loses an element. What does this print, and what is the fix?

#include <iostream>
#include <set>

struct Point {
    int x, y;
    friend bool operator<(const Point& a, const Point& b) { return a.x < b.x; }
    friend bool operator==(const Point&, const Point&) = default;
};

int main() {
    std::set<Point> pts{{1, 2}, {1, 3}, {2, 0}};
    std::cout << pts.size() << ' ' << pts.count({1, 99}) << '\n';
    Point p{1, 2}, q{1, 3};
    std::cout << (p == q) << (p < q) << (q < p) << '\n';
}
Answer
2 1
000

Answer. std::set never calls ==. It treats a and b as the same key when !(a < b) && !(b < a), and this operator< looks only at x, so {1, 3} counts as a duplicate of {1, 2} and is dropped, and count({1, 99}) finds a "match". Meanwhile == says p and q differ, so the type has two inconsistent notions of sameness.

Why. Ordered containers and algorithms use equivalence derived from the comparator, not equality. The fix is to compare every member that == compares, in a fixed order: friend auto operator<=>(const Point&, const Point&) = default;, which also keeps == consistent, or std::tie(a.x, a.y) < std::tie(b.x, b.y) before C++20. The common wrong answer is "the set uses == to detect duplicates". A worse variant, a.x < b.x || a.y < b.y, is not a strict weak ordering at all, and using it in a std::set is undefined behaviour.

OutputDefaulted comparisons. What does this print?

#include <cmath>
#include <compare>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

struct Version {
    int major, minor, patch;
    auto operator<=>(const Version&) const = default;
};
struct Player {
    std::string name;
    int score;
    auto operator<=>(const Player&) const = default;
};

int main() {
    Version a{1, 10, 0}, b{1, 9, 7};
    std::cout << (a > b) << (a == Version{1, 10, 0}) << '\n';
    Player p{"bob", 10}, q{"alice", 99};
    std::cout << (p < q) << '\n';
    auto c = 1.0 <=> std::nan("");
    std::cout << (c == std::partial_ordering::unordered) << (1.0 < std::nan("")) << '\n';
}
Answer
11
0
10

Why. A defaulted <=> compares members lexicographically in declaration order. 1.10.0 > 1.9.7 because the minor field 10 is greater than 9 (which a string comparison of "1.10.0" and "1.9.7" would get wrong). Player compares name first, so "bob" < "alice" is false and the score is never looked at: member order is part of the meaning. For double, <=> returns std::partial_ordering, and any comparison with NaN is unordered, so 1.0 < NaN is false.

Find the bugA Liskov violation. What does this print, and which design rule does it break?

#include <iostream>

class Rectangle {
public:
    virtual ~Rectangle() = default;
    virtual void set_width(int w) { w_ = w; }
    virtual void set_height(int h) { h_ = h; }
    int area() const { return w_ * h_; }
protected:
    int w_ = 0, h_ = 0;
};

class Square : public Rectangle {
public:
    void set_width(int w) override { w_ = h_ = w; }
    void set_height(int h) override { w_ = h_ = h; }
};

static void stretch(Rectangle& r) {
    r.set_width(5);
    r.set_height(4);
    std::cout << "expected 20, got " << r.area() << '\n';
}

int main() {
    Rectangle r;
    Square s;
    stretch(r);
    stretch(s);
}
Answer
expected 20, got 20
expected 20, got 16

Answer. Square breaks the Liskov substitution principle: stretch relies on the rectangle's promise that set_height does not change the width, and the square's override silently changes both.

Why. The code compiles and every class is "correct" in isolation; the bug only appears when a Square is used where a Rectangle is expected, which is the whole point of public inheritance. Fixes: drop the inheritance and make both siblings under an abstract Shape with area(), or make the shapes immutable so there are no setters to break. Throwing from Square::set_width when the sides differ is not a fix: it adds a failure mode the base never had, which is also a Liskov violation.

Find the bugWhy does this not compile, and what is the right fix?

#include <vector>

class Account {
public:
    long balance() const {
        audit();
        return balance_;
    }
    void audit() { log_.push_back(balance_); }
private:
    long balance_ = 0;
    std::vector<long> log_;
};

int main() {
    const Account acct;
    return static_cast<int>(acct.balance());
}
Answer

Answer. balance() is const, so this is const Account*, and it calls the non-const member audit(). Calling a non-const member function on a const object is an error ("passing const Account as this argument discards qualifiers").

Why. The fix depends on whether the audit log is part of the account's observable value. It is not: reading a balance should not count as changing the account. So declare mutable std::vector<long> log_; and make audit() const, and add a mutable std::mutex if the class may be read from several threads, because const member functions are expected to be safe to call concurrently. The wrong fixes are removing const from balance() (then no const reference can read the balance) and const_cast<Account*>(this)->audit() (undefined behaviour here, because acct was defined const).

OutputConstruct on first use. What does this print?

#include <iostream>

struct Logger {
    Logger() { std::cout << "Logger ready\n"; }
    ~Logger() { std::cout << "Logger gone\n"; }
    void log(const char* msg) { std::cout << msg << '\n'; }
};

static Logger& logger() {
    static Logger instance;
    return instance;
}

struct App {
    App() { logger().log("App starting"); }
    ~App() { std::cout << "App gone\n"; }
};

static App app;

int main() {
    std::cout << "main\n";
    logger().log("hello");
}
Answer
Logger ready
App starting
main
hello
App gone
Logger gone

Why. The global app is dynamically initialised before main (all mainstream implementations do this at start-up). Its constructor calls logger(), which constructs the function-local static on first use, so the logger exists before App needs it, whichever file either lives in. At exit, statics are destroyed in reverse order of completed construction: the logger finished constructing first (inside App's constructor), so app is destroyed first and the logger last. That is exactly the order that keeps ~App safe if it logs. If logger were a plain global in another file, App() could run before it was constructed: the fiasco.

OutputA member operator<<. What does this print, and why does std::cout << t not compile?

#include <iostream>

struct Temp {
    double celsius;
    std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os) const { return os << celsius << 'C'; }
};

int main() {
    Temp t{21.5};
    t << std::cout;  // the object is the left operand
    std::cout << '\n';
    // std::cout << t;  // error: no operator<< for (ostream, Temp)
}
Answer
21.5C

Why. A member binary operator always takes the object as its left operand, so this operator<< means t.operator<<(std::cout), written t << std::cout. For std::cout << t the compiler looks for a member of std::ostream or a non-member taking (std::ostream&, const Temp&), and finds neither. The fix is the canonical hidden friend: friend std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const Temp& t).

Find the bugThe fragile base class. The counter should report 4 insertion attempts. What does it print, and what is the robust fix?

#include <iostream>
#include <set>
#include <vector>

class IntSet {
public:
    virtual ~IntSet() = default;
    virtual bool insert(int x) { return items_.insert(x).second; }
    virtual void insert_all(const std::vector<int>& xs) { for (int x : xs) insert(x); }
    std::size_t size() const { return items_.size(); }
private:
    std::set<int> items_;
};

class CountingSet : public IntSet {
public:
    bool insert(int x) override { ++attempts; return IntSet::insert(x); }
    void insert_all(const std::vector<int>& xs) override {
        attempts += xs.size();
        IntSet::insert_all(xs);
    }
    std::size_t attempts = 0;
};

int main() {
    CountingSet s;
    s.insert_all({1, 2, 3});
    s.insert(3);
    std::cout << s.attempts << ' ' << s.size() << '\n';
}
Answer
7 3

Answer. IntSet::insert_all calls the virtual insert for each element, which dispatches to CountingSet::insert, so the three elements are counted twice: 3 + 3 + 1 = 7.

Why. The derived class depends on an undocumented implementation detail of the base (whether insert_all calls insert). Removing the override of insert_all gives the right answer today, but breaks again if the base author later optimises insert_all to bypass insert. The robust fix is composition: a CountingSet that holds an IntSet and forwards to it, counting in its own functions, depends only on the public behaviour. This is Effective Java item 18 ("favour composition over inheritance") and applies unchanged to C++.

Find the bugA copy-paste error in a CRTP hierarchy. What is wrong? (Output is not compared: the behaviour is undefined.)

#include <iostream>

template <class D>
struct Shape {
    double area() const { return static_cast<const D*>(this)->area_impl(); }
};

struct Square : Shape<Square> {
    double side = 2;
    double area_impl() const { return side * side; }
};

struct Circle : Shape<Square> {  // should be Shape<Circle>
    double radius = 1;
    double area_impl() const { return 3.14159 * radius * radius; }
};

int main() {
    Circle c;
    std::cout << c.area() << '\n';
}
Answer

Answer. Circle derives from Shape<Square>, so area() casts a Circle to Square and calls Square::area_impl on it. That is undefined behaviour; in practice it reads radius as if it were side and prints 1 instead of about 3.14.

Why. static_cast down a hierarchy is unchecked, and both are valid-looking types, so nothing complains. The guard is to make the base's constructor private and befriend the template parameter; then Circle cannot construct a Shape<Square> and the mistake becomes a compile error:

template <class D>
class Shape {
public:
    double area() const { return static_cast<const D*>(this)->area_impl(); }
private:
    Shape() = default;
    friend D;  // only D may construct Shape<D>
};

struct Square : Shape<Square> {
    double side = 2;
    double area_impl() const { return side * side; }
};

struct Circle : Shape<Square> {
    double radius = 1;
    double area_impl() const { return 3.14159 * radius * radius; }
};

int main() {
    Circle c;  // error: Shape<Square>::Shape() is private within this context
    return static_cast<int>(c.area());
}

Write the code

Coding

CodeA Fraction value type. Store a numerator and denominator in std::int64_t, always normalised (lowest terms, positive denominator). Provide + - * / and their compound forms, unary minus, ==, a correct <=>, operator<< (print 3 rather than 3/1) and an explicit conversion to double. Integers must mix freely on either side (1 + f). A zero denominator, including division by zero, throws std::domain_error.

Answer

Approach. Normalise in the constructor so every object is canonical; then equality is member-wise and can be defaulted. Compound assignments do the work and build a new normalised fraction; the binary operators are hidden friends that take the left operand by value. A non-explicit constructor from int64_t plus non-member operators gives mixed arithmetic on both sides. Ordering cross-multiplies, which is correct because both denominators are positive.

#include <compare>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <numeric>
#include <stdexcept>

class Fraction {
public:
    Fraction(std::int64_t num = 0, std::int64_t den = 1) : num_(num), den_(den) {
        if (den_ == 0) throw std::domain_error("zero denominator");
        if (den_ < 0) { num_ = -num_; den_ = -den_; }
        std::int64_t g = std::gcd(num_, den_);  // gcd(0, d) == d, so 0/d becomes 0/1
        num_ /= g;
        den_ /= g;
    }
    std::int64_t num() const { return num_; }
    std::int64_t den() const { return den_; }

    Fraction& operator+=(const Fraction& r) { return *this = Fraction(num_ * r.den_ + r.num_ * den_, den_ * r.den_); }
    Fraction& operator-=(const Fraction& r) { return *this += -r; }
    Fraction& operator*=(const Fraction& r) { return *this = Fraction(num_ * r.num_, den_ * r.den_); }
    Fraction& operator/=(const Fraction& r) { return *this = Fraction(num_ * r.den_, den_ * r.num_); }  // throws if r == 0
    Fraction operator-() const { return Fraction(-num_, den_); }

    friend Fraction operator+(Fraction a, const Fraction& b) { return a += b; }
    friend Fraction operator-(Fraction a, const Fraction& b) { return a -= b; }
    friend Fraction operator*(Fraction a, const Fraction& b) { return a *= b; }
    friend Fraction operator/(Fraction a, const Fraction& b) { return a /= b; }

    friend bool operator==(const Fraction&, const Fraction&) = default;  // valid: always normalised
    friend std::strong_ordering operator<=>(const Fraction& a, const Fraction& b) {
        return a.num_ * b.den_ <=> b.num_ * a.den_;  // denominators are positive
    }
    explicit operator double() const { return static_cast<double>(num_) / static_cast<double>(den_); }

    friend std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const Fraction& f) {
        os << f.num_;
        if (f.den_ != 1) os << '/' << f.den_;
        return os;
    }
private:
    std::int64_t num_, den_;
};

int main() {
    Fraction a(1, 2), b(-3, 4);
    std::cout << a + b << ' ' << a - b << ' ' << a * b << ' ' << a / b << '\n';
    std::cout << Fraction(6, -8) << ' ' << Fraction(0, 5) << ' ' << 1 + a << ' ' << a * 4 << '\n';
    std::cout << (a > b) << (Fraction(2, 4) == a) << (a != 1) << (Fraction(1, 3) < a) << '\n';
    std::cout << static_cast<double>(b) << '\n';
    try {
        (void)(a / Fraction(0));
    } catch (const std::domain_error& e) {
        std::cout << e.what() << '\n';
    }
}
-1/4 5/4 -3/8 -2/3
-3/4 0 3/2 2
1111
-0.75
zero denominator

Complexity and pitfalls. Each operation is O(log n) for the gcd. Pitfalls: the products overflow int64_t for large terms (reduce by the gcd of cross terms first, or use __int128 for the intermediate products and comparison); defaulting == is only correct because of the normalisation invariant, so a constructor that skipped it would make 1/2 != 2/4; and return a += b; returns an lvalue reference expression, so the result is copied out of the parameter; the two-statement form a += b; return a; moves instead (a by-value parameter is never eligible for NRVO, but returning it by name is an implicit move). For two int64_t fields the difference is nil; for a big type it matters.

Estimated rating: ~1400 · straightforward, but tests every canonical signature and the invariant that makes defaulted equality valid

CodeA dense Matrix of double. Requirements: construction from a size or from nested braces (Matrix{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}), element access with m(r, c) that works on const and non-const matrices, +=, +, *, ==, a static identity(n), and operator<<. Shape mismatches throw std::invalid_argument. Store the elements contiguously.

Answer

Approach. One std::vector<double> in row-major order plus the two dimensions, so the class follows the rule of zero (Ch 1). operator() is overloaded on const: a reference for writing, a value for reading. Multiplication uses the i-k-j loop order so the inner loop walks both b and the result contiguously, which matters for cache behaviour (Ch 19). Defaulted == compares dimensions and data.

#include <initializer_list>
#include <iostream>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <vector>

class Matrix {
public:
    Matrix(std::size_t rows, std::size_t cols, double fill = 0.0)
        : rows_(rows), cols_(cols), data_(rows * cols, fill) {}
    Matrix(std::initializer_list<std::initializer_list<double>> init)
        : rows_(init.size()), cols_(init.size() ? init.begin()->size() : 0) {
        data_.reserve(rows_ * cols_);
        for (const auto& row : init) {
            if (row.size() != cols_) throw std::invalid_argument("ragged rows");
            data_.insert(data_.end(), row.begin(), row.end());
        }
    }
    static Matrix identity(std::size_t n) {
        Matrix m(n, n);
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) m(i, i) = 1.0;
        return m;
    }

    std::size_t rows() const { return rows_; }
    std::size_t cols() const { return cols_; }
    double& operator()(std::size_t r, std::size_t c) { return data_[r * cols_ + c]; }
    double operator()(std::size_t r, std::size_t c) const { return data_[r * cols_ + c]; }

    Matrix& operator+=(const Matrix& o) {
        if (rows_ != o.rows_ || cols_ != o.cols_) throw std::invalid_argument("shape mismatch");
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < data_.size(); ++i) data_[i] += o.data_[i];
        return *this;
    }
    friend Matrix operator+(Matrix a, const Matrix& b) { a += b; return a; }
    friend Matrix operator*(const Matrix& a, const Matrix& b) {
        if (a.cols_ != b.rows_) throw std::invalid_argument("shape mismatch");
        Matrix m(a.rows_, b.cols_);
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < a.rows_; ++i)
            for (std::size_t k = 0; k < a.cols_; ++k) {
                const double aik = a(i, k);
                for (std::size_t j = 0; j < b.cols_; ++j) m(i, j) += aik * b(k, j);
            }
        return m;
    }
    friend bool operator==(const Matrix&, const Matrix&) = default;
    friend std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const Matrix& m) {
        for (std::size_t r = 0; r < m.rows_; ++r) {
            if (r) os << '\n';
            os << '[';
            for (std::size_t c = 0; c < m.cols_; ++c) os << (c ? " " : "") << m(r, c);
            os << ']';
        }
        return os;
    }
private:
    std::size_t rows_, cols_;
    std::vector<double> data_;
};

int main() {
    Matrix a{{1, 2}, {3, 4}};
    Matrix b{{0, 1}, {1, 0}};
    const Matrix& ca = a;
    std::cout << a * b << '\n';
    std::cout << (a * Matrix::identity(2) == a) << ' ' << ca(1, 0) << '\n';
    std::cout << a + a << '\n';
    try {
        (void)(Matrix(2, 3) * Matrix(2, 3));
    } catch (const std::invalid_argument& e) {
        std::cout << e.what() << '\n';
    }
}
[2 1]
[4 3]
1 3
[2 4]
[6 8]
shape mismatch

Complexity and pitfalls. Multiplication is O(n·m·p); addition is O(n·m). Pitfalls: the const operator() must return by value or const double&, never double&; Matrix{2, 3} with braces picks the initialiser-list constructor and is easy to misuse, so size construction uses parentheses; and exact == on floating point is only meaningful for exactly representable values like these (real code compares with a tolerance). C++23 allows m[r, c] with a multi-argument operator[].

Estimated rating: ~1300 · routine class design; the cache-friendly loop order and the const overload are the discussion points

CodePIMPL with value semantics. Write a Phonebook whose header exposes only add(name, number), find(name) returning std::optional<std::string>, and size(), with all data hidden in an Impl. It must be copyable (deep copy) and cheaply movable, and sizeof(Phonebook) must equal one pointer. Put the "header" and "source" parts in one file, marked with comments.

Answer

Approach. Hold std::unique_ptr<Impl>. Declare all five special members in the header and define them in the source after Impl is complete, which avoids the incomplete-type error. Copy construction clones the Impl; copy assignment uses copy-and-swap for the strong guarantee; the move operations are defaulted (in the source file) and leave the source with a null pointer.

#include <iostream>
#include <map>
#include <memory>
#include <optional>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

// ---- phonebook.h: what clients include ----
class Phonebook {
public:
    Phonebook();
    ~Phonebook();
    Phonebook(const Phonebook& other);
    Phonebook& operator=(const Phonebook& other);
    Phonebook(Phonebook&& other) noexcept;
    Phonebook& operator=(Phonebook&& other) noexcept;

    void add(std::string name, std::string number);
    std::optional<std::string> find(const std::string& name) const;
    std::size_t size() const;
private:
    struct Impl;
    std::unique_ptr<Impl> p_;  // a moved-from Phonebook holds null: assign or destroy only
};

// ---- phonebook.cpp: the only file that sees Impl ----
struct Phonebook::Impl {
    std::map<std::string, std::string> entries;
};

Phonebook::Phonebook() : p_(std::make_unique<Impl>()) {}
Phonebook::~Phonebook() = default;
Phonebook::Phonebook(const Phonebook& other)
    : p_(other.p_ ? std::make_unique<Impl>(*other.p_) : nullptr) {}
Phonebook& Phonebook::operator=(const Phonebook& other) {
    Phonebook tmp(other);  // may throw; *this is untouched if it does
    p_.swap(tmp.p_);
    return *this;
}
Phonebook::Phonebook(Phonebook&&) noexcept = default;
Phonebook& Phonebook::operator=(Phonebook&&) noexcept = default;

void Phonebook::add(std::string name, std::string number) {
    p_->entries[std::move(name)] = std::move(number);
}
std::optional<std::string> Phonebook::find(const std::string& name) const {
    auto it = p_->entries.find(name);
    if (it == p_->entries.end()) return std::nullopt;
    return it->second;
}
std::size_t Phonebook::size() const { return p_->entries.size(); }

// ---- main.cpp ----
int main() {
    Phonebook a;
    a.add("alice", "555-0100");
    a.add("bob", "555-0199");
    Phonebook b = a;  // deep copy
    b.add("carol", "555-0123");
    Phonebook c = std::move(b);
    std::cout << a.size() << ' ' << c.size() << '\n';
    a = c;            // copy assignment
    std::cout << a.size() << ' ' << a.find("carol").value_or("?") << ' '
              << c.find("dave").value_or("none") << '\n';
    std::cout << "one pointer: " << (sizeof(Phonebook) == sizeof(void*)) << '\n';
}
2 3
3 555-0123 none
one pointer: 1

Complexity and pitfalls. Every operation costs one extra pointer dereference, construction costs a heap allocation, and nothing in Impl can be inlined into callers. Pitfalls: defining the destructor or move operations in the header (or leaving them implicit) brings back the incomplete-type error; in a const member function p_->entries.clear() would compile, because constness does not propagate through the pointer; and the copy constructor must handle a moved-from source, or copying such an object dereferences null.

Estimated rating: ~1500 · the code is short; knowing exactly which special members must be out of line, and why, is the test

CodeCRTP mixins. Write two mixins: Printable<T>, which gives any T with a print(std::ostream&) const member an operator<<, and Counted<T>, which keeps a live-instance count per type, correct under copying. Apply both to two unrelated classes. The mixins must add no size to the classes and must not be usable on their own.

Answer

Approach. Printable<T> defines a hidden friend operator<<(std::ostream&, const T&); ADL finds it because Printable<T> is a base class of T, and base classes are associated classes. Counted<T> holds an inline static counter, so each T gets its own, and increments in every constructor including the copy constructor. Both have protected constructors and destructors (not usable alone, no virtual destructor needed) and no data, so the empty base optimisation makes them free.

#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

template <class T>
class Printable {
public:
    friend std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const T& x) {
        x.print(os);
        return os;
    }
protected:
    Printable() = default;
    ~Printable() = default;
};

template <class T>
class Counted {
public:
    static int alive() { return alive_; }
protected:
    Counted() { ++alive_; }
    Counted(const Counted&) { ++alive_; }  // copies are new objects too
    Counted& operator=(const Counted&) = default;
    ~Counted() { --alive_; }
private:
    inline static int alive_ = 0;          // one counter per T
};

class Point : public Printable<Point>, public Counted<Point> {
public:
    Point(int x, int y) : x_(x), y_(y) {}
    void print(std::ostream& os) const { os << '(' << x_ << ", " << y_ << ')'; }
private:
    int x_, y_;
};

class Order : public Printable<Order>, public Counted<Order> {
public:
    Order(std::string id, int qty) : id_(std::move(id)), qty_(qty) {}
    void print(std::ostream& os) const { os << "order " << id_ << " x" << qty_; }
private:
    std::string id_;
    int qty_;
};

int main() {
    Point p(1, 2);
    {
        Point q = p;
        Order o("A1", 5);
        std::cout << p << ' ' << q << ' ' << o << '\n';
        std::cout << Point::alive() << ' ' << Order::alive() << '\n';
    }
    std::cout << Point::alive() << ' ' << Order::alive() << '\n';
    std::cout << "sizeof(Point) = " << sizeof(Point) << '\n';
}
(1, 2) (1, 2) order A1 x5
2 1
1 0
sizeof(Point) = 8

Complexity and pitfalls. Everything is resolved at compile time; there is no run-time cost beyond the counter update. Pitfalls: forgetting the counting copy constructor gives negative counts (the Counted drill in Ch 1); the counter is not thread-safe (use std::atomic<int> if objects are created on several threads); and two empty bases of the same type cannot share an address, so Counted<Base> inherited twice would add a byte. Before C++20, CRTP mixins were also the way to derive !=, > and friends from == and < (Boost.Operators); defaulted comparisons replace that use.

Estimated rating: ~1500 · needs ADL through base classes, per-instantiation statics and EBO, all small but easy to get wrong

CodeA testable rate limiter. Implement a token bucket: capacity burst tokens, refilled continuously at rate tokens per second, with bool try_acquire() that takes one token if available. The class must not call the system clock directly: inject a Clock interface so a unit test can drive time with a fake clock. Avoid floating-point drift.

Answer

Approach. Dependency inversion: TokenBucket depends on an abstract Clock returning microseconds, with a real implementation on std::chrono::steady_clock and a fake for tests. Refill lazily on each call from the elapsed time. Store the level in micro-tokens (tokens × 10⁶): then elapsed microseconds × tokens per second is exactly the number of micro-tokens earned, so all arithmetic is integer and exact.

#include <algorithm>
#include <chrono>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

class Clock {
public:
    virtual ~Clock() = default;
    virtual std::int64_t now_us() const = 0;
};

class SteadyClock final : public Clock {
public:
    std::int64_t now_us() const override {
        using namespace std::chrono;
        return duration_cast<microseconds>(steady_clock::now().time_since_epoch()).count();
    }
};

class FakeClock final : public Clock {
public:
    std::int64_t now_us() const override { return t_; }
    void advance_us(std::int64_t us) { t_ += us; }
private:
    std::int64_t t_ = 0;
};

class TokenBucket {
public:
    TokenBucket(const Clock& clock, std::int64_t rate_per_sec, std::int64_t burst)
        : clock_(clock), rate_(rate_per_sec), cap_(burst * kScale), level_(cap_), last_(clock.now_us()) {}

    bool try_acquire() {
        refill();
        if (level_ < kScale) return false;
        level_ -= kScale;
        return true;
    }
private:
    static constexpr std::int64_t kScale = 1'000'000;  // micro-tokens per token
    void refill() {
        const std::int64_t now = clock_.now_us();
        const std::int64_t elapsed = std::min<std::int64_t>(now - last_, 3'600'000'000);  // cap at 1 h: no overflow
        level_ = std::min(cap_, level_ + elapsed * rate_);
        last_ = now;
    }
    const Clock& clock_;
    std::int64_t rate_, cap_, level_, last_;
};

static std::string attempts(TokenBucket& tb, int n) {
    std::string s;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) s += tb.try_acquire() ? '1' : '0';
    return s;
}

int main() {
    FakeClock clock;
    TokenBucket tb(clock, 10, 3);    // 10 per second, burst of 3
    std::cout << attempts(tb, 4) << '\n';
    clock.advance_us(100'000);       // 0.1 s earns exactly one token
    std::cout << attempts(tb, 2) << '\n';
    clock.advance_us(5'000'000);     // long idle: capped at the burst size
    std::cout << attempts(tb, 4) << '\n';

    SteadyClock real;
    TokenBucket live(real, 1000, 5);
    std::cout << live.try_acquire() << '\n';
}
1110
10
1110
1

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) per call, no background thread. Pitfalls: using double tokens makes "exactly one token after 0.1 s" fail by one ulp, which produces flaky tests; using system_clock breaks when the wall clock jumps (NTP, daylight saving), so rate limiters use a monotonic clock; storing the Clock by reference requires it to outlive the bucket; and the class is not thread-safe (add a mutex, or a CAS loop on a packed state word for a lock-free version, Ch 5).

Estimated rating: ~1500 · simple algorithm; the interview is about injecting time and getting exact integer arithmetic

CodeIterators for a fixed-capacity ring buffer. Implement RingBuffer<T, N> where push overwrites the oldest element when full, with iterator and const_iterator that visit elements oldest first. They must satisfy std::forward_iterator (check with static_assert), support prefix and postfix ++, *, -> and ==, and an iterator must convert to a const_iterator. Range-for and standard algorithms must work.

Answer

Approach. Store std::array<T, N>, the index of the oldest element and the size. An iterator holds the buffer pointer and a logical index from 0 to size; dereferencing maps it to (head + i) % N, so end() is simply index size. One template Iter<bool Const> produces both iterator types, with the conversion constrained to the non-const one. The member types (value_type, difference_type, iterator_concept) plus a default constructor and defaulted == are what the C++20 concept checks.

#include <algorithm>
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <iostream>
#include <iterator>
#include <numeric>
#include <string>
#include <type_traits>

template <class T, std::size_t N>
class RingBuffer {
    template <bool Const>
    class Iter {
        using Buf = std::conditional_t<Const, const RingBuffer, RingBuffer>;
    public:
        using iterator_concept = std::forward_iterator_tag;
        using iterator_category = std::forward_iterator_tag;
        using value_type = T;
        using difference_type = std::ptrdiff_t;
        using reference = std::conditional_t<Const, const T&, T&>;
