        Iter() = default;
        Iter(Buf* buf, std::size_t i) : buf_(buf), i_(i) {}
        operator Iter<true>() const requires(!Const) { return {buf_, i_}; }

        reference operator*() const { return buf_->data_[(buf_->head_ + i_) % N]; }
        auto operator->() const { return &**this; }
        Iter& operator++() { ++i_; return *this; }
        Iter operator++(int) { Iter old = *this; ++*this; return old; }
        friend bool operator==(const Iter&, const Iter&) = default;
    private:
        Buf* buf_ = nullptr;
        std::size_t i_ = 0;
    };

public:
    using iterator = Iter<false>;
    using const_iterator = Iter<true>;

    void push(const T& v) {
        data_[(head_ + size_) % N] = v;
        if (size_ < N) ++size_;
        else head_ = (head_ + 1) % N;  // full: the oldest element was overwritten
    }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    iterator begin() { return {this, 0}; }
    iterator end() { return {this, size_}; }
    const_iterator begin() const { return {this, 0}; }
    const_iterator end() const { return {this, size_}; }
private:
    std::array<T, N> data_{};
    std::size_t head_ = 0, size_ = 0;
};

static_assert(std::forward_iterator<RingBuffer<int, 4>::iterator>);
static_assert(std::forward_iterator<RingBuffer<int, 4>::const_iterator>);

template <class Range>
static void print(const Range& r) {
    bool first = true;
    for (const auto& x : r) { std::cout << (first ? "" : " ") << x; first = false; }
    std::cout << '\n';
}

int main() {
    RingBuffer<int, 4> rb;
    for (int i = 1; i <= 6; ++i) rb.push(i);  // keeps the last four
    print(rb);
    std::cout << "sum " << std::accumulate(rb.begin(), rb.end(), 0) << '\n';
    for (int& x : rb) x *= 10;
    const auto& crb = rb;
    print(crb);
    auto it = rb.begin();
    auto old = it++;
    std::cout << *old << ' ' << *it << '\n';
    RingBuffer<int, 4>::const_iterator cit = it;  // iterator converts to const_iterator
    auto found = std::find(crb.begin(), crb.end(), 50);
    std::cout << "found " << *found << " at " << std::distance(crb.begin(), found)
              << ", cit==it " << (cit == crb.begin()) << '\n';
    RingBuffer<std::string, 2> names;
    names.push("ab");
    names.push("cde");
    std::cout << names.begin()->size() << '\n';
}
3 4 5 6
sum 18
30 40 50 60
30 40
found 50 at 2, cit==it 0
2

Complexity and pitfalls. Every operation is O(1); std::distance is O(n) because the iterator is only forward (adding +=, - and <=> would make it random access). Pitfalls: storing a physical index makes end() equal begin() when the buffer is full, which is why the reference uses a logical index; postfix must return the old iterator by value; omitting the default constructor or difference_type makes std::forward_iterator fail with a long concept error; and pushing invalidates the meaning of existing iterators, which the class should document. The last comparison prints 0 because cit was taken after one increment, so it is not begin().

Estimated rating: ~1600 · the ring arithmetic is easy; the C++20 iterator requirements and the const/non-const pair are where candidates get stuck

Cheat sheet

Theory
  • Abstraction picks the operations; encapsulation hides the representation so only the class can break its invariant. Access control is per class, not per object.
  • Interfaces are classes with only pure virtual functions, no data, a public virtual or protected destructor, and protected copy operations. Use concepts or CRTP instead when the type is known at compile time.
  • Operators: = () [] -> and conversions must be members; compound assignment and ++ are members by convention; symmetric binary operators and << are non-members, ideally hidden friends. Build + from +=, take the left side by value, return a plain value. Postfix ++ takes a dummy int and returns the old value by copy.
  • C++20 comparisons: == also provides != and reversed operands; <=> provides the four relational operators. A defaulted <=> declares a defaulted ==, a user-written one does not. Members compare in declaration order. double gives partial_ordering.
  • Statics: inline static members need no out-of-class definition (C++17). Cross-TU dynamic initialisation order is unspecified: use constinit/constexpr or a function-local static (thread-safe since C++11). Destruction runs in reverse order of completed construction.
  • const: a const member function makes this a const T*; constness is shallow through pointers. Use mutable for caches and mutexes and synchronise it. Provide const and non-const overloads of accessors, or one C++23 deducing-this template.
  • Design: SOLID; Liskov is about behavioural promises (mutable square/rectangle fails, immutable passes); prefer composition, because inheriting implementation creates the fragile base class problem. Mark classes not designed for inheritance final.
  • PIMPL needs the destructor and move operations defined in the .cpp; write the deep copy yourself; remember constness does not propagate. CRTP gives inlinable static dispatch but no heterogeneous containers; guard it with a private base constructor and friend Derived;.

Part B · Threads · Chapter 4

Threads in the operating system

A thread is a scheduled stream of execution that shares its process's memory with every other thread in that process. This chapter builds the operating-system picture (what the kernel tracks, how threads are created, scheduled and switched) and then maps it onto pthread_create, std::thread and std::jthread. Interviewers use it to check that you know what is shared, what it costs, and how C++ thread objects end their lives.

TheoryDrillsCoding· about 5 hours· prerequisites: basic C++, RAII, lambdas

Process vs thread

Theory

Mental model. A process is a container of resources: one virtual address space, a table of open file descriptors, signal handlers, credentials and resource limits. A thread is a unit of execution inside that container: a program counter, a stack pointer, a register set and a stack. Every process starts with one thread. Creating more threads adds more streams of execution that all see the same memory.

The consequence that drives this whole part of the guide: two threads can read and write the same global, the same heap block and even each other's stack variables (if they are handed a pointer), with no copy and no permission check. That makes communication cheap and makes data races possible (Ch 5).

What is shared and what is private

ResourceShared by all threadsPrivate to each threadNote
Address space (code, globals, heap, mappings)yesOne set of page tables; a write by one thread is visible to all (subject to the memory model)
StackyesPrivate by convention only: it is ordinary memory any thread can address
Registers, PC, SPyesSaved into the thread's kernel structure on a context switch
thread_local variables, errnoyesFound through a per-thread base register
File descriptors and file offsetsyesclose(fd) in one thread closes it for all
Signal handlers (dispositions)yesThe signal mask is per thread
Process id, cwd, umask, uid/gid, rlimitsyeschdir affects every thread
Thread id, scheduling priority, CPU affinityyesLinux schedules threads, not processes

Both facts are visible from user code. A thread sees the same process id as main but a different thread id, and globals and heap memory written by one thread are read back by another:

#include <iostream>
#include <thread>
#include <unistd.h>

int main() {
    const pid_t main_pid = getpid();
    const std::thread::id main_id = std::this_thread::get_id();
    bool same_pid = false, same_tid = true;
    std::thread t([&] {
        same_pid = (getpid() == main_pid);
        same_tid = (std::this_thread::get_id() == main_id);
    });
    t.join();  // join makes the writes above visible to main
    std::cout << "same process id: " << same_pid << '\n';
    std::cout << "same thread id:  " << same_tid << '\n';
}
same process id: 1
same thread id:  0
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <latch>
#include <memory>
#include <thread>

static int global_value = 0;   // data segment: one copy per process

int main() {
    auto heap_value = std::make_unique<int>(0);   // heap: one copy per process
    std::uintptr_t local_addr[2] = {0, 0};
    std::latch both_alive(2);

    auto body = [&](int idx) {
        int local = idx;               // lives on this thread's own stack
        local_addr[idx] = reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t>(&local);
        both_alive.arrive_and_wait();  // keep both stacks alive at the same time
        if (idx == 0) global_value = 10;
        else *heap_value = 20;
    };
    std::thread a(body, 0), b(body, 1);
    a.join();
    b.join();

    std::cout << "global written by a: " << global_value << '\n';
    std::cout << "heap written by b:   " << *heap_value << '\n';
    std::cout << "locals at different addresses: " << (local_addr[0] != local_addr[1]) << '\n';
}
global written by a: 10
heap written by b:   20
locals at different addresses: 1

Know this cold

Threads in a process share everything except the execution context: registers (PC, SP), the stack, thread-local storage, the signal mask, the thread id and scheduling attributes. Processes share nothing by default; they communicate through pipes, sockets, files or explicitly shared memory.

Why use threads at all

  • Parallelism: use several cores for one job (number crunching, compression, a parallel build).
  • Overlapping waits: one thread blocks on disk or network while another keeps computing or serving the UI.
  • Cheaper than processes: creation needs no new page tables, a switch inside one process keeps the TLB valid, and communication is a memory write.

The price is isolation. A wild pointer in one thread corrupts the whole process, and a crash in any thread kills all of them. Browsers and databases use separate processes exactly where they want that isolation back.

PCB, TCB and Linux tasks

Theory

Mental model. The kernel needs a record for everything it manages. The classic textbook split is a process control block (PCB) for the resource container and a thread control block (TCB) for each execution stream inside it.

PCB (per process)TCB (per thread)
pid, parent, credentialsthread id, state (ready, running, blocked)
memory map: pointer to page tables, list of regionssaved registers: PC, SP, flags, general and FP/SIMD registers
open file table, cwd, umaskkernel stack pointer, user stack location
signal handlers, pending process-wide signalssignal mask, pending thread-directed signals
resource limits, accounting totalspriority, scheduling policy, CPU affinity, time used
list of its threadsTLS base, pointer back to its process

On Linux, threads are tasks

Linux has no separate PCB and TCB types. Every schedulable entity is a task_struct, a task. Resources live in separately allocated, reference-counted objects (mm_struct for memory, files_struct for descriptors, sighand_struct for handlers, fs_struct for cwd). A "process" is a group of tasks that point at the same objects.

The system call that creates tasks is clone() (and the newer clone3()). Its flags choose what the child shares with the caller:

fork()            ≈ clone(SIGCHLD)                          share nothing: copy-on-write copy of memory
pthread_create()  ≈ clone(CLONE_VM | CLONE_FS | CLONE_FILES | CLONE_SIGHAND |
                          CLONE_THREAD | CLONE_SYSVSEM | CLONE_SETTLS |
                          CLONE_PARENT_SETTID | CLONE_CHILD_CLEARTID)
                                                            share memory, fds, cwd, handlers; join the thread group
  • CLONE_VM shares the address space, which is what makes it a thread.
  • CLONE_THREAD puts the new task in the caller's thread group. The group id (tgid) is what getpid() returns; each task's own id is what gettid() returns. For the first thread, pid equals tid.
  • CLONE_SETTLS sets the new thread's TLS base register; CLONE_CHILD_CLEARTID makes the kernel zero a word and wake a futex when the thread exits, which is how pthread_join waits.

This is why ps -eLf or top -H show threads as separate lines, why /proc/<pid>/task/ lists one directory per thread, and why a thread is sometimes called a "light-weight process" (LWP). The scheduler sees only tasks; it never needs to know which tasks form a process.

Interview trap

"Linux threads are processes" is half right. They are tasks, scheduled exactly like processes, but tasks in one thread group share one pid, one address space and one set of handlers, and a fatal signal kills the whole group. The old LinuxThreads library (before glibc 2.3 and NPTL) really did give each thread its own pid, which broke POSIX signal semantics; that is where the folklore comes from.

User-level vs kernel-level threads

Theory

Kernel-level threads are known to the kernel: each has a kernel record, the kernel scheduler places them on cores, and a blocking system call blocks only the calling thread. User-level threads are implemented by a library inside one process: the library keeps its own run queue, saves and restores registers itself, and the kernel sees only the threads that carry them.

ModelExamplesStrengthsWeaknesses
N:1 (many user threads on one kernel thread)early Java green threads, GNU Pthswitches are function-call cheap, no kernel involvementa blocking syscall or page fault stops every thread; one core only
1:1Linux NPTL, Windows, macOS, std::thread everywherereal parallelism, blocking is per thread, kernel handles signals and prioritiescreation and switch go through the kernel; each thread reserves a full stack
M:NGo goroutines, Java 21 virtual threads, Erlang processes, old Solarismillions of cheap threads, still parallelthe runtime must avoid blocking carriers (it wraps I/O), harder debugging, priority inversion between levels

IBM built an M:N library for Linux (NGPT) at the same time as NPTL; NPTL won because a 1:1 design with a fast kernel was simpler and fast enough. C++ std::thread is specified as an OS thread, so on every mainstream platform it is 1:1. Cheap user-level concurrency in C++ comes from coroutines and executors, covered at the end of this chapter.

Thread states and lifecycle

Theory

A thread moves between a small number of states. The names vary between textbooks, but the machine is the same:

  • New: the thread object and its stack are being set up. For std::thread this is inside the constructor; when the constructor returns, the thread is already Ready or Running.
  • Ready: runnable and waiting for a core. Linux keeps one run queue per CPU.
  • Running: executing on a core. At most one thread per hardware thread.
  • Blocked (waiting, sleeping): waiting for an event, such as a mutex, a condition variable, I/O, a timer or another thread's exit. It uses no CPU.
  • Terminated: the function returned or the thread called pthread_exit. Its stack and result stay allocated until someone calls join, unless the thread was detached.

Tip

Linux does not distinguish Ready from Running in ps: both show as R. A thread spinning on a lock is Running and burns CPU; a thread sleeping in futex() is S and costs nothing. That difference is the core of the spinlock vs mutex trade-off in Ch 5.

Context switches and scheduling

Theory

Mental model. A core can run one thread at a time. A context switch saves the running thread's state into its kernel record and loads another thread's state, so the core continues where the other thread left off.

What happens during a switch

  1. Entry to the kernel. Something transfers control: a timer interrupt (preemption), a blocking system call (read, futex wait), or a voluntary sched_yield.
  2. Save state. The user registers are already on the thread's kernel stack from the entry path. The scheduler saves the callee-saved registers and stack pointer into the task, and the FP/SIMD state is saved as well (on x86-64 Linux it is restored lazily, on the way back to user space).
  3. Pick the next task. The scheduler chooses from this CPU's run queue.
  4. Switch memory if needed. If the next task belongs to a different process, the kernel loads its page-table root (CR3 on x86-64, TTBR0 on arm64). Inside the same process this step is skipped.
  5. Restore state of the next task, including its TLS base register, and return to user space.

What it costs

The direct cost, the instructions above, is on the order of a microsecond on current hardware (much more with KPTI page-table isolation or with large SIMD state). The indirect cost is usually larger: the next thread finds caches, branch predictors and the TLB full of the previous thread's data.

Thread switch (same process)Process switch
Registers saved and restoredyesyes
Page-table root reloadednoyes
TLBstays validflushed, or kept but tagged with PCID/ASID so old entries are ignored
Cache contentsoften useful: same code, shared datamostly cold for the new process

The TLB caches virtual-to-physical translations. Without address-space tags, loading a new page-table root must discard them, and the new process then takes page-walk misses until the TLB warms up. PCID (x86-64) and ASID (arm64) tags reduce this, but a thread switch inside one process still avoids the question entirely.

Interview trap

"Threads switch faster because they do not save registers" is wrong: both save the same register state. The saving is in the memory context (no page-table switch, no TLB invalidation) and in warmer caches. And user-level switches (coroutines, green threads) are faster still because they never enter the kernel.

Scheduling basics that matter for threads

  • The unit is the thread. A process with 8 threads competes with 8 entries; Linux has no per-process fairness unless you use cgroups.
  • Policies. SCHED_OTHER (the default, time-shared fair scheduling with nice values -20 to 19; CFS until Linux 6.6, EEVDF since), SCHED_FIFO and SCHED_RR (fixed real-time priorities 1 to 99, which always beat SCHED_OTHER), SCHED_DEADLINE, SCHED_BATCH and SCHED_IDLE.
  • Preemption. A normal thread runs until it blocks, yields or uses up its slice (a few milliseconds). A SCHED_FIFO thread runs until it blocks or a higher-priority thread wakes, so a busy loop at real-time priority can starve its whole core.
  • Affinity. pthread_setaffinity_np or sched_setaffinity pins a thread to chosen cores. Low-latency systems pin one busy-polling thread per isolated core so it never migrates or gets preempted.
  • Oversubscription. More runnable threads than cores means time slicing: total throughput does not rise, and switching, cache thrashing and lock holder preemption make it fall. This is the main argument for thread pools.

Thread-local storage

Theory

Mental model. A thread_local variable has one instance per thread. Each thread reads and writes its own copy with no synchronisation, because no other thread can name that copy.

#include <iostream>
#include <thread>

thread_local int calls = 0;   // one instance per thread, zero-initialised in each

static int work(int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) ++calls;   // no lock needed: nobody else sees this copy
    return calls;
}

int main() {
    int r1 = 0, r2 = 0;
    std::thread a([&] { r1 = work(3); });
    std::thread b([&] { r2 = work(5); });
    a.join();
    b.join();
    std::cout << "a: " << r1 << ", b: " << r2 << ", main: " << calls << '\n';
}
a: 3, b: 5, main: 0

Rules

  • thread_local can apply to namespace-scope variables, static data members and block-scope variables (where it implies static). Storage duration is "thread": the object lives as long as its thread.
  • Initialisation. Constant-initialised values are set up when the thread starts. Dynamically initialised namespace-scope ones are initialised before their first odr-use in that thread (implementations do it lazily), and block-scope ones the first time control passes the declaration in that thread.
  • Destruction. At thread exit, in reverse order of construction, before the thread's completion is signalled to join(). Thread-locals of the main thread are destroyed when main returns or exit is called, before static objects.
  • Implementation. The TLS base lives in a register (FS on x86-64, TPIDR_EL0 on arm64). Access in the main executable is one load at a fixed offset; access across shared libraries may call __tls_get_addr, and dynamically initialised variables add a wrapper that checks an initialisation flag.
  • Uses: per-thread caches and allocators (glibc's tcache, jemalloc arenas), random number engines, errno, per-thread counters merged later (the coding drill below), and avoiding locks on hot paths.

Interview trap

Thread pools reuse threads, so a thread_local survives between unrelated tasks. A cache keyed on "the current request" leaks data from one task to the next unless the task resets it. And the address of a thread_local handed to another thread is a plain pointer: the other thread can use it (it is shared memory), and it dangles once the owner exits.

pthreads, std::thread and std::jthread

Theory

The POSIX API

POSIX threads are a C API. The thread function has the fixed type void* (*)(void*), so arguments travel through a void* and the result comes back through pthread_join. Functions return an error number; they do not set errno.

#include <cstdio>
#include <cstring>
#include <pthread.h>

struct Job {
    int a, b;
    int sum;
};

static void* add(void* arg) {          // the only signature pthreads accepts
    auto* job = static_cast<Job*>(arg);
    job->sum = job->a + job->b;
    return job;                        // returned pointer is collected by pthread_join
}

int main() {
    Job job{2, 3, 0};
    pthread_t tid;
    if (int rc = pthread_create(&tid, nullptr, add, &job); rc != 0) {
        std::fprintf(stderr, "pthread_create: %s\n", std::strerror(rc));   // errors are returned, not errno
        return 1;
    }
    void* result = nullptr;
    pthread_join(tid, &result);
    std::printf("sum = %d, same object: %d\n", static_cast<Job*>(result)->sum, result == &job);
}
sum = 5, same object: 1
  • pthread_create(&tid, attr, fn, arg): starts the thread. attr sets stack size, detach state and scheduling policy.
  • pthread_join(tid, &ret): blocks until the thread ends and frees its resources. Joining twice, or joining a detached thread, is undefined.
  • pthread_detach(tid): resources are freed automatically when the thread ends; nobody can join it any more.
  • pthread_exit(ret): ends the calling thread. Called from main, it ends the main thread but keeps the process alive until the other threads finish.
  • pthread_self(), pthread_equal(), pthread_key_create() (the older dynamic TLS API).

std::thread

std::thread wraps one OS thread. The constructor takes any callable plus arguments and starts the thread before it returns. The object is a move-only handle; the thread itself is not the object.

#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <thread>

static void greet(std::string name, int times, std::string& out) {
    for (int i = 0; i < times; ++i) out += "hi " + name + "; ";
}

int main() {
    std::string out;
    std::thread t(greet, "ada", 2, std::ref(out));   // args are copied, std::ref opts out
    t.join();
    std::cout << out << '\n';

    int answer = 0;
    std::jthread j([&answer] { answer = 42; });      // C++20: joins in its destructor
    j.join();                                        // or let the destructor do it
    std::cout << "answer = " << answer << '\n';
}
hi ada; hi ada; 
answer = 42
  • joinable() is true from construction until join() or detach(), or until the handle is moved from. A default-constructed thread is not joinable.
  • join() waits for the thread to finish. Everything the thread did happens-before join() returns, so results written by the thread can be read afterwards without a lock.
  • detach() lets the thread run on alone; the handle becomes empty. You lose every way of knowing when it finishes.
  • Destructor: if the thread is still joinable, ~thread() calls std::terminate(). Move assignment onto a joinable thread does the same.

Know this cold

Destroying a joinable std::thread calls std::terminate. The committee rejected both implicit choices: an implicit join can hang during exception unwinding, and an implicit detach leaves a thread running with references to destroyed locals. C++20's std::jthread picks join, made safe by asking the thread to stop first.

Passing arguments

The constructor decay-copies the callable and every argument into storage owned by the new thread (this copy happens in the calling thread), then invokes the callable with those copies as rvalues. Three consequences:

  1. A parameter of type const T& binds to the internal copy, never to your original. Use std::ref or std::cref to pass a reference, and then you own the lifetime problem.
  2. A parameter of type T& does not compile without std::ref, because an rvalue cannot bind to a non-const lvalue reference.
  3. Implicit conversions (for example char* to std::string) happen in the new thread, possibly after the source buffer is gone. Convert explicitly before the call.

Lambdas follow their capture list instead: [=] copies when the lambda is created, [&] captures references. Capturing a loop variable or a local by reference in a thread that may outlive it is the most common thread bug in interviews.

std::jthread (C++20)

std::jthread behaves like std::thread with two additions. Its destructor calls request_stop() and then join(), so it can never terminate the program. And if the callable accepts a std::stop_token as its first parameter, the jthread passes one in, giving a standard cooperative cancellation channel (stop_requested(), std::stop_callback, and condition_variable_any::wait overloads that wake on a stop request).

Interview trap

A stop request is only a flag. A jthread whose function never checks its token, or is blocked in a plain read(), still makes the destructor wait forever. Cancellation is cooperative in C++; there is no portable way to kill a thread.

hardware_concurrency and stack size

std::thread::hardware_concurrency() returns a hint: the number of hardware threads the implementation knows about, or 0 if it cannot tell. On Linux, libstdc++ uses get_nprocs(), the online CPU count, which ignores CPU affinity masks and container CPU quotas. Treat it as an upper bound, clamp 0 to 1, and prefer sched_getaffinity when it matters.

std::thread has no way to set the stack size. glibc uses the RLIMIT_STACK soft limit (usually 8 MiB) for new threads, while macOS gives secondary threads 512 KiB. Use pthread_attr_setstacksize through the native API when you need control. The memory is virtual and committed page by page, so many threads cost address space more than RAM.

Thread pools, fork, signals and green threads

Theory

Why thread pools

Creating a thread costs a system call, a stack mapping and scheduler bookkeeping (tens of microseconds). A thread per request also lets the thread count grow with load, which leads to oversubscription and memory pressure. A thread pool creates a fixed set of workers once; producers push tasks into a shared queue and workers pop and run them. Benefits: creation cost paid once, concurrency bounded at about the core count, and a natural place for back-pressure and shutdown. The pool's queue is a producer-consumer problem solved with a mutex and condition variable (Ch 6); the coding section builds one.

Sizing rule of thumb: about the number of cores for CPU-bound tasks; more for tasks that block on I/O, roughly cores × (1 + wait time / compute time).

fork() in a multithreaded process

fork() copies the whole address space but creates only one thread in the child: a copy of the caller. Every other thread vanishes in the child, mid-instruction, without running destructors or unlocking anything. Any mutex another thread held at the moment of the fork (including the ones inside malloc, printf or the dynamic loader) stays locked forever in the child.

  • POSIX says that after fork() in a multithreaded process, the child may only call async-signal-safe functions until it calls exec. fork then exec immediately (or posix_spawn) is safe; doing real work in the child is not.
  • pthread_atfork(prepare, parent, child) lets a library take its locks before the fork and release them in both processes afterwards. glibc does this for malloc, which is why malloc usually works in such a child, but you cannot rely on it for other libraries.
  • Unflushed stdio buffers are copied too, so buffered output can be printed twice (see the drills).

Signals and threads, briefly

  • Signal handlers are per process; the signal mask is per thread (pthread_sigmask, never sigprocmask in threaded code).
  • A process-directed signal (kill, Ctrl-C) is delivered to one arbitrary thread that does not block it. A synchronous fault (SIGSEGV, SIGFPE) goes to the thread that caused it. pthread_kill targets one thread.
  • The robust pattern: block the signals in main before creating threads (new threads inherit the mask), then dedicate one thread to sigwait and handle signals as ordinary events there.
  • Handlers may only call async-signal-safe functions: no malloc, no locks, no std::cout. Setting a volatile std::sig_atomic_t or a lock-free atomic flag is the safe minimum.

Green threads and coroutines

OS threadGreen thread / fiber (stackful)C++20 coroutine (stackless)
Scheduled bykernel, preemptiveuser-space runtime, usually cooperativeyour code or an executor, cooperative at co_await
State kept infull stack (MiB reserved) + kernel taskits own small stack (KiB, sometimes growable)a heap frame holding only locals that live across suspension points
Switch costabout 1 µs plus cache effectstens of nsa function call
Parallel on many coresyesonly with M:N carriersonly if resumed on several threads
Blocking syscallblocks that thread onlyblocks the carrier unless the runtime wraps I/Oblocks the thread running it
Can suspend in a nested callyesyesno: only the coroutine body itself can co_await

Coroutines are a concurrency tool, not a parallelism tool. They let one thread interleave thousands of I/O-bound tasks; you still need threads to use more than one core, and once a coroutine is resumed on another thread all the data-race rules apply again.

Concept and tricky questions

Drills

ConceptList what threads of one process share and what each thread has privately.

Answer

Answer. Shared: the address space (code, globals, heap, memory mappings), file descriptors, cwd, signal handlers, pid, credentials and limits. Private: registers including PC and SP, the stack, thread-local storage (including errno), the signal mask, the thread id and scheduling attributes.

Why. Linux creates threads with clone(CLONE_VM | CLONE_FILES | CLONE_SIGHAND | CLONE_THREAD | ...), so the resource objects are shared by reference and only the task's execution context is new. The common mistake is to say "each thread has its own heap". There is one heap; allocators keep per-thread caches (glibc tcache and arenas) for speed, but memory allocated by one thread can be freed by another. Another subtle point: a stack is "private" only by convention. Another thread can read and write it through a pointer.

ConceptWhy is a context switch between two threads of the same process usually cheaper than a switch between two processes?

Answer

Answer. The register save and restore is the same. The thread switch skips loading a new page-table root, so the TLB stays valid, and the new thread often finds useful code and data already in the caches.

Why. A process switch writes CR3 (x86-64) or TTBR0 (arm64). Without PCID or ASID tags that flushes the TLB, and even with tags the new process has few entries cached and takes page walks. Most of the measured cost of a switch is this indirect cache and TLB warm-up, not the switch code. The wrong answer is "threads have fewer registers to save".

TrickyOn Linux, what do getpid() and gettid() return in a second thread, and does the scheduler know which tasks form a process?

Answer

Answer. getpid() returns the thread group id, the same as in main. gettid() returns the task's own id, which differs. The scheduler schedules tasks individually and does not care about the grouping (apart from cgroups and group scheduling).

Why. Every Linux thread is a task_struct. CLONE_THREAD places the new task in the caller's thread group, and the group's id (the tgid, equal to the first thread's tid) is what POSIX calls the pid. People who learned from LinuxThreads-era material say each thread has its own pid; that was true before NPTL (glibc 2.3, 2003) and broke POSIX semantics such as signals sent to the process.

ConceptCompare the N:1, 1:1 and M:N threading models. Which does std::thread use on Linux?

Answer

Answer. N:1 puts all user threads on one kernel thread: cheap switches, but no parallelism and one blocking call stalls everything. 1:1 gives every user thread a kernel thread: true parallelism and per-thread blocking, at kernel cost. M:N multiplexes many user threads on a pool of kernel threads: cheap and parallel, but the runtime is complex. std::thread on Linux is 1:1 (glibc NPTL).

Why. In N:1 the kernel sees one thread, so it cannot run two of them at once and cannot know that a user thread blocked. M:N (Go, Java virtual threads) solves this by converting blocking I/O into non-blocking calls plus a scheduler park, and by moving goroutines off a carrier stuck in a syscall. A trap: M:N does not remove the need for locks. Two goroutines on two carriers race exactly like two OS threads.

TrickyWhy does destroying a joinable std::thread call std::terminate instead of joining or detaching? How does C++20 change this?

Answer

Answer. Both automatic choices are dangerous, so the standard makes forgetting a hard error. std::jthread (C++20) chooses to request a stop and join in its destructor.

Why. Implicit detach would leave a running thread that may still reference locals of the scope being destroyed: silent use-after-free. Implicit join can deadlock or hang during stack unwinding, for example when the thread waits for something the unwinding code would have done. std::terminate forces the programmer to decide. jthread makes join safe enough by first calling request_stop(), which a cooperative worker checks through its stop_token. The same terminate rule applies to move assignment onto a joinable thread ([thread.thread.assign]). Candidates often say "the destructor joins": that is jthread, not std::thread.

TrickyA program detaches a worker thread and then main returns while the worker is still running. What happens to the worker, and what can go wrong just before it dies?

Answer

Answer. Returning from main calls exit(), which runs static destructors and then ends the process with exit_group, killing every thread. The worker dies mid-instruction. Before that, while static destructors run, the worker may still be using those objects: undefined behaviour.

Why. Detach does not make a thread independent of its process. The classic crash is a detached logger thread writing to std::cout or a global logger while exit destroys them. Only pthread_exit from main (or quick_exit after the main thread reaches a safe point) keeps the process alive or skips destructors. The wrong answer is "the detached thread keeps running in the background". That is only true while the process lives.

TrickyCan a thread join itself? What happens if you call join() twice on the same std::thread?

#include <iostream>
#include <latch>
#include <system_error>
#include <thread>

static std::thread t;
static std::latch assigned(1), tried(1);

int main() {
    t = std::thread([] {
        assigned.wait();   // make sure t is fully assigned before the worker reads it
        try {
            t.join();      // the worker tries to wait for itself
        } catch (const std::system_error& e) {
            std::cout << "self join: " << (e.code() == std::errc::resource_deadlock_would_occur) << '\n';
        }
        tried.count_down();
    });
    assigned.count_down();
    tried.wait();          // never join one thread from two threads at once
    t.join();
    try {
        t.join();          // already joined: no longer joinable
    } catch (const std::system_error& e) {
        std::cout << "join twice: " << (e.code() == std::errc::invalid_argument) << '\n';
    }
}
Answer
self join: 1
join twice: 1

Answer. No. A thread waiting for its own termination could never finish, so std::thread::join() throws std::system_error with resource_deadlock_would_occur when get_id() == std::this_thread::get_id(). A second join() throws with invalid_argument, because after the first join the handle is no longer joinable.

Why. Both are specified error conditions in [thread.thread.member], so they are defined behaviour for std::thread (pthreads returns EDEADLK for a self-join, while joining an already joined pthread_t is undefined, because the id may already belong to a new thread). The common wrong answers are "it deadlocks forever" for the self-join and "the second join returns immediately". The two latches matter. Without assigned, the worker could read t while main is still move-assigning it, which is a data race. Without tried, main could already be inside join() when the worker calls it, and two simultaneous joins of one thread are undefined (macOS then reports EINVAL instead of EDEADLK). (ThreadSanitizer's pthread_join interceptor aborts on a deliberate self-join, so this program is run without it.)

ConceptWhen is a thread_local variable constructed and destroyed, and how does a thread find its copy?

Answer

Answer. Each thread gets its own instance. Constant-initialised ones are ready when the thread starts; dynamically initialised ones are constructed before first use in that thread (block-scope ones when control first passes the declaration). They are destroyed at thread exit in reverse order, before join() returns. The thread finds its copy through a per-thread base register (FS on x86-64, TPIDR_EL0 on arm64) plus an offset.

Why. The ELF TLS model lays out a template that the loader copies for each new thread. Variables defined in the main executable use a fixed offset from the register (one instruction); shared libraries loaded later may need __tls_get_addr. A common mistake is to think thread_local implies a lock or atomic: it needs neither, because only one thread can name each instance.

TrickyCan a thread pass a pointer to one of its stack variables to another thread? Is that safe?

Answer

Answer. Yes, it compiles and works: all stacks are in the shared address space. It is safe only while the variable is alive and the accesses are synchronised. Once the owning function returns or the thread exits, the pointer dangles.

Why. The OS does not protect one thread's stack from another; there is only a guard page below each stack to catch overflow. The standard library itself relies on this: std::ref(local) passed to a thread that is joined before the scope ends is fine. The bug is the lifetime, not the address: detaching such a thread, or returning before join, is the classic dangling reference.

ConceptWhat does std::thread::hardware_concurrency() return, and why can it be the wrong number for sizing a pool?

Answer

Answer. A hint: the number of hardware threads (logical CPUs) the implementation can see, or 0 if unknown. In a container with a CPU quota, or a process pinned to a subset of cores, it still reports the machine's online CPUs.

Why. The standard only says "number of concurrent threads supported... should be considered only a hint". libstdc++ uses get_nprocs(); it does not look at sched_getaffinity or cgroup cpu.max. It also counts SMT siblings, which share execution units. Always handle 0, and for CPU-bound work consider the affinity mask; for I/O-bound work more threads than cores is normal.

TrickyA multithreaded server calls fork() to run some work in a child, and the child sometimes hangs forever in malloc or a logging call. Why, and what are the safe options?

Answer

Answer. The child contains only a copy of the forking thread. If another thread held a lock (in the allocator, the logger, stdio, the loader) at the moment of the fork, the lock's memory is copied in the locked state and no thread exists in the child to release it. Safe options: call exec straight after fork (or use posix_spawn), fork before creating threads, or use pthread_atfork handlers to quiesce your own locks.

Why. POSIX restricts the child of a multithreaded process to async-signal-safe functions until exec. glibc registers atfork handlers for malloc, which is why it often works, but third-party libraries usually do not. The wrong answer is "fork copies all threads": only Solaris had a forkall.

ConceptA process receives SIGTERM. Which thread runs the handler, and what is the recommended way to handle signals in a multithreaded program?

Answer

Answer. Any one thread that does not block SIGTERM; the choice is up to the kernel. The recommended pattern is to block the signals with pthread_sigmask in main before creating threads (the mask is inherited), then have one dedicated thread call sigwait and turn each signal into a normal event, such as setting a stop flag or notifying a condition variable.

Why. Handlers are shared by the process, masks are per thread, and a handler interrupts whatever the chosen thread was doing, possibly while it holds a lock. Inside a handler only async-signal-safe functions are allowed, so locking a mutex or calling notify_one there can deadlock or corrupt state. Synchronous signals like SIGSEGV are the exception: they go to the faulting thread.

Tricky"C++20 coroutines are lightweight threads, so I can use them instead of a thread pool to speed up a CPU-bound computation." What is wrong with that statement?

Answer

Answer. Coroutines give concurrency, not parallelism. A coroutine runs on whichever thread resumes it; with one thread, a thousand coroutines still use one core. To speed up CPU-bound work you need several OS threads (often a pool that resumes coroutines).

Why. C++20 coroutines are stackless: a coroutine frame stores locals that cross a suspension point, and co_await returns control to the caller or resumer. There is no scheduler and no preemption in the language. They shine for I/O-bound work where most tasks wait. Also, a coroutine that calls a blocking function blocks its whole thread, and a coroutine resumed on a different thread can see thread_local values change across a co_await.

TrickyA program creates 10,000 threads, each doing a tiny recursive computation, and fails with "Resource temporarily unavailable" although only a few GB of RAM are in use. What limits apply?

Answer

Answer. Thread creation fails with EAGAIN (thrown as std::system_error by std::thread) when a limit is hit: the per-user process/task limit (RLIMIT_NPROC, ulimit -u), /proc/sys/kernel/threads-max, cgroup pids.max (common in containers), the number of memory mappings, or virtual address space for the stacks (8 MiB reserved each by default).

Why. On Linux, threads count as tasks against the same limits as processes. Stack memory is reserved virtually and committed lazily, so RSS stays low while the reservation can still exhaust a limited address space or vm.max_map_count (each stack plus guard page is a mapping). The real fix is a thread pool sized near the core count; shrinking stacks with pthread_attr_setstacksize only treats the symptom.

ConceptWhy use a thread pool instead of creating a thread per task?

Answer

Answer. A pool pays thread creation once, bounds the number of runnable threads (avoiding oversubscription), keeps caches and thread-locals warm, and gives one place for queueing, back-pressure and orderly shutdown.

Why. Each creation is a clone system call, a stack mapping and scheduler work, tens of microseconds, which is more than many tasks take. With one thread per request, a load spike creates thousands of threads that thrash the scheduler and memory. The pitfalls a good answer also names: tasks that block on other tasks in the same pool can deadlock it when every worker waits, and long blocking I/O tasks starve CPU tasks unless they get a separate pool.

Predict the output and find the bug

Drills

OutputWhat does this print? Each thread is joined before the next starts.

#include <functional>
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>

static int g = 0;

static void check(const int& r) {
    std::cout << (&r == &g ? "same object" : "a copy") << '\n';
}

int main() {
    std::thread t1(check, g);
    t1.join();
    std::thread t2(check, std::cref(g));
    t2.join();
    std::thread t3([] { check(g); });
    t3.join();
}
Answer
a copy
same object
same object

Answer. Only the first call sees a copy.

Why. std::thread t1(check, g) decay-copies g into the thread's own storage and the const int& binds to that copy ([thread.thread.constr]). std::cref(g) copies a reference_wrapper, which converts back to a reference to g. The lambda calls check(g) directly, so no copy is involved. People expect "same object" for the first line because the parameter is a reference; the reference binds to the thread's copy.

Find the bugWhy does this not compile, and what are the two fixes?

#include <iostream>
#include <thread>

static void increment(int& x) { ++x; }

int main() {
    int n = 0;
    std::thread t(increment, n);
    t.join();
    std::cout << n << '\n';
}
Answer

Answer. The thread stores a copy of n and calls increment with that copy as an rvalue, and an rvalue int cannot bind to int&. GCC reports "std::thread arguments must be invocable after conversion to rvalues". Fix with std::thread t(increment, std::ref(n)); or with a lambda std::thread t([&n] { increment(n); });. Either way it prints 1.

Why. The library deliberately passes rvalues so that a function taking int& cannot silently modify a temporary copy, which would look like it worked but leave n at 0. The compile error is a feature. The common wrong answer is "it compiles and prints 1 because the parameter is a reference": the reference would bind to the thread's internal copy, if it were allowed to bind at all.

Find the bugThe author expects sum = 6. What is wrong? (The sum is atomic.)

#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::atomic<int> sum{0};
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i)
        threads.emplace_back([&] { sum += i; });   // expected 0+1+2+3 = 6
    for (auto& t : threads) t.join();
    std::cout << "sum = " << sum << '\n';
}
Answer

Answer. The lambda captures the loop variable i by reference. Each thread reads i whenever it gets to run, while main keeps incrementing it: a data race on i, so undefined behaviour. In practice the printed sum varies from run to run, because a thread that starts late sees a larger i (often 4). ThreadSanitizer reports the race. Fix: capture by value, [&sum, i] { sum += i; }.

Why. Making sum atomic protects only sum. The read of i in the thread and the write ++i in main are unsynchronised conflicting accesses, which is a data race by definition ([intro.races]). After the loop i is also out of scope, so a late thread reads a dead variable. The output is not shown because it is nondeterministic.

OutputWhat does this print?

#include <iostream>
#include <thread>

static void work() {}

int main() {
    std::thread t1(work);
    std::thread t2 = std::move(t1);
    std::cout << t1.joinable() << t2.joinable() << '\n';
    t1 = std::thread(work);
    std::cout << t1.joinable() << t2.joinable() << '\n';
    t1.join();
    t2.join();
    std::cout << t1.joinable() << t2.joinable() << '\n';
    std::thread t3;
    std::cout << t3.joinable() << (t3.get_id() == std::thread::id{}) << '\n';
}
Answer
01
11
00
01

Answer. 01, 11, 00, 01.

Why. Moving transfers ownership of the OS thread, leaving t1 empty (not joinable). Assigning a new thread to the empty t1 is fine; had t1 still been joinable, the move assignment would have called std::terminate. After join() both handles are empty. A default-constructed thread is not joinable and its id compares equal to std::thread::id{}, the "no thread" id.

Find the bugThe author expects caught boom and end. What actually happens?

#include <iostream>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <thread>

static void work() {}
static void risky() { throw std::runtime_error("boom"); }

int main() {
    try {
        std::thread t(work);
        risky();
        t.join();
    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        std::cout << "caught " << e.what() << '\n';
    }
    std::cout << "end\n";
}
Answer

Answer. Nothing is printed and the program aborts: risky() throws, unwinding destroys t while it is still joinable, and ~thread() calls std::terminate. libstdc++ prints "terminate called without an active exception" to stderr. (The snippet is tagged as not compared because it aborts.)

Why. The join() after the throwing call is skipped. This is the main reason never to hold a raw std::thread across code that can throw. Fixes: use std::jthread, or an RAII joining guard (coding drill 2), or join in a catch block and rethrow. Candidates sometimes expect the catch block to run; it cannot, because terminate happens during unwinding before the handler is reached.

OutputBoth workers spin until stopped. What does this print, and in what order?

#include <iostream>
#include <stop_token>
#include <thread>

static std::jthread make(const char* name) {
    return std::jthread([name](std::stop_token st) {
        while (!st.stop_requested()) std::this_thread::yield();
        std::cout << name << " stopped\n";
    });
}

int main() {
    std::jthread a = make("a");
    std::jthread b = make("b");
    std::cout << "end of main\n";
}
Answer
end of main
b stopped
a stopped

Answer. end of main, then b stopped, then a stopped. The order is deterministic.

Why. Neither worker can print before its stop is requested. Locals are destroyed in reverse order of construction, so b's destructor runs first: request_stop() and then join(), which waits for "b stopped". Only then is a destroyed and stopped. With std::thread instead, the program would terminate at the end of main. Note that make returns the jthread by value; moving a jthread moves its stop state with it.

OutputWhat does this print? Watch when the thread-local object is created and destroyed.

#include <iostream>
#include <thread>

struct Tracker {
    int id;
    explicit Tracker(int i) : id(i) { std::cout << "ctor " << id << '\n'; }
    ~Tracker() { std::cout << "dtor " << id << '\n'; }
};

static int next_id = 0;   // touched by one thread at a time (the joins order them)

static Tracker& tracker() {
    thread_local Tracker t(++next_id);
    return t;
}

int main() {
    std::thread a([] {
        int x = tracker().id;
        std::cout << "a uses " << x << '\n';
    });
    a.join();
    std::cout << "joined a\n";
    std::thread b([] {
        int x = tracker().id;
        int y = tracker().id;
        std::cout << "b uses " << x << ' ' << y << '\n';
    });
    b.join();
    std::cout << "joined b\n";
}
Answer
ctor 1
a uses 1
dtor 1
joined a
ctor 2
b uses 2 2
dtor 2
joined b

Answer. Each thread constructs its own Tracker on first use and destroys it when the thread exits, before join() returns. Thread b calls tracker() twice but constructs only once. main never calls it, so no third object exists.

Why. A block-scope thread_local is initialised the first time control passes its declaration in each thread, and destroyed at that thread's exit. The standard sequences thread-local destructors before the thread's completion, and completion synchronises with the return from join() ([thread.thread.member]), so "dtor 1" always precedes "joined a". The local variable x exists so that construction ("ctor") is printed on its own line; with C++17's left-to-right sequencing of <<, putting tracker() inside the output statement would print "a uses ctor 1".

OutputThe test harness captures stdout through a pipe. What does it see?

#include <cstdio>
#include <sys/wait.h>
#include <unistd.h>

int main() {
    std::printf("start\n");
    pid_t pid = fork();
    if (pid == 0) {
        std::printf("child\n");
        return 0;              // exit() flushes the child's copy of the stdio buffer
    }
    waitpid(pid, nullptr, 0);
    std::printf("parent\n");
}
Answer
start
child
start
parent

Answer. start appears twice. On a terminal you would see start, child, parent.

Why. stdout is line buffered only on a terminal; on a pipe or file it is fully buffered, so "start\n" is still in the user-space buffer when fork() copies the address space. Each process flushes its own copy at exit. The child exits first (the parent waits for it), giving start child, then the parent prints start parent. Fix: fflush(stdout) before fork(), and use _exit in a child that should not flush inherited buffers. The same memory-copy rule is why locks held by other threads stay locked in the child (next drill).

Find the bugRun this and it never prints "child got the lock". Why? (Tagged compile-only because it hangs.)

#include <chrono>
#include <cstdio>
#include <mutex>
#include <sys/wait.h>
#include <thread>
#include <unistd.h>

static std::mutex m;

int main() {
    std::thread holder([] {
        std::lock_guard lk(m);
        std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::seconds(1));
    });
    std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(100));
    pid_t pid = fork();
    if (pid == 0) {
        std::lock_guard lk(m);
        std::puts("child got the lock");
        _exit(0);
    }
    waitpid(pid, nullptr, 0);
    holder.join();
    std::puts("parent done");
}
Answer

Answer. The child deadlocks forever, and so does the parent in waitpid. At the fork, holder owns m. The child gets a copy of the mutex in the locked state but no copy of holder, so nobody will ever unlock it.

Why. fork() duplicates only the calling thread. Locking a mutex in the child of a multithreaded process breaks the POSIX rule that only async-signal-safe functions may be called before exec. Fixes: fork before creating threads, exec immediately, or register pthread_atfork handlers that acquire m in "prepare" and release it in both "parent" and "child". The sleeps only make the timing reliable for the demonstration; they are not a synchronisation tool.

Find the bugSometimes this prints garbage or nothing. Explain the exact moment the bug happens. (Compile-only: the result is undefined.)

#include <chrono>
#include <cstdio>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <thread>

static void log_line(const std::string& s) { std::cout << s << '\n'; }

static void start_job(int id) {
    char buf[32];
    std::snprintf(buf, sizeof buf, "job %d started", id);
    std::thread t(log_line, buf);
    t.detach();
}

int main() {
    start_job(1);
    std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(100));
}
Answer

Answer. std::thread decay-copies the argument, and buf decays to a char*. The conversion from char* to std::string happens later, inside the new thread, when log_line is invoked. By then start_job may have returned and buf is dead. Fix: std::thread t(log_line, std::string(buf)); so the string is built and copied before the constructor returns.

Why. This is the classic example from Anthony Williams' "C++ Concurrency in Action". detach() hides the lifetime problem: if start_job called t.join() before returning, buf would still be alive during the conversion and the code would happen to work. The bug is the combination of a deferred conversion and a buffer that dies first. People often think "the parameter is a std::string, so it was copied": the parameter type does not matter, the stored type is the decayed argument type.

Write the code

Coding

CodeParallel sum. Write std::int64_t parallel_sum(const std::vector<int>& v, unsigned n_threads) that splits the vector into contiguous chunks, sums each in its own thread and combines the results. Requirements: correct for any size including empty and for more threads than elements; no locks or atomics on the hot path; no thread is left joinable if something throws.

Answer

Approach. Clamp the thread count to the range 1 to v.size(). Give thread i a chunk of size / n elements, plus one for the first size % n threads, so chunk sizes differ by at most one. Each thread sums into a local variable and writes its result once into its own slot of a partial vector. Joining the threads makes those writes visible to the caller, which adds them up.

#include <algorithm>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <numeric>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

static std::int64_t parallel_sum(const std::vector<int>& v, unsigned n_threads) {
    if (v.empty()) return 0;
    n_threads = std::clamp<unsigned>(n_threads, 1, static_cast<unsigned>(v.size()));
    std::vector<std::int64_t> partial(n_threads, 0);
    const std::size_t chunk = v.size() / n_threads;
    const std::size_t extra = v.size() % n_threads;
    {
        std::vector<std::jthread> workers;   // jthread joins even if a later emplace_back throws
        workers.reserve(n_threads);
        std::size_t begin = 0;
        for (unsigned i = 0; i < n_threads; ++i) {
            const std::size_t end = begin + chunk + (i < extra ? 1 : 0);
            workers.emplace_back([&v, &partial, i, begin, end] {
                std::int64_t s = 0;          // local accumulator: one write to shared memory
                for (std::size_t k = begin; k < end; ++k) s += v[k];
                partial[i] = s;
            });
            begin = end;
        }
    }   // all workers joined here
    return std::accumulate(partial.begin(), partial.end(), std::int64_t{0});
}

int main() {
    std::vector<int> v(1'000'001);
    std::iota(v.begin(), v.end(), 1);
    for (unsigned n : {1u, 3u, 8u, 64u})
        std::cout << n << " threads: " << parallel_sum(v, n) << '\n';
    std::cout << "tiny: " << parallel_sum({5, 7}, 16) << '\n';
    std::cout << "empty: " << parallel_sum({}, 4) << '\n';
}
1 threads: 500001500001
3 threads: 500001500001
8 threads: 500001500001
64 threads: 500001500001
tiny: 12
empty: 0

Complexity and pitfalls. O(n / threads) time per thread plus O(threads) to combine. Accumulating directly into partial[i] inside the loop would be correct but slow: adjacent slots share a cache line, so every write invalidates the line in the other cores (false sharing, Ch 19). Using std::jthread in a vector means that if the fifth thread fails to start, the first four are joined during unwinding instead of calling terminate. Use a 64-bit accumulator: the sum of a million ints overflows 32 bits.

Estimated rating: ~1200 · straightforward partitioning, with the off-by-one chunking and empty input as the only traps

CodeRAII joining thread. Implement JoiningThread, a move-only wrapper around std::thread that joins in its destructor and on move assignment instead of terminating. It must forward any callable and arguments, expose join, detach and joinable, and survive an exception thrown after the thread starts.

Answer

Approach. Hold a std::thread member and perfect-forward the constructor arguments to it. Delete copying, default the move constructor (it leaves the source empty), and write move assignment to join the current thread before taking the new one, because std::thread's own move assignment terminates if the target is joinable. The destructor joins if joinable.

#include <iostream>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <thread>
#include <utility>

class JoiningThread {
public:
    JoiningThread() noexcept = default;
    template <class F, class... Args>
    explicit JoiningThread(F&& f, Args&&... args)
        : t_(std::forward<F>(f), std::forward<Args>(args)...) {}

    JoiningThread(JoiningThread&&) noexcept = default;
    JoiningThread& operator=(JoiningThread&& other) noexcept {
        if (this != &other) {
            join_if_needed();          // std::thread would call terminate here instead
            t_ = std::move(other.t_);
        }
        return *this;
    }
    JoiningThread(const JoiningThread&) = delete;
    JoiningThread& operator=(const JoiningThread&) = delete;
    ~JoiningThread() { join_if_needed(); }

    bool joinable() const noexcept { return t_.joinable(); }
    void join() { t_.join(); }
    void detach() { t_.detach(); }

private:
    void join_if_needed() noexcept {
        if (t_.joinable()) t_.join();
    }
    std::thread t_;
};

int main() {
    int result = 0;
    try {
        JoiningThread worker([&result] { result = 7 * 6; });
        throw std::runtime_error("boom");   // unwinding joins the worker, no terminate
    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        std::cout << "caught " << e.what() << ", result " << result << '\n';
    }

    int a = 0, b = 0;
    JoiningThread t([&a] { a = 1; });
    t = JoiningThread([&b] { b = 2; });     // joins the first thread, then takes the second
    std::cout << "a after reassignment: " << a << '\n';
    t.join();
    std::cout << "b: " << b << ", joinable: " << t.joinable() << '\n';
}
caught boom, result 42
a after reassignment: 1
b: 2, joinable: 0

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) apart from the join itself. Guard the move assignment against self-assignment, or t = std::move(t) would join and then move from itself. The variadic constructor is explicit so that a lambda does not silently convert to a JoiningThread. A joining destructor can hang if the thread waits for something that the unwinding code was going to provide; that is the gap std::jthread fills with a stop token. In C++20 code, prefer std::jthread; this exercise is how interviewers check that you know why it exists.

Estimated rating: ~1300 · small class, but move assignment and the terminate rule must both be right

CodeFixed-size thread pool. Implement ThreadPool(unsigned n) with template <class F> std::future<R> submit(F f) where R is the callable's return type. Exceptions thrown by a task must reach the caller through the future. The destructor must finish all queued tasks and then join the workers. Submitting after shutdown begins must fail loudly.

Answer

Approach. Workers loop: lock the mutex, wait on a condition variable until there is a job or the pool is stopping, pop one job, unlock, run it. submit wraps the callable in a std::packaged_task, which captures the return value or exception into the shared state behind the future. Because packaged_task is move-only and std::function needs a copyable target, the task is held by a shared_ptr (in C++23, std::move_only_function removes that allocation). The destructor sets stopping_ under the lock, notifies all, and joins; workers only exit when the queue is empty, so queued work is drained.

#include <condition_variable>
#include <functional>
#include <future>
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <mutex>
#include <queue>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <thread>
#include <type_traits>
#include <vector>

class ThreadPool {
public:
    explicit ThreadPool(unsigned n) {
        if (n == 0) n = 1;
        workers_.reserve(n);
        for (unsigned i = 0; i < n; ++i) workers_.emplace_back([this] { run(); });
    }
    ThreadPool(const ThreadPool&) = delete;
    ThreadPool& operator=(const ThreadPool&) = delete;
    ~ThreadPool() {
        {
            std::lock_guard lk(m_);
            stopping_ = true;
        }
        cv_.notify_all();
        for (auto& w : workers_) w.join();   // workers drain the queue first
    }

    template <class F>
    auto submit(F f) -> std::future<std::invoke_result_t<F&>> {
        using R = std::invoke_result_t<F&>;
        // packaged_task is move-only and std::function needs a copyable target: share it
        auto task = std::make_shared<std::packaged_task<R()>>(std::move(f));
        std::future<R> fut = task->get_future();
        {
            std::lock_guard lk(m_);
            if (stopping_) throw std::runtime_error("submit on a stopped pool");
            jobs_.emplace([task] { (*task)(); });
        }
        cv_.notify_one();
        return fut;
    }

private:
    void run() {
        for (;;) {
            std::function<void()> job;
            {
                std::unique_lock lk(m_);
                cv_.wait(lk, [this] { return stopping_ || !jobs_.empty(); });
                if (jobs_.empty()) return;   // stopping and nothing left to do
                job = std::move(jobs_.front());
                jobs_.pop();
            }
            job();   // run outside the lock
        }
    }

    std::mutex m_;
    std::condition_variable cv_;
    std::queue<std::function<void()>> jobs_;
    bool stopping_ = false;
    std::vector<std::thread> workers_;
};

int main() {
    ThreadPool pool(4);
    std::vector<std::future<int>> results;
    for (int i = 1; i <= 10; ++i)
        results.push_back(pool.submit([i] { return i * i; }));
    int total = 0;
    for (auto& f : results) total += f.get();
    std::cout << "sum of squares: " << total << '\n';

    auto bad = pool.submit([]() -> int { throw std::runtime_error("task failed"); });
    try {
        std::cout << bad.get() << '\n';
    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        std::cout << "rethrown: " << e.what() << '\n';
    }

    auto text = pool.submit([] { return std::string("done"); });
    std::cout << text.get() << '\n';
}
sum of squares: 385
rethrown: task failed
done

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) per submit and per pop, plus one lock round trip each. Pitfalls: run the job outside the lock, or the pool serialises; set stopping_ while holding the mutex, or a worker can check the predicate, miss the notification and sleep forever (a lost wake-up, Ch 6); declare workers_ after the mutex, queue and condition variable so they exist before any worker starts. A task that waits on another task's future can deadlock the pool when all workers are waiting. A single shared queue becomes a contention point at high task rates; production pools use per-worker queues with work stealing.

Estimated rating: ~1900 · combines condition variables, type deduction, packaged_task and a correct drain-then-join shutdown

CodePer-thread counters. A hot function record_hit() is called millions of times from many threads. Make it lock-free and atomic-free on the hot path by counting in thread-local storage, and merge each thread's count into a global total when the thread exits. After all workers are joined, the global total must be exact.

Answer

Approach. A thread_local object holds a plain counter. Its destructor runs at thread exit and adds the count into a global total under a mutex, which is taken once per thread instead of once per hit. Because thread-local destructors complete before join() returns, main sees the final totals after joining.

#include <iostream>
#include <mutex>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

struct Totals {
    std::mutex m;
    long hits = 0;
    int threads_merged = 0;
};
static Totals totals;

struct LocalCounter {
    long hits = 0;
    ~LocalCounter() {                 // runs at thread exit, before join() returns
        std::lock_guard lk(totals.m);
        totals.hits += hits;
        ++totals.threads_merged;
    }
};
thread_local LocalCounter local;

static void record_hit() { ++local.hits; }   // hot path: no lock, no atomic

int main() {
    std::vector<std::thread> workers;
    for (int t = 0; t < 4; ++t)
        workers.emplace_back([t] {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100000 * (t + 1); ++i) record_hit();
        });
    for (auto& w : workers) w.join();
    std::lock_guard lk(totals.m);
    std::cout << "hits: " << totals.hits << ", threads merged: " << totals.threads_merged << '\n';
}
hits: 1000000, threads merged: 4

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) per hit with no shared writes; O(threads) lock acquisitions in total. Pitfalls: the global must outlive every thread-local that merges into it, which holds here because workers are joined before main returns (a detached thread exiting during static destruction would touch a destroyed mutex). The main thread's counter would merge only when main exits, after the print. Totals are only complete at join points; for a live total readable at any time, use one cache-line-aligned atomic per thread and sum them on read.

Estimated rating: ~1500 · needs precise knowledge of thread_local lifetime and the join guarantee rather than much code

Codeparallel_for with exceptions. Implement parallel_for(n, threads, f) that calls f(i) for every i in the range 0 to n-1 using up to threads threads. If any call throws, parallel_for must rethrow one of the exceptions in the calling thread after all threads have finished. The program must never terminate because of an exception in a worker.

Answer

Approach. Split the range into contiguous chunks with n * t / threads boundaries, which distributes the remainder evenly without special cases. Each worker wraps its loop in try { ... } catch (...) and stores std::current_exception() into its own slot, so no lock is needed. After the jthreads are joined at the end of the block, rethrow the first stored exception.

#include <algorithm>
#include <exception>
#include <iostream>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <string>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

template <class F>
void parallel_for(std::size_t n, unsigned threads, F f) {
    threads = std::max(1u, threads);
    std::vector<std::exception_ptr> errors(threads);
    {
        std::vector<std::jthread> pool;
        pool.reserve(threads);
        for (unsigned t = 0; t < threads; ++t) {
            const std::size_t begin = n * t / threads, end = n * (t + 1) / threads;
            pool.emplace_back([&f, &errors, t, begin, end] {
                try {
                    for (std::size_t i = begin; i < end; ++i) f(i);
                } catch (...) {
                    errors[t] = std::current_exception();   // an escaping exception would terminate
                }
            });
        }
    }
    for (auto& e : errors)
        if (e) std::rethrow_exception(e);   // report the first chunk that failed
}

int main() {
    std::vector<long> sq(20);
    parallel_for(sq.size(), 4, [&sq](std::size_t i) { sq[i] = static_cast<long>(i * i); });
    std::cout << "sq[19] = " << sq[19] << ", sq[7] = " << sq[7] << '\n';

    try {
        parallel_for(100, 8, [](std::size_t i) {
            if (i == 42) throw std::out_of_range("bad index " + std::to_string(i));
        });
    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        std::cout << "caught: " << e.what() << '\n';
    }
}
sq[19] = 361, sq[7] = 49
caught: bad index 42

Complexity and pitfalls. O(n / threads) per worker. An exception that escapes a thread function calls std::terminate, so the catch-all is mandatory. std::exception_ptr keeps the exception object alive and can be rethrown in another thread. The other chunks keep running after one fails; add a shared std::atomic<bool> "cancelled" flag (or a stop_source) to stop early. Writes by different threads to different elements of sq are not a data race: distinct objects, even in one vector, are distinct memory locations.

Estimated rating: ~1600 · the chunking is easy; exception transport across threads is what interviewers look for

CodeDynamic work distribution. Count the primes below limit with n_threads threads. Cost per number grows with its size, so a static split gives the last thread the most work. Distribute work dynamically in blocks of block numbers, using no mutex.

Answer

Approach. A shared std::atomic<int> cursor hands out blocks: each fetch_add(block) atomically claims the range starting at the returned value. A worker stops when the claimed start is past the limit. Each worker counts locally and adds its count to the total once at the end. Relaxed ordering is enough because the only requirement is that each block is claimed exactly once, and the joins publish the totals.

#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

static bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) return false;
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; ++d)
        if (n % d == 0) return false;
    return true;
}

static int count_primes(int limit, unsigned n_threads, int block) {
    std::atomic<int> next{0};      // shared cursor: each fetch_add claims one block
    std::atomic<int> total{0};
    {
        std::vector<std::jthread> workers;
        for (unsigned t = 0; t < n_threads; ++t)
            workers.emplace_back([&] {
                int mine = 0;
                for (;;) {
                    const int start = next.fetch_add(block, std::memory_order_relaxed);
                    if (start >= limit) break;
                    const int stop = std::min(limit, start + block);
                    for (int n = start; n < stop; ++n) mine += is_prime(n);
                }
                total.fetch_add(mine, std::memory_order_relaxed);
            });
    }   // the joins order every fetch_add before the load below
    return total.load();
}

int main() {
    std::cout << count_primes(200000, 4, 1000) << '\n';
    std::cout << count_primes(200000, 7, 1) << '\n';
    std::cout << count_primes(10, 3, 4) << '\n';
}
17984
17984
4

Complexity and pitfalls. About limit × √limit / threads work, with one atomic operation per block. Block size trades contention (too small: every number is a contended fetch_add on one cache line) against load balance (too large: the last blocks leave cores idle). The cursor can overshoot limit by up to threads × block, which is harmless with int here but needs care near the type's maximum. This pattern is the core of OpenMP's schedule(dynamic).

Estimated rating: ~1400 · one atomic fetch_add and a clean loop, with block size as the design discussion

Cheat sheet

Theory
  • Threads share the address space, fds, handlers and pid; each owns registers, stack, TLS, signal mask and tid. On Linux every thread is a task created by clone(CLONE_VM | CLONE_THREAD | ...); getpid() is the group id, gettid() the task id.
  • Models: N:1 (no parallelism, a block stalls all), 1:1 (Linux NPTL, std::thread), M:N (Go, Java virtual threads).
  • States: New, Ready, Running, Blocked, Terminated. Wake-ups go to Ready, never straight to Running.
  • Thread switch vs process switch: same register work, but no page-table reload and no TLB invalidation, and warmer caches.
  • A joinable std::thread destroyed or move-assigned over calls std::terminate. std::jthread requests stop and joins. Stop is cooperative.
  • Thread arguments are decay-copied and passed as rvalues: use std::ref for references, convert char* buffers to std::string before the call, capture loop variables by value.
  • thread_local: one instance per thread, destroyed at thread exit before join() returns; beware reuse in pools.
  • fork() in a threaded process copies one thread and every lock state: exec straight away. Signals: block in main, sigwait in one thread. Coroutines give concurrency, not parallelism.
