Part C · Locks and mutexes · Chapter 5

Races, locks and mutex internals

Two threads that touch the same memory without coordination give you lost updates at best and undefined behaviour at worst. This chapter builds mutual exclusion from the ground up: why counter++ breaks, the classic software solutions and why they fail on real CPUs, the atomic instructions hardware gives you, and how a real mutex uses a futex to stay in user space when nobody is waiting. Interviewers at systems and low-latency firms ask about this because it separates people who use locks from people who understand them.

TheoryDrillsCoding· about 5 hours· prerequisites: Ch 4 (threads), basic C++

Race conditions and data races

Theory

Two terms get mixed up in interviews, and the difference matters. Keep them apart from the first minute.

Race condition: a logic bug about timing

A race condition is any bug where the result depends on the relative timing of threads. The classic shape is check-then-act: a thread checks a condition, and by the time it acts on the answer, another thread has changed the world. Two ATM withdrawals both see a balance of 100, both decide 80 is affordable, and the account goes to minus 60. A race condition is a property of your program's logic. It can exist even when every single memory access is perfectly atomic.

Data race: undefined behaviour in the C++ memory model

A data race is a precise term from the C++ standard ([intro.races]). Two expressions conflict if they access the same memory location and at least one of them writes. A program has a data race if two conflicting actions happen in different threads, at least one of them is not atomic, and neither happens before the other. A data race is undefined behaviour. The whole program has no meaning, not just the racing variable.

Why so harsh? Because the compiler optimises each thread as if it ran alone. If a variable is not atomic and nothing synchronises, the compiler may keep it in a register, merge two stores into one, hoist a load out of a loop, or invent a temporary store. The hardware also reorders. Making races UB is what allows all of those optimisations in ordinary single-threaded code.

bool stop = false;            // plain bool, shared between threads
void worker() {
    while (!stop) { /* work */ }  // compiler may load stop once: infinite loop
}
// Fix: std::atomic<bool> stop{false};
Race conditionData race
Defined byYour program's intentThe C++ memory model, [intro.races]
ConsequenceWrong answer for some interleavingsUndefined behaviour for the whole program
Possible with only atomics?Yes (check-then-act on an atomic)No, by definition
Found by ThreadSanitizer?No, it is a logic errorYes, when the racy interleaving runs under test
FixMake the check and the act one atomic step (lock or CAS)Atomics or a lock that orders the accesses

Finding data races with ThreadSanitizer

ThreadSanitizer (-fsanitize=thread, in both GCC and Clang) instruments every memory access and tracks happens-before through mutexes, atomics, thread creation and join. It reports two accesses that conflict and are not ordered, even if they did not overlap in time on this run. It cannot find race conditions that involve only atomics, and it only sees code paths your test actually executes. Every correct multithreaded program in this guide is run clean under TSan, and every race drill is proven by a TSan report.

Interview trap

"The race is benign, it only reads a flag" is not an argument in C++. A racy read of a plain bool is UB even if the hardware load is a single instruction. Use std::atomic<bool> (with memory_order_relaxed if you truly need no ordering). It costs nothing extra on x86 or ARM for a plain load or store.

Why counter++ is not atomic

Theory

The mental model: ++counter is three steps, a read, a modify and a write. Any thread can be interrupted or run in parallel between those steps, so two increments can read the same old value and both write back old + 1.

What the CPU executes

Without optimisation, GCC on x86-64 emits a load into a register, an add, and a store. With optimisation it may emit a single add DWORD PTR counter[rip], 1, which looks atomic but is not: inside the core it is still a load micro-op, an add and a store, and another core can grab the cache line in between. Only the lock prefix (lock add, lock xadd) makes the read-modify-write indivisible across cores. On ARM the plain version is ldr, add, str; the atomic one is an ldxr/stxr retry loop or an ARMv8.1 ldadd.

; ++counter on x86-64, no lock prefix     ; counter.fetch_add(1)
mov  eax, DWORD PTR counter[rip]          lock xadd DWORD PTR counter[rip], eax
add  eax, 1
mov  DWORD PTR counter[rip], eax

Three correct fixes

  • An atomic read-modify-write: std::atomic<int> and fetch_add (or ++ on the atomic, which is the same operation). Best for one independent counter.
  • A mutex around the increment. Needed when the counter must change together with other data (an invariant spanning several variables).
  • No sharing: give each thread its own counter and sum at the end. Fastest, and the only option that scales with core count (see the sharded counter drill and Ch 19 on false sharing).
#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>

static std::atomic<int> counter{0};

static void work() {
    for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) counter.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
}

int main() {
    std::thread a(work), b(work);
    a.join();
    b.join();
    std::cout << counter.load() << '\n';
}
200000

memory_order_relaxed is enough here: the increments are still indivisible, and join() gives the main thread a happens-before edge, so the final load sees every increment. Relaxed only drops ordering with respect to other variables.

Interview trap

hits = hits + 1 on a std::atomic<int> is an atomic load followed by an atomic store. Each half is atomic, the pair is not, so updates are lost exactly as in the figure. There is no data race, so TSan stays silent. Only ++hits, hits += 1 or fetch_add are single RMW operations.

The critical section problem

Theory

A critical section is the code that touches shared state. The classic OS formulation (Dijkstra 1965, the version in every textbook) asks for an entry protocol and an exit protocol around it, making no assumptions about the relative speed of threads or the number of CPUs.

The three requirements

RequirementMeaningBroken by
Mutual exclusionAt most one thread is inside the critical section at any time."Wait while locked, then set locked" with two separate steps
ProgressIf nobody is inside and some threads want in, one of them gets in in finite time. Threads that are not trying cannot block the decision.Strict alternation; "set my flag, wait for yours" (both wait forever)
Bounded waitingAfter a thread asks to enter, there is a limit on how many times others can enter before it does. No starvation.A plain test-and-set spinlock (an unlucky thread can lose every race)

Deadlock freedom is part of progress; starvation freedom is bounded waiting. Real locks add practical goals the textbook omits: low uncontended cost, no wasted CPU while waiting, and fairness that does not destroy throughput.

Failed software attempts (two threads)

// Attempt 1: strict alternation. Mutual exclusion holds, progress does not:
// if thread 0 never wants in again, thread 1 waits forever after one turn.
int turn = 0;
void lock(int me)   { while (turn != me) {} }
void unlock(int me) { turn = 1 - me; }

// Attempt 2: intent flags. Mutual exclusion holds, but if both set
// their flag at the same moment, both spin forever (deadlock).
bool want[2];
void lock(int me)   { want[me] = true; while (want[1 - me]) {} }
void unlock(int me) { want[me] = false; }

(These are pseudo-code in the textbook sense: written with plain variables they also contain data races. Peterson combines both ideas, as the next section shows.)

Disabling interrupts

On a single CPU, a thread loses the processor only through an interrupt (timer, device) or by blocking. So the kernel can make a sequence atomic by disabling interrupts (cli/sti on x86) around it. This fails as a general solution:

  • It is privileged. User code cannot execute cli; a user process that could would own the machine.
  • It does nothing on a multiprocessor. Disabling interrupts on CPU 0 does not stop CPU 1 from running the same code at the same time.
  • It hurts latency. While interrupts are off, timer ticks and device events wait. A long or buggy critical section freezes the system.

Linux still uses it, combined with spinlocks: spin_lock_irqsave() takes a spinlock (excludes other CPUs) and disables local interrupts (so an interrupt handler on this CPU that takes the same lock cannot deadlock against the code it interrupted).

Peterson's algorithm and why it breaks on modern CPUs

Theory

Peterson's algorithm (1981) solves the two-thread critical section problem with only loads and stores. It is a favourite interview question because it is short, provably correct on paper, and wrong on every modern CPU unless you add fences.

The algorithm

// Textbook form (shared: bool flag[2]; int turn;)
void lock(int me) {
    int other = 1 - me;
    flag[me] = true;    // I want to enter
    turn = other;       // but you go first if you also want to
    while (flag[other] && turn == other) { }  // wait
}
void unlock(int me) { flag[me] = false; }

Why it works (sequentially consistent memory). If both threads are in the loop, turn holds one value, so exactly one of them sees turn == other false and enters: mutual exclusion and progress. When the thread inside leaves and tries again, it sets turn to the other thread, so the waiting thread enters next: bounded waiting with a bound of one.

Where it breaks

The proof assumes each thread's write to flag[me] is visible to the other thread before its own read of flag[other]. Two layers violate that:

  1. The compiler. With plain variables, the loop condition reads data nobody in this thread writes, so the compiler may load it once and spin forever, or reorder the stores. And it is a data race, so the program is UB anyway. volatile stops the compiler from caching the loads, but does nothing about the CPU and does not remove the data race.
  2. The CPU's store buffer. Even x86, the most strongly ordered mainstream architecture (x86-TSO), lets a later load complete before an earlier store to a different address becomes globally visible. The store sits in the core's store buffer while the load reads memory. Both threads write their flag into their own buffer, both read the other flag from memory as false, and both enter.

The fix in C++

Make the shared variables std::atomic and use the default memory_order_seq_cst. Sequential consistency guarantees a single total order over all seq_cst operations that agrees with each thread's program order, which is exactly the assumption in the proof. On x86 the compiler emits xchg (or mov + mfence) for the seq_cst stores; on ARMv8 it emits stlr and ldar, which are defined not to reorder with each other.

#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>

class PetersonLock {
    std::atomic<bool> flag_[2] = {false, false};
    std::atomic<int> turn_{0};
public:
    void lock(int me) {
        int other = 1 - me;
        flag_[me].store(true);   // seq_cst by default
        turn_.store(other);
        while (flag_[other].load() && turn_.load() == other) { }
    }
    void unlock(int me) { flag_[me].store(false); }
};

static PetersonLock lk;
static int counter = 0;  // guarded by lk

static void work(int me) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 50000; ++i) {
        lk.lock(me);
        ++counter;
        lk.unlock(me);
    }
}

int main() {
    std::thread a(work, 0), b(work, 1);
    a.join();
    b.join();
    std::cout << counter << '\n';
}
100000

Know this cold

Peterson needs store→load ordering, the one reordering x86 permits. Acquire loads and release stores are not enough, because release/acquire never orders an earlier store before a later load. That is the textbook example of why seq_cst exists. In practice nobody uses Peterson: it needs one slot per thread, generalises poorly (Lamport's bakery handles N threads), and a hardware RMW does the job in one instruction.

Hardware primitives: TAS, CAS and fetch-add

Theory

Mutual exclusion with only loads and stores is possible (Peterson, bakery) but slow and fragile. Every real lock instead uses an atomic read-modify-write (RMW) instruction: the CPU reads a location, computes, and writes back with a guarantee that no other core can write the location in between. Under the hood the core takes the cache line in the exclusive (Modified) state of the coherence protocol (MESI and its variants) and holds it for the duration of the operation.

Key facts: the primitives

PrimitiveSemantics (all one indivisible step)x86-64ARMv8C++Consensus number
Test-and-set (TAS)set to 1, return the old valuexchg, lock btsswpal (v8.1 LSE) or an LL/SC loopatomic_flag::test_and_set2
Exchange (swap)old = *p; *p = v; return oldxchg (implicitly locked)swpal or LL/SCexchange2
Fetch-and-addold = *p; *p = old + v; return oldlock xaddldaddal or LL/SCfetch_add, ++, +=2
Compare-and-swap (CAS)if *p == expected then *p = desired; report success and the value seenlock cmpxchg (16-byte: cmpxchg16b)casal or LL/SCcompare_exchange_strong/weak∞
Load-linked / store-conditionalload and watch the line; the store fails if anyone wrote it sincenoneldaxr / stlxrnot exposed; it is why _weak exists∞

The consensus number (Herlihy, 1991) is the largest number of threads for which the primitive can solve wait-free consensus. Plain loads and stores have consensus number 1, TAS, swap and fetch-add have 2, and CAS and LL/SC are universal: any concurrent object can be built lock-free from them. That is why CAS is the workhorse of lock-free programming.

The CAS loop

CAS lets you build any atomic update out of "read, compute, publish if nobody interfered". The pattern:

// Atomically value = max(value, x)
void fetch_max(std::atomic<int>& value, int x) {
    int cur = value.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
    while (cur < x && !value.compare_exchange_weak(cur, x, std::memory_order_relaxed)) {
        // on failure, cur now holds the value another thread wrote: recompute and retry
    }
}

Three facts make this loop correct. On failure compare_exchange writes the current value into expected (here cur), so you never reload by hand. The _weak form may fail spuriously even when the values are equal, because on LL/SC machines the reservation can be lost to an interrupt or a write to a nearby address in the same line; inside a loop that costs nothing and avoids a nested retry loop. The _strong form never fails spuriously; use it when a failure would make you do expensive work or when there is no loop.

The ABA problem

CAS compares values, not histories. Thread 1 reads head pointer A, gets preempted; thread 2 pops A, pops B, frees both, and pushes a new node that the allocator happens to place at address A. Thread 1 wakes, its CAS sees A and succeeds, installing a stale next pointer. Fixes: a version counter packed next to the pointer (double-width CAS), hazard pointers, epoch-based reclamation, or a design that never reuses memory while readers may hold it (the push-and-drain stack in the coding drills avoids ABA by taking the whole list with one exchange).

Spinlocks

Theory

A spinlock is the simplest lock built on an RMW: try to flip a flag from free to taken, and if it was already taken, loop. Waiting threads stay on the CPU, which is ideal when the holder will release within a few hundred nanoseconds and terrible when it will not.

A spinlock with std::atomic_flag

std::atomic_flag is the only type the standard has always guaranteed to be lock-free (C++20 adds the aliases std::atomic_signed_lock_free and std::atomic_unsigned_lock_free, which are too). Since C++20 it is default-initialised to clear (before C++20 you needed ATOMIC_FLAG_INIT) and it gained test(), a plain read, plus wait/notify. Providing lock() and unlock() makes the class BasicLockable, so std::lock_guard works with it.

#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>
#include <mutex>
#include <thread>

class Spinlock {
    std::atomic_flag f_;  // clear since C++20
public:
    void lock() {
        while (f_.test_and_set(std::memory_order_acquire)) {
            while (f_.test(std::memory_order_relaxed)) { }  // spin on a read
        }
    }
    void unlock() { f_.clear(std::memory_order_release); }
};

static Spinlock sl;
static int counter = 0;  // guarded by sl

int main() {
    auto work = [] {
        for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) {
            std::lock_guard<Spinlock> g(sl);
            ++counter;
        }
    };
    std::thread a(work), b(work);
    a.join();
    b.join();
    std::cout << counter << '\n';
}
200000

Acquire on lock, release on unlock. The successful test_and_set is an acquire operation and clear is a release, so everything written inside the previous critical section is visible inside the next one. The inner loop is the test-and-test-and-set (TTAS) idea, explained next.

Why spinning on a read is faster

Every test_and_set is a write, even when it fails. With four cores spinning on TAS, the cache line holding the flag bounces between their caches in the Modified state on every attempt, flooding the interconnect and slowing down the holder, which needs that same line to release. Spinning on a plain load keeps a Shared copy in each waiter's cache, so waiting generates no traffic. When the holder releases, the line is invalidated, all waiters see "free" and race with one RMW each. Two refinements:

  • A pause hint in the spin loop (_mm_pause / pause on x86, yield or isb on ARM) saves power, gives the sibling hyperthread the core, and avoids a memory-order pipeline flush when the loop exits.
  • Exponential backoff: wait longer after each failed attempt, so fewer threads stampede when the lock frees up. Eventually call std::this_thread::yield() or fall back to sleeping.

Fairness: ticket locks and queue locks

A TAS spinlock has no bounded waiting: whichever core sees the release first wins, and a core that is far away on the interconnect may lose for a long time. A ticket lock fixes that with two counters: fetch_add on next takes a ticket, and you wait until serving equals it. It is FIFO, but every waiter still spins on the same line. MCS and similar queue locks give each waiter its own node to spin on, so a handoff touches only one other cache. The Linux kernel used ticket spinlocks from 2.6.25 and moved to MCS-based queued spinlocks (qspinlock) in 4.2.

Spinlock vs mutex

SpinlockMutex (futex-based)
Uncontended lock + unlockone RMW + one release storeone RMW + one RMW (unlock must read the state to learn whether anyone sleeps), all in user space
While waitingburns a CPUsleeps in the kernel, CPU free for other work
Handoff latencya cache-line transfer, tens of nsa wake-up syscall plus scheduling, usually microseconds
Holder preempted or blockedwaiters spin for a whole time slicewaiters sleep, no waste
Single corepathological: the waiter spins until its slice ends, because the holder cannot runfine
Typical usekernel code with preemption off, interrupt handlers, latency-critical user code on pinned, isolated coresdefault for user space

Tip

Spin only if the critical section is shorter than the cost of sleeping and waking (a few microseconds) and the holder cannot be preempted. In ordinary user space you cannot promise the second part, which is why std::mutex is the default and why good mutexes are already fast when uncontended. Linus Torvalds' well-known advice is that user-space spinlocks are almost always a mistake unless you control the scheduling.

How a mutex is implemented

Theory

The mental model: a mutex is a spinlock that knows how to sleep. The uncontended case must cost one atomic instruction and no system call, and only threads that actually have to wait should enter the kernel. On Linux the bridge between the two worlds is the futex.

std::mutex in one minute

std::mutex has lock(), try_lock() and unlock(). It is neither copyable nor movable, and its default constructor is constexpr, so a namespace-scope std::mutex is constant-initialised and immune to the static initialisation order problem. libstdc++ and libc++ wrap pthread_mutex_t on POSIX systems. The rules that interviewers probe:

  • Locking a std::mutex the calling thread already owns is undefined behaviour (in practice a self-deadlock). Use std::recursive_mutex if you truly need that, see Ch 6.
  • Unlocking a mutex you do not own, or destroying a mutex that is still locked, is undefined behaviour.
  • try_lock() may fail spuriously even if no thread holds the mutex ([thread.mutex.requirements.mutex]). Never use it to test whether a mutex is free.
  • Call lock() and unlock() directly only in lock implementations. Everywhere else use an RAII wrapper (std::lock_guard, std::scoped_lock, std::unique_lock), covered in Ch 6, so an exception cannot leave the mutex locked.
#include <iostream>
#include <mutex>
#include <thread>

static std::mutex m;
static long counter = 0;  // guarded by m

static void work() {
    for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(m);
        ++counter;
    }
}

int main() {
    std::thread a(work), b(work);
    a.join();
    b.join();
    std::cout << counter << '\n';
}
200000

What a futex is

A futex ("fast user-space mutex", Linux 2.6) is not a lock. It is a 32-bit integer in ordinary user memory plus two system calls that let the kernel park and wake threads keyed by that integer's address:

  • futex(&word, FUTEX_WAIT, val): atomically check that word == val and, if so, put the caller to sleep on a kernel wait queue for that address. If the value differs, return EAGAIN at once.
  • futex(&word, FUTEX_WAKE, n): wake up to n threads sleeping on that address.

The atomic check inside FUTEX_WAIT is the whole trick. Between "I saw the lock taken" in user space and "I am asleep" in the kernel, the holder might unlock and call wake. If the kernel simply slept, that wake-up would be lost and the waiter would sleep forever. Because the kernel re-checks the value under its wait-queue lock, a waiter whose value is stale returns immediately and retries. The kernel keeps no state for a futex nobody waits on, so an uncontended mutex costs the kernel nothing.

The three-state mutex

The standard design, from Ulrich Drepper's paper "Futexes Are Tricky", uses three values: 0 unlocked, 1 locked with no waiters, 2 locked and possibly with waiters. The third state lets unlock() skip the system call when nobody is sleeping.

A woken waiter sets the state to 2 (not 1) when it takes the lock, because it cannot know whether other waiters are still asleep. That costs at most one unnecessary wake call later, which is the price of never losing one. In Linux code, the slow path looks like this (a fragment for Linux only; the portable version is a coding drill below, using C++20 std::atomic::wait, which libstdc++ implements with futexes on Linux):

#include <atomic>
#include <linux/futex.h>
#include <sys/syscall.h>
#include <unistd.h>

// Relies on std::atomic<int> having the size and layout of int, true on Linux.
static void futex_wait(std::atomic<int>* w, int val) {
    syscall(SYS_futex, reinterpret_cast<int*>(w), FUTEX_WAIT_PRIVATE, val, nullptr, nullptr, 0);
}
static void futex_wake_one(std::atomic<int>* w) {
    syscall(SYS_futex, reinterpret_cast<int*>(w), FUTEX_WAKE_PRIVATE, 1, nullptr, nullptr, 0);
}

void lock(std::atomic<int>& state) {
    int c = 0;
    if (state.compare_exchange_strong(c, 1, std::memory_order_acquire)) return;
    if (c != 2) c = state.exchange(2, std::memory_order_acquire);
    while (c != 0) {
        futex_wait(&state, 2);
        c = state.exchange(2, std::memory_order_acquire);
    }
}
void unlock(std::atomic<int>& state) {
    if (state.exchange(0, std::memory_order_release) == 2) futex_wake_one(&state);
}

What production mutexes add

  • Adaptive spinning. Spin briefly before sleeping, betting that the holder is running on another core and will release soon. glibc offers it as PTHREAD_MUTEX_ADAPTIVE_NP; its default mutex type goes straight to the futex.
  • Lock types. Error-checking and recursive pthread mutexes store the owner thread id in the mutex.
  • Priority inheritance (PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT, FUTEX_LOCK_PI): the kernel boosts the owner's priority while a higher-priority thread waits. See priority inversion in Ch 6.
  • Other systems: Windows has WaitOnAddress and SRW locks, macOS has os_unfair_lock and the private ulock wait calls. The idea is the same everywhere: an atomic word in user space, a kernel queue only for waiters.

What a lock guarantees about memory

Theory

A lock does two jobs. Mutual exclusion is the obvious one. The second is visibility: data written by one critical section must be seen by the next, even though compilers and CPUs reorder memory operations freely.

Acquire and release, intuitively

  • Release (unlocking): every read and write before it in program order is completed before the release becomes visible. Think "publish everything I did".
  • Acquire (locking): every read and write after it in program order happens after it. Think "subscribe to what was published".
  • An unlock of mutex m synchronises with the next lock of m, so it creates a happens-before edge: the writer's critical section happens before the reader's. That edge is exactly what turns two conflicting accesses into a non-race.

The roach motel rule follows: operations may move into a critical section (a load after unlock may be performed before it), but never out of it. Compilers and CPUs exploit that freedom, which is why locks are cheap.

// Publishing with an atomic flag needs the same pairing
int payload;                          // plain data
std::atomic<bool> ready{false};
// producer                           // consumer
payload = 42;                         // while (!ready.load(std::memory_order_acquire)) {}
ready.store(true, std::memory_order_release);   // use(payload);  sees 42

With memory_order_relaxed on both sides there is no happens-before edge and reading payload is a data race (see the reading drills). Locks, seq_cst atomics and acquire/release pairs all create the edge; relaxed atomics do not.

Atomics or a lock?

Use an atomic whenUse a lock when
The shared state is one word: a counter, a flag, a pointerAn invariant spans several variables (size and buffer, balance and history)
The update is a single RMW or a short CAS loopThe update needs a check and an act that must not be split
You need progress even if a thread is descheduled (lock-free)Simplicity and reviewability matter more than the last 20 ns
Readers are frequent and must never blockWaiters should sleep rather than spin

"Lock-free" is not "fast". A contended atomic counter still bounces one cache line between cores and may be slower than per-thread counters merged at the end. std::atomic<T> for large T is not lock-free at all: the library hides a lock (check is_always_lock_free, and note that GCC may need -latomic).

Key facts: rough costs on a modern x86 server

OperationOrder of magnitude
Uncontended atomic RMW on a line in your own cacheabout 5 to 20 ns (tens of cycles)
Uncontended std::mutex lock + unlockabout 15 to 30 ns (two atomics, no syscall)
Moving a contended cache line to another coreabout 50 to 150 ns, more across sockets
Futex wait and wake round trip, thread context switchabout 1 to 10 µs

These are order-of-magnitude figures; measure on your hardware. The shape is what matters in interviews: uncontended locking is cheap, contention is expensive, and sleeping is the most expensive of all.

False sharing in one paragraph

Coherence works on whole cache lines (64 bytes on x86 and most ARM servers, 128 bytes on Apple M-series). Two threads updating different variables that share a line still bounce the line, so per-thread counters packed into one array can be as slow as one shared atomic. Pad or align hot per-thread data to the line size (alignas(64) or std::hardware_destructive_interference_size). The full treatment, with measurements, is in Ch 19.

Concept and tricky questions

Drills

ConceptWhat exactly is a data race in C++, and what is the consequence?

Answer

Answer. Two conflicting accesses to the same memory location (at least one a write), in different threads, at least one not atomic, with neither happening before the other. The consequence is undefined behaviour for the entire program.

Why. The rule is [intro.races]. Making races UB lets the compiler optimise every non-atomic access as if the thread were alone: keep values in registers, merge or split stores, hoist loads out of loops. The common wrong answer is "you might read a stale or torn value". That describes one possible outcome, but the standard promises nothing at all, and real compilers produce infinite loops and impossible values from racy code. The fix is to order the accesses with a lock, an atomic, or thread start and join.

ConceptGive an example of a race condition that has no data race, and explain why ThreadSanitizer will not report it.

Answer

Answer. Check-then-act on a "thread-safe" container whose every member function locks an internal mutex: if (!q.empty()) { int v = q.front(); q.pop(); }. Two consumers can both see one item, both read the same front, and the second pop() runs on an empty queue.

Why. Every access to the queue's data happens under its mutex, so there is no data race and TSan, which looks for unordered conflicting accesses where at least one is non-atomic, has nothing to report. The bug is in the interface: the check and the act are separate critical sections, and another thread can run between them. Fix it by making the combined operation one call that holds the lock throughout (std::optional<int> try_pop()), so a concurrent queue must not copy the split front()/pop() interface that std::queue uses for exception safety. The same pattern on a single atomic (load the balance, then fetch_sub) appears as a find-the-bug drill below. Interviewers use this to test whether you think "every call is locked" means "correct".

TrickyA colleague says a plain bool stop flag is fine on x86 because aligned byte loads and stores are atomic in hardware. Is it?

Answer

Answer. No. It is a data race, so it is UB, and in practice the compiler may read the flag once and turn while (!stop) into an infinite loop.

Why. Hardware atomicity is irrelevant: the C++ abstract machine decides what the compiler may do, and a non-atomic variable that this thread never writes inside the loop is assumed not to change. GCC and Clang at -O2 really do hoist such loads. std::atomic<bool> costs the same plain mov on x86 for a relaxed or acquire load, so there is no performance argument for the plain bool.

TrickyDoes declaring a shared counter volatile int make counter++ safe across threads?

Answer

Answer. No. volatile gives neither atomicity nor inter-thread ordering, and the accesses still form a data race.

Why. volatile only tells the compiler that each access is an observable side effect it must perform (for memory-mapped I/O and, with sig_atomic_t, signal handlers). counter++ is still a separate load, add and store, the CPU may still reorder around it, and the standard does not exempt volatile from [intro.races]. C++20 even deprecates ++ and compound assignment on volatile variables because people kept misreading them as atomic. Java's volatile is a different thing (closer to a seq_cst atomic), which is where much of the confusion comes from.

TrickyWith optimisation, GCC compiles ++counter to the single instruction add DWORD PTR counter[rip], 1. Is that atomic on a multicore x86? On a single-core machine?

Answer

Answer. On multicore: no, it needs the lock prefix. On a single core the single instruction happens to be atomic with respect to interrupts, but the C++ program is still a data race and the compiler is free to emit three instructions instead.

Why. A memory-destination add is decoded into load, add and store micro-ops. Without lock, another core can take the cache line between the load and the store. Interrupts are only taken at instruction boundaries, so on one core no other thread can run in the middle, which is why old uniprocessor kernels got away with it. Relying on the instruction choice is relying on codegen, which is not a contract. fetch_add guarantees lock xadd or lock add.

ConceptState the three requirements for a solution to the critical section problem, and say which one strict alternation (while (turn != me) {}, then turn = other on exit) violates.

Answer

Answer. Mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting. Strict alternation violates progress.

Why. Mutual exclusion holds because only the thread whose turn it is can enter. But if thread 0 finishes and never wants the lock again, thread 1 can enter once and then waits forever for a turn that thread 0 will never hand over, even though the critical section is empty. Progress says a thread outside the critical section and not trying to enter must not block the others. People often answer "bounded waiting", but strict alternation actually has perfect bounded waiting (a bound of one); the failure is progress.

TrickyWhy can't a user-space program implement a lock by disabling interrupts, and why would it not work on a multiprocessor even in the kernel?

Answer

Answer. Disabling interrupts is a privileged instruction (cli faults in ring 3), and it only affects the current CPU, so other CPUs keep running and can enter the same critical section.

Why. On a uniprocessor, preemption arrives only through interrupts, so masking them makes a code sequence atomic. On SMP, two CPUs execute in parallel and interrupts are irrelevant to that. Kernels therefore combine both: a spinlock excludes other CPUs and local_irq_save stops an interrupt handler on this CPU from trying to take the same spinlock and deadlocking against the code it interrupted (spin_lock_irqsave). Long sections with interrupts off also hurt latency because timer and device interrupts are delayed.

Trickyx86 is "strongly ordered". Does Peterson's algorithm with plain variables (or with release stores and acquire loads) work on x86?

Answer

Answer. No. x86-TSO allows a later load to complete before an earlier store to a different address is visible, and Peterson needs exactly that store-then-load order. Release/acquire does not forbid that reordering either. You need seq_cst operations or a full fence (mfence) between the stores and the loop's loads.

Why. Each core puts flag[me] = true in its store buffer, then reads flag[other] from cache, where the other core's store has not arrived yet. Both read false and both enter (see the store buffer figure). x86 forbids load-load, store-store and load-store reordering, which is why people believe it is "sequentially consistent", but store-load is the one it permits. Release only orders earlier operations before the release store; acquire only orders later operations after the acquire load; neither orders a store before a later load.

ConceptCompare test-and-set, fetch-and-add and compare-and-swap. Which would you pick to build a fair (FIFO) spinlock, and which to build a lock-free stack?

Answer

Answer. TAS sets a flag and returns the old value; fetch-and-add adds and returns the old value; CAS writes only if the current value equals the expected one. A FIFO ticket lock uses fetch-and-add to hand out tickets; a lock-free stack needs CAS to swing the head pointer.

Why. Fetch-and-add always succeeds, so each arriving thread gets a unique ticket in arrival order, which gives fairness for free. A stack push must say "set head to my node only if head is still what I linked to", which is a conditional update: only CAS (or LL/SC) expresses it. Herlihy's consensus hierarchy makes it formal: TAS, swap and fetch-add have consensus number 2, CAS is universal. TAS is the cheapest option for a simple unfair spinlock.

TrickyWhy does compare_exchange_weak exist, if it can fail even when the value matches? When should you use _strong?

Answer

Answer. On LL/SC architectures (classic ARM, POWER, RISC-V) one LL/SC pair can fail spuriously, for example after an interrupt or a write elsewhere in the same cache line. _weak maps to a single attempt; _strong must hide spurious failures with an internal retry loop. Use _weak inside your own retry loop and _strong for one-shot attempts.

Why. If you are already looping, a nested loop inside _strong is wasted code. If there is no loop (for example "try to claim this slot once"), a spurious failure would be a logic error, so you need _strong. On x86 both compile to lock cmpxchg, which never fails spuriously, so the difference only shows up on other targets. In both forms, a failure stores the observed value into expected.

ConceptWhen is a spinlock better than a mutex, and why is a spinlock a bad idea on a single-core machine?

Answer

Answer. Spin when the critical section is shorter than a sleep and wake-up (a few microseconds) and the holder is guaranteed to be running, for example in the kernel with preemption disabled or on pinned, isolated cores in a low-latency system. On one core the holder cannot run while the waiter spins, so the waiter wastes its whole time slice every time.

Why. A mutex costs about the same as a spinlock when uncontended (one atomic operation each way, all in user space). Under contention the mutex puts waiters to sleep, which costs a system call and a context switch but frees the CPU. A spinlock hands over in tens of nanoseconds when the holder runs on another core, but if the holder is preempted the waiters burn CPU until the scheduler brings it back. Uniprocessor kernels compile spinlocks down to "disable preemption" for this reason.

TrickyDoes std::mutex::lock() make a system call every time?

Answer

Answer. No. On Linux an uncontended lock is a single CAS in user space and an uncontended unlock is a single atomic exchange or decrement. Only a thread that must wait calls futex(FUTEX_WAIT), and unlock calls futex(FUTEX_WAKE) only if the state word says there may be waiters.

Why. That is the whole point of the futex design (Linux 2.6): the kernel keeps no state for an uncontended lock. The wrong answer "a mutex is slow because it enters the kernel" is twenty years out of date. A mutex becomes slow when it is contended, and then the cost is the cache-line transfers plus sleeping and waking, not the uncontended path.

TrickyIs std::atomic<T> always lock-free? What about std::atomic<Big> where Big is a 24-byte struct?

Answer

Answer. No. Only std::atomic_flag (and, since C++20, the std::atomic_signed_lock_free and std::atomic_unsigned_lock_free aliases) is guaranteed lock-free. std::atomic<Big> compiles for any trivially copyable type, but for sizes the hardware cannot handle in one instruction the library protects it with an internal lock (a hashed table of locks), so is_lock_free() is false.

Why. std::atomic<T>::is_always_lock_free (C++17) tells you at compile time. On x86-64, sizes 1, 2, 4 and 8 are lock-free; 16 bytes depends on cmpxchg16b and the library. With GCC, non-lock-free atomics call into libatomic, so you may need -latomic to link. A lock-based atomic is not safe in a signal handler and can be much slower, which surprises people who chose atomics "to avoid locks".

TrickyMay m.try_lock() return false when no thread holds m? Thread A sets x = 1 and locks m; thread B sees m.try_lock() fail and concludes that it may now read x. Is that safe?

Answer

Answer. Yes, try_lock() may fail spuriously ([thread.mutex.requirements.mutex]), and no, B's reasoning is broken: a failed try_lock tells you nothing and creates no happens-before edge, so reading x is a data race.

Why. If a failed try_lock were a reliable sign that someone holds the lock, programs could use it as a signal, and then lock() would have to order the earlier write of x before itself, which costs a full fence on every acquisition. Hans Boehm's analysis of this for the C++11 memory model is why the standard allows spurious failure: it keeps lock() a plain acquire. Only a successful lock synchronises with the previous unlock. The practical rule is to use try_lock only to attempt, never to ask "is it free?" or "is it taken?". The common wrong answer is "spurious failure only exists for LL/SC hardware"; a mutex's try_lock can be built with a strong CAS and the standard still permits it to fail. (Relocking a std::mutex you already own is covered in Ch 6.)

TrickyWhat do "lock-free" and "wait-free" mean? Is a CAS retry loop wait-free, and is a lock-free counter always faster than a mutex-protected one?

Answer

Answer. Lock-free: some thread always completes its operation in a finite number of steps, even if other threads are suspended at any point. Wait-free: every thread completes in a bounded number of its own steps. A CAS loop is lock-free but not wait-free, because one unlucky thread can keep losing the CAS while others succeed. And no, lock-free is not automatically faster.

Why. A thread that fails a CAS failed because another thread's CAS succeeded, so the system as a whole progresses, but nothing bounds how often a given thread loses (starvation is possible). A hardware fetch_add (lock xadd, ldadd) completes in one instruction for every caller, so a counter built on it is wait-free. Below lock-free sits obstruction-free (a thread finishes if it runs alone), and anything using a mutex is blocking: a holder descheduled inside the critical section stops everyone. The speed question is separate: under contention a lock-free counter still bounces one cache line between cores, and a mutex with short critical sections can match it; per-thread counters beat both. People say "lock-free means no locks so it is faster"; the real benefit is progress when threads are preempted, killed or running in a signal handler, not raw speed.

ConceptBesides mutual exclusion, what guarantee does a mutex give about memory? Can the compiler move a load from after unlock() to before it?

Answer

Answer. Visibility and ordering: unlock() is a release and lock() is an acquire, so an unlock synchronises with the next lock of the same mutex and everything done in the earlier critical section happens before the later one. Yes, the compiler or CPU may move a later load into the critical section, but nothing may move out of it.

Why. This is the "roach motel" rule: accesses can check in but not check out. Moving work into a critical section never breaks correctness, only increases the hold time slightly, so the memory model allows it; moving work out would expose it to other threads unprotected. Without the release/acquire pairing, a reader could take the lock and still see stale data, which is the bug in the "relaxed publish" reading drill.

TrickyWhat is the ABA problem, and why does a CAS-based lock-free stack pop suffer from it while push does not?

Answer

Answer. CAS succeeds if the value equals what you read earlier, even if it changed to something else and back in between. In pop you read head = A and next = A->next; if A is popped, freed and reallocated as a new node pushed back on top, your CAS from A to the stale next succeeds and corrupts the stack.

Why. pop dereferences a node that another thread may free, and its CAS decision depends on that dereferenced value. push only links a node it owns to the current head and swings head; if head changed, the CAS fails and the loop retries with the fresh head, so A to B to A is harmless. Fixes for pop: tagged pointers with a version counter (double-width CAS), hazard pointers, epoch-based reclamation, or garbage collection. A garbage collector removes the "freed and reused" step entirely, which is why ABA is mainly a C and C++ problem.

ConceptWhy does a test-and-test-and-set spinlock scale better than a plain test-and-set spinlock?

Answer

Answer. Plain TAS writes the lock's cache line on every attempt, so the line ping-pongs between waiting cores in the Modified state. TTAS spins on an ordinary load, which each core can serve from its own Shared copy, and only attempts the RMW after it sees the lock free.

Why. Under MESI, a write needs exclusive ownership, which invalidates every other copy. With N waiters doing TAS, every attempt is an invalidation broadcast, and the holder's own release has to fight for the line. With TTAS, the line stays shared while the lock is held and there is one burst of traffic per release. Backoff and a pause instruction reduce that burst further; queue locks (MCS) remove it by giving each waiter its own line.

Predict the output and find the bug

Drills

OutputWhat does this print? Watch which operations return the old value and which return the new one.

#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::atomic<int> a{5};
    int r1 = a.fetch_add(3);
    int r2 = ++a;
    int r3 = a++;
    int r4 = a.exchange(100);
    std::cout << r1 << ' ' << r2 << ' ' << r3 << ' ' << r4 << ' ' << a.load() << '\n';
}
Answer
5 9 9 10 100

Answer. 5 9 9 10 100.

Why. fetch_add(3) returns the old value 5 and leaves 8. Pre-increment on an atomic returns the new value, 9. Post-increment returns the old value 9 and leaves 10. exchange(100) returns the previous value 10. All of these are single RMW operations, and they return a value rather than a reference: ++a on a std::atomic yields T, not atomic&, because a reference would invite a second, racy read. People who expect fetch_add to return the new value (like __sync_add_and_fetch) answer 8 first.

Find the bugTwo threads each add 100000. What can this print, and what is wrong?

#include <iostream>
#include <thread>

static int counter = 0;

static void work() {
    for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) ++counter;
}

int main() {
    std::thread a(work), b(work);
    a.join();
    b.join();
    std::cout << counter << '\n';  // often less than 200000
}
Answer

Answer. A data race on counter, so the behaviour is undefined. In practice it prints anything from about 100000 to 200000, and it may print exactly 200000 every time on one compiler. ThreadSanitizer reports the race. Fix: std::atomic<int> with fetch_add, or a mutex.

Why. Each ++counter is load, add, store, and interleavings lose updates (see the counter figure). The surprise is the 200000: at -O1 Clang may turn the whole loop into counter += 100000, one load and one store, so the window for losing an update shrinks to almost nothing, and the first thread often finishes before the second starts. That is the danger of UB: the program "passes" on your machine and fails elsewhere. Output is deliberately not compared here.

OutputWhat does this print? bool prints as 0 or 1.

#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::atomic<int> x{10};
    int expected = 7;
    bool ok1 = x.compare_exchange_strong(expected, 20);
    std::cout << ok1 << ' ' << expected << ' ' << x << '\n';
    bool ok2 = x.compare_exchange_strong(expected, 20);
    std::cout << ok2 << ' ' << expected << ' ' << x << '\n';
}
Answer
0 10 10
1 10 20

Answer. First line 0 10 10, second line 1 10 20.

Why. The first CAS compares 10 with the expected 7 and fails. On failure it writes the current value into expected, so expected becomes 10 and x is unchanged. The second CAS now expects 10, which matches, so it stores 20 and returns true; on success expected is left alone. This write-back is what makes CAS loops tidy: the next iteration already has the fresh value. The usual wrong answer is 0 7 10, from treating expected as an input only.

Find the bugThis home-made lock uses an atomic, so it should be safe. Why does the counter come out wrong?

#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>

static std::atomic<bool> locked{false};
static int counter = 0;

static void lock() {
    while (locked.load()) { }  // wait until free
    locked.store(true);        // then take it
}
static void unlock() { locked.store(false); }

static void work() {
    for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) {
        lock();
        ++counter;
        unlock();
    }
}

int main() {
    std::thread a(work), b(work);
    a.join();
    b.join();
    std::cout << counter << '\n';
}
Answer

Answer. The check (load) and the claim (store(true)) are two separate atomic operations. Both threads can see false, both store true, and both enter. Mutual exclusion fails, so counter has a data race, which TSan reports. Fix: claim with one RMW, while (locked.exchange(true, std::memory_order_acquire)) {}, and unlock with a release store.

Why. Atomic operations are indivisible individually, not in combination. This is the same check-then-act race condition as the bank account, here breaking the lock itself. The other weakness, the default seq_cst on every access, only costs speed. A correct test-and-test-and-set lock keeps the read loop but follows it with exchange and retries if the exchange returns true.

OutputWhat does this print (C++20)?

#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::atomic_flag f;  // starts clear (C++20)
    std::cout << f.test_and_set() << f.test_and_set() << f.test() << ' ';
    f.clear();
    std::cout << f.test() << f.test_and_set() << '\n';
}
Answer
011 00

Answer. 011 00.

Why. Since C++20 a default-constructed atomic_flag is clear (P0883; before C++20 its state was unspecified unless you used ATOMIC_FLAG_INIT). The first test_and_set returns the old value false, the second returns true, and test() (new in C++20) reads true without modifying it. After clear(), test() is false and test_and_set returns false again while setting the flag. The left-to-right evaluation of the << chain is guaranteed since C++17, so the order of the three calls is well defined.

Find the bughits is atomic and ThreadSanitizer runs clean, yet the result is usually below 200000. Why?

#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>

static std::atomic<int> hits{0};

static void work() {
    for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) hits = hits + 1;
}

int main() {
    std::thread a(work), b(work);
    a.join();
    b.join();
    std::cout << hits << '\n';  // usually less than 200000
}
Answer

Answer. hits = hits + 1 is an atomic load, then an addition on a plain int, then an atomic store. Another thread can update hits between the load and the store, and that update is overwritten. Use ++hits, hits += 1 or hits.fetch_add(1).

Why. std::atomic overloads operator=, operator++ and operator+= as single atomic operations, but hits + 1 goes through the implicit conversion operator T(), a separate load. There is no data race (every access is atomic), so TSan is right to stay quiet: this is a pure race condition. The output depends on timing and is not compared.

OutputTwo threads each double value ten times using a CAS loop. Is the output deterministic? What is it?

#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>

static std::atomic<long> value{1};

static void times(long k) {
    long old = value.load();
    while (!value.compare_exchange_weak(old, old * k)) { }
}

int main() {
    auto work = [] { for (int i = 0; i < 10; ++i) times(2); };
    std::thread a(work), b(work);
    a.join();
    b.join();
    std::cout << value << '\n';
}
Answer
1048576

Answer. Yes: always 1048576, which is 2 to the power 20.

Why. Every multiplication is applied exactly once: if another thread changes value between the load and the CAS, the CAS fails, refreshes old and recomputes from the new value. Twenty doublings in any order give the same product because multiplication commutes. The interleaving still varies from run to run; only the final value is fixed. Using _weak is correct because a spurious failure just causes one more iteration.

Find the bugPeterson's algorithm, with volatile added so the compiler cannot cache the flags. Is it correct now?

#include <iostream>
#include <thread>

static volatile bool flag[2] = {false, false};
static volatile int turn = 0;
static int counter = 0;

static void lock(int me) {
    int other = 1 - me;
    flag[me] = true;
    turn = other;
    while (flag[other] && turn == other) { }
}

static void unlock(int me) { flag[me] = false; }

static void work(int me) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 50000; ++i) {
        lock(me);
        ++counter;
        unlock(me);
    }
}

int main() {
    std::thread a(work, 0), b(work, 1);
    a.join();
    b.join();
    std::cout << counter << '\n';
}
Answer

Answer. No. volatile stops the compiler from hoisting the loads, but every access is still a data race (TSan reports it), and the CPU's store buffer can let both threads read the other flag as false, so both enter and increments are lost. Fix: std::atomic<bool> and std::atomic<int> with seq_cst, as in the theory section and the coding drill.

Why. Peterson's proof assumes sequential consistency: the store to flag[me] is visible before the load of flag[other]. Both x86 (store buffer) and ARM (much weaker ordering) break that without a full fence. volatile emits no fence. On Apple silicon or a multicore x86, runs of this program typically end short of 100000.

Find the bugThe consumer waits for ready, then reads payload. It prints 42 on every run you try. Why is it still broken?

#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>

static int payload = 0;
static std::atomic<bool> ready{false};

int main() {
    std::thread producer([] {
        payload = 42;
        ready.store(true, std::memory_order_relaxed);
    });
    std::thread consumer([] {
        while (!ready.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)) { }
        std::cout << payload << '\n';
    });
    producer.join();
    consumer.join();
}
Answer

Answer. Relaxed operations create no happens-before edge, so the write of payload and the read in the consumer are unordered conflicting accesses: a data race. TSan reports it. Fix: store(true, std::memory_order_release) and load(std::memory_order_acquire) (or the seq_cst default).

Why. Relaxed guarantees only atomicity of ready itself. The compiler may sink payload = 42 below the flag store, and ARM or POWER may make the flag visible first. x86 happens not to reorder these two stores, which is why it "works" in testing, and why such bugs appear when code moves to ARM servers or Apple silicon. Release/acquire is the minimum that makes the publish correct, and it is free on x86 (plain movs).

Find the bugThe writer locks the mutex. The reader only reads, so it skips the lock "for speed". What is wrong?

#include <iostream>
#include <mutex>
#include <thread>

static std::mutex m;
static long total = 0;

static void writer() {
    for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(m);
        ++total;
    }
}

static void reader() {
    long seen = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) seen = total;  // "reads are harmless"
    std::cout << (seen >= 0) << '\n';
}

int main() {
    std::thread w(writer), r(reader);
    w.join();
    r.join();
}
Answer

Answer. A lock protects data only if every access, reads included, goes through it. The unlocked read of total conflicts with the locked write, nothing orders them, so it is a data race (UB), which TSan reports. Fix: lock in the reader too, or make total a std::atomic<long> if it is a standalone value.

Why. Happens-before through a mutex needs both sides to take it: the writer's unlock synchronises with a later lock, and the reader never locks. "Reads are harmless" is wrong twice: the read may be torn on a platform where long is not written in one instruction, and the compiler may hoist the load out of the loop entirely (here it would read total once). For many readers and few writers use std::shared_mutex (Ch 6), not no lock at all.

Find the bugTwo threads try to withdraw 80 from a balance of 100. Every access is atomic. What can the final balance be?

#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>

static std::atomic<int> balance{100};

static void withdraw(int amount) {
    if (balance.load() >= amount) {   // check
        balance.fetch_sub(amount);    // act
    }
}

int main() {
    std::thread a(withdraw, 80), b(withdraw, 80);
    a.join();
    b.join();
    std::cout << balance << '\n';  // 20 or -60, depending on the interleaving
}
Answer

Answer. Either 20 (one withdrawal succeeds) or minus 60 (both pass the check before either subtracts). It is a race condition without a data race, so TSan runs clean. Fix with a CAS loop that checks and subtracts in one step:

static bool withdraw(int amount) {
    int cur = balance.load();
    while (cur >= amount) {
        if (balance.compare_exchange_weak(cur, cur - amount)) return true;
    }
    return false;  // insufficient funds, decided on the value we failed to change
}

Why. The check and the act are two atomic operations with a window between them. The CAS version makes the decision and the update a single step on the same observed value: if anyone changed the balance, the CAS fails and the condition is re-evaluated on the fresh value. Thread start-up latency makes either outcome common, which is why output is not compared here.

OutputWhat does this print on a 64-bit desktop or server platform (x86-64 or ARM64)?

#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>

struct Big { long a, b, c; };

int main() {
    std::cout << std::atomic<int>::is_always_lock_free
              << std::atomic<long long>::is_always_lock_free
              << std::atomic<Big>::is_always_lock_free << '\n';
    std::atomic<Big> big{Big{1, 2, 3}};
    Big copy = big.load();
    std::cout << copy.a + copy.b + copy.c << '\n';
}
Answer
110
6

Answer. 110, then 6.

Why. 4-byte and 8-byte atomics map onto native instructions, so they are always lock-free. A 24-byte struct has no native atomic instruction on these targets, so std::atomic<Big> is implemented with a lock hidden inside the library (GCC's libatomic or libc++'s lock table); it still works, as the second line shows, but it is a lock under the hood. The exact answer is implementation-specific, which is why the standard offers is_always_lock_free and is_lock_free(). On some Linux toolchains, GCC needs -latomic to link the third case.

Write the code

Coding

CodeImplement a test-and-test-and-set spinlock with exponential backoff. It must satisfy Lockable (lock(), try_lock(), unlock()) so that std::lock_guard works, use the weakest correct memory orders, and stop hammering the cache line while the lock is held. Test it with four threads incrementing a shared counter.

Answer

Approach. Acquire with one exchange(true, acquire); if it returns true the lock was taken, so spin on a relaxed load (which hits the local cache) until it looks free, pausing between checks with a growing backoff, then retry the exchange. try_lock checks with a cheap load first so a failing try_lock does not steal the line. Unlock is a release store.

#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>
#include <mutex>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

class TTASLock {
    std::atomic<bool> locked_{false};

    static void pause() {
#if defined(__x86_64__) || defined(__i386__)
        __builtin_ia32_pause();
#elif defined(__aarch64__)
        asm volatile("yield");
#endif
    }

public:
    void lock() {
        int backoff = 1;
        for (;;) {
            if (!locked_.exchange(true, std::memory_order_acquire)) return;
            while (locked_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)) {
                for (int i = 0; i < backoff; ++i) pause();
                if (backoff < 1024) backoff *= 2;
                else std::this_thread::yield();
            }
        }
    }
    bool try_lock() {
        return !locked_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed) &&
               !locked_.exchange(true, std::memory_order_acquire);
    }
    void unlock() { locked_.store(false, std::memory_order_release); }
};

int main() {
    TTASLock lk;
    long counter = 0;  // guarded by lk
    std::vector<std::thread> ts;
    for (int t = 0; t < 4; ++t)
        ts.emplace_back([&] {
            for (int i = 0; i < 50000; ++i) {
                std::lock_guard<TTASLock> g(lk);
                ++counter;
            }
        });
    for (auto& t : ts) t.join();
    std::cout << counter << '\n';
    std::cout << lk.try_lock() << lk.try_lock() << '\n';
    lk.unlock();
}
200000
10

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) uncontended: one RMW to lock, one store to unlock. Pitfalls: spinning on exchange instead of a load (cache-line ping-pong); using seq_cst everywhere (correct but slower on ARM); unbounded spinning when the holder may be preempted, which is why the loop eventually yields; forgetting that this lock is unfair, so a thread can starve. The pause/yield hint is guarded by architecture macros so the code stays portable.

Estimated rating: ~1400 · short code, but needs the TTAS insight and correct acquire/release placement

CodeImplement a FIFO ticket lock with two counters, so threads acquire the lock in the order they arrived (bounded waiting). Provide lock(), unlock() and a non-blocking try_lock(), and test it with four threads.

Answer

Approach. next_ hands out tickets with fetch_add, which always succeeds and orders arrivals. Each thread waits until serving_ equals its ticket, with an acquire load. Only the owner changes serving_, so unlock is a relaxed load plus a release store of the next number, not an RMW. try_lock takes a ticket only if it would be served at once: read serving_ as s, then CAS next_ from s to s + 1. If the CAS succeeds, nobody else held or was queued for the lock, and since serving_ never passes next_, it still equals s.

#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>
#include <mutex>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

class TicketLock {
    std::atomic<unsigned> next_{0};     // next ticket to hand out
    std::atomic<unsigned> serving_{0};  // ticket allowed in
public:
    void lock() {
        unsigned my = next_.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
        while (serving_.load(std::memory_order_acquire) != my) std::this_thread::yield();
    }
    bool try_lock() {
        unsigned s = serving_.load(std::memory_order_acquire);
        // succeed only if the next ticket is the one being served: no holder, no queue
        return next_.compare_exchange_strong(s, s + 1, std::memory_order_acquire,
                                             std::memory_order_relaxed);
    }
    void unlock() {
        // only the owner writes serving_, so a plain load plus store is enough
        unsigned s = serving_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        serving_.store(s + 1, std::memory_order_release);
    }
};

int main() {
    TicketLock lk;
    long counter = 0;        // guarded by lk
    std::vector<std::thread> ts;
    for (int t = 0; t < 4; ++t)
        ts.emplace_back([&] {
            for (int i = 0; i < 20000; ++i) {
                std::lock_guard<TicketLock> g(lk);
                ++counter;
            }
        });
    for (auto& t : ts) t.join();
    std::cout << counter << '\n';
    std::cout << lk.try_lock() << lk.try_lock() << '\n';
    lk.unlock();
}
80000
10

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) per operation, strict FIFO. Unsigned wrap-around is harmless because only equality is compared. Pitfalls: all waiters spin on serving_, so every release invalidates every waiter's cache line (MCS or Linux's qspinlock fix this); and strict FIFO hurts badly if the thread whose turn it is gets preempted, since everyone behind it waits (a "convoy"). That is why the demo yields in the spin loop. A common mistake in try_lock is to take a ticket with fetch_add and give up if it is not served yet: the ticket cannot be handed back, so every later thread waits forever. The CAS only takes a ticket that is already being served.

Estimated rating: ~1600 · needs fetch_add ordering and the single-writer unlock argument

CodeImplement Peterson's lock for two threads in portable C++ so that it is correct on x86 and ARM. Prove mutual exclusion in your test by tracking the maximum number of threads inside the critical section at once.

Answer

Approach. Use std::atomic for both flags and the victim variable, with seq_cst on the two stores and the loads in the wait loop: the algorithm needs the store-then-load order that only sequential consistency (or a full fence) provides. Writing "victim = me" is equivalent to the textbook "turn = other". The unlock can be a release store. A side atomic counts how many threads are inside.

#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>

class Peterson {
    std::atomic<bool> interested_[2] = {false, false};
    std::atomic<int> victim_{0};
public:
    void lock(int me) {
        const int other = 1 - me;
        interested_[me].store(true, std::memory_order_seq_cst);
        victim_.store(me, std::memory_order_seq_cst);  // "after you"
        while (interested_[other].load(std::memory_order_seq_cst) &&
               victim_.load(std::memory_order_seq_cst) == me) {
            std::this_thread::yield();
        }
    }
    void unlock(int me) { interested_[me].store(false, std::memory_order_release); }
};

int main() {
    Peterson p;
    int counter = 0;      // guarded by p
    int max_inside = 0;   // guarded by p
    std::atomic<int> inside{0};
    auto work = [&](int me) {
        for (int i = 0; i < 50000; ++i) {
            p.lock(me);
            int now = inside.fetch_add(1) + 1;
            if (now > max_inside) max_inside = now;
            ++counter;
            inside.fetch_sub(1);
            p.unlock(me);
        }
    };
    std::thread a(work, 0), b(work, 1);
    a.join();
    b.join();
    std::cout << counter << ' ' << max_inside << '\n';
}
100000 1

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) per acquisition without contention, with a bound of one bypass under contention. Pitfalls: weakening the stores to release or the loads to acquire (store-load reordering returns and the lock breaks); using volatile; extending it to N threads naively (use Lamport's bakery or a filter lock). It is a teaching algorithm: a single exchange does the same job for any number of threads.

Estimated rating: ~1700 · easy to type, hard to justify the memory orders correctly

CodeImplement a lock-free multi-producer stack of int that supports concurrent push and a drain_sum() that atomically takes all current elements and returns their sum. It must not suffer from ABA and must not leak memory.

Answer

Approach. push is the classic Treiber CAS loop: point the new node at the current head, then CAS the head from that value to the new node; on failure CAS refreshes n->next with the head it saw. Instead of a single-node pop (which has the ABA and reclamation problems), drain_sum takes the entire list with one exchange(nullptr), after which the detached nodes belong to one thread and can be freed safely.

#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

class PushStack {
    struct Node { int value; Node* next; };
    std::atomic<Node*> head_{nullptr};
public:
    ~PushStack() { free_list(head_.load()); }

    void push(int v) {
        Node* n = new Node{v, head_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)};
        // on failure, n->next is refreshed with the current head
        while (!head_.compare_exchange_weak(n->next, n, std::memory_order_release,
                                            std::memory_order_relaxed)) { }
    }

    // Detach the whole list in one atomic step: no ABA, no use after free.
    long drain_sum() {
        Node* n = head_.exchange(nullptr, std::memory_order_acquire);
        long sum = 0;
        for (Node* p = n; p; p = p->next) sum += p->value;
        free_list(n);
        return sum;
    }

private:
    static void free_list(Node* n) {
        while (n) { Node* next = n->next; delete n; n = next; }
    }
};

int main() {
    PushStack s;
    std::vector<std::thread> ts;
    for (int t = 0; t < 4; ++t)
        ts.emplace_back([&s, t] { for (int i = 1; i <= 1000; ++i) s.push(t * 1000 + i); });
    for (auto& t : ts) t.join();
    std::cout << s.drain_sum() << '\n';
    std::cout << s.drain_sum() << '\n';
}
8002000
0

Complexity and pitfalls. Push is lock-free (some thread always makes progress) with O(1) expected work; drain is O(n) after one atomic. The release on push pairs with the acquire on drain, so node contents are visible to the draining thread. Pitfalls: a single-node pop with head.compare_exchange(old, old->next) is the textbook ABA bug and also reads old->next after another thread may have freed old; and every lock-free container needs a reclamation plan (hazard pointers, epochs, or a design like this one). This "push many, take all" shape is used in real systems, for example for deferred work queues.

Estimated rating: ~1800 · the CAS loop is standard; seeing that exchange sidesteps ABA is the insight

CodeImplement a futex-style mutex with the three-state algorithm (0 free, 1 locked, 2 locked with possible waiters). Waiters must sleep rather than spin, the uncontended path must not touch the kernel, and unlock must wake a sleeper only when one may exist. Use C++20 std::atomic::wait and notify_one so it is portable. Test with eight threads.

Answer

Approach. Lock tries CAS 0 → 1. If that fails, set the state to 2 with exchange: if the old value was 0 you now own it (pessimistically marked contended); otherwise sleep with wait(2), which returns immediately if the value is no longer 2, then retry the exchange. Unlock exchanges to 0 and calls notify_one only if the old value was 2. std::atomic::wait is built on futex on Linux, ulock on macOS and WaitOnAddress on Windows.

#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>
#include <mutex>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

// 0 = unlocked, 1 = locked with no waiters, 2 = locked and maybe waiters
class FutexMutex {
    std::atomic<int> state_{0};
public:
    void lock() {
        int c = 0;
        if (state_.compare_exchange_strong(c, 1, std::memory_order_acquire)) return;  // fast path
        if (c != 2) c = state_.exchange(2, std::memory_order_acquire);
        while (c != 0) {
            state_.wait(2, std::memory_order_relaxed);  // sleeps only while state_ == 2
            c = state_.exchange(2, std::memory_order_acquire);
        }
    }
    bool try_lock() {
        int c = 0;
        return state_.compare_exchange_strong(c, 1, std::memory_order_acquire);
    }
    void unlock() {
        if (state_.exchange(0, std::memory_order_release) == 2) state_.notify_one();  // slow path
    }
};

int main() {
    FutexMutex m;
    long counter = 0;  // guarded by m
    std::vector<std::thread> ts;
    for (int t = 0; t < 8; ++t)
        ts.emplace_back([&] {
            for (int i = 0; i < 20000; ++i) {
                std::lock_guard<FutexMutex> g(m);
                ++counter;
            }
        });
    for (auto& t : ts) t.join();
    std::cout << counter << '\n';
    std::cout << m.try_lock() << m.try_lock() << '\n';
    m.unlock();
}
160000
10

Complexity and pitfalls. Uncontended lock and unlock are one atomic each, no system call. Pitfalls: a two-state version (0/1) must call wake on every unlock, because it cannot tell whether anyone sleeps; setting the state to 1 instead of 2 after waking can lose a wake-up for the remaining sleepers; and checking "is it 2?" then sleeping as two steps reintroduces the lost wake-up that the atomic compare inside FUTEX_WAIT (and atomic::wait) exists to prevent. Unlock uses exchange, not a store, because it must learn the old state.

Estimated rating: ~2100 · subtle protocol; lost wake-ups and the reason for state 2 are the interview

CodeA single std::atomic<long> hit counter is the hottest line in your service. Implement a sharded counter: add(shard, v) from many threads and an approximate read() that is exact once writers stop. Avoid false sharing.

Answer

Approach. Give each shard its own atomic, aligned to a cache line so two shards never share one, and let each thread pick a shard (its index, or a hash of its thread id). add is a relaxed fetch_add on a line that, ideally, only one core writes. read sums the shards with relaxed loads. Relaxed is enough because no other data is published through the counter.

#include <atomic>
#include <cstddef>
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

class ShardedCounter {
    static constexpr std::size_t kLine = 64;  // typical cache line size
    struct alignas(kLine) Slot { std::atomic<long> n{0}; };
    std::vector<Slot> slots_;
public:
    explicit ShardedCounter(std::size_t shards) : slots_(shards) {}
    void add(std::size_t shard, long v) {
        slots_[shard % slots_.size()].n.fetch_add(v, std::memory_order_relaxed);
    }
    long read() const {  // a snapshot; exact once writers have stopped
        long sum = 0;
        for (const Slot& s : slots_) sum += s.n.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        return sum;
    }
};

int main() {
    ShardedCounter c(4);
    std::vector<std::thread> ts;
    for (std::size_t t = 0; t < 4; ++t)
        ts.emplace_back([&c, t] { for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) c.add(t, 1); });
    for (auto& t : ts) t.join();
    std::cout << c.read() << '\n';
}
400000

Complexity and pitfalls. add is O(1) with no cross-core traffic when shards are thread-private; read is O(shards). Pitfalls: packing shards into a plain std::atomic<long>[] puts eight of them on one 64-byte line and recreates the contention (false sharing, Ch 19); read() during updates is a snapshot, not a linearisable total; and before C++17, std::vector did not honour over-aligned element types (C++17 aligned new fixed that). std::hardware_destructive_interference_size is the standard name for the padding size, but using it in a header can change ABI between compiler flags, so many codebases hard-code 64 or 128.

Estimated rating: ~1300 · simple code; the value is knowing why one atomic does not scale

Cheat sheet

Theory
  • Data race = conflicting accesses, one non-atomic, no happens-before: UB for the whole program. Race condition = timing-dependent logic bug, possible with atomics only. TSan finds the first, not the second.
  • counter++ is load, add, store. Fix with fetch_add, a mutex, or per-thread counters. x = x + 1 on an atomic is still two operations. volatile fixes nothing.
  • Critical section: mutual exclusion, progress, bounded waiting. Disabling interrupts is privileged and useless on multiprocessors. Strict alternation fails progress; TAS spinlocks fail bounded waiting.
  • Peterson needs store→load ordering: breaks on x86 and ARM without seq_cst or a full fence. Release/acquire is not enough.
  • Primitives: TAS, swap, fetch-add (consensus 2) and CAS, LL/SC (universal). CAS writes the observed value into expected on failure; _weak may fail spuriously, use it in loops. Watch for ABA.
  • Spinlock: TTAS plus pause and backoff, acquire on lock, release on unlock. Spin only for very short sections with a running holder; never on one core. Ticket and MCS locks add fairness.
  • Mutex = atomic word + futex. Fast path: one CAS, no syscall. Slow path: FUTEX_WAIT re-checks the value atomically, so wakes are not lost. Three states let unlock skip the wake.
  • Unlock is a release, lock is an acquire: they create happens-before. Lock every access to guarded data, reads included. Uncontended locks are cheap; contention and false sharing (Ch 19) are what hurt.

Part C · Locks and mutexes · Chapter 6

Mutex types, condition variables and deadlock

This chapter covers the synchronisation toolbox you use every day in C++: the mutex family, the RAII lock wrappers, condition variables, semaphores, latches and barriers. It then covers what goes wrong with them (deadlock, livelock, starvation, priority inversion) and the classic problems interviewers use to test all of it: producer-consumer, readers-writers and the dining philosophers.

TheoryDrillsCoding· about 5 hours· prerequisites: Ch 4 threads, Ch 5 races and mutex internals

The mutex family

Theory

Mental model. A mutex is a token that only one thread can hold at a time. A thread that wants the token and finds it taken goes to sleep until the holder gives it back. Ch 5 explains how that sleep works (a futex fast path in user space, a system call only on contention). This chapter is about the C++ types built on top of it and how to combine them.

The standard library gives you six mutex types in <mutex> and <shared_mutex>. They differ along three axes: can the owner lock it again (recursive), can you give up after a timeout (timed), and can many readers hold it at once (shared).

std::mutex

std::mutex has three operations: lock(), try_lock() and unlock(). It is not copyable and not movable, because other threads hold its address. Its rules are preconditions, so breaking them is undefined behaviour, not an error you can catch:

  • Locking a std::mutex that the calling thread already owns is undefined. On Linux it usually deadlocks the thread against itself; an implementation may also throw std::system_error with resource_deadlock_would_occur.
  • Unlocking a mutex the calling thread does not own is undefined. A mutex has an owner; this is the key difference from a semaphore.
  • Destroying a mutex that is still locked is undefined.
  • try_lock() is allowed to fail spuriously, that is, return false even when no thread holds the mutex. Never use it to ask "is it locked?".

On the plus side, std::mutex has a constexpr default constructor, so a global or static mutex is constant-initialised and cannot suffer from the static initialisation order problem.

recursive_mutex

std::recursive_mutex keeps an owner thread id and a count. The owner may lock it again, and it becomes free only after as many unlock() calls as lock() calls. The maximum depth is unspecified; past it, lock() throws and try_lock() returns false.

It exists for code where a public locked function calls another public locked function on the same object. Most reviewers treat it as a design smell: the inner call runs while the invariant may be half updated by the outer call, and you lose the ability to reason about "inside the lock, the invariant holds on entry". The usual fix is a private do_x_locked() helper that assumes the lock is held, called by thin public wrappers that take the lock.

timed_mutex and shared_mutex

std::timed_mutex and std::recursive_timed_mutex add try_lock_for(duration) and try_lock_until(time_point). Use them when a caller must give up, for example to report a likely deadlock or to keep a latency budget. Prefer steady_clock for deadlines, because system_clock can jump.

std::shared_mutex (C++17) is a readers-writer lock: lock() takes it exclusively, lock_shared() takes a shared (read) hold, and any number of shared holders may coexist while no exclusive holder exists. std::shared_timed_mutex (C++14, older) adds timed variants. The standard does not say whether readers or writers get priority. In practice it differs: libstdc++ builds std::shared_mutex on pthread_rwlock_t, and glibc's default rwlock prefers readers, so on Linux with GCC a steady stream of overlapping readers can starve a writer; libc++ implements its own lock that blocks new readers once a writer is waiting. The section on classic problems shows how to build a writer-preferring lock yourself.

Interview trap

"Use shared_mutex for read-heavy data" is not automatically a win. Every lock_shared() still writes to the mutex (it bumps a reader count), so with many cores the cache line holding the mutex bounces between them just as it would for a plain mutex. When critical sections are a few nanoseconds long, a plain std::mutex is often faster. Shared locking pays off when readers hold the lock for a long time.

Key facts

TypeHeader, standardRe-lock by ownerTimeoutShared modeTypical use
mutex<mutex>, C++11UBnonodefault choice
recursive_mutex<mutex>, C++11yes, countednonolegacy re-entrant APIs

recursive_timed_mutex<mutex>, C++11yesyesnorare
