The handshake is completed by the kernel, not by accept(). A client's connect() succeeds as soon as the server kernel answers, even if the server process never calls accept().

The four-way teardown, half-close and RST

Each direction is closed separately, because TCP is full duplex. The side that closes first (the active closer) sends FIN; the peer ACKs it, may keep sending data (the connection is half-closed), and later sends its own FIN, which the active closer ACKs. The middle ACK and FIN are often combined, which gives three segments on the wire. shutdown(fd, SHUT_WR) sends FIN while keeping the read direction open, which is how a client says "request finished" while still reading the response. close() releases the descriptor and closes both directions once the last descriptor for the socket is gone.

A RST aborts a connection immediately, with no TIME_WAIT. Causes: a SYN to a port with no listener (the client sees "connection refused"), a segment for a connection the host does not know (for example after a reboot), close() while unread data sits in the receive buffer, or SO_LINGER with a zero timeout.

The TCP state machine and TIME_WAIT

Theory

TIME_WAIT and 2·MSL

The active closer stays in TIME_WAIT for twice the maximum segment lifetime (MSL, nominally 2 minutes in RFC 793 and RFC 9293; Linux hard-codes TIME_WAIT at 60 seconds). Two reasons:

  1. Reliable close. If the final ACK is lost, the peer retransmits its FIN. The TIME_WAIT side must still exist to ACK it again; otherwise it would answer with RST and the peer would report an error. One MSL for the lost ACK to die and one MSL for the retransmitted FIN to arrive gives 2·MSL.
  2. No ghost segments. Delayed segments of the old connection must expire before a new connection with the same 4-tuple can start, or they could be accepted as data of the new one.

TIME_WAIT costs only a small kernel structure (no file descriptor), but a busy client opening many short connections to the same server can run out of ephemeral ports (the 4-tuple must be unique, and Linux's default range 32768 to 60999 gives about 28 thousand). Fixes: connection reuse (keep-alive, pooling), more ephemeral ports or more client IPs, and net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse, which lets a new outgoing connection reuse a TIME_WAIT 4-tuple when timestamps prove it safe. (The old tcp_tw_recycle broke clients behind NAT and was removed in Linux 4.12.)

SO_REUSEADDR and SO_REUSEPORT

A server that restarts while connections it closed are still in TIME_WAIT gets EADDRINUSE from bind(). Setting SO_REUSEADDR before bind() allows binding a port that has TIME_WAIT connections on it. Every TCP server should set it. On Linux it does not allow two sockets to listen on the same address and port; that is SO_REUSEPORT (Linux 3.9), which lets several sockets (usually one per worker thread or process) bind the same port, with the kernel load-balancing incoming connections between them. BSD and macOS semantics differ in details, so check the platform when it matters.

Interview trap

"The server is in TIME_WAIT" is not a property of servers. Whichever side calls close() first enters TIME_WAIT. HTTP servers that close idle keep-alive connections accumulate TIME_WAIT sockets; clients that close first push the cost to the client side. Conversely, thousands of sockets in CLOSE_WAIT mean your application received FIN and never called close(): a descriptor leak in your code, not a kernel tuning problem.

Sequence numbers, ACKs and retransmission

Theory

Mental model. TCP numbers every byte. The receiver says "I have everything before byte N" (a cumulative ACK of N). The sender keeps every unacknowledged byte in its send buffer and resends whatever is not acknowledged in time.

  • Sequence number of a segment = stream position of its first byte. A segment with sequence number 1001 and 100 bytes of data covers 1001 to 1100, and the receiver acknowledges it with ACK 1101.
  • Cumulative ACKs mean a lost segment holds back the ACK number even if later segments arrive; the receiver buffers out-of-order data and sends duplicate ACKs for the hole. SACK (RFC 2018) adds option blocks that tell the sender exactly which later ranges arrived, so it only resends the holes.
  • Sequence numbers are 32-bit and wrap around (after 4 GiB of data). Comparisons use serial arithmetic: a is before b when (int32_t)(a - b) < 0. On very fast links, timestamps (PAWS, RFC 7323) guard against an old segment from the previous wrap being accepted.

Retransmission timeout

The sender measures round-trip times and keeps a smoothed RTT and its variance. RFC 6298 sets RTO = SRTT + 4·RTTVAR, with an initial RTO of 1 second and a recommended minimum of 1 second (Linux uses a 200 ms minimum). Each timeout doubles the RTO (exponential backoff). Karn's algorithm: never take an RTT sample from a retransmitted segment, because you cannot tell which transmission the ACK answers. A timeout is treated as a strong congestion signal (see below).

Fast retransmit

Waiting a full RTO for each loss is slow. When the sender receives three duplicate ACKs (four ACKs with the same number), it assumes the segment at that number was lost, because later segments are clearly arriving, and retransmits it immediately (RFC 5681). Modern stacks also use RACK (time-based loss detection, RFC 8985) and tail loss probes.

Flow control vs congestion control

Theory

Mental model. Two different limits stop a sender from sending too fast. Flow control protects the receiver: do not send more than its buffer can hold. Congestion control protects the network: do not send more than the path can carry. The sender may have at most min(rwnd, cwnd) unacknowledged bytes in flight.

Flow control: the receive window

Every segment carries the receiver's free buffer space (rwnd) in the window field. If the application stops reading, the window shrinks to zero and the sender stops; it then sends periodic zero-window probes until the window opens. The 16-bit field caps the window at 64 KB, so the window scale option (RFC 7323, negotiated in the SYN) shifts it left by up to 14 bits, allowing windows up to 1 GiB. To fill a path, the window must cover the bandwidth-delay product: 1 Gbit/s × 100 ms = 12.5 MB in flight. A 64 KB window on that path gives at most 64 KB per 100 ms, about 5 Mbit/s.

Congestion control: slow start and AIMD

The sender keeps a congestion window (cwnd), which it learns by probing, and a threshold (ssthresh). Classic Reno (RFC 5681):

  • Slow start (cwnd < ssthresh): start with an initial window of up to 10 segments (RFC 6928, the Linux default) and add one MSS per ACK, so cwnd doubles every RTT. "Slow" refers to starting small, not to the growth rate.
  • Congestion avoidance (cwnd ≥ ssthresh): add about one MSS per RTT (MSS·MSS/cwnd per ACK). This is the additive increase.
  • Fast retransmit and fast recovery on three duplicate ACKs: set ssthresh = max(FlightSize / 2, 2·MSS), retransmit the lost segment, set cwnd = ssthresh + 3·MSS and inflate it per further duplicate ACK; when new data is acknowledged, deflate cwnd to ssthresh and continue in congestion avoidance. This is the multiplicative decrease.
  • Timeout: ssthresh = max(FlightSize / 2, 2·MSS) and cwnd = 1 MSS, then slow start again. A timeout means the ACK clock stopped, which is worse news than a few duplicate ACKs.

Linux uses CUBIC by default (RFC 9438): it grows cwnd as a cubic function of the time since the last loss, which recovers faster on high-bandwidth, long-delay paths and is fairer between flows with different RTTs. BBR (Google) instead models the bottleneck bandwidth and minimum RTT and paces packets to match, so it does not need loss as its signal. ECN lets routers mark packets (CE) instead of dropping them; the receiver echoes ECE and the sender reacts as if a loss had happened and answers with CWR.

Know this cold

Flow control is end to end and receiver driven (rwnd in every ACK). Congestion control is a sender-side estimate of the network (cwnd, never sent on the wire). In flight ≤ min(rwnd, cwnd). Slow start is exponential, congestion avoidance is linear, a loss signal halves (AIMD), a timeout resets to 1.

Nagle, delayed ACK and head-of-line blocking

Theory

Nagle's algorithm and delayed ACKs

Nagle (RFC 896) reduces tiny packets: while any sent data is unacknowledged, small writes are buffered and sent together, either when the ACK arrives or when a full MSS has accumulated. Delayed ACK (RFC 1122, RFC 9293) reduces pure ACKs: the receiver waits a little (it must ACK within 500 ms and should ACK at least every second full-size segment; Linux uses 40 ms to 200 ms) hoping to piggyback the ACK on response data.

Each is fine alone; together they stall. A client that does write, write, read (for example a header and a body in two send() calls) sends the first small segment at once. The second is held by Nagle until the first is ACKed, and the server holds its ACK hoping to piggyback it on a response it cannot produce until it gets the second part. The connection sits idle until the delayed-ACK timer fires, adding about 40 ms (Linux) or up to 200 ms per request.

Fixes, best first: build the whole message and send it in one call (or use writev/sendmsg with an iovec); set TCP_NODELAY to disable Nagle, which every latency-sensitive system does (trading, RPC frameworks, games, interactive protocols); or on Linux, use TCP_CORK to batch explicitly and uncork to flush. TCP_QUICKACK turns off delayed ACKs temporarily on Linux.

int one = 1;
setsockopt(fd, IPPROTO_TCP, TCP_NODELAY, &one, sizeof one);  // needs <netinet/tcp.h>

Head-of-line blocking

Because TCP delivers a single ordered byte stream, one lost segment blocks delivery of everything after it, even data that has already arrived, until the retransmission fills the hole. This is head-of-line (HOL) blocking, and it appears at two levels:

  • HTTP/1.1: a connection carries one request/response at a time (pipelining exists but is effectively unused), so a slow response blocks the requests behind it. Browsers open about 6 connections per host to compensate.
  • HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection, which fixes HTTP-level HOL blocking, but a single lost TCP segment still stalls every stream, which is worse than HTTP/1.1's six independent connections on lossy networks.
  • HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP, where each stream is ordered independently, so a loss only stalls the stream it belongs to.

The BSD sockets API in C and C++

Theory

Mental model. A socket is a file descriptor that names one end of a communication channel inside the kernel. The kernel owns the protocol state, the send buffer and the receive buffer; your calls only copy bytes between your memory and those buffers, and ask the kernel to change state.

CallServerClientWhat it really does
socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0)yesyescreates an unconnected socket, returns an fd
setsockopt(SO_REUSEADDR)before bindrarelyallows rebinding a port with TIME_WAIT connections
bind(fd, addr, len)yesoptionalattaches a local address and port (port 0 lets the kernel choose)
listen(fd, backlog)yesmarks it passive: the kernel now completes handshakes
accept(fd, peer, len)yestakes one finished connection from the accept queue; returns a new fd
connect(fd, addr, len)yespicks an ephemeral port, runs the 3-way handshake
send/recv (or write/read)yesyescopy into the send buffer / out of the receive buffer; may do less than asked
shutdown(fd, SHUT_WR)optionaloptionalsends FIN, keeps reading
close(fd)yesyesreleases the fd; FIN when the last reference goes

A blocking echo server

The minimal correct server. Notice the new descriptor returned by accept, the loop around send, the n == 0 end-of-stream check, and the byte-order conversions. This program blocks forever, so it is compile-only here.

#include <arpa/inet.h>
#include <netinet/in.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <cerrno>
#include <cstdio>

static bool send_all(int fd, const char* p, size_t n) {
    while (n > 0) {
        ssize_t w = send(fd, p, n, MSG_NOSIGNAL);  // no SIGPIPE if the peer is gone
        if (w < 0) {
            if (errno == EINTR) continue;
            return false;
        }
        p += w;
        n -= size_t(w);
    }
    return true;
}

int main() {
    int lfd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
    if (lfd < 0) { std::perror("socket"); return 1; }
    int yes = 1;
    setsockopt(lfd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_REUSEADDR, &yes, sizeof yes);  // before bind

    sockaddr_in addr{};
    addr.sin_family = AF_INET;
    addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(INADDR_ANY);  // all interfaces
    addr.sin_port = htons(9000);               // network byte order
    if (bind(lfd, reinterpret_cast<sockaddr*>(&addr), sizeof addr) < 0) { std::perror("bind"); return 1; }
    if (listen(lfd, SOMAXCONN) < 0) { std::perror("listen"); return 1; }

    for (;;) {
        sockaddr_in peer{};
        socklen_t plen = sizeof peer;
        int cfd = accept(lfd, reinterpret_cast<sockaddr*>(&peer), &plen);
        if (cfd < 0) {
            if (errno == EINTR) continue;
            std::perror("accept");
            break;
        }
        char ip[INET_ADDRSTRLEN];
        inet_ntop(AF_INET, &peer.sin_addr, ip, sizeof ip);
        std::printf("client %s:%d\n", ip, ntohs(peer.sin_port));
        char buf[4096];
        for (;;) {
            ssize_t n = recv(cfd, buf, sizeof buf, 0);
            if (n == 0) break;  // peer sent FIN
            if (n < 0) {
                if (errno == EINTR) continue;
                break;
            }
            if (!send_all(cfd, buf, size_t(n))) break;
        }
        close(cfd);  // forgetting this leaks fds and leaves peers in FIN_WAIT_2
    }
    close(lfd);
}

This server handles one client at a time. Real servers use a thread per connection (simple, but costly beyond thousands of connections), a thread pool, or an event loop with non-blocking sockets and epoll.

A client with getaddrinfo

getaddrinfo resolves names for IPv4 and IPv6 alike and returns a list of candidate addresses; a robust client tries each in turn. Never hand-fill sockaddr_in from a hostname, and never use the obsolete gethostbyname (not thread-safe, IPv4 only).

#include <netdb.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <cstdio>
#include <string>

static int connect_to(const char* host, const char* port) {
    addrinfo hints{};
    hints.ai_family = AF_UNSPEC;  // IPv4 or IPv6
    hints.ai_socktype = SOCK_STREAM;
    addrinfo* res = nullptr;
    if (int rc = getaddrinfo(host, port, &hints, &res); rc != 0) {
        std::fprintf(stderr, "getaddrinfo: %s\n", gai_strerror(rc));
        return -1;
    }
    int fd = -1;
    for (addrinfo* ai = res; ai; ai = ai->ai_next) {
        fd = socket(ai->ai_family, ai->ai_socktype, ai->ai_protocol);
        if (fd < 0) continue;
        if (connect(fd, ai->ai_addr, ai->ai_addrlen) == 0) break;
        close(fd);
        fd = -1;
    }
    freeaddrinfo(res);
    return fd;
}

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
    const char* host = argc > 1 ? argv[1] : "example.com";
    int fd = connect_to(host, "80");
    if (fd < 0) return 1;
    std::string req = std::string("GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: ") + host + "\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n";
    send(fd, req.data(), req.size(), 0);  // small request; production code loops like send_all
    char buf[4096];
    ssize_t n;
    while ((n = recv(fd, buf, sizeof buf, 0)) > 0) std::fwrite(buf, 1, size_t(n), stdout);
    close(fd);
}

Byte order

Every multi-byte field in IP, TCP and UDP headers is big-endian ("network byte order"). The sockets API passes ports and IPv4 addresses in network order inside sockaddr_in, so convert with htons/htonl on the way in and ntohs/ntohl on the way out. Use inet_pton and inet_ntop for text conversion. Your own wire formats should also pick one order explicitly and serialise byte by byte (or with std::byteswap in C++23), never by memcpy of a struct, which also copies padding and host byte order.

Blocking vs non-blocking, select, poll and epoll

By default accept, connect, recv and (when the send buffer is full) send block the thread. With fcntl(fd, F_SETFL, flags | O_NONBLOCK) they return −1 with errno set to EAGAIN/EWOULDBLOCK instead, and a non-blocking connect returns EINPROGRESS; you then wait for writability and read SO_ERROR. To wait on many sockets at once you use a readiness API:

APIInterfaceCost per waitLimits
selectthree fd_set bitmaps, rebuilt every call, nfds = highest fd + 1O(highest fd)FD_SETSIZE, usually 1024; fds above it overflow the bitmap
pollarray of pollfd {fd, events, revents}O(number of fds)no fixed limit
epoll (Linux)kernel-side interest set: epoll_create1, epoll_ctl, epoll_waitO(ready fds)Linux only; BSD and macOS have kqueue, Windows has IOCP

epoll is level-triggered by default (reports a socket as long as it has data). With EPOLLET (edge-triggered) it reports only changes, so you must read until EAGAIN every time, or the remaining data is never reported again. A Linux-only sketch of the loop:

int ep = epoll_create1(0);
epoll_event ev{};
ev.events = EPOLLIN;
ev.data.fd = listen_fd;
epoll_ctl(ep, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, listen_fd, &ev);
epoll_event ready[64];
for (;;) {
    int n = epoll_wait(ep, ready, 64, -1);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        if (ready[i].data.fd == listen_fd) { /* accept, set O_NONBLOCK, EPOLL_CTL_ADD the new fd */ }
        else { /* recv until EAGAIN; on 0 or error: EPOLL_CTL_DEL and close */ }
    }
}

Newer Linux code can also use io_uring, which submits the operations themselves (completion-based, like IOCP) instead of waiting for readiness.

Message framing: TCP is a byte stream

TCP preserves the order of bytes and nothing else. One send of 12 bytes can arrive as one recv of 12, as 12 reads of 1 byte, or merged with the next message. recv(fd, buf, n, 0) returns whatever is available, between 1 and n bytes (0 means the peer closed). Any protocol on TCP therefore needs framing: a delimiter (HTTP header lines end with CRLF, Redis uses CRLF), a length prefix (most binary protocols, gRPC, Kafka) or a fixed message size. The receiver keeps a buffer, appends what each recv returns, and extracts complete messages from the front.

#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <cstdio>

int main() {
    int sv[2];
    if (socketpair(AF_UNIX, SOCK_STREAM, 0, sv) < 0) return 1;
    write(sv[0], "HELLO ", 6);  // the sender's 12-byte message arrives in two pieces
    char buf[12];
    ssize_t n = recv(sv[1], buf, sizeof buf, 0);
    std::printf("asked for %zu, got %zd\n", sizeof buf, n);
    write(sv[0], "WORLD!", 6);
    ssize_t m = recv(sv[1], buf + n, sizeof buf - size_t(n), 0);
    std::printf("then got %zd: %.12s\n", m, buf);
    close(sv[0]);
    close(sv[1]);
}
asked for 12, got 6
then got 6: HELLO WORLD!

Interview trap

Code that does a single recv per message works on localhost and in tests, because small messages usually arrive whole, and then fails under load or over a real network. Interviewers often hand you exactly this bug. The same is true of send: on a blocking socket it normally sends everything, but it can return less (signals, non-blocking mode), so loop until all bytes are written.

Tip

Two more production habits: ignore SIGPIPE (or pass MSG_NOSIGNAL), because writing to a socket the peer has reset kills the process by default; and treat EINTR as "retry", not as an error.

HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3

Theory

HTTP/1.1 messages

HTTP semantics are in RFC 9110 and the HTTP/1.1 wire format in RFC 9112. A request is a request line, header lines, an empty line, and an optional body, with CRLF line endings:

GET /search?q=tcp HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
User-Agent: curl/8.5.0
Accept: */*

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 1256
Cache-Control: max-age=60

<!doctype html>...
  • Host is mandatory in HTTP/1.1 (a server answers 400 without it), which is what lets one IP address host many sites.
  • Header names are case-insensitive. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 send them lowercase.
  • The body length is known from Content-Length, or from Transfer-Encoding: chunked (hex size lines, terminated by a zero-size chunk), or, for responses only, by the server closing the connection.
  • Persistent connections are the default in HTTP/1.1 ("keep-alive"): the connection stays open for further requests until either side sends Connection: close or times out. HTTP/1.0 needed Connection: keep-alive explicitly. Reusing connections avoids a new TCP and TLS handshake and a new slow start per request.

Methods and status codes

MethodSafeIdempotentUse
GET, HEADyesyesread a resource (HEAD: headers only)
OPTIONSyesyescapabilities, CORS preflight
PUTnoyescreate or replace at a known URL
DELETEnoyesremove
POSTnonocreate under a collection, or any non-idempotent action
PATCHnonot guaranteedpartial update (RFC 5789)

Safe means no intended side effects. Idempotent means sending it twice has the same effect as once, which is what makes a request safe to retry after a timeout. Status classes: 1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.

CodeMeaningCodeMeaning
200OK400Bad Request (malformed)
201Created (with Location)401Unauthorized: not authenticated
204No Content403Forbidden: authenticated but not allowed
206Partial Content (Range)404Not Found
301 / 308Moved permanently (308 keeps the method)409 / 429Conflict / Too Many Requests
302 / 307Found, temporary (307 keeps the method)500Internal Server Error
304Not Modified (cache revalidation)502 / 503 / 504Bad Gateway / Service Unavailable / Gateway Timeout

HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 in one breath

  • HTTP/2 (RFC 9113): same semantics, binary framing, many concurrent streams multiplexed on one TCP connection, header compression with HPACK (RFC 7541), stream priorities and flow control. Browsers use it only over TLS (negotiated with ALPN "h2"); cleartext h2c appears mainly between backend services, for example gRPC. It removes HTTP-level HOL blocking but keeps TCP's.
  • HTTP/3 (RFC 9114): HTTP over QUIC (RFC 9000), a transport on UDP that builds in TLS 1.3 (RFC 9001), independent streams (no cross-stream HOL blocking), 1-RTT setup for transport and crypto together (0-RTT on resumption), connection IDs that survive a change of IP address (Wi-Fi to cellular), and QPACK header compression (RFC 9204). Servers advertise it with an Alt-Svc header or an HTTPS DNS record.

HTTPS and the TLS 1.3 handshake

Theory

Mental model. TLS turns a TCP connection into an authenticated, encrypted, integrity-protected byte stream. Asymmetric crypto is used only during the handshake, to agree on symmetric keys (ephemeral Diffie-Hellman) and to prove the server's identity (a certificate signature); the data itself is protected with fast symmetric AEAD ciphers such as AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305.

  1. ClientHello: supported versions and cipher suites, a random value, an ephemeral (EC)DHE public key share (usually X25519, increasingly a hybrid post-quantum group), SNI (the hostname, still sent in clear unless Encrypted Client Hello is used) and ALPN (h2 or http/1.1).
  2. ServerHello: the chosen suite and the server's key share. Both sides now compute the shared secret and derive handshake keys (HKDF). Everything from here is encrypted.
  3. The server sends EncryptedExtensions, its Certificate chain, CertificateVerify (a signature over the handshake transcript with the certificate's private key, which proves it owns the key) and Finished (a MAC over the transcript).
  4. The client validates the certificate: chain to a trusted root CA, hostname matches the subject alternative name, within its validity dates, not revoked. Then it checks CertificateVerify and Finished, sends its own Finished, and starts sending application data.

TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) removed RSA key transport and static Diffie-Hellman, so every connection has forward secrecy: stealing the server's private key later does not decrypt recorded traffic. On resumption, a pre-shared key from an earlier session allows 0-RTT early data, which can be replayed by an attacker and is not forward secret with respect to the resumption key, so servers should accept only idempotent requests as early data. HSTS (a response header) tells browsers to use HTTPS only for a domain, which prevents downgrade to plain HTTP.

What happens when you type a URL

Theory

The classic open question. A strong answer walks the layers in order, says what is cached at each step, and offers depth where the interviewer wants it. For https://www.example.com/index.html:

  1. Parse the input. The browser decides it is a URL (not a search), extracts scheme, host, port (443 by default for https) and path, and checks the HSTS list (an http URL for an HSTS host is upgraded to https before anything is sent).
  2. Reuse check. If an open connection to that origin exists (keep-alive, or an HTTP/2 connection whose certificate covers the name), the browser skips to step 6. It also checks its HTTP cache: a fresh cached response skips the network entirely.
  3. DNS. Browser cache, then OS cache and /etc/hosts, then a recursive query to the configured resolver, which iterates from root to com to example.com (Ch 7). The browser asks for A and AAAA (and possibly HTTPS records, which can advertise HTTP/3).
  4. Route the first packet. The destination is off-subnet, so the OS sends to the default gateway, using ARP (or cached ARP) for the gateway's MAC. The home router applies NAT, and routers hop by hop forward on longest-prefix match.
  5. Transport. A TCP 3-way handshake to port 443 (or a QUIC handshake over UDP for HTTP/3, which merges this step with the next).
  6. TLS 1.3. ClientHello with SNI and ALPN, server certificate validated against the hostname, keys derived, 1 RTT.
  7. HTTP request. GET /index.html with Host, cookies and accept headers, over HTTP/2 if ALPN chose h2.
  8. Server side. A CDN edge or load balancer terminates TLS, routes the request (L4 or L7) to an application server, which may hit caches and databases, and produces a response with a status code and caching headers.
  9. Response and rendering. The browser parses HTML into the DOM, discovers CSS, JavaScript and images and fetches them (over the same connection with HTTP/2), builds the CSSOM, runs scripts, computes layout and paints.
  10. Afterwards. The connection stays open for reuse until idle timeout; DNS answers and cacheable responses stay cached for their TTL and max-age.

Tip

Count the round trips: DNS (often 0 if cached), TCP 1, TLS 1, HTTP 1, so about 3 RTTs before the first byte on a cold HTTPS connection over TCP, and 2 with HTTP/3 (QUIC combines the transport and TLS handshakes). On a 100 ms RTT that is the difference between 300 ms and 200 ms, which is why CDNs put servers close to users.

Concept and tricky questions

Drills

ConceptGive four differences between TCP and UDP, and three situations where UDP is the better choice.

Answer

Answer. TCP is connection-oriented, reliable, ordered, a byte stream, and flow and congestion controlled, with a 20 to 60 byte header. UDP is connectionless, best effort, unordered, message-oriented, with an 8-byte header and no handshake. UDP wins for DNS queries (one request, one reply, no handshake), real-time media and games (late data is useless, so retransmission only adds delay), multicast (market data feeds, service discovery) and protocols that implement their own reliability, such as QUIC.

Why. TCP's guarantees come from state and waiting: a handshake before data, retransmission timers, and in-order delivery that holds back later data behind a loss. When the application would rather skip a lost packet than wait for it, those guarantees hurt. The wrong answer "UDP is faster" is too vague: UDP has no setup round trip and no head-of-line blocking, but raw throughput on a clean path is similar, and UDP without congestion control can be worse for everyone.

TrickyWhy does TCP need a three-way handshake? Why would two messages not be enough?

Answer

Answer. Both sides must choose an initial sequence number and learn that the other side received it. The client's ISN is confirmed by the SYN+ACK, and the server's ISN is confirmed only by the third message. With two messages the server would never know its ISN arrived, and a delayed duplicate SYN from an old connection would make the server create a connection that the client does not want.

Why. RFC 9293 section 3.5 describes exactly the old-duplicate case: with the third step, the client sees a SYN+ACK for a SYN it did not just send and answers with RST, so the bogus half-open connection dies. The "four messages, two piggybacked into one" view explains the count: SYN, ACK, SYN, ACK, with the server's ACK and SYN combined. An answer about "checking that the network works" misses the point that the purpose is synchronising sequence numbers (that is what SYN stands for).

TrickyWhich side of a TCP connection enters TIME_WAIT, how long does it stay there, and why is the duration 2·MSL?

Answer

Answer. The side that sends the first FIN (the active closer), whether client or server. It stays for 2·MSL, nominally 4 minutes by RFC (MSL is 2 minutes), 60 seconds on Linux. The two reasons: to re-ACK the peer's FIN if the last ACK is lost, and to let delayed segments of this connection expire before the same 4-tuple can be reused.

Why. If the final ACK is lost, the peer in LAST_ACK retransmits its FIN; that FIN can arrive up to one MSL after the lost ACK would have expired, so the active closer must survive two segment lifetimes. Without TIME_WAIT the retransmitted FIN would get a RST and the peer's close would be reported as an error. The common wrong answers are "the server" and "the client": it depends only on who closes first. Disabling TIME_WAIT (with SO_LINGER and a zero timeout, which sends RST) is almost always the wrong fix; reusing connections is the right one.

TrickyDoes SO_REUSEADDR let two server processes listen on the same TCP port on Linux? What does?

Answer

Answer. No. On Linux SO_REUSEADDR lets a socket bind a port that still has connections in TIME_WAIT (so a restarted server can bind at once), but a second listener on the same address and port still fails with EADDRINUSE. SO_REUSEPORT (Linux 3.9 and later) allows several sockets, owned by the same user, to bind and listen on the same port, and the kernel distributes new connections between them by hashing the 4-tuple.

Why. The two options solve different problems: restart after close (REUSEADDR) and load-balancing across workers without a shared accept queue (REUSEPORT, used by nginx with reuseport and by many multi-threaded servers). On BSD and macOS, SO_REUSEADDR also allows binding a specific address while another socket holds the wildcard address, which is where the confusion comes from. The option must be set before bind().

ConceptExplain the difference between flow control and congestion control. Which variable implements each, and who sets it?

Answer

Answer. Flow control stops the sender from overrunning the receiver's buffer; it uses the receive window (rwnd), which the receiver advertises in every segment. Congestion control stops the sender from overloading the network; it uses the congestion window (cwnd), which the sender estimates from ACKs, losses and delay and never transmits. The sender keeps in flight at most min(rwnd, cwnd).

Why. A fast server talking to a slow phone is limited by rwnd even on an empty network; a fast phone and fast server across a congested link are limited by cwnd even with large buffers. Mixing them up is the classic mistake, as is saying "slow start is flow control". The window scale option only affects rwnd. A useful follow-up: throughput ≤ window / RTT, so a 64 KB window over a 100 ms RTT gives at most about 5 Mbit/s regardless of link speed.

TrickyWhat is a SYN flood, and how do SYN cookies let a server survive one without keeping state? What does the server give up while cookies are in use?

Answer

Answer. An attacker sends many SYNs, usually from spoofed source addresses, and never completes the handshake. Each SYN creates a half-open entry in the listener's SYN queue, and once the queue is full, real clients' SYNs are dropped. With SYN cookies the server stores nothing: it encodes a coarse timestamp, an index for the client's MSS and a keyed hash of the 4-tuple into the ISN of its SYN+ACK. A real client's final ACK carries that value plus one, and the server checks the hash and rebuilds the connection from it. While cookies are active, the server loses options that need state from the SYN: window scale and SACK survive only if TCP timestamps are on (Linux stores them in the timestamp value), and the MSS is rounded to one of a few values.

Why. The attack exhausts state, not bandwidth, so the fix is to stop holding state before the client proves it can receive packets at its claimed address. A spoofed SYN never produces a valid ACK. Linux turns cookies on automatically when the SYN queue overflows (net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1, the default), so normal traffic keeps every option. A common wrong answer is "increase the backlog": that only delays the overflow. Another is "SYN cookies stop DDoS": they do nothing against floods that saturate the link or against attackers that complete real handshakes. RFC 4987 surveys this and the other mitigations.

Trickysend() returned the full length of your message. Has the peer received it? And if you call close() right after, is delivery guaranteed?

Answer

Answer. No and no. A successful send means only that the bytes were copied into the local kernel send buffer. After close the kernel keeps trying to deliver them in the background, but your process gets no report if that fails, and if unread data is still sitting in your receive buffer at close time, Linux sends RST instead of FIN, and the peer may discard data it has not read yet.

Why. TCP acknowledgements are between kernels, never surfaced to the application, so "delivered to the peer application" needs an application-level reply. The RST-on-close-with-unread-data behaviour (described in RFC 1122 and RFC 2525) catches servers that send an error response and close without draining the request body: the client sees "connection reset" and loses the response. The graceful pattern is shutdown(fd, SHUT_WR), read until 0, then close. SO_LINGER with a timeout makes close block until the data is acknowledged or the timeout expires.

ConceptA request/response protocol shows a steady 40 ms latency per request on Linux, although the server answers in microseconds. The client writes a header and then a body with two send calls. What is happening and how do you fix it?

Answer

Answer. Nagle's algorithm holds the second small write until the first is acknowledged, and the server's delayed-ACK timer (40 ms minimum on Linux) holds the ACK because the server has nothing to send until it has the whole request. Fix by writing the request in one call (writev or one buffer), or set TCP_NODELAY on the client.

Why. Nagle (RFC 896) allows only one small unacknowledged segment in flight; delayed ACK (RFC 1122) waits to piggyback. Each is sensible alone, and together they wait for each other until the timer fires. The pattern is write-write-read; write-read-write-read does not trigger it. Turning off delayed ACK on the server (TCP_QUICKACK) also helps but must be re-armed, and disabling Nagle without batching your writes produces many tiny packets, so the best fix is one write per message plus TCP_NODELAY.

TrickyDoes HTTP/2 solve head-of-line blocking?

Answer

Answer. Only at the HTTP layer. HTTP/2 multiplexes streams on one TCP connection, so a slow response no longer blocks others, but one lost TCP segment still stalls every stream until it is retransmitted. HTTP/3 over QUIC removes transport-level HOL blocking because QUIC orders each stream independently.

Why. TCP delivers one ordered byte stream and knows nothing about HTTP/2 streams; bytes after a hole wait in the kernel even if they belong to a different stream. On lossy links, HTTP/2 on one connection can perform worse than HTTP/1.1 on six. "Yes, HTTP/2 fixed it" is the half-right answer interviewers are listening for. QUIC still has HOL blocking within a single stream, which is inherent to ordered delivery.

Conceptss -tan on your server shows 20,000 sockets in CLOSE_WAIT and the count keeps rising. What does that mean and where is the bug?

Answer

Answer. The peers have closed their side (sent FIN, which the kernel ACKed), but your application never called close() on those sockets. The bug is in your code: a missing close on some path (often an error path or a recv returning 0 that is not handled), or threads stuck elsewhere. Eventually the process runs out of file descriptors (EMFILE).

Why. CLOSE_WAIT has no timeout in TCP: the kernel waits for the application indefinitely, since only the application knows whether it still wants to send. Contrast TIME_WAIT, which is normal, bounded by a timer, and holds no descriptor. Tuning kernel parameters does not fix CLOSE_WAIT. Look for the code path that reads EOF and does not close, and use RAII wrappers for descriptors in C++ so every path closes.

TrickyCan you call connect() on a UDP socket? What does it do, given that UDP has no connection?

Answer

Answer. Yes. It sends nothing; it records a default peer address. Afterwards you can use send/recv without addresses, the kernel discards datagrams from other sources, and asynchronous ICMP errors (such as port unreachable) are reported to you as ECONNREFUSED on a later call.

Why. A connected UDP socket also lets the kernel cache the route, which makes sending slightly cheaper, and it is how you find your own outgoing address: connect a UDP socket to a remote IP and call getsockname, with no packet sent. On an unconnected UDP socket ICMP errors are not delivered, because the kernel cannot tell which destination they belong to. Saying "connect is TCP-only" is the common wrong answer.

TrickyWhat does the backlog argument to listen() limit on Linux, and what happens to new clients when that limit is reached?

Answer

Answer. It sizes the accept queue: connections whose handshake has completed but that the application has not yet accepted, capped by net.core.somaxconn. When the queue is full, Linux drops the client's final ACK (and may drop new SYNs), so clients see retransmissions and connection delays of a second or more, not an immediate refusal.

Why. Since Linux 2.2 the half-open (SYN_RCVD) connections live in a separate SYN queue sized by tcp_max_syn_backlog, protected by SYN cookies. Older BSD semantics counted both together, which is the source of the classic "backlog is the number of pending connections" answer. The client may already believe it is connected (it got the SYN+ACK) and send data that the server silently drops until the handshake completes. net.ipv4.tcp_abort_on_overflow=1 makes Linux send RST instead. The real fix is to call accept faster.

TrickyThe peer has closed its socket. You call write() twice on yours. What happens on each call?

Answer

Answer. Over TCP, the first write usually succeeds: the data is buffered and sent. The peer's kernel has no socket for it any more and replies with RST. The second write then fails with EPIPE, and by default the kernel also sends SIGPIPE, which terminates the process (exit status 141 from a shell) unless it is ignored or MSG_NOSIGNAL is used.

Why. Receiving the peer's FIN only means "they will send no more"; they might still be reading (half-close), so TCP cannot fail the first write. Only the RST proves nobody is listening. Many servers have died "mysteriously" with no log line because of SIGPIPE. Standard practice: signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN) at startup or MSG_NOSIGNAL on every send (on macOS, the SO_NOSIGPIPE socket option is the traditional equivalent), and handle EPIPE and ECONNRESET as ordinary errors.

ConceptWalk through the TLS 1.3 handshake. How many round trips does it take, what is encrypted, and what is the risk of 0-RTT?

Answer

Answer. One round trip. ClientHello carries an ephemeral key share; ServerHello returns the server's share, after which both derive keys, and the server sends encrypted EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished. The client verifies the certificate chain and hostname and the signature, sends Finished, and its first request goes with it. Everything after ServerHello is encrypted, including the certificate; SNI in the ClientHello is still visible unless ECH is used. 0-RTT early data on resumption can be replayed by an attacker, so it must only carry idempotent requests.

Why. TLS 1.2 needed two round trips because the key exchange parameters came only after the server picked a cipher suite. TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) cut the options to a few (EC)DHE groups so the client can guess and send its share up front (if it guesses wrong, HelloRetryRequest costs an extra round trip). Ephemeral keys give forward secrecy. Certificates authenticate; Diffie-Hellman provides the key; symmetric AEAD protects the data. The common error is "the client encrypts a session key with the server's RSA public key", which is TLS 1.2 RSA key exchange and was removed in 1.3.

Tricky"TCP guarantees delivery." True or false?

Answer

Answer. False as stated. TCP guarantees that the bytes the receiver gets are in order, without gaps or duplicates, and that loss is retried while the connection lives. It cannot guarantee delivery if the connection breaks: bytes in the send buffer or in flight are lost, and the sender learns only that the connection failed, not which bytes the peer application processed.

Why. This is why payment systems, message queues and RPC frameworks add application-level acknowledgements, request ids and idempotent retries. A related trap is the "exactly once" claim: after a timeout the client cannot tell whether the server processed the request, so retries need idempotency keys. Also note that TCP's 16-bit checksum is weak; very rare corruption can pass it, which is one reason TLS (with its MAC) also gives integrity.

TrickyA server listens on port 443. Is the number of simultaneous clients limited to about 65 thousand because ports are 16-bit?

Answer

Answer. No. A connection is identified by the 4-tuple (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port), and all server-side connections share the server port. The real limits are memory, file descriptors (ulimit -n) and CPU. The 16-bit limit applies to a client host: about 28 thousand ephemeral ports (Linux default range) per (destination IP, destination port) pair, per source IP.

Why. accept returns a new socket that shares the listening port; the kernel demultiplexes incoming segments by the full tuple. Servers handle millions of connections on one port. The client-side limit bites load generators and proxies that open many connections to one backend, especially with TIME_WAIT on the client side; fixes include more source IPs, a wider ip_local_port_range and connection pooling.

ConceptExplain these pairs of HTTP status codes: 401 vs 403, 301 vs 308, 502 vs 504. Which methods are idempotent, and why does that matter?

Answer

Answer. 401 means "not authenticated" (send credentials; it comes with WWW-Authenticate), 403 means "authenticated, or authentication would not help, but not allowed". 301 and 308 are both permanent redirects, but clients may change a POST to GET after 301, while 308 requires keeping the method and body (307 is the temporary version of 308). 502 means the gateway got an invalid response from the upstream (for example a crash or reset), 504 means the upstream did not answer in time. GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not, and PATCH is not guaranteed to be.

Why. Idempotency (RFC 9110 section 9.2.2) decides what a client, proxy or library may retry automatically after a timeout or connection reset: retrying an idempotent request cannot double its effect, while retrying a POST might charge a card twice. That is why APIs add idempotency keys to POST. Idempotent is not the same as safe: DELETE changes state but is idempotent.

ConceptCompare select, poll and epoll. Why does epoll scale to 100,000 idle connections when the other two do not, and what extra rule does edge-triggered mode impose?

Answer

Answer. All three tell you which descriptors are ready. select passes three bitmaps limited to FD_SETSIZE (usually 1024) and rewrites them, so you rebuild them every call. poll passes an array with no fixed limit. Both copy the whole interest set into the kernel on every call and scan all of it, so each wait costs O(n) even when only one descriptor is ready. epoll keeps the interest set inside the kernel (epoll_ctl once per descriptor), and the kernel puts descriptors on a ready list as events arrive, so epoll_wait costs O(ready). In edge-triggered mode (EPOLLET) you are told only when a descriptor becomes ready, so you must use non-blocking sockets and read (or accept, or write) until EAGAIN. Otherwise the data left behind is never reported again.

Why. With 100,000 connections and 10 active, poll copies and scans 100,000 entries per wakeup, while epoll returns 10. The common wrong answer is "epoll is always faster": with a few busy descriptors poll is just as fast, and epoll costs one system call per interest change. Level-triggered epoll (the default) behaves like poll and is the safer choice. Edge-triggered mode saves wakeups but turns a missed drain into a hung connection. With several threads waiting on one epoll set, use EPOLLEXCLUSIVE or EPOLLONESHOT to avoid thundering-herd wakeups and two threads handling the same socket. All three report readiness, which differs from completion: io_uring and Windows IOCP perform the I/O and tell you when it is done.

TrickyHow many round trips pass before the first response byte of an HTTPS request on a new connection, with DNS already cached, for: TCP + TLS 1.2, TCP + TLS 1.3, TCP + TLS 1.3 with 0-RTT resumption, and HTTP/3 (QUIC) on a first and on a resumed connection?

Answer

Answer. TCP + TLS 1.2: 4 (TCP 1, TLS 2, HTTP 1). TCP + TLS 1.3: 3. TCP + TLS 1.3 with 0-RTT: 2, because the request rides in the first TLS flight but the TCP handshake still costs a round trip. QUIC first connection: 2 (one combined transport and crypto handshake, then the request). QUIC with 0-RTT: 1, since the request goes in the first packet.

Why. TLS 1.3 saves a round trip because the client sends its key share in ClientHello. 0-RTT reuses a pre-shared key from an earlier session, so it is available only on resumption. QUIC also merges the transport handshake into the TLS one. The trap is the name: "0-RTT TLS" over TCP still costs at least one round trip, unless TCP Fast Open also carries the ClientHello in the SYN, which is rarely deployed because middleboxes interfere with it. A cold DNS lookup adds at least one round trip to the resolver, plus the resolver's own queries on a cache miss. On a 100 ms path, going from 4 round trips to 1 saves 300 ms, which is why CDNs and HTTP/3 matter most on mobile networks. 0-RTT data can be replayed, so servers accept only idempotent requests in it.

Predict the output and find the bug

Drills

Programs that run use only a socketpair or pure computation, so they are deterministic. Programs that would block or need a network are compile-only. Byte-order answers assume a little-endian machine (x86-64, ARM64).

OutputThis decodes the first 20 bytes of a captured TCP segment. What does it print, and what kind of segment is it?

#include <arpa/inet.h>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstring>

int main() {
    const uint8_t seg[20] = {0xc3, 0x50, 0x01, 0xbb,
                             0x00, 0x00, 0x03, 0xe8,
                             0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00,
                             0x50, 0x02, 0xfa, 0xf0,
                             0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00};
    uint16_t sport, dport, win;
    uint32_t seq;
    std::memcpy(&sport, seg, 2);
    std::memcpy(&dport, seg + 2, 2);
    std::memcpy(&seq, seg + 4, 4);
    std::memcpy(&win, seg + 14, 2);
    int hlen = (seg[12] >> 4) * 4;
    uint8_t f = seg[13];
    std::printf("%d -> %d seq=%u hlen=%d win=%d\n", ntohs(sport), ntohs(dport), ntohl(seq), hlen, ntohs(win));
    std::printf("SYN=%d ACK=%d FIN=%d RST=%d\n", (f >> 1) & 1, (f >> 4) & 1, f & 1, (f >> 2) & 1);
}
Answer

Answer. A SYN from ephemeral port 50000 to HTTPS (443), the first segment of a handshake.

50000 -> 443 seq=1000 hlen=20 win=64240
SYN=1 ACK=0 FIN=0 RST=0

Why. Ports and numbers are big-endian on the wire: 0xc350 = 50000, 0x01bb = 443, 0x000003e8 = 1000. The data offset is the top nibble of byte 12, in 32-bit words: 5 × 4 = 20 bytes, so no options (a real SYN almost always carries MSS and other options, so you would usually see 0xa0, 40 bytes). The flag byte 0x02 is SYN alone; the bit order from the low end is FIN, SYN, RST, PSH, ACK, URG, ECE, CWR. Using memcpy plus ntohs avoids both the byte-order bug and the misaligned-pointer cast that *(uint16_t*)(seg + 2) would be.

OutputFill in the numbers: what does this connection trace print?

#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>

int main() {
    uint32_t c = 1000, s = 5000;
    std::printf("C->S SYN seq=%u\n", c);
    std::printf("S->C SYN+ACK seq=%u ack=%u\n", s, c + 1);
    c += 1;
    s += 1;
    std::printf("C->S ACK seq=%u ack=%u\n", c, s);
    for (int i = 0; i < 2; ++i) {
        std::printf("C->S data seq=%u len=100\n", c);
        c += 100;
    }
    std::printf("S->C ACK ack=%u\n", c);
    std::printf("C->S FIN seq=%u\n", c);
    c += 1;
    std::printf("S->C ACK ack=%u\n", c);
}
Answer

Answer.

C->S SYN seq=1000
S->C SYN+ACK seq=5000 ack=1001
C->S ACK seq=1001 ack=5001
C->S data seq=1001 len=100
C->S data seq=1101 len=100
S->C ACK ack=1201
C->S FIN seq=1201
S->C ACK ack=1202

Why. The SYN occupies sequence number 1000, so the first data byte is 1001, and the server's SYN+ACK acknowledges 1001 ("next byte I expect"). The server's own SYN uses 5000, so the client acknowledges 5001. Two 100-byte segments cover 1001 to 1200; one cumulative ACK of 1201 acknowledges both (with delayed ACK, a receiver typically sends one ACK per two full segments). The FIN takes 1201 and is acknowledged with 1202. The pure ACK in the third line consumes nothing, which is why the first data segment also carries 1001. In real captures the ISNs are random 32-bit values; Wireshark shows "relative sequence numbers" starting at 0 to make traces like this readable.

OutputTwo sends of two bytes each, then one receive of up to 16 bytes, on a stream socket pair and on a datagram socket pair. What does each first receive return?

#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <cstdio>
#include <initializer_list>

int main() {
    for (int type : {SOCK_STREAM, SOCK_DGRAM}) {
        int sv[2];
        if (socketpair(AF_UNIX, type, 0, sv) < 0) return 1;
        send(sv[0], "ab", 2, 0);
        send(sv[0], "cd", 2, 0);
        char buf[16];
        ssize_t n = recv(sv[1], buf, sizeof buf, 0);
        std::printf("%s: first recv got \"%.*s\"\n", type == SOCK_STREAM ? "stream" : "dgram", int(n), buf);
        close(sv[0]);
        close(sv[1]);
    }
}
Answer

Answer.

stream: first recv got "abcd"
dgram: first recv got "ab"

Why. A stream socket has no message boundaries: both writes sit in one receive buffer and one read returns everything available. A datagram socket returns exactly one datagram per receive, and the second recv would return "cd". TCP behaves like the stream case and UDP like the datagram case. On a local socket pair the merge is reliable; over a network, a TCP reader may see "abcd", "ab" then "cd", or "a" then "bcd", which is why protocols on TCP need explicit framing. With UDP, a buffer smaller than the datagram silently truncates it (the excess is discarded, and MSG_TRUNC is set in recvmsg flags).

Find the bugThe socket has data waiting, yet select reports nothing ready. Why?

#include <sys/select.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <cstdio>

int main() {
    int sv[2];
    if (socketpair(AF_UNIX, SOCK_STREAM, 0, sv) < 0) return 1;
    send(sv[0], "x", 1, 0);  // sv[1] is now readable
    int fd = sv[1];
    fd_set rd;
    FD_ZERO(&rd);
    FD_SET(fd, &rd);
    timeval tv{0, 0};        // check without blocking
    int ready = select(fd, &rd, nullptr, nullptr, &tv);
    std::printf("ready = %d\n", ready);
    close(sv[0]);
    close(sv[1]);
}
Answer

Answer. The first argument of select is the highest descriptor plus one, not the highest descriptor. With nfds = fd the kernel checks descriptors 0 to fd − 1 and never looks at fd.

ready = 0

Why. nfds is a count of bits to scan in the bitmaps. Here sv[1] is the highest open descriptor, so it is skipped and the call times out immediately with 0; with select(fd + 1, ...) it returns 1. Two more select traps: the sets are modified in place, so you must rebuild them before every call, and FD_SET on a descriptor ≥ FD_SETSIZE (usually 1024) writes past the bitmap, which is memory corruption. Use poll or epoll in new code.

Find the bugwrite_some behaves like send under pressure: it may write fewer bytes than asked. What does the peer receive?

#include <algorithm>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstring>
#include <string>

static std::string wire;  // what the peer receives

static long write_some(const char* p, size_t n) {
    size_t k = std::min<size_t>(n, 4);
    wire.append(p, k);
    return long(k);
}

static void send_all(const char* buf, size_t len) {
    size_t sent = 0;
    while (sent < len) {
        long n = write_some(buf, len - sent);
        if (n < 0) return;
        sent += size_t(n);
    }
}

int main() {
    const char* msg = "hello world";
    send_all(msg, std::strlen(msg));
    std::printf("peer got \"%s\"\n", wire.c_str());
}
Answer

Answer. The loop tracks how much was sent but always passes buf, not buf + sent, so it resends the start of the message.

peer got "hellhellhel"

Why. The calls write "hell" (4), then "hell" again (4), then "hel" (the remaining length is 3), and the loop ends believing 11 bytes went out. The fix is write_some(buf + sent, len - sent). A real send_all must also retry on EINTR, treat EAGAIN on a non-blocking socket as "wait for POLLOUT", and stop on other errors. Partial writes are rare on blocking sockets, so this bug survives testing and appears under load.

Find the bugThis echo server compiles, accepts connections, and never echoes anything. After running for a while it stops accepting. Find two bugs.

#include <arpa/inet.h>
#include <netinet/in.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <unistd.h>

int main() {
    int lfd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
    sockaddr_in a{};
    a.sin_family = AF_INET;
    a.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(INADDR_ANY);
    a.sin_port = htons(9000);
    bind(lfd, reinterpret_cast<sockaddr*>(&a), sizeof a);
    listen(lfd, 16);
    for (;;) {
        int cfd = accept(lfd, nullptr, nullptr);
        if (cfd < 0) continue;
        char buf[1024];
        ssize_t n = recv(lfd, buf, sizeof buf, 0);
        if (n > 0) send(cfd, buf, size_t(n), 0);
    }
}
Answer

Answer. (1) It reads from the listening socket lfd instead of the connected socket cfd; recv on a listening socket fails with ENOTCONN, so nothing is echoed. (2) It never closes cfd, so every client leaks a descriptor; at the ulimit -n limit (often 1024) accept fails with EMFILE, and the continue turns that into a busy loop at 100% CPU.

Why. accept returns a new descriptor per connection; the listening socket only produces connections, never data. Leaked sockets also leave clients hanging, since no FIN is ever sent. Further problems: no error checks on bind (a port in use goes unnoticed), no SO_REUSEADDR, a single recv per connection instead of a loop until 0, and no send_all. In C++, wrap descriptors in an RAII type so the close cannot be forgotten.

Find the bugAfter a restart, this server fails with "bind: Address already in use" for about a minute, even though it sets SO_REUSEADDR. Why?

#include <arpa/inet.h>
#include <netinet/in.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <cstdio>

int main() {
    int fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
    sockaddr_in a{};
    a.sin_family = AF_INET;
    a.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(INADDR_ANY);
    a.sin_port = htons(8080);
    if (bind(fd, reinterpret_cast<sockaddr*>(&a), sizeof a) < 0) {
        std::perror("bind");
        return 1;
    }
    int yes = 1;
    setsockopt(fd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_REUSEADDR, &yes, sizeof yes);
    listen(fd, SOMAXCONN);
    for (;;) {
        int c = accept(fd, nullptr, nullptr);
        if (c >= 0) close(c);
    }
}
Answer

Answer. The option is set after bind. The address check happens inside bind, so SO_REUSEADDR must be set between socket and bind.

Why. This server closes every connection first (close(c) right after accept), so each of those connections sits in TIME_WAIT on the server for 60 seconds on Linux. A restarted process trying to bind port 8080 then conflicts with them unless SO_REUSEADDR was already set when it called bind. Many socket options have the same "before the call that uses them" rule: SO_REUSEPORT before bind, and buffer sizes (SO_RCVBUF) before listen/connect because the window scale is negotiated in the SYN.

Find the bugA client reads the body length from a response. It works against one server and reads an empty body from another. What does it print?

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

static size_t content_length(std::string_view head) {
    size_t pos = head.find("Content-Length:");
    if (pos == std::string_view::npos) return 0;
    return std::stoul(std::string(head.substr(pos + 15)));
}

int main() {
    std::string_view a = "HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 42\r\n\r\n";
    std::string_view b = "HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\ncontent-length: 42\r\n\r\n";
    std::printf("%zu %zu\n", content_length(a), content_length(b));
}
Answer

Answer. HTTP header field names are case-insensitive (RFC 9110 section 5.1), and the lookup is case-sensitive.

42 0

Why. Servers, proxies and especially HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 (which require lowercase names on the wire) send content-length. Parse each header line into a name and a value, lowercase the name, and trim optional whitespace from the value. The substring search has more bugs: it would match "X-Content-Length:", it would find the text inside the body, and a missing header should not mean "length 0" (it means chunked encoding or read-until-close). std::stoul also throws on garbage, which a network parser must not do on hostile input.

OutputA server stores the peer address from accept in a sockaddr_in. What does this print, and what breaks when IPv6 clients arrive?

#include <netinet/in.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <cstdio>

int main() {
    std::printf("sockaddr %zu\n", sizeof(sockaddr));
    std::printf("sockaddr_in %zu\n", sizeof(sockaddr_in));
    std::printf("sockaddr_in6 %zu\n", sizeof(sockaddr_in6));
    std::printf("sockaddr_storage %zu\n", sizeof(sockaddr_storage));
}
Answer

Answer.

sockaddr 16
sockaddr_in 16
sockaddr_in6 28
sockaddr_storage 128

Why. An IPv6 address alone is 16 bytes, so sockaddr_in6 (family, port, flow info, address, scope id) does not fit in the 16-byte sockaddr or sockaddr_in. accept truncates the address to the length you pass and reports the real length, so code using sockaddr_in on a dual-stack listener silently gets a cut-off address. Use sockaddr_storage, which is large enough and suitably aligned for every family, and switch on ss_family. The sizes are the same on Linux and macOS (macOS adds a length byte but keeps the totals).

OutputThe peer has gone away. What does this print? What happens if you delete the signal line?

#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <cerrno>
#include <csignal>
#include <cstdio>

int main() {
    std::signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN);
    int sv[2];
    if (socketpair(AF_UNIX, SOCK_STREAM, 0, sv) < 0) return 1;
    close(sv[1]);
    ssize_t w = write(sv[0], "x", 1);
    std::printf("write returned %zd, EPIPE=%d\n", w, errno == EPIPE);
    char c;
    ssize_t r = read(sv[0], &c, 1);
    std::printf("read returned %zd\n", r);
    close(sv[0]);
}
Answer

Answer.

write returned -1, EPIPE=1
read returned 0

Why. Writing to a stream socket whose peer is closed raises SIGPIPE; ignored, the write fails with EPIPE instead. Without the signal line the default action of SIGPIPE terminates the process on the write, before anything is printed, with no error message. Reading returns 0, which is end of stream, not an error. With a local socket pair the kernel knows at once that the peer is gone; over TCP, as the drill in the concept section explains, the first write usually succeeds and the error appears on a later one, after the peer's RST.

Write the code

Coding

Every reference solution here runs: framing and parsing are tested on buffers, and the socket solutions use a socketpair or a loopback server on an ephemeral port with receive timeouts, so they cannot hang.

CodeImplement a length-prefixed message framer for a TCP stream. Each frame is a 4-byte big-endian length followed by that many payload bytes. FrameDecoder::feed(data, n, out) is called with whatever each recv returned (any split, including one byte at a time) and appends every complete frame to out. Reject frames larger than a configured maximum. Show that the output does not depend on how the stream is split.

Answer

Approach. Keep one buffer of unconsumed bytes. After appending new data, loop: if fewer than 4 bytes are buffered, stop; decode the length; if the whole payload is not buffered yet, stop; otherwise emit the frame and advance. Erase the consumed prefix once per call rather than once per frame, which keeps the cost linear. Check the length against the maximum before waiting for the payload, so a hostile peer cannot make you buffer 4 GiB.

#include <algorithm>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

static std::string encode_frame(const std::string& payload) {
    uint32_t n = static_cast<uint32_t>(payload.size());
    std::string out = {char(n >> 24), char(n >> 16), char(n >> 8), char(n)};
    return out + payload;
}

class FrameDecoder {
public:
    explicit FrameDecoder(uint32_t max_frame) : max_(max_frame) {}

    // Returns false if the stream is corrupt; the connection should then be closed.
    bool feed(const char* data, size_t n, std::vector<std::string>& out) {
        buf_.append(data, n);
        size_t pos = 0;
        while (buf_.size() - pos >= 4) {
            const auto* p = reinterpret_cast<const unsigned char*>(buf_.data() + pos);
            uint32_t len = uint32_t(p[0]) << 24 | uint32_t(p[1]) << 16 | uint32_t(p[2]) << 8 | p[3];
            if (len > max_) return false;
            if (buf_.size() - pos - 4 < len) break;  // payload not complete yet
            out.emplace_back(buf_, pos + 4, len);
            pos += 4 + size_t(len);
        }
        buf_.erase(0, pos);
        return true;
    }
    size_t buffered() const { return buf_.size(); }

private:
    std::string buf_;
    uint32_t max_;
};

static std::vector<std::string> decode(const std::string& stream, const std::vector<size_t>& sizes, bool& ok) {
    FrameDecoder d(1 << 20);
    std::vector<std::string> frames;
    size_t pos = 0, k = 0;
    ok = true;
    while (ok && pos < stream.size()) {
        size_t n = std::min(sizes[k++ % sizes.size()], stream.size() - pos);
        ok = d.feed(stream.data() + pos, n, frames);
        pos += n;
    }
    ok = ok && d.buffered() == 0;
    return frames;
}

int main() {
    std::vector<std::string> msgs = {"hello", "", "a longer message with spaces", std::string(300, 'z')};
    std::string stream;
    for (const auto& m : msgs) stream += encode_frame(m);
    std::vector<std::pair<const char*, std::vector<size_t>>> patterns = {
        {"1 byte at a time", {1}}, {"chunks 1,2,3,5,7", {1, 2, 3, 5, 7}}, {"all at once", {stream.size()}}};
    for (const auto& [name, sizes] : patterns) {
        bool ok;
        auto frames = decode(stream, sizes, ok);
        std::printf("%s: %zu frames, %s\n", name, frames.size(), ok && frames == msgs ? "match" : "MISMATCH");
    }
    FrameDecoder d(1 << 20);
    std::vector<std::string> out;
    const char evil[4] = {char(0xFF), char(0xFF), char(0xFF), char(0xFF)};
    std::printf("4 GiB length accepted: %s\n", d.feed(evil, 4, out) ? "yes" : "no");
}
1 byte at a time: 4 frames, match
chunks 1,2,3,5,7: 4 frames, match
all at once: 4 frames, match
4 GiB length accepted: no

Complexity and pitfalls. O(total bytes) time; memory is bounded by one maximum frame plus one recv buffer. Pitfalls: assuming the 4-byte header arrives in one piece, reading the length with memcpy into a uint32_t and forgetting ntohl, erasing from the front of the buffer after every frame (quadratic with many small frames), treating a zero-length frame as "no frame", and trusting the length before checking it. A ring buffer or a read offset with occasional compaction avoids the copy in erase.

Estimated rating: ~1500 · simple state machine, but partial headers and hostile lengths are where solutions break

CodeWrite send_all(fd, p, n) and recv_exact(fd, p, n) for a blocking stream socket. send_all must handle partial writes and EINTR and never raise SIGPIPE. recv_exact must return the number of bytes read, fewer than n only if the peer closed early, and −1 on error. Test by moving 1 MiB through a socket pair, which is far bigger than the socket buffer.

Answer

Approach. Both are loops that advance a pointer by whatever each call managed to transfer. EINTR means a signal interrupted the call before any data moved, so retry. recv returning 0 is end of stream. Because 1 MiB does not fit in the kernel buffer, the writer must run concurrently with the reader, so it gets its own thread.

#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <cerrno>
#include <cstdio>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

static bool send_all(int fd, const char* p, size_t n) {
    while (n > 0) {
        ssize_t w = send(fd, p, n, MSG_NOSIGNAL);
        if (w < 0) {
            if (errno == EINTR) continue;
            return false;
        }
        p += w;
        n -= size_t(w);
    }
    return true;
}

static ssize_t recv_exact(int fd, char* p, size_t n) {
    size_t got = 0;
    while (got < n) {
        ssize_t r = recv(fd, p + got, n - got, 0);
        if (r == 0) break;  // peer closed
        if (r < 0) {
            if (errno == EINTR) continue;
            return -1;
        }
        got += size_t(r);
    }
    return ssize_t(got);
}

int main() {
    int sv[2];
    if (socketpair(AF_UNIX, SOCK_STREAM, 0, sv) < 0) return 1;
    std::vector<char> data(1 << 20);
    for (size_t i = 0; i < data.size(); ++i) data[i] = char(i * 31 + 7);
    std::thread writer([&data, fd = sv[0]] {
        send_all(fd, data.data(), data.size());
        close(fd);  // FIN: the reader will see end of stream
    });
    std::vector<char> in(data.size());
    ssize_t got = recv_exact(sv[1], in.data(), in.size());
    char extra;
    ssize_t tail = recv_exact(sv[1], &extra, 1);
    writer.join();
    std::printf("received %zd bytes, match=%d, next read %zd (EOF)\n", got, int(in == data), tail);
    close(sv[1]);
}
received 1048576 bytes, match=1, next read 0 (EOF)

Complexity and pitfalls. O(n) bytes copied, in as many system calls as the buffers require (hundreds here). Pitfalls: not advancing the pointer (see the reading drills), treating 0 as an error or as "try again" (an infinite loop on a closed socket), retrying on EAGAIN in a busy loop on a non-blocking socket (wait with poll instead), and forgetting MSG_NOSIGNAL. The writer thread captures the descriptor by value, so the two threads share no mutable state and the program is clean under ThreadSanitizer.

Estimated rating: ~1200 · short loops, judged on error handling and EOF semantics

CodeWrite a single-threaded TCP echo server that serves many clients at once with poll and non-blocking sockets. It must cope with partial writes (keep unsent bytes per client and wait for POLLOUT), clients that disconnect, and a clean shutdown request. Test it in-process: run the server on 127.0.0.1 with an ephemeral port in one thread, and two clients with receive timeouts in the main thread.

Answer

Approach. Keep a pollfd array: the listening socket, a pipe used as a stop signal, then one entry per client, with a parallel array of pending output. On readiness, accept all new clients, read each readable client until EAGAIN and append to its pending output, then write as much pending output as the socket takes. Ask for POLLOUT only while output is pending (otherwise poll returns at once forever). Close clients on EOF or error, and compact the arrays after each round.

#include <arpa/inet.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <netinet/in.h>
#include <poll.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <cerrno>
#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

static void set_nonblocking(int fd) { fcntl(fd, F_SETFL, fcntl(fd, F_GETFL, 0) | O_NONBLOCK); }

static bool would_block() { return errno == EAGAIN || errno == EWOULDBLOCK || errno == EINTR; }

// Echoes every byte back to its sender until stop_fd becomes readable.
static void echo_server(int lfd, int stop_fd) {
    std::vector<pollfd> fds = {{lfd, POLLIN, 0}, {stop_fd, POLLIN, 0}};
    std::vector<std::string> out(2);  // pending output, parallel to fds
    for (;;) {
        if (poll(fds.data(), nfds_t(fds.size()), -1) < 0) {
            if (errno == EINTR) continue;
            break;
        }
        if (fds[1].revents) break;
        if (fds[0].revents & POLLIN) {
            for (int c; (c = accept(lfd, nullptr, nullptr)) >= 0;) {
                set_nonblocking(c);
                fds.push_back({c, POLLIN, 0});
                out.emplace_back();
            }
        }
        for (size_t i = 2; i < fds.size(); ++i) {
            bool dead = false;
            if (fds[i].revents & (POLLIN | POLLHUP | POLLERR)) {
                char buf[4096];
                for (;;) {
                    ssize_t n = recv(fds[i].fd, buf, sizeof buf, 0);
                    if (n > 0) { out[i].append(buf, size_t(n)); continue; }
                    if (n == 0 || !would_block()) dead = true;  // EOF or a real error
                    break;
                }
            }
            while (!out[i].empty()) {
                ssize_t w = send(fds[i].fd, out[i].data(), out[i].size(), MSG_NOSIGNAL);
                if (w > 0) { out[i].erase(0, size_t(w)); continue; }
                if (w < 0 && !would_block()) dead = true;
                break;
            }
            fds[i].events = short(out[i].empty() ? POLLIN : (POLLIN | POLLOUT));
            if (dead) {
                close(fds[i].fd);
                fds[i].fd = -1;
            }
        }
        size_t keep = 2;
        for (size_t i = 2; i < fds.size(); ++i) {
            if (fds[i].fd < 0) continue;
            fds[keep] = fds[i];
            out[keep] = std::move(out[i]);
            ++keep;
        }
        fds.resize(keep);
        out.resize(keep);
    }
    for (size_t i = 2; i < fds.size(); ++i) close(fds[i].fd);
}

static std::string roundtrip(int fd, const std::string& msg) {
    if (send(fd, msg.data(), msg.size(), 0) != ssize_t(msg.size())) return "send failed";
    std::string got(msg.size(), '\0');
    size_t have = 0;
    while (have < got.size()) {
        ssize_t r = recv(fd, got.data() + have, got.size() - have, 0);
        if (r <= 0) return "timeout or error";
        have += size_t(r);
    }
    return got;
}

int main() {
    int lfd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
    sockaddr_in addr{};
    addr.sin_family = AF_INET;
    addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(INADDR_LOOPBACK);
    addr.sin_port = 0;  // let the kernel choose a free port
    socklen_t len = sizeof addr;
    if (lfd < 0 || bind(lfd, reinterpret_cast<sockaddr*>(&addr), sizeof addr) < 0 || listen(lfd, 16) < 0 ||
        getsockname(lfd, reinterpret_cast<sockaddr*>(&addr), &len) < 0) {
        std::perror("setup");
        return 1;
    }
    set_nonblocking(lfd);
    int stop[2];
    if (pipe(stop) < 0) return 1;
    std::thread server(echo_server, lfd, stop[0]);

    auto client = [&addr] {
        int fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
        timeval tv{2, 0};
        setsockopt(fd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_RCVTIMEO, &tv, sizeof tv);  // a broken server cannot hang the test
        connect(fd, reinterpret_cast<const sockaddr*>(&addr), sizeof addr);
        return fd;
    };
    int a = client(), b = client();
    std::printf("a: %s\n", roundtrip(a, "hello from a").c_str());
    std::printf("b: %s\n", roundtrip(b, "hello from b").c_str());
    std::string big(100000, 'x');
    std::printf("a: %s\n", roundtrip(a, big) == big ? "100000 bytes echoed" : "mismatch");
    close(a);
    std::printf("b after a left: %s\n", roundtrip(b, "still here").c_str());
    close(b);

    if (write(stop[1], "q", 1) != 1) return 1;
    server.join();
    close(stop[0]);
    close(stop[1]);
    close(lfd);
}
a: hello from a
b: hello from b
a: 100000 bytes echoed
b after a left: still here

Complexity and pitfalls. Each poll costs O(clients); for tens of thousands of clients switch to epoll or kqueue, keeping the same structure. Pitfalls: a blocking listening socket (one spurious wakeup and accept blocks the whole server), always requesting POLLOUT (busy loop), dropping unsent bytes after a short write, erasing from fds while iterating, and unbounded pending output: a client that sends but never reads makes this server buffer forever. Production servers stop reading from a client while its output exceeds a limit, which pushes backpressure to the client through TCP flow control.

Estimated rating: ~1900 · event-loop bookkeeping with several subtle readiness rules

CodeParse a complete HTTP/1.1 response held in a buffer: the status line, headers (case-insensitive names, trimmed values) and the body, using Transfer-Encoding: chunked if present, else Content-Length, else everything until the end. Return nothing for malformed or truncated input; never throw.

Answer

Approach. Split head and body at the first blank line (CRLF CRLF). Validate the status line by position: "HTTP/x.y", space, three digits, optional reason. Store header names lowercased. For chunked bodies loop: read a hex size line (ignoring extensions after ';'), copy that many bytes, require CRLF, stop at size 0. Parse numbers by hand, so bad input yields "invalid" instead of an exception.

#include <cctype>
#include <cstdio>
#include <optional>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Response {
    int status = 0;
    std::string reason;
    std::vector<std::pair<std::string, std::string>> headers;  // names lowercased
    std::string body;
    const std::string* header(std::string_view name) const {
        for (const auto& [k, v] : headers)
            if (k == name) return &v;
        return nullptr;
    }
};

static std::string lower(std::string_view s) {
    std::string r(s);
    for (char& c : r) c = char(std::tolower(static_cast<unsigned char>(c)));
    return r;
}

static std::string_view trim(std::string_view s) {
    while (!s.empty() && (s.front() == ' ' || s.front() == '\t')) s.remove_prefix(1);
    while (!s.empty() && (s.back() == ' ' || s.back() == '\t')) s.remove_suffix(1);
    return s;
}

static std::optional<size_t> parse_num(std::string_view s, int base) {
    if (s.empty() || s.size() > 12) return std::nullopt;
    size_t v = 0;
    for (char c : s) {
        int d;
        if (c >= '0' && c <= '9') d = c - '0';
        else if (base == 16 && c >= 'a' && c <= 'f') d = c - 'a' + 10;
        else if (base == 16 && c >= 'A' && c <= 'F') d = c - 'A' + 10;
        else return std::nullopt;
        v = v * size_t(base) + size_t(d);
    }
    return v;
}

static std::optional<std::string> decode_chunked(std::string_view s) {
    std::string body;
    for (;;) {
        size_t eol = s.find("\r\n");
        if (eol == std::string_view::npos) return std::nullopt;
        std::string_view line = s.substr(0, eol);
        auto n = parse_num(trim(line.substr(0, line.find(';'))), 16);
        if (!n) return std::nullopt;
        s.remove_prefix(eol + 2);
        if (*n == 0) return body;  // trailers (if any) are ignored here
        if (s.size() < *n + 2 || s.substr(*n, 2) != "\r\n") return std::nullopt;
        body.append(s.substr(0, *n));
        s.remove_prefix(*n + 2);
    }
}

static std::optional<Response> parse_response(std::string_view raw) {
    size_t end = raw.find("\r\n\r\n");
    if (end == std::string_view::npos) return std::nullopt;
    std::string_view head = raw.substr(0, end), rest = raw.substr(end + 4);
    size_t eol = head.find("\r\n");
    std::string_view status = head.substr(0, eol);
    if (status.size() < 12 || status.substr(0, 5) != "HTTP/" || status[8] != ' ') return std::nullopt;
    auto code = parse_num(status.substr(9, 3), 10);
    if (!code || *code < 100 || *code > 599 || (status.size() > 12 && status[12] != ' ')) return std::nullopt;
    Response r;
    r.status = int(*code);
    r.reason = std::string(status.size() > 13 ? status.substr(13) : std::string_view{});
    head = eol == std::string_view::npos ? std::string_view{} : head.substr(eol + 2);
    while (!head.empty()) {
        size_t e = head.find("\r\n");
        std::string_view line = head.substr(0, e);
        head = e == std::string_view::npos ? std::string_view{} : head.substr(e + 2);
        size_t colon = line.find(':');
        if (colon == std::string_view::npos || colon == 0) return std::nullopt;
        r.headers.emplace_back(lower(line.substr(0, colon)), std::string(trim(line.substr(colon + 1))));
    }
    if (const std::string* te = r.header("transfer-encoding"); te && lower(*te).find("chunked") != std::string::npos) {
        auto body = decode_chunked(rest);
        if (!body) return std::nullopt;
        r.body = std::move(*body);
    } else if (const std::string* cl = r.header("content-length")) {
        auto n = parse_num(*cl, 10);
        if (!n || rest.size() < *n) return std::nullopt;
        r.body = std::string(rest.substr(0, *n));
    } else {
        r.body = std::string(rest);  // delimited by the server closing the connection
    }
    return r;
}

int main() {
    const char* tests[] = {
        "HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: text/plain\r\nContent-Length: 5\r\n\r\nhelloEXTRA",
        "HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nTransfer-Encoding: chunked\r\n\r\n7\r\nMozilla\r\n11\r\nDeveloper Network\r\n0\r\n\r\n",
        "HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found\r\ncontent-length:   9  \r\n\r\nnot found",
        "HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 10\r\n\r\nshort",
        "HTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n\r\n",
    };
    for (const char* t : tests) {
        auto r = parse_response(t);
        if (!r) {
            std::printf("invalid\n");
            continue;
        }
        const std::string* type = r->header("content-type");
        std::printf("%d %s type=%s body=\"%s\"\n", r->status, r->reason.c_str(), type ? type->c_str() : "-", r->body.c_str());
    }
}
200 OK type=text/plain body="hello"
200 OK type=- body="MozillaDeveloper Network"
404 Not Found type=- body="not found"
invalid
invalid

Complexity and pitfalls. O(n). In the first test "EXTRA" is not part of the body: on a keep-alive connection it is the start of the next response, which is why Content-Length must be honoured exactly. Security pitfalls: a message with both Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length must use chunked (and proxies should reject it), because disagreeing parsers enable request smuggling; chunk sizes must be bounded; and headers must not be accepted without a colon.
