A streaming parser would also need to work incrementally, like the frame decoder above.

Estimated rating: ~1600 · careful string handling with a protocol state machine for chunked bodies

CodeModel TCP Reno's congestion window in segments at RTT granularity. Events: R (a round trip in which everything was acknowledged), D (three duplicate ACKs) and T (retransmission timeout). Start with cwnd 1 and ssthresh 16, print cwnd after each event, and report the send window for a given receive window.

Answer

Approach. Follow RFC 5681 with FlightSize approximated by cwnd. Per RTT: below ssthresh, double (capped at ssthresh, so slow start ends exactly there); otherwise add one. Triple duplicate ACK: ssthresh = max(cwnd/2, 2) and, after fast recovery completes, cwnd = ssthresh. Timeout: same ssthresh, cwnd = 1. The usable window is min(cwnd, rwnd).

#include <algorithm>
#include <cstdio>
#include <string>

class Reno {
public:
    explicit Reno(int ssthresh) : ssthresh_(ssthresh) {}
    void on_rtt_all_acked() {
        if (cwnd_ < ssthresh_) cwnd_ = std::min(cwnd_ * 2, ssthresh_);  // slow start
        else cwnd_ += 1;                                                // congestion avoidance
    }
    void on_triple_dupack() {  // fast retransmit, then fast recovery ends at ssthresh
        ssthresh_ = std::max(cwnd_ / 2, 2);
        cwnd_ = ssthresh_;
    }
    void on_timeout() {
        ssthresh_ = std::max(cwnd_ / 2, 2);
        cwnd_ = 1;
    }
    int cwnd() const { return cwnd_; }
    int ssthresh() const { return ssthresh_; }
    int send_window(int rwnd) const { return std::min(cwnd_, rwnd); }

private:
    int cwnd_ = 1;
    int ssthresh_;
};

int main() {
    Reno r(16);
    const std::string events = "RRRRRRRRRRDRRRRRTRRRRR";
    for (char e : events) {
        if (e == 'R') r.on_rtt_all_acked();
        else if (e == 'D') r.on_triple_dupack();
        else r.on_timeout();
        std::printf("%c:%d ", e, r.cwnd());
    }
    std::printf("\nssthresh=%d, send window with rwnd=6: %d\n", r.ssthresh(), r.send_window(6));
}
R:2 R:4 R:8 R:16 R:17 R:18 R:19 R:20 R:21 R:22 D:11 R:12 R:13 R:14 R:15 R:16 T:1 R:2 R:4 R:8 R:9 R:10
ssthresh=8, send window with rwnd=6: 6

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) per event. This is exactly the sawtooth in the congestion control figure. Real stacks count in bytes and update per ACK (slow start adds one MSS per ACK, congestion avoidance adds MSS·MSS/cwnd), inflate cwnd by one MSS per duplicate ACK during fast recovery, and use CUBIC rather than Reno's linear growth by default on Linux. Interview follow-ups: why a timeout is punished harder than duplicate ACKs (the ACK clock has stopped), and why the final window is 6 here (flow control, the receiver's limit, wins over congestion control).

Estimated rating: ~1300 · simulation is easy once the rules are known; the test is knowing them

CodeImplement a TCP receive-side reassembler. on_segment(seq, data) receives segments in any order, possibly duplicated, overlapping or outside the window, and appends bytes to the in-order stream as soon as they become contiguous. ack() returns the next expected sequence number. Sequence numbers are 32-bit and wrap around; test with an ISN just below 232.

Answer

Approach. Compare sequence numbers with serial arithmetic: the offset of a segment from the next expected byte is int32_t(seq - next), which is correct across wrap-around while the window is below 231. Trim the part of a segment we already have, drop it if nothing remains or it falls outside the window, then store it in an ordered map keyed by a 64-bit absolute stream offset (which never wraps). After each insert, drain map entries that start at or before the delivered offset.

#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <map>
#include <string>

class Reassembler {
public:
    Reassembler(uint32_t isn, uint32_t window) : next_(isn), window_(window) {}

    void on_segment(uint32_t seq, std::string data) {
        int32_t off = int32_t(seq - next_);  // serial number arithmetic
        if (off < 0) {
            uint64_t have = uint64_t(-int64_t(off));
            if (have >= data.size()) return;  // pure duplicate
            data.erase(0, size_t(have));
            off = 0;
        }
        if (uint64_t(off) + data.size() > window_) return;  // outside the receive window
        std::string& slot = pending_[delivered_ + uint64_t(off)];
        if (data.size() > slot.size()) slot = std::move(data);
        while (!pending_.empty() && pending_.begin()->first <= delivered_) {
            auto it = pending_.begin();
            uint64_t skip = delivered_ - it->first;
            if (skip < it->second.size()) {
                uint64_t added = it->second.size() - skip;
                stream_.append(it->second, size_t(skip), std::string::npos);
                delivered_ += added;
                next_ += uint32_t(added);
            }
            pending_.erase(it);
        }
    }
    uint32_t ack() const { return next_; }
    const std::string& stream() const { return stream_; }

private:
    uint32_t next_;
    uint32_t window_;
    uint64_t delivered_ = 0;
    std::map<uint64_t, std::string> pending_;  // keyed by absolute stream offset
    std::string stream_;
};

int main() {
    const uint32_t isn = 0xFFFFFFF0;  // wraps after 16 bytes
    Reassembler r(isn, 64);
    struct Seg { uint32_t seq; const char* data; };
    const Seg segs[] = {{isn + 10, "KLMNO"}, {isn, "ABCDE"}, {isn + 5, "FGHIJ"},
                        {isn, "ABC"}, {isn + 13, "NOPQRSTU"}, {isn + 500, "far"}};
    for (const Seg& s : segs) {
        r.on_segment(s.seq, s.data);
        std::printf("seg %08x %-8s -> ack %08x stream %s\n", s.seq, s.data, r.ack(), r.stream().c_str());
    }
}
seg fffffffa KLMNO    -> ack fffffff0 stream
seg fffffff0 ABCDE    -> ack fffffff5 stream ABCDE
seg fffffff5 FGHIJ    -> ack ffffffff stream ABCDEFGHIJKLMNO
seg fffffff0 ABC      -> ack ffffffff stream ABCDEFGHIJKLMNO
seg fffffffd NOPQRSTU -> ack 00000005 stream ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTU
seg 000001e4 far      -> ack 00000005 stream ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTU

Complexity and pitfalls. O(log k) per segment for k buffered segments, plus copying. The decisive bug to avoid is comparing raw 32-bit sequence numbers with <: after the wrap, 0x00000005 is "after" 0xfffffffd. Keying the map by raw sequence numbers fails the same way, hence the 64-bit offsets. The out-of-order "KLMNO" segment is held, and the cumulative ACK stays at the hole until "FGHIJ" fills it, which is when a real receiver would have been sending duplicate ACKs (and SACK blocks). Real TCP also trims segments to the window instead of dropping them, and bounds total buffered bytes.

Estimated rating: ~1800 · interval merging plus wrap-around arithmetic that most first attempts get wrong

Cheat sheet

Theory
  • TCP vs UDP: TCP (RFC 9293) = connection, reliable, ordered byte stream, flow and congestion control, 20 to 60 B header. UDP (RFC 768) = datagrams, best effort, boundaries kept, 8 B header, multicast. QUIC builds TCP-like reliability on UDP.
  • Handshake: SYN(x), SYN+ACK(y, x+1), ACK(y+1). SYN and FIN each consume one sequence number. The kernel completes handshakes; accept just dequeues. Backlog = accept queue, capped by somaxconn.
  • Teardown: FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK; half-close with shutdown(SHUT_WR). Active closer gets TIME_WAIT for 2·MSL (60 s on Linux) to re-ACK a lost FIN and let old segments die. Many CLOSE_WAIT = your app forgot close. Set SO_REUSEADDR before bind.
  • Reliability: cumulative ACKs, SACK, RTO = SRTT + 4·RTTVAR (RFC 6298) with backoff and Karn's rule, fast retransmit after 3 duplicate ACKs. Compare sequence numbers with (int32_t)(a - b) < 0.
  • Windows: in flight ≤ min(rwnd, cwnd). rwnd = receiver buffer (flow control, window scale up to 1 GiB). cwnd: slow start doubles per RTT, congestion avoidance +1 MSS per RTT, 3 dup ACKs halve, timeout resets to 1 (RFC 5681). Linux default CUBIC.
  • Latency: Nagle + delayed ACK on write-write-read costs 40 to 200 ms; send each message in one call and set TCP_NODELAY. TCP HOL blocking remains in HTTP/2; HTTP/3 over QUIC removes it.
  • Sockets: socket, (setsockopt), bind, listen, accept (new fd) / connect; loop on send and recv; recv 0 = EOF; htons/htonl for ports and addresses; ignore SIGPIPE or use MSG_NOSIGNAL; frame messages (length prefix or delimiter); select nfds = max fd + 1; epoll for scale.
  • HTTP and TLS: HTTP/1.1 needs Host, keeps connections alive by default, bodies by Content-Length or chunked; idempotent = GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS. TLS 1.3 = 1 RTT, ephemeral key share in ClientHello, certificate encrypted, forward secrecy, 0-RTT replayable. A cold HTTPS fetch over TCP costs about 3 RTTs before the first byte.

Part E · Memory management · Chapter 9

new/delete vs malloc/free

A new-expression is two operations glued together: it gets raw memory from an allocation function, then runs a constructor in it. malloc does only the first half. This chapter takes both apart, from failure modes and array cookies to what glibc does under the hood, because interviewers use the topic to test whether you understand object lifetime and the heap at the same time.

TheoryDrillsCoding· about 3 hours· prerequisites: Ch 1 (constructors, destructors, lifetime)

What a new-expression actually does

Theory

Mental model. new T(args) is a language construct, not a function. The compiler turns it into: call an allocation function named operator new to get sizeof(T) raw bytes, then run T's constructor in those bytes, then hand you a typed T*. delete p is the mirror image: run p->~T(), then call operator delete to give the bytes back. malloc and free are plain library functions that only deal in bytes; they know nothing about types, constructors or destructors.

"new operator" vs "operator new"

Interviewers like this pair of names. The new operator (the standard calls it a new-expression) is the thing you write: new Widget(3). You cannot change what it does. operator new is the allocation function it calls. You can replace it globally or overload it per class, and you can call it directly: void* raw = ::operator new(64); gives you 64 bytes and constructs nothing. The same split exists for delete: the delete-expression always runs the destructor, then calls operator delete, which only frees.

When the constructor throws

The language guarantees no leak if a constructor called from a new-expression throws: [expr.new] requires the implementation to call the deallocation function that matches the allocation function used. That is why every placement form of operator new you write should have a matching placement operator delete. If it does not, the compiler cannot free the memory when the constructor throws, and you leak silently. The program below traces both paths with a class-specific allocation function (class-specific functions are never elided, so the trace is reliable).

#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <new>
#include <stdexcept>

struct Widget {
    int id;
    explicit Widget(int i) : id(i) {
        if (i < 0) throw std::invalid_argument("negative id");
        std::printf("  Widget(%d)\n", id);
    }
    ~Widget() { std::printf("  ~Widget(%d)\n", id); }

    static void* operator new(std::size_t n) {
        std::printf("  operator new(%zu)\n", n);
        if (void* p = std::malloc(n)) return p;
        throw std::bad_alloc{};
    }
    static void operator delete(void* p) noexcept {
        std::puts("  operator delete");
        std::free(p);
    }
};

int main() {
    std::puts("new Widget(7):");
    Widget* w = new Widget(7);
    std::puts("delete w:");
    delete w;
    std::puts("new Widget(-1):");
    try {
        Widget* bad = new Widget(-1);
        delete bad;
    } catch (const std::invalid_argument& e) {
        std::printf("  caught: %s\n", e.what());
    }
}
new Widget(7):
  operator new(4)
  Widget(7)
delete w:
  ~Widget(7)
  operator delete
new Widget(-1):
  operator new(4)
  operator delete
  caught: negative id

Notice that the failed construction prints no destructor. A destructor runs only for an object whose constructor finished; the members and bases that were fully built are destroyed, and the storage is released.

What malloc gives you

void* malloc(std::size_t n) returns a pointer to at least n bytes aligned for any fundamental type (at least alignof(std::max_align_t): 16 on x86-64 and arm64 Linux; on Apple arm64 max_align_t is only 8, though macOS malloc still returns 16-byte aligned blocks), or a null pointer on failure. No object of class type exists in that memory until you create one, usually with placement new (Ch 14). Since C++20 (P0593, "implicit creation of objects") malloc does implicitly create objects of implicit-lifetime types such as int, arrays and aggregates without a user-provided destructor, which made the decades-old C idiom int* a = (int*)malloc(10 * sizeof(int)); officially well-defined. For a type like std::string it is still undefined behaviour to use the memory without constructing an object first.

Failure behaviour: bad_alloc, nothrow and the new_handler

Theory

Mental model. malloc reports failure by returning null. A plain new-expression never returns null: the global operator new either returns memory or throws std::bad_alloc. Before it gives up it calls a user-installable hook, the new_handler, in a loop.

The operator new loop

The standard ([new.delete.single]) describes the default operator new(std::size_t) as this loop:

void* operator new(std::size_t n) {
    if (n == 0) n = 1;                       // must return a unique non-null pointer
    for (;;) {
        if (void* p = std::malloc(n)) return p;
        std::new_handler h = std::get_new_handler();
        if (!h) throw std::bad_alloc{};
        h();                                 // then try again
    }
}

A new_handler must do one of four things: make more memory available (for example release an emergency reserve), install a different handler, uninstall itself with std::set_new_handler(nullptr) so the next iteration throws, or not return at all (throw bad_alloc or call std::abort). A handler that returns without changing anything turns the loop into an infinite loop.

nothrow new

new (std::nothrow) T calls operator new(std::size_t, const std::nothrow_t&), which returns null instead of throwing. Two details catch people out. First, it only suppresses allocation failure: if T's constructor throws, the exception still propagates. Second, since C++11 the default nothrow version is specified as calling the throwing version inside a try block, so it still runs the new_handler loop first. There is also std::bad_array_new_length (derived from bad_alloc), which new T[n] throws when n is negative or n * sizeof(T) overflows. GCC follows that rule; Clang passes SIZE_MAX to operator new[] instead, which then throws a plain bad_alloc, so always catch bad_alloc.

Interview trap

"On Linux, if new succeeded, the memory exists." Not necessarily. With the default overcommit policy (vm.overcommit_memory = 0) the kernel hands out virtual address space and only finds physical pages when you first touch them. A large new can succeed and the process can be killed later by the OOM killer while writing to the memory, with no exception anywhere. Mode 0 refuses only obviously impossible requests (more than RAM plus swap); mode 2 does strict accounting against CommitLimit, which is when bad_alloc becomes reliable. Checking for bad_alloc is still correct code; just do not promise the interviewer that it protects you from running out of RAM.

Seeing the failure modes

Asking for 262 bytes fails on any real machine, so the program below shows all three behaviours. The volatile sink stops the compiler from removing the allocations, which C++14 allows (see the tricky drills), and the volatile size stops Clang from rejecting the constant array bound at compile time ("array is too large").

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>

static void* volatile sink;
static volatile std::size_t huge_v = std::size_t(1) << 62;  // hides the constant from Clang

int main() {
    const std::size_t huge = huge_v;

    char* p = new (std::nothrow) char[huge];
    sink = p;
    std::puts(p ? "nothrow: got memory" : "nothrow: null");

    try {
        char* q = new char[huge];
        sink = q;
    } catch (const std::bad_alloc&) {
        std::puts("plain new: bad_alloc");
    }

    std::size_t n = SIZE_MAX / 2;           // n * sizeof(int) overflows
    try {
        int* r = new int[n];
        sink = r;
    } catch (const std::bad_alloc& e) {     // bad_array_new_length is a bad_alloc
        std::puts("overflowing array size: caught a bad_alloc");
    }
}
nothrow: null
plain new: bad_alloc
overflowing array size: caught a bad_alloc

This program is not tagged for ASan on purpose: ASan treats a request that large as a bug in its own right and aborts unless you set allocator_may_return_null=1.

Type safety, sizes and the comparison table

Theory

Mental model. new knows the type, so it computes the size, returns a correctly typed pointer and runs constructors. malloc knows only a byte count, so you must compute the size, cast the result and construct objects yourself. Everything else in the table follows from that.

// C style: three chances to get it wrong (size, cast, no construction)
Point* a = static_cast<Point*>(std::malloc(sizeof(Point)));
// C++ style: size, type and construction come from the type
Point* b = new Point{1, 2};

A classic C bug is malloc(sizeof(p)) instead of malloc(sizeof(*p)), which allocates the size of a pointer. new cannot make that mistake. In C you do not cast malloc's result (the implicit conversion from void* hides a missing #include in old C); in C++ the cast is required because void* does not convert implicitly to T*.

new / deletemalloc / free
What it isLanguage expression (calls operator new)Library function
SizeComputed from the typeYou pass bytes
Return typeT*void*, cast needed in C++
ConstructionRuns constructor / destructorNone (C++20: implicit-lifetime types only)
FailureThrows std::bad_alloc (nothrow form returns null)Returns null
Hook on failurestd::set_new_handlerNone
Arraysnew[] / delete[], may store a cookieOne block, you do the arithmetic
ResizeNo equivalentrealloc
CustomisableReplace globally, overload per class, placement formsOnly by interposing the symbol (LD_PRELOAD)
Over-aligned typesAutomatic since C++17 (align_val_t)aligned_alloc, posix_memalign
Null argumentdelete nullptr is a no-opfree(NULL) is a no-op
Size 0Unique non-null pointerNull or a unique pointer (implementation-defined)

Know this cold

new = operator new + constructor; delete = destructor + operator delete. new throws, malloc returns null. Pair every allocation with its own deallocation form: new/delete, new[]/delete[], malloc/free. Anything else is undefined behaviour even when it seems to work.

new[], delete[] and the array cookie

Theory

Mental model. delete[] p receives only a pointer, yet it must run the destructor on every element. So when the element type has a non-trivial destructor, new T[n] asks for a few extra bytes and stores n just before the first element. That hidden header is the array cookie.

When there is a cookie

  • Trivially destructible element type (int, a POD struct): no cookie. Nothing must run per element, and the allocator knows the block size anyway. This is why int* p = new int[10]; delete p; usually "works": it is still undefined behaviour.
  • Non-trivial destructor: cookie present. delete p on such an array runs one destructor and passes the wrong address to operator delete, which typically crashes the allocator or corrupts the heap.
  • Sized array delete: if the usual deallocation function for the class is operator delete[](void*, std::size_t), the cookie is present even for a trivially destructible type, because the size passed to delete[] must be recomputed from the count. Give struct Plain below such a class-specific operator and GCC asks for 20 bytes instead of 12.
  • The cookie is an ABI detail, not a language rule. MSVC does something similar. The language rule is only: use delete[] for new[].
  • Elements are destroyed in reverse order of construction. If the k-th constructor throws during new T[n], the k already-built elements are destroyed in reverse order and the storage is released with operator delete[].

You can see the cookie by replacing operator new[] and printing the requested size:

#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <new>

void* operator new[](std::size_t n) {
    std::printf("operator new[](%zu)\n", n);
    if (void* p = std::malloc(n)) return p;
    throw std::bad_alloc{};
}
void operator delete[](void* p) noexcept { std::free(p); }

struct Plain { int v; };                 // trivial destructor
struct Owner { int v; ~Owner() {} };     // user-provided destructor

static void* volatile sink;              // keeps the allocations alive

int main() {
    Plain* a = new Plain[3]; sink = a; delete[] a;
    Owner* b = new Owner[3]; sink = b; delete[] b;
}
operator new[](12)
operator new[](20)

The output shown is GCC's (Itanium ABI: 12 bytes of elements plus an 8-byte cookie). Clang on Linux prints the same. Clang on Apple arm64 prints 28 for the second line because Apple's ABI cookie is 16 bytes.

Mismatched allocation and deallocation

Theory

Mental model. Each allocation family owns its own bookkeeping. Handing a pointer to the wrong family is undefined behaviour ([expr.delete]: the operand of non-array delete must come from a non-array new-expression, and vice versa; C says free must receive a pointer from malloc, calloc, realloc or aligned_alloc).

PairWhy it breaksWhat usually happens
new T then freeDestructor skipped; operator new may not be malloc (replaced, class-specific, aligned)Leak of whatever the object owned; heap corruption if operator new is not malloc
malloc then deleteDestructor runs on an object that never existed; operator delete may not be freeUB in the destructor; works by luck for int
new T[n] then deleteOne destructor; wrong address freed when there is a cookieCrash or heap corruption for non-trivial T
new T then delete[]Reads a cookie that does not existRuns a garbage number of destructors
new of derived, delete via base without virtual destructorWrong destructor and wrong size (Ch 2)Leaks, sized-delete mismatch

On glibc, global operator new happens to call malloc, so new int followed by free appears to work. That is the most dangerous kind of UB: it passes tests and breaks the day someone links tcmalloc, adds a class-specific operator new, or compiles with ASan. On Linux, ASan reports alloc-dealloc-mismatch for the first four rows of the table; the last row shows up as new-delete-type-mismatch when sized deallocation is on. On macOS the check is off by default (ASAN_OPTIONS=alloc_dealloc_mismatch=1 turns it on), which is why the drills in this chapter prove the array case with a type whose cookie makes the bug visible everywhere.

Tip

The real fix is to stop writing delete at all. std::vector, std::unique_ptr<T[]> and std::make_unique (Ch 11) pick the right deallocation form for you.

realloc, and why C++ has no renew

Theory

realloc(p, n) grows or shrinks a malloc block. If it can extend in place it returns p; otherwise it allocates a new block, copies the old bytes with the equivalent of memcpy, frees the old block and returns the new pointer. On failure it returns null and leaves the old block alive, so p = realloc(p, n); leaks p when it fails. Write void* q = realloc(p, n); if (!q) { /* p is still valid */ } else p = q;.

C++ has no equivalent for objects because a bytewise copy is not a valid way to move most objects:

  • An object may point into itself. libstdc++'s std::string holds a pointer to its own small buffer, so after a memcpy to a new address the copy points into freed memory.
  • Other objects may hold pointers to it (an intrusive list node, an observer registration). Moving the bytes does not update them.
  • Moving requires running move constructors and destructors, which can throw, so containers need std::move_if_noexcept to keep the strong guarantee (Ch 20).

So std::vector grows by allocating a new block, move-constructing elements into it, destroying the old ones and freeing the old block. Libraries such as folly's fbvector use realloc for types they mark as relocatable. The standard has crept towards the missing pieces: C++23 added std::allocator::allocate_at_least, which tells you how much memory you really got. Trivial relocation is not in C++26. P2786 was voted into the C++26 working draft in February 2025 (Hagenberg), then removed again in November 2025 (Kona, P3920) because of unresolved design concerns; the competing P1144 was never adopted. The committee aims to return to the topic for C++29, so today "relocatable" is still a library-specific trait.

One glibc detail worth knowing: when the block is large enough to have been served by mmap, realloc uses mremap, which moves page table entries instead of copying bytes. Growing a 1 GB buffer that way costs almost nothing.

#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <cstring>

int main() {
    int* a = static_cast<int*>(std::malloc(4 * sizeof(int)));
    if (!a) return 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) a[i] = i * i;

    int* grown = static_cast<int*>(std::realloc(a, 1000 * sizeof(int)));
    if (!grown) { std::free(a); return 1; }  // on failure a is still ours
    a = grown;                               // the old value of a is now invalid
    for (int i = 4; i < 1000; ++i) a[i] = i * i;

    std::printf("%d %d %d\n", a[0], a[3], a[999]);
    std::free(a);
}
0 9 998001

Overloading operator new and operator delete

Theory

Mental model. You cannot change what a new-expression does, but you choose which allocation function it calls. Name lookup for new T first looks in the scope of T (class-specific operator new), then at global scope. ::new T skips the class and goes straight to the global one.

Replacing the global functions

The standard library defines the global allocation functions as replaceable: if your program defines void* operator new(std::size_t) at global scope with exactly that signature, the linker uses yours everywhere, including inside the standard library. The full set is: single and array, throwing and nothrow, with and without std::align_val_t (C++17), and sized delete (C++14). The defaults are defined in terms of each other: operator new[] calls operator new, sized delete calls unsized delete, and the nothrow forms call the throwing ones. Replacing the plain operator new and operator delete therefore catches most allocations, but replace the aligned pair as well if you track over-aligned types. Rules for a replacement:

  • Return memory suitably aligned for any object of that size (at least __STDCPP_DEFAULT_NEW_ALIGNMENT__, 16 on mainstream 64-bit targets).
  • Size 0 must return a unique non-null pointer. Failure must throw bad_alloc (or call the new_handler loop).
  • Do not call anything that allocates through operator new from inside it (std::cout, std::string, std::map), or you recurse. Use printf or write and fixed-size storage.
  • Do not put it in an inline function or a namespace; it must be a global, non-inline definition.

Class-specific allocation

Declaring static void* operator new(std::size_t) in a class (the static is implicit even if you omit it) makes every new T use it. Typical uses: a free-list pool for a hot node type (Ch 15), tracking, or placing objects in shared memory. Two rules: it is inherited, so a derived class that is bigger gets the base's allocator with a larger n (check n == sizeof(Base) or forward to ::operator new); and you should declare the matching operator delete, otherwise the global one frees memory your allocator handed out.

struct Node {
    static void* operator new(std::size_t n);           // used by new Node
    static void  operator delete(void* p) noexcept;     // used by delete and on ctor throw
    static void* operator new(std::size_t n, Arena& a); // placement form: new (arena) Node
    static void  operator delete(void* p, Arena& a) noexcept; // called only if the ctor throws
};

Placement forms, sized and destroying delete

Any operator new with extra parameters is a "placement" form, invoked as new (args...) T. The one in <new> that takes a void* and returns it unchanged is the famous placement new, which constructs an object at an address you provide; it gets its own chapter (Ch 14). Sized delete (C++14) gives operator delete(void*, std::size_t) the object size, so allocators with size classes skip a lookup; GCC enables it by default, and Clang does since version 19. Destroying delete (C++20), void operator delete(T*, std::destroying_delete_t), receives the object before the destructor has run and becomes responsible for destroying it, which lets a class with a variable-length tail compute its real size.

Aligned new (C++17) and zero-size allocations

Theory

Over-aligned types

Before C++17, new on a type declared alignas(64) only guaranteed the default alignment (16), so cache-line aligned structures silently came out misaligned and SIMD code crashed. C++17 (P0035) added operator new(std::size_t, std::align_val_t). When alignof(T) > __STDCPP_DEFAULT_NEW_ALIGNMENT__, the new-expression calls the aligned form and the delete-expression calls the matching operator delete(void*, std::align_val_t). You get this for free with new, std::make_unique and std::vector; with malloc you must call aligned_alloc(alignment, size) (size must be a multiple of the alignment in C11; C17 relaxed that) or posix_memalign.

#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <vector>

struct alignas(64) CacheLine { long counter = 0; };

static bool aligned64(const void* p) {
    return reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t>(p) % 64 == 0;
}

int main() {
    std::printf("default new alignment: %zu\n", std::size_t(__STDCPP_DEFAULT_NEW_ALIGNMENT__));
    auto* a = new CacheLine;
    auto b = std::make_unique<CacheLine>();
    std::vector<CacheLine> v(3);
    std::printf("new: %d, make_unique: %d, vector: %d\n",
                aligned64(a), aligned64(b.get()), aligned64(v.data()));
    delete a;   // calls operator delete(void*, std::align_val_t)
}
default new alignment: 16
new: 1, make_unique: 1, vector: 1

Zero-size allocations

  • operator new(0) and new T[0] must return a non-null pointer distinct from every other live allocation. You may not dereference it, but you must delete it (delete[] for the array). Implementations treat the request as 1 byte or as the minimum chunk.
  • malloc(0) is implementation-defined: either null or a unique pointer that must be passed to free. glibc and macOS return a unique minimum-size chunk; code that treats a null return from malloc(0) as out of memory is not portable.
  • realloc(p, 0) is the nastiest: historically it freed p on some systems and returned a minimum block on others. C23 made it undefined behaviour. Do not use it.
  • Why must C++ return unique pointers? Distinct objects must have distinct addresses, so two live allocations cannot compare equal.

What malloc does under the hood (glibc ptmalloc)

Theory

Mental model. malloc is a user-space library that buys memory from the kernel in large pieces and sells it to you in small pieces. Each piece is a chunk with a small header. Freed chunks are kept in caches and bins for reuse, and only rarely go back to the kernel. Interviewers at systems and HFT firms expect you to sketch this.

Getting memory from the kernel

  • brk/sbrk moves the end of the process's data segment (the "program break"). glibc's main arena grows its heap this way. Only the top of that heap can be given back, by moving the break down.
  • mmap maps fresh anonymous pages anywhere in the address space. Requests at or above M_MMAP_THRESHOLD (128 KiB by default) get their own mapping, which free returns to the kernel immediately with munmap. The threshold is dynamic: freeing an mmapped chunk raises it to that chunk's size, up to 32 MiB on 64-bit, so a program that repeatedly allocates 1 MiB buffers stops paying for mmap/munmap.
  • Additional arenas (for other threads) get their memory from mmapped "heaps" of up to 64 MiB each.

Where a request is served from

  1. tcache (glibc 2.26+): a per-thread cache with 64 size-indexed singly linked lists, 7 chunks each by default, for chunks up to 1040 bytes (requests up to 1032). No lock, a handful of instructions. Most small malloc/free pairs never leave it. Since glibc 2.42 the tcache can also cache large blocks (up to 4 MiB) if you raise the glibc.malloc.tcache_max tunable; the default limit is unchanged.
  2. fastbins: per-arena singly linked LIFO lists for small chunks (chunks up to 128 bytes by default, M_MXFAST, so requests up to 120 bytes). Freed chunks here are not coalesced right away.
  3. small bins (62 exact-size doubly linked lists below 1024 bytes) and large bins (ranges, kept sorted by size, best fit). Freed chunks first go to the unsorted bin, a one-shot staging list that malloc sorts into bins while it searches.
  4. top chunk: if no bin fits, malloc carves from the free space at the end of the heap and extends it with brk (main arena) when needed.

Free does roughly the reverse: put the chunk in the tcache if there is room; otherwise coalesce it with free neighbours (using the P bit and boundary tag) and put it in the unsorted bin; if it borders the top chunk, merge into top, and if top grows beyond M_TRIM_THRESHOLD (128 KiB default) shrink the heap with brk. Why freed memory often does not lower RSS is a fragmentation question, covered in Ch 10.

Arenas and threads

One global lock would serialise every thread's malloc. ptmalloc keeps several arenas, each with its own lock and bins. A thread is attached to an arena at its first malloc and keeps using it: glibc creates a new arena for each new thread until there are 8 × number of cores arenas on 64-bit (2 × cores on 32-bit), and after that threads share the existing ones. The cost is memory: each arena holds its own free chunks, so a program with many threads can use much more RSS than its live data. MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 (or the tunable glibc.malloc.arena_max) is a common fix in production. jemalloc, tcmalloc and mimalloc take different approaches (Ch 10).

Know this cold

Small requests: tcache, then bins, then the top chunk, grown with brk. Large requests (128 KiB and up by default): a private mmap, returned with munmap on free. The size lives in a header just before the pointer. Several arenas reduce lock contention at the price of memory.

Memory leaks and how to find them

Theory

Mental model. A leak is memory that is still allocated but that no live pointer can reach any more, so nobody can free it. In a long-running server, a leak of a few bytes per request becomes gigabytes. "Still reachable at exit" (a global cache never freed) is not the same thing, and tools report it separately.

Typical causes in C++

  • An early return or an exception between new and delete. RAII fixes this class of leak completely.
  • Ownership confusion: unique_ptr::release() with the result ignored, a raw pointer stored in a container of raw pointers, or a C API that returns memory you must free.
  • shared_ptr cycles (Ch 13): every count stays above zero.
  • A base class without a virtual destructor, so derived members are never destroyed.
  • Logical leaks: a cache or map that only grows. No tool calls this a leak because it is reachable.

Tools

ToolHowCostFinds
ASan + LeakSanitizer-fsanitize=address -g; LSan runs at exit (on by default on Linux; off by default on macOS, where ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=1 enables it if your toolchain supports it)About 2× time, 2 to 3× memoryLeaks with allocation stacks, plus use-after-free, double free, overflows, mismatches
Valgrind memcheckvalgrind --leak-check=full ./a.out, no rebuild10 to 50× slower"definitely lost", "indirectly lost", "possibly lost", "still reachable"; uninitialised reads
heaptrack, massifRecord every allocation over timeModerateWho allocates the most, growth over time (logical leaks)
Counting operator newReplace the global functions (coding drills below)TinyLive count and bytes in tests
g++ -std=c++20 -g -O1 -fsanitize=address leak.cpp -o leak && ./leak
# ==1234==ERROR: LeakSanitizer: detected memory leaks
# Direct leak of 40 byte(s) in 1 object(s) allocated from:
#     #0 ... in operator new[](unsigned long)
#     #1 ... in make_buffer() leak.cpp:5

valgrind --leak-check=full --show-leak-kinds=all ./leak_without_asan

"Indirectly lost" in valgrind means a block reachable only from another leaked block: fix the definitely lost one and the indirect ones usually disappear. Do not run ASan and valgrind on the same binary; they both intercept malloc.

Concept and tricky questions

Drills

ConceptWhat are the steps of new T(args) and of delete p, and what happens if T's constructor throws?

Answer

Answer. new: call operator new(sizeof(T)) (class-specific if T declares one, else global), construct T in the storage, yield a T*. delete: call p->~T() (virtually if the destructor is virtual), then call operator delete. If the constructor throws, the matching operator delete releases the storage and the exception propagates; no destructor runs.

Why. [expr.new] requires the matching deallocation on constructor failure, so new on its own never leaks. A common wrong answer is "the destructor cleans up": the destructor runs only for objects whose construction completed. Subobjects that were completed are destroyed by the normal unwinding rules.

ConceptHow does free(p) know how many bytes to release when you never told it the size?

Answer

Answer. The allocator records the size itself. glibc stores it in an 8-byte header immediately before the pointer it returned (with flag bits in the low three bits). Size-class allocators such as jemalloc or tcmalloc look the size class up from the page the pointer lives in.

Why. The C API predates sized deallocation, so the allocator must recover the size from the address. C++14 sized delete passes the size explicitly, which lets size-class allocators skip that lookup. "The OS tracks it" is the usual wrong answer: the kernel knows only about pages and mappings, not individual malloc blocks.

ConceptCan you release memory from new with free()? And if free() manages without a count, why does delete[] need to know how many elements there are?

Answer

Answer. No: memory from a new-expression must go back through the matching delete-expression, and anything else is undefined behaviour. delete[] needs the count because it must run one destructor per element; the allocator only knows the byte size of the block, which may be rounded up, so it cannot tell how many objects live there. That is why compilers store the count in an array cookie when the elements have non-trivial destructors.

Why. free skips the destructor, and operator new need not be malloc at all (replaced, class-specific, aligned or tcmalloc-backed), so free may receive an address its heap never handed out. The common wrong answer is "yes, new calls malloc anyway": that is true of glibc's default, and it is exactly why the bug passes tests and then breaks when the allocator changes. For the count, the usual wrong answer is "delete[] asks the allocator for the block size": the block can be larger than n * sizeof(T), so dividing would run destructors on objects that never existed.

ConceptWhat may a new_handler do, and what happens if it simply returns?

Answer

Answer. It must make progress: free some memory (for example an emergency reserve), install another handler, uninstall itself with std::set_new_handler(nullptr), or not return (throw std::bad_alloc, or abort). If it returns having done none of these, operator new retries, fails, calls it again, forever.

Why. The standard specifies operator new as a loop: try to allocate; on failure, if a handler is installed call it and retry, otherwise throw bad_alloc. The handler is process-wide and is consulted only by operator new, not by malloc.

ConceptWhy does C++ have no renew or object-aware realloc, and how does std::vector grow instead?

Answer

Answer. realloc may move the block with a raw byte copy, and a byte copy is not a valid move for objects that point into themselves or are pointed to by others. vector allocates a new buffer, move-constructs (or copies, if the move constructor may throw) each element into it, destroys the old elements and frees the old buffer.

Why. Object lifetime in C++ is tied to an address; moving means running constructors. libstdc++'s std::string with its internal SSO pointer is the standard example of a type that breaks under memcpy. The "just realloc the vector's buffer" answer is correct only for trivially copyable types, which is why some libraries special-case them.

ConceptWhen does malloc call brk and when does it call mmap?

Answer

Answer. In glibc, requests at or above the mmap threshold (128 KiB by default, raised dynamically up to 32 MiB on 64-bit) get a private anonymous mmap that free returns with munmap. Smaller requests come from an arena; the main arena grows its heap with brk when the top chunk is too small, and other arenas use mmapped heaps.

Why. mmap avoids fragmenting the main heap with big blocks and gives the memory back immediately on free, but each call is a system call plus page faults, so small requests are pooled. The dynamic threshold exists because a program that repeatedly allocates and frees 1 MiB buffers would otherwise pay mmap and munmap every time.

ConceptWhat do valgrind's "definitely lost", "indirectly lost" and "still reachable" mean, and which do you fix first?

Answer

Answer. Definitely lost: no pointer to the block exists at exit. Indirectly lost: the block is reachable only through a definitely lost block (the nodes of a leaked list). Still reachable: a live pointer exists (often a global), the program just never freed it. Fix definitely lost first; the indirect ones usually go with it.

Why. Freeing the root of a leaked structure frees its children. "Still reachable" is often deliberate (singletons torn down by the OS), but it hides logical leaks such as caches that only grow, which you find with heap profilers rather than leak checkers. "Possibly lost" means only an interior pointer points into the block.

TrickyDoes new (std::nothrow) Widget guarantee that no exception escapes?

Answer

Answer. No. It only turns allocation failure into a null result. If Widget's constructor throws, the exception propagates as usual (after the storage is freed with the nothrow operator delete).

Why. The std::nothrow tag selects the allocation function operator new(std::size_t, const std::nothrow_t&) noexcept. It has nothing to do with construction. People also forget that the default nothrow version runs the new_handler loop before returning null, and that on an overcommitting Linux system it rarely returns null at all.

Trickyint* p = new int[10]; delete p; runs without a crash on GCC and Clang. Is it correct?

Answer

Answer. No, it is undefined behaviour by [expr.delete]. It appears to work only because int is trivially destructible, so the Itanium ABI stores no cookie, and the global array and single operator delete both end in free.

Why. Change int to a type with a destructor and the pointer passed to operator delete is 8 bytes past the start of the block, which crashes or corrupts the heap. ASan on Linux reports alloc-dealloc-mismatch even for int. "It's fine for built-in types" is the wrong answer interviewers listen for.

TrickyYou replace global operator new with a version that counts calls, then write int* p = new int(5); std::printf("%d", *p); delete p;. At -O2 the counter says zero. Is the compiler allowed to do that?

Answer

Answer. Yes. Since C++14 (N3664, now [expr.new]) an implementation may omit or merge calls to replaceable global allocation functions made by new-expressions, even if your replacement has side effects. Clang and GCC both do it when the pointer does not escape.

Why. The rule exists so that short-lived heap objects can live on the stack or in registers. It applies to new-expressions only: direct calls such as ::operator new(n), class-specific operator new and malloc are not covered by that permission (GCC still treats malloc as a builtin it can sometimes optimise). To make a counting test reliable, let the pointer escape, for example by storing it in a volatile global, as the programs in this chapter do.

TrickyIs int* a = static_cast<int*>(std::malloc(4 * sizeof(int))); a[0] = 1; undefined behaviour in C++?

Answer

Answer. Not since C++20. P0593 says malloc, operator new, memcpy and a few others implicitly create objects of implicit-lifetime types (scalars, arrays, aggregates whose destructor is not user-provided, and classes with a trivial non-deleted destructor and at least one trivial eligible constructor) when that would give the program defined behaviour. Before C++20 it was technically UB, though every compiler accepted it.

Why. The rule was applied retroactively as a defect report, so the answer for "C++17" is debated; say "formally UB before P0593, fine now". For std::string or anything with a non-trivial constructor, using malloc'd memory without placement new is still UB. Candidates often say "always UB" or "always fine"; both are wrong.

TrickyCan you delete a pointer to const? Can you call delete this?

Answer

Answer. Both are legal. const Widget* p = new const Widget; delete p; is fine: constness controls modification during the object's lifetime, not who may end it (a const local is destroyed at scope exit, too). delete this is legal if the object was created by a non-array new-expression and nothing touches the object (members, virtual calls, this) after the delete.

Why. [expr.delete] accepts a pointer to cv-qualified type. delete this appears in intrusive reference counting (COM's Release). It is a bug for stack objects, members, arrays or objects from make_shared. The common wrong answer to the first part is "no, delete modifies the object".

TrickyWhat do malloc(0), new int[0] and ::operator new(0) return, and must you free them?

Answer

Answer. malloc(0) returns either null or a unique pointer (implementation-defined; glibc returns a minimum 32-byte chunk) and the non-null result must be freed. new int[0] and ::operator new(0) must return unique non-null pointers that you must release with delete[] and ::operator delete respectively. None may be dereferenced.

Why. C++ requires distinct live allocations to have distinct addresses, so it cannot return null or a shared dummy. The trap is code that checks if (!malloc(n)) out_of_memory(); with n == 0: on a platform that returns null for zero it reports a false out-of-memory. realloc(p, 0) is UB in C23.

Predict the output and find the bug

Drills

OutputThe third element's constructor throws during new Item[4]. What does the program print?

#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <new>
#include <stdexcept>

static int built = 0;

struct Item {
    int id;
    Item() : id(built) {
        if (built == 2) throw std::runtime_error("boom");
        ++built;
        std::printf("Item(%d) ", id);
    }
    ~Item() { std::printf("~Item(%d) ", id); }
    static void* operator new[](std::size_t n) {
        if (void* p = std::malloc(n)) return p;
        throw std::bad_alloc{};
    }
    static void operator delete[](void* p) noexcept {
        std::printf("operator delete[] ");
        std::free(p);
    }
};

int main() {
    try {
        Item* items = new Item[4];
        delete[] items;
    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        std::printf("caught %s\n", e.what());
    }
}
Answer
Item(0) Item(1) ~Item(1) ~Item(0) operator delete[] caught boom

Answer. Two items are built, the third throws, the two built items are destroyed in reverse order, the storage is released, and then the handler runs.

Why. An array new-expression is exception-safe on its own: the implementation destroys the fully constructed elements in reverse order ([expr.new], [dcl.init]) and calls the matching operator delete[]. Element 2 never gets a destructor because its constructor did not finish. A common wrong answer prints ~Item(2) or destroys in forward order.

OutputThe new_handler counts calls and gives up after the third. What is printed?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>

static int calls = 0;
static void* volatile sink;
static volatile std::size_t huge = std::size_t(1) << 62;

static void handler() {
    ++calls;
    std::printf("handler call %d\n", calls);
    if (calls == 3) std::set_new_handler(nullptr);
}

int main() {
    std::set_new_handler(handler);
    try {
        char* p = new char[huge];
        sink = p;
        std::puts("allocated");
    } catch (const std::bad_alloc&) {
        std::printf("bad_alloc after %d handler calls\n", calls);
    }
}
Answer
handler call 1
handler call 2
handler call 3
bad_alloc after 3 handler calls

Answer. The handler runs three times; after the third it uninstalls itself, so the fourth allocation attempt finds no handler and throws.

Why. This is the operator new loop from [new.delete.single]. Each failure calls the current handler and retries. If the handler never uninstalled itself and never freed anything, the program would loop forever, which is the main bug in hand-written handlers. (Not tagged for ASan: ASan aborts on impossible sizes by default.)

Find the bugThis compiles cleanly and the destructor message even prints once. What is wrong?

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>

struct Record {
    std::string name = "row";
    ~Record() { std::puts("~Record"); }
};

int main() {
    Record* rows = new Record[3];
    delete rows;
}
Answer

Answer. new[] paired with plain delete. Use delete[] rows;, or better, std::vector<Record> rows(3);.

Why. Record has a non-trivial destructor, so the block starts with an array cookie and rows points past it. Plain delete runs one destructor and passes rows itself to operator delete, an address malloc never returned. ASan reports "attempting free on address which was not malloc()-ed"; without ASan the result ranges from silence to a glibc abort ("free(): invalid pointer"). Output is not compared because the behaviour is undefined.

Find the bugA cleanup path frees a node twice. Spot it.

#include <cstdio>

struct Node { int value; Node* next; };

static void destroy(Node* n) {
    while (n) {
        Node* next = n->next;
        delete n;
        n = next;
    }
}

int main() {
    Node* tail = new Node{2, nullptr};
    Node* head = new Node{1, tail};
    std::printf("%d %d\n", head->value, head->next->value);
    destroy(head);
    delete tail;   // "just to be safe"
}
Answer

Answer. destroy(head) already deleted tail; the extra delete tail is a double free. Remove it, and model the list with a single owner (for example std::unique_ptr<Node> next or a std::forward_list).

Why. Deleting a pointer does not change other pointers to the same object, so tail still holds the old address. A double free can corrupt glibc's bins (the classic "tcache double free" exploit primitive); glibc detects some cases and aborts with "free(): double free detected in tcache 2". ASan reports "attempting double-free". Setting a pointer to null after delete only protects that one variable, not its copies.

Find the bugThe buffer grows with realloc. Where is the use-after-free?

#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>

int main() {
    int* data = static_cast<int*>(std::malloc(2 * sizeof(int)));
    if (!data) return 1;
    data[0] = 10;
    data[1] = 20;
    int* first = &data[0];

    int* bigger = static_cast<int*>(std::realloc(data, 100000 * sizeof(int)));
    if (!bigger) { std::free(data); return 1; }
    data = bigger;

    std::printf("%d\n", *first);
    std::free(data);
}
Answer

Answer. first points into the old block. If realloc moved the data (here it must, from 8 bytes to 400 KB), the old block is freed and *first reads freed memory. Keep an index instead of a pointer, or recompute first after the realloc.

Why. realloc may return a different address; every pointer and reference into the old block is invalid afterwards, exactly like iterators after std::vector reallocation. ASan always moves on realloc growth and reports heap-use-after-free. Without ASan the program may print 10 and look correct, which is why this bug survives code review.

Find the bugA C library returns a malloc'd string and the C++ caller releases it. What is wrong, and why might ASan stay quiet on some machines?

#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <cstring>

extern "C" char* c_duplicate(const char* s) {   // stands in for a C API such as strdup
    std::size_t n = std::strlen(s) + 1;
    char* p = static_cast<char*>(std::malloc(n));
    if (p) std::memcpy(p, s, n);
    return p;
}

int main() {
    char* copy = c_duplicate("hello");
    std::printf("%s\n", copy);
    delete[] copy;
}
Answer

Answer. Memory from malloc must go back with free(copy). Better: wrap it at the boundary, std::unique_ptr<char, decltype(&std::free)> copy(c_duplicate("hello"), &std::free); (custom deleters are Ch 12).

Why. delete[] must receive a pointer from new[]. With glibc the default operator delete[] ends in free, so it appears to work, until a replaced or class-specific allocator, a different heap (Windows DLLs each have their own CRT heap) or a cookie read gets involved. ASan on Linux reports alloc-dealloc-mismatch (malloc vs operator delete []). On macOS that check is off by default (alloc_dealloc_mismatch=0), so this drill is marked UB without the sanitizer-must-fail flag.

OutputWhich allocation function does each expression call?

#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <new>

struct Base {
    static void* operator new(std::size_t n) {
        std::printf("Base::operator new(%zu)\n", n);
        return ::operator new(n);
    }
    static void operator delete(void* p) noexcept {
        std::puts("Base::operator delete");
        ::operator delete(p);
    }
    virtual ~Base() = default;
    long a = 0;
};

struct Derived : Base { long b = 0; long c = 0; };

int main() {
    Base* x = new Derived;
    delete x;
    Base* y = ::new Base;
    ::delete y;
}
Answer
Base::operator new(32)
Base::operator delete

Answer. new Derived finds Base::operator new by inheritance and asks for sizeof(Derived) = 32 (vptr + three longs on a 64-bit target). delete x calls Base::operator delete, found through the virtual destructor. The ::new and ::delete forms skip the class functions and print nothing.

Why. Lookup for the allocation function starts in the class scope of the allocated type, and class-specific functions are inherited. That is why a pool allocator written for sizeof(Base) must check n: here it would receive 32 instead of 16. The deallocation function is looked up in the scope of the dynamic type's destructor, so the virtual destructor matters for picking the right operator delete too.

OutputZero-size requests. What is printed?

#include <cstdio>
#include <new>

int main() {
    int* a = new int[0];
    int* b = new int[0];
    void* c = ::operator new(0);
    std::printf("a non-null: %d\n", a != nullptr);
    std::printf("a != b: %d\n", a != b);
    std::printf("c non-null: %d\n", c != nullptr);
    delete[] a;
    delete[] b;
    ::operator delete(c);
}
Answer
a non-null: 1
a != b: 1
c non-null: 1

Answer. All non-null, and the two arrays have distinct addresses.

Why. [basic.stc.dynamic.allocation]: a successful allocation of size zero returns a non-null pointer that differs from every other live allocation. You must still release each one. Compare malloc(0), which may legally return null.

Find the bugA string pool keeps raw pointers into a vector of strings. Where does it read freed memory?

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<std::string> names;
    names.reserve(1);
    names.push_back("a fairly long string that lives on the heap");
    const char* first = names[0].c_str();
    names.push_back("another long string that also lives on the heap");
    names.clear();
    std::printf("%s\n", first);
}
Answer

Answer. names.clear() destroys the strings, which frees the heap buffer that first points into; the printf reads freed memory. (The second push_back also reallocates the vector; for a long string the character buffer survives the move, but nothing guarantees that.)

Why. c_str() is valid only while the string is alive and unmodified. Raw pointers do not extend lifetime. ASan reports heap-use-after-free at the printf. The usual wrong answer blames only the reallocation; the guaranteed bug is the destruction.

Write the code

Coding

CodeCounting allocator. Replace the global operator new and operator delete so that a test can ask how many allocations are live, how many bytes are live and what the peak was. Requirements: correct alignment (at least 16), size 0 handled, failure throws bad_alloc, no allocation through operator new inside the hooks, thread-safe counters.

Answer

Approach. Prefix every block with a 16-byte header that stores the requested size, so operator delete can subtract it without a lookup table. Use std::atomic counters and a compare-exchange loop for the peak. Hand the caller the address just past the header, which keeps malloc's 16-byte alignment. Use a volatile sink in the test so the compiler cannot elide the allocations.

#include <atomic>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <new>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

namespace stats {
std::atomic<std::size_t> live_blocks{0}, live_bytes{0}, peak_bytes{0};
}

static constexpr std::size_t kHeader = 16;   // keeps 16-byte alignment

void* operator new(std::size_t n) {
    void* raw = std::malloc(n + kHeader);
    if (!raw) throw std::bad_alloc{};
    *static_cast<std::size_t*>(raw) = n;
    stats::live_blocks.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
    std::size_t now = stats::live_bytes.fetch_add(n, std::memory_order_relaxed) + n;
    std::size_t peak = stats::peak_bytes.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
    while (now > peak && !stats::peak_bytes.compare_exchange_weak(peak, now)) {}
    return static_cast<char*>(raw) + kHeader;
}

void operator delete(void* p) noexcept {
    if (!p) return;
    void* raw = static_cast<char*>(p) - kHeader;
    std::size_t n = *static_cast<std::size_t*>(raw);
    stats::live_blocks.fetch_sub(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
    stats::live_bytes.fetch_sub(n, std::memory_order_relaxed);
    std::free(raw);
}

void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { ::operator delete(p); }

static void* volatile sink;

static void report(const char* label) {
    std::printf("%-14s blocks=%zu bytes=%zu\n", label,
                stats::live_blocks.load(), stats::live_bytes.load());
}

int main() {
    std::size_t base_blocks = stats::live_blocks, base_bytes = stats::live_bytes;
    stats::peak_bytes = base_bytes;
    int* one = new int(42);
    sink = one;
    double* arr = new double[10];
    sink = arr;
    std::printf("after 2 news: +%zu blocks, +%zu bytes\n",
                stats::live_blocks - base_blocks, stats::live_bytes - base_bytes);
    delete one;
    delete[] arr;
    {
        std::vector<int> v(1000);
        sink = v.data();
    }
    std::printf("back to base: %d\n", stats::live_blocks == base_blocks && stats::live_bytes == base_bytes);
    std::printf("peak above base: %zu\n", stats::peak_bytes - base_bytes);
    (void)report;
}
after 2 news: +2 blocks, +84 bytes
back to base: 1
peak above base: 4000

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) per call plus malloc. The header costs 16 bytes per block. The counts are relative to a baseline because the runtime may allocate before main (iostream buffers, locale data). Pitfalls: forgetting that operator new[] and sized delete default to the replaced functions (fine here, but replace them too if you use a different scheme), forgetting the aligned overloads (align_val_t allocations bypass this header and would be freed through the default aligned delete, which is fine, but not counted), and calling anything that allocates inside the hooks.

Estimated rating: ~1500 · straightforward header trick, but alignment, elision and baseline details trip people up

CodeLeak detector with file and line. Provide a macro TRACK_NEW so that TRACK_NEW Widget(3) records the file and line, and a function report_leaks() that lists every tracked allocation not yet deleted. Constraint: the bookkeeping must not itself call operator new.

Answer

Approach. Add a placement form operator new(std::size_t, const char* file, int line) and define TRACK_NEW as new (__FILE__, __LINE__). Store each allocation in a fixed-size open table allocated with malloc semantics (a static array), protected by a mutex. Provide the matching placement operator delete so a throwing constructor does not leak a table entry, and a replaced plain operator delete that removes entries.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <mutex>
#include <new>
#include <stdexcept>

namespace leak {
struct Entry { void* p; std::size_t size; const char* file; int line; };
constexpr int kMax = 1024;
Entry table[kMax];
std::mutex mu;

void add(void* p, std::size_t n, const char* file, int line) {
    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mu);
    for (Entry& e : table)
        if (!e.p) { e = {p, n, file, line}; return; }
}
void remove(void* p) {
    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mu);
    for (Entry& e : table)
        if (e.p == p) { e.p = nullptr; return; }
}
int report() {
    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mu);
    int count = 0;
    for (const Entry& e : table) {
        if (!e.p) continue;
        std::printf("leak: %zu bytes from line %d\n", e.size, e.line);
        ++count;
    }
    return count;
}
}  // namespace leak

void* operator new(std::size_t n, const char* file, int line) {
    void* p = std::malloc(n ? n : 1);
    if (!p) throw std::bad_alloc{};
    leak::add(p, n, file, line);
    return p;
}
void operator delete(void* p, const char*, int) noexcept {   // used if the ctor throws
    leak::remove(p);
    std::free(p);
}
void* operator new(std::size_t n) {
    void* p = std::malloc(n ? n : 1);
    if (!p) throw std::bad_alloc{};
    return p;
}
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept {
    leak::remove(p);
    std::free(p);
}
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { ::operator delete(p); }

#define TRACK_NEW new (__FILE__, __LINE__)

struct Widget {
    int id;
    explicit Widget(int i) : id(i) { if (i < 0) throw std::invalid_argument("bad id"); }
};

int main() {
    Widget* kept = TRACK_NEW Widget(1);
    Widget* freed = TRACK_NEW Widget(2);
    delete freed;
    try { Widget* bad = TRACK_NEW Widget(-1); delete bad; } catch (const std::exception&) {}
    int n = leak::report();
    std::printf("%d leak(s)\n", n);
    delete kept;
    std::printf("%d leak(s) after cleanup\n", leak::report());
}
leak: 4 bytes from line 65
1 leak(s)
0 leak(s) after cleanup

Complexity and pitfalls. O(table size) per operation; a real tool uses a hash table keyed by address with its own malloc-backed storage. Pitfalls: delete on a tracked pointer goes through the plain operator delete (there is no placement delete-expression), so that one must remove the entry; the placement operator delete is called only when a constructor throws; TRACK_NEW breaks code that already uses placement syntax; arrays need operator new[] overloads too. The demo prints only the line; a real report prints e.file too.

Estimated rating: ~1700 · needs placement new/delete pairing and recursion-free bookkeeping

CodeAligned allocation on top of malloc. Implement void* aligned_malloc(std::size_t size, std::size_t align) and void aligned_free(void* p) using only std::malloc and std::free. align is a power of two. This is a frequent phone-screen question.

Answer

Approach. Over-allocate by align - 1 + sizeof(void*) bytes. Skip past room for one pointer, round the address up to the next multiple of align with (addr + align - 1) & ~(align - 1), and store the original malloc pointer in the word just before the aligned address. aligned_free reads that word and frees it.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <cstring>
#include <initializer_list>

static bool is_pow2(std::size_t x) { return x && !(x & (x - 1)); }

void* aligned_malloc(std::size_t size, std::size_t align) {
    if (!is_pow2(align)) return nullptr;
    if (align < alignof(void*)) align = alignof(void*);
    std::size_t extra = align - 1 + sizeof(void*);
    if (size > SIZE_MAX - extra) return nullptr;          // overflow guard
    void* raw = std::malloc(size + extra);
    if (!raw) return nullptr;
    std::uintptr_t start = reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t>(raw) + sizeof(void*);
    std::uintptr_t aligned = (start + align - 1) & ~(std::uintptr_t(align) - 1);
    void* result = reinterpret_cast<void*>(aligned);
    std::memcpy(static_cast<char*>(result) - sizeof(void*), &raw, sizeof raw);
    return result;
}

void aligned_free(void* p) {
    if (!p) return;
    void* raw;
    std::memcpy(&raw, static_cast<char*>(p) - sizeof(void*), sizeof raw);
    std::free(raw);
}

int main() {
    bool ok = true;
    for (std::size_t align : {8, 16, 64, 256, 4096}) {
        for (std::size_t size : {1, 7, 100, 5000}) {
            void* p = aligned_malloc(size, align);
            ok = ok && p && reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t>(p) % align == 0;
            std::memset(p, 0xAB, size);                     // whole range is writable
            aligned_free(p);
        }
    }
    std::printf("all aligned: %d\n", ok);
    std::printf("bad alignment gives null: %d\n", aligned_malloc(10, 24) == nullptr);
}
all aligned: 1
bad alignment gives null: 1

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1), wasting at most align - 1 + 8 bytes per block. Pitfalls: forgetting the room for the stored pointer (then the header can land before the malloc block), rounding with % on signed types, not guarding size + extra against overflow, and freeing the aligned pointer with plain free. In production use std::aligned_alloc, posix_memalign or aligned new; this exercise shows how they can be built.

Estimated rating: ~1400 · classic bit trick plus a stored back-pointer

CodeEmulate new T[n] and delete[]. Write template<class T> T* new_array(std::size_t n) that allocates raw memory with ::operator new, stores the count in a cookie, default-constructs the elements with placement new, and destroys the ones already built in reverse order if a constructor throws. Write delete_array(T*) that reads the cookie, destroys in reverse order and frees.

Answer

Approach. The cookie must keep the elements aligned, so its size is max(sizeof(std::size_t), alignof(T)), which is what the Itanium ABI does. Construct in a loop counting successes; on an exception, destroy [0, built) backwards, free and rethrow. delete_array steps back by the cookie size to find the count and the original block.

#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>
#include <stdexcept>

template <class T>
constexpr std::size_t cookie_size = std::max(sizeof(std::size_t), alignof(T));

template <class T>
T* new_array(std::size_t n) {
    static_assert(alignof(T) <= __STDCPP_DEFAULT_NEW_ALIGNMENT__, "use aligned new for this");
    char* raw = static_cast<char*>(::operator new(cookie_size<T> + n * sizeof(T)));
    ::new (raw + cookie_size<T> - sizeof(std::size_t)) std::size_t(n);
    T* first = reinterpret_cast<T*>(raw + cookie_size<T>);
    std::size_t built = 0;
    try {
        for (; built < n; ++built) ::new (first + built) T();
    } catch (...) {
        while (built > 0) first[--built].~T();
        ::operator delete(raw);
        throw;
    }
    return first;
}

template <class T>
void delete_array(T* first) {
    if (!first) return;
    char* raw = reinterpret_cast<char*>(first) - cookie_size<T>;
    std::size_t n = *reinterpret_cast<std::size_t*>(raw + cookie_size<T> - sizeof(std::size_t));
    while (n > 0) first[--n].~T();
    ::operator delete(raw);
}

static int next_id = 0;
static int fail_at = -1;

struct Probe {
    int id;
    Probe() : id(next_id++) {
        if (id == fail_at) throw std::runtime_error("ctor failed");
        std::printf("+%d ", id);
    }
    ~Probe() { std::printf("-%d ", id); }
};

int main() {
    Probe* a = new_array<Probe>(3);
    std::printf("| built\n");
    delete_array(a);
    std::printf("| deleted\n");

    next_id = 0;
    fail_at = 2;
    try {
        new_array<Probe>(4);
    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        std::printf("| %s\n", e.what());
    }
}
+0 +1 +2 | built
-2 -1 -0 | deleted
+0 +1 -1 -0 | ctor failed

Complexity and pitfalls. O(n) construction and destruction. Pitfalls: a cookie smaller than alignof(T) misaligns every element; destroying in forward order; destroying the element whose constructor threw; leaking the block on exception; forgetting that a real implementation skips the cookie for trivially destructible types. Placing the count with placement new (instead of a cast and assignment) starts the lifetime of the size_t properly.

Estimated rating: ~1700 · placement new plus exception-safe partial construction and alignment arithmetic

CodeImplement the operator new loop with an emergency reserve. Write void* allocate(std::size_t n) that behaves like the standard operator new (retry, call the current new_handler, throw bad_alloc when there is none) on top of a pluggable low-level allocator. Then write a handler that releases a reserved block the first time memory runs out and uninstalls itself the second time. Test it with a low-level allocator that has a fixed budget.

Answer

Approach. Model the heap as a budget of bytes so failure is deterministic. allocate loops: try the low-level allocator; on failure read std::get_new_handler(), throw if null, otherwise call it and retry. The handler gives the reserve back to the budget once; on the next call it sets the handler to null so the loop throws.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <new>

namespace heap {
std::size_t budget = 1000;                 // bytes the fake heap can still hand out
void* low_level(std::size_t n) {
    if (n > budget) return nullptr;
    budget -= n;
    return std::malloc(n);
}
void release(void* p, std::size_t n) { budget += n; std::free(p); }
}

void* allocate(std::size_t n) {
    if (n == 0) n = 1;
    for (;;) {
        if (void* p = heap::low_level(n)) return p;
        std::new_handler h = std::get_new_handler();
        if (!h) throw std::bad_alloc{};
        h();
    }
}

static void* reserve = nullptr;
constexpr std::size_t kReserve = 300;

static void emergency_handler() {
    if (reserve) {
        std::puts("handler: releasing reserve");
        heap::release(reserve, kReserve);
        reserve = nullptr;
    } else {
        std::puts("handler: nothing left, giving up");
        std::set_new_handler(nullptr);
    }
}

int main() {
    reserve = allocate(kReserve);                 // budget 700 left
    std::set_new_handler(emergency_handler);
    void* a = allocate(600);                      // fits: 100 left
    std::puts("a ok");
    void* b = allocate(350);                      // needs the reserve: 400 -> 50
    std::puts("b ok");
    try {
        allocate(200);
        std::puts("c ok");
    } catch (const std::bad_alloc&) {
        std::puts("c: bad_alloc");
    }
    heap::release(a, 600);
    heap::release(b, 350);
    std::printf("budget restored: %zu\n", heap::budget);
}
a ok
handler: releasing reserve
b ok
handler: nothing left, giving up
c: bad_alloc
budget restored: 1000

Complexity and pitfalls. Each failure costs one handler call and one retry. The final line checks the bookkeeping: the reserve went back during the handler call and a and b go back at the end, so the fake heap is whole again. Pitfalls: a handler that returns without changing state loops forever; a handler that allocates through operator new re-enters the failing path; the handler is global state, so libraries should not install one behind the application's back. Real reserves are megabytes, used to log and shut down cleanly.

Estimated rating: ~1500 · requires knowing the standard loop exactly and designing a deterministic test

CodeA class-specific free-list allocator. Give struct Order (40 bytes) a class-specific operator new/operator delete that recycles freed blocks through an intrusive singly linked free list and only falls back to ::operator new when the list is empty. Derived classes of a different size must still work. Report how many blocks came from the system.

Answer

Approach. A freed block is at least as big as a pointer, so its first bytes can hold the next-free link. operator new pops from the list when n == sizeof(Order), otherwise forwards to the global allocator (the inherited-size trap). operator delete takes the size (sized class-specific delete) so it can make the same decision on the way back. Pools in depth are Ch 15.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>
#include <vector>

struct Order {
    long id = 0;
    double price = 0, qty = 0;
    long side = 0, venue = 0;

    static void* operator new(std::size_t n) {
        if (n != sizeof(Order)) return ::operator new(n);    // a bigger derived class
        if (free_list) {
            FreeNode* head = free_list;
            free_list = head->next;
            return head;
        }
        ++from_system;
        return ::operator new(n);
    }
    static void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t n) noexcept {
        if (!p) return;
        if (n != sizeof(Order)) { ::operator delete(p); return; }
        free_list = ::new (p) FreeNode{free_list};
    }
    static void release_all() noexcept {
        while (free_list) {
            FreeNode* next = free_list->next;
            ::operator delete(free_list);
            free_list = next;
        }
    }
    virtual ~Order() = default;

    struct FreeNode { FreeNode* next; };
    static inline FreeNode* free_list = nullptr;
    static inline int from_system = 0;
};

struct BigOrder : Order { char note[64] = {}; };

int main() {
    std::vector<Order*> live;
    for (int round = 0; round < 3; ++round) {
        for (int i = 0; i < 100; ++i) live.push_back(new Order);
        for (Order* o : live) delete o;
        live.clear();
    }
    Order* big = new BigOrder;      // must not come from the 40-byte free list
    delete big;
    std::printf("sizeof(Order) = %zu\n", sizeof(Order));
    std::printf("blocks from system: %d\n", Order::from_system);
    Order::release_all();
}
sizeof(Order) = 48
blocks from system: 100

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) allocate and free, 300 objects served from 100 system blocks. Note that sizeof(Order) is 48, not 40: the virtual destructor adds a vptr. That is exactly why the size check matters. Because the destructor is virtual, the sized operator delete receives the dynamic type's size, so BigOrder blocks go back to the global allocator. Pitfalls: not thread-safe (add a mutex or a thread-local list), never returns memory to the system until release_all, and a use-after-free on an Order now corrupts your free list instead of being caught by ASan.

Estimated rating: ~1600 · intrusive free list plus the inherited operator new size trap

Cheat sheet

Theory
  • new = operator new + constructor; delete = destructor + operator delete. malloc/free only move bytes. If a constructor throws inside new, the matching operator delete frees the storage and no destructor runs.
  • Failure: new throws std::bad_alloc after looping through the new_handler; new (std::nothrow) returns null but does not stop constructor exceptions; malloc returns null. On Linux, overcommit means real exhaustion usually shows up as the OOM killer.
  • Pair the families: new/delete, new[]/delete[], malloc/free. Mixing them is UB; the array cookie (present for non-trivial destructors) is why new[] + delete crashes for class types.
  • No renew: objects cannot be moved by memcpy in general, so containers allocate, move and destroy. On realloc failure the old block survives; never write p = realloc(p, n).
  • Customise by replacing the global functions (all forms default to plain new/delete) or with class-specific ones (inherited, so check the size). Always pair a placement new with a placement delete. C++17 aligned new handles alignas beyond 16 automatically.
  • Zero size: new returns a unique non-null pointer; malloc(0) is implementation-defined; realloc(p, 0) is UB in C23.
  • glibc malloc: an 8-byte size word just before your pointer (the chunk starts 16 bytes earlier), tcache then bins then top chunk; brk for the main heap, mmap at 128 KiB and above; per-thread arenas trade memory for less locking.
  • Leaks: RAII prevents most; find the rest with ASan/LSan (-fsanitize=address), valgrind memcheck, or heap profilers for growth that is still reachable.
