Part E · Memory management · Chapter 10

Memory fragmentation

Fragmentation is memory you own but cannot use: bytes wasted inside blocks, or free space split into holes too small for the next request. This chapter explains where it comes from, how allocators fight it (fit policies, size classes, buddies, slabs, coalescing), why a process's RSS stays high after free, and what you can do about it in a long-running C++ service. Interviewers at HFT firms and systems teams ask about it because it explains real production incidents: latency spikes, slow memory growth and out-of-memory kills with plenty of "free" memory.

TheoryDrillsCoding· about 3 hours· prerequisites: Ch 9 (how malloc works)

Internal vs external fragmentation

Theory

Mental model. An allocator hands out blocks from a bigger region. Internal fragmentation is waste inside a block: you asked for 33 bytes and got a 48-byte block, so 15 bytes are allocated but useless. External fragmentation is waste between blocks: the free memory exists, but it is split into many small holes, so a large request fails even though the total free space would be enough.

Sources of internal fragmentation

  • Alignment and minimum size. glibc rounds every request up to a multiple of 16 bytes plus an 8-byte header, with a 32-byte minimum chunk on 64-bit, so malloc(1) occupies 32 bytes.
  • Size classes. Allocators that keep one free list per size round up to the class: jemalloc's spacing keeps the worst-case waste near 20% once sizes pass the first few tiny classes (a 17-byte request still takes a 32-byte slot), while a power-of-two scheme wastes up to 50% at every size.
  • Pages. The kernel maps memory in 4 KiB pages (or 2 MiB huge pages), so the last page of every mapping is on average half empty.
  • Padding inside objects (Ch 1) and container slack: a std::vector with capacity 1024 and size 513 wastes 511 elements.

Sources of external fragmentation

External fragmentation needs two ingredients: varying sizes and interleaved lifetimes. If every block were the same size, any hole would fit any request. If everything were freed in reverse allocation order (a stack), holes would always merge back into the top. Real programs break both: a server allocates a 200-byte request object, then a 4 KiB buffer, then a 48-byte session entry that lives for an hour. When the short-lived neighbours are freed, the long-lived entry pins the middle of the region, and the space around it can only be reused by requests that fit exactly.

How fragmentation builds up in long-running processes

Theory

Mental model. A fresh heap is one big free block. Every allocation that outlives its neighbours becomes a pin. After hours of traffic the heap looks like a car park after a busy day: many single empty spaces scattered between parked cars, and no room for a bus.

The typical patterns behind production incidents:

  • Mixed lifetimes in one heap. Long-lived cache entries allocated between short-lived request buffers. Each cache entry prevents its neighbours from coalescing.
  • Growing then shrinking containers. A burst makes a std::vector or std::string grow through 1, 2, 4, ... 64 MB; the freed smaller buffers leave holes behind that only small requests can use.
  • Size drift. The workload changes from many 64-byte objects to many 80-byte objects. The free 64-byte chunks (or a size class's dedicated pages) cannot serve the new size, so the heap grows while old free memory sits idle.
  • Per-thread caches and arenas. Memory freed by thread A is cached for thread A. If thread B now does the allocating, the heap grows again. glibc's per-thread arenas make this visible as RSS that is several times the live data (Ch 9).
  • Producer-consumer across threads. One thread allocates messages, another frees them. Allocators with thread-local caches must ship the memory back, and some (older ptmalloc versions especially) do this badly.

Know this cold

C++ cannot compact the heap. Raw pointers and references are plain addresses, the language allows hiding them in integers, and nothing records where they are, so an allocator can never move a live block to close a hole. Fragmentation therefore only goes down when blocks next to each other are both freed. Java and .NET compacting collectors can move objects because the runtime knows every reference.

Placement policies: first, best, next and worst fit

Theory

Mental model. Given a list of free holes and a request, which hole do you carve the block from? The answer changes both speed and how the holes evolve.

PolicyRuleStrengthWeakness
First fitScan from the start, take the first hole that fitsSimple; address-ordered first fit keeps low addresses denseSmall leftovers pile up at the front, so scans get slower
Next fitLike first fit, but resume where the last search stoppedSpreads work across the listScatters long-lived blocks everywhere; measured fragmentation is worse than first fit
Best fitTake the smallest hole that fitsKeeps big holes intact for big requestsLeaves tiny slivers; needs an ordered structure to be fast
Worst fitTake the largest holeLeftovers stay usableDestroys large holes; performs badly in practice

What measurements say

The classic survey by Wilson, Johnstone, Neely and Boles (1995) replayed real program traces and found that address-ordered first fit and best fit both fragment very little on real workloads, while next fit is noticeably worse. Two older results are interview favourites. Knuth's fifty-percent rule: in an allocator that always coalesces adjacent free blocks, at equilibrium with N allocated blocks there are about N/2 free holes, so roughly a third of all blocks are holes. (It is a statistical result under steady-state assumptions, and it says nothing about how big the holes are.) Robson's bound: for any allocator that cannot move blocks there exist adversarial request sequences that need memory proportional to M·log2 n, where M is the maximum live data and n the ratio of largest to smallest block size. Robson proved a lower bound of roughly ½·M·log2 n for every non-moving allocator and gave one that stays within about M·log2 n. No placement policy can prevent fragmentation in the worst case; the good ones exploit the fact that real programs are not adversarial.

Splitting and coalescing

Theory

Mental model. Splitting carves the requested size off a larger hole and keeps the remainder as a smaller hole. Coalescing is the reverse: when a block is freed, merge it with a free neighbour on either side so that holes grow back. Without coalescing, a heap that has served many small requests can never serve a large one again.

Immediate vs deferred coalescing

Coalescing on every free costs time and can be wasted work if the program immediately asks for the same size again (free 64, malloc 64, free 64...). So allocators often defer it: glibc's tcache and fastbins keep small chunks unmerged and marked "in use", and coalesce the fastbins in bulk (malloc_consolidate) when a large-bin request arrives or when a free produces a merged chunk of 64 KiB or more. Chunks in the tcache are never coalesced while they sit there. The trade-off: deferred coalescing is faster for repeating sizes and worse for fragmentation when the size mix changes. Size-class allocators (next section) mostly avoid the question: blocks in a size-class page never merge with each other; the whole page becomes free when its last block is freed.

Segregated lists, size classes, buddies and slabs

Theory

Segregated free lists and size classes

Mental model. Instead of one list of holes of every size, keep a separate free list per size class, and carve each class from its own pages. A request is rounded up to its class and popped from that list in O(1). Since every block on a list is the same size, any free block fits any request of that class: external fragmentation within the class disappears. The price is internal fragmentation from rounding, plus pages that belong to one class sitting half-empty when the program stops using that size.

Class spacing is the main design knob. Powers of two are simple but waste up to 50%. jemalloc uses four classes per doubling (for example 80, 96, 112, 128, then 160, 192, 224, 256), capping waste at about 20% of the block (the request is rounded up by at most a quarter of the class's power of two). tcmalloc uses a hand-tuned table of roughly 60 to 90 classes (Google's documentation says 60 to 80, gperftools about 88), chosen from allocation profiles to keep rounding waste small; it publishes no single worst-case bound, so do not quote one.

The buddy system

The buddy allocator manages a power-of-two region. Every block has size 2k times a minimum unit, and every block (except the whole region) has a unique buddy of the same size: the other half of the block it was split from. The buddy's address is found with one XOR: buddy = offset ^ size. Allocation rounds up to a power of two, takes a free block of that order, or splits a larger one in halves repeatedly. Freeing checks whether the buddy is free; if so, merges and repeats one level up.

The Linux kernel's page allocator is a buddy system over physical page frames with orders 0 to 10 (4 KiB up to 4 MiB with 4 KiB pages). cat /proc/buddyinfo shows how many free blocks of each order every memory zone has; a machine with plenty of order-0 pages and no order-9 pages cannot satisfy a 2 MiB huge page without compaction.

Slab allocation

A slab allocator (Bonwick, SunOS 1994; SLUB in today's Linux kernel) dedicates one or more pages to objects of a single type or size, for example all struct inode objects or all 64-byte kmalloc requests. Each slab is carved into equal slots tracked by a free list. Benefits: no external fragmentation within a slab, O(1) allocation, good cache behaviour, and (in the original design) objects kept in a constructed state so initialisation is not repeated. /proc/slabinfo or slabtop shows the caches. User-space equivalents are fixed-size pools (Ch 15) and object pools (Ch 16).

Measuring fragmentation

Theory

There is no single number, so say which one you mean.

MetricFormulaReads as
Internal fragmentation(bytes allocated − bytes requested) / bytes allocatedRounding and header waste
External fragmentation1 − largest free block / total free bytes0 when all free space is one hole; near 1 when it is shattered
Heap overhead ratioheap size from the OS / live bytes requestedEverything together, plus allocator metadata
RSS ratio (Redis mem_fragmentation_ratio)RSS / live bytes requestedWhat operators see; above about 1.5 usually means fragmentation, below 1 means swapping
Kernel: /proc/buddyinfo, extfrag_indexFree blocks per orderWhether high-order (contiguous) allocations can succeed

Tools: glibc malloc_stats() and malloc_info(0, stdout) print per-arena totals; mallinfo2() returns them as numbers. jemalloc has malloc_stats_print and the stats.* mallctl namespace, tcmalloc has MallocExtension::GetStats. For RSS, read VmRSS in /proc/self/status or use smem/pmap.

Key facts

FactValue (Linux, glibc, 64-bit)
Minimum chunk / alignment32 bytes / 16 bytes
mmap threshold128 KiB default, dynamic up to 32 MiB
Trim threshold (top of heap returned with brk)128 KiB default
Max arenas8 × cores (tunable MALLOC_ARENA_MAX)
Page size / huge page4 KiB / 2 MiB (x86-64)
Kernel buddy orders0 to 10 (4 KiB to 4 MiB)
Power-of-two classes, worst internal wasteJust under 50%
vector growth factor2 (libstdc++, libc++), 1.5 (MSVC, folly)

RSS, virtual memory and why free() does not shrink the process

Theory

Mental model. Three different numbers describe a process's memory. Virtual size (VSZ) is all mapped address space, including reserved and never-touched regions. Resident set size (RSS) is the physical pages currently mapped in. Live heap is what your program has allocated and not freed. free() lowers the third; whether RSS goes down depends on whether the allocator gives pages back to the kernel.

Why RSS stays high after free

  • brk can only shrink from the top. The main glibc heap is one contiguous segment. If one live chunk sits near the top, nothing below it can be released with brk, however much is free. glibc trims automatically only when the free top chunk exceeds M_TRIM_THRESHOLD (128 KiB by default).
  • Free chunks stay in caches and bins, ready for reuse. That is the point of an allocator: going back to the kernel costs a system call and later page faults.
  • Fragmentation inside pages. A 4 KiB page that holds one live 32-byte chunk stays resident.
  • Arenas. Each thread's arena holds its own free memory.
  • Lazy release. Allocators that release pages with madvise(MADV_FREE) (Linux 4.5+; jemalloc's "muzzy" stage when it is enabled, some Go runtime versions) tell the kernel it may take the pages, but RSS only drops when the kernel actually reclaims them under memory pressure. Monitoring then shows "high" RSS that is in fact reclaimable.

What you can do

#include <malloc.h>   // glibc only

// Return free memory to the kernel: trims the top of the main heap and, since
// glibc 2.8, calls madvise(MADV_DONTNEED) on whole free pages inside every arena.
malloc_trim(0);

// Tune at startup (or with GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.malloc.trim_threshold=...).
mallopt(M_MMAP_THRESHOLD, 64 * 1024);   // fixing it also disables the dynamic threshold
mallopt(M_ARENA_MAX, 2);

Large allocations (above the mmap threshold) avoid the problem entirely: each one is its own mapping and free unmaps it at once. That is also why a program that frees one huge buffer sees RSS drop immediately, while one that frees a million small nodes does not.

Interview trap

"Our service leaks: RSS grows and never comes down." Before blaming a leak, check the live heap (allocator stats or a heap profiler). If live bytes are flat while RSS is high, the problem is fragmentation, arena count or retention policy, not a leak, and the fixes are different: fewer arenas, another allocator, malloc_trim, or changing allocation patterns.

jemalloc, tcmalloc and mimalloc in brief

Theory

All three replace malloc and operator new (by linking or LD_PRELOAD), use size classes for small objects plus thread-local caches, and give memory back to the OS more actively than ptmalloc. The differences that come up in interviews:

AllocatorSmall objectsConcurrencyReturning memoryKnown for
jemalloc (FreeBSD, Meta)Size classes, 4 per doubling, in "slabs" within extentsThread cache in front of several arenas (4 × cores)Time-based decay purging with madvise (dirty pages, then optionally "muzzy" lazily freed ones; muzzy decay is off by default since 5.2)Low fragmentation, rich statistics and profiling
tcmalloc (Google)About 60 to 90 hand-tuned size classes, spans of pagesPer-thread or per-CPU caches (per-CPU uses Linux restartable sequences), central free lists, page heapBackground release of free spans at a configurable rateVery fast small allocations, huge-page aware design
mimalloc (Microsoft)Free-list sharding: a free list per page, not per size classPages owned by a thread; cross-thread frees go to a separate per-page listEager page reset and segment releaseSmall code base, consistently fast in benchmarks

Switching allocators is a common production fix for RSS bloat in multithreaded C++ services. Measure first: each allocator wins on some workloads and loses on others, and the decision is usually made from a load test that records both RSS and tail latency.

Mitigation: pools, arenas, preallocation and growth policy

Theory

Mental model. Fragmentation comes from mixing sizes and lifetimes in one heap. Every mitigation separates them: same-size objects together, same-lifetime objects together, or no allocation at all on the hot path.

  • Fixed-size pools for hot objects (orders, nodes, messages): one size, so no external fragmentation, O(1) allocation (Ch 15, Ch 16).
  • Arenas per lifetime: everything allocated for one request or one frame goes into a bump allocator that is reset at the end; no individual frees, so no holes (Ch 17). std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource is the standard one.
  • Preallocate at startup: HFT systems size every buffer, ring and pool before the market opens, then never call malloc on the hot path. A heap that does not change cannot fragment.
  • reserve() for containers whose final size you know, so they never pass through the 1, 2, 4, 8... sequence of intermediate buffers.
  • Reuse objects instead of freeing and reallocating: clear() a vector or string and keep its capacity.
  • Avoid node-based containers on hot paths: std::list and std::map make one allocation per element; a sorted std::vector or a flat hash map makes a few large ones.
  • Small-buffer optimisation keeps short strings and small functors inside the object (Ch 18).

The vector growth factor

libstdc++ and libc++ double a vector's capacity on reallocation; MSVC and folly's fbvector multiply by 1.5. Both give amortised O(1) push_back. The fragmentation argument for 1.5: with factor f, can the new buffer ever fit in the space released by all the previous buffers? During reallocation the current buffer is still live (its elements are being moved), so the new size fn+1 must fit into the sum of the older blocks 1 + f + ... + fn−1. For f = 2 that sum is 2n − 1, always less than the old block alone, so the new buffer never fits in the old space and the vector keeps walking forward through memory. The condition can hold only when f is below the golden ratio, about 1.618; at 1.5 the old space becomes reusable after a few reallocations. The argument assumes the freed blocks are adjacent and get coalesced, which real allocators with size classes and mmap thresholds do not guarantee, so treat it as a tie-breaker, not a law.

Tip

clear() keeps capacity and shrink_to_fit() is only a request. To really release a vector's buffer, swap with an empty one: std::vector<T>().swap(v);. In a long-running process, prefer keeping the capacity if the vector will grow again, since repeated grow-shrink cycles are a fragmentation source.

The paging angle: physical memory and huge pages

Theory

Mental model. Virtual memory solves external fragmentation of physical memory: the page table can map any free physical frame behind any virtual page, so a process that needs 1 GB of contiguous addresses gets them even if its frames are scattered all over RAM. What it does not solve:

  • Internal fragmentation in pages. Memory is mapped in whole pages, so every mapping wastes on average half a page at its end. With 2 MiB huge pages that average waste is 1 MiB per mapping, which is why huge pages suit big heaps and hurt programs with many small mappings.
  • Fragmentation of the virtual address space. On 32-bit systems a long-running process could fail to find 500 MB of contiguous virtual addresses with gigabytes of RAM free. On 64-bit with 47 bits of user address space it is rarely a problem.
  • Physically contiguous requests. Huge pages, DMA buffers for devices without an IOMMU and some kernel allocations need contiguous frames, which brings back external fragmentation at the physical level. Linux fights it with the buddy allocator, by grouping pages by mobility (movable user pages apart from unmovable kernel pages), and with compaction (kcompactd), which migrates movable pages to build large free blocks. Transparent huge pages depend on compaction succeeding; when it stalls, page faults can take milliseconds, a known cause of latency spikes in trading systems.
  • Fragmentation inside the heap (the rest of this chapter) happens in virtual addresses, above the page tables, and paging does nothing for it.

So the accurate interview answer to "doesn't paging eliminate fragmentation?" is: it eliminates external fragmentation of physical memory for ordinary page-sized mappings, it introduces internal fragmentation at page granularity, and it does nothing about fragmentation inside your process's heap.

Concept and tricky questions

Drills

ConceptDefine internal and external fragmentation and give one cause of each.

Answer

Answer. Internal: memory allocated to a block but not requested by the program (a 33-byte request served from a 48-byte class wastes 15). External: free memory split into holes too small to satisfy a request although the total would suffice. Internal comes from rounding (alignment, size classes, page granularity); external comes from mixed sizes with interleaved lifetimes.

Why. The distinction matters because the fixes differ: finer size classes reduce internal waste, while separating lifetimes or sizes (pools, arenas) reduces external waste. A common slip is calling a leak "fragmentation": leaked memory is live from the allocator's point of view.

ConceptA heap has free blocks of 64, 16, 16 and 32 bytes. Compute the external fragmentation metric and say whether malloc(100) can succeed without growing the heap.

Answer

Answer. Total free = 128, largest = 64, so external fragmentation = 1 − 64/128 = 0.5. A 100-byte request fails without growing the heap, even though 128 bytes are free.

Why. A request needs one contiguous block. The metric is 0 when all free memory is a single hole and approaches 1 when it is shattered into tiny pieces. The heap would extend the top chunk (brk) or mmap, so RSS grows while free memory sits unused.

ConceptHow does the buddy system find a block's buddy, and what is its worst-case internal fragmentation?

Answer

Answer. For a block of size 2k at offset off (relative to the region start), the buddy is at off ^ 2k. Worst-case internal fragmentation is just under 50%: a request of 2k + 1 units gets a 2k+1 block.

Why. Splitting a block of size 2k+1 aligned to its size produces two halves that differ only in bit k of their offset, so flipping that bit finds the other half. That makes merging a constant-time check per level. Average waste for uniformly distributed sizes is about 25%.

ConceptWhat is a slab allocator and why does the Linux kernel use one on top of its buddy allocator?

Answer

Answer. A slab allocator dedicates pages to objects of one size or type and hands out equal slots from them via a free list. The buddy allocator only deals in whole pages (4 KiB and up), so allocating a 64-byte kernel object from it directly would waste most of a page; SLUB carves pages from the buddy allocator into many small slots.

Why. One size per slab means no external fragmentation within it and O(1) operations, and grouping same-type objects is cache friendly. The original Bonwick design also cached constructed objects to skip initialisation. User-space pools apply the same idea.

ConceptA service's live heap is flat at 2 GB but its RSS has grown to 6 GB over a week. Give three likely causes and how you would confirm each.

Answer

Answer. (1) Heap fragmentation: compare allocator stats (malloc_info, jemalloc stats) for free-but-retained bytes. (2) Too many glibc arenas holding per-thread free memory: count arenas in malloc_info, try MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2. (3) Memory not returned to the kernel (no trim, or lazy MADV_FREE): call malloc_trim(0) in a test and watch RSS drop, or check LazyFree in /proc/PID/smaps.

Why. A flat live heap rules out a classic leak. The usual production fixes are fewer arenas, a different allocator (jemalloc/tcmalloc), separating long-lived from short-lived allocations, or periodic trimming. Heap profilers (heaptrack, jemalloc prof) confirm which call sites dominate.

ConceptWhy do HFT and game engines preallocate everything at startup instead of trusting a good malloc?

Answer

Answer. Predictability. A hot-path malloc can take a lock, walk bins, call brk or mmap, take page faults on fresh memory, or trigger consolidation; the average is fast but the tail is not. A heap that does not change after startup cannot fragment and never needs the kernel.

Why. Latency-sensitive code cares about the 99.9th percentile. Preallocation plus pools, arenas and rings turns allocation into a pointer bump or a free-list pop, and prefaulting (touching or mlocking the memory) removes page faults too.

Tricky"Paging eliminates fragmentation." True or false?

Answer

Answer. Partly false. Paging eliminates external fragmentation of physical memory for page-sized mappings, because any free frame can back any virtual page. It introduces internal fragmentation (on average half a page per mapping), does nothing about fragmentation inside a process's heap, and physical external fragmentation returns for anything that needs contiguous frames: huge pages, DMA buffers, high-order kernel allocations.

Why. That is why Linux has compaction and groups pages by mobility, and why transparent huge pages can stall page faults on a fragmented machine. The one-word "true" is the answer the interviewer is fishing for.

TrickyBest fit picks the tightest hole. Does it always fragment less than first fit?

Answer

Answer. No. Best fit tends to leave tiny unusable slivers, and for some request sequences first fit succeeds where best fit fails (and vice versa). On real program traces, address-ordered first fit and best fit perform similarly well; next fit is the one measurably worse.

Why. Robson showed every non-moving policy has adversarial inputs, and Wilson et al. (1995) found trace behaviour, not the policy name, dominates. Example where first fit wins: holes 20 and 15, requests 10, 10, 15. First fit puts both 10s into the 20 hole and the 15 into the 15 hole. Best fit puts the first 10 into the 15 hole (leaving 5), the second into the 20 (leaving 10), and the 15 fails.

TrickyWhy can a C++ allocator not compact the heap the way the JVM does?

Answer

Answer. Moving a block requires updating every pointer to it, and in C++ nothing knows where those pointers are. They can live in registers, on the stack, inside other objects, be cast to std::uintptr_t, XOR-ed, or written to a file. The JVM's collector knows the exact location of every reference.

Why. Without compaction, external fragmentation only shrinks through coalescing of adjacent free blocks. Systems that need compaction in C++ use handles (an index into a table that the allocator can update) instead of raw pointers, which is what some game engines and databases do.

TrickyWhy does MSVC grow vectors by 1.5 while libstdc++ uses 2, and is the "1.5 lets you reuse memory" argument actually true?

Answer

Answer. With factor f, the new buffer can fit into the coalesced space of all earlier buffers only if f is below the golden ratio (about 1.618), because the current buffer is still live during the copy. At 2 the sum of earlier buffers (2n − 1) is always smaller than the next request, so memory is never reused by the vector itself. Factor 2 wins on fewer reallocations and copies.

Why. The argument assumes the old buffers were adjacent, freed and merged, and that nothing else claimed them. Size-class allocators, the mmap threshold for big buffers and other allocations break those assumptions, so in practice the benefit is small. Both factors give amortised O(1) push_back; the trade-off is copies vs memory.

TrickyA program frees a 1 GB buffer and a million 1 KB nodes (another 1 GB). RSS drops by about 1 GB, not 2. Why?

Answer

Answer. The 1 GB buffer was above the mmap threshold, so it had its own mapping and free unmapped it immediately. The nodes came from the brk heap and arenas; their freed chunks stay in bins and caches, and the heap can only shrink from the top, so most of that memory stays resident until reused or until malloc_trim releases whole free pages.

Why. glibc returns memory to the kernel automatically only for mmapped chunks and for a free top chunk above the trim threshold. People assume free means "give back to the OS"; for small blocks it almost never does.

TrickyDoes std::list fragment the heap more than std::vector? Does reserve() help with fragmentation or only with speed?

Answer

Answer. Usually yes: a list makes one small allocation per element, interleaved with everything else the program allocates, and freeing elements in arbitrary order leaves holes all over the heap. A vector makes O(log n) large allocations. reserve() helps both: it removes the reallocation copies and the trail of discarded intermediate buffers (1, 2, 4, ... n/2) that would otherwise become holes.

Why. Each node also carries allocator overhead (header plus rounding: a 4-byte int in a list node uses a 32-byte chunk with glibc). The counter-argument is that list nodes are all the same size, so their holes are reusable by other nodes; mixed with other sizes, they still fragment.

Tricky"Size-class allocators such as jemalloc and tcmalloc have no external fragmentation, because every block in a class is the same size." True?

Answer

Answer. False. Within one class any free slot fits any request of that class, so there is no hole-too-small problem. But free slots are tied to their class and their page: a run of 64-byte slots with one live object cannot serve a 96-byte request and cannot go back to the OS. After a burst of 64-byte objects is mostly freed, those pages sit nearly empty while the 96-byte class asks for new pages. This is external fragmentation one level up, between classes and pages.

Why. The allocator can only release a page (or span, or extent) when every slot on it is free, and a single long-lived object pins the whole page. That is why these allocators track per-page occupancy, prefer to allocate from the fullest pages so the emptier ones can drain, and report "fragmentation" as resident bytes in partly used runs. The common wrong answer is "size classes trade external for internal fragmentation completely": they only remove the within-class part.

Predict the output and find the bug

Drills

OutputPrint a vector's capacity each time it changes during 17 push_backs.

#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<int> v;
    std::size_t last = v.capacity();
    std::printf("%zu", last);
    for (int i = 0; i < 17; ++i) {
        v.push_back(i);
        if (v.capacity() != last) {
            last = v.capacity();
            std::printf(" %zu", last);
        }
    }
    std::printf("\n");
}
Answer
0 1 2 4 8 16 32

Answer. libstdc++ and libc++ both start at 0 and double: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. The 17th push_back moves from 16 to 32.

Why. The growth factor is unspecified; the standard only requires amortised constant time. MSVC would print 0 1 2 3 4 6 9 13 19 (factor 1.5, with a minimum growth of one). Each step allocates a new buffer and frees the old one, so without reserve(17) this loop performs six allocations and leaves five freed buffers behind.

OutputWhat are size and capacity after clear(), after shrink_to_fit(), and after the swap trick?

#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<double> v(1000);
    v.clear();
    std::printf("after clear: size=%zu capacity=%zu\n", v.size(), v.capacity());
    v.shrink_to_fit();
    std::printf("after shrink_to_fit: capacity=%zu\n", v.capacity());

    std::vector<double> w(1000);
    std::vector<double>().swap(w);
    std::printf("after swap: capacity=%zu\n", w.capacity());
}
Answer
after clear: size=0 capacity=1000
after shrink_to_fit: capacity=0
after swap: capacity=0

Answer. clear() destroys the elements but keeps the 8000-byte buffer. shrink_to_fit() releases it on both libstdc++ and libc++. The swap trick releases it on every implementation.

Why. shrink_to_fit is a non-binding request ([vector.capacity]), so portable code that must release memory uses the swap idiom. Keeping capacity after clear() is deliberate: a vector that is refilled every iteration then never reallocates, which is a fragmentation and latency win in loops.

OutputA size-class allocator with classes 16, 32, 48, 64, 96 and 128 serves five requests. What does it report?

#include <cstdio>

static const int kClasses[] = {16, 32, 48, 64, 96, 128};

static int class_for(int n) {
    for (int c : kClasses)
        if (n <= c) return c;
    return -1;
}

int main() {
    const int requests[] = {1, 17, 33, 65, 100};
    int asked = 0, given = 0;
    for (int r : requests) {
        int c = class_for(r);
        std::printf("%d->%d ", r, c);
        asked += r;
        given += c;
    }
    std::printf("\nrequested %d, allocated %d, internal waste %.1f%%\n",
                asked, given, 100.0 * (given - asked) / given);
}
Answer
1->16 17->32 33->48 65->96 100->128
requested 216, allocated 320, internal waste 32.5%

Answer. Each request rounds up to the next class; 104 of the 320 allocated bytes are waste, 32.5%.

Why. Internal fragmentation is (allocated − requested) / allocated. The worst offenders are requests just above a class boundary (17, 33, 65). Finer class spacing reduces this at the cost of more free lists and more partly used pages, which is the trade-off every size-class allocator tunes.

OutputHoles of 100, 30 and 60 bytes; requests of 25, 55 and 90. What do first fit and best fit do?

#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

static int pick(const std::vector<int>& holes, int n, bool best) {
    int chosen = -1;
    for (int i = 0; i < static_cast<int>(holes.size()); ++i) {
        if (holes[i] < n) continue;
        if (!best) return i;
        if (chosen < 0 || holes[i] < holes[chosen]) chosen = i;
    }
    return chosen;
}

static void run(bool best) {
    std::vector<int> holes = {100, 30, 60};
    std::printf("%s:", best ? "best " : "first");
    for (int n : {25, 55, 90}) {
        int i = pick(holes, n, best);
        if (i < 0) { std::printf(" %d->fail", n); continue; }
        holes[i] -= n;
        std::printf(" %d->hole%d", n, i);
    }
    std::printf(" | left:");
    for (int h : holes) std::printf(" %d", h);
    std::printf("\n");
}

int main() {
    run(false);
    run(true);
}
Answer
first: 25->hole0 55->hole0 90->fail | left: 20 30 60
best : 25->hole1 55->hole2 90->hole0 | left: 10 5 5

Answer. First fit carves both small requests from the big hole and then cannot serve 90. Best fit puts them into the tight holes and keeps the big hole for 90.

Why. This sequence favours best fit; others favour first fit (see the tricky drill on best fit). Note the cost: best fit leaves two 5-byte slivers, which are likely too small to ever be used, the classic best-fit weakness.

Find the bugA bump arena aligns every allocation to 8 bytes. Two allocations later the program corrupts the heap. Why?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstring>

class Arena {
public:
    explicit Arena(std::size_t cap) : buf_(new char[cap]), cap_(cap) {}
    ~Arena() { delete[] buf_; }
    Arena(const Arena&) = delete;
    Arena& operator=(const Arena&) = delete;

    void* alloc(std::size_t n) {
        std::size_t start = (used_ + 7) & ~std::size_t(7);
        if (used_ + n > cap_) return nullptr;
        used_ = start + n;
        return buf_ + start;
    }

private:
    char* buf_;
    std::size_t cap_;
    std::size_t used_ = 0;
};

int main() {
    Arena arena(64);
    char* a = static_cast<char*>(arena.alloc(5));
    char* b = static_cast<char*>(arena.alloc(58));
    if (!a || !b) { std::puts("out of space"); return 0; }
    std::memset(a, 'a', 5);
    std::memset(b, 'b', 58);
    std::puts("done");
}
Answer

Answer. The capacity check uses used_ instead of the aligned start. The second call computes start = 8 but checks 5 + 58 = 63 <= 64, so it returns [8, 66), two bytes past the end of the buffer. Fix: if (start + n > cap_ || start + n < start) return nullptr; (the second test guards overflow).

Why. Alignment padding is internal fragmentation that the bounds check must account for. ASan reports a heap-buffer-overflow in the second memset. Without ASan the two bytes land in the allocator's next chunk header, and the crash happens much later, in an unrelated free. Arenas are covered fully in Ch 17.

Find the bugThe code keeps a reference to the first element while the vector grows.

#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<int> prices = {100, 101, 102};
    int& best = prices[0];
    for (int i = 0; i < 10; ++i) prices.push_back(103 + i);
    best = 99;
    std::printf("%d\n", prices[0]);
}
Answer

Answer. The fourth push_back exceeds capacity 3, so the vector moves to a new buffer and frees the old one. best still refers to the old buffer, and best = 99 writes freed memory. Store an index, take the reference after the growth, or reserve enough first.

Why. Reallocation invalidates all references, pointers and iterators ([vector.modifiers]). Under glibc the write lands in a freed chunk that may now be a tcache entry, corrupting the allocator's own list. ASan reports heap-use-after-free on the assignment.

Find the bugThis toy allocator should end with one free 128-byte block after everything is freed, but it prints something else. What is printed, and what is missing?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <iterator>
#include <map>

struct Heap {
    std::map<std::size_t, std::size_t> free_blocks;   // offset -> size, address ordered
    explicit Heap(std::size_t n) { free_blocks[0] = n; }

    std::size_t alloc(std::size_t n) {                // first fit, assumes success
        for (auto it = free_blocks.begin(); it != free_blocks.end(); ++it) {
            if (it->second < n) continue;
            std::size_t off = it->first, rest = it->second - n;
            free_blocks.erase(it);
            if (rest) free_blocks[off + n] = rest;
            return off;
        }
        return SIZE_MAX;
    }

    void release(std::size_t off, std::size_t n) {
        auto it = free_blocks.emplace(off, n).first;
        auto next = std::next(it);
        if (next != free_blocks.end() && off + n == next->first) {
            it->second += next->second;
            free_blocks.erase(next);
        }
    }
};

int main() {
    Heap h(128);
    std::size_t a = h.alloc(32), b = h.alloc(32), c = h.alloc(32);
    h.release(a, 32);
    h.release(b, 32);
    h.release(c, 32);
    std::size_t largest = 0;
    for (auto& [off, size] : h.free_blocks) largest = size > largest ? size : largest;
    std::printf("free blocks: %zu, largest: %zu\n", h.free_blocks.size(), largest);
}
Answer
free blocks: 3, largest: 64

Answer. It prints three free blocks with the largest only 64. release merges with the following block but never with the preceding one. Freeing a then b leaves [0,32) and [32,64) separate; freeing c merges it only with the tail. Add the backward merge: if it != begin and prev.offset + prev.size == off, grow prev and erase it.

Why. Coalescing must look both ways, or the heap slowly turns into slivers and large requests fail with plenty of free bytes, which is exactly external fragmentation. Real allocators use boundary tags so the previous block can be found in O(1); an address-ordered map gives O(log n).

OutputA buddy allocator over 1024 KiB receives requests of 100, 200, 60 and 300 KiB. What block sizes are used and how much is wasted?

#include <cstdio>

static unsigned round_pow2(unsigned n) {
    unsigned p = 1;
    while (p < n) p <<= 1;
    return p;
}

int main() {
    const unsigned requests[] = {100, 200, 60, 300};
    unsigned total_req = 0, total_block = 0;
    for (unsigned r : requests) {
        unsigned b = round_pow2(r);
        std::printf("%u KiB -> %u KiB block (waste %u)\n", r, b, b - r);
        total_req += r;
        total_block += b;
    }
    std::printf("requested %u of 1024, blocks use %u, fits: %s\n",
                total_req, total_block, total_block <= 1024 ? "maybe" : "no");
}
Answer
100 KiB -> 128 KiB block (waste 28)
200 KiB -> 256 KiB block (waste 56)
60 KiB -> 64 KiB block (waste 4)
300 KiB -> 512 KiB block (waste 212)
requested 660 of 1024, blocks use 960, fits: maybe

Answer. Blocks of 128, 256, 64 and 512 KiB; 300 KiB wastes 212 KiB because it sits just above 256. The blocks total 960 KiB, so they fit, but only because their placement works out: 512 + 256 + 128 + 64 can all be carved from one 1024 region.

Why. Buddy allocation trades internal fragmentation (here 300 of 960 KiB, 31%) for O(log n) splits and merges with no searching. "Maybe" is the honest answer for total ≤ capacity in general: a buddy system can also fail on external fragmentation if the free blocks are not buddies of each other.

Write the code

Coding

CodeFirst-fit allocator simulation with splitting and coalescing. Manage a region of N bytes by offset. alloc(n) rounds n up to 8, uses first fit and returns an offset or std::nullopt. release(off) frees the block and merges it with both neighbours. Expose total free bytes, largest free block and the external fragmentation metric.

Answer

Approach. Keep free blocks in an address-ordered std::map<offset, size> and live blocks in another map so release knows the size. Allocation scans in address order (first fit) and splits. Release inserts the block, then merges with the successor and the predecessor if they touch.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <iterator>
#include <map>
#include <optional>

class FirstFit {
public:
    explicit FirstFit(std::size_t size) { free_[0] = size; }

    std::optional<std::size_t> alloc(std::size_t n) {
        n = (n + 7) & ~std::size_t(7);
        if (n == 0) n = 8;
        for (auto it = free_.begin(); it != free_.end(); ++it) {
            if (it->second < n) continue;
            std::size_t off = it->first, rest = it->second - n;
            free_.erase(it);
            if (rest) free_[off + n] = rest;
            used_[off] = n;
            return off;
        }
        return std::nullopt;
    }

    void release(std::size_t off) {
        auto u = used_.find(off);
        if (u == used_.end()) return;                    // unknown or double free
        std::size_t n = u->second;
        used_.erase(u);
        auto it = free_.emplace(off, n).first;
        if (auto next = std::next(it); next != free_.end() && it->first + it->second == next->first) {
            it->second += next->second;
            free_.erase(next);
        }
        if (it != free_.begin()) {
            auto prev = std::prev(it);
            if (prev->first + prev->second == it->first) {
                prev->second += it->second;
                free_.erase(it);
            }
        }
    }

    std::size_t total_free() const {
        std::size_t t = 0;
        for (auto& [off, size] : free_) t += size;
        return t;
    }
    std::size_t largest_free() const {
        std::size_t m = 0;
        for (auto& [off, size] : free_) m = size > m ? size : m;
        return m;
    }
    double external_frag() const {
        std::size_t t = total_free();
        return t ? 1.0 - double(largest_free()) / double(t) : 0.0;
    }
    std::size_t holes() const { return free_.size(); }

private:
    std::map<std::size_t, std::size_t> free_, used_;
};

static void show(const char* label, const FirstFit& h) {
    std::printf("%-12s holes=%zu free=%zu largest=%zu frag=%.2f\n", label,
                h.holes(), h.total_free(), h.largest_free(), h.external_frag());
}

int main() {
    FirstFit h(256);
    auto a = h.alloc(64), b = h.alloc(64), c = h.alloc(64), d = h.alloc(30);
    show("4 allocs", h);
    h.release(*a);
    h.release(*c);
    show("free a, c", h);
    std::printf("alloc(100): %s\n", h.alloc(100) ? "ok" : "fails");
    h.release(*b);
    show("free b", h);
    auto e = h.alloc(100);
    std::printf("alloc(100): at %zu\n", *e);
    h.release(*e);
    h.release(*d);
    show("free all", h);
}
4 allocs     holes=1 free=32 largest=32 frag=0.00
free a, c    holes=3 free=160 largest=64 frag=0.60
alloc(100): fails
free b       holes=2 free=224 largest=192 frag=0.14
alloc(100): at 0
free all     holes=1 free=256 largest=256 frag=0.00

Complexity and pitfalls. Allocation is O(h) in the number of holes (first fit scans), release is O(log h). The d = alloc(30) request rounds to 32, so only 32 bytes remain at first. With a and c free there are 160 free bytes and the 100-byte request still fails: external fragmentation in action. After freeing b, three adjacent blocks merge into one 192-byte hole. Pitfalls: forgetting the backward merge, double free (handled by the used_ lookup), and taking iterators after erase.

Estimated rating: ~1500 · ordered-map bookkeeping with careful two-sided merging

CodeBuddy allocator. Manage 2K units. alloc(units) rounds up to a power of two, takes the smallest free block that fits, and splits it; release(off) merges with free buddies all the way up. Show the free lists after a few operations.

Answer

Approach. One std::set of offsets per order. To allocate order k, find the smallest order j ≥ k with a free block, remove it, and split down: each split puts the upper half (off + 2j−1) on list j−1. Remember the order of each live block. To free, repeatedly check whether off ^ 2k is on list k; if so remove it, take the lower offset and go up one order.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <map>
#include <optional>
#include <set>
#include <vector>

class Buddy {
public:
    explicit Buddy(int max_order) : max_(max_order), free_(max_order + 1) {
        free_[max_].insert(0);
    }

    std::optional<std::size_t> alloc(std::size_t units) {
        int k = 0;
        while ((std::size_t(1) << k) < units) ++k;
        int j = k;
        while (j <= max_ && free_[j].empty()) ++j;
        if (j > max_) return std::nullopt;
        std::size_t off = *free_[j].begin();
        free_[j].erase(free_[j].begin());
        while (j > k) {
            --j;
            free_[j].insert(off + (std::size_t(1) << j));   // upper half stays free
        }
        order_of_[off] = k;
        return off;
    }

    void release(std::size_t off) {
        auto it = order_of_.find(off);
        if (it == order_of_.end()) return;
        int k = it->second;
        order_of_.erase(it);
        while (k < max_) {
            std::size_t buddy = off ^ (std::size_t(1) << k);
            auto b = free_[k].find(buddy);
            if (b == free_[k].end()) break;
            free_[k].erase(b);
            off = off < buddy ? off : buddy;
            ++k;
        }
        free_[k].insert(off);
    }

    void dump(const char* label) const {
        std::printf("%-10s", label);
        for (int k = 0; k <= max_; ++k)
            for (std::size_t off : free_[k]) std::printf(" [%zu:%zu]", off, std::size_t(1) << k);
        std::printf("\n");
    }

private:
    int max_;
    std::vector<std::set<std::size_t>> free_;
    std::map<std::size_t, int> order_of_;
};

int main() {
    Buddy b(10);                         // 1024 units, think KiB
    auto x = b.alloc(100);               // 128
    auto y = b.alloc(200);               // 256
    auto z = b.alloc(60);                // 64
    std::printf("x=%zu y=%zu z=%zu\n", *x, *y, *z);
    b.dump("allocated");
    b.release(*x);
    b.dump("free x");
    b.release(*z);
    b.dump("free z");
    b.release(*y);
    b.dump("free y");
}
x=0 y=256 z=128
allocated  [192:64] [512:512]
free x     [192:64] [0:128] [512:512]
free z     [0:256] [512:512]
free y     [0:1024]

Complexity and pitfalls. O(K log n) per operation with sets (O(K) with intrusive lists and a bitmap of free blocks, as the kernel does). Freeing x cannot merge because its buddy at 128 is split; freeing z (64 units at 128) merges it with its free buddy at 192 into a 128-unit block at 128, which then merges with x's block at 0 into 256 at 0. Pitfalls: computing the buddy with + instead of XOR, merging with a buddy that is free but of a different order (the per-order set prevents it), and forgetting to keep the lower offset after a merge.

Estimated rating: ~1700 · split/merge invariants and XOR buddy addressing

CodeBest fit in O(log n) with coalescing. Same interface as the first-fit drill, but choose the smallest hole that fits using an index by size. Create holes of 100, 30 and 60 bytes and serve 25, 55, 90.

Answer

Approach. Keep two indexes over the same free blocks: by_addr (offset to size) for coalescing, and by_size, a std::set of (size, offset) pairs for best fit via lower_bound({n, 0}). Every insertion and removal updates both. No rounding here so the numbers match the reading drill.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <iterator>
#include <map>
#include <optional>
#include <set>
#include <utility>

class BestFit {
public:
    explicit BestFit(std::size_t size) { add(0, size); }

    std::optional<std::size_t> alloc(std::size_t n) {
        auto it = by_size_.lower_bound({n, 0});
        if (it == by_size_.end()) return std::nullopt;
        auto [size, off] = *it;
        remove(off, size);
        if (size > n) add(off + n, size - n);
        used_[off] = n;
        return off;
    }

    void release(std::size_t off) {
        auto u = used_.find(off);
        if (u == used_.end()) return;
        std::size_t n = u->second;
        used_.erase(u);
        auto next = by_addr_.lower_bound(off);
        if (next != by_addr_.end() && off + n == next->first) {
            std::size_t ns = next->second;
            remove(next->first, ns);
            n += ns;
        }
        auto after = by_addr_.lower_bound(off);
        if (after != by_addr_.begin()) {
            auto prev = std::prev(after);
            if (prev->first + prev->second == off) {
                std::size_t po = prev->first, ps = prev->second;
                remove(po, ps);
                off = po;
                n += ps;
            }
        }
        add(off, n);
    }

    void dump() const {
        for (auto& [off, size] : by_addr_) std::printf(" [%zu:%zu]", off, size);
        std::printf("\n");
    }

private:
    void add(std::size_t off, std::size_t size) { by_addr_[off] = size; by_size_.insert({size, off}); }
    void remove(std::size_t off, std::size_t size) { by_addr_.erase(off); by_size_.erase({size, off}); }

    std::map<std::size_t, std::size_t> by_addr_, used_;
    std::set<std::pair<std::size_t, std::size_t>> by_size_;
};

int main() {
    BestFit h(220);
    auto a = h.alloc(100); h.alloc(10);
    auto c = h.alloc(30);  h.alloc(10);
    auto e = h.alloc(60);  h.alloc(10);
    h.release(*a); h.release(*c); h.release(*e);
    std::printf("holes:"); h.dump();
    for (std::size_t n : {25, 55, 90}) {
        auto off = h.alloc(n);
        if (off) std::printf("alloc(%zu) -> %zu\n", n, *off);
        else std::printf("alloc(%zu) -> fail\n", n);
    }
    std::printf("holes:"); h.dump();
}
holes: [0:100] [110:30] [150:60]
alloc(25) -> 110
alloc(55) -> 150
alloc(90) -> 0
holes: [90:10] [135:5] [205:5]

Complexity and pitfalls. O(log n) allocate and free. The 10-byte separators keep the three holes from merging. Pitfalls: updating one index and forgetting the other (the private add/remove pair prevents that), using a std::multimap by size and then erasing the wrong block with the same size (the (size, offset) pair makes keys unique), and invalidated iterators after remove (the code re-queries lower_bound). Note the two 5-byte slivers: best fit's characteristic leftover.

Estimated rating: ~1700 · two synchronised ordered indexes with merge in both directions

CodeSegregated size-class allocator. Over a fixed 4096-byte arena, serve requests up to 128 bytes from classes 16, 32, 64 and 128. Each class has an intrusive free list; when empty it carves a 512-byte run from the arena. Larger requests return null (they would go to a different path). Track requested and allocated bytes to report internal fragmentation, and show that a freed block is reused by the next request of the same class.

Answer

Approach. Map size to class index with a loop over four classes. A free block stores the next pointer in its first bytes. Refill carves a run of 512 / class blocks from the arena's bump pointer and threads them onto the list. free needs the size (as with sized delete) to find the class.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>

class SizeClassHeap {
public:
    static constexpr std::size_t kClass[] = {16, 32, 64, 128};
    static constexpr int kNum = 4;
    static constexpr std::size_t kRun = 512;

    void* alloc(std::size_t n) {
        int c = class_of(n);
        if (c < 0) return nullptr;
        if (!lists_[c] && !refill(c)) return nullptr;
        Free* f = lists_[c];
        lists_[c] = f->next;
        requested_ += n;
        allocated_ += kClass[c];
        return f;
    }

    void free(void* p, std::size_t n) {
        int c = class_of(n);
        lists_[c] = ::new (p) Free{lists_[c]};
        requested_ -= n;
        allocated_ -= kClass[c];
    }

    std::size_t offset(const void* p) const { return static_cast<const char*>(p) - arena_; }
    double internal_frag() const { return allocated_ ? 1.0 - double(requested_) / double(allocated_) : 0.0; }
    std::size_t arena_used() const { return bump_; }

private:
    struct Free { Free* next; };

    static int class_of(std::size_t n) {
        for (int c = 0; c < kNum; ++c)
            if (n <= kClass[c]) return c;
        return -1;
    }

    bool refill(int c) {
        if (bump_ + kRun > sizeof arena_) return false;
        char* run = arena_ + bump_;
        bump_ += kRun;
        for (std::size_t off = kRun; off >= kClass[c]; off -= kClass[c])
            lists_[c] = ::new (run + off - kClass[c]) Free{lists_[c]};
        return true;
    }

    alignas(16) char arena_[4096];
    std::size_t bump_ = 0;
    Free* lists_[kNum] = {};
    std::size_t requested_ = 0, allocated_ = 0;
};

int main() {
    static SizeClassHeap heap;
    void* a = heap.alloc(10);      // class 16
    void* b = heap.alloc(20);      // class 32, new run
    void* c = heap.alloc(100);     // class 128, new run
    std::printf("a@%zu b@%zu c@%zu, arena used %zu\n",
                heap.offset(a), heap.offset(b), heap.offset(c), heap.arena_used());
    std::printf("internal fragmentation: %.3f\n", heap.internal_frag());
    heap.free(b, 20);
    void* d = heap.alloc(30);      // same class as b
    std::printf("d reuses b: %d\n", d == b);
    std::printf("too big: %s\n", heap.alloc(200) ? "served" : "null");
    heap.free(a, 10); heap.free(c, 100); heap.free(d, 30);
    std::printf("after freeing all: arena used %zu (runs are kept)\n", heap.arena_used());
}
a@0 b@512 c@1024, arena used 1536
internal fragmentation: 0.261
d reuses b: 1
too big: null
after freeing all: arena used 1536 (runs are kept)

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) allocate and free after refill. The three live requests total 10 + 20 + 100 = 130 bytes in blocks of 16 + 32 + 128 = 176 bytes, so internal fragmentation is 1 − 130/176 = 0.261. Each class owns its own 512-byte run, so the arena is 1536 bytes used for 176 bytes of blocks: unused slots in a class's run are the size-class version of external fragmentation, and freeing every block does not give the runs back. Pitfalls: free with the wrong size puts the block on the wrong list (sized delete has the same contract), class sizes must be multiples of the alignment you promise, and the free-list pointer overwrites the first bytes of a freed block, so use-after-free bugs corrupt the list.

Estimated rating: ~1600 · intrusive free lists plus run carving and per-class accounting

CodeGrowth factor experiment. Model a vector that starts at capacity 1000 and grows by factor f (new capacity = max(old + 1, floor(old · f))). Old buffers are freed after the copy and coalesce into one region at the start of memory; the current buffer is live while the next one is allocated. For f = 1.5, 1.6, 1.7 and 2.0, report the first reallocation whose new buffer fits into the freed region, within 40 reallocations.

Answer

Approach. Track freed (sum of all buffers before the current one) and cur. At each step compute next; if next <= freed the allocator could place it in the old space. Otherwise the current buffer joins the freed region after the copy and cur becomes next. The golden-ratio argument predicts reuse for f below about 1.618 and never for f above it.

#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>
#include <initializer_list>

static int first_reuse(double f, long long* at_capacity) {
    long long cur = 1000, freed = 0;
    for (int step = 1; step <= 40; ++step) {
        long long next = static_cast<long long>(std::floor(cur * f));
        if (next < cur + 1) next = cur + 1;
        if (next <= freed) { *at_capacity = next; return step; }
        freed += cur;          // the old buffer is released after the copy
        cur = next;
    }
    return -1;
}

int main() {
    for (double f : {1.5, 1.6, 1.7, 2.0}) {
        long long cap = 0;
        int step = first_reuse(f, &cap);
        if (step > 0) std::printf("f=%.1f: reuse at reallocation %d (capacity %lld)\n", f, step, cap);
        else std::printf("f=%.1f: never within 40 reallocations\n", f);
    }
}
f=1.5: reuse at reallocation 5 (capacity 7593)
f=1.6: reuse at reallocation 8 (capacity 42940)
f=1.7: never within 40 reallocations
f=2.0: never within 40 reallocations

Complexity and pitfalls. O(steps). The result matches the theory: below the golden ratio the freed prefix eventually catches up (after 5 reallocations at 1.5, after 8 at 1.6, and later the closer f gets to 1.618), above it never does. For f = 1.5 the condition is 2(1.5n − 1) ≥ 1.5n+1, which first holds at n = 4 previous buffers, the fifth reallocation. Starting at 1000 keeps integer rounding out of the way: from capacity 1 the forced minimum growth (1, 2, 3, 4, 6...) produces early "reuse" that is an artefact of rounding, not of the factor. The model ignores size classes, other allocations and the mmap threshold, so real allocators show a weaker effect; say so when you quote it.

Estimated rating: ~1300 · simple simulation, the insight is in setting up the invariant correctly

Cheat sheet

Theory
  • Internal = waste inside blocks (rounding, headers, pages). External = free memory split into holes too small to use. External frag metric: 1 − largest free / total free.
  • Fragmentation needs mixed sizes and interleaved lifetimes. C++ cannot compact, so only coalescing adjacent free blocks reduces it.
  • Fit policies: first and best fit both do well on real traces; next fit is worse; none is safe against adversarial sequences (Robson). Best fit leaves slivers.
  • Coalescing with boundary tags is O(1); allocators defer it for small sizes (tcache, fastbins) for speed. Size classes remove external frag per class at the cost of rounding; buddy splits and merges by XOR with up to 50% internal waste; slab = pages per object size.
  • RSS stays high after free because brk only shrinks from the top, free chunks are cached, pages are partly used, threads have their own arenas, and MADV_FREE is lazy. Large blocks (above 128 KiB by default) are mmapped and returned at once. malloc_trim(0) and MALLOC_ARENA_MAX are the glibc levers.
  • Mitigate by separating sizes and lifetimes: pools, arenas, preallocation, reserve, reusing capacity, flat containers instead of node-based ones, or a different allocator (jemalloc, tcmalloc, mimalloc).
  • Growth factor: 2 in libstdc++/libc++, 1.5 in MSVC; only factors below about 1.618 can ever reuse their own freed buffers.
  • Paging removes external fragmentation of physical memory, adds internal fragmentation per page, and brings external fragmentation back for contiguous needs (huge pages, DMA), which the kernel handles with buddy lists and compaction.
