Part E · Memory management · Chapter 11

Smart pointers

Smart pointers turn ownership into a type: unique_ptr means "I alone own this", shared_ptr means "we own this together", and weak_ptr means "I want to look at it if it still exists". This chapter covers what each one costs, how the control block works, and the pitfalls that come up in almost every C++ interview: make_shared trade-offs, the aliasing constructor, enable_shared_from_this, double ownership and thread safety.

TheoryDrillsCoding· about 4 hours· prerequisites: Ch 9 (new and delete), Ch 20 (move semantics)

Ownership models

Theory

Mental model. Every heap object needs exactly one answer to "who calls delete, and when?". A raw T* cannot express that answer; it looks the same whether it owns, borrows or points into an array. Smart pointers are RAII classes (Ch 1) whose destructor releases the object, and whose copy and move rules encode the ownership policy.

ModelTypeCopyCostUse for
Exclusive ownershipstd::unique_ptr<T>Move onlySame as a raw pointerThe default for owning heap objects: factories, pimpl, trees, polymorphic members
Shared ownershipstd::shared_ptr<T>Copy increments an atomic countTwo pointers plus a control blockLifetime genuinely shared by independent parties: caches, async callbacks, graph-like data
Non-owning observer that can detect expirystd::weak_ptr<T>Copy increments the weak countTwo pointersCaches, observers, breaking cycles (Ch 13)
Non-owning borrowT&, T*, std::spanFreeNoneFunction parameters, back pointers whose target outlives the pointer

The guideline is: own with values first, then with unique_ptr, and reach for shared_ptr only when you cannot name a single owner. With smart pointers as members, a class usually needs no destructor, copy or move operations of its own (the rule of zero). Raw pointers stay perfectly fine as non-owning parameters and observers; the C++ Core Guidelines (R.3) say a raw T* is non-owning by convention.

Know this cold

unique_ptr: single owner, move-only, zero overhead with a stateless deleter. shared_ptr: shared owners, copyable, an atomic reference count in a separately allocated control block. weak_ptr: observes a shared_ptr-managed object without keeping it alive; call lock() to use it.

unique_ptr

Theory

Mental model. A unique_ptr<T, D> is a pointer plus a deleter D (by default std::default_delete<T>, which calls delete). Its copy constructor and copy assignment are deleted; its move operations transfer the pointer and leave the source null. The destructor calls the deleter if the pointer is non-null.

The API in one program

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>

struct Res {
    int id;
    explicit Res(int i) : id(i) { std::printf("+Res%d\n", id); }
    ~Res() { std::printf("-Res%d\n", id); }
};

int main() {
    auto a = std::make_unique<Res>(1);        // C++14
    std::unique_ptr<Res> b = std::move(a);    // ownership moves, a becomes null
    std::printf("a is null: %d, b->id = %d\n", a == nullptr, b->id);

    b.reset(new Res(2));                      // Res2 built first, then Res1 deleted
    Res* raw = b.release();                   // b gives up ownership, deletes nothing
    std::printf("b is null: %d\n", !b);
    std::unique_ptr<Res> c(raw);              // someone must own it again

    auto arr = std::make_unique<int[]>(3);    // value-initialised: 0 0 0
    arr[1] = 7;
    std::printf("arr: %d %d %d\n", arr[0], arr[1], arr[2]);
}
+Res1
a is null: 1, b->id = 1
+Res2
-Res1
b is null: 1
arr: 0 7 0
-Res2
  • get() returns the pointer and keeps ownership. release() returns it and gives up ownership: the caller must delete it, and ignoring the result is a leak (it is [[nodiscard]] in recent libraries). reset(p) stores p and then deletes the old pointer, so reset is safe even if the old object's destructor somehow reaches the unique_ptr.
  • std::make_unique<T>(args...) (C++14) avoids writing new, and before C++17 it also avoided a leak in expressions such as f(std::unique_ptr<T>(new T), g()). C++20 adds std::make_unique_for_overwrite, which default-initialises (no zeroing) for large buffers you are about to fill.
  • unique_ptr<T[]> calls delete[], offers operator[] and no * or ->. Prefer std::vector unless you need exactly a fixed-size heap buffer without size and capacity members.
  • A unique_ptr<Derived> converts to unique_ptr<Base>. The deletion then goes through Base*, so Base needs a virtual destructor (Ch 2).
  • A unique_ptr converts to a shared_ptr by move: std::shared_ptr<T> s = std::move(u);. That is why factories should return unique_ptr: the caller can still choose to share.

Size and the deleter

The deleter is part of the type and is stored inside the unique_ptr. Implementations use the empty base optimisation (or [[no_unique_address]]) so a stateless deleter takes no space. A function pointer deleter costs a pointer, and a std::function deleter costs much more. Custom deleters in depth are Ch 12.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

static void free_int(int* p) { delete p; }

int main() {
    auto lambda = [](int* p) { delete p; };
    std::printf("unique_ptr<int>:               %zu\n", sizeof(std::unique_ptr<int>));
    std::printf("unique_ptr<int, lambda>:       %zu\n", sizeof(std::unique_ptr<int, decltype(lambda)>));
    std::printf("unique_ptr<int, void(*)(int*)>: %zu\n", sizeof(std::unique_ptr<int, void (*)(int*)>));
    std::printf("shared_ptr<int>:               %zu\n", sizeof(std::shared_ptr<int>));
    std::printf("weak_ptr<int>:                 %zu\n", sizeof(std::weak_ptr<int>));
    std::unique_ptr<int, void (*)(int*)> p(new int(1), free_int);
}
unique_ptr<int>:               8
unique_ptr<int, lambda>:       8
unique_ptr<int, void(*)(int*)>: 16
shared_ptr<int>:               16
weak_ptr<int>:                 16

unique_ptr and incomplete types (pimpl)

std::default_delete<T> requires T to be complete where the deleter is instantiated, which is wherever the unique_ptr's destructor is instantiated. In the pimpl idiom, if the outer class has an implicitly defined destructor, it is generated inline in the header where Impl is incomplete, and compilation fails with "invalid application of sizeof to an incomplete type". The fix: declare ~Widget(); in the header and define Widget::~Widget() = default; in the .cpp file after Impl is defined (the same applies to the move operations). shared_ptr does not have this problem because it captures the deleter when the pointer is first stored.

Passing smart pointers to functions

Theory

Mental model. The parameter type is a statement about ownership. Pass a smart pointer only when the function does something to the ownership; if it only uses the object, pass a reference or raw pointer.

ParameterMeansCaller writes
Widget& / const Widget&Uses the object, must not be null, ownership irrelevantf(*up)
Widget*Uses the object, may be null, does not ownf(up.get())
std::unique_ptr<Widget> by valueSink: takes ownershipf(std::move(up))
std::unique_ptr<Widget>&May reseat or reset the caller's pointerf(up)
const std::unique_ptr<Widget>&Nothing useful; use Widget* or Widget&Avoid
std::shared_ptr<Widget> by valueShares ownership (stores a copy)f(sp) or f(std::move(sp))
const std::shared_ptr<Widget>&Might share (copies only on some path)f(sp)
void render(const Widget& w);                       // just uses it
void attach(std::unique_ptr<Widget> w);             // sink: now owns it
void replace(std::unique_ptr<Widget>& slot);        // may reset or reseat
void subscribe(std::shared_ptr<Listener> l) {       // stores a copy
    listeners_.push_back(std::move(l));             // move the parameter into place
}

Passing shared_ptr by value to a function that only reads the object costs two atomic operations (increment and decrement), which matters on hot paths and in contention (see the next section). Returning: return unique_ptr by value from factories; return p; moves implicitly from a local, so return std::move(p); is unnecessary.

shared_ptr and the control block

Theory

Mental model. A shared_ptr<T> is two pointers: one to the object (what get() returns) and one to a control block shared by every shared_ptr and weak_ptr that manages the same object. The control block holds the strong count (number of shared_ptrs), the weak count, the deleter and the allocator. When the strong count reaches zero the object is destroyed; when the weak count also reaches zero the control block is freed.

Strong and weak counts

  • Copying a shared_ptr increments the strong count; destroying or resetting one decrements it. Moving transfers ownership without touching the count, which is why std::move into a member or container is cheaper than copying.
  • When the strong count drops to zero, the deleter destroys the object. Then the "strong owners" share of the weak count is dropped; if no weak_ptr remains, the control block is deallocated.
  • use_count() returns the strong count. In multithreaded code it is a snapshot that can be stale before you read it, so never use it for synchronisation. unique() was deprecated in C++17 and removed in C++20 for that reason.
  • The deleter is type-erased: shared_ptr<Widget> has the same type whatever deleter or allocator it uses, unlike unique_ptr. A consequence many people do not know: std::shared_ptr<Base> p(new Derived); deletes through Derived*, so ~Derived runs even without a virtual destructor. The same is true for shared_ptr<void>.

The cost of atomic reference counting

The counts must be updated atomically because copies of the same shared_ptr may be created and destroyed in different threads. On x86-64 each increment is a lock xadd or lock inc (roughly 5 to 20 ns uncontended, much more under contention), and each decrement also needs acquire-release ordering so the thread that destroys the object sees all writes made through other copies. When many threads copy the same shared_ptr, the control block's cache line bounces between cores, which is a scalability bottleneck that does not show in single-threaded benchmarks. Mitigations: pass by reference, move instead of copy, keep one shared_ptr per thread and hand out references, or use unique_ptr or intrusive counting where ownership allows. (libstdc++ skips the atomic instructions while the process is single-threaded: on glibc 2.32 and later it checks __libc_single_threaded at run time, so a program pays for atomics only once it has started a second thread. libc++ always uses atomics. Do not let a single-threaded benchmark convince you copies are free.)

make_shared: one allocation, and its trade-off

Theory

std::make_shared<T>(args...) allocates the control block and the object together. Advantages: one allocation instead of two (faster, less overhead, better locality because the counts and the object share cache lines), no visible new, and (before C++17) protection against the interleaving leak in f(std::shared_ptr<T>(new T), g()).

The trade-off is memory lifetime. Because the object lives inside the control block's allocation, its memory cannot be freed until the weak count reaches zero. The destructor runs on time, but the bytes stay allocated as long as any weak_ptr exists. For a large object observed by long-lived weak_ptrs (a cache), shared_ptr<T>(new T) frees the object's memory sooner. The program below shows the difference by tracing operator new and operator delete.

#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <new>

static bool trace = false;

void* operator new(std::size_t n) {
    if (trace) std::printf("    allocate %s\n", n > 200 ? "large block" : "small block");
    if (void* p = std::malloc(n)) return p;
    throw std::bad_alloc{};
}
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept {
    if (trace && p) std::puts("    deallocate");
    std::free(p);
}
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { ::operator delete(p); }

struct Big {
    char data[256];
    ~Big() { std::puts("    ~Big"); }
};

static void* volatile sink;

int main() {
    trace = true;
    std::puts("make_shared:");
    {
        auto sp = std::make_shared<Big>();
        sink = sp.get();
        std::weak_ptr<Big> wp = sp;
        std::puts("  reset shared_ptr");
        sp.reset();
        std::puts("  reset weak_ptr");
        wp.reset();
    }
    std::puts("shared_ptr(new Big):");
    {
        std::shared_ptr<Big> sp(new Big);
        sink = sp.get();
        std::weak_ptr<Big> wp = sp;
        std::puts("  reset shared_ptr");
        sp.reset();
        std::puts("  reset weak_ptr");
        wp.reset();
    }
    trace = false;
}
make_shared:
    allocate large block
  reset shared_ptr
    ~Big
  reset weak_ptr
    deallocate
shared_ptr(new Big):
    allocate large block
    allocate small block
  reset shared_ptr
    ~Big
    deallocate
  reset weak_ptr
    deallocate

When make_shared is not an option

  • Custom deleter: make_shared has no deleter parameter; it always destroys the object in place and frees the combined block itself. Use the shared_ptr(p, deleter) constructor (Ch 12).
  • Private or protected constructors: make_shared constructs from inside the library, so it cannot call them. Use a passkey type or std::shared_ptr<T>(new T(...)) from a static factory.
  • Class-specific operator new: make_shared bypasses it (it allocates the combined block with std::allocator). Use std::allocate_shared with a custom allocator instead.
  • Large objects with long-lived weak_ptrs: the memory trade-off above.
  • Adopting an existing pointer (from a C API or a unique_ptr): there is nothing to make.

C++20 added std::make_shared<T[]>(n) and make_shared_for_overwrite; shared_ptr<T[]> itself works since C++17.

The aliasing constructor

Theory

Mental model. The two pointers inside a shared_ptr do not have to agree. std::shared_ptr<U> alias(owner, ptr) shares owner's control block (so it keeps the owner alive) but get() returns ptr, usually a member or subobject of the owned object.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <string>

struct Order {
    int id;
    std::string venue;
    Order(int i, std::string v) : id(i), venue(std::move(v)) {}
    ~Order() { std::puts("~Order"); }
};

int main() {
    auto order = std::make_shared<Order>(7, "XNAS");
    std::shared_ptr<std::string> venue(order, &order->venue);   // aliasing constructor
    std::printf("use_count = %ld\n", order.use_count());
    order.reset();
    std::printf("venue = %s, use_count = %ld\n", venue->c_str(), venue.use_count());
    venue.reset();
    std::puts("end");
}
use_count = 2
venue = XNAS, use_count = 1
~Order
end

Uses: handing out a pointer to a member or an array element while guaranteeing the container stays alive, implementing std::static_pointer_cast/dynamic_pointer_cast (same control block, converted pointer), and node-based structures where many views share one allocation. Pitfall: std::shared_ptr<T>(std::shared_ptr<void>{}, p) creates a non-null pointer with no owner (use_count() == 0), which nothing will ever delete; that is occasionally used on purpose for objects with static lifetime.

enable_shared_from_this and double ownership

Theory

Two shared_ptrs from one raw pointer

Every shared_ptr constructor that takes a raw pointer creates a new control block. So this code creates two independent owners of the same object, each with a count of one, and the object is deleted twice:

Widget* raw = new Widget;
std::shared_ptr<Widget> a(raw);
std::shared_ptr<Widget> b(raw);     // second control block: double delete later
std::shared_ptr<Widget> c(this);    // inside a member function: same bug

The rule: a raw pointer becomes a shared_ptr exactly once, ideally at the new (or with make_shared, so no raw pointer exists). Afterwards, copy the shared_ptr.

enable_shared_from_this

Sometimes a member function needs a shared_ptr to its own object, for example to register itself as a callback that may outlive the call (async I/O sessions in Asio are the classic case). Inherit publicly from std::enable_shared_from_this<T>. It contains a hidden weak_ptr<T> that the shared_ptr constructor (and make_shared) fills in when it first takes ownership. shared_from_this() then locks that weak_ptr, producing a shared_ptr that shares the existing control block.

#include <cstdio>
#include <functional>
#include <memory>
#include <vector>

class Session : public std::enable_shared_from_this<Session> {
public:
    void start(std::vector<std::function<void()>>& loop) {
        auto self = shared_from_this();              // keeps us alive in the callback
        loop.push_back([self] { self->on_read(); });
    }
    void on_read() { std::puts("on_read"); }
    ~Session() { std::puts("~Session"); }
};

int main() {
    std::vector<std::function<void()>> loop;
    {
        auto s = std::make_shared<Session>();
        s->start(loop);
        std::printf("use_count = %ld\n", s.use_count());
    }                                                // s gone, callback still owns it
    std::puts("running callbacks");
    for (auto& cb : loop) cb();
    loop.clear();
    std::puts("end");
}
use_count = 2
running callbacks
on_read
~Session
end

Interview trap

shared_from_this() works only after a shared_ptr owns the object. Calling it on a stack object, on an object owned by unique_ptr, or inside the constructor (the owning shared_ptr does not exist yet) throws std::bad_weak_ptr since C++17; before C++17 it was undefined behaviour. The usual fix is a static factory: static std::shared_ptr<Session> create() that calls make_shared and then does the registration. Also: inherit publicly, or the shared_ptr constructor cannot see the base and silently skips the setup. C++17's weak_from_this() returns an empty weak_ptr instead of throwing.

Thread safety: the control block vs the pointer vs the pointee

Theory

Mental model. There are three separate things, with three separate answers:

  1. The control block is thread-safe. Different shared_ptr objects that share it can be copied, assigned and destroyed concurrently in different threads; the counts are atomic and the object is destroyed exactly once.
  2. One shared_ptr object is not thread-safe, like any other standard library object: concurrent reads (copying from it, get()) are fine, but a write (assignment, reset) concurrent with any other access is a data race. Copying is a two-step operation (read the pointers, increment the count), and an assignment in between can free the control block. C++20 offers std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>> for this case (libstdc++ since GCC 12 and MSVC have it; libc++ still does not, as of LLVM 22, where std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<int>> fails with "requires that T be a trivially copyable type"); otherwise protect the shared variable with a mutex. The C++11 free functions such as std::atomic_load(&sp) are deprecated in C++20 and removed in C++26 (P2869). Note that libstdc++'s atomic<shared_ptr> uses an internal lock bit, so is_lock_free() is false: it is correct, not necessarily faster than a mutex.
  3. The pointee has whatever thread safety its own type has. shared_ptr<std::vector<int>> does nothing to make push_back safe.

The correct pattern for a configuration object that a writer replaces while readers use it: readers take a copy of the current shared_ptr under a short lock (or an atomic load), then use the immutable snapshot without any lock; the writer builds a new object and swaps the pointer.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <mutex>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

struct Config { int limit; };

class ConfigHolder {
public:
    std::shared_ptr<const Config> get() const {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mu_);
        return current_;                      // copy under the lock: count +1
    }
    void set(std::shared_ptr<const Config> c) {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mu_);
        current_.swap(c);                     // old config released after unlock, by c
    }
private:
    mutable std::mutex mu_;
    std::shared_ptr<const Config> current_ = std::make_shared<const Config>(Config{0});
};

int main() {
    ConfigHolder holder;
    std::thread writer([&] {
        for (int i = 1; i <= 1000; ++i) holder.set(std::make_shared<const Config>(Config{i}));
    });
    std::vector<std::thread> readers;
    long seen_max[3] = {};
    for (int t = 0; t < 3; ++t) {
        readers.emplace_back([&, t] {
            for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) {
                std::shared_ptr<const Config> snap = holder.get();   // no lock while reading
                if (snap->limit > seen_max[t]) seen_max[t] = snap->limit;
            }
        });
    }
    writer.join();
    for (auto& r : readers) r.join();
    std::printf("final limit = %d\n", holder.get()->limit);
}
final limit = 1000

weak_ptr: observers and caches

Theory

Mental model. A weak_ptr holds a reference to the control block, not to the object. It does not keep the object alive and you cannot dereference it. To use the object, call lock(), which atomically checks the strong count and, if it is non-zero, increments it and returns a shared_ptr; otherwise it returns an empty one.

std::weak_ptr<Texture> cached = texture;          // does not extend the lifetime
if (std::shared_ptr<Texture> t = cached.lock()) { // atomic check and acquire
    draw(*t);                                     // safe: t keeps it alive
} else {
    reload();                                     // the object is gone
}
  • expired() is true when the strong count is zero. In multithreaded code if (!w.expired()) use(w.lock()) is a race: the object can die between the two calls. Always use the result of lock().
  • std::shared_ptr<T>(weak) (the constructor) throws std::bad_weak_ptr if expired, unlike lock().
  • weak_ptr has no operator<, == or std::hash. To key a std::map by it, use std::owner_less, which compares control blocks (owner_before) and so stays valid after the object dies. C++26 adds std::owner_hash and std::owner_equal for unordered containers.
  • Typical uses: caches that hand out shared objects but do not keep them alive (the coding drills build one), observer lists where subjects must not keep observers alive, and back pointers (child to parent) that break ownership cycles (Ch 13).

auto_ptr, deleters and cycles

Theory

Why auto_ptr was removed

C++98's std::auto_ptr tried to express unique ownership before the language had move semantics. Its "copy" constructor and copy assignment silently transferred ownership and set the source to null. So auto_ptr<T> b = a; left a null, passing one by value to a function destroyed the caller's object at the end of the call, and it could not be safely stored in standard containers or used with algorithms that copy elements (sort can keep a copy as a pivot). It also called delete, never delete[]. C++11 introduced unique_ptr, which makes the transfer explicit with std::move; auto_ptr was deprecated in C++11 and removed in C++17.

Custom deleters and cycles

Both smart pointers accept a custom deleter, which turns them into RAII wrappers for any resource: FILE* with fclose, sockets, memory from malloc or a C library. For unique_ptr the deleter is part of the type and its size; for shared_ptr it is type-erased into the control block. The details and size trade-offs are Ch 12. Reference counting cannot reclaim cycles: two objects that hold shared_ptrs to each other keep both counts at one forever. Breaking cycles with weak_ptr and parent pointers is Ch 13.

Key facts

unique_ptrshared_ptrweak_ptr
Size (64-bit, default deleter)8 bytes16 bytes + control block16 bytes
CopyableNo (move only)Yes (atomic increment)Yes (atomic weak increment)
DeleterPart of the type, stored inlineType-erased in the control blockn/a
Arraysunique_ptr<T[]>shared_ptr<T[]> (C++17)n/a
Factorymake_unique (C++14)make_shared, allocate_sharedfrom a shared_ptr
Incomplete T at destructionError with default deleterFine (deleter captured earlier)Fine
Thread safetyLike a raw pointerControl block safe; one instance not; pointee notlock() is atomic
HistoryC++11 (replaces auto_ptr, removed in C++17)C++11 (from Boost and TR1)C++11

Concept and tricky questions

Drills

ConceptWhen do you use unique_ptr, shared_ptr, weak_ptr and a raw pointer or reference?

Answer

Answer. unique_ptr whenever one owner can be named (the default for heap objects). shared_ptr when the lifetime really is shared by parties that end independently (async callbacks, caches handing out objects). weak_ptr to observe a shared object without keeping it alive. A raw pointer or reference for non-owning access, especially function parameters.

Why. The type documents ownership and the compiler enforces it. Overusing shared_ptr hides who is responsible for lifetime, costs atomic operations on every copy and invites cycles. "Never use raw pointers" is the over-correction interviewers push back on: raw pointers are fine when they do not own.

ConceptWhat is the difference between get(), release() and reset() on a unique_ptr?

Answer

Answer. get() returns the pointer and keeps ownership. release() returns the pointer, sets the unique_ptr to null and gives up ownership without deleting. reset(p) takes ownership of p (or null) and deletes the previously owned object.

Why. Confusing release with reset is a classic leak: p.release(); with the result discarded leaks the object. reset assigns the new pointer before deleting the old one, so a destructor that reaches back into the owner sees a consistent state.

ConceptHow should a function take a smart pointer if it (a) only reads the object, (b) takes ownership, (c) may replace the caller's object, (d) stores a shared copy?

Answer

Answer. (a) const T& or const T*. (b) std::unique_ptr<T> by value, called with std::move. (c) std::unique_ptr<T>&. (d) std::shared_ptr<T> by value, then move it into the member.

Why. These are the C++ Core Guidelines R.30 to R.37. Taking a smart pointer for (a) restricts callers to one ownership model for no reason and, for shared_ptr by value, costs two atomic operations. const unique_ptr& is almost always a mistake: it cannot transfer or reset, so it just means T* with extra indirection.

ConceptGive the advantages of make_shared over std::shared_ptr<T>(new T), and the cases where you cannot or should not use it.

Answer

Answer. Advantages: one allocation instead of two, better cache locality, less allocator overhead, no naked new, and exception safety in pre-C++17 argument lists. Cannot: custom deleter, private constructor, or adopting an existing pointer. Should not: large object observed by long-lived weak_ptrs (its memory stays allocated until the last weak_ptr goes), or a class with its own operator new that you want honoured (make_shared bypasses it; use allocate_shared).

Why. The combined block is the source of both the speed and the memory trade-off: the object's storage is inside the control block, which lives until the weak count is zero.

ConceptWhat exactly does a shared_ptr control block contain?

Answer

Answer. The strong (use) count, the weak count, the deleter, the allocator and either a pointer to the managed object (separate allocation) or the object itself (make_shared). Implementations use a vtable (libstdc++ _Sp_counted_base, libc++ __shared_weak_count) to dispatch to the right deleter and deallocation code, which is how the deleter type is erased.

Why. The pointer stored in the control block can differ from the one in the shared_ptr (aliasing, base class conversions), and the control block's copy is the one that gets deleted. That is why shared_ptr<Base>(new Derived) deletes as Derived. Typical size: 16 bytes of header (vptr plus two 32-bit counts on libstdc++) plus the stored pointer and deleter.

ConceptWhy was std::auto_ptr removed, and what replaced it?

Answer

Answer. Its copy operations transferred ownership and nulled the source, so ordinary-looking copies (passing by value, storing in a container, an algorithm keeping a temporary) silently destroyed or stole objects. unique_ptr replaced it in C++11 with explicit, move-only transfer; auto_ptr was deprecated in C++11 and removed in C++17.

Why. Copy that mutates the source breaks the requirements of containers and algorithms (CopyConstructible means the source is unchanged). Without rvalue references C++98 had no other way to spell "transfer". auto_ptr also had no array form and no custom deleter.

TrickyWhat is sizeof of a unique_ptr<int> with (a) the default deleter, (b) a captureless lambda, (c) a function pointer, (d) a lambda that captures a pointer?

Answer

Answer. On 64-bit: (a) 8, (b) 8, (c) 16, (d) 16.

Why. The deleter is stored in the unique_ptr, but empty classes take no space thanks to the empty base optimisation (libstdc++ uses a tuple with EBO, libc++ a compressed pair). A captureless lambda is an empty class. A function pointer is 8 bytes of state, and a capture is too. People often answer "always 8" or "16 because it stores a deleter". shared_ptr is 16 regardless of deleter, because the deleter lives in the control block.

Tricky"Is shared_ptr thread-safe?" Give the precise answer.

Answer

Answer. The reference counting is: distinct shared_ptr objects sharing one control block may be copied and destroyed concurrently. A single shared_ptr object is not: writing it (assign, reset) while another thread reads or writes it is a data race. The pointee is not protected at all.

Why. The standard gives shared_ptr the same guarantee as other library types ([res.on.data.races]) and additionally makes the count updates atomic. For a shared variable that is swapped while read, use a mutex or C++20 std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>>. "Yes" and "no" are both wrong; interviewers want the three-part answer.

TrickyA class derived from enable_shared_from_this calls shared_from_this() in its constructor to register itself. What happens?

Answer

Answer. It throws std::bad_weak_ptr (C++17 and later; undefined behaviour before). During construction no shared_ptr owns the object yet, so the internal weak_ptr is still empty.

Why. The hidden weak_ptr is assigned by the shared_ptr constructor (or make_shared) after the object is fully constructed. Fix: a static create() factory that calls make_shared and then registers, with the constructor made private (and a passkey so make_shared can still call it). The same exception occurs for stack objects and objects owned by unique_ptr.

TrickyWhat is wrong with if (!weak.expired()) weak.lock()->update();?

Answer

Answer. It is a check-then-act race. Another thread can drop the last shared_ptr between expired() and lock(), so lock() returns null and ->update() dereferences it. Write if (auto sp = weak.lock()) sp->update();.

Why. lock() is the only atomic "check and acquire" operation: it increments the strong count only if it is non-zero (a compare-exchange loop). expired() is useful only as a hint, for example when purging dead cache entries. Even single-threaded, the version with lock() is shorter.

TrickyA pimpl class has std::unique_ptr<Impl> impl_; with Impl only forward-declared in the header, and no user-declared destructor. Why does code that destroys a Widget fail to compile, and why would shared_ptr<Impl> compile?

Answer

Answer. The implicit ~Widget() is defined inline wherever it is used, which instantiates std::default_delete<Impl>::operator() while Impl is incomplete; the library's static_assert (or sizeof) rejects it. Fix: declare ~Widget(); in the header and define it as = default in the .cpp after Impl's definition (also the move operations). shared_ptr compiles because its deleter is created where the pointer is first stored (in the .cpp, where Impl is complete) and called through the control block.

Why. Deleting a pointer to an incomplete class type is undefined behaviour if the class has a non-trivial destructor, so default_delete forbids it at compile time. This difference between the two pointers is a favourite follow-up question.

TrickyBefore C++17, could process(std::shared_ptr<Widget>(new Widget), priority()); leak? Can it in C++17? Is make_shared still worth using?

Answer

Answer. Before C++17, yes: the compiler could evaluate new Widget, then priority(), then the shared_ptr constructor. If priority() threw, the Widget leaked. In C++17 (P0145) each function argument is evaluated completely before another starts (they are indeterminately sequenced, not interleaved), so that leak is gone. make_shared is still worth it for the single allocation and for never writing new.

Why. Many candidates still give the pre-C++17 reasoning as the main reason for make_shared. The argument order remains unspecified in C++17; only interleaving was removed.

Trickyauto order = std::make_shared<Order>(); std::shared_ptr<std::string> v(order, &order->venue); order.reset(); Is v dangling? And what does std::shared_ptr<int>(std::shared_ptr<int>{}, &global) give you?

Answer

Answer. v is not dangling: the aliasing constructor shares order's control block, so v is now the only strong owner (use_count() == 1) and the whole Order stays alive until v goes. The second expression gives a non-null shared_ptr that owns nothing: get() returns &global, use_count() is 0 and nothing is ever deleted.

Why. A shared_ptr carries two independent pointers: the stored pointer (what get() and * use) and the control block (what decides lifetime). The aliasing constructor copies the second and sets the first. The usual wrong answers are "v points into a destroyed object" for the first part and "an empty owner means a null pointer" for the second; if (p) tests the stored pointer, not ownership, so an ownerless aliasing pointer tests true. C++20 adds a move overload, shared_ptr(shared_ptr<Y>&&, T*), which steals the owner instead of incrementing the count.

TrickyA function returns a local std::unique_ptr<T> p with return p;. Why does that compile when unique_ptr cannot be copied, and should you write return std::move(p);?

Answer

Answer. A returned local variable is treated as an rvalue first (implicit move, [class.copy.elision]), so the move constructor is chosen, or the copy is elided entirely by NRVO. Do not add std::move: it makes the expression a different kind and disables NRVO, and GCC and Clang warn about it (-Wpessimizing-move, -Wredundant-move).

Why. C++11 already moved from returned locals; C++20 (P1825) and C++23 (P2266) extended the implicit move to more cases, such as returning an rvalue reference parameter. Returning a unique_ptr<Derived> local from a function returning unique_ptr<Base> also moves implicitly since C++14's CWG 1579. NRVO details are Ch 24.

Predict the output and find the bug

Drills

OutputTrack the reference count.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>

int main() {
    auto a = std::make_shared<int>(5);
    std::printf("%ld ", a.use_count());
    auto b = a;
    std::printf("%ld ", a.use_count());
    auto c = std::move(b);
    std::printf("%ld %ld ", a.use_count(), b.use_count());
    std::weak_ptr<int> w = a;
    std::printf("%ld ", a.use_count());
    {
        auto d = w.lock();
        std::printf("%ld ", a.use_count());
    }
    a.reset();
    std::printf("%ld %d ", c.use_count(), w.expired());
    c.reset();
    std::printf("%ld %d\n", w.use_count(), w.expired());
}
Answer
1 2 2 0 2 3 1 0 0 1

Answer. 1 after creation; 2 after copying into b; moving b into c leaves the count at 2 and b empty (0); a weak_ptr does not change it (2); lock() adds a strong owner (3); after d dies and a resets, c is the only owner (1) and w is not expired; after c resets the count is 0 and w is expired.

Why. use_count() counts strong owners only; an empty shared_ptr reports 0. Moves transfer ownership without touching the count, which is why they are cheaper than copies.

Find the bugTwo owners are built from the same raw pointer.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct Account {
    long balance = 100;
    ~Account() { std::puts("~Account"); }
};

int main() {
    Account* raw = new Account;
    std::shared_ptr<Account> owner(raw);
    std::shared_ptr<Account> audit(raw);
    std::printf("%ld %ld\n", owner.use_count(), audit.use_count());
}
Answer

Answer. Each raw-pointer constructor creates its own control block, so both report use_count() == 1 and each deletes the object: a double free at the end of main. Fix: auto owner = std::make_shared<Account>(); auto audit = owner;.

Why. A shared_ptr cannot find an existing control block from a raw pointer (only enable_shared_from_this provides a way back). ASan reports "attempting double-free"; without it glibc may abort with "free(): double free detected in tcache 2" after printing ~Account twice. The output is not compared because the behaviour is undefined.

Outputshared_from_this() on objects with different owners. What is printed?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct Node : std::enable_shared_from_this<Node> {
    long owners() { return shared_from_this().use_count() - 1; }
};

int main() {
    auto shared = std::make_shared<Node>();
    std::printf("shared: %ld\n", shared->owners());

    auto unique = std::make_unique<Node>();
    try {
        unique->owners();
    } catch (const std::bad_weak_ptr&) {
        std::puts("unique: bad_weak_ptr");
    }

    Node local;
    std::printf("local weak_from_this expired: %d\n", local.weak_from_this().expired());
}
Answer
shared: 1
unique: bad_weak_ptr
local weak_from_this expired: 1

Answer. The make_shared object works (one owner besides the temporary). The unique_ptr-owned object throws std::bad_weak_ptr, and the stack object's weak_from_this() is empty.

Why. Only a shared_ptr constructor fills the internal weak_ptr. Since C++17 shared_from_this() on an unowned object is specified to throw (it was UB in C++11 and C++14); weak_from_this() (C++17) is the non-throwing way to ask.

Find the bugAn array is put in a unique_ptr.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <string>

struct Level {
    std::string name = "level";
};

int main() {
    std::unique_ptr<Level> levels(new Level[4]);
    std::printf("%s\n", levels->name.c_str());
}
Answer

Answer. unique_ptr<Level> uses default_delete<Level>, which calls delete, but the memory came from new[]. Use std::unique_ptr<Level[]> (or std::make_unique<Level[]>(4)), or simply std::vector<Level>.

Why. Level has a non-trivial destructor, so new Level[4] stores an array cookie before the first element (Ch 9). Plain delete destroys one element and frees an address malloc never returned; ASan reports "attempting free on address which was not malloc()-ed". Nothing in the type system catches it because new Level[4] has type Level*.

Find the bugA raw pointer from get() is kept for later.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct Quote { double bid = 99.5, ask = 100.5; };

struct Book {
    std::unique_ptr<Quote> top = std::make_unique<Quote>();
    void refresh() { top = std::make_unique<Quote>(); }
};

int main() {
    Book book;
    const Quote* q = book.top.get();
    book.refresh();
    std::printf("%.1f\n", q->bid);
}
Answer

Answer. refresh() assigns a new unique_ptr, which deletes the old Quote; q now dangles and q->bid reads freed memory. Re-read book.top.get() after any operation that can reseat it, or do not cache the pointer.

Why. get() returns a non-owning pointer whose validity is tied to the owner's next modification. It is the smart-pointer version of iterator invalidation. ASan reports heap-use-after-free; without it the program likely prints 99.5 because the freed memory still holds the old bytes.

OutputThe object is held only through shared_ptr<Base>, and Base has no virtual destructor. Which destructors run?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct Base { ~Base() { std::puts("~Base"); } };
struct Derived : Base { ~Derived() { std::puts("~Derived"); } };

int main() {
    {
        std::shared_ptr<Base> p(new Derived);
    }
    std::puts("--");
    {
        std::shared_ptr<void> v = std::make_shared<Derived>();
    }
}
Answer
~Derived
~Base
--
~Derived
~Base

Answer. Both run in both cases.

Why. The shared_ptr constructor is a template that remembers the pointer's original type (Derived*) in the control block and deletes through it, whatever the shared_ptr's own element type. std::unique_ptr<Base>(new Derived) would delete through Base*, which is undefined behaviour without a virtual destructor. Do not rely on this to skip the virtual destructor: as soon as the object is created as a Base* first, or owned elsewhere, the protection is gone.

Find the bugThis counts live Order objects. Why does it report one at the end?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct Order {
    static inline int live = 0;
    Order() { ++live; }
    ~Order() { --live; }
};

static void archive(Order* o) { (void)o; /* writes it somewhere, does not delete */ }

int main() {
    {
        auto o = std::make_unique<Order>();
        archive(o.release());
        auto p = std::make_unique<Order>();
        p.reset();
    }
    std::printf("live orders: %d\n", Order::live);
}
Answer
live orders: 1

Answer. release() gives up ownership, and archive does not take it, so the first Order is never deleted. Pass o.get() (or *o) to a function that only uses the object; use release() only to hand ownership to something that will delete it, ideally a function taking std::unique_ptr<Order> by value.

Why. release and reset sound alike but are opposites: reset() deletes, release() does not. LeakSanitizer would report the leak at exit (it is disabled in this chapter's test harness, which is why the counter is used).

Find the bugWhy does this not compile, and what are the two correct fixes?

#include <memory>
#include <vector>

struct Task { int id; };

int main() {
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Task>> queue;
    auto t = std::make_unique<Task>(Task{1});
    queue.push_back(t);
}
Answer

Answer. push_back(t) tries to copy a unique_ptr, whose copy constructor is deleted. Either move it, queue.push_back(std::move(t)); (and stop using t), or construct it in place, queue.push_back(std::make_unique<Task>(Task{1}));.

Why. Move-only types work in every standard container as long as you move them in. The compile error is the point of unique_ptr: with auto_ptr this line would have compiled and silently nulled t. Copying a vector of unique_ptr also fails to compile, for the same reason.

Find the bugA writer replaces a global configuration while a reader copies it. The counts are atomic, so what is wrong?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <thread>

static std::shared_ptr<int> config = std::make_shared<int>(0);

int main() {
    std::thread writer([] {
        for (int i = 1; i <= 1000; ++i) config = std::make_shared<int>(i);
    });
    std::thread reader([] {
        long sum = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) {
            std::shared_ptr<int> local = config;
            sum += *local;
        }
        std::printf("%d\n", sum >= 0);
    });
    writer.join();
    reader.join();
}
Answer

Answer. Both threads access the same shared_ptr object config, and one of them writes it. Copying reads the two internal pointers and then increments the count; the assignment can replace the pointers and drop the old control block's last reference in between, so the reader increments a freed count. Fix: guard config with a mutex (as in the snapshot example) or use std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<int>> (C++20).

Why. Atomic reference counts make different shared_ptr objects safe to use concurrently, not one object. ThreadSanitizer reports a data race on config. Output is not compared because the program has undefined behaviour.

OutputA sink function takes the unique_ptr by value. In what order do the lines appear?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>

struct Job {
    ~Job() { std::puts("~Job"); }
};

static void consume(std::unique_ptr<Job> j) {
    std::puts("consume: start");
    (void)j;
    std::puts("consume: end");
}

static void inspect(const Job&) { std::puts("inspect"); }

int main() {
    auto job = std::make_unique<Job>();
    inspect(*job);
    consume(std::move(job));
    std::printf("after consume, job is null: %d\n", job == nullptr);
}
Answer
inspect
consume: start
consume: end
~Job
after consume, job is null: 1

Answer. The Job is destroyed together with the parameter j, after consume's body has finished and before the next statement in main runs; job is null afterwards.

Why. Taking unique_ptr by value makes the function the owner, so the object dies with the parameter. Exactly when a parameter is destroyed is implementation-defined ([expr.call]): at the end of the function or at the end of the caller's full-expression. GCC and Clang follow the Itanium ABI, where the caller destroys a parameter with a non-trivial destructor at the end of the full-expression consume(std::move(job));; MSVC destroys it in the callee. Both put ~Job before the next line, so the output is the same everywhere. A common wrong answer is that ~Job prints at the end of main, as if job still owned it. inspect takes a reference because it only uses the object.

Write the code

Coding

CodeImplement my::unique_ptr<T, D>: default and nullptr construction, construction from a pointer (and deleter), move construction and assignment (including from unique_ptr<U, E> when U* converts to T*), deleted copies, get, release, reset, operator*, operator->, explicit operator bool, get_deleter, and a make_unique. A stateless deleter must add no size.

Answer

Approach. Store the pointer and the deleter, marking the deleter [[no_unique_address]] so empty deleters take no space. Every ownership transfer goes through release() and reset(), which keeps the logic in two places: release exchanges the pointer with null, reset exchanges in the new pointer and then deletes the old one. That ordering makes self-move-assignment safe.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>

namespace my {

template <class T>
struct default_delete {
    default_delete() = default;
    template <class U, class = std::enable_if_t<std::is_convertible_v<U*, T*>>>
    default_delete(const default_delete<U>&) noexcept {}
    void operator()(T* p) const noexcept {
        static_assert(sizeof(T) > 0, "cannot delete an incomplete type");
        delete p;
    }
};

template <class T, class D = default_delete<T>>
class unique_ptr {
public:
    constexpr unique_ptr() noexcept = default;
    constexpr unique_ptr(std::nullptr_t) noexcept {}
    explicit unique_ptr(T* p) noexcept : p_(p) {}
    unique_ptr(T* p, D d) noexcept : p_(p), d_(std::move(d)) {}

    unique_ptr(unique_ptr&& o) noexcept : p_(o.release()), d_(std::move(o.d_)) {}
    template <class U, class E, class = std::enable_if_t<std::is_convertible_v<U*, T*>>>
    unique_ptr(unique_ptr<U, E>&& o) noexcept : p_(o.release()), d_(std::move(o.get_deleter())) {}

    unique_ptr& operator=(unique_ptr&& o) noexcept {
        reset(o.release());
        d_ = std::move(o.d_);
        return *this;
    }
    unique_ptr& operator=(std::nullptr_t) noexcept { reset(); return *this; }

    unique_ptr(const unique_ptr&) = delete;
    unique_ptr& operator=(const unique_ptr&) = delete;
    ~unique_ptr() { if (p_) d_(p_); }

    T* get() const noexcept { return p_; }
    D& get_deleter() noexcept { return d_; }
    T* release() noexcept { return std::exchange(p_, nullptr); }
    void reset(T* p = nullptr) noexcept {
        T* old = std::exchange(p_, p);
        if (old) d_(old);
    }
    T& operator*() const noexcept { return *p_; }
    T* operator->() const noexcept { return p_; }
    explicit operator bool() const noexcept { return p_ != nullptr; }

private:
    T* p_ = nullptr;
    [[no_unique_address]] D d_{};
};

template <class T, class... Args>
unique_ptr<T> make_unique(Args&&... args) {
    return unique_ptr<T>(new T(std::forward<Args>(args)...));
}

}  // namespace my

struct Shape {
    static inline int live = 0;
    Shape() { ++live; }
    virtual ~Shape() { --live; }
    virtual int sides() const { return 0; }
};
struct Square : Shape { int sides() const override { return 4; } };

static int deleted_by_lambda = 0;

int main() {
    static_assert(sizeof(my::unique_ptr<int>) == sizeof(int*));
    static_assert(!std::is_copy_constructible_v<my::unique_ptr<int>>);

    my::unique_ptr<Shape> s = my::make_unique<Square>();          // converting move
    std::printf("sides=%d live=%d\n", s->sides(), Shape::live);

    my::unique_ptr<Shape> t;
    t = std::move(s);
    std::printf("s empty=%d t ok=%d\n", !s, static_cast<bool>(t));
    t = std::move(t);                                              // self-move is safe
    std::printf("after self-move live=%d\n", Shape::live);

    Shape* raw = t.release();
    std::printf("released, live=%d\n", Shape::live);
    t.reset(raw);
    t.reset();
    std::printf("after reset live=%d\n", Shape::live);

    auto del = [](int* p) { ++deleted_by_lambda; delete p; };
    {
        my::unique_ptr<int, decltype(del)> q(new int(3), del);
        std::printf("custom deleter size=%zu value=%d\n", sizeof q, *q);
    }
    std::printf("lambda deleter calls=%d\n", deleted_by_lambda);
}
sides=4 live=1
s empty=1 t ok=1
after self-move live=1
released, live=1
after reset live=0
custom deleter size=8 value=3
lambda deleter calls=1

Complexity and pitfalls. Everything is O(1) and as cheap as a raw pointer. Pitfalls: deleting in reset before storing the new pointer (breaks self-reset and reentrancy), forgetting explicit on operator bool (allows int x = p;), a converting constructor without the convertibility constraint, and forgetting that the converting move needs default_delete<Derived> to convert to default_delete<Base>. The real one also has an array specialisation, comparison operators and swap. Clang and GCC honour [[no_unique_address]]; MSVC needs [[msvc::no_unique_address]].

Estimated rating: ~1600 · move-only RAII with EBO and the converting constructor constraint

CodeImplement my::shared_ptr<T> and my::weak_ptr<T> with a separately allocated control block and atomic counts: copy and move, reset, use_count, weak_ptr::lock and expired. The object must be destroyed when the last shared_ptr goes and the control block freed when the last weak_ptr goes too. Copies in several threads must be safe.

Answer

Approach. The control block holds strong and weak atomics; weak starts at 1, representing all strong owners together, so freeing happens in one place. Increments can be relaxed (you already hold a reference). Decrements use acquire-release so the thread that destroys sees every other thread's writes. lock() must never resurrect a dead object, so it uses a compare-exchange loop that increments only from a non-zero value.

#include <atomic>
#include <cstdio>
#include <thread>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

namespace my {

struct control_block {
    std::atomic<long> strong{1};
    std::atomic<long> weak{1};                 // +1 held by the strong owners as a group
    virtual void destroy_object() noexcept = 0;
    virtual ~control_block() = default;

    void release_weak() noexcept {
        if (weak.fetch_sub(1, std::memory_order_acq_rel) == 1) delete this;
    }
    void release_strong() noexcept {
        if (strong.fetch_sub(1, std::memory_order_acq_rel) == 1) {
            destroy_object();
            release_weak();
        }
    }
};

template <class T>
struct block_for : control_block {
    T* ptr;
    explicit block_for(T* p) : ptr(p) {}
    void destroy_object() noexcept override { delete ptr; }
};

template <class T> class weak_ptr;

template <class T>
class shared_ptr {
public:
    shared_ptr() noexcept = default;
    explicit shared_ptr(T* p) : ptr_(p) {
        try { cb_ = new block_for<T>(p); } catch (...) { delete p; throw; }
    }
    shared_ptr(const shared_ptr& o) noexcept : ptr_(o.ptr_), cb_(o.cb_) {
        if (cb_) cb_->strong.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
    }
    shared_ptr(shared_ptr&& o) noexcept
        : ptr_(std::exchange(o.ptr_, nullptr)), cb_(std::exchange(o.cb_, nullptr)) {}
    shared_ptr& operator=(shared_ptr o) noexcept { swap(o); return *this; }   // copy and swap
    ~shared_ptr() { if (cb_) cb_->release_strong(); }

    void reset() noexcept { shared_ptr().swap(*this); }
    void swap(shared_ptr& o) noexcept { std::swap(ptr_, o.ptr_); std::swap(cb_, o.cb_); }
    long use_count() const noexcept { return cb_ ? cb_->strong.load(std::memory_order_relaxed) : 0; }
    T* get() const noexcept { return ptr_; }
    T& operator*() const noexcept { return *ptr_; }
    T* operator->() const noexcept { return ptr_; }
    explicit operator bool() const noexcept { return ptr_ != nullptr; }

private:
    friend class weak_ptr<T>;
    shared_ptr(T* p, control_block* cb) noexcept : ptr_(p), cb_(cb) {}   // adopts a strong ref
    T* ptr_ = nullptr;
    control_block* cb_ = nullptr;
};

template <class T>
class weak_ptr {
public:
    weak_ptr() noexcept = default;
    weak_ptr(const shared_ptr<T>& s) noexcept : ptr_(s.ptr_), cb_(s.cb_) { acquire(); }
    weak_ptr(const weak_ptr& o) noexcept : ptr_(o.ptr_), cb_(o.cb_) { acquire(); }
    weak_ptr(weak_ptr&& o) noexcept
        : ptr_(std::exchange(o.ptr_, nullptr)), cb_(std::exchange(o.cb_, nullptr)) {}
    weak_ptr& operator=(weak_ptr o) noexcept {
        std::swap(ptr_, o.ptr_);
        std::swap(cb_, o.cb_);
        return *this;
    }
    ~weak_ptr() { if (cb_) cb_->release_weak(); }

    long use_count() const noexcept { return cb_ ? cb_->strong.load(std::memory_order_relaxed) : 0; }
    bool expired() const noexcept { return use_count() == 0; }
    shared_ptr<T> lock() const noexcept {
        if (!cb_) return {};
        long n = cb_->strong.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        while (n != 0) {
            if (cb_->strong.compare_exchange_weak(n, n + 1, std::memory_order_acq_rel,
                                                  std::memory_order_relaxed))
                return shared_ptr<T>(ptr_, cb_);
        }
        return {};
    }

private:
    void acquire() noexcept { if (cb_) cb_->weak.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed); }
    T* ptr_ = nullptr;
    control_block* cb_ = nullptr;
};

}  // namespace my

struct Probe {
    static inline std::atomic<int> live{0};
    int value;
    explicit Probe(int v) : value(v) { ++live; }
    ~Probe() { --live; }
};

int main() {
    my::weak_ptr<Probe> w;
    {
        my::shared_ptr<Probe> a(new Probe(42));
        my::shared_ptr<Probe> b = a;
        w = a;
        std::printf("use_count=%ld value=%d\n", a.use_count(), b->value);
        if (auto c = w.lock()) std::printf("locked, use_count=%ld\n", c.use_count());
        a.reset();
        std::printf("after reset: b.use_count=%ld expired=%d\n", b.use_count(), w.expired());
    }
    std::printf("scope left: expired=%d live=%d lock null=%d\n", w.expired(), Probe::live.load(), !w.lock());

    my::shared_ptr<Probe> shared(new Probe(7));
    my::weak_ptr<Probe> watcher = shared;
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;
    for (int t = 0; t < 4; ++t) {
        threads.emplace_back([shared, watcher] {          // each thread owns its own copies
            for (int i = 0; i < 10000; ++i) {
                my::shared_ptr<Probe> copy = shared;
                my::shared_ptr<Probe> locked = watcher.lock();
                (void)copy;
                (void)locked;
            }
        });
    }
    for (auto& th : threads) th.join();
    std::printf("after threads: use_count=%ld\n", shared.use_count());
    shared.reset();
    std::printf("final: live=%d expired=%d\n", Probe::live.load(), watcher.expired());
}
use_count=2 value=42
locked, use_count=3
after reset: b.use_count=1 expired=0
scope left: expired=1 live=0 lock null=1
after threads: use_count=1
final: live=0 expired=1

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) per operation, one extra allocation per object (make_shared would remove it by storing T inside the block). Pitfalls: a lock() that does if (strong > 0) ++strong in two steps (resurrects objects being destroyed), relaxed decrements (the destroying thread might not see other threads' writes to the object), freeing the control block when the strong count hits zero although weak_ptrs still read it, and not deleting the pointer when allocating the control block throws. The standard version adds aliasing, deleters, allocators, conversions and enable_shared_from_this support.

Estimated rating: ~1900 · two-count lifetime protocol, memory ordering and a correct lock() loop

CodeImplement an intrusive reference-counted pointer. Classes inherit from RefCounted, which holds an atomic count; intrusive_ptr<T> increments on copy and deletes the object when the count reaches zero. Show that it is one pointer wide and that wrapping the same raw pointer twice is safe, unlike shared_ptr.

Answer

Approach. The count lives in the object, so there is no control block, no second allocation and no way to create two disagreeing counts. The base class has a protected virtual destructor so the pointer can delete the most derived object. Copies are relaxed increments; the decrement that reaches zero uses acquire-release before deleting.

#include <atomic>
#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>

class RefCounted {
public:
    void add_ref() const noexcept { refs_.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed); }
    void release() const noexcept {
        if (refs_.fetch_sub(1, std::memory_order_acq_rel) == 1) delete this;
    }
    int ref_count() const noexcept { return refs_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed); }
protected:
    RefCounted() = default;
    RefCounted(const RefCounted&) {}                   // copies start with their own count
    virtual ~RefCounted() = default;
private:
    mutable std::atomic<int> refs_{0};
};

template <class T>
class intrusive_ptr {
public:
    intrusive_ptr() noexcept = default;
    intrusive_ptr(T* p) noexcept : p_(p) { if (p_) p_->add_ref(); }
    intrusive_ptr(const intrusive_ptr& o) noexcept : intrusive_ptr(o.p_) {}
    intrusive_ptr(intrusive_ptr&& o) noexcept : p_(std::exchange(o.p_, nullptr)) {}
    intrusive_ptr& operator=(intrusive_ptr o) noexcept { std::swap(p_, o.p_); return *this; }
    ~intrusive_ptr() { if (p_) p_->release(); }
    T* get() const noexcept { return p_; }
    T* operator->() const noexcept { return p_; }
    T& operator*() const noexcept { return *p_; }
    explicit operator bool() const noexcept { return p_ != nullptr; }
private:
    T* p_ = nullptr;
};

struct Texture : RefCounted {
    int id;
    explicit Texture(int i) : id(i) {}
    ~Texture() override { std::printf("~Texture(%d)\n", id); }
};

int main() {
    static_assert(sizeof(intrusive_ptr<Texture>) == sizeof(Texture*));
    Texture* raw = new Texture(1);
    intrusive_ptr<Texture> a(raw);
    intrusive_ptr<Texture> b(raw);                     // safe: same count, now 2
    std::printf("count=%d\n", raw->ref_count());
    {
        intrusive_ptr<Texture> c = a;
        std::printf("count=%d\n", c->ref_count());
    }
    a = intrusive_ptr<Texture>();
    std::printf("count=%d\n", b->ref_count());
    b = new Texture(2);                                // releases Texture 1
    std::printf("b->id=%d\n", b->id);
}
count=2
count=3
count=1
~Texture(1)
b->id=2
~Texture(2)

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1), 8 bytes per pointer, one allocation per object. Trade-offs vs shared_ptr: no weak_ptr (adding one needs a separate block again), the type must opt in by inheriting, and the object cannot live on the stack or be owned any other way. Pitfalls: the copy constructor of RefCounted must not copy the count; the destructor must be virtual or the deleting call must know the concrete type; and an object whose count was never incremented (created and never wrapped) leaks. Used by COM, Boost.intrusive_ptr, LLVM's IntrusiveRefCntPtr and many game engines.

Estimated rating: ~1500 · small, but the count-in-object design and copy semantics need care

CodeA thread-safe cache with weak_ptr. TextureCache::get(name) returns a std::shared_ptr<const Texture>: if a live texture with that name exists, return it; otherwise load a new one. The cache must not keep textures alive. Add purge() to drop expired entries. Explain the make_shared choice.

Answer

Approach. Map names to weak_ptrs under a mutex. get tries lock(); on failure it creates the texture and stores a weak reference. The texture is created with shared_ptr(new ...), not make_shared, so that an expired texture's memory is freed immediately even though its weak_ptr remains in the map until purge(). This is Herb Sutter's "favourite C++ 10-liner" with that refinement.

#include <atomic>
#include <cstdio>
#include <map>
#include <memory>
#include <mutex>
#include <string>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

struct Texture {
    std::string name;
    std::vector<unsigned char> pixels;
    explicit Texture(std::string n) : name(std::move(n)), pixels(4096) {}
};

class TextureCache {
public:
    std::shared_ptr<const Texture> get(const std::string& name) {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mu_);
        std::weak_ptr<const Texture>& slot = cache_[name];
        if (std::shared_ptr<const Texture> hit = slot.lock()) return hit;
        std::shared_ptr<const Texture> fresh(new Texture(name));   // not make_shared, see text
        slot = fresh;
        ++loads_;
        return fresh;
    }

    std::size_t purge() {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mu_);
        std::size_t removed = 0;
        for (auto it = cache_.begin(); it != cache_.end();) {
            if (it->second.expired()) { it = cache_.erase(it); ++removed; }
            else ++it;
        }
        return removed;
    }

    int loads() const { std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mu_); return loads_; }

private:
    mutable std::mutex mu_;
    std::map<std::string, std::weak_ptr<const Texture>> cache_;
    int loads_ = 0;
};

int main() {
    TextureCache cache;
    auto stone = cache.get("stone");                    // keep one alive for the whole test
    std::atomic<int> same{0};
    std::vector<std::thread> workers;
    for (int t = 0; t < 4; ++t) {
        workers.emplace_back([&] {
            for (int i = 0; i < 500; ++i)
                if (cache.get("stone") == stone) ++same;
        });
    }
    for (auto& w : workers) w.join();
    std::printf("loads=%d, all hits returned the same object: %d\n", cache.loads(), same.load() == 2000);

    {
        auto grass = cache.get("grass");
        std::printf("loads=%d\n", cache.loads());
    }                                                   // grass expires here
    std::printf("purged=%zu\n", cache.purge());
    stone.reset();
    std::printf("purged=%zu\n", cache.purge());
    auto again = cache.get("stone");
    std::printf("reload: loads=%d\n", cache.loads());
}
loads=1, all hits returned the same object: 1
loads=2
purged=1
purged=1
reload: loads=3

Complexity and pitfalls. O(log n) per lookup under one mutex; a high-traffic cache would shard the map or load outside the lock (with care to avoid two threads loading the same name). Pitfalls: storing shared_ptr in the cache (then nothing ever expires), checking expired() then calling lock() (race), and using make_shared here, which would keep each dead texture's 4 KB alive inside its control block until purge() removes the weak_ptr. Without periodic purging, the map itself grows with every distinct name ever requested: a logical leak.

Estimated rating: ~1500 · weak_ptr lock pattern plus locking and the make_shared memory trade-off

CodeA singly linked list owned by unique_ptr. Implement push_front, pop_front, reverse (in place, no allocation) and sum. The list must survive one million nodes: explain why the default destructor would not, and write one that does.

Answer

Approach. Each node owns the next through std::unique_ptr<Node>, so ownership is automatic. The implicit destructor would destroy head, whose destructor destroys next, recursively: one stack frame per node, which overflows an 8 MB stack long before a million nodes. The destructor instead detaches nodes in a loop: head_ = std::move(head_->next) first takes the successor out of the old head (via release), then deletes the old head, which now owns nothing.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <optional>
#include <utility>

class IntList {
public:
    IntList() = default;
    IntList(IntList&&) noexcept = default;
    IntList& operator=(IntList&& o) noexcept { clear(); head_ = std::move(o.head_); return *this; }
    ~IntList() { clear(); }

    void push_front(int v) {
        auto n = std::make_unique<Node>();
        n->value = v;
        n->next = std::move(head_);
        head_ = std::move(n);
    }
    std::optional<int> pop_front() {
        if (!head_) return std::nullopt;
        int v = head_->value;
        head_ = std::move(head_->next);
        return v;
    }
    void reverse() noexcept {
        std::unique_ptr<Node> done;
        while (head_) {
            std::unique_ptr<Node> rest = std::move(head_->next);
            head_->next = std::move(done);
            done = std::move(head_);
            head_ = std::move(rest);
        }
        head_ = std::move(done);
    }
    long long sum() const noexcept {
        long long s = 0;
        for (const Node* n = head_.get(); n; n = n->next.get()) s += n->value;
        return s;
    }
    void clear() noexcept {
        while (head_) head_ = std::move(head_->next);   // iterative: no deep recursion
    }

private:
    struct Node {
        int value = 0;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
    };
    std::unique_ptr<Node> head_;
};

int main() {
    IntList small;
    for (int i = 1; i <= 4; ++i) small.push_front(i);   // 4 3 2 1
    small.reverse();                                    // 1 2 3 4
    std::printf("pop: %d %d\n", *small.pop_front(), *small.pop_front());
    std::printf("sum of rest: %lld\n", small.sum());

    IntList big;
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000000; ++i) big.push_front(1);
    big.reverse();
    std::printf("big sum: %lld\n", big.sum());
}                                                       // destroys a million nodes safely
pop: 1 2
sum of rest: 7
big sum: 1000000

Complexity and pitfalls. push and pop O(1), reverse and sum O(n), destruction O(n) time with O(1) stack. Pitfalls: relying on the recursive default destructor (stack overflow, often only in production with large inputs), writing head_ = std::move(head_->next) with your own pointer class that deletes before moving (that destroys the node you are reading from), and a defaulted move assignment that would destroy the old list recursively (hence the explicit one). Copy is deliberately not provided. The same recursion problem hits trees of unique_ptr and long shared_ptr chains.

Estimated rating: ~1400 · unique_ptr ownership transfer plus the recursive-destructor trap

CodeCopy-on-write string with shared_ptr. CowString copies share one buffer; the first modifying operation on a shared buffer makes a private copy. Provide str(), append, set(i, c) and shares_buffer_with, and state why this design is not thread-safe as written.

Answer

Approach. Hold std::shared_ptr<std::string>. Copying a CowString copies the pointer (cheap). Every mutator calls detach() first, which clones the buffer if use_count() > 1. Readers return a const reference to the shared buffer.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

class CowString {
public:
    explicit CowString(std::string s = {}) : buf_(std::make_shared<std::string>(std::move(s))) {}

    const std::string& str() const noexcept { return *buf_; }
    void append(const std::string& s) { detach(); buf_->append(s); }
    void set(std::size_t i, char c) { detach(); (*buf_)[i] = c; }
    bool shares_buffer_with(const CowString& o) const noexcept { return buf_ == o.buf_; }

private:
    void detach() {
        if (buf_.use_count() > 1) buf_ = std::make_shared<std::string>(*buf_);
    }
    std::shared_ptr<std::string> buf_;
};

int main() {
    CowString a("order book");
    CowString b = a;                       // shares
    CowString c = a;
    std::printf("b shares with a: %d\n", b.shares_buffer_with(a));
    b.append(" v2");                       // b detaches
    c.set(0, 'O');                         // c detaches
    std::printf("a=\"%s\" b=\"%s\" c=\"%s\"\n", a.str().c_str(), b.str().c_str(), c.str().c_str());
    std::printf("shares: a-b %d, a-c %d\n", a.shares_buffer_with(b), a.shares_buffer_with(c));
    a.append("!");                         // a is the sole owner now: no copy
    std::printf("a=\"%s\"\n", a.str().c_str());
}
b shares with a: 1
a="order book" b="order book v2" c="Order book"
shares: a-b 0, a-c 0
a="order book!"

Complexity and pitfalls. Copies are O(1); the first write after sharing is O(n). Not thread-safe: use_count() is a snapshot, so two threads holding copies could both see 2 and both clone (harmless), or one could see 1 while another thread is in the middle of copying it from a third object, and then write into a buffer that just became shared. Also, str() returns a reference into a buffer that a later mutation may replace. This is why C++11 banned copy-on-write for std::string (references and iterators must stay valid, and operator[] must not invalidate them); libstdc++ switched to SSO with its new ABI in GCC 5.

Estimated rating: ~1300 · simple with shared_ptr, but explaining the thread-safety hole is the real test

Cheat sheet

Theory
  • Default to unique_ptr (8 bytes, move-only, zero overhead with a stateless deleter); use make_unique; return it from factories; convert to shared_ptr by move when sharing is needed.
  • Parameters: T&/T* to use, unique_ptr by value to take ownership, unique_ptr& to reseat, shared_ptr by value to share. Avoid const unique_ptr&.
  • shared_ptr = object pointer + control block (strong count, weak count, type-erased deleter). Copies cost atomic operations and can bounce cache lines; move when you can.
  • make_shared: one allocation and better locality, but the object's memory lives until the last weak_ptr dies; cannot take a custom deleter or call private constructors.
  • Never build two shared_ptrs from one raw pointer (two control blocks, double delete). Inside the object use enable_shared_from_this (public base), and never call shared_from_this() in the constructor or on an unowned object (bad_weak_ptr).
  • Aliasing constructor shares ownership of a whole object while pointing at a member; it is how the pointer casts work.
  • Thread safety: the counts are atomic; one shared_ptr instance written concurrently is a race (mutex or atomic<shared_ptr>); the pointee is unprotected. Use weak.lock(), never expired() then lock().
  • auto_ptr moved on copy and was removed in C++17. Custom deleters: Ch 12. Cycles and weak back pointers: Ch 13.
