Part E · Memory management · Chapter 12

Custom deleters

A smart pointer is a pointer plus a rule for releasing it. This chapter is about that rule: how unique_ptr stores it in its type (and what that costs in bytes), how shared_ptr hides it in the control block, and how to wrap C handles, file descriptors, pool memory and mappings safely. Interviewers use deleters to test whether you understand type erasure, the empty base optimisation and the exact null and exception rules.

TheoryDrillsCoding· about 3 hours· prerequisites: Ch 11 smart pointers, Ch 9 new/delete

Why custom deleters exist

Theory

Mental model. Ownership is about resources, and memory is only one kind of resource. A FILE* must go back through fclose, a file descriptor through close, a mapping through munmap, a block from a pool back to that pool, and an array from new[] through delete[]. If a smart pointer could only call delete, every one of these would need a hand-written RAII class. A custom deleter lets you reuse the whole smart pointer machinery (move semantics, exception safety, reset, release, comparison) and change only the last step.

Under the hood. std::unique_ptr<T, D> stores a pointer of type D::pointer (or T* if D has no such member) and an object of type D. Its destructor is, in effect:

~unique_ptr() {
    if (get() != nullptr) get_deleter()(get());
}

std::shared_ptr<T> does the same thing later, when the strong count reaches zero, and it keeps the deleter in the control block instead of in the pointer object (Ch 11 covers the control block itself).

ResourceAcquireRelease (the deleter calls)Null value
C streamfopen, tmpfile, popenfclose (pclose for popen)nullptr
File descriptor, socketopen, socket, accept, pipeclose-1 (0 is a valid fd)
Memory mappingmmapmunmap(addr, length), needs the lengthMAP_FAILED, which is not nullptr
C allocationmalloc, strdup, getlinefreenullptr
C library handlesqlite3_open, EVP_MD_CTX_new, curl_easy_initthe matching *_close or *_freenullptr
Arraynew T[n]delete[] (use unique_ptr<T[]>)nullptr
Pool or arena blockpool.acquire()pool.release(p), needs the poolnullptr

Two columns in that table drive the design of a deleter. The release column decides whether the deleter needs state (a length, a pool pointer). The null value column decides whether a plain pointer type can represent "no resource" at all. For a file descriptor it cannot, and a custom pointer type fixes that.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct FileCloser {
    void operator()(std::FILE* f) const noexcept {
        std::puts("fclose");
        std::fclose(f);
    }
};
using File = std::unique_ptr<std::FILE, FileCloser>;

static File open_temp() { return File(std::tmpfile()); }

int main() {
    File f = open_temp();
    if (!f) return 1;
    std::fputs("hello\n", f.get());
    std::rewind(f.get());
    char line[16];
    if (std::fgets(line, sizeof line, f.get())) std::printf("read: %s", line);
    File g = std::move(f);
    std::printf("f empty: %d\n", f == nullptr);
}
read: hello
f empty: 1
fclose

The stream is closed exactly once, by g, at the end of main. The moved-from f holds nullptr, so its destructor does not call the deleter. Early returns and exceptions get the same guarantee for free.

unique_ptr<T, D>: three ways to spell the deleter

Theory

Mental model. For unique_ptr the deleter is part of the type. unique_ptr<FILE, A> and unique_ptr<FILE, B> are unrelated types: you cannot assign one to the other or put both in one vector. That is the price of zero overhead, because the compiler sees the exact deleter and can inline it.

Function object, lambda, function pointer

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct FileCloser {                       // 1. a named function-object type
    void operator()(std::FILE* f) const noexcept { std::fclose(f); }
};

static void close_file(std::FILE* f) { std::fclose(f); }

int main() {
    std::unique_ptr<std::FILE, FileCloser> a(std::tmpfile());

    using LambdaCloser = decltype([](std::FILE* f) { std::fclose(f); });  // 2. C++20 only
    std::unique_ptr<std::FILE, LambdaCloser> b(std::tmpfile());

    auto closer = [](std::FILE* f) { std::fclose(f); };                   // 2b. lambda object
    std::unique_ptr<std::FILE, decltype(closer)> c(std::tmpfile(), closer);

    std::unique_ptr<std::FILE, decltype(&close_file)> d(std::tmpfile(), &close_file);  // 3. pointer

    std::printf("%d %d %d %d\n", a != nullptr, b != nullptr, c != nullptr, d != nullptr);
}
1 1 1 1
  • Function-object type. The best default. It is default constructible, so File(fopen(...)) works with one argument, it costs no space, and the name documents the intent. Mark operator() noexcept.
  • Lambda. Before C++20 a lambda closure type has no default constructor and a lambda cannot appear in decltype, so you must pass the lambda object to every constructor (form 2b). C++20 made captureless lambdas default constructible and allowed lambdas in unevaluated operands, which gives form 2. A stateless lambda costs no space either.
  • Function pointer. decltype(&fclose) is int (*)(FILE*). The pointer is a runtime value, so it takes 8 bytes inside every unique_ptr, the call is indirect unless the optimiser proves the value, and you must pass it at every construction: a value-initialised function pointer is null, so the one-argument constructor does not take part in overload resolution for pointer deleters (it would leave you with a null deleter to call later).

Interview trap

std::unique_ptr<FILE, decltype(&fclose)> f(fopen("a", "r")); does not compile. The single-argument constructor requires D to be default constructible and not a pointer type ([unique.ptr.single.ctor]). Write f(fopen("a", "r"), &fclose), or better, use a function-object type.

A note on taking the address of library functions

C++20 [namespace.std] says the behaviour is unspecified (possibly ill-formed) if a program takes the address of a standard library function that is not designated addressable, and almost none are. &std::fclose works on every real implementation, but the strictly portable spelling is a lambda or function object that calls fclose. It also avoids a GCC -Wignored-attributes warning on glibc, where fclose carries a nonnull attribute that is lost in decltype(&fclose). One more trick you may see in code reviews turns a function pointer into a zero-size type:

template <auto F>
struct FnDeleter {
    template <class P> void operator()(P p) const noexcept { F(p); }
};
using File = std::unique_ptr<std::FILE, FnDeleter<&std::fclose>>;   // pointer is a template argument, 0 bytes

What unique_ptr requires of D

  • d(ptr) must be well-formed and must not throw. The destructor and reset call it.
  • get_deleter() returns a reference to the stored deleter, so a stateful deleter can be inspected or changed.
  • D may be an lvalue reference type, unique_ptr<T, D&>. Then the pointer stores a reference to an external deleter object, which must outlive it. This is how several pointers share one stateful deleter without copying it.
  • If D has a nested type pointer, that type is stored instead of T*. It must satisfy NullablePointer: value-initialises to null, compares with nullptr, converts to bool in a condition.
  • release() gives up ownership without calling the deleter. reset(q) stores q first and then deletes the old pointer, so a deleter that inspects the smart pointer sees the new state.

The size cost and the empty base optimisation

Theory

Mental model. An empty class still has sizeof 1, so a naive struct { T* p; D d; } would be 16 bytes even for an empty D, because of padding. Library implementations avoid this. libstdc++ stores the pair in a std::tuple whose elements are base classes when they are empty, and libc++ uses a __compressed_pair. Both rely on the empty base optimisation (EBO): an empty base class subobject may occupy zero bytes. In your own code, C++20 [[no_unique_address]] on a member gives the same effect without inheritance.

#include <cstdio>
#include <functional>
#include <memory>

struct CloseFile { void operator()(std::FILE* f) const noexcept { std::fclose(f); } };
static void close_file(std::FILE* f) { std::fclose(f); }

int main() {
    auto lam = [](std::FILE* f) { std::fclose(f); };
    int log_fd = 2;
    auto stateful = [log_fd](std::FILE* f) { (void)log_fd; std::fclose(f); };
    using F = std::FILE;
    std::printf("default_delete   %zu\n", sizeof(std::unique_ptr<int>));
    std::printf("function object  %zu\n", sizeof(std::unique_ptr<F, CloseFile>));
    std::printf("stateless lambda %zu\n", sizeof(std::unique_ptr<F, decltype(lam)>));
    std::printf("function pointer %zu\n", sizeof(std::unique_ptr<F, decltype(&close_file)>));
    std::printf("stateful lambda  %zu\n", sizeof(std::unique_ptr<F, decltype(stateful)>));
    std::printf("std::function    %zu\n", sizeof(std::unique_ptr<F, std::function<void(F*)>>));
}
default_delete   8
function object  8
stateless lambda 8
function pointer 16
stateful lambda  16
std::function    40

These numbers are for 64-bit Linux and macOS with both libstdc++ and libc++. The last line depends on sizeof(std::function), which is 32 on both libraries today but is not fixed by the standard. The stateful lambda captures an int (4 bytes), and alignment pads the pair to 16.

Why the size matters. A vector<unique_ptr<Node, decltype(&free_node)>> with ten million entries wastes 80 MB on copies of the same function pointer, and halves the number of pointers per cache line. In latency-sensitive code the indirect call also blocks inlining. Prefer an empty function-object type whenever the release action is fixed at compile time.

Doing it yourself: [[no_unique_address]]

template <class T, class D>
class Handle {
    T* p_ = nullptr;
    [[no_unique_address]] D d_;     // occupies no storage if D is empty (GCC, Clang; MSVC ignores it)
};

MSVC accepts but ignores the standard attribute for ABI reasons and offers [[msvc::no_unique_address]] instead. Before C++20 the portable technique was to inherit privately from D when std::is_empty_v<D> and D is not final.

shared_ptr deleters: type-erased, in the control block

Theory

Mental model. For shared_ptr<T> the deleter is not part of the type. Every shared_ptr<int> is the same 16-byte object, two pointers: one to the int and one to a control block. The control block is a class template instantiated for the exact pointer, deleter and allocator types, and the shared_ptr talks to it through virtual functions. That is classic type erasure.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <vector>

static int global_counter = 3;

int main() {
    std::vector<std::shared_ptr<int>> v;
    v.push_back(std::shared_ptr<int>(new int(1)));
    v.push_back(std::shared_ptr<int>(new int(2), [](int* p) {
        std::printf("lambda frees %d\n", *p);
        delete p;
    }));
    v.push_back(std::shared_ptr<int>(&global_counter, [](int*) { std::puts("no-op for a static"); }));
    std::printf("all the same type, sizeof %zu\n", sizeof(v[0]));
    for (auto& p : v) p.reset();
}
all the same type, sizeof 16
lambda frees 2
no-op for a static

Rules that differ from unique_ptr

  • Capture at construction. The constructor template<class Y, class D> shared_ptr(Y* p, D d) records Y and D in the control block type. Later conversions to shared_ptr<Base> or shared_ptr<void> keep calling the original deleter with the original Y*, which is why shared_ptr<void>(new Foo) runs ~Foo and shared_ptr<Base>(new Derived) is correct even without a virtual destructor.
  • Requirements on D. D must be move constructible, and d(p) must be well-formed and must not throw.
  • Allocation failure. The constructor allocates the control block. If that throws, it calls d(p) before rethrowing, so the resource never leaks. That is why shared_ptr<FILE>(fopen(...), fclose) is exception safe on its own.
  • Inspection. std::get_deleter<D>(sp) returns a D* to the stored deleter, or nullptr if the type does not match exactly. There is no way to ask "what is the deleter type?", only "is it this type?".
  • Cost. The deleter is stored once per owned object, in the control block, not once per pointer. Calling it is a virtual call, which is irrelevant compared with the atomic decrement before it.
  • Conversion from unique_ptr. shared_ptr<T>(std::move(u)) moves the unique_ptr's deleter into the new control block, so a unique_ptr<FILE, FileCloser> becomes a shared_ptr<FILE> that still calls FileCloser. If D is a reference type, the control block stores std::ref(u.get_deleter()) instead, so the external deleter object must outlive every copy of the shared_ptr.

Know this cold

unique_ptr: deleter in the type, stored inline, zero cost if empty, statically dispatched. shared_ptr: deleter erased, stored in the control block, one virtual call, any deleter fits the same shared_ptr<T>.

When is the deleter object itself destroyed?

The deleter is called when the strong count reaches zero. When the deleter object is destroyed is left to the implementation: the standard only promises that get_deleter stays valid while some shared_ptr or weak_ptr shares ownership. libstdc++ destroys the deleter together with the control block, when the weak count also reaches zero. libc++ destroys it right after calling it. If your deleter captures something heavy (a shared_ptr to a pool, a big buffer), a long-lived weak_ptr may keep that alive on libstdc++.

Deleters and the make functions

Theory

Mental model. make_unique and make_shared both decide how the object is allocated, so they also decide how it is freed. There is no overload that takes a deleter, and there cannot be a sensible one: a deleter is the answer to "how do I free memory someone else allocated?", and with a make function nobody else allocated it.

  • make_unique<T>(args...) is unique_ptr<T>(new T(args...)), always with default_delete. For a custom deleter, call the constructor: unique_ptr<T, D>(pool.acquire(), D{&pool}).
  • make_shared<T>(args...) allocates the control block and the object in one block, and destroys the object with a direct destructor call, not with delete. A user deleter would have nothing valid to free.
  • std::allocate_shared<T>(alloc, args...) is the customisation point instead. It takes an allocator, rebinds it to the internal control-block-plus-object type, allocates once through it and constructs the object with allocator_traits::construct. Use it when the memory must come from a pool or arena but you still want a single allocation.
  • The three-argument constructor shared_ptr(p, d, alloc) uses alloc only for the control block. The object was allocated by you, and d frees it.
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <new>

static int allocations = 0;

template <class T>
struct CountingAlloc {
    using value_type = T;
    CountingAlloc() = default;
    template <class U> CountingAlloc(const CountingAlloc<U>&) {}
    T* allocate(std::size_t n) {
        ++allocations;
        return static_cast<T*>(::operator new(n * sizeof(T)));
    }
    void deallocate(T* p, std::size_t) noexcept { ::operator delete(p); }
    friend bool operator==(const CountingAlloc&, const CountingAlloc&) { return true; }
};

struct Point { int x, y; };

int main() {
    auto a = std::allocate_shared<Point>(CountingAlloc<Point>{}, 1, 2);
    std::printf("allocate_shared: %d allocation(s) through the allocator\n", allocations);

    allocations = 0;
    std::shared_ptr<Point> b(new Point{3, 4}, std::default_delete<Point>{}, CountingAlloc<Point>{});
    std::printf("shared_ptr(p, d, a): %d allocation(s) through the allocator, plus the new\n", allocations);
    std::printf("%d %d\n", a->x + a->y, b->x + b->y);
}
allocate_shared: 1 allocation(s) through the allocator
shared_ptr(p, d, a): 1 allocation(s) through the allocator, plus the new
3 7

Tip

For "objects from my pool, shared ownership", you have two designs. allocate_shared with a pool allocator gives one allocation and the pool sees the combined block size. A raw pool pointer plus a PoolDeleter gives two allocations (the control block comes from the global heap) but keeps the pool's block size equal to sizeof(T). Pick the second if the pool is a fixed-size block pool (Ch 15).

Null handles, exceptions and close errors

Theory

Is the deleter called for a null pointer?

This is the single most asked deleter question, and the two smart pointers answer it differently.

  • unique_ptr: no. The destructor and reset only call the deleter if the stored pointer is not null ([unique.ptr.single.dtor]). So unique_ptr<FILE, FileCloser>(fopen("missing", "r")) is safe even though fclose(nullptr) is undefined.
  • shared_ptr: yes, if you gave it a deleter. shared_ptr(nullptr_t, D d) and shared_ptr(p, d) with p == nullptr both create a control block that owns the null pointer. use_count() is 1, and when it drops to 0 the deleter is called with nullptr. A default-constructed shared_ptr has no control block, so nothing is called.
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

static void say(int* p) {
    std::printf("deleter called with %s\n", p ? "an object" : "nullptr");
    delete p;
}

int main() {
    {
        std::unique_ptr<int, void (*)(int*)> u(nullptr, say);
        std::puts("unique_ptr leaves scope");
    }
    {
        std::shared_ptr<int> s(nullptr, say);
        std::printf("use_count %ld\n", s.use_count());
        std::puts("shared_ptr leaves scope");
    }
    {
        std::shared_ptr<int> e;
        std::printf("empty use_count %ld\n", e.use_count());
    }
}
unique_ptr leaves scope
use_count 1
shared_ptr leaves scope
deleter called with nullptr
empty use_count 0

So a shared_ptr deleter for a C API that rejects null must check: [](FILE* f) { if (f) fclose(f); }. Note also that a shared_ptr holding null with a deleter is non-empty but if (sp) is false, because operator bool tests the stored pointer, not the control block.

Handles that are not pointers

A file descriptor is an int whose null value is -1. unique_ptr<int, D> would store an int*, which is wrong. Give the deleter a nested pointer type that wraps the fd and satisfies NullablePointer, and unique_ptr stores that instead. The coding section builds this completely. The common alternative is a 30-line dedicated UniqueFd class, which is what most codebases (for example Android's unique_fd) actually ship. Both are fine answers in an interview, as long as you say why int* is wrong and why 0 is a valid descriptor.

Deleters must not throw

The standard requires that the deleter call does not throw, and destructors are implicitly noexcept. If a deleter throws from inside ~unique_ptr, std::terminate is called. Mark your deleter noexcept so the contract is visible and checked.

A deleter also has no way to report an error. fclose flushes buffered output, and the flush can fail (disk full, NFS errors). close on some file systems reports deferred write errors. If the error matters, close explicitly on the success path and check the result:

bool save(const char* path, const std::string& data) {
    File f(std::fopen(path, "w"));
    if (!f) return false;
    if (std::fwrite(data.data(), 1, data.size(), f.get()) != data.size()) return false;
    return std::fclose(f.release()) == 0;   // explicit close: the error is observed; the deleter only covers failure paths
}

Interview trap

Retrying close after EINTR is wrong on Linux: the descriptor is already released, and a retry may close a descriptor another thread just received. A deleter should call close once and ignore the result.

Key factsunique_ptr<T, D>shared_ptr<T>
Deleter part of the typeyesno (type-erased)
Where it is storedinside the pointer object (EBO if empty)in the control block
Size with a stateless deleter8 bytes16 bytes (always)
Size with a function pointer deleter16 bytes16 bytes (the pointer is in the control block)
Deleter called for nullneveryes, if constructed with a deleter
Works with the make functionno, call the constructorno, use allocate_shared for allocator control
Inspect the deleterget_deleter() memberstd::get_deleter<D>(sp) free function
Incomplete T at destructionerror with default_deletefine, deleter captured at construction
Custom handle type (fd)yes, via D::pointerno, always stores T*

Arrays, no-op deleters, pools and mmap

Theory

Arrays

unique_ptr<T[]> uses default_delete<T[]>, which calls delete[], and provides operator[] instead of * and ->. It also refuses conversions from Derived*, because indexing an array through a base pointer is broken. shared_ptr<T[]> works the same way since C++17, and make_shared<T[]>(n) since C++20. Before C++17 you had to write shared_ptr<T>(new T[n], std::default_delete<T[]>()), and forgetting the deleter meant delete on a new[] pointer, which is undefined behaviour (Ch 9 explains the array cookie). For buffers from malloc use unique_ptr<char[], FreeDeleter>. In most code, std::vector is still the better array owner.

No-op deleters

A deleter that does nothing turns a smart pointer into a non-owning one: shared_ptr<Logger>(&global_logger, [](Logger*) {}). It is useful when an interface demands a shared_ptr and you want to pass a static or stack object that is known to outlive every user. It is also a design smell, because the type now lies: it says "shared ownership" while nobody owns the object, and if the stack object dies first you get a dangling pointer that the type system cannot see. The aliasing constructor (Ch 11) is the better tool when there is a real owner to tie the lifetime to. The cleaner fix is to change the interface to take T& or T*.

Stateful deleters: pools and mappings

A pool deleter must know which pool to return to, so it carries a Pool*, and every unique_ptr grows to 16 bytes. If there is exactly one pool per type, a stateless deleter that calls a static or thread-local pool keeps the size at 8. A munmap deleter must know the length. Store it in the deleter, or wrap the mapping in a span-like type and give the deleter a pointer typedef.

struct Unmap {
    std::size_t len;
    void operator()(void* p) const noexcept { ::munmap(p, len); }
};
void* raw = ::mmap(nullptr, len, PROT_READ, MAP_PRIVATE, fd, 0);
if (raw == MAP_FAILED) throw std::system_error(errno, std::generic_category());   // MAP_FAILED is (void*)-1, not null
std::unique_ptr<void, Unmap> map(raw, Unmap{len});

Interview trap

Check for MAP_FAILED before handing the pointer to the smart pointer. unique_ptr only skips the deleter for nullptr, so a MAP_FAILED pointer would be passed to munmap. The same applies to INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE on Windows and SIG_ERR-style sentinels.

A pool deleter also creates a lifetime rule: the pool must outlive every pointer it handed out. Declare the pool before the pointers (members are destroyed in reverse order of declaration), or make the deleter hold a shared_ptr to the pool. The reading drills include the bug you get when this is wrong.

default_delete and incomplete types: the PIMPL destructor

Theory

Mental model. std::default_delete<T>::operator() contains static_assert(sizeof(T) > 0) (in effect), so it refuses to compile if T is incomplete at the point where it is instantiated. That is deliberate: delete on a pointer to an incomplete class type compiles with a warning but is undefined behaviour if the class has a non-trivial destructor, because the destructor is never called. C++26 goes further and makes deleting a pointer to an incomplete class type ill-formed (P3144).

In the PIMPL idiom the header only declares struct Impl;. If the class does not declare a destructor, the compiler defines one implicitly inline, wherever it is used, which is in client code that only saw the header. There Impl is incomplete, so default_delete<Impl> fails.

// parser.h
class Parser {
public:
    Parser();
    ~Parser();                              // declared only
    Parser(Parser&&) noexcept;              // these also destroy an Impl
    Parser& operator=(Parser&&) noexcept;
    int parse(std::string_view s);
private:
    struct Impl;
    std::unique_ptr<Impl> impl_;
};

// parser.cpp
struct Parser::Impl { std::vector<int> tokens; };
Parser::Parser() : impl_(std::make_unique<Impl>()) {}
Parser::~Parser() = default;                // Impl is complete here
Parser::Parser(Parser&&) noexcept = default;
Parser& Parser::operator=(Parser&&) noexcept = default;

The same error appears with any class that has a unique_ptr member to a forward-declared type, not only PIMPL. Note that unique_ptr<Impl> as a member is fine while Impl is incomplete: only the functions that destroy (destructor, reset, move assignment) need the complete type.

C++23 std::out_ptr and std::inout_ptr

Theory

C APIs often return a handle through an output parameter: int sqlite3_open(const char*, sqlite3** out). Before C++23 you wrote a temporary raw pointer, called the function and then reset the smart pointer, and every early return between the two steps was a leak. std::out_ptr(sp) (in <memory>) creates a temporary object that converts to T**, and at the end of the full expression its destructor calls sp.reset(p) if the C function wrote a non-null pointer. It also resets sp first, so the old handle is released before the call. std::inout_ptr is for APIs that take an existing handle, free or reallocate it and write back the new one: it passes the current pointer in after calling release().

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct Widget { int id; };
// A C-style API: the handle comes back through an out parameter.
static int widget_create(Widget** out, int id) { *out = new Widget{id}; return 0; }
static void widget_destroy(Widget* w) { std::printf("destroy %d\n", w->id); delete w; }

struct WidgetDeleter { void operator()(Widget* w) const noexcept { widget_destroy(w); } };

int main() {
    std::unique_ptr<Widget, WidgetDeleter> w;
    if (widget_create(std::out_ptr(w), 7) != 0) return 1;
    std::printf("got %d\n", w->id);
    widget_create(std::out_ptr(w), 8);   // w is reset (destroy 7) before the call
    std::printf("got %d\n", w->id);
}
got 7
destroy 7
got 8
destroy 8

For a shared_ptr, out_ptr needs the deleter as an extra argument, std::out_ptr(sp, WidgetDeleter{}), because shared_ptr::reset(p) alone would use delete. inout_ptr does not work with shared_ptr at all, because a shared object cannot be released.

Concept and tricky questions

Drills

ConceptWhy does a smart pointer need a custom deleter at all? Give three resources where delete is the wrong release.

Answer

Answer. Because the release action depends on how the resource was acquired. FILE* from fopen needs fclose, a buffer from malloc needs free, an mmap region needs munmap(addr, len), a pool block needs pool.release, and new T[n] needs delete[].

Why. Calling the wrong release is undefined behaviour: delete on malloc memory or on a FILE* corrupts the heap or skips flushing. The deleter lets you keep all of unique_ptr's guarantees (single owner, exception safety, moves) and change only the last step. A weak answer says "for logging"; that is a use, but not the reason the feature exists.

TrickyYour stateless deleter is declared struct Closer final { void operator()(int* p) const noexcept { delete p; } };. It is still an empty class. Is unique_ptr<int, Closer> still 8 bytes?

Answer

Answer. No. With both libstdc++ (GCC 16) and libc++ (LLVM 22) it is 16 bytes, the same as a function pointer deleter. Remove final and it goes back to 8. A hand-written pair with [[no_unique_address]] stays at 8 even for a final type.

Why. The library size optimisation is the empty base optimisation, and you cannot derive from a final class. So the libraries store the deleter as an ordinary member instead, which takes 1 byte and is padded to pointer alignment. [[no_unique_address]] works on a member, so it does not care about final. The standard fixes neither size. The usual wrong answer is "8, the deleter is empty". Being empty is necessary for the zero-cost layout, but it is not enough. (The basic sizes for function pointers and lambdas are a Ch 11 drill.)

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct Closer { void operator()(int* p) const noexcept { delete p; } };
struct FinalCloser final { void operator()(int* p) const noexcept { delete p; } };

template <class T, class D>
struct Pair { T* p; [[no_unique_address]] D d; };

int main() {
    std::printf("plain %zu, final %zu, no_unique_address final %zu\n",
                sizeof(std::unique_ptr<int, Closer>), sizeof(std::unique_ptr<int, FinalCloser>),
                sizeof(Pair<int, FinalCloser>));
}
plain 8, final 16, no_unique_address final 8

TrickyIs the deleter called when the managed pointer is null? Answer for unique_ptr and for shared_ptr.

Answer

Answer. unique_ptr: never. shared_ptr: yes, if it was constructed with a deleter, even from nullptr; no, if it is default-constructed or constructed from a plain nullptr without a deleter.

Why. ~unique_ptr is specified as "if get() != nullptr, calls get_deleter()(get())". shared_ptr(nullptr_t, D) is specified to own p (a null pointer): a control block is allocated, use_count() is 1, and when it drops to zero the deleter runs with nullptr. So a shared_ptr<FILE>(fopen(...), fclose) whose fopen failed calls fclose(nullptr), which is undefined. Guard inside the deleter. People usually assume the two smart pointers agree.

TrickyCan you store a shared_ptr<int> with a lambda deleter and one with default_delete in the same vector? What about unique_ptr?

Answer

Answer. Yes for shared_ptr: both are shared_ptr<int>. No for unique_ptr: unique_ptr<int> and unique_ptr<int, Lambda> are different types.

Why. shared_ptr's deleter is type-erased into the control block; the pointer object only holds a pointer to a polymorphic control block base. unique_ptr carries the deleter as a template parameter so it can store it inline and call it without indirection. To mix deleters in a unique_ptr container you would need a type-erased deleter such as std::function<void(int*)>, at a cost of 32 extra bytes per element and a possible allocation.

ConceptWhy is there no make_shared or make_unique overload that takes a deleter? What do you use instead?

Answer

Answer. A make function allocates the object itself, so it already knows how to free it; a deleter only makes sense for memory or a resource that someone else acquired. Use the constructor (unique_ptr<T, D>(p, d) or shared_ptr<T>(p, d)) when you acquired the resource, and std::allocate_shared when you want to control where make_shared's single block comes from.

Why. make_shared places the object inside the control block allocation and destroys it with a direct destructor call. A user deleter receiving that pointer could not legally free it, since it is not the start of any allocation. The allocator is the right customisation point: it controls both allocation and deallocation of the combined block. Saying "it was just forgotten" is the common wrong answer.

TrickyCan unique_ptr manage a POSIX file descriptor? What goes wrong with unique_ptr<int, FdCloser> written naively?

Answer

Answer. Yes, but only if the deleter defines a nested pointer type that holds the fd and satisfies NullablePointer, with -1 as its null state. Written naively, unique_ptr<int, FdCloser> stores an int*, so you would have to heap-allocate the int or cast the fd to a pointer.

Why. unique_ptr stores D::pointer if it exists, otherwise T*. Casting an fd to int* (reinterpret_cast<int*>(fd)) breaks for fd 0, which is a valid descriptor (stdin) but would compare equal to nullptr, so it would never be closed, while an invalid fd -1 would be "non-null" and passed to close. A small dedicated UniqueFd class is often clearer; the coding section shows both.

ConceptWhat happens if a deleter throws an exception?

Answer

Answer. The standard requires that the deleter call does not throw, so it is a contract violation. In practice the exception leaves ~unique_ptr (or the shared_ptr release path), which is noexcept, and std::terminate is called.

Why. Destructors are implicitly noexcept(true) since C++11 unless a member or base has a throwing destructor, and unique_ptr's destructor is not one of those. Even outside a destructor, a throwing release would make reset unable to give the strong exception guarantee. Mark deleters noexcept, swallow or log errors inside, and close explicitly on the success path if the error must be observed.

Trickyu is a std::unique_ptr<int, Counter&> that refers to an external counting deleter. Which deleter does std::shared_ptr<int> s(std::move(u)); store, and what follows from that? Can you go the other way, from a shared_ptr to a unique_ptr?

Answer

Answer. For a reference deleter type, the converting constructor stores std::ref(u.get_deleter()), a std::reference_wrapper<Counter>. It does not store a copy of the Counter. So std::get_deleter<Counter>(s) is null, and the external Counter must outlive every copy of s, including copies on other threads. For a non-reference D, the deleter is moved into the control block. The other direction does not exist: shared_ptr has no release().

Why. [util.smartptr.shared.const] specifies the unique_ptr<Y, D>&& constructor as shared_ptr(r.release(), std::ref(r.get_deleter())) when D is a reference, because a reference cannot be stored in a control block. A shared_ptr cannot give up ownership, because other owners or weak_ptrs may exist and the deleter belongs to the control block. Even with use_count() == 1, there is no way to take the object out. The usual wrong answers are "it copies the Counter" and "call release() when you are the last owner". If you may need unique ownership later, keep the unique_ptr and convert as late as possible.

#include <cstdio>
#include <functional>
#include <memory>

struct Counter {
    int n = 0;
    void operator()(int* p) noexcept { ++n; delete p; }
};

int main() {
    Counter c;
    {
        std::unique_ptr<int, Counter&> u(new int(1), c);
        std::shared_ptr<int> s(std::move(u));
        std::printf("reference_wrapper stored: %d, Counter stored: %d\n",
                    std::get_deleter<std::reference_wrapper<Counter>>(s) != nullptr,
                    std::get_deleter<Counter>(s) != nullptr);
    }
    std::printf("external counter: %d\n", c.n);
}
reference_wrapper stored: 1, Counter stored: 0
external counter: 1

ConceptHow does shared_ptr<T> store a deleter of any type without the deleter becoming part of its own type? Sketch the mechanism.

Answer

Answer. It uses type erasure. The shared_ptr holds a pointer to a non-template control block base class that has virtual functions. The constructor template shared_ptr(Y* p, D d) knows Y and D, so it allocates a derived class template instantiated for exactly those types. That derived class stores p and d and overrides the virtual "dispose" function to call d(p).

struct ControlBase {
    std::atomic<long> strong{1}, weak{1};
    virtual void dispose() noexcept = 0;   // destroy the object: strong count hit 0
    virtual void destroy() noexcept = 0;   // free this block: weak count hit 0
    virtual ~ControlBase() = default;
};

template <class Y, class D>
struct ControlWithDeleter final : ControlBase {
    Y* p;
    D d;
    ControlWithDeleter(Y* p, D d) : p(p), d(std::move(d)) {}
    void dispose() noexcept override { d(p); }
    void destroy() noexcept override { delete this; }
};
// shared_ptr<T> = { T* ptr; ControlBase* ctrl; }: the same layout for every D

Why. The type information is captured once, at construction, inside a class the shared_ptr only sees through its base. That is why any deleter fits the same shared_ptr<T>, why shared_ptr<void>(new Foo) still runs ~Foo (it stores a Foo*), and why std::get_deleter must check the type at run time. The costs are a virtual call when the count reaches zero and a separate allocation for the block (unless you use make_shared). A common wrong answer is "it stores a std::function". That would also work, but real implementations use a hand-written virtual base, with no extra allocation for the callable.

ConceptWhat does std::get_deleter do, and why is it a free function template rather than a member like unique_ptr::get_deleter?

Answer

Answer. std::get_deleter<D>(sp) returns a D* to the deleter stored in sp's control block if its type is exactly D, and nullptr otherwise.

Why. The deleter type is erased, so shared_ptr<T> has no static knowledge of it; the caller must guess the type and the control block checks it at run time (implementations compare typeid). unique_ptr::get_deleter() can be a member returning D& because D is in the type. Use cases: reading state from a stateful deleter (a pool id, a length), or detecting that a pointer came from a particular factory.

ConceptWrite the custom deleter you would use in production to own a FILE* with unique_ptr, and justify each choice. What is wrong with std::unique_ptr<FILE> f(fopen("a.txt", "r"));?

Answer

Answer.

struct FileCloser {
    void operator()(std::FILE* f) const noexcept { std::fclose(f); }
};
using File = std::unique_ptr<std::FILE, FileCloser>;

File f(std::fopen("a.txt", "r"));   // one argument: FileCloser is default constructible
if (!f) { /* handle the error */ }

The version with the default deleter calls delete on a pointer that came from fopen. That is undefined behaviour: the stream is never flushed or closed, and the C library's memory goes back to the wrong allocator.

Why. An empty function object costs no space and lets the one-argument constructor work, and its call can be inlined. It is noexcept because it runs from a destructor. It needs no null check, because unique_ptr never calls the deleter on null (a shared_ptr deleter would need if (f)). It calls fclose rather than taking &fclose, which avoids the 8-byte function pointer, the extra constructor argument and the rule that standard library functions are not addressable. It ignores the return value. When you wrote data and need to know that the close succeeded, call std::fclose(f.release()) and check it. The common wrong answers are unique_ptr<FILE, decltype(&fclose)> f(fopen(...)), which does not compile, and the default deleter.

TrickyWhen is the deleter object of a shared_ptr destroyed: when the strong count reaches zero, or when the control block is freed?

Answer

Answer. The standard leaves it to the implementation. libstdc++ destroys it with the control block (when the weak count also reaches zero); libc++ destroys it immediately after calling it.

Why. [util.smartptr.getdeleter] only says the returned pointer stays valid while a shared_ptr or weak_ptr shares ownership of the deleter, and that it is unspecified whether it remains valid longer. Programs that depend on the deleter's destructor running at a specific time (for example a deleter that captures a shared_ptr to a pool and you expect the pool to die with the last strong reference) behave differently across libraries when weak_ptrs are alive. The program below shows it.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct D {
    D() = default;
    D(const D&) = default;
    D(D&&) noexcept = default;
    void operator()(int* p) const noexcept { std::puts("deleter called"); delete p; }
    ~D() { if (live) std::puts("deleter destroyed"); }
    bool live = false;
};

int main() {
    std::weak_ptr<int> w;
    {
        std::shared_ptr<int> s(new int(1), D{});
        std::get_deleter<D>(s)->live = true;  // mark the stored copy only
        w = s;
    }
    std::puts("only a weak_ptr left");
    w.reset();
    std::puts("end");
}

libstdc++ prints "deleter called", "only a weak_ptr left", "deleter destroyed", "end". libc++ prints "deleter called", "deleter destroyed", "only a weak_ptr left", "end". The output is not compared because it is implementation-specific.

ConceptWhy should a deleter for fclose or close ignore the return value, and how do you handle close errors that matter?

Answer

Answer. The deleter runs from a destructor, often during stack unwinding, so it cannot throw and has no caller to return an error to. When the error matters (a file you wrote), call fclose(f.release()) explicitly on the success path and check it; the deleter then only covers failure paths, where the data is being abandoned anyway.

Why. fclose flushes the stdio buffer, so it is where "disk full" is first reported. Silently ignoring it in a destructor can lose data. Throwing from the deleter is worse: it calls std::terminate. For close on Linux, do not retry on EINTR: the fd is gone regardless and a retry can close someone else's new descriptor.

ConceptWhat problem does C++23 std::out_ptr solve?

Answer

Answer. It lets you pass a smart pointer directly to a C function that returns a handle through a T** out parameter. The temporary adaptor converts to T**, and when the full expression ends it calls reset on the smart pointer with whatever the function wrote.

Why. The manual pattern (raw temporary, call, then reset) has a window where the handle is owned by nobody, and it is easy to forget the reset on one path. out_ptr also resets the smart pointer before the call, so the old handle is released first. For shared_ptr you must pass the deleter: std::out_ptr(sp, Deleter{}). std::inout_ptr covers APIs that consume the old handle and write a new one.

Predict the output and find the bug

Drills

OutputWhat does this print on a 64-bit target with GCC or Clang?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct Empty { void operator()(int* p) const noexcept { delete p; } };
struct WithId {
    int id = 0;
    void operator()(int* p) const noexcept { delete p; }
};

template <class T, class D>
struct Naive { T* p; D d; };

template <class T, class D>
struct Compressed { T* p; [[no_unique_address]] D d; };

int main() {
    std::printf("%zu %zu\n", sizeof(Naive<int, Empty>), sizeof(Compressed<int, Empty>));
    std::printf("%zu %zu\n", sizeof(std::unique_ptr<int, Empty>), sizeof(std::unique_ptr<int, WithId>));
    std::printf("%zu\n", sizeof(std::unique_ptr<int, Empty&>));
}
Answer
16 8
8 16
16

Answer. The naive pair is 16 because the empty member takes 1 byte and is padded to pointer alignment; [[no_unique_address]] lets the empty member overlap, giving 8. unique_ptr with an empty deleter is 8 and with an int member is 16. A reference deleter type Empty& stores a reference, which is a pointer under the hood, so it is 16 even though Empty is empty.

Why. EBO and [[no_unique_address]] only apply to empty class types. A reference is not an object of class type, it is stored as an address. People often answer 8 for the last line because "the deleter is empty". (MSVC ignores the standard [[no_unique_address]], so the second number would be 16 there.)

Find the bugWhy does this not compile, and what are two fixes?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

static void close_file(std::FILE* f) { std::fclose(f); }

int main() {
    std::unique_ptr<std::FILE, decltype(&close_file)> f(std::tmpfile());
    std::fputs("x", f.get());
}
Answer

Answer. The one-argument constructor of unique_ptr<T, D> is constrained to deleters that are default constructible and are not pointer types. D here is void (*)(FILE*), so overload resolution finds no viable constructor. Fix 1: pass the function, f(std::tmpfile(), &close_file). Fix 2 (better): use a function-object type, struct CloseFile { void operator()(FILE* f) const noexcept { fclose(f); } };, which also halves the size.

Why. A value-initialised function pointer is null; if the constructor were allowed, the destructor would call a null function pointer. The standard rules it out at compile time ([unique.ptr.single.ctor]: "Constraints: is_pointer_v<deleter_type> is false and is_default_constructible_v<deleter_type> is true").

OutputWhat does this print?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct Base { ~Base() { std::puts("~Base"); } };         // not virtual
struct Derived : Base { ~Derived() { std::puts("~Derived"); } };

int main() {
    {
        std::shared_ptr<void> v(new Derived);
    }
    std::puts("--");
    {
        std::shared_ptr<Base> b(new Derived);
    }
    std::puts("--");
    {
        std::shared_ptr<Base> c(static_cast<Base*>(new Derived));
        std::shared_ptr<Base> keep = c;
    }
}
Answer
~Derived
~Base
--
~Derived
~Base
--
~Base

Answer. The first two blocks run the full Derived destructor; the third runs only ~Base, which is undefined behaviour (deleting a Derived through a Base* without a virtual destructor).

Why. The shared_ptr(Y* p) constructor deduces Y from the argument and builds a control block that deletes a Y*. In the first two blocks Y = Derived. In the third, the cast happened before the constructor saw the pointer, so Y = Base. Copying (keep) never changes the stored deleter. This is a favourite because candidates either say "always ~Base without a virtual destructor" or "shared_ptr always gets it right". (ASan does not flag the third block because Derived adds no members, so the sizes match; it is still UB.)

Find the bugA connection pool counts open and closed handles. At the end it reports one leak. Where is it?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

static int opened = 0, closed = 0;

struct Conn { int id; };
struct ConnCloser { void operator()(Conn* c) const noexcept { ++closed; delete c; } };
using ConnPtr = std::unique_ptr<Conn, ConnCloser>;

static ConnPtr connect(int id) { ++opened; return ConnPtr(new Conn{id}); }

int main() {
    ConnPtr a = connect(1);
    ConnPtr b = connect(2);
    ConnPtr c = connect(3);
    a.reset();            // done with 1
    b.release();          // done with 2
    c = connect(4);       // replace 3
    std::printf("opened %d closed-before-exit %d\n", opened, closed);
    c.reset();
    std::printf("opened %d closed %d\n", opened, closed);
}
Answer
opened 4 closed-before-exit 2
opened 4 closed 3

Answer. b.release() drops ownership without calling the deleter, and the returned pointer is discarded, so connection 2 leaks. It should be b.reset(). The move assignment c = connect(4) correctly closes connection 3.

Why. release means "I take the resource back", and clang-tidy's bugprone-unused-return-value check flags a discarded release() by default, because discarding its result is almost always a leak. LeakSanitizer would also catch this on Linux, but the counters prove it on any platform.

OutputIn what order do the lines appear?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct Noisy {
    int id;
    ~Noisy() { std::printf("~Noisy %d\n", id); }
};

struct Tell {
    const std::unique_ptr<Noisy, Tell>* owner = nullptr;
    void operator()(Noisy* p) const noexcept {
        std::printf("deleting %d, owner now holds %d\n", p->id, (*owner) ? (*owner)->id : -1);
        delete p;
    }
};

int main() {
    std::unique_ptr<Noisy, Tell> u(new Noisy{1});
    u.get_deleter().owner = &u;
    u.reset(new Noisy{2});
    u.reset();
    std::puts("end");
}
Answer
deleting 1, owner now holds 2
~Noisy 1
deleting 2, owner now holds -1
~Noisy 2
end

Answer. In reset(q) the new pointer is stored first and the old one is deleted afterwards, so the deleter already sees the new value. reset() stores null first, then deletes.

Why. [unique.ptr.single.modifiers] specifies: assign p to the stored pointer, then if the old value was not null call get_deleter()(old). That order makes reset safe if the deleted object's destructor reaches back into the owner (for example a node that resets its parent's child pointer). Many candidates assume "delete old, then assign new".

Find the bugThis compiles cleanly. What happens at run time?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

static int sum(const std::unique_ptr<int[]>& a, int n) {
    int s = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) s += a[i];
    return s;
}

int main() {
    int scratch[4] = {1, 2, 3, 4};
    std::unique_ptr<int[]> view(scratch);   // "just to pass it to sum"
    std::printf("%d\n", sum(view, 4));
}
Answer

Answer. When view is destroyed, default_delete<int[]> calls delete[] on a stack array. That is undefined behaviour; ASan reports "attempting free on address which was not malloc()-ed", and without it the program usually crashes in the allocator.

Why. A smart pointer with the default deleter asserts ownership of heap memory from new[]. To pass a non-owning view, take a std::span<const int> (or const int* and a size). A no-op deleter would silence the crash but keep the misleading type. GCC may also warn with -Wfree-nonheap-object.

Find the bugA pool hands out objects with a deleter that returns them to the pool. Sometimes the program crashes on exit. Why?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <vector>

struct Pool {
    std::vector<int*> free_list;
    ~Pool() { for (int* p : free_list) delete p; }
    int* acquire() {
        if (free_list.empty()) return new int(0);
        int* p = free_list.back();
        free_list.pop_back();
        return p;
    }
    void release(int* p) { free_list.push_back(p); }
};

struct ToPool {
    Pool* pool;
    void operator()(int* p) const noexcept { pool->release(p); }
};

struct Service {
    std::unique_ptr<int, ToPool> current;   // declared first
    Pool pool;                              // declared second
    Service() : current(nullptr, ToPool{&pool}) {
        for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) pool.release(new int(i));
        current.reset(pool.acquire());
    }
};

int main() {
    Service s;
    std::printf("value %d\n", *s.current);
}
Answer

Answer. Members are destroyed in reverse order of declaration, so pool is destroyed before current. Then current's deleter calls release on a destroyed pool, and push_back writes into the vector's freed buffer: heap-use-after-free, which ASan reports.

Why. A stateful deleter that points to its pool creates a lifetime dependency the type system does not check. Fix: declare Pool pool; before every member that holds pointers from it, or let the deleter hold a shared_ptr<Pool> (or a weak_ptr and fall back to delete when the pool is gone). Using pool in current's member initialiser is also suspicious, since pool is not yet constructed there; taking its address is fine, calling it would not be. Compilers warn about that with -Wuninitialized only in some cases.

OutputTwo unique_ptrs share one counting deleter through a reference type. What is printed?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct Counter {
    int freed = 0;
    void operator()(int* p) noexcept { ++freed; delete p; }
};

int main() {
    Counter shared_counter;
    {
        std::unique_ptr<int, Counter&> a(new int(1), shared_counter);
        std::unique_ptr<int, Counter&> b(new int(2), shared_counter);
        std::unique_ptr<int, Counter> c(new int(3), shared_counter);   // copies the deleter
    }
    std::printf("freed through the reference: %d\n", shared_counter.freed);
}
Answer
freed through the reference: 2

Answer. 2. a and b store a Counter& and increment the same object. c stores its own copy of Counter, so its increment goes to the copy, which dies with c.

Why. With D = Counter& the deleter is a reference to an external object, so state is shared and the external object must outlive the pointers. With D = Counter the constructor copies the argument. Note that operator() here is non-const, which works because unique_ptr calls the deleter through a non-const reference. The common wrong answer is 3.

Find the bugThis shared_ptr wrapper for a C stream crashes on some platforms when the file is missing. Why, and what is the one-line fix?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

static int closes = 0;
static int checked_close(std::FILE* f) {
    ++closes;
    std::printf("fclose called with %s\n", f ? "a stream" : "nullptr");
    return f ? std::fclose(f) : EOF;   // stand-in: real fclose(nullptr) is undefined
}

int main() {
    std::shared_ptr<std::FILE> log(std::fopen("/no/such/dir/log.txt", "r"), checked_close);
    if (!log) std::puts("open failed");
}
Answer

Answer. When fopen fails, the shared_ptr still owns the null pointer through a control block, and its deleter is called with nullptr. With the real fclose as the deleter that is undefined behaviour (glibc crashes). Fix: guard in the deleter, [](FILE* f) { if (f) std::fclose(f); }, or construct the shared_ptr only after checking the result. The program prints "open failed" and then "fclose called with nullptr".

Why. shared_ptr(p, d) takes ownership of p whatever its value; only unique_ptr skips null. if (!log) is true because operator bool checks the stored pointer, yet use_count() is 1. It is marked data-mode="ub" because the path being demonstrated is undefined with the real fclose, even though this stand-in is safe.

Find the bugWhy does this PIMPL class fail to compile in main? (Imagine Engine in a header and Engine::Impl defined in another file that main.cpp never sees.)

#include <memory>

class Engine {
public:
    Engine() = default;
    ~Engine() = default;        // "I declared the destructor"
private:
    struct Impl;
    std::unique_ptr<Impl> impl_;
};

int main() {
    Engine e;
}
Answer

Answer. ~Engine() = default; inside the class is a definition, so the destructor is still defined in the header, where Impl is incomplete. Destroying impl_ instantiates default_delete<Impl>::operator(), whose static assertion fails. Fix: write ~Engine(); in the header and Engine::~Engine() = default; in the .cpp after struct Engine::Impl { ... };.

Why. Defaulting on first declaration makes the function inline and defined at that point. Only an out-of-line definition moves the instantiation to the translation unit that has the complete type. GCC reports "invalid application of 'sizeof' to incomplete type"; Clang reports the same in default_delete.

Find the bugTwo smart pointers manage one buffer from malloc. What goes wrong?

#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <cstring>
#include <memory>

struct Free { void operator()(void* p) const noexcept { std::free(p); } };
using Buf = std::unique_ptr<char[], Free>;

static Buf duplicate(const char* s) {
    char* raw = static_cast<char*>(std::malloc(std::strlen(s) + 1));
    std::strcpy(raw, s);
    return Buf(raw);
}

int main() {
    Buf a = duplicate("hello");
    Buf b(a.get());          // "share" it
    std::printf("%s %s\n", a.get(), b.get());
}
Answer

Answer. b(a.get()) creates a second owner of the same pointer, so free runs twice: a double free, reported by ASan as "attempting double-free".

Why. Constructing a smart pointer from a raw pointer always means "take ownership". The deleter does not change that rule. To share, use shared_ptr<char[]>(a.release(), Free{}) and copy the shared_ptr; to lend, pass a.get() as a plain const char*. The same bug with shared_ptr (two control blocks for one pointer) is in Ch 11.

Write the code

Coding

CodeMake std::unique_ptr own a POSIX file descriptor. Write a deleter FdCloser with a nested pointer type so that using UniqueFd = std::unique_ptr<int, FdCloser>; stores an int fd (not an int*), treats -1 as null, treats 0 as a valid descriptor, and closes exactly once. Test it with pipe(): write through one end, read from the other, move a handle, and count the closes.

Answer

Approach. unique_ptr stores D::pointer when that type exists. Make it a tiny struct holding the fd, with a default constructor and a nullptr_t constructor that both give -1, an explicit operator bool that tests fd >= 0, and defaulted equality. That satisfies NullablePointer, so unique_ptr skips the deleter for -1 and moves set the source to -1.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <unistd.h>

static int close_calls = 0;

struct FdCloser {
    struct pointer {
        int fd = -1;
        pointer() = default;
        pointer(std::nullptr_t) {}
        explicit pointer(int f) : fd(f) {}
        explicit operator bool() const { return fd >= 0; }
        friend bool operator==(pointer, pointer) = default;
    };
    void operator()(pointer p) const noexcept {
        ++close_calls;
        ::close(p.fd);    // once, result ignored: no retry on EINTR
    }
};
using UniqueFd = std::unique_ptr<int, FdCloser>;

static int fd_of(const UniqueFd& u) { return u.get().fd; }

int main() {
    int fds[2];
    if (::pipe(fds) != 0) return 1;
    UniqueFd rd(FdCloser::pointer{fds[0]}), wr(FdCloser::pointer{fds[1]});

    const char msg[] = "ping";
    if (::write(fd_of(wr), msg, sizeof msg) != static_cast<ssize_t>(sizeof msg)) return 1;
    char buf[8] = {};
    if (::read(fd_of(rd), buf, sizeof buf) <= 0) return 1;
    std::printf("read: %s\n", buf);

    UniqueFd moved = std::move(wr);
    std::printf("after move: wr %s, moved %s\n", wr ? "valid" : "null", moved ? "valid" : "null");

    UniqueFd zero(FdCloser::pointer{0});              // fd 0 is valid: must not count as null
    std::printf("fd 0 is %s\n", zero ? "valid" : "null");
    (void)zero.release();                               // do not close our stdin

    UniqueFd none;                                      // null: deleter never called
    moved.reset();
    rd.reset();
    std::printf("close calls: %d\n", close_calls);
    std::printf("sizeof(UniqueFd) = %zu\n", sizeof(UniqueFd));
}
read: ping
after move: wr null, moved valid
fd 0 is valid
close calls: 2
sizeof(UniqueFd) = 4

Complexity and pitfalls. Every operation is O(1) and the handle is the size of an int. Pitfalls: using int* or casting the fd to a pointer (fd 0 becomes "null"); testing fd != 0 instead of fd >= 0; retrying close on EINTR; forgetting the nullptr_t constructor, which unique_ptr's default constructor and reset() need. release() returns the pointer struct, so give the class a helper if callers need the raw fd.

Estimated rating: ~1600 · knowing the D::pointer hook and NullablePointer requirements is the whole problem

CodeImplement ScopeGuard: auto g = make_scope_exit([&] { ... }); runs the callable when g leaves scope, unless g.dismiss() was called. It must be movable (the moved-from guard does nothing), not copyable, and must not add overhead for a captureless or reference-capturing lambda beyond the lambda and one bool. Show the classic use: roll back a two-step update if the second step throws.

Answer

Approach. A class template over the callable type F, storing F and an active flag. The destructor calls f_() if active. The move constructor steals the callable and dismisses the source. A deleter-based version (unique_ptr<void, Lambda> with a dummy pointer) also works, but it abuses the pointer and cannot be dismissed without release; the dedicated class is clearer. This is the shape of std::experimental::scope_exit from the Library Fundamentals TS v3.

#include <cstdio>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

template <class F>
class ScopeGuard {
public:
    explicit ScopeGuard(F f) noexcept(std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<F>) : f_(std::move(f)) {}
    ScopeGuard(ScopeGuard&& o) noexcept(std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<F>)
        : f_(std::move(o.f_)), active_(std::exchange(o.active_, false)) {}
    ScopeGuard(const ScopeGuard&) = delete;
    ScopeGuard& operator=(const ScopeGuard&) = delete;
    ScopeGuard& operator=(ScopeGuard&&) = delete;
    ~ScopeGuard() { if (active_) f_(); }      // f_ must not throw: we may be unwinding
    void dismiss() noexcept { active_ = false; }
private:
    F f_;
    bool active_ = true;
};

template <class F>
ScopeGuard<F> make_scope_exit(F f) { return ScopeGuard<F>(std::move(f)); }

static void step_two(int value) {
    if (value < 0) throw std::invalid_argument("negative");
}

static void add_both(std::vector<int>& a, std::vector<int>& b, int value) {
    a.push_back(value);
    auto undo = make_scope_exit([&] { a.pop_back(); std::puts("rolled back"); });
    step_two(value);
    b.push_back(value);
    undo.dismiss();               // commit
}

int main() {
    std::vector<int> a, b;
    add_both(a, b, 1);
    try { add_both(a, b, -5); } catch (const std::exception& e) { std::printf("caught %s\n", e.what()); }
    std::printf("a=%zu b=%zu\n", a.size(), b.size());

    int n = 0;
    {
        auto g1 = make_scope_exit([&n] { ++n; });
        auto g2 = std::move(g1);  // only g2 fires
    }
    std::printf("fired %d time(s), sizeof %zu\n", n, sizeof(ScopeGuard<void (*)()>));
}
rolled back
caught negative
a=1 b=1
fired 1 time(s), sizeof 16

Complexity and pitfalls. Zero allocation; the size is the closure plus a bool plus padding (a function pointer callable gives 16). Pitfalls: a copyable guard runs the action twice; forgetting to dismiss the moved-from guard; throwing from the action during unwinding calls std::terminate; writing make_scope_exit(...) without naming the result destroys the temporary immediately (mark the class [[nodiscard]] in production). Guaranteed copy elision in C++17 makes returning the guard from make_scope_exit free.

Estimated rating: ~1400 · small class, but move semantics and unwinding rules must be right

CodeWrite a fixed-capacity ObjectPool<T, N> whose acquire(args...) returns std::unique_ptr<T, Returner>. When the pointer dies, the object is destroyed and its slot goes back to the pool. acquire returns a null pointer when the pool is full. The pool must not be moved while handles exist (make it non-movable). Report how many slots are free.

Answer

Approach. The pool owns an aligned byte array of N slots and a free list of slot indices. acquire pops an index and constructs T there with placement new (Ch 14). The deleter holds a Pool* (stateful, so the handle is 16 bytes) and calls pool->give_back(p), which runs ~T and pushes the index. If the constructor throws, the slot must be returned before propagating.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <new>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

template <class T, std::size_t N>
class ObjectPool {
public:
    struct Returner {
        ObjectPool* pool = nullptr;
        void operator()(T* p) const noexcept { pool->give_back(p); }
    };
    using Handle = std::unique_ptr<T, Returner>;

    ObjectPool() { for (std::size_t i = 0; i < N; ++i) free_[i] = N - 1 - i; }
    ObjectPool(const ObjectPool&) = delete;
    ObjectPool& operator=(const ObjectPool&) = delete;

    template <class... Args>
    Handle acquire(Args&&... args) {
        if (nfree_ == 0) return Handle(nullptr, Returner{this});
        std::size_t idx = free_[--nfree_];
        T* p;
        try {
            p = ::new (slot(idx)) T(std::forward<Args>(args)...);
        } catch (...) {
            free_[nfree_++] = idx;
            throw;
        }
        return Handle(p, Returner{this});
    }
    std::size_t available() const { return nfree_; }

private:
    void* slot(std::size_t i) { return storage_ + i * sizeof(T); }
    void give_back(T* p) noexcept {
        std::size_t idx = static_cast<std::size_t>(reinterpret_cast<std::byte*>(p) - storage_) / sizeof(T);
        p->~T();
        free_[nfree_++] = idx;
    }
    alignas(T) std::byte storage_[N * sizeof(T)];
    std::size_t free_[N];
    std::size_t nfree_ = N;
};

int main() {
    ObjectPool<std::string, 2> pool;
    {
        auto a = pool.acquire("first, long enough to need a heap buffer");
        auto b = pool.acquire(3, 'x');
        auto c = pool.acquire("no room");
        std::printf("%s | %s | c is %s | free %zu\n", a->substr(0, 5).c_str(), b->c_str(),
                    c ? "set" : "null", pool.available());
        a.reset();
        std::printf("after reset free %zu\n", pool.available());
        auto d = pool.acquire("reused");
        std::printf("%s free %zu\n", d->c_str(), pool.available());
    }
    std::printf("all returned, free %zu, handle size %zu\n", pool.available(),
                sizeof(ObjectPool<int, 1>::Handle));
}
first | xxx | c is null | free 0
after reset free 1
reused free 0
all returned, free 2, handle size 16

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) acquire and release, no heap allocation by the pool. Pitfalls: the pool must outlive every handle (declare it first; see the reading drill); the slot must be returned if the constructor throws; the storage must be aligned for T; destroying T in the deleter, not only marking the slot free, or std::string buffers leak. If there is one global pool per type, a stateless deleter brings the handle back to 8 bytes.

Estimated rating: ~1800 · combines a stateful deleter, placement new, alignment and exception safety

CodeBuild a Registry of named resources: open(name) returns a std::shared_ptr<Resource>; opening a name that is already open returns the same object; when the last user drops it, a custom deleter closes it and removes the entry. The registry must not keep resources alive by itself.

Answer

Approach. Store weak_ptr<Resource> values in a map, so the registry observes without owning. open tries lock(); on a miss it creates the resource with shared_ptr(new Resource, Closer{this, name}). The deleter erases the entry and deletes the resource. Because the deleter runs when the strong count is zero, the map entry is already expired and safe to erase; check that the entry is still the expired one, in case a new resource with the same name was opened in between. A single-threaded version is shown; with threads, guard the map with a mutex taken in both open and the deleter.

#include <cstdio>
#include <map>
#include <memory>
#include <string>

struct Resource {
    std::string name;
    explicit Resource(std::string n) : name(std::move(n)) { std::printf("open %s\n", name.c_str()); }
    ~Resource() { std::printf("close %s\n", name.c_str()); }
};

class Registry {
public:
    std::shared_ptr<Resource> open(const std::string& name) {
        if (auto it = live_.find(name); it != live_.end())
            if (auto sp = it->second.lock()) return sp;
        std::shared_ptr<Resource> sp(new Resource(name), Closer{this, name});
        live_[name] = sp;
        return sp;
    }
    std::size_t size() const { return live_.size(); }

private:
    struct Closer {
        Registry* reg;
        std::string name;
        void operator()(Resource* r) const noexcept {
            auto it = reg->live_.find(name);
            if (it != reg->live_.end() && it->second.expired()) reg->live_.erase(it);
            delete r;
        }
    };
    std::map<std::string, std::weak_ptr<Resource>> live_;
};

int main() {
    Registry reg;
    auto a = reg.open("db");
    auto b = reg.open("db");
    auto c = reg.open("cache");
    std::printf("same object: %d, entries %zu, db users %ld\n", a == b, reg.size(), a.use_count());
    a.reset();
    b.reset();
    std::printf("entries %zu\n", reg.size());
    auto d = reg.open("db");
    std::printf("entries %zu\n", reg.size());
}
open db
open cache
same object: 1, entries 2, db users 2
close db
entries 1
open db
entries 2
close db
close cache

Complexity and pitfalls. O(log n) per open and close. Pitfalls: storing shared_ptr in the map (nothing ever closes); Closer holding a raw Registry*, so the registry must outlive all handles (here reg is declared first, so it is destroyed last); erasing an entry that already belongs to a newer resource; locking order with threads (the deleter can run on any thread that drops the last reference, so it must take the same mutex, and open must not hold that mutex while a shared_ptr it obtained might be destroyed). Destruction order at the end: d is declared last and destroyed first, then c.

Estimated rating: ~1900 · weak_ptr cache plus a deleter that reaches back into its owner

CodeWrite your own Unique<T, D = std::default_delete<T>> with move-only semantics, get, release, reset, get_deleter and operator->. It must be 8 bytes with an empty deleter, use the store-then-delete order in reset, never call the deleter on null, and prove its size with static_assert.

Answer

Approach. Store T* p_ and [[no_unique_address]] D d_. Moves use std::exchange on the pointer and move the deleter. reset(q) exchanges the stored pointer with q and then deletes the old value if it was not null. Move assignment is reset(other.release()) plus moving the deleter.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>

template <class T, class D = std::default_delete<T>>
class Unique {
public:
    Unique() noexcept = default;
    explicit Unique(T* p) noexcept : p_(p) {}
    Unique(T* p, D d) noexcept : p_(p), d_(std::move(d)) {}
    Unique(Unique&& o) noexcept : p_(std::exchange(o.p_, nullptr)), d_(std::move(o.d_)) {}
    Unique& operator=(Unique&& o) noexcept {
        if (this != &o) {
            reset(o.release());
            d_ = std::move(o.d_);
        }
        return *this;
    }
    Unique(const Unique&) = delete;
    Unique& operator=(const Unique&) = delete;
    ~Unique() { if (p_) d_(p_); }

    T* get() const noexcept { return p_; }
    T* operator->() const noexcept { return p_; }
    T& operator*() const noexcept { return *p_; }
    explicit operator bool() const noexcept { return p_ != nullptr; }
    D& get_deleter() noexcept { return d_; }
    [[nodiscard]] T* release() noexcept { return std::exchange(p_, nullptr); }
    void reset(T* q = nullptr) noexcept {
        T* old = std::exchange(p_, q);   // store first
        if (old) d_(old);                // then delete
    }

private:
    T* p_ = nullptr;
    [[no_unique_address]] D d_{};
};

struct Loud {
    int id;
    ~Loud() { std::printf("~Loud %d\n", id); }
};
struct CountingDelete {
    int* count;
    void operator()(Loud* p) const noexcept { ++*count; delete p; }
};

static_assert(sizeof(Unique<Loud>) == sizeof(Loud*));
static_assert(sizeof(Unique<Loud, CountingDelete>) == 2 * sizeof(void*));

int main() {
    Unique<Loud> a(new Loud{1});
    Unique<Loud> b = std::move(a);
    std::printf("a %s, b holds %d\n", a ? "set" : "null", b->id);
    b.reset(new Loud{2});

    int deletes = 0;
    {
        Unique<Loud, CountingDelete> c(new Loud{3}, CountingDelete{&deletes});
        Unique<Loud, CountingDelete> d(nullptr, CountingDelete{&deletes});
        d = std::move(c);
    }
    std::printf("counted deletes: %d\n", deletes);
}
a null, b holds 1
~Loud 1
~Loud 3
counted deletes: 1
~Loud 2

Complexity and pitfalls. All operations O(1). Pitfalls: self-move-assignment (guarded); deleting before storing in reset; calling the deleter on null in the destructor (the counter shows only one delete, for the object that existed); forgetting noexcept on moves: std::vector<Unique> still compiles and still moves (move_if_noexcept uses a throwing move when there is no copy constructor), but it loses the strong exception guarantee on reallocation. The real unique_ptr also supports converting moves from Unique<Derived>, array specialisation and D::pointer.

Estimated rating: ~1700 · standard interview implementation, the EBO detail and reset order separate good answers

CodeMap an anonymous memory region with mmap and own it with std::unique_ptr<std::byte[], Unmap>, where Unmap remembers the length. Handle MAP_FAILED correctly, write and read the region, and expose the size through get_deleter().

Answer

Approach. munmap needs the address and the length, so the deleter is stateful and stores the length. Call mmap first and check for MAP_FAILED (which is (void*)-1, not null) before constructing the smart pointer; on failure return an empty pointer. Using the array form gives operator[].

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstring>
#include <memory>
#include <sys/mman.h>

static int unmaps = 0;

struct Unmap {
    std::size_t len = 0;
    void operator()(std::byte* p) const noexcept {
        ++unmaps;
        ::munmap(p, len);
    }
};
using Mapping = std::unique_ptr<std::byte[], Unmap>;

static Mapping map_anonymous(std::size_t len) {
    void* raw = ::mmap(nullptr, len, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE, MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANON, -1, 0);
    if (raw == MAP_FAILED) return Mapping(nullptr, Unmap{0});
    return Mapping(static_cast<std::byte*>(raw), Unmap{len});
}

int main() {
    Mapping m = map_anonymous(1 << 16);
    if (!m) return 1;
    std::printf("mapped %zu bytes, zero-filled: %d\n", m.get_deleter().len, m[100] == std::byte{0});
    std::memcpy(m.get(), "mapped", 7);
    std::printf("%s\n", reinterpret_cast<const char*>(m.get()));
    m[65535] = std::byte{42};
    std::printf("last byte %d\n", static_cast<int>(m[65535]));

    Mapping huge = map_anonymous(static_cast<std::size_t>(1) << 62);   // fails: too big
    std::printf("huge %s\n", huge ? "mapped" : "failed");
    m.reset();
    std::printf("unmaps %d\n", unmaps);
}
mapped 65536 bytes, zero-filled: 1
mapped
last byte 42
huge failed
unmaps 1

Complexity and pitfalls. The mapping is lazy: pages are faulted in on first touch, so "allocating" 64 KiB costs almost nothing until written. Pitfalls: passing MAP_FAILED to the smart pointer (it is non-null, so munmap((void*)-1, len) would be called); losing the length (a stateless deleter cannot unmap); MAP_ANON vs MAP_ANONYMOUS spelling (Linux has both, macOS prefers MAP_ANON); the handle is 16 bytes because of the length.

Estimated rating: ~1500 · stateful deleter plus the MAP_FAILED sentinel trap

Cheat sheet

Theory
  • unique_ptr<T, D>: deleter in the type, stored inline. Empty D (function object, captureless lambda) costs 0 bytes through EBO; a function pointer or captured state costs 8 or more.
  • Prefer struct Closer { void operator()(T*) const noexcept; };. Function pointer deleters must be passed at every construction and cannot be default-constructed.
  • shared_ptr<T>: deleter type-erased into the control block, captured at construction with the real pointer type, so shared_ptr<void> and non-virtual bases still destroy correctly. Inspect with std::get_deleter<D>.
  • Null: unique_ptr never calls the deleter on null; shared_ptr built with a deleter calls it even for nullptr. Check sentinels like MAP_FAILED and -1 yourself.
  • No deleter overloads for make_unique/make_shared; use the constructor, or allocate_shared to control the single allocation.
  • Deleters must not throw (destructors are noexcept). Close explicitly with fclose(f.release()) when you need the error.
  • PIMPL with unique_ptr<Impl>: declare the destructor and moves in the header, define them = default in the .cpp. shared_ptr does not need this.
  • Stateful deleters (pool, mmap length) add a lifetime rule: whatever they point to must outlive every handle. C++23 std::out_ptr adapts smart pointers to T** out parameters.
