Part E · Memory management · Chapter 13

Cyclic reference issues

Reference counting frees an object when nobody points to it, so two objects that point to each other are never freed. This chapter shows exactly how shared_ptr cycles form (including the hidden ones inside callbacks), how to prove a leak, and the standard ways to break a cycle: weak_ptr, raw back pointers and an ownership graph with no cycles. Interviewers ask about it because it separates people who use shared_ptr everywhere from people who design ownership.

TheoryDrillsCoding· about 3 hours· prerequisites: Ch 11 smart pointers, Ch 12 custom deleters

How a shared_ptr cycle leaks

Theory

Mental model. A shared_ptr answers one local question: "how many owners point at this object?". It never asks whether those owners are themselves reachable from the program. When object A owns B and B owns A, each count includes the other's pointer, so neither count can reach zero once the outside world lets go. The objects are unreachable, yet every count is 1. That is a leak, and their destructors never run, so any resource they hold (sockets, files, threads) leaks too.

Under the hood. Each make_shared creates a control block with a strong count (owners) and a weak count. Copying a shared_ptr increments the strong count atomically, and destroying one decrements it. The destructor of the managed object runs only when the strong count goes from 1 to 0 (Ch 11 has the full control block).

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <string>

static int alive = 0;

struct Person {
    std::string name;
    std::shared_ptr<Person> partner;
    explicit Person(std::string n) : name(std::move(n)) { ++alive; std::printf("hello %s\n", name.c_str()); }
    ~Person() { --alive; std::printf("bye %s\n", name.c_str()); }
};

int main() {
    {
        auto alice = std::make_shared<Person>("alice");
        auto bob = std::make_shared<Person>("bob");
        alice->partner = bob;
        bob->partner = alice;
        std::printf("counts: alice %ld, bob %ld\n", alice.use_count(), bob.use_count());
    }
    std::printf("after scope: %d alive\n", alive);
}
hello alice
hello bob
counts: alice 2, bob 2
after scope: 2 alive

No "bye" line is ever printed. At the closing brace the local bob is destroyed first (strong count 2 to 1), then alice (2 to 1). Both counts stop at 1, held by the other object's partner member.

Where cycles come from in real code

  • Bidirectional relationships: parent and child in a tree, prev and next in a doubly linked list, a session and its connection, a document and its views.
  • Callbacks: an object stores a std::function (a handler, a timer, a completion callback) whose lambda captured a shared_ptr to the same object. The cycle is invisible in the class definition.
  • Registries: a manager owns a list of shared_ptr<Client> and each client owns a shared_ptr<Manager> to talk back.
  • Self-ownership: an object stores shared_from_this() in one of its own members, a cycle of length one.
  • Longer rings: A to B to C to A, often created by three different teams, which is why ownership rules must be global (see the rules).

Detecting cycles

Theory

A cycle does not crash. It shows up as memory growth, files that stay open, or destructors whose side effects never happen. You need tools that make "never destroyed" visible.

Destructor printouts and instance counters

The cheapest proof is a static counter incremented in every constructor and decremented in the destructor, checked at the end of a test. It works on every platform and in release builds. Destructor printouts are the same idea for quick experiments, and they are what most interview answers use.

The weak_ptr probe

In a unit test, keep a weak_ptr to the object, drop all the strong pointers you know about, and assert that the weak_ptr has expired. If it has not, something still owns the object, and probe.use_count() tells you how many owners are left. This needs no change to the class under test.

#include <cstdio>
#include <functional>
#include <memory>

struct Widget {
    std::function<void()> on_click;
    int clicks = 0;
};

static void check(const char* label, const std::weak_ptr<Widget>& probe) {
    if (probe.expired()) std::printf("%s: freed\n", label);
    else std::printf("%s: LEAK, %ld owner(s) left\n", label, probe.use_count());
}

int main() {
    std::weak_ptr<Widget> probe;
    {
        auto w = std::make_shared<Widget>();
        w->on_click = [w] { ++w->clicks; };          // the lambda owns w, and w owns the lambda
        probe = w;
    }
    check("capture shared_ptr", probe);
    probe.lock()->on_click = nullptr;               // break the cycle by hand, so the test cleans up
    check("after clearing", probe);

    {
        auto w = std::make_shared<Widget>();
        Widget* raw = w.get();
        w->on_click = [raw] { ++raw->clicks; };      // the object owns the lambda, the lambda only observes
        probe = w;
    }
    check("capture raw pointer", probe);
}
capture shared_ptr: LEAK, 1 owner(s) left
after clearing: freed
capture raw pointer: freed

Leak detectors

  • LeakSanitizer (-fsanitize=address on Linux, or -fsanitize=leak alone) scans memory at exit and reports heap blocks that no live pointer reaches, with allocation stacks. A cycle is exactly that, so it is reported. On Linux it is on by default with ASan. On macOS, Apple's Xcode clang does not support it, but upstream LLVM clang (for example Homebrew's) does with ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=1. The harness for this guide leaves it off, which is why the drills prove leaks with counters.
  • Valgrind memcheck reports cycles as "definitely lost" or "indirectly lost" blocks, more slowly but without recompiling.
  • Heap profilers (heaptrack, jemalloc or tcmalloc profiling) show steady growth by allocation site, which is how cycles are usually found in long-running servers where the process never exits.

Tip

A leak checker only reports at exit. In a server, a cycle that forms per request is found by a test that runs the request 1000 times and checks the instance counter is back to its starting value.

Breaking cycles with weak_ptr

Theory

Mental model. A weak_ptr is a non-owning reference that knows whether its target is still alive. It increments the weak count, not the strong count, so it does not keep the object alive. To use the object you call lock(), which atomically returns a shared_ptr (owning, for as long as you hold it) or an empty one if the object is gone. Breaking a cycle means choosing one edge in each cycle and making it weak.

Which edge? Make weak the edge that points back toward the owner, that is, from the part to the whole, from the child to the parent, from the observer target to the observer, from the cache to the cached value. The rule of thumb: the weak edge must point at something that has another owner. If you make the wrong edge weak, the object you still need is destroyed immediately.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct Node {
    std::string name;
    std::weak_ptr<Node> parent;                       // observes
    std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Node>> children;      // owns
    explicit Node(std::string n) : name(std::move(n)) {}
    ~Node() { std::printf("~%s\n", name.c_str()); }
};

static std::shared_ptr<Node> add_child(const std::shared_ptr<Node>& parent, std::string name) {
    auto c = std::make_shared<Node>(std::move(name));
    c->parent = parent;
    parent->children.push_back(c);
    return c;
}

int main() {
    auto root = std::make_shared<Node>("root");
    auto usr = add_child(root, "usr");
    auto bin = add_child(usr, "bin");

    std::string path;
    for (auto n = bin; n; n = n->parent.lock()) path = "/" + n->name + path;
    std::printf("%s\n", path.c_str());
    std::printf("root %ld owner(s), usr %ld owner(s)\n", root.use_count(), usr.use_count());

    usr.reset();
    bin.reset();
    std::puts("dropping root");
    root.reset();
}
/root/usr/bin
root 1 owner(s), usr 2 owner(s)
dropping root
~root
~usr
~bin

The destructor body of root runs first, then its members are destroyed, which destroys usr, whose members destroy bin. The parent links never contribute to a count.

Doubly linked lists

Same rule: next owns, prev observes. The list owns head, every node owns its successor, and tail is a weak_ptr or raw pointer.

template <class T>
struct DNode {
    T value;
    std::shared_ptr<DNode> next;   // owning
    std::weak_ptr<DNode> prev;     // breaks the next/prev cycle
};

Two practical notes. First, a long owning chain is destroyed recursively (each node's destructor destroys next), so a list of a million nodes can overflow the stack; write an iterative clear(). Second, weak_ptr::lock() on every backward step costs two atomic operations; if the list owns all nodes, a raw prev pointer is just as safe and much cheaper (next section).

What weak_ptr costs

  • Size: 16 bytes, the same as shared_ptr (object pointer and control block pointer).
  • lock(): an atomic compare-and-swap loop on the strong count (it must not resurrect an object whose count already hit 0), then an atomic decrement when the returned shared_ptr dies.
  • Memory: the control block stays allocated until the weak count also reaches 0. With make_shared the object and control block are one allocation, so a long-lived weak_ptr keeps the whole block (including the dead object's bytes) allocated, although the destructor has already run. With shared_ptr<T>(new T) only the small control block stays.

Raw non-owning back pointers

Theory

Mental model. A back pointer needs to be a weak_ptr only if the target can die while the pointer still exists. If the structure guarantees that a child never outlives its parent, the parent link can be a plain T* (or T&): it is 8 bytes, needs no atomics and no lock(). The guarantee usually comes from unique_ptr ownership: the parent owns its children exclusively, nobody else holds an owning pointer to a child, so a child exists only inside its parent.

struct Node {
    Node* parent = nullptr;                          // valid for the child's whole life
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Node>> children;     // exclusive ownership

    Node& add_child() {
        auto c = std::make_unique<Node>();
        c->parent = this;
        children.push_back(std::move(c));
        return *children.back();
    }
};
Back edgeSafe whenCost per accessFailure mode
weak_ptr<T>always; target may die firstlock(): 2 atomic opsreturns null, which you must handle
T* / T&target is guaranteed to outlive the pointernonedangling pointer, use-after-free if the guarantee breaks
shared_ptr<T>never for a back edgecopy: 1 atomic opcycle, leak
index or id into a containertarget stored in a stable containera lookupstale id, detectable with generation counters

Interview trap

The raw back pointer breaks silently when ownership changes. If someone later hands out shared_ptr<Node> to children (for example to return them from an API), a child can outlive its parent, and child->parent dangles. Write the lifetime assumption down in a comment, or use weak_ptr whenever ownership is shared.

Moving the parent object is another trap. If Node objects live in a std::vector<Node> and the vector reallocates, every parent pointer to them dangles. Owning children through unique_ptr (stable heap addresses) avoids that.

Observers and caches

Theory

The observer pattern

A subject that stores shared_ptr<Observer> keeps every observer alive forever, and if the observer also holds the subject, you have a cycle. Storing raw Observer* instead means an observer that dies without unsubscribing leaves a dangling pointer, a classic crash. Storing weak_ptr<Observer> fixes both: the subject does not own its observers, and on each notification it locks each entry, calls live observers and erases expired ones.

void notify(const Event& e) {
    std::erase_if(observers_, [&](const std::weak_ptr<Observer>& w) {
        if (auto o = w.lock()) { o->on_event(e); return false; }
        return true;                                    // expired: drop it
    });
}

Locking before the call matters: the observer cannot be destroyed in the middle of on_event, even if another thread drops the last external owner. Be aware that an observer that unsubscribes (modifies observers_) from inside its own callback invalidates the iteration; real implementations copy the list, or mark entries and erase after the loop.

Caches of shared objects

A cache that stores shared_ptr<Texture> never frees anything. A cache that stores weak_ptr<Texture> returns the existing object while someone uses it and lets it die when the last user drops it. This "weak cache" or flyweight is common for fonts, compiled shaders, DNS results and parsed configs. Expired entries remain in the map until you purge them (on lookup, periodically, or from a custom deleter as in Ch 12), otherwise the map itself grows without bound.

Callbacks, enable_shared_from_this and capturing self

Theory

Mental model. A lambda's captures are members of its closure object. A std::function that holds the closure owns those members. So obj->handler = [self = obj] { ... }; stores, inside obj, an object that owns obj. The cycle runs through a type that does not mention shared_ptr at all.

enable_shared_from_this

A member function sometimes needs a shared_ptr to its own object, for example to register itself with an event loop. shared_ptr<T>(this) would create a second control block and a double delete. Instead, inherit publicly from std::enable_shared_from_this<T>. The base contains a mutable weak_ptr<T>; when a shared_ptr constructor (or make_shared) takes ownership of an object with an unambiguous, accessible enable_shared_from_this base, it stores a weak reference to itself there. shared_from_this() then just locks that member.

  • Since C++17, shared_from_this() throws std::bad_weak_ptr if the object is not owned by any shared_ptr (a stack object, a unique_ptr, or inside the constructor, before ownership exists). Before C++17 it was undefined behaviour.
  • C++17 weak_from_this() returns the stored weak_ptr, which is empty in those cases, without throwing.
  • The base must be public. With private inheritance the shared_ptr constructor cannot see it, the weak member stays empty and shared_from_this() throws.
  • Inside the destructor the strong count is already 0, so shared_from_this() throws and weak_from_this().lock() is empty.

Which capture to use in a callback

Who stores the callbackCaptureWhy
The object itself (a member std::function)thisthe callback cannot outlive the object that owns it; capturing shared_from_this() is a cycle
Someone else, and the object may die first (timer queue, event bus, UI)w = weak_from_this(), then if (auto self = w.lock())no ownership, no dangling; a dead object's callback becomes a no-op
Someone else, and the operation must keep the object alive until it completes (async read, Asio handler)self = shared_from_this()intentional, temporary ownership; the cycle ends when the one-shot handler runs and is destroyed
Someone else, forever (periodic timer owned by the object)never shared_from_this()the handler is never destroyed, so the object is never destroyed
#include <cstdio>
#include <functional>
#include <memory>
#include <vector>

static std::vector<std::function<void()>> timer_queue;   // stands in for an event loop

struct Session : std::enable_shared_from_this<Session> {
    int id;
    explicit Session(int i) : id(i) {}
    ~Session() { std::printf("~Session %d\n", id); }
    void schedule_ping() {
        timer_queue.push_back([w = weak_from_this()] {
            if (auto self = w.lock()) std::printf("ping %d\n", self->id);
            else std::puts("ping skipped: session gone");
        });
    }
};

int main() {
    auto a = std::make_shared<Session>(1);
    auto b = std::make_shared<Session>(2);
    a->schedule_ping();
    b->schedule_ping();
    b.reset();                       // b dies now: the queue does not own it
    for (auto& f : timer_queue) f();
    timer_queue.clear();
    std::puts("end of main");
}
~Session 2
ping 1
ping skipped: session gone
end of main
~Session 1

Capturing this here would be a use-after-free for session 2, and capturing shared_from_this() would have kept session 2 alive until the queue ran. Neither is a cycle, but only the weak capture matches the intent "ping if still connected".

Why reference counting cannot collect cycles

Theory

Mental model. Garbage is defined globally: an object is garbage if no chain of pointers leads to it from a root (stack slots, registers, globals). A reference count is purely local: the number of pointers into the object. Every object in an unreachable cycle has a non-zero count that comes from inside the cycle, so local information cannot distinguish "kept alive by the program" from "kept alive by garbage". Detecting cycles needs a global traversal from the roots, which is what a tracing collector does.

C++ cannot bolt a tracing collector onto shared_ptr, because the runtime does not know where the roots are (any word on the stack might be a pointer, pointers can be hidden in integers or unions) and because destructors must run deterministically. C++11 even had minimal "garbage collection support" APIs (std::declare_reachable and friends), which no implementation used, and C++23 removed them.

Language or runtimeStrategyCyclesDestruction timing
C++ shared_ptratomic reference countingleak; break with weak_ptr or designdeterministic, at the last release
Rust Rc/Arcreference countingleak (safe, but a leak); break with Weakdeterministic
Swift, Objective-C ARCcompiler-inserted reference countingleak; weak and unowned references, [weak self] in closuresdeterministic
CPythonreference counting plus a generational cycle detector (gc module)collected by the detector, which finds groups whose counts are fully explained by internal referencesimmediate for acyclic objects, delayed for cycles
Java, Go, C#, JavaScripttracing garbage collection from rootscollectednondeterministic; finalisers are unreliable, so resources use try-with-resources, defer, using

The trade-off is the interview point. Reference counting gives deterministic destruction, which is what makes RAII work for files, locks and sockets, and it spreads cost evenly (no pauses). The price is that cycles are the programmer's job. Tracing GC handles cycles and is often faster in throughput, but it cannot tell you when a resource is released.

weak_ptr and threads: lock races

Theory

Mental model. The control block's counts are atomic, so different shared_ptr and weak_ptr objects that share one control block can be copied, locked and destroyed from different threads safely. What is not safe is a check followed by a separate use.

if (!w.expired()) w.lock()->refresh();   // BUG: may dereference null
if (auto sp = w.lock()) sp->refresh();   // correct: one atomic step, then you own it

Between expired() returning false and lock(), another thread can drop the last owner, so lock() returns an empty pointer. lock() itself is atomic: it increments the strong count only if it is still non-zero, so it never resurrects a dying object. For the same reason, use_count() is only a hint in multithreaded code; C++20 removed shared_ptr::unique() because it suggested otherwise.

#include <atomic>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <thread>

struct Config { int version; };

int main() {
    auto owner = std::make_shared<Config>(Config{1});
    std::weak_ptr<Config> w = owner;
    std::atomic<bool> go{false};
    int alive_hits = 0, null_hits = 0;

    std::thread reader([w, &go, &alive_hits, &null_hits] {   // the thread has its own copy of w
        while (!go.load()) {}
        for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) {
            if (auto sp = w.lock()) alive_hits += (sp->version == 1);
            else ++null_hits;
        }
    });
    go = true;
    owner.reset();                    // races with lock(), and that is fine
    reader.join();
    std::printf("every lock() saw a live object or null: %d\n", alive_hits + null_hits == 100000);
}
every lock() saw a live object or null: 1

The split between alive_hits and null_hits depends on timing, so the program prints only the invariant. What would be a data race is two threads using the same shared_ptr or weak_ptr object while one of them modifies it (assigns, resets). For that, protect the pointer object with a mutex or use C++20 std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>> and std::atomic<std::weak_ptr<T>> (available in libstdc++ since GCC 12; libc++ as of LLVM 22 does not provide it yet).

Know this cold

Locking a weak_ptr is the only correct way to use it: if (auto sp = w.lock()). Never test expired() and then use. expired() is useful only as a cheap "definitely dead" check, for example to purge cache entries.

Ownership design rules

Theory

Mental model. Draw every owning pointer as an arrow. If the arrows form a directed acyclic graph (DAG), reference counting frees everything: when the roots go, counts cascade to zero in topological order. A cycle anywhere in the owning graph is a leak waiting to happen. All the techniques in this chapter are ways to keep that graph acyclic.

  1. Give every object one clear owner by default. Use values and unique_ptr. Reach for shared_ptr only when the lifetime is genuinely shared and not known statically (an object used by several asynchronous operations, a cache entry). Exclusive ownership cannot form a shared_ptr cycle.
  2. Keep the owning graph a DAG. Owners point down, from the whole to the parts. Anything pointing up or sideways is non-owning: weak_ptr if the target can die first, a raw pointer or reference if it cannot.
  3. Treat captures as edges. A lambda stored in an object or in something the object owns must not capture a shared_ptr to the object. Review [self = shared_from_this()] in code review the way you review new.
  4. Prefer explicit teardown for graphs that really are cyclic. Some domains (graph editors, object graphs loaded from files) have arbitrary cycles. Store all nodes in an owning container (a vector<unique_ptr<Node>> or an arena, Ch 17), and let edges be raw pointers or indices. The container frees everything at once.
  5. Test for leaks. A weak probe or an instance counter in unit tests catches the cycle that someone adds next year.
Key facts
Destructor runs whenstrong count reaches 0 (weak count irrelevant)
Control block freed whenstrong and weak counts both reach 0
make_shared memory with a live weak_ptrwhole block stays allocated until the last weak_ptr goes
weak_ptr::lock()atomic; returns empty if the object is dead; never resurrects
shared_from_this() without an ownerthrows std::bad_weak_ptr (C++17), UB before
weak_from_this()C++17; empty weak_ptr instead of a throw
Can unique_ptr leak through a cycle?yes, if you build an ownership ring by hand (A owns B owns A)
LeakSanitizerfinds cycles at exit; default with ASan on Linux; on macOS only with upstream clang and detect_leaks=1

Concept and tricky questions

Drills

ConceptExplain precisely why two objects that hold shared_ptrs to each other are never destroyed.

Answer

Answer. Each object's strong count includes the pointer stored in the other object. When all outside pointers are gone, both counts are still 1, and the destructor runs only when a count reaches 0. Since the destructor of A is what would release A's pointer to B (and vice versa), neither can start.

Why. Reference counting decides liveness locally, from the number of incoming owning pointers, not from reachability. An unreachable cycle has non-zero counts that are all internal. "The memory is freed at program exit" is not an answer: destructors still never run, so files are not flushed and sockets are not closed in an orderly way, and in a long-running server the leak grows per request.

TrickyA Parent owns a shared_ptr<Child> and the child owns a shared_ptr<Parent>. Your colleague breaks the cycle by making the Parent::child member a weak_ptr. Does it leak? Is it correct?

Answer

Answer. It no longer leaks, but it is wrong: if nothing else owns the child, the child is destroyed as soon as it is created, and parent->child.lock() returns null. Make the child-to-parent edge weak instead.

Why. Any weak edge in the cycle stops the leak, but a weak_ptr only works if the target has another owner. The child's only owner is the parent, so that edge must be owning. The parent has another owner (whoever created the tree), so the child can observe it weakly. The rule: weak edges point back toward the owner.

TrickyCan you leak memory through a cycle with only unique_ptr?

Answer

Answer. Yes. If A's unique_ptr member owns B and you then move ownership of A into B's member, A and B own each other and no outside pointer owns either. Both leak. A circular singly linked list built with unique_ptr<Node> next is the usual way it happens.

Why. unique_ptr guarantees one owner per object, not an acyclic ownership graph. "Unique ownership cannot cycle" is the common wrong answer. It is harder to do by accident than with shared_ptr, because you must explicitly move the last outside owner into the ring, and the reading drills include it.

ConceptWhat does weak_ptr::lock() do, and why can't you dereference a weak_ptr directly?

Answer

Answer. lock() atomically increments the strong count if it is non-zero and returns a shared_ptr that owns the object; if the count is already 0, it returns an empty shared_ptr. weak_ptr has no operator* or operator->.

Why. A direct dereference could not guarantee the object stays alive during the access: another thread might drop the last owner in the middle. Forcing you through lock() makes you hold an owner for exactly as long as you use the object. Internally lock() is a CAS loop, since a plain increment could revive an object whose count already hit zero.

TrickyAn object is created with make_shared. Its last shared_ptr is gone, but a weak_ptr to it lives on in a cache for hours. Has the object's memory been freed? Has its destructor run?

Answer

Answer. The destructor has run, but the memory has not been freed. The object's storage is inside the same allocation as the control block, and the control block must live until the weak count reaches 0.

Why. make_shared does one allocation for counts plus object. The strong count reaching 0 calls the destructor; the weak count reaching 0 frees the block. For a large object (say a 1 MB buffer member stored inline) a lingering weak_ptr keeps the whole 1 MB allocated. shared_ptr<T>(new T) frees the object at strong count 0 and keeps only the small control block. Many candidates think a weak_ptr holds nothing at all.

ConceptHow does enable_shared_from_this work internally?

Answer

Answer. The base class holds a mutable weak_ptr<T>. When a shared_ptr takes ownership of a raw pointer (or make_shared creates the object), its constructor checks at compile time whether T has an unambiguous, accessible enable_shared_from_this base, and if so assigns itself to that weak_ptr. shared_from_this() returns shared_ptr<T>(weak_this), which throws if expired.

Why. This lets a member function get a shared_ptr that shares the existing control block, instead of creating a second one with shared_ptr<T>(this), which would delete the object twice. It also explains its limits: the weak member is filled only after the constructor finishes and only if inheritance is public.

TrickyTo fix the alice/bob cycle, a colleague adds ~Person() { partner.reset(); }. Does that stop the leak?

Answer

Answer. No. The destructor is exactly the code that never runs. It would run only when a strong count reaches 0, and the cycle is what keeps both counts at 1. Adding a reset to it changes nothing, and the program still prints no "bye" lines.

Why. Breaking a cycle must happen either from outside while an external owner still exists (an explicit close() or unlink() that resets partner before the last outside shared_ptr goes), or structurally, by making one edge a weak_ptr. The explicit teardown works but relies on every caller remembering it on every path, including exceptions, so the structural fix is preferred. The same mistake appears as "reset the callbacks in the destructor" for a std::function that captured shared_from_this(). Many candidates suggest the destructor reset because it is how you would release resources in ordinary RAII code.

TrickyA Parent owns its Child through unique_ptr. The child needs the parent's settings, so the parent gives it std::shared_ptr<const Settings>(self, &self->settings), where self is the parent's own shared_ptr. No type in Child mentions Parent. Is there a cycle?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct Settings { int level = 3; };
struct Child { std::shared_ptr<const Settings> settings; };

struct Parent {
    Settings settings;
    std::unique_ptr<Child> child;
    ~Parent() { std::puts("~Parent"); }
};

int main() {
    std::weak_ptr<Parent> probe;
    {
        auto p = std::make_shared<Parent>();
        p->child = std::make_unique<Child>();
        p->child->settings = std::shared_ptr<const Settings>(p, &p->settings);   // aliasing constructor
        probe = p;
        std::printf("parent owners %ld\n", p.use_count());
    }
    std::printf("after scope: expired %d, owners %ld\n", probe.expired(), probe.use_count());
}
Answer
parent owners 2
after scope: expired 0, owners 1

Answer. Yes, and the parent leaks. The aliasing constructor creates a shared_ptr that points to the Settings member but shares ownership of the whole Parent (same control block). So the parent owns the child, and the child owns the parent. ~Parent never prints.

Why. An owning edge is defined by the control block a pointer shares, not by its element type. That makes aliasing pointers the hardest cycles to spot in review. Fixes: give the child a std::weak_ptr<const Settings> made from the aliasing pointer (it observes the parent's block), a plain const Settings* (the parent outlives its exclusively owned child), or a copy of the settings. The common wrong answer is "no cycle, it is only a pointer to Settings".

ConceptWhen is a raw pointer a better back pointer than a weak_ptr?

Answer

Answer. When the structure guarantees that the target outlives the pointer, typically when the parent owns its children exclusively with unique_ptr (or by value in a node container with stable addresses). Then child->parent can never dangle, and a raw pointer is cheaper: 8 bytes, no atomics, no null check after lock().

Why. weak_ptr exists to handle "the target might be gone". If that is impossible by construction, it adds cost and suggests a lifetime uncertainty that does not exist. The risk is future changes: as soon as children can be shared outside the parent, the guarantee is gone and the raw pointer becomes a use-after-free.

TrickyA class stores a std::function<void()> on_timeout and sets it to a lambda that captures this. Is that a cycle? What if it captures shared_from_this()?

Answer

Answer. Capturing this is not a cycle and is safe as long as only the object itself invokes on_timeout: the closure cannot outlive the object that owns it. Capturing shared_from_this() is a cycle: object owns function owns closure owns object, so it leaks.

Why. Raw this is a non-owning edge, so it adds nothing to any count. The danger with this appears only when a copy of the callback is handed to someone else (a timer queue, another thread) that may call it after the object died; then use weak_from_this(). Many candidates say "always capture shared_from_this() to be safe", which is the leak.

ConceptWhy can a tracing garbage collector free a cycle when reference counting cannot? How does CPython deal with cycles?

Answer

Answer. A tracing collector marks everything reachable from the roots (stacks, registers, globals) and frees the rest, so an unreachable cycle is simply never marked. Reference counting only knows incoming pointer counts. CPython uses reference counting plus a periodic cycle detector: for container objects it subtracts references that come from other tracked objects, and any group whose count is fully explained by internal references is unreachable garbage.

Why. Reachability is a global property and counts are local. C++ chooses local counting because it gives deterministic destruction (RAII) and needs no knowledge of roots, which C++ cannot provide precisely. The price is that cycle avoidance is a design responsibility, handled with weak_ptr, raw back pointers or owning containers.

ConceptIn the observer pattern, why store weak_ptr<Observer> in the subject rather than shared_ptr or a raw pointer?

Answer

Answer. shared_ptr makes the subject keep every observer alive (and forms a cycle if the observer holds the subject). A raw pointer dangles when an observer is destroyed without unsubscribing. A weak_ptr does neither: the subject locks each observer during notify, calls the live ones and erases the expired ones.

Why. Subscription is not ownership. Locking also protects the call: while on_event runs, the subject holds a temporary owner, so the observer cannot be destroyed mid-call by another thread. The cost is two atomic operations per observer per notification, which is usually negligible next to the callback.

TrickyIn an Asio-style server every handler captures self = shared_from_this(). Isn't that a cycle? Why doesn't it leak?

Answer

Answer. It is a temporary ownership edge, not a permanent cycle. The handler is owned by the I/O service (not by the session), runs once and is then destroyed, which releases self. When the last pending operation completes without starting a new one, the session's count drops to 0 and it is destroyed. That is the intended "keep alive while an operation is in flight" pattern.

Why. A leak needs the closure to be owned, directly or indirectly, by the object it captures, and never released. If the session stored a copy of the handler in a member (or a periodic timer it owns re-arms forever with self), the edge would become permanent and leak. The usual way to stop such a session is to close its socket, so the pending operations complete with an error and do not re-arm.

Predict the output and find the bug

Drills

OutputFollow the counts. What does this print?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct B;
struct A { std::shared_ptr<B> b; ~A() { std::puts("~A"); } };
struct B { std::shared_ptr<A> a; ~B() { std::puts("~B"); } };

int main() {
    std::weak_ptr<A> wa;
    std::weak_ptr<B> wb;
    {
        auto a = std::make_shared<A>();
        auto b = std::make_shared<B>();
        wa = a;
        wb = b;
        a->b = b;
        std::printf("%ld %ld\n", a.use_count(), b.use_count());
        b->a = a;
        std::printf("%ld %ld\n", a.use_count(), b.use_count());
    }
    std::printf("%ld %ld\n", wa.use_count(), wb.use_count());
    wa.lock()->b.reset();
    std::printf("%ld %ld\n", wa.use_count(), wb.use_count());
}
Answer
1 2
2 2
1 1
~B
~A
0 0

Answer. After the scope both counts are 1 (the cycle). wa.lock() creates a temporary owner of A (count 2). Resetting A::b drops B to 0, so ~B runs, and destroying B's member a drops A to 1. At the end of the full expression the temporary from lock() dies, A drops to 0 and ~A runs.

Why. weak_ptr::use_count() reports the strong count, not the weak count. The temporary shared_ptr returned by lock() lives until the semicolon, which is why ~A comes after ~B and not in the middle. Breaking any one edge of a cycle lets the whole cycle cascade.

Find the bugA doubly linked list reports that its nodes are still alive after the list is destroyed. Why?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

static int live_nodes = 0;

struct Node {
    int value;
    std::shared_ptr<Node> next;
    std::shared_ptr<Node> prev;
    explicit Node(int v) : value(v) { ++live_nodes; }
    ~Node() { --live_nodes; }
};

struct List {
    std::shared_ptr<Node> head, tail;
    void push_back(int v) {
        auto n = std::make_shared<Node>(v);
        if (!head) { head = tail = n; return; }
        n->prev = tail;
        tail->next = n;
        tail = n;
    }
};

int main() {
    {
        List l;
        for (int i = 0; i < 5; ++i) l.push_back(i);
        std::printf("live inside: %d\n", live_nodes);
    }
    std::printf("live after the list is gone: %d\n", live_nodes);
}
Answer
live inside: 5
live after the list is gone: 5

Answer. Every adjacent pair of nodes owns each other through next and prev, so the list is a chain of cycles. When head and tail are released, every node still has count at least 1. Fix: make prev (and the list's tail) a weak_ptr or a raw Node*.

Why. With prev weak, the owning graph is a single chain from head, and dropping head cascades down the list. Note that the cascade is recursive (each destructor destroys next), so for very long lists add an iterative clear(). LeakSanitizer on Linux would report all five nodes; the counter proves it here.

Find the bugThis timer callback crashes intermittently in production. What is wrong?

#include <cstdio>
#include <functional>
#include <memory>
#include <vector>

struct EventLoop {
    std::vector<std::function<void()>> pending;
    void post(std::function<void()> f) { pending.push_back(std::move(f)); }
    void run() { for (auto& f : pending) f(); pending.clear(); }
};

struct Session {
    int bytes_sent = 0;
    void start(EventLoop& loop) {
        loop.post([this] { bytes_sent += 100; std::printf("sent %d\n", bytes_sent); });
    }
};

int main() {
    EventLoop loop;
    auto s = std::make_unique<Session>();
    s->start(loop);
    s.reset();          // client disconnected before the loop ran
    loop.run();
}
Answer

Answer. The callback captured raw this, and the event loop (not the session) owns the callback. The session is destroyed before the loop runs, so the callback writes to freed memory: heap-use-after-free, which ASan reports.

Why. A raw capture is safe only when the object owns the callback. Here the callback is stored by someone else and may run later. Fix: own the session with shared_ptr, inherit enable_shared_from_this, capture w = weak_from_this() and lock() inside, or capture shared_from_this() if the operation must keep the session alive until it runs. Capturing shared_from_this() is not a cycle here because the loop, not the session, owns the closure.

OutputWhat does each shared_from_this call do?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct W : std::enable_shared_from_this<W> {
    W() {
        try {
            auto self = shared_from_this();
            (void)self;
            std::puts("ctor: got a shared_ptr");
        } catch (const std::bad_weak_ptr&) {
            std::puts("ctor: bad_weak_ptr");
        }
    }
};

int main() {
    auto p = std::make_shared<W>();
    auto q = p->shared_from_this();
    std::printf("use_count %ld\n", p.use_count());

    W on_stack;
    try {
        auto r = on_stack.shared_from_this();
        (void)r;
    } catch (const std::bad_weak_ptr&) {
        std::puts("stack: bad_weak_ptr");
    }
    std::printf("weak_from_this expired: %d\n", on_stack.weak_from_this().expired());
}
Answer
ctor: bad_weak_ptr
use_count 2
ctor: bad_weak_ptr
stack: bad_weak_ptr
weak_from_this expired: 1

Answer. Inside the constructor nothing owns the object yet, so both constructions print bad_weak_ptr. After make_shared returns, shared_from_this() shares the existing control block (count 2). The stack object is never owned, so it throws, and its weak_from_this() is empty.

Why. The internal weak_ptr in enable_shared_from_this is assigned by the owning shared_ptr after the object has been fully constructed. C++17 specifies the throw; before C++17 these calls were undefined behaviour.

Find the bugA developer needed a shared_ptr to the current object inside a member function and did not want to change the base classes. What happens?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <vector>

struct Job;
static std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Job>> registry;

struct Job {
    int id;
    explicit Job(int i) : id(i) {}
    void enqueue() { registry.push_back(std::shared_ptr<Job>(this)); }
};

int main() {
    auto job = std::make_shared<Job>(7);
    job->enqueue();
    std::printf("registered %zu job(s)\n", registry.size());
    registry.clear();
    std::printf("job id %d\n", job->id);
}
Answer

Answer. shared_ptr<Job>(this) creates a second, independent control block for an object that is already owned. When registry is cleared, that control block's count reaches 0 and it deletes the job, while job still points to it. The next line reads freed memory, and at the end the original owner destroys the object again. Under ASan the first error is an invalid free ("attempting free on address which was not malloc()-ed"): the object lives inside make_shared's combined block, so its address was never returned by new.

Why. Constructing a shared_ptr from a raw pointer always means "I am the first owner". Inherit from enable_shared_from_this<Job> and use shared_from_this(), which shares the existing control block. If the registry should not keep jobs alive, store weak_from_this() instead.

Find the bugA tree uses raw parent pointers. The code that prints a node's parent crashes. Why?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct Node {
    std::string name;
    Node* parent = nullptr;
    std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Node>> children;
    explicit Node(std::string n) : name(std::move(n)) {}
};

static std::shared_ptr<Node> add(Node& parent, std::string name) {
    auto c = std::make_shared<Node>(std::move(name));
    c->parent = &parent;
    parent.children.push_back(c);
    return c;
}

int main() {
    std::shared_ptr<Node> keep;
    {
        auto root = std::make_shared<Node>("root, with a name long enough to live on the heap");
        keep = add(*root, "leaf");
    }
    std::printf("leaf's parent is %s\n", keep->parent->name.c_str());
}
Answer

Answer. The children are shared, so keep can (and does) outlive the root. When root goes out of scope the root node is destroyed, and keep->parent dangles: heap-use-after-free.

Why. A raw back pointer is valid only if the parent is guaranteed to outlive the child. That holds when the parent owns its children exclusively (unique_ptr), and fails once children are handed out as shared_ptr. Fix: make parent a weak_ptr<Node> and check lock(), or keep exclusive ownership.

OutputA ring built from unique_ptr. How many nodes are alive at the end?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

static int alive = 0;

struct Node {
    std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
    Node() { ++alive; }
    ~Node() { --alive; }
};

int main() {
    {
        auto a = std::make_unique<Node>();
        a->next = std::make_unique<Node>();
        a->next->next = std::make_unique<Node>();
        Node* last = a->next->next.get();
        last->next = std::move(a);      // close the ring
        std::printf("a is %s\n", a ? "set" : "null");
    }
    std::printf("alive: %d\n", alive);
}
Answer
a is null
alive: 3

Answer. All three nodes leak. After the move, the first node is owned by the last node, which is owned by the second, which is owned by the first. The local a is null, so nothing outside the ring owns any of them.

Why. unique_ptr guarantees a single owner per object, which the ring satisfies. It does not guarantee the ownership graph is acyclic. The same structure with shared_ptr would also leak. Circular lists need a non-owning link somewhere, or an owning container for all nodes.

    int total = 0;
    Widget() { ++widgets; }
    ~Widget() { --widgets; std::puts("~Widget"); }
    void add_logging() {
        auto self = shared_from_this();
        handlers.push_back([self](int v) { self->total += v; });
    }
    void fire(int v) { for (auto& h : handlers) h(v); }
};

int main() {
    {
        auto w = std::make_shared<Widget>();
        w->add_logging();

    }
    std::printf("widgets alive: %d\n", widgets);
}

total 5, use_count 2
widgets alive: 1

Answer. The handler lambda captures self, a shared_ptr to the widget, and the widget stores the handler in its own handlers vector. Widget owns closure owns widget, so the count never drops below 1 and ~Widget never prints. Fix: capture this (the widget owns the handler, so it cannot outlive the widget), or weak_from_this() if handlers can be copied out.

Why. use_count 2 is the giveaway: one owner is w, the other is hidden inside a std::function. Cycles through captures do not show up in the class definition, which is why reviewers should treat [self = shared_from_this()] in a stored callback as a red flag.

OutputWhen does the destructor run relative to the weak pointer's lifetime?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct Big {
    char payload[4096];
    ~Big() { std::puts("~Big"); }
};

int main() {
    std::weak_ptr<Big> w;
    {
        auto sp = std::make_shared<Big>();
        w = sp;
        std::printf("inside: expired %d, use_count %ld\n", w.expired(), w.use_count());
    }
    std::printf("outside: expired %d, use_count %ld\n", w.expired(), w.use_count());
    auto again = w.lock();
    std::printf("lock gave %s\n", again ? "an object" : "null");
    w.reset();
    std::puts("weak reset: now the 4 KiB block is freed");

Answer
inside: expired 0, use_count 1
~Big
outside: expired 1, use_count 0
lock gave null
weak reset: now the 4 KiB block is freed

Answer. ~Big runs at the end of the inner scope, when the strong count reaches 0, even though w still exists. After that w is expired and lock() returns null. The allocation (control block plus the 4 KiB payload, since it came from make_shared) is freed only when w is reset.

Why. Destruction is driven by the strong count, deallocation by both counts. A weak_ptr cannot keep an object alive and cannot revive it. The last line is a comment about memory, not something the program can observe without a custom allocator.

#include <cstdio>
#include <map>
#include <memory>
#include <string>

struct Glyph { int code; };

struct GlyphCache {
    std::map<int, std::weak_ptr<Glyph>> entries;
    std::shared_ptr<Glyph> get(int code) {
        auto& slot = entries[code];
        if (auto sp = slot.lock()) return sp;
        auto sp = std::make_shared<Glyph>(Glyph{code});
        slot = sp;
        return sp;
    }
};

int main() {
    GlyphCache cache;
    long used = 0;
    for (int code = 0; code < 1000; ++code) used += cache.get(code)->code;   // each glyph used once
    std::size_t expired = 0;
    for (auto& [code, w] : cache.entries) expired += w.expired();
    std::printf("entries %zu, expired %zu, sum %ld\n", cache.entries.size(), expired, used);
}
Answer
entries 1000, expired 1000, sum 499500

Answer. The glyphs themselves are destroyed, but every expired weak_ptr stays in the map, and each one pins its control block, which (because of make_shared) also contains the dead glyph's storage. The map grows with every distinct key. Fix: purge expired entries (on lookup misses, periodically, or from a custom deleter that erases the key).

Why. weak_ptr solves ownership, not eviction. A cache keyed by an unbounded set of keys needs a removal policy regardless of how the values are held.

Coding

CodeImplement a tree of named nodes with shared ownership of children and weak_ptr parents. Provide add_child(parent, name), path(node) (from the root, separated by /), depth(node) and detach(node), which removes a node (and its subtree) from its parent. Prove with an instance counter that detached subtrees are freed once no one else holds them, and that dropping the root frees everything.

Answer

Approach. Each node owns vector<shared_ptr<Node>> children and observes weak_ptr<Node> parent. path and depth walk up with lock(). detach locks the parent, erases the child from the parent's vector (comparing raw addresses) and resets the child's parent link. Freeing then follows automatically from the counts.

#include <algorithm>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

static int live = 0;

struct Node {
    std::string name;
    std::weak_ptr<Node> parent;
    std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Node>> children;
    explicit Node(std::string n) : name(std::move(n)) { ++live; }
    ~Node() { --live; }
};
using NodePtr = std::shared_ptr<Node>;

static NodePtr add_child(const NodePtr& parent, std::string name) {
    auto c = std::make_shared<Node>(std::move(name));
    c->parent = parent;
    parent->children.push_back(c);
    return c;
}

static std::string path(NodePtr n) {
    std::string out;
    for (; n; n = n->parent.lock()) out = "/" + n->name + out;
    return out;
}

static int depth(const NodePtr& n) {
    int d = 0;
    for (auto p = n->parent.lock(); p; p = p->parent.lock()) ++d;
    return d;
}

static void detach(const NodePtr& n) {
    if (auto p = n->parent.lock()) {
        auto& v = p->children;
        v.erase(std::remove_if(v.begin(), v.end(), [&](const NodePtr& c) { return c.get() == n.get(); }), v.end());
    }
    n->parent.reset();
}

int main() {
    auto root = std::make_shared<Node>("root");
    auto home = add_child(root, "home");
    auto ana = add_child(home, "ana");
    add_child(ana, "notes");
    add_child(root, "tmp");
    std::printf("%s depth %d, live %d\n", path(ana).c_str(), depth(ana), live);

    detach(home);
    std::printf("after detach: %s, root children %zu, live %d\n", path(ana).c_str(), root->children.size(), live);
    home.reset();
    std::printf("ana still held: live %d\n", live);
    ana.reset();
    std::printf("subtree released: live %d\n", live);
    root.reset();
    std::printf("all released: live %d\n", live);
}
/root/home/ana depth 2, live 5
after detach: /home/ana, root children 1, live 5
ana still held: live 4
subtree released: live 2
all released: live 0

Complexity and pitfalls. path and depth are O(depth) with two atomics per step; detach is O(siblings). After home.reset() the home node is freed (live 4), but ana survives because the local variable owns it, and its parent link is now expired, which is exactly what weak_ptr is for. Pitfalls: a shared_ptr parent (cycle), forgetting to reset the parent link on detach, recursion depth on destruction of very deep trees.

CodeWrite DList<T>, a doubly linked list with shared_ptr forward links and weak_ptr backward links. Support push_back, push_front, pop_back, forward and backward traversal, and a destructor that frees 200000 nodes without recursing (no stack overflow). Count live nodes to prove nothing leaks.

Answer

Approach. head is the only outside owner; next owns and prev observes, and tail is a weak_ptr too. pop_back locks the tail, finds its predecessor through prev, and resets that node's next (which destroys the old tail). The destructor detaches nodes one at a time: move head->next out before releasing head, so each node dies with a null next and destruction never recurses.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

static long live = 0;

template <class T>
class DList {
    struct Node {
        T value;
        std::shared_ptr<Node> next;
        std::weak_ptr<Node> prev;
        explicit Node(T v) : value(std::move(v)) { ++live; }
        ~Node() { --live; }
    };
    std::shared_ptr<Node> head_;
    std::weak_ptr<Node> tail_;

public:
    DList() = default;
    DList(const DList&) = delete;
    DList& operator=(const DList&) = delete;
    ~DList() { clear(); }

    void clear() {
        while (head_) head_ = std::move(head_->next);   // old head dies with next already empty
        tail_.reset();
    }
    void push_back(T v) {
        auto n = std::make_shared<Node>(std::move(v));
        if (auto t = tail_.lock()) { n->prev = t; t->next = n; }
        else head_ = n;
        tail_ = n;
    }
    void push_front(T v) {
        auto n = std::make_shared<Node>(std::move(v));
        n->next = head_;
        if (head_) head_->prev = n; else tail_ = n;
        head_ = std::move(n);
    }
    bool pop_back() {
        auto t = tail_.lock();
        if (!t) return false;
        if (auto p = t->prev.lock()) { p->next.reset(); tail_ = p; }
        else { head_.reset(); tail_.reset(); }
        return true;
    }
    template <class F> void for_each(F f) const {
        for (auto n = head_; n; n = n->next) f(n->value);
    }
    template <class F> void for_each_reverse(F f) const {
        for (auto n = tail_.lock(); n; n = n->prev.lock()) f(n->value);
    }
};

int main() {
    {
        DList<int> l;
        for (int i = 1; i <= 3; ++i) l.push_back(i);
        l.push_front(0);
        l.pop_back();
        l.for_each([](int v) { std::printf("%d ", v); });
        std::printf("| ");
        l.for_each_reverse([](int v) { std::printf("%d ", v); });
        std::printf("| live %ld\n", live);
    }
    std::printf("after small list: live %ld\n", live);
    {
        DList<int> big;
        for (int i = 0; i < 200000; ++i) big.push_back(i);
        std::printf("big list: live %ld\n", live);
    }
    std::printf("after big list: live %ld\n", live);
}
0 1 2 | 2 1 0 | live 3
after small list: live 0
big list: live 200000
after big list: live 0

Complexity and pitfalls. Pushes and pop_back are O(1); every backward step costs a lock(). The non-recursive clear works because head_ = std::move(head_->next) empties the old head's next before the old head is released, so each node is destroyed with nothing left to cascade into. Without it, destroying 200000 nodes recurses 200000 levels deep, which can overflow the stack (and does under ASan, whose frames are larger). Pitfalls: a shared_ptr prev (every adjacent pair becomes a cycle); forgetting to update tail_ in push_front on an empty list; pop_back on a one-element list must reset head_. If the list owns all nodes and never hands them out, raw prev pointers are cheaper and equally safe.

CodeImplement Subject with subscribe(std::weak_ptr<Observer>) and notify(int event), where Observer has a virtual on_event(int). notify must skip and erase observers that have died, return how many observers it delivered to, and remain correct if an observer subscribes another observer from inside on_event.

Answer

Approach. Store vector<weak_ptr<Observer>>. In notify, first take a snapshot: lock every entry into a local vector<shared_ptr<Observer>> and erase expired entries from the member list. Then call the observers from the snapshot. Holding strong pointers during the calls means no observer dies mid-notification, and iterating the snapshot means subscriptions made during a callback do not invalidate the loop (they take effect on the next notification).

#include <algorithm>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct Observer {
    virtual ~Observer() = default;
    virtual void on_event(int e) = 0;
};

class Subject {
public:
    void subscribe(std::weak_ptr<Observer> o) { observers_.push_back(std::move(o)); }
    int notify(int event) {
        std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Observer>> live;
        live.reserve(observers_.size());
        std::erase_if(observers_, [&](const std::weak_ptr<Observer>& w) {
            if (auto sp = w.lock()) { live.push_back(std::move(sp)); return false; }
            return true;
        });
        for (auto& o : live) o->on_event(event);
        return static_cast<int>(live.size());
    }
    std::size_t size() const { return observers_.size(); }
private:
    std::vector<std::weak_ptr<Observer>> observers_;
};

struct Printer : Observer {
    std::string name;
    explicit Printer(std::string n) : name(std::move(n)) {}
    void on_event(int e) override { std::printf("%s got %d\n", name.c_str(), e); }
};

struct Recruiter : Observer {
    Subject* subject;
    std::shared_ptr<Observer> recruit = std::make_shared<Printer>("recruit");
    bool done = false;
    explicit Recruiter(Subject* s) : subject(s) {}
    void on_event(int e) override {
        std::printf("recruiter got %d\n", e);
        if (!done) { subject->subscribe(recruit); done = true; }   // subscribe during notify
    }
};

int main() {
    Subject s;
    auto a = std::make_shared<Printer>("a");
    auto r = std::make_shared<Recruiter>(&s);
    s.subscribe(a);
    s.subscribe(r);
    {
        auto temp = std::make_shared<Printer>("temp");
        s.subscribe(temp);
        std::printf("delivered %d\n", s.notify(1));
    }
    std::printf("delivered %d\n", s.notify(2));
    std::printf("registered %zu\n", s.size());
}
a got 1
recruiter got 1
temp got 1
delivered 3
a got 2
recruiter got 2
recruit got 2
delivered 3
registered 3

Complexity and pitfalls. O(n) per notification plus two atomics per observer; the snapshot costs one allocation, which a reused member buffer can avoid. Pitfalls: calling on_event while iterating observers_ (a subscribe inside the callback reallocates the vector and invalidates the iterator); expired() followed by lock(); storing shared_ptr, which keeps observers alive forever. With threads, guard observers_ with a mutex during the snapshot only, and never hold it while calling observers (a callback that subscribes would deadlock).

Estimated rating: ~1600 · weak_ptr purge plus re-entrancy during notification

CodeWrite an EventLoop with post(std::function<void()>) and run(), and a Connection class owned by shared_ptr with two methods: ping(), which posts a callback that runs only if the connection is still alive, and send(msg), which posts a callback that must keep the connection alive until the message has been sent. Show that a connection dropped by its owner is destroyed immediately unless a send is pending, and destroyed right after its last pending send runs.

Answer

Approach. Connection inherits enable_shared_from_this and has a private constructor plus a static create factory, so it can only be owned by shared_ptr (otherwise shared_from_this would throw). ping captures weak_from_this() and locks inside. send captures shared_from_this(): the loop owns that closure, so this is temporary ownership, not a cycle. run moves the queue out before executing it so that callbacks can post safely and so that each closure is destroyed right after it runs.

#include <cstdio>
#include <deque>
#include <functional>
#include <memory>
#include <string>

class EventLoop {
public:
    void post(std::function<void()> f) { q_.push_back(std::move(f)); }
    void run() {
        while (!q_.empty()) {
            auto f = std::move(q_.front());
            q_.pop_front();
            f();
        }                                   // f, and anything it captured, dies here
    }
private:
    std::deque<std::function<void()>> q_;
};

class Connection : public std::enable_shared_from_this<Connection> {
    struct Key {};
public:
    Connection(Key, EventLoop& loop, int id) : loop_(loop), id_(id) {}
    static std::shared_ptr<Connection> create(EventLoop& loop, int id) {
        return std::make_shared<Connection>(Key{}, loop, id);
    }
    ~Connection() { std::printf("~Connection %d\n", id_); }

    void ping() {
        loop_.post([w = weak_from_this()] {
            if (auto self = w.lock()) std::printf("ping %d\n", self->id_);
            else std::puts("ping dropped");
        });
    }
    void send(std::string msg) {
        loop_.post([self = shared_from_this(), msg = std::move(msg)] {
            std::printf("conn %d sent '%s'\n", self->id_, msg.c_str());
        });
    }
private:
    EventLoop& loop_;
    int id_;
};

int main() {
    EventLoop loop;
    auto c1 = Connection::create(loop, 1);
    auto c2 = Connection::create(loop, 2);
    c1->ping();
    c2->ping();
    c2->send("bye");
    c1.reset();                 // no send pending: destroyed now
    c2.reset();                 // a send is pending: kept alive by the loop
    std::puts("running loop");
    loop.run();
    std::puts("loop done");
}
~Connection 1
running loop
ping dropped
ping 2
conn 2 sent 'bye'
~Connection 2
loop done

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) per post and per callback. Connection 1 has no pending strong capture, so c1.reset() destroys it at once and its ping is dropped. Connection 2 is owned only by the queued send closure after c2.reset(); its ping still succeeds, because lock() only needs some owner to exist. When the send closure has run and is destroyed, the count reaches 0. Pitfalls: running callbacks while iterating the queue (a callback that posts invalidates the iteration); keeping executed closures in the queue, which would keep connection 2 alive forever; capturing this in ping (use-after-free for connection 1); a public constructor, which lets someone create a stack Connection whose send throws bad_weak_ptr.

CodeSimulate both memory managers on an ownership graph. Input: n objects, a list of owning edges u → v and a set of roots (objects owned by the stack). When the program drops all roots, which objects does reference counting free and which does it leak? Which would a tracing collector free? Print the leaked objects for each strategy.

Answer

Approach. Reference counting: once the stack references are gone, an object's count is its number of incoming owning edges. Put every object with count 0 on a worklist; freeing one decrements each object it owns, and any that reach 0 join the worklist (Kahn's algorithm). Whatever is never freed is the refcount leak: exactly the objects on a cycle or reachable from one. A tracing collector with no roots left frees everything, so the interesting comparison is while the roots are alive: tracing frees everything unreachable from the roots right away, including unreachable cycles. The program reports both.

#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

struct Graph {
    int n;
    std::vector<std::vector<int>> owns;
    std::vector<int> roots;
};

// Objects that reference counting never frees after every root is dropped.
static std::vector<int> refcount_leaks(const Graph& g) {
    std::vector<int> count(g.n, 0);
    for (int u = 0; u < g.n; ++u) for (int v : g.owns[u]) ++count[v];
    // Each root adds one stack reference, and dropping the roots removes it again,
    // so after the drop the count is the in-degree. Zero means "freed".
    std::vector<int> work;
    for (int u = 0; u < g.n; ++u) if (count[u] == 0) work.push_back(u);
    std::vector<bool> freed(g.n, false);
    while (!work.empty()) {
        int u = work.back(); work.pop_back();
        freed[u] = true;
        for (int v : g.owns[u]) if (--count[v] == 0) work.push_back(v);
    }
    std::vector<int> leaked;
    for (int u = 0; u < g.n; ++u) if (!freed[u]) leaked.push_back(u);
    return leaked;
}

// Objects unreachable from the roots while the roots are still alive: tracing frees them now.
static std::vector<int> unreachable_now(const Graph& g) {
    std::vector<bool> seen(g.n, false);
    std::vector<int> st(g.roots.begin(), g.roots.end());
    for (int r : g.roots) seen[r] = true;
    while (!st.empty()) {
        int u = st.back(); st.pop_back();
        for (int v : g.owns[u]) if (!seen[v]) { seen[v] = true; st.push_back(v); }
    }
    std::vector<int> out;
    for (int u = 0; u < g.n; ++u) if (!seen[u]) out.push_back(u);
    return out;
}

static void print(const char* label, const std::vector<int>& v) {
    std::printf("%s:", label);
    for (int x : v) std::printf(" %d", x);
    std::printf("%s\n", v.empty() ? " none" : "");
}

int main() {
    // 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 1 (cycle 1,2), 2 -> 3, 0 -> 4, 5 <-> 6 never reachable, 7 isolated
    Graph g{8, {{1, 4}, {2}, {1, 3}, {}, {}, {6}, {5}, {}}, {0}};
    print("refcount leaks after dropping roots", refcount_leaks(g));
    print("tracing frees while roots alive", unreachable_now(g));
}
refcount leaks after dropping roots: 1 2 3 5 6
tracing frees while roots alive: 5 6 7

Complexity and pitfalls. Both passes are O(n + e). Object 7 has no owner at all, so reference counting frees it immediately (in C++ it would have died with its last owner), and tracing also lists it as unreachable. Objects 5 and 6 are the unreachable cycle that only tracing can free. Object 3 is not on a cycle, but it leaks under reference counting because a cycle owns it. Pitfalls: forgetting that objects reachable from a cycle leak too; treating a root that is also owned by another object as freed when the stack drops it (its count stays above 0).

CodeSome graphs really are cyclic (A → B → A, self-loops). Store one without any shared_ptr: a Graph owns every node, and edges are non-owning. Provide add_node(name), which returns a stable NodeId; add_edge(a, b); remove_node(id), which also removes every edge into the node; neighbours(id); and detection of stale ids, so a removed node's id does not silently refer to a newer node that reuses its slot. Prove with an instance counter that destroying the graph frees every node, cycles included.

Answer

Approach. This is ownership rule 4: one owning container, non-owning edges. Slots hold a unique_ptr<Node> and a generation counter. A NodeId is (slot index, generation), and it is valid only while the generation matches. Removing a node destroys it, bumps the slot's generation (so every old id goes stale), puts the slot on a free list and erases the edges that point to it. Edges are ids, so they can form any cycle, and destroying the graph destroys the slot vector, which frees every node whatever the edges look like.

#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

static int live = 0;

struct NodeId { std::uint32_t index, gen; };

class Graph {
    struct Node {
        std::string name;
        std::vector<NodeId> out;                 // non-owning edges
        explicit Node(std::string n) : name(std::move(n)) { ++live; }
        ~Node() { --live; }
    };
    struct Slot { std::unique_ptr<Node> node; std::uint32_t gen = 0; };
    std::vector<Slot> slots_;                   // the only owner of nodes
    std::vector<std::uint32_t> free_;

    Node* get(NodeId id) const {
        if (id.index >= slots_.size()) return nullptr;
        const Slot& s = slots_[id.index];
        return s.gen == id.gen ? s.node.get() : nullptr;
    }

public:
    NodeId add_node(std::string name) {
        std::uint32_t i;
        if (!free_.empty()) { i = free_.back(); free_.pop_back(); }
        else { i = static_cast<std::uint32_t>(slots_.size()); slots_.emplace_back(); }
        slots_[i].node = std::make_unique<Node>(std::move(name));
        return {i, slots_[i].gen};
    }
    bool add_edge(NodeId from, NodeId to) {
        Node* f = get(from);
        if (!f || !get(to)) return false;
        f->out.push_back(to);
        return true;
    }
    bool remove_node(NodeId id) {
        if (!get(id)) return false;
        Slot& s = slots_[id.index];
        s.node.reset();
        ++s.gen;                                  // every old id for this slot is now stale
        free_.push_back(id.index);
        for (Slot& other : slots_)
            if (other.node)
                std::erase_if(other.node->out, [&](NodeId e) { return e.index == id.index && e.gen == id.gen; });
        return true;
    }
    bool alive(NodeId id) const { return get(id) != nullptr; }
    std::string neighbours(NodeId id) const {
        std::string out;
        if (Node* n = get(id))
            for (NodeId e : n->out)
                if (Node* t = get(e)) out += t->name + " ";
        return out;
    }
};

int main() {
    {
        Graph g;
        NodeId a = g.add_node("a"), b = g.add_node("b"), c = g.add_node("c");
        g.add_edge(a, b);
        g.add_edge(b, a);                         // a 2-cycle
        g.add_edge(b, c);
        g.add_edge(c, c);                         // a self-loop
        std::printf("b -> %s| live %d\n", g.neighbours(b).c_str(), live);
        g.remove_node(a);
        std::printf("after removing a: b -> %s| live %d\n", g.neighbours(b).c_str(), live);
        NodeId d = g.add_node("d");               // reuses a's slot
        bool stale_edge = g.add_edge(a, d);
        std::printf("d in slot %u, old id a alive %d, edge from a accepted %d\n", d.index, g.alive(a), stale_edge);
    }
    std::printf("graph destroyed: live %d\n", live);
}
b -> a c | live 3
after removing a: b -> c | live 2
d in slot 0, old id a alive 0, edge from a accepted 0
graph destroyed: live 0

Complexity and pitfalls. add_node, add_edge and lookups are O(1); remove_node is O(V + E) because it scans for incoming edges (keep reverse edge lists if removals are frequent). Pitfalls: storing raw Node* edges without removing them (dangling after a removal); reusing a slot without a generation, so an old id silently names the new node (the ABA problem); storing nodes by value in the vector and handing out Node*, which dangle when the vector reallocates. With shared_ptr edges, the 2-cycle and the self-loop would both leak.

Estimated rating: ~1600 · generation-checked handles plus edge cleanup, the standard answer for genuinely cyclic data

Cheat sheet

Theory
  • Reference counting frees an object when its strong count hits 0. Objects in a cycle keep each other at 1 or more, so their destructors never run.
  • Break each cycle with one non-owning edge, pointing back toward the owner: weak_ptr if the target may die first, a raw pointer if structure guarantees it outlives the pointer.
  • Use a weak_ptr only through if (auto sp = w.lock()). Never expired() then lock(); use_count() is a hint.
  • Captured shared_ptrs are owning edges. A callback stored in the object captures this; a callback stored elsewhere captures weak_from_this(); a one-shot async handler may capture shared_from_this().
  • shared_from_this() needs public enable_shared_from_this and an existing owner; it throws bad_weak_ptr in constructors, destructors and on unowned objects (C++17).
  • The destructor runs at strong count 0, the block is freed at weak count 0; with make_shared, lingering weak_ptrs pin the object's memory.
  • Prove leaks with instance counters or a weak_ptr probe in tests; LeakSanitizer (default with ASan on Linux; Apple's clang lacks it on macOS).
  • Design rule: one clear owner, owning graph is a DAG, arbitrary graphs live in an owning container with non-owning edges.
