Part E · Memory management · Chapter 14

Placement new

Placement new separates the two jobs that a normal new does: getting memory and constructing an object in it. With it you construct objects in storage you already own, which is how std::vector, std::optional, std::variant, pools and arenas work. Interviewers ask about it to check that you understand object lifetime as distinct from memory: alignment, explicit destruction, std::launder and the undefined behaviour waiting at each step.

TheoryDrillsCoding· about 3.5 hours· prerequisites: Ch 9 new/delete vs malloc/free, Ch 1 object lifetime

What placement new does

Theory

Mental model. An ordinary new T(args) is two steps: call an allocation function, operator new(sizeof(T)), to get raw bytes, then run T's constructor on those bytes. Placement new is the same expression with extra arguments in parentheses, new (place) T(args). The extra arguments are passed to the allocation function, and the standard one, operator new(std::size_t, void* p), simply returns p. So no memory is allocated: you supply the storage, and the expression only constructs.

// What <new> declares (the non-allocating forms; they cannot be replaced by the program):
void* operator new  (std::size_t, void* p) noexcept { return p; }
void* operator new[](std::size_t, void* p) noexcept { return p; }
void  operator delete  (void*, void*) noexcept {}   // matching "placement delete": does nothing
void  operator delete[](void*, void*) noexcept {}

Under the hood. The result is a T* to a new object whose lifetime has begun at that address. The storage is still owned by whoever owned it before (a stack buffer, a pool, a malloc block), and placement new has no record of it. That means you, not the runtime, are responsible for ending the object's lifetime with an explicit destructor call, and for releasing the storage in whatever way it was obtained.

#include <cstdio>
#include <new>
#include <string>

struct Widget {
    std::string name;
    explicit Widget(std::string n) : name(std::move(n)) { std::printf("construct %s\n", name.c_str()); }
    ~Widget() { std::printf("destroy %s\n", name.c_str()); }
};

int main() {
    alignas(Widget) unsigned char buf[sizeof(Widget)];
    Widget* w = new (buf) Widget("gear");      // no allocation: buf is the storage
    std::printf("same address: %d\n", static_cast<void*>(w) == static_cast<void*>(buf));
    w->~Widget();                              // ends the lifetime; the bytes stay
    w = new (buf) Widget("spring");            // reuse the same bytes for a new object
    w->~Widget();
}
construct gear
same address: 1
destroy gear
construct spring
destroy spring

The new expression versus operator new

Keep three names apart. The new expression (new T, new (args) T) is language syntax: it calls an allocation function and then a constructor, and if the constructor throws, it calls the matching deallocation function. operator new is an ordinary function that only returns memory; you can call it directly, void* p = ::operator new(64);. Placement new is the informal name for a new expression with extra arguments, most often the void* form. Any extra argument types work: new (arena) T calls a user-declared operator new(std::size_t, Arena&).

  • Write ::new (p) T in generic code. The leading :: skips class-specific operator new overloads that T might declare.
  • Cast the address to void*: ::new (static_cast<void*>(p)) T. Otherwise a user overload like operator new(std::size_t, Foo*) could be a better match. std::construct_at does both for you.
  • new (p) T default-initialises (an int or a POD member is left indeterminate); new (p) T() and new (p) T{} value-initialise (zero for scalars). Same rules as ordinary new.

Storage: size and alignment

Theory

Mental model. The storage must be large enough (sizeof(T) bytes) and its address must be a multiple of alignof(T). Placement new checks neither. A plain unsigned char buf[sizeof(T)] on the stack has alignment 1, so it may start at an odd address; constructing a double or a std::string there is undefined behaviour. On x86 a misaligned ordinary load usually just works (slowly, across cache lines), but SSE aligned loads, atomics and many ARM instructions fault, and the optimiser is allowed to assume alignment, so "it worked on my laptop" proves nothing.

Getting correctly aligned storage

  • A typed byte array. alignas(T) std::byte buf[sizeof(T)]; (or unsigned char). This is the modern idiom. Arrays of std::byte, unsigned char or char are special: they can provide storage for other objects without ending their own lifetime ([intro.object]).
  • std::aligned_storage is deprecated in C++23. std::aligned_storage_t<sizeof(T), alignof(T)> did the same job, but P1413 deprecated it (and aligned_union) because it is easy to misuse: forgetting _t or ::type gives you a tiny struct with the wrong size, the default alignment argument is implementation-defined, and every access needs a reinterpret_cast plus std::launder anyway. Replace it with the alignas byte array.
  • Heap storage. ::operator new(n) and malloc return memory aligned for any fundamental type (__STDCPP_DEFAULT_NEW_ALIGNMENT__, 16 on x86-64 Linux). For over-aligned types use C++17 ::operator new(n, std::align_val_t{64}), which must be paired with the matching aligned operator delete.
  • Inside a larger buffer. std::align(alignment, size, ptr, space) advances ptr to the next aligned address and decreases space, or returns nullptr if the object does not fit. Arenas use it on every allocation (Ch 17).
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <new>

struct alignas(32) Block { float v[8]; };

static bool aligned(const void* p, std::size_t a) {
    return reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t>(p) % a == 0;
}

int main() {
    std::printf("alignof(Block) %zu, sizeof(Block) %zu\n", alignof(Block), sizeof(Block));
    alignas(Block) std::byte good[sizeof(Block)];
    std::printf("alignas buffer aligned: %d\n", aligned(good, alignof(Block)));

    alignas(Block) std::byte pool[128];
    void* p = pool + 1;                          // a deliberately misaligned cursor
    std::size_t space = sizeof pool - 1;
    void* q = std::align(alignof(Block), sizeof(Block), p, space);
    std::printf("std::align: found %d, aligned %d, skipped %zu bytes\n",
                q != nullptr, aligned(q, alignof(Block)), (sizeof pool - 1) - space);
    Block* b = ::new (q) Block{};
    b->v[7] = 1.5f;
    std::printf("%.1f\n", b->v[7]);              // Block is trivially destructible: no destructor call needed
}
alignof(Block) 32, sizeof(Block) 32
alignas buffer aligned: 1
std::align: found 1, aligned 1, skipped 31 bytes
1.5

Ending the lifetime: explicit destructor calls, destroy_at and construct_at

Theory

Mental model. An object built with placement new is destroyed by calling its destructor explicitly, p->~T(). That ends the object's lifetime and releases whatever the object owns (a string's heap buffer, a mutex), but it does not touch the storage. Never write delete p: that would call operator delete on memory that did not come from operator new (a stack buffer, the middle of a pool), which is undefined behaviour and usually a crash in the allocator.

  • std::destroy_at(p) (C++17) calls p->~T(). Unlike the raw syntax, it also works for arrays (destroying each element, C++20) and reads better in generic code. For scalars, p->~T() with T = int is a legal "pseudo-destructor call" that does nothing, so generic code needs no special case.
  • std::construct_at(p, args...) (C++20) is ::new (static_cast<void*>(p)) T(std::forward<Args>(args)...) and returns T*. It is constexpr, which placement new is not until C++26 (P2747), so it is how std::vector and std::optional became usable in constant expressions in C++20. It takes a typed pointer T*, not void*.
  • Range helpers in <memory>: std::destroy, destroy_n, uninitialized_copy, uninitialized_move, uninitialized_fill, uninitialized_value_construct_n, uninitialized_default_construct_n. The uninitialized_* algorithms destroy what they already built if a constructor throws.
  • Order. Built-in arrays and class members are destroyed in reverse order of construction. std::destroy(first, last) destroys forward. If the order matters, destroy in a reverse loop yourself.
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct Tracer {
    int id;
    explicit Tracer(int i) : id(i) { std::printf("+%d ", id); }
    ~Tracer() { std::printf("-%d ", id); }
};

int main() {
    alignas(Tracer) std::byte raw[3 * sizeof(Tracer)];
    Tracer* first = reinterpret_cast<Tracer*>(raw);
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) std::construct_at(first + i, i);
    std::puts("");
    std::destroy(first, first + 3);              // forward order
    std::puts("");

    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) std::construct_at(first + i, i + 10);
    std::puts("");
    for (int i = 3; i-- > 0;) std::destroy_at(first + i);   // reverse, like a built-in array
    std::puts("");
}
+0 +1 +2
-0 -1 -2
+10 +11 +12
-12 -11 -10

Interview trap

Calling the destructor does not make the memory reusable "for free": if you skip it, the object's resources leak, and if you call it twice, the second call runs on a dead object (double free of the string's buffer, for example). Every placement new needs exactly one matching destruction, on every path, including exceptions.

Placement delete: called only when a constructor throws

Theory

Mental model. There is no "placement delete expression". You cannot write delete (arena) p. A placement deallocation function, operator delete(void*, Args...) with the same extra parameters as a placement operator new, is called in exactly one situation: when the constructor in a placement new expression throws. The new expression then has memory it obtained but no object, and it calls the matching deallocation function with the same extra arguments so that the memory is not lost ([expr.new]).

  • For the standard void* form, the matching operator delete(void*, void*) does nothing, which is correct: the storage belongs to you.
  • For your own forms (operator new(std::size_t, Arena&)), declare the matching operator delete(void*, Arena&). If there is no match, nothing is called when the constructor throws, and the memory leaks (or the arena space is wasted).
  • For normal destruction you call the destructor and then release the memory by hand (p->~T(); arena.release(p);), because no expression can pass the extra arguments.
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>
#include <stdexcept>

struct Arena {
    alignas(16) std::byte buf[256];
    std::size_t used = 0, last = 0;
    void* take(std::size_t n) {
        last = used;
        used += (n + 15) & ~std::size_t{15};
        return buf + last;
    }
    void undo_last() { used = last; }
};

void* operator new(std::size_t n, Arena& a) {
    std::puts("arena operator new");
    return a.take(n);
}
void operator delete(void*, Arena& a) noexcept {   // the matching placement delete
    std::puts("placement delete: the constructor threw");
    a.undo_last();
}

struct Fragile {
    int v;
    explicit Fragile(int x) : v(x) { if (x < 0) throw std::invalid_argument("negative"); }
};

int main() {
    Arena arena;
    Fragile* ok = new (arena) Fragile(1);
    std::printf("ok->v %d, used %zu\n", ok->v, arena.used);
    ok->~Fragile();                                    // trivial here, but write it anyway
    try {
        new (arena) Fragile(-1);
    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        std::printf("caught %s, used %zu\n", e.what(), arena.used);
    }
}
arena operator new
ok->v 1, used 16
arena operator new
placement delete: the constructor threw
caught negative, used 16

Reusing storage and std::launder

Theory

Mental model. A pointer in C++ is more than an address: it points to a particular object. When you destroy an object and construct a new one in the same storage, the question is whether old pointers (and the old name) refer to the new object. The rule is [basic.life]/8: they do if the new object transparently replaces the old one, which in C++20 means it occupies exactly the same storage, has the same type (ignoring top-level cv), the old object was not a const complete object, and neither is a base class subobject or a [[no_unique_address]] member.

When those conditions fail, the compiler may assume the old pointer still sees the old object. For example, it may keep a const member's value in a register across the replacement. std::launder(p) (C++17, <new>) is the escape hatch: given a pointer that represents the right address, it returns a pointer to the object that currently lives there, and it is an optimisation barrier for that purpose. It generates no code.

When you actually need std::launder

  • Pointers derived from the raw storage. The main case today. reinterpret_cast<T*>(buf) where buf is a std::byte array gives a pointer whose value still points to the byte, because the array and the T nested in it are not pointer-interconvertible. Writing std::launder(reinterpret_cast<T*>(buf)) gets you the T. Containers that keep only a byte buffer (no stored T*) do this on every access. Keeping the pointer returned by placement new avoids the need.
  • Different type. The new object has a different type from the old one; old pointers do not refer to it at all, and launder on the old pointer (cast to the new type) is how you reach it.
  • const complete objects and base class subobjects, which are never transparently replaceable.
  • Before C++20, const and reference members. In C++17 a class with a const or reference non-static member was not transparently replaceable either, which is why early std::optional implementations needed launder after re-emplacing such a type (P0532 discussed the problem). C++20 relaxed the rule (P1971R0, resolving national body comments RU 007 and US 047), so replacing a struct { const int v; } through the old pointer is now well-defined.
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>

struct Config {
    const int version;      // const member: Config cannot be assigned, only rebuilt
    int flags;
};

int main() {
    alignas(Config) unsigned char storage[sizeof(Config)];
    Config* p = new (storage) Config{1, 0};
    std::printf("v%d\n", p->version);

    p->~Config();
    new (storage) Config{2, 0};               // result discarded on purpose
    std::printf("v%d\n", p->version);          // C++20: fine (transparent replacement); C++17: UB

    Config* q = std::launder(reinterpret_cast<Config*>(storage));   // from raw storage: launder
    std::printf("v%d\n", q->version);
}
v1
v2
v2

Know this cold

The simplest correct rule: use the pointer that placement new (or construct_at) returned. Use std::launder when you have to recompute a T* from the raw storage, or when the type changed. launder does not create an object; there must already be a live T at that address.

Implicit lifetime types and implicit object creation (C++20)

Theory

Mental model. Before C++20, the code every C programmer writes, Point* p = (Point*)malloc(sizeof(Point)); p->x = 3;, was technically undefined in C++: malloc returns storage, not a Point, and nothing started a Point's lifetime. P0593 fixed this in C++20 (and as a defect report against earlier standards). Certain operations now implicitly create objects of implicit-lifetime types in the storage they touch, if doing so gives the program defined behaviour.

  • Implicit-lifetime types: scalars, arrays (of anything), and class types that are aggregates without a user-provided destructor, or that have at least one trivial eligible constructor and a trivial, non-deleted destructor. struct Point { int x, y; }; qualifies; std::string does not.
  • Operations that create objects implicitly: malloc, calloc, realloc, operator new, operator new[], std::allocator<T>::allocate, memcpy and memmove (into the destination), and starting the lifetime of an array of char, unsigned char or std::byte.
  • For anything with a non-trivial constructor or destructor you still need placement new or construct_at. Implicit creation does not run constructors.
  • C++23 adds std::start_lifetime_as<T>(p) for "these bytes I received from the network are a T now", without copying. libstdc++ ships it from GCC 16, but libc++ (LLVM 22) does not yet, so memcpy into a local T remains the portable choice.
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <cstring>
#include <type_traits>

struct Point { int x, y; };                   // implicit-lifetime: aggregate, trivial destructor

int main() {
    static_assert(std::is_trivially_copyable_v<Point>);
    auto* p = static_cast<Point*>(std::malloc(sizeof(Point)));   // C++20: a Point is implicitly created
    if (!p) return 1;
    p->x = 3;
    p->y = 4;

    unsigned char wire[sizeof(Point)];
    std::memcpy(wire, p, sizeof wire);        // "send" the bytes
    Point q;
    std::memcpy(&q, wire, sizeof q);          // "receive": memcpy creates the object representation
    std::printf("%d %d\n", q.x, q.y);
    std::free(p);
}
3 4

This is also why a std::byte buffer can serve as storage for an array of T: arrays are implicit-lifetime types, so the buffer can implicitly contain a T[N] array object whose elements you then construct one by one. That makes pointer arithmetic across the slots of a container's buffer well-defined.

How vector, optional and variant use placement new

Theory

Mental model. Every standard container that can hold "room for a T but no T yet" is built from three pieces: raw storage of the right size and alignment, placement construction into it, and explicit destruction out of it. The container tracks which slots are live, because the language does not.

  • std::vector allocates with its allocator, constructs through allocator_traits::construct (placement new or construct_at for std::allocator) and destroys through allocator_traits::destroy. On reallocation it builds the elements in the new buffer with uninitialized_move if the move constructor is noexcept (otherwise it copies, to keep the strong guarantee), then destroys the old elements and frees the old buffer.
  • std::optional<T> stores the value in an anonymous union next to a bool. A union member is not constructed automatically, so the union acts as raw storage with the right size and alignment. emplace destroys any current value, constructs the new one with construct_at on the union member and sets the flag; reset destroys and clears it. If the constructor throws, the optional is left empty.
  • std::variant<Ts...> is the same idea with storage for the largest alternative and an index instead of a bool. Assigning a different alternative destroys the old one first; if the new constructor then throws, the variant can become valueless_by_exception().
  • Small-buffer types (std::function, std::any, SSO strings, Ch 18) placement-construct small objects in an internal buffer and fall back to the heap for large ones.
template <class T>
class TinyOptional {                 // the core of std::optional, without the API
    union { T value_; };             // no T constructed by default
    bool engaged_ = false;
public:
    TinyOptional() {}
    ~TinyOptional() { reset(); }
    template <class... A> T& emplace(A&&... a) {
        reset();
        std::construct_at(&value_, std::forward<A>(a)...);   // may throw: engaged_ is still false
        engaged_ = true;
        return value_;
    }
    void reset() noexcept { if (engaged_) { std::destroy_at(&value_); engaged_ = false; } }
};

A union member is an object of type T at a fixed address, so &value_ is already a T* and no launder is needed. That is one reason modern implementations prefer the union over a byte array.

Placement new with arrays: the overhead problem

Theory

Mental model. new T[n] for a type with a non-trivial destructor stores the element count in a hidden array cookie in front of the elements, so that delete[] knows how many destructors to run (Ch 9). The array new expression therefore asks the allocation function for n * sizeof(T) + overhead bytes and places the elements after the cookie. For placement array new, new (buf) T[n], older standards left the overhead unspecified, so a buffer of exactly n * sizeof(T) bytes could overflow, and the pointer returned was not necessarily buf.

CWG issue 2382 (accepted as a defect report in November 2019, so it applies to C++20 and to earlier modes) says the overhead is zero for the non-allocating form operator new[](std::size_t, void*). Any other placement array form, such as your own operator new[](std::size_t, Arena&), still gets the cookie when T is not trivially destructible, and its size is ABI-specific: 8 bytes on x86-64 (Itanium ABI); on Apple arm64, Clang uses a 16-byte ARM-style cookie while GCC uses 8.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>

struct Arena {};
static std::size_t requested = 0;
void* operator new[](std::size_t n, Arena&) { requested = n; return ::operator new(n); }
void operator delete[](void* p, Arena&) noexcept { ::operator delete(p); }

struct Trivial { int x; };
struct NonTrivial { int x; ~NonTrivial() {} };

int main() {
    Arena a;
    Trivial* t = new (a) Trivial[4];
    std::printf("trivial: extra bytes %zu\n", requested - 4 * sizeof(Trivial));
    NonTrivial* n = new (a) NonTrivial[4];
    std::printf("non-trivial: extra bytes > 0: %d\n", requested > 4 * sizeof(NonTrivial));

    alignas(NonTrivial) std::byte buf[4 * sizeof(NonTrivial)];
    NonTrivial* in_place = new (buf) NonTrivial[4];
    std::printf("void* form starts at buf: %d\n", static_cast<void*>(in_place) == static_cast<void*>(buf));
    for (int i = 4; i-- > 0;) in_place[i].~NonTrivial();

    ::operator delete(t);               // trivial: the elements start at the allocation
    for (int i = 4; i-- > 0;) n[i].~NonTrivial();
    ::operator delete(reinterpret_cast<std::byte*>(n) - (requested - 4 * sizeof(NonTrivial)));
}
trivial: extra bytes 0
non-trivial: extra bytes > 0: 1
void* form starts at buf: 1

The last two lines of main show why custom array forms are painful: to free the block you must undo the cookie offset yourself. The practical advice has not changed: do not use placement array new. Construct elements one at a time in a loop, or with std::uninitialized_value_construct_n, and destroy them in a reverse loop. You keep full control of the layout and of the exception cleanup.

Undefined behaviour pitfalls

Theory
MistakeWhat happensHow to catch or avoid it
Misaligned storageUB; slow or faulting loads, wrong code from the optimiseralignas(T) buffers, std::align; UBSan reports "misaligned address"

Forgetting the destructorthe object's resources leak; the storage is fineRAII owner for the slot, instance counters
Destroying twicethe destructor runs on a dead object: double free insidetrack liveness (a flag, a size counter)
Constructing over a live objectthe old object's lifetime ends without its destructor; its resources leakdestroy first, or assign instead of reconstructing
delete p on a placement objectfrees memory that operator new never returneddestroy explicitly, release storage the way it was obtained; ASan "free on address which was not malloc()-ed"

Old pointer after reuse with a different typeUB; strict aliasing lets the compiler use stale valuesuse the new pointer only

Key facts
new (p) T(args)calls operator new(sizeof(T), p), which returns p; then constructs; no allocation
Header<new> (the void* forms); construct_at/destroy_at in <memory>
Destroyp->~T() or std::destroy_at(p); never delete p
Placement delete is calledonly if the constructor throws during that placement new expression

Concept and tricky questions

Drills

ConceptWhat does new (buf) T(args) do, and does it allocate memory?

Answer

Answer. It calls the allocation function operator new(sizeof(T), buf), which returns buf unchanged, and then runs T's constructor at that address, returning a T*. It does not allocate.

Why. The new expression is always "allocation function, then constructor"; the extra arguments in parentheses select which allocation function. The standard void* overload is a no-op, so only the construction remains. People sometimes say "placement new allocates on the stack"; the storage can be anywhere, and it is whatever you passed in. Typical uses, the follow-up interviewers ask for: containers that separate capacity from size (vector, optional, variant, inplace_vector), object pools and arenas, small-buffer optimisation, constructing objects in shared memory or a memory-mapped file, and wrappers such as NoDestructor.

TrickyAn object was created with placement new in a stack buffer. Can you destroy it with delete p? What if the buffer came from ::operator new?

Answer

Answer. Not for the stack buffer: delete p runs the destructor and then calls operator delete(p) on memory the heap never handed out, which is undefined behaviour (ASan: "attempting free on address which was not malloc()-ed"). For a buffer from ::operator new(sizeof(T)) it happens to match what new T would have done, but it is still poor style; write p->~T(); ::operator delete(buf); so that destruction and deallocation are visibly paired with how they were obtained.

Why. A delete expression always does both halves. With placement new you did the halves separately, so you undo them separately. For arrays or class-specific allocators, delete would even pick the wrong deallocation function.

TrickyWhen is a placement operator delete called? Can you call it with a delete expression?

Answer

Answer. Only when the constructor throws inside a placement new expression; then the runtime calls the operator delete whose extra parameters match the operator new that was used, with the same arguments. There is no delete expression syntax that passes extra arguments, so you never trigger it by writing delete.

Why. At that moment the memory has been obtained but no object exists, so the program has nothing to call delete on; the language cleans up for you ([expr.new]). If no matching placement delete is declared, nothing is called and the memory leaks. The standard operator delete(void*, void*) is a no-op, which is correct for caller-owned storage.

ConceptWhy must the buffer be declared alignas(T)? What can go wrong on x86, which tolerates misaligned loads?

Answer

Answer. Every object must live at an address that is a multiple of alignof(T); a char array only guarantees alignment 1. Constructing at a misaligned address is undefined behaviour regardless of the CPU.

Why. On x86 ordinary integer loads still work (possibly split across cache lines), but aligned SSE/AVX instructions (movaps) fault, lock-prefixed atomics that cross a cache line are extremely slow or trap with split-lock detection, and the compiler is allowed to emit those instructions because it assumes alignment. On ARM many instructions (exclusive loads, some SIMD) fault. UBSan reports misaligned accesses at run time.

TrickyWhy was std::aligned_storage deprecated in C++23, and what replaces it?

Answer

Answer. P1413 deprecated aligned_storage and aligned_union because they are easy to misuse and give no real benefit. Replace them with alignas(T) std::byte buf[sizeof(T)];.

Why. Classic bugs: writing std::aligned_storage<sizeof(T)> without ::type or _t (you get the trait class itself, a 1-byte empty struct); relying on the default alignment argument, which is implementation-defined and may be smaller than alignof(T) for over-aligned types; and the type gives no access to the object anyway, so you need reinterpret_cast and std::launder. A byte array with alignas states size and alignment explicitly and can legally provide storage.

TrickyIs alignas(T) std::byte buf[n * sizeof(T)]; T* a = new (buf) T[n]; safe?

Answer

Answer. Since CWG 2382 (C++20, also treated as a defect fix), yes for the standard void* form: the array allocation overhead is required to be zero, so the elements start at buf. Before that resolution it was unspecified, and implementations were allowed to add a cookie and overrun the buffer. With any custom placement form (an arena overload), a non-trivially destructible T gets a cookie (8 bytes on x86-64 Linux; 16 with Clang on Apple arm64, 8 with GCC there).

Why. The cookie exists so that delete[] knows how many destructors to run. You never use delete[] on placement arrays, but the expression rules applied anyway. Even now, the idiomatic answer is "construct the elements in a loop" or std::uninitialized_value_construct_n, which also handles exceptions. Interviewers often expect "unsafe, unspecified overhead", so mention both the history and the fix.

ConceptWhat is std::launder for? Give a case that needs it in C++20.

Answer

Answer. It takes a pointer that holds the address of a live object of type T but does not formally point to it, and returns a pointer that does. The common C++20 case is a container that stores only a byte buffer and recomputes element pointers with reinterpret_cast<T*>(buf): that pointer still points to the byte, so you write std::launder(reinterpret_cast<T*>(buf)).

Why. The object model tracks which object a pointer points to, and optimisers use it (for example to cache const values or vtable pointers). launder tells the compiler to forget those assumptions for this pointer. It does not create an object and generates no instructions. If you keep the pointer that placement new returned, you never need it.

TrickyAfter p->~T(); new (p) T(2); can you keep using the old pointer p? Does the answer change if T has a const int member, and does it differ between C++17 and C++20?

Answer

Answer. Yes, as long as the new object transparently replaces the old one: same storage, same type, the old object is not a const complete object and not a base subobject. In C++17 a const or reference member also disqualified the replacement, so p could not be used and you needed std::launder(p). C++20 (P1971R0, from the RU 007 and US 047 national body comments) removed that member condition, so the code is fine.

Why. The C++17 rule let compilers assume a const member never changes through the same pointer, which made std::optional<S> with a const member hard to implement correctly. Many answers still quote the C++17 rule; mention the change. A const complete object (const T obj;) still cannot be replaced transparently.

ConceptWhat do std::construct_at and std::destroy_at add over placement new and an explicit destructor call?

Answer

Answer. construct_at(p, args...) (C++20) is constexpr, always uses the global non-allocating form through ::new (static_cast<void*>(p)), and returns the typed pointer. destroy_at(p) (C++17) is the explicit destructor call as a function, and in C++20 it also destroys arrays element by element and is constexpr.

Why. A placement new expression is not allowed in constant evaluation before C++26 (P2747 makes it constexpr), so constexpr std::vector and std::optional in C++20 depend on construct_at. The :: and the void* cast protect generic code from class-specific or oddly-typed operator new overloads. As free functions they also work with algorithms and allocators.

TrickyWhat happens if you placement-new a second object into storage that still holds a live std::string, without destroying the first?

Answer

Answer. The first string's lifetime ends when its storage is reused, but its destructor never runs, so its heap buffer leaks. That alone is not undefined behaviour: [basic.life]/5 allows reusing storage without calling a non-trivial destructor, as long as the program does not depend on the destructor's side effects.

Why. "It is UB to construct over a live object" is the common wrong answer. The real consequences are the leak and any broken invariants (an unlocked mutex that never unlocks, a registration never removed). Containers avoid this by destroying before reconstructing, or by assigning to the live object.

ConceptWhat are implicit-lifetime types, and what did C++20 change about malloc?

Answer

Answer. Implicit-lifetime types are scalars, arrays, and classes that are aggregates without user-provided destructors or that have a trivial eligible constructor and a trivial non-deleted destructor. Since C++20 (P0593, applied as a defect report), operations like malloc, operator new, memcpy and creating a byte array implicitly create objects of such types when that is needed to give the program defined behaviour.

Why. Before that, (Point*)malloc(sizeof(Point)) followed by p->x = 1 was formally undefined, because nothing began the Point's lifetime, even though every C-compatible program relied on it. It does not help types with real constructors: a std::string in malloc memory still needs placement new.

ConceptHow do vector::reserve and push_back use placement new? Why doesn't reserve construct anything?

Answer

Answer. reserve(n) allocates raw storage for n elements through the allocator and moves existing elements into it. push_back constructs the new element at end() with allocator_traits::construct, which is placement new (or construct_at) for std::allocator. reserve constructs nothing because capacity is storage, not elements: size() does not change.

Why. If reserve default-constructed elements, it would require T to be default constructible and would waste work that push_back then overwrites. The separation between allocation and construction is the reason placement new exists. resize(n), in contrast, constructs elements.

Trickyalignas(int) std::byte b[sizeof(int)]; What is the difference between new (b) int and new (b) int()?

Answer

Answer. new (b) int default-initialises, which for int means no initialisation: the value is indeterminate and reading it is undefined behaviour. C++26 "erroneous behaviour" (P2795) covers uninitialised automatic variables, not objects created by a new expression, so this read stays undefined. new (b) int() (or int{}) value-initialises it to 0.

Why. Placement new follows exactly the same initialisation rules as ordinary new. People assume the bytes already in the buffer become the value, or that new always zeroes. For class types with a user-provided default constructor both forms call it; for aggregates, T() zeroes members that have no initialiser and T leaves them indeterminate.

Predict the output and find the bug

Drills

OutputIn what order are the objects constructed and destroyed?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>

struct T {
    char c;
    explicit T(char x) : c(x) { std::printf("+%c", c); }
    ~T() { std::printf("-%c", c); }
};

int main() {
    alignas(T) std::byte buf[3 * sizeof(T)];
    T* p[3];
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) p[i] = ::new (buf + i * sizeof(T)) T(static_cast<char>('a' + i));
    std::printf("\n");
    {
        T local[2] = {T('x'), T('y')};
    }
    std::printf("\n");
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) p[i]->~T();
    std::printf("\n");
}
Answer
+a+b+c
+x+y-y-x
-a-b-c

Answer. The built-in array is destroyed in reverse order of construction (-y-x). The placement objects are destroyed in whatever order you write, here forward (-a-b-c).

Why. The language guarantees reverse destruction for arrays, members and automatic objects. For placement-constructed objects there is no automatic destruction at all, so the order is the programmer's choice; mimic the reverse order when objects may depend on earlier ones. T local[2] = {T('x'), T('y')} constructs each element directly (guaranteed copy elision since C++17), so no extra copies print.

Find the bugA market data decoder places a payload struct right after a 4-byte header. It works on the developer's machine. What is wrong?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>

struct Payload {
    double price;
    long qty;
};

int main() {
    alignas(8) std::byte packet[64];
    // bytes 0..3 hold a header
    Payload* p = ::new (packet + 4) Payload{101.25, 300};
    std::printf("%.2f x %ld\n", p->price, p->qty);
}
Answer

Answer. Payload requires 8-byte alignment, and packet + 4 is only 4-byte aligned, so the object is created at a misaligned address: undefined behaviour. UBSan reports "member access within misaligned address ... which requires 8 byte alignment".

Why. alignas on the buffer aligns its start, not every offset. For wire formats with packed fields, do not place structs into the buffer at all: memcpy the bytes into a properly aligned local Payload (the compiler turns it into plain loads), or use std::align to pick a valid offset when you control the layout. x86 hides the bug for plain loads, while ARM and vectorised code expose it.

Find the bugA message slot API constructs messages into caller-provided memory. What goes wrong here?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>

struct Order {
    long id;
    double px;
    long qty;
    char side;
};

static Order* make_order(void* where, std::size_t capacity, long id) {
    (void)capacity;                        // "we always pass enough"
    return ::new (where) Order{id, 99.5, 10, 'B'};
}

int main() {
    alignas(Order) std::byte slot[16];     // sized for an old version of Order
    Order* o = make_order(slot, sizeof slot, 42);
    std::printf("%ld %c\n", o->id, o->side);
}
Answer

Answer. Order grew to 32 bytes, but the slot has 16, so the constructor writes past the end of slot: a stack buffer overflow. With -fsanitize=address,undefined the first report comes from UBSan's object-size check ("store to address ... with insufficient space for an object of type 'long'"); ASan alone reports a stack-buffer-overflow.

Why. Placement new trusts the caller completely; it neither knows nor checks the size. Validate capacity >= sizeof(Order) and alignment at run time, and when the buffer type is known at compile time use static_assert(sizeof(Order) <= sizeof slot). GCC's -Wplacement-new catches the case where it can see both sizes in one expression, which is exactly what the indirection here hides.

OutputA class has a custom placement operator new with a tag argument but only the usual operator delete. What is printed when the constructor throws?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>
#include <stdexcept>

static int allocs = 0, frees = 0;

struct Tagged {
    int v;
    explicit Tagged(int x) : v(x) { if (x < 0) throw std::runtime_error("bad"); }
    static void* operator new(std::size_t n, int /*tag*/) { ++allocs; return ::operator new(n); }
    static void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { ++frees; ::operator delete(p); }
};

int main() {
    Tagged* ok = new (1) Tagged(5);
    delete ok;                                   // the usual delete: fine
    try {
        new (2) Tagged(-1);
    } catch (const std::exception&) {
        std::puts("caught");
    }
    std::printf("allocs %d frees %d\n", allocs, frees);
}
Answer
caught
allocs 2 frees 1

Answer. The second allocation is never freed. When the constructor throws, the new expression looks for a deallocation function whose parameters after the first match the placement arguments, operator delete(void*, int). There is none, so no deallocation function is called and the block leaks.

Why. The usual operator delete(void*) is only used for the non-placement new Tagged(5) form and for delete expressions. Whenever you declare a placement operator new, declare the matching placement operator delete. (LeakSanitizer would flag the leak on Linux; the counters prove it here.)

Find the bugA developer cleans up a placement-constructed object the "normal" way. What happens?

#include <cstdio>
#include <new>
#include <string>

int main() {
    alignas(std::string) unsigned char buf[sizeof(std::string)];
    auto* s = new (buf) std::string("constructed in a stack buffer");
    std::printf("%s\n", s->c_str());
    delete s;
}
Answer

Answer. delete s runs ~basic_string correctly and then calls operator delete on a stack address, which is undefined behaviour. ASan reports "attempting free on address which was not malloc()-ed"; without ASan the allocator usually aborts or corrupts its metadata.

Why. A delete expression always pairs the destructor with deallocation. The storage did not come from operator new, so only the destructor may be called: s->~basic_string(); or, more readably, std::destroy_at(s);.

Find the bugReusing a buffer for a different type. What does the last line print, and why is the question meaningless?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>

int main() {
    alignas(8) std::byte buf[8];
    auto* i = ::new (buf) std::int64_t(42);
    auto* d = ::new (buf) double(1.0);     // ends the int64's lifetime
    std::printf("%.1f\n", *d);
    std::printf("%lld\n", static_cast<long long>(*i));
}
Answer

Answer. Reading *i is undefined behaviour: the int64_t it pointed to no longer exists, and a double cannot transparently replace an int64_t because the types differ. In practice it prints either the bit pattern of 1.0 (4607182418800017408) or 42, depending on whether the optimiser forwarded the earlier store through the type-based aliasing rules.

Why. Old pointers survive storage reuse only for transparent replacement (same type). To reinterpret bits, use std::bit_cast<std::int64_t>(1.0) or memcpy, never a stale pointer. This is the same rule that makes type punning through pointer casts unsafe.

OutputCount the constructions. What does this print?

#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

struct C {
    static inline int ctor = 0, copy = 0, move = 0, dtor = 0;
    C() { ++ctor; }
    C(const C&) { ++copy; }
    C(C&&) noexcept { ++move; }
    ~C() { ++dtor; }
};

int main() {
    std::vector<C> v;
    v.reserve(4);
    std::printf("after reserve: ctor %d dtor %d size %zu\n", C::ctor, C::dtor, v.size());
    v.emplace_back();
    v.emplace_back();
    C c;
    v.push_back(c);
    std::printf("ctor %d copy %d move %d\n", C::ctor, C::copy, C::move);
    v.pop_back();
    std::printf("after pop: dtor %d size %zu capacity >= 4: %d\n", C::dtor, v.size(), v.capacity() >= 4);
}
Answer
after reserve: ctor 0 dtor 0 size 0
ctor 3 copy 1 move 0
after pop: dtor 1 size 2 capacity >= 4: 1

Answer. reserve constructs nothing. Two emplace_back() calls default-construct in place, C c is the third default construction, and push_back(c) copy-constructs into the next raw slot. No reallocation happens, so there are no moves. pop_back runs one destructor and keeps the capacity.

Why. The vector separates storage (capacity) from objects (size) and uses placement construction for every element. A frequent wrong answer is "reserve(4) constructs 4 objects", which is what resize(4) would do.

Find the bugA hand-written "copy into raw storage" leaks when a copy throws. Where?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <stdexcept>

static int live = 0;

struct Item {
    int v;
    explicit Item(int x) : v(x) { ++live; }
    Item(const Item& o) : v(o.v) {
        if (o.v == 3) throw std::runtime_error("copy failed");
        ++live;
    }
    ~Item() { --live; }
};

template <class T>
static void copy_into(const T* src, std::size_t n, T* dst) {
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) std::construct_at(dst + i, src[i]);
}

int main() {
    Item src[5] = {Item(0), Item(1), Item(2), Item(3), Item(4)};
    alignas(Item) std::byte raw[5 * sizeof(Item)];
    try {
        copy_into(src, 5, reinterpret_cast<Item*>(raw));
    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        std::printf("%s, live objects: %d (expected 5)\n", e.what(), live);
    }
}
Answer
copy failed, live objects: 8 (expected 5)

Answer. When the fourth copy throws, the three copies already constructed in raw are never destroyed, so their resources leak (here, the counter stays 3 too high). Fix: wrap the loop in try, and in catch (...) destroy dst[i-1] ... dst[0] in reverse order and rethrow. Or call std::uninitialized_copy_n, which does exactly that.

Why. Raw storage has no destructor to fall back on: no container owns those objects yet, so stack unwinding cannot clean them up. This is the core of the strong exception guarantee in vector's copy constructor and reallocation.

Find the bugA reusable connection slot is re-initialised with placement new. Why do the counts not balance?

#include <cstdio>
#include <new>

static int opened = 0, closed = 0;

struct Conn {
    int id;
    explicit Conn(int i) : id(i) { ++opened; }
    ~Conn() { ++closed; }
};

class Slot {
    alignas(Conn) unsigned char buf_[sizeof(Conn)];
    Conn* c_ = nullptr;
public:
    void open(int id) { c_ = new (buf_) Conn(id); }
    void close() { if (c_) { c_->~Conn(); c_ = nullptr; } }
    ~Slot() { close(); }
};

int main() {
    {
        Slot s;
        s.open(1);
        s.open(2);      // reconnect
        s.open(3);      // reconnect again
    }
    std::printf("opened %d closed %d\n", opened, closed);
}
Answer
opened 3 closed 1

Answer. open constructs a new Conn over a live one without destroying it first, so connections 1 and 2 are never closed. Only connection 3 is destroyed, by ~Slot. Fix: call close() at the start of open, then construct.

Why. Reusing the storage ends the old object's lifetime silently, skipping its destructor (allowed by [basic.life]/5, but its side effects are lost). Any type that wraps placement-constructed storage must track whether the slot is live, exactly like std::optional::emplace does.

OutputWhat state is the std::optional in after emplace throws?

#include <cstdio>
#include <optional>
#include <stdexcept>

struct Picky {
    int v;
    explicit Picky(int x) : v(x) {
        if (x < 0) throw std::invalid_argument("negative");
        std::printf("+%d\n", v);
    }
    ~Picky() { std::printf("-%d\n", v); }
};

int main() {
    std::optional<Picky> o;
    o.emplace(1);
    try {
        o.emplace(-1);
    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        std::printf("caught %s, has_value %d\n", e.what(), o.has_value());
    }
    o.emplace(2);
}
Answer
+1
-1
caught negative, has_value 0
+2
-2

Answer. emplace first destroys the current value (-1 prints), then tries to construct the new one in the same storage. The constructor throws, so the optional is left empty, not holding the old value. The final emplace(2) succeeds and is destroyed at the end of main.

Why. In-place construction cannot offer the strong guarantee: the old object had to die to free the storage. The standard specifies "if an exception is thrown during the call to T's constructor, *this does not contain a value". The flag is set only after the constructor succeeds, which is the pattern your own implementation should copy.

Write the code

Coding

CodeImplement Optional<T> using an aligned byte buffer and placement new: default constructor (empty), construction from T, copy and move construction and assignment, emplace(args...), reset(), has_value(), operator*, operator-> and value() (throws when empty). If the constructor in emplace throws, the optional must end up empty. Test with a type that counts live instances.

Answer

Approach. Store alignas(T) std::byte buf_[sizeof(T)] and bool engaged_. emplace calls reset(), constructs with ::new, and sets engaged_ only afterwards. Access goes through std::launder(reinterpret_cast<T*>(buf_)), since the pointer is recomputed from raw storage. Copy and move assignment have four cases: both engaged (assign the value), only the source engaged (construct), only this engaged (reset), neither (nothing).

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <string>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>

template <class T>
class Optional {
public:
    Optional() noexcept {}
    Optional(const T& v) { emplace(v); }
    Optional(T&& v) { emplace(std::move(v)); }
    Optional(const Optional& o) { if (o.engaged_) emplace(*o); }
    Optional(Optional&& o) noexcept(std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<T>) {
        if (o.engaged_) emplace(std::move(*o));
    }
    Optional& operator=(const Optional& o) {
        if (this == &o) return *this;
        if (engaged_ && o.engaged_) **this = *o;
        else if (o.engaged_) emplace(*o);
        else reset();
        return *this;
    }
    Optional& operator=(Optional&& o) noexcept(std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<T> &&
                                               std::is_nothrow_move_assignable_v<T>) {
        if (this == &o) return *this;
        if (engaged_ && o.engaged_) **this = std::move(*o);
        else if (o.engaged_) emplace(std::move(*o));
        else reset();
        return *this;
    }
    ~Optional() { reset(); }

    template <class... A>
    T& emplace(A&&... a) {
        reset();
        T* p = ::new (static_cast<void*>(buf_)) T(std::forward<A>(a)...);   // may throw: still empty
        engaged_ = true;
        return *p;
    }
    void reset() noexcept {
        if (engaged_) { ptr()->~T(); engaged_ = false; }
    }
    bool has_value() const noexcept { return engaged_; }
    explicit operator bool() const noexcept { return engaged_; }
    T& operator*() noexcept { return *ptr(); }
    const T& operator*() const noexcept { return *ptr(); }
    T* operator->() noexcept { return ptr(); }
    T& value() {
        if (!engaged_) throw std::logic_error("Optional is empty");
        return *ptr();
    }

private:
    T* ptr() noexcept { return std::launder(reinterpret_cast<T*>(buf_)); }
    const T* ptr() const noexcept { return std::launder(reinterpret_cast<const T*>(buf_)); }
    alignas(T) std::byte buf_[sizeof(T)];
    bool engaged_ = false;
};

static int live = 0;
struct Tracked {
    std::string s;
    explicit Tracked(std::string v) : s(std::move(v)) {
        if (s.empty()) throw std::invalid_argument("empty");
        ++live;
    }
    Tracked(const Tracked& o) : s(o.s) { ++live; }
    Tracked(Tracked&& o) noexcept : s(std::move(o.s)) { ++live; }
    Tracked& operator=(const Tracked&) = default;
    Tracked& operator=(Tracked&&) noexcept = default;
    ~Tracked() { --live; }
};

int main() {
    {
        Optional<Tracked> a;
        std::printf("a empty: %d, live %d\n", !a, live);
        a.emplace("alpha, long enough to allocate on the heap");
        Optional<Tracked> b = a;                     // copy construct
        Optional<Tracked> c = std::move(a);          // move construct (a stays engaged, moved-from)
        std::printf("b %.5s, c %.5s, live %d\n", b->s.c_str(), c->s.c_str(), live);
        b = Optional<Tracked>();                     // assign empty: destroys b's value
        std::printf("b empty: %d, live %d\n", !b, live);
        try {
            c.emplace("");                           // constructor throws
        } catch (const std::exception& e) {
            std::printf("emplace threw %s, c empty: %d, live %d\n", e.what(), !c, live);
        }
        try {
            c.value();
        } catch (const std::logic_error& e) {
            std::printf("value(): %s\n", e.what());
        }
    }
    std::printf("after scope: live %d\n", live);
    std::printf("sizeof Optional<int> %zu, Optional<double> %zu\n", sizeof(Optional<int>), sizeof(Optional<double>));
}
a empty: 1, live 0
b alpha, c alpha, live 3
b empty: 1, live 2
emplace threw empty, c empty: 1, live 1
value(): Optional is empty
after scope: live 0
sizeof Optional<int> 8, Optional<double> 16

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) apart from T's own operations, no heap use by Optional. Pitfalls: setting engaged_ before construction (a throwing constructor leaves a "full" optional with garbage); forgetting reset in emplace (leaks the old value); using the moved-from source as if empty (a moved-from optional is still engaged, as with std::optional); missing std::launder when recomputing the pointer. The real std::optional uses a union so that it can be constexpr and trivially copyable when T is.

Estimated rating: ~1800 · four-way assignment logic, exception safety and lifetime rules in one class

CodeImplement StaticVector<T, N>: a vector with inline storage for at most N elements and no heap allocation. Provide push_back (copy and move), emplace_back, pop_back, operator[], size, clear, begin/end, a copy constructor that cleans up if an element copy throws, and a destructor. emplace_back on a full vector throws std::length_error. (This is C++26 std::inplace_vector.)

Answer

Approach. An aligned byte array of N * sizeof(T) and a size counter. Elements [0, size) are live. emplace_back checks capacity, constructs at slot size with construct_at, then increments. pop_back decrements and destroys. clear destroys in reverse. The copy constructor appends element by element inside try; on failure it clears what it built and rethrows, because the destructor of a partially constructed object never runs.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <new>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

template <class T, std::size_t N>
class StaticVector {
public:
    StaticVector() = default;
    StaticVector(const StaticVector& o) {
        try {
            for (const T& x : o) push_back(x);
        } catch (...) {
            clear();
            throw;
        }
    }
    StaticVector& operator=(const StaticVector&) = delete;   // kept short; see pitfalls
    ~StaticVector() { clear(); }

    template <class... A>
    T& emplace_back(A&&... a) {
        if (size_ == N) throw std::length_error("StaticVector is full");
        T* p = std::construct_at(slot(size_), std::forward<A>(a)...);
        ++size_;                          // only after the constructor succeeded
        return *p;
    }
    void push_back(const T& v) { emplace_back(v); }
    void push_back(T&& v) { emplace_back(std::move(v)); }
    void pop_back() noexcept { std::destroy_at(&(*this)[--size_]); }
    void clear() noexcept { while (size_) pop_back(); }   // reverse order

    T& operator[](std::size_t i) noexcept { return *std::launder(slot(i)); }
    const T& operator[](std::size_t i) const noexcept { return *std::launder(cslot(i)); }
    std::size_t size() const noexcept { return size_; }
    static constexpr std::size_t capacity() noexcept { return N; }
    T* begin() noexcept { return size_ ? &(*this)[0] : slot(0); }
    T* end() noexcept { return begin() + size_; }
    const T* begin() const noexcept { return size_ ? &(*this)[0] : cslot(0); }
    const T* end() const noexcept { return begin() + size_; }

private:
    T* slot(std::size_t i) noexcept { return reinterpret_cast<T*>(buf_ + i * sizeof(T)); }
    const T* cslot(std::size_t i) const noexcept { return reinterpret_cast<const T*>(buf_ + i * sizeof(T)); }
    alignas(T) std::byte buf_[N * sizeof(T)];
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};

static int live = 0;
struct Name {
    std::string s;
    Name(const char* v) : s(v) { ++live; }
    Name(const Name& o) : s(o.s) {
        if (s == "boom") throw std::runtime_error("copy failed");
        ++live;
    }
    Name(Name&& o) noexcept : s(std::move(o.s)) { ++live; }
    ~Name() { --live; }
};

int main() {
    {
        StaticVector<Name, 4> v;
        v.emplace_back("ada");
        v.push_back(Name("grace"));
        v.emplace_back("linus");
        for (const Name& n : v) std::printf("%s ", n.s.c_str());
        std::printf("| size %zu live %d\n", v.size(), live);
        v.pop_back();
        std::printf("after pop: size %zu live %d\n", v.size(), live);
        v.emplace_back("boom");
        v.emplace_back("dennis");
        try {
            v.emplace_back("overflow");
        } catch (const std::length_error& e) {
            std::printf("%s\n", e.what());
        }
        try {
            StaticVector<Name, 4> copy = v;      // the third copy throws
        } catch (const std::exception& e) {
            std::printf("copy: %s, live %d\n", e.what(), live);
        }
    }
    std::printf("after scope: live %d\n", live);
    std::printf("sizeof StaticVector<int, 8> = %zu\n", sizeof(StaticVector<int, 8>));
}
ada grace linus | size 3 live 3
after pop: size 2 live 2
StaticVector is full
copy: copy failed, live 4
after scope: live 0
sizeof StaticVector<int, 8> = 40

Complexity and pitfalls. All operations O(1) except clear and copying, which are O(n); no allocation. The size is N * sizeof(T) plus the counter (32 + 8 for int, 8). Pitfalls: incrementing size_ before construction; destroying forward instead of backward (fine for independent elements, wrong for elements that refer to earlier ones); relying on ~StaticVector to clean up a throwing copy constructor (it does not run); a defaulted copy constructor, which would copy raw bytes of non-trivial objects. Copy assignment is deleted to keep the solution short; a correct one is clear() then append with the same rollback (basic guarantee), or copy-and-swap via a temporary and element-wise moves.

Estimated rating: ~1900 · placement construction with exact liveness tracking and exception-safe copying

CodeWrite RingBuffer<T, N>, a fixed-capacity FIFO queue with inline raw storage: bool push(T) (false when full), std::optional<T> pop() (empty when the queue is empty), size(), and a destructor that destroys exactly the live elements. Elements must be constructed only when pushed and destroyed when popped.

Answer

Approach. Keep head_ (next to pop), count_, and the raw slots. push constructs at (head_ + count_) % N. pop moves the front element into the returned optional, destroys the slot, and advances head_. The destructor pops (destroys) the remaining count_ elements starting at head_, wrapping around.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <new>
#include <optional>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

template <class T, std::size_t N>
class RingBuffer {
public:
    RingBuffer() = default;
    RingBuffer(const RingBuffer&) = delete;
    RingBuffer& operator=(const RingBuffer&) = delete;
    ~RingBuffer() { while (count_) destroy_front(); }

    bool push(T v) {
        if (count_ == N) return false;
        std::construct_at(slot((head_ + count_) % N), std::move(v));
        ++count_;
        return true;
    }
    std::optional<T> pop() {
        if (count_ == 0) return std::nullopt;
        std::optional<T> out(std::move(front()));
        destroy_front();
        return out;
    }
    std::size_t size() const noexcept { return count_; }

private:
    T& front() noexcept { return *std::launder(slot(head_)); }
    void destroy_front() noexcept {
        std::destroy_at(&front());
        head_ = (head_ + 1) % N;
        --count_;
    }
    T* slot(std::size_t i) noexcept { return reinterpret_cast<T*>(buf_ + i * sizeof(T)); }
    alignas(T) std::byte buf_[N * sizeof(T)];
    std::size_t head_ = 0, count_ = 0;
};

static int live = 0;
struct Msg {
    std::string text;
    explicit Msg(std::string t) : text(std::move(t)) { ++live; }
    Msg(Msg&& o) noexcept : text(std::move(o.text)) { ++live; }
    ~Msg() { --live; }
};

int main() {
    {
        RingBuffer<Msg, 3> q;
        bool a = q.push(Msg("a"));
        bool b = q.push(Msg("b"));
        bool c = q.push(Msg("c"));
        bool d = q.push(Msg("d"));                // full
        std::printf("push: %d %d %d %d\n", a, b, c, d);
        std::printf("live after pushes: %d\n", live);
        auto first = q.pop();
        std::printf("popped %s, size %zu\n", first->text.c_str(), q.size());
        q.push(Msg("e"));                          // wraps around to slot 0
        while (auto m = q.pop()) std::printf("%s ", m->text.c_str());
        std::printf("| empty pop: %d\n", !q.pop().has_value());
        q.push(Msg("left in the queue"));
        std::printf("live before destruction: %d\n", live);
    }
    std::printf("after scope: live %d\n", live);
}
push: 1 1 1 0
live after pushes: 3
popped a, size 2
b c e | empty pop: 1
live before destruction: 2
after scope: live 0

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) push and pop. "live before destruction: 2" counts the queued message plus first, which still holds "a". Pitfalls: destroying all N slots in the destructor instead of only the live ones (destructors on raw memory); forgetting to wrap indices; putting the four push calls directly into one printf call would make the test nondeterministic, because the evaluation order of function arguments is unspecified (GCC and Clang really do differ). Using a power-of-two N lets the modulo become a mask.

Estimated rating: ~1600 · raw slots with wrap-around and exact destruction of live elements

CodeImplement copy_construct_n(src, n, dst), which copy-constructs n objects into uninitialised storage at dst with the strong guarantee: if any copy throws, every object already constructed is destroyed (in reverse order) and the exception propagates. Show it next to std::uninitialized_copy_n.

Answer

Approach. Count constructed elements in i. Construct in a try; in the handler destroy dst[i-1] down to dst[0], then rethrow. The function owns the partially built range only during the call; on success the caller owns [dst, dst+n).

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <new>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <string>

template <class T>
T* copy_construct_n(const T* src, std::size_t n, T* dst) {
    std::size_t i = 0;
    try {
        for (; i < n; ++i) std::construct_at(dst + i, src[i]);
    } catch (...) {
        while (i > 0) std::destroy_at(dst + --i);   // reverse order
        throw;
    }
    return dst + n;
}

static int live = 0;
struct Cell {
    std::string s;
    int fail_on_copy;
    Cell(std::string v, int f) : s(std::move(v)), fail_on_copy(f) { ++live; }
    Cell(const Cell& o) : s(o.s), fail_on_copy(o.fail_on_copy) {
        if (fail_on_copy) throw std::runtime_error("copy of " + s + " failed");
        ++live;
    }
    ~Cell() { --live; }
};

int main() {
    const Cell src[4] = {{"w", 0}, {"x", 0}, {"y", 1}, {"z", 0}};
    alignas(Cell) std::byte raw[4 * sizeof(Cell)];
    Cell* dst = reinterpret_cast<Cell*>(raw);
    std::printf("live before: %d\n", live);
    try {
        copy_construct_n(src, 4, dst);
    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        std::printf("mine: %s, live %d\n", e.what(), live);
    }
    try {
        std::uninitialized_copy_n(src, 4, dst);
    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        std::printf("std: %s, live %d\n", e.what(), live);
    }
    Cell* end = copy_construct_n(src, 2, dst);      // succeeds
    std::printf("copied %td, live %d\n", end - dst, live);
    std::destroy(dst, end);
    std::printf("after destroy: live %d\n", live);
}
live before: 4
mine: copy of y failed, live 4
std: copy of y failed, live 4
copied 2, live 6
after destroy: live 4

Complexity and pitfalls. O(n) copies. Pitfalls: destroying dst[i] (the one that threw was never constructed); destroying all n; swallowing the exception; catching only std::exception (any type can be thrown). This loop is the building block for vector's copy constructor and for reallocation when the move constructor is not noexcept.

Estimated rating: ~1300 · short, but the off-by-one in the rollback is exactly what interviewers look for

CodeBuild an Arena with create<T>(args...) that bump-allocates correctly aligned storage from one heap block and placement-constructs a T. reset() must run the destructors of all non-trivially destructible objects in reverse creation order and make the memory reusable. Trivially destructible objects must not cost any bookkeeping. Throw std::bad_alloc when full. Test with strings and an alignas(64) type.

Answer

Approach. allocate(size, align) uses std::align on the cursor. For non-trivially destructible T, also allocate a small Finalizer node (function pointer, object pointer, next) and push it on a linked list; LIFO order gives reverse destruction for free. Allocate the node before constructing the object, so that a failure to get the node cannot leave a constructed object with no destructor registered. If the constructor throws, the space is simply wasted until reset.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <new>
#include <string>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>

class Arena {
public:
    explicit Arena(std::size_t cap) : buf_(static_cast<std::byte*>(::operator new(cap))), cap_(cap) {}
    Arena(const Arena&) = delete;
    Arena& operator=(const Arena&) = delete;
    ~Arena() { reset(); ::operator delete(buf_); }

    void* allocate(std::size_t n, std::size_t align) {
        void* p = buf_ + used_;
        std::size_t space = cap_ - used_;
        if (!std::align(align, n, p, space)) throw std::bad_alloc();
        used_ = (cap_ - space) + n;
        return p;
    }

    template <class T, class... A>
    T* create(A&&... a) {
        if constexpr (std::is_trivially_destructible_v<T>) {
            return ::new (allocate(sizeof(T), alignof(T))) T(std::forward<A>(a)...);
        } else {
            void* node = allocate(sizeof(Finalizer), alignof(Finalizer));
            void* mem = allocate(sizeof(T), alignof(T));
            T* obj = ::new (mem) T(std::forward<A>(a)...);
            fins_ = ::new (node) Finalizer{[](void* p) noexcept { static_cast<T*>(p)->~T(); }, obj, fins_};
            return obj;
        }
    }

    void reset() noexcept {
        for (Finalizer* f = fins_; f; f = f->next) f->destroy(f->obj);   // newest first
        fins_ = nullptr;
        used_ = 0;
    }
    std::size_t used() const noexcept { return used_; }

private:
    struct Finalizer {
        void (*destroy)(void*) noexcept;
        void* obj;
        Finalizer* next;
    };
    std::byte* buf_;
    std::size_t cap_, used_ = 0;
    Finalizer* fins_ = nullptr;
};

struct Loud {
    std::string name;
    explicit Loud(std::string n) : name(std::move(n)) {}
    ~Loud() { std::printf("~%s\n", name.c_str()); }
};
struct alignas(64) CacheLine { int v[16]; };

int main() {
    Arena arena(1024);
    int* n = arena.create<int>(7);
    auto* a = arena.create<Loud>("first loud object, long enough to own heap memory");
    auto* line = arena.create<CacheLine>();
    auto* b = arena.create<Loud>("second");
    line->v[15] = *n;
    std::printf("cache line aligned: %d, value %d\n",
                reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t>(line) % 64 == 0, line->v[15]);
    std::printf("%.5s %s\n", a->name.c_str(), b->name.c_str());

    std::puts("reset:");
    arena.reset();
    std::printf("used after reset %zu\n", arena.used());
    try {
        for (;;) arena.create<CacheLine>();
    } catch (const std::bad_alloc&) {
        std::puts("arena full");
    }
}
cache line aligned: 1, value 7
first second
reset:
~second
~first loud object, long enough to own heap memory
used after reset 0
arena full

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) per create, O(k) reset for k non-trivial objects. The heap block from ::operator new is only guaranteed 16-byte aligned, but std::align handles larger alignments by skipping bytes. Pitfalls: forgetting destructors (leaks the strings' buffers); destroying in creation order; registering the finaliser after construction with an allocation that can throw (the object would never be destroyed); handing out pointers that outlive reset. Ch 17 covers arenas and std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource in depth.

Estimated rating: ~2000 · alignment arithmetic, type-erased destructors and ordering under exceptions

CodeWrite NoDestructor<T>: a wrapper that constructs a T in inline storage and deliberately never destroys it. Use it for a function-local static registry, and show why it matters: a global object's destructor uses the registry during program shutdown, after an ordinary function-local static would already have been destroyed.

Answer

Approach. Construct T with placement new into alignas(T) std::byte storage in the constructor, and give NoDestructor a trivial (defaulted) destructor that does not touch T. Function-local statics are constructed on first use (thread-safely since C++11) and destroyed in reverse order of construction completion at exit; a NoDestructor registry is never destroyed, so it stays usable by any destructor that runs during shutdown. The leaked memory is reclaimed by the OS at exit and is still reachable through the static, so leak checkers do not report it.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <map>
#include <new>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

template <class T>
class NoDestructor {
public:
    template <class... A>
    explicit NoDestructor(A&&... a) { ::new (static_cast<void*>(storage_)) T(std::forward<A>(a)...); }
    NoDestructor(const NoDestructor&) = delete;
    NoDestructor& operator=(const NoDestructor&) = delete;
    ~NoDestructor() = default;                      // T is intentionally never destroyed

    T& get() noexcept { return *std::launder(reinterpret_cast<T*>(storage_)); }
    T* operator->() noexcept { return &get(); }
private:
    alignas(T) std::byte storage_[sizeof(T)];
};

static std::map<std::string, int>& registry() {
    static NoDestructor<std::map<std::string, int>> r;   // constructed on first use, never destroyed
    return r.get();
}

struct Plugin {
    std::string name;
    explicit Plugin(std::string n) : name(std::move(n)) { registry()[name] = 1; }
    ~Plugin() {
        registry().erase(name);                       // runs during static destruction
        std::printf("unregistered %s, %zu left\n", name.c_str(), registry().size());
    }
};

static Plugin audio("audio");    // constructed before main; the registry is created inside its constructor
static Plugin video("video");

int main() {
    std::printf("registered: %zu\n", registry().size());
    std::printf("sizeof(NoDestructor<std::string>) == sizeof(std::string): %d\n",
                sizeof(NoDestructor<std::string>) == sizeof(std::string));
}
registered: 2
sizeof(NoDestructor<std::string>) == sizeof(std::string): 1
unregistered video, 1 left
unregistered audio, 0 left

Complexity and pitfalls. Zero overhead: same size as T, one placement construction. Without NoDestructor this particular program would also work, because the registry's static finishes construction during audio's constructor and is therefore destroyed after audio; but as soon as some other static touches registry() first, or plugins live in another translation unit with a different initialisation order, a destructor can run against a destroyed map. NoDestructor removes the order question entirely. Pitfalls: using it for objects whose destructor must run (flushing a log file); destroying it manually; forgetting launder when recomputing the pointer. Chromium's base::NoDestructor and Abseil's absl::NoDestructor are production versions.

Estimated rating: ~1500 · small class, but explaining static destruction order is the real test

Cheat sheet

Theory
  • new (p) T(args) constructs at p without allocating. In generic code use std::construct_at(p, args...) (C++20, constexpr) or ::new (static_cast<void*>(p)) T(...).
  • Storage must be big enough and aligned: alignas(T) std::byte buf[sizeof(T)];. std::aligned_storage is deprecated in C++23. Use std::align inside larger buffers.
  • Destroy with p->~T() or std::destroy_at(p), exactly once, on every path. Never delete a placement object. Destroy in reverse order to mimic the language.
  • Placement operator delete(void*, Args...) is called only when the constructor throws in the matching placement new expression; declare it for every custom placement operator new.
  • Keep the pointer placement new returned. Use std::launder when you recompute a T* from raw storage or the type changed. C++20 lets old pointers see a same-type replacement even with const members.
  • C++20 implicit object creation makes malloc/memcpy of implicit-lifetime types (aggregates, scalars, arrays) well-defined; non-trivial types still need construction.
  • vector, optional, variant and SBO types are raw storage plus placement construction plus a liveness record (size, bool, index). Set the record only after the constructor succeeds.
  • Avoid placement array new: construct elements in a loop or with std::uninitialized_*, which roll back on exceptions.

Part E · Memory management · Chapter 15

Memory pools

A memory pool hands out fixed-size blocks from memory it already owns, so allocation becomes a pointer pop and freeing becomes a pointer push. This chapter builds pools from the free list up, covers size classes, thread safety, std::pmr and STL allocators, and shows how to debug and measure them. Low-latency firms and game studios ask about pools because they show whether you understand what malloc really costs.

TheoryDrillsCoding· about 5 hours· prerequisites: Ch 9, Ch 10, Ch 14

Why pools exist

Theory

Mental model. malloc is a general-purpose service: any size, any thread, any order of frees, and memory can go back to the OS. A pool gives up that generality. It serves one block size (or a few), usually from one thread, and keeps its memory until it is destroyed. In exchange, every allocation costs a handful of instructions and takes the same time every time.

What malloc actually does

A modern allocator (glibc ptmalloc, jemalloc, tcmalloc, mimalloc, macOS libmalloc) works roughly like this on each call:

  • Map the request size to a size class and look in a per-thread cache for a free block of that class.
  • If the cache is empty, refill it from a shared arena, which may take a lock or an atomic operation.
  • If the arena is empty, grow the heap with brk or mmap. That is a system call, and the first touch of each new page is a page fault (a few hundred nanoseconds to microseconds).
  • On free, find the block's metadata (a header before the block, or a page map lookup), handle frees that come from a different thread, and sometimes coalesce neighbours or return pages with madvise.

The fast path is good, often 10 to 30 ns. The problem is the variance: slow paths happen at moments you do not control, and a trading system that answers a tick in 2 microseconds cannot afford a 20 microsecond page fault on one order in ten thousand.

What a pool buys you

  • Constant, small cost. Allocation pops the head of a singly linked list. Freeing pushes onto it. No size lookup, no lock, no system call.
  • No external fragmentation inside the pool. Every block has the same size, so any free block fits any request. See Ch 10 for the general fragmentation story.
  • Predictable memory. You can allocate and touch all of it at start-up (and mlock it), so no page faults happen on the hot path.
  • Locality. Blocks sit next to each other in a few large chunks, and a LIFO free list returns the block that was freed most recently, which is probably still in cache.
  • Bulk teardown. Destroying the pool frees everything at once, which is useful when the objects die together.

The costs: memory is held at its peak until the pool dies, a block cannot be bigger than the block size, and a pool is one more piece of code that can corrupt memory in ways tools find hard to see (debugging pools covers this).

Know this cold

Interviewers want the trade-off in one sentence: a pool trades generality (any size, any order, any thread, memory returned to the OS) for constant-time allocation, no external fragmentation and no latency spikes. If you only say "pools are faster", you have missed the point that the tail latency is what matters on hot paths.

Fixed-size pools and the intrusive free list

Theory

Mental model. Take one big buffer and cut it into equal blocks. A free block is not being used for anything, so it can store the pointer to the next free block in its own first bytes. The pool keeps one pointer, head, to the first free block. That chain of pointers threaded through the free blocks is the intrusive free list: the list nodes are the free blocks themselves, so it costs no extra memory.

The core code

This is the whole idea in 30 lines. The pool computes a block size that can hold both the user's object and a pointer, carves the buffer, and pushes every block onto the list.

#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>

class FixedPool {
    struct Node { Node* next; };
    static constexpr std::size_t kAlign = __STDCPP_DEFAULT_NEW_ALIGNMENT__;   // what operator new guarantees
    static std::size_t round_up(std::size_t n, std::size_t a) { return (n + a - 1) / a * a; }

    std::size_t block_;
    std::byte* buf_;
    Node* head_ = nullptr;

public:
    FixedPool(std::size_t object_size, std::size_t count)
        : block_(round_up(std::max(object_size, sizeof(Node)), kAlign)),
          buf_(static_cast<std::byte*>(::operator new(block_ * count))) {
        for (std::size_t i = count; i-- > 0;)          // push in reverse so block 0 comes out first
            head_ = ::new (buf_ + i * block_) Node{head_};
    }
    ~FixedPool() { ::operator delete(buf_); }
    FixedPool(const FixedPool&) = delete;
    FixedPool& operator=(const FixedPool&) = delete;

    void* allocate() {
        if (!head_) return nullptr;                    // exhausted
        Node* n = head_;
        head_ = n->next;
        return n;
    }
    void deallocate(void* p) { head_ = ::new (p) Node{head_}; }
    std::size_t block_size() const { return block_; }
};

int main() {
    FixedPool pool(24, 4);
    std::printf("block size %zu\n", pool.block_size());
    void* a = pool.allocate();
    void* b = pool.allocate();
    pool.deallocate(a);
    void* c = pool.allocate();
    std::printf("c reuses a: %s\n", c == a ? "yes" : "no");
    std::printf("b - a = %td bytes\n", static_cast<std::byte*>(b) - static_cast<std::byte*>(a));
    pool.deallocate(b);
    pool.deallocate(c);
}
block size 32
c reuses a: yes
b - a = 32 bytes

Points to notice:

  • allocate and deallocate are a few loads and stores each: O(1), independent of how many blocks are in use.
  • The free list is LIFO: the next allocation gets the block just freed, which is probably still in L1. Good for speed, bad for catching use-after-free (the stale pointer now aliases a live object).
  • Placement new (Ch 14) starts a Node's lifetime in freed storage, and the caller placement-news its own object into the block it gets, so no object is read through the wrong type.
  • ::operator new returns memory aligned to at least __STDCPP_DEFAULT_NEW_ALIGNMENT__ (16 on mainstream 64-bit platforms), and the block size is a multiple of that, so every block is suitably aligned for any type that is not over-aligned. Do not assume alignof(std::max_align_t) is the same number: on Apple arm64 it is 16 with GCC but 8 with Clang, so a pool that rounds to max_align_t gets different block sizes from the two compilers.

Alignment and the minimum block size

Two rules decide the block size:

  1. It must hold a free-list pointer, so it is at least sizeof(void*) (8 bytes on 64-bit). A pool of char or int16_t still uses 8-byte blocks, unless you store 16-bit or 32-bit indices instead of pointers.
  2. It must be a multiple of the strictest alignment you serve. If block 0 is aligned to 16 and the block size is 24, block 1 starts at offset 24, which is only 8-aligned. A type with alignas(16) placed there is misaligned, which is undefined behaviour and can fault with SIMD loads.

The rounding formula for a power-of-two alignment a is (n + a - 1) & ~(a - 1), which equals (n + a - 1) / a * a. For a pool dedicated to one type T, use block = round_up(max(sizeof(T), sizeof(void*)), max(alignof(T), alignof(void*))), and make the buffer itself at least that aligned (::operator new(size, std::align_val_t{alignof(T)}) for over-aligned types, paired with the matching aligned operator delete).

A neat way to express a typed block is a union:

template <class T>
union Slot {
    Slot* next;                                  // valid while free
    alignas(T) unsigned char storage[sizeof(T)]; // valid while in use
};
// sizeof(Slot<T>) and alignof(Slot<T>) are already the max of both members, rounded correctly.

Why both operations are O(1), and what "O(1)" hides

Neither operation loops or searches, so both are constant time in the strict sense. The constant still includes a possible cache miss: popping the head reads head->next, which lives in the block itself.
