If that block has not been touched for a while, the pop costs a trip to L2 or DRAM. Prefetching the next head on each pop (__builtin_prefetch(head_)) is a known trick in very hot pools.

Key factsFixed-size poolGeneral-purpose malloc
AllocatePop the free-list head: O(1), a few nsFast path 10 to 30 ns; slow path takes locks, system calls, page faults
FreePush onto the head: O(1)Metadata lookup, cross-thread handling, sometimes coalescing
Sizes servedOne block size (or a few classes)Any size
Per-block overheadNone: the link lives inside free blocksA header or page-map metadata, plus size-class rounding
External fragmentationNone inside the poolPossible over long runs
Internal fragmentationBlock size minus object sizeSize-class rounding
Thread safetyNone unless you add itYes
Memory back to the OSWhen the pool is destroyedSometimes (trim, madvise)
Minimum blocksizeof(void*), rounded to the alignmentUsually 16 bytes

Growing by chunks vs a fixed capacity

Theory

A pool needs a policy for the moment the free list is empty.

  • Fixed capacity. Allocate all blocks up front and return nullptr (or throw, or fall back to malloc) when they run out. This is the HFT choice: size the pool for the worst day, pre-fault the pages at start-up, and treat exhaustion as an alarm. Memory use is known before the market opens.
  • Grow by chunks. When the list is empty, get a new chunk of N blocks from the upstream allocator, thread its blocks onto the free list and continue. Chunks are often doubled (64, 128, 256 blocks) to keep the number of upstream calls logarithmic. The chunks are linked together so the destructor can free them.

Growing never moves existing blocks, so pointers into the pool stay valid (unlike a std::vector of objects). Freed blocks are not returned upstream: a chunk can go back only when all its blocks are free, which needs per-chunk counters, so most pools keep every chunk until destruction.

The chunk header can live at the start of each chunk (one allocation per chunk), or the pool can keep a std::vector<std::unique_ptr<std::byte[]>> of chunks. The second is simpler and the cost is irrelevant because it runs once per chunk.

Tip

Pre-faulting matters as much as pre-allocating. operator new for a large buffer usually maps fresh pages that the kernel has not backed yet, so the first write to each 4 KiB (16 KiB on Apple Silicon) page still faults. Touch every page at start-up (write one byte per page, or memset the buffer) and, on Linux, consider mlock or MAP_POPULATE.

Multiple size classes

Theory

One pool serves one size. A small-object allocator serves many sizes by keeping an array of pools, one per size class, and routing each request to the smallest class that fits. This is exactly how jemalloc, tcmalloc and mimalloc work internally, and it is how std::pmr::unsynchronized_pool_resource is built.

  • Mapping. A common scheme is 16-byte steps up to 128 bytes, then powers of two up to a limit such as 4 KiB. The index is (n + 15) / 16 - 1 in the small range, or std::bit_width(n - 1) for powers of two.
  • Internal fragmentation. A 65-byte request in a power-of-two scheme takes 128 bytes, wasting 63 (49 percent). Finer classes waste less but need more pools, each with partly empty chunks.
  • Large requests above the biggest class go straight to the upstream allocator.
  • Freeing needs the size. The pool must know which class a pointer belongs to. Either the caller passes the size back (C++ sized deallocation, std::allocator::deallocate(p, n) and memory_resource::deallocate(p, bytes, align) all do), or the allocator looks it up from the address (page-to-class maps in jemalloc and tcmalloc).
// 16-byte classes: 1..16 -> 0, 17..32 -> 1, ..., 113..128 -> 7
constexpr std::size_t size_class(std::size_t n) { return (n + 15) / 16 - 1; }
static_assert(size_class(1) == 0 && size_class(16) == 0 && size_class(17) == 1 && size_class(128) == 7);

The coding section builds a complete size-class allocator with a fallback to malloc.

Thread safety options

Theory

The basic pool is a single-threaded data structure: two threads popping the head at the same time can both get the same block. There are three standard fixes, in increasing order of difficulty.

1. A mutex around the pool

Simple and correct. An uncontended std::mutex lock and unlock costs roughly 10 to 25 ns (two atomic read-modify-write operations on the lock word), which is often more than the pool operation itself, and under contention threads queue on the lock (Ch 5 explains the futex path). Fine when allocation is not the bottleneck.

2. Thread-local pools

Give each thread its own pool (thread_local, or one pool per worker passed explicitly). No synchronisation at all on the fast path. The hard case is a cross-thread free: thread A allocates an order object, hands it to thread B, and B frees it. Options:

  • Forbid it by design: the object goes back to the thread that owns it (via a queue) and is freed there.
  • Each pool has a lock-free "remote free" stack that other threads push to, and the owner drains it into its local list when the local list runs dry. mimalloc and snmalloc use this design.
  • Let the block join the freeing thread's pool. This works only if all pools share one block size and pools never free their chunks, and memory can drift between threads.

3. A lock-free free list and the ABA problem

The free list is a stack, so the classic lock-free version is a Treiber stack: pop reads head and head->next, then uses compare-and-swap to move head from the old value to next. It fails in a specific way called ABA.

Standard fixes, at the level interviews expect:

  • Tagged pointers / version counters. Store a counter next to the head and increment it on every change. CAS compares both, so A-with-version-5 is different from A-with-version-7. Needs a double-width CAS (cmpxchg16b on x86-64, CASP on arm64 with LSE), or pack a 32-bit block index with a 32-bit tag into one 64-bit word. The coding section uses the index trick.
  • Hazard pointers or epoch-based reclamation. A thread announces which node it is reading, and nobody reuses that node until the announcement is cleared. C++26 adds <hazard_pointer> (P2530) and <rcu> (P2545), but neither GCC 16's libstdc++ nor libc++ ships those headers yet, so today you use a library such as Folly or write your own.
  • LL/SC hardware. ARM's load-exclusive / store-exclusive fails if the location was written at all, which avoids ABA in principle, but C++ only exposes CAS, so you cannot rely on it from portable code.

There is a second, quieter problem: reading A->next while another thread may be writing the user's data into A is a data race in the C++ memory model. Lock-free free lists make next an atomic or use indices into an array of atomics. Pools never return memory to the OS, which at least means the read cannot fault.

Interview trap

"Just use std::atomic<Node*> and CAS" is the answer that gets the follow-up "what about ABA?". Have the timeline ready (pop A, pop B, push A, stale CAS succeeds) and name one fix. Also say that a mutex or thread-local pools are usually the better engineering choice: lock-free is not automatically faster under contention, because the cache line holding head still bounces between cores.

std::pmr: polymorphic memory resources

Theory

Mental model. C++17's <memory_resource> separates what a container is from where its memory comes from. A std::pmr::memory_resource is an abstract class with a virtual allocate and deallocate. A std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<T> is a small allocator that holds a pointer to a resource and forwards to it. Because the allocator type is always the same, std::pmr::vector<int> backed by a pool and one backed by new have the same type, and you can pass both to the same function.

memory_resource and the standard resources

class memory_resource {
public:
    void* allocate(std::size_t bytes, std::size_t align = alignof(std::max_align_t));
    void  deallocate(void* p, std::size_t bytes, std::size_t align = alignof(std::max_align_t));
    bool  is_equal(const memory_resource& other) const noexcept;
private:   // you override these
    virtual void* do_allocate(std::size_t bytes, std::size_t align) = 0;
    virtual void  do_deallocate(void* p, std::size_t bytes, std::size_t align) = 0;
    virtual bool  do_is_equal(const memory_resource& other) const noexcept = 0;
};
ResourceBehaviourThread safe
new_delete_resource()Calls global operator new / delete (with alignment). The initial default resource.Yes
null_memory_resource()Every allocate throws std::bad_alloc. Used as an upstream to prove nothing spills to the heap.Yes
unsynchronized_pool_resourceSize-class pools carved from chunks obtained upstream. Requests larger than largest_required_pool_block go straight upstream.No
synchronized_pool_resourceSame interface, safe to share between threads. libc++ wraps the unsynchronised pool in a mutex; libstdc++ keeps per-thread pools behind a shared mutex.Yes
monotonic_buffer_resourceA bump-pointer arena: deallocate is a no-op. Covered in Ch 17.No

Facts that come up:

  • std::pmr::pool_options has two fields, max_blocks_per_chunk and largest_required_pool_block; implementations may adjust them, and chunks grow geometrically up to the maximum.
  • release() (also called by the destructor) returns everything upstream, even blocks never deallocated. A plain deallocate puts the block back in the pool, not upstream.
  • get_default_resource() and set_default_resource() manage a process-wide default. A default-constructed polymorphic_allocator captures the default at construction time.
  • Pool resources are not copyable and must outlive every container that uses them.

polymorphic_allocator and pmr containers

Every standard container has a std::pmr alias, for example std::pmr::vector<T> is std::vector<T, std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<T>>. The allocator is scoped: when a pmr::vector<pmr::string> constructs an element, uses-allocator construction passes the vector's allocator to the string, so the characters come from the same resource. That is the main reason to prefer pmr over a hand-written allocator for nested containers.

Propagation rules are the classic source of surprises:

  • Copy construction calls select_on_container_copy_construction(), which for polymorphic_allocator returns a default-constructed allocator. The copy uses the default resource, not the source's resource, so a hot path that copies pmr containers quietly calls operator new. Pass the resource explicitly: std::pmr::vector<T> copy(src, &pool);.
  • Move construction moves the allocator, so the new container keeps the same resource and steals the buffer.
  • Copy and move assignment do not propagate the allocator (propagate_on_container_*_assignment are false). Move-assigning between containers with unequal resources moves element by element, O(n), and may allocate.
  • swap between containers with unequal resources is undefined behaviour.

C++20 made polymorphic_allocator<> (defaulting to std::byte) a general-purpose "vocabulary" allocator with allocate_bytes, allocate_object<T>, new_object<T>(args...) and delete_object(p).

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <list>
#include <memory_resource>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

// Counts what reaches the upstream: shows that the pool batches requests into chunks.
class CountingResource : public std::pmr::memory_resource {
    std::pmr::memory_resource* up_ = std::pmr::new_delete_resource();
public:
    std::size_t calls = 0, live = 0;
private:
    void* do_allocate(std::size_t n, std::size_t a) override { ++calls; live += n; return up_->allocate(n, a); }
    void do_deallocate(void* p, std::size_t n, std::size_t a) override { live -= n; up_->deallocate(p, n, a); }
    bool do_is_equal(const memory_resource& o) const noexcept override { return this == &o; }
};

int main() {
    CountingResource upstream;
    {
        std::pmr::unsynchronized_pool_resource pool(
            std::pmr::pool_options{.max_blocks_per_chunk = 256, .largest_required_pool_block = 512}, &upstream);

        std::pmr::list<int> nodes(&pool);
        for (int i = 0; i < 10000; ++i) nodes.push_back(i);
        std::printf("10000 list nodes took fewer than 100 upstream calls: %s\n", upstream.calls < 100 ? "yes" : "no");

        std::pmr::vector<std::pmr::string> names(&pool);
        names.emplace_back("a string long enough to need a heap buffer");
        std::printf("element uses the pool: %s\n", names[0].get_allocator().resource() == &pool ? "yes" : "no");

        auto copy = names;   // copy construction: default resource
        std::printf("copy uses the pool: %s\n", copy.get_allocator().resource() == &pool ? "yes" : "no");
        auto moved = std::move(names);   // move construction: same resource
        std::printf("moved-to uses the pool: %s\n", moved.get_allocator().resource() == &pool ? "yes" : "no");
    }
    std::printf("bytes still held upstream after the pool died: %zu\n", upstream.live);
}
10000 list nodes took fewer than 100 upstream calls: yes
element uses the pool: yes
copy uses the pool: no
moved-to uses the pool: yes
bytes still held upstream after the pool died: 0

Writing an STL-compatible allocator

Theory

Before pmr, the way to put a container on a pool was a custom allocator type. It is still common in trading code because it avoids the virtual call and lets the compiler inline the pool. Since C++11, std::allocator_traits fills in almost everything, so the minimal allocator is short.

The minimal requirements

  • using value_type = T;
  • T* allocate(std::size_t n): room for n objects, uninitialised. Throws on failure (do not return null).
  • void deallocate(T* p, std::size_t n): n is the same value passed to allocate.
  • A converting constructor template <class U> A(const A<U>&) noexcept, so the container can make an allocator for a different type from yours.
  • operator==: two allocators compare equal when memory from one can be freed through the other. (!= is generated from == in C++20.)
  • Copies must compare equal to the original and share its memory source. In practice an allocator is a handle (a pointer to the real pool), not the pool itself.

Everything else (construct, destroy, max_size, pointer, the propagate_on_* traits, is_always_equal) has a default in allocator_traits. is_always_equal defaults to std::is_empty, so a stateless allocator is always equal.

rebind: why std::list never allocates a T

std::list<int, A<int>> never allocates an int. It allocates nodes (two pointers and an int), using std::allocator_traits<A<int>>::rebind_alloc<Node>, which for a class template A<T> without a rebind member is simply A<Node>, built from your allocator through the converting constructor. Maps, sets and unordered_map (nodes plus a bucket array) do the same, and deque rebinds for its block map.

Consequences:

  • A pool sized for sizeof(T) is the wrong size for a list. Size the pool from the type the allocator is instantiated with, inside allocate, not from the type the user wrote.
  • Several rebound copies can exist at once (node allocator, bucket allocator), so they must share state through a pointer, and that state must handle different sizes or keep one pool per size.
  • Since C++20 std::allocator no longer has a rebind member. Code that writes A::rebind<U>::other by hand should use allocator_traits instead.
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <list>
#include <new>
#include <vector>

template <class T>
struct Tracing {
    using value_type = T;
    Tracing() = default;
    template <class U> Tracing(const Tracing<U>&) noexcept {}
    T* allocate(std::size_t n) {
        std::printf("  allocate %zu x %zu bytes%s\n", n, sizeof(T), sizeof(T) == sizeof(int) ? " (an int)" : " (not an int)");
        return static_cast<T*>(::operator new(n * sizeof(T)));
    }
    void deallocate(T* p, std::size_t) noexcept { ::operator delete(p); }
    template <class U> bool operator==(const Tracing<U>&) const noexcept { return true; }
};

int main() {
    std::puts("vector<int>:");
    std::vector<int, Tracing<int>> v;
    v.reserve(4);
    std::puts("list<int>:");
    std::list<int, Tracing<int>> l;
    l.push_back(1);
    l.push_back(2);
}

Expected output (the node size is 24 bytes on both libstdc++ and libc++ for 64-bit targets, but it is printed indirectly so the test does not depend on it):

vector<int>:
  allocate 4 x 4 bytes (an int)
list<int>:
  allocate 1 x 24 bytes (not an int)
  allocate 1 x 24 bytes (not an int)

Debugging pools

Theory

A pool hides memory bugs. Freed blocks stay inside a buffer that the system allocator considers live, so AddressSanitizer and Valgrind see every access as valid. A use-after-free reads another live object, a double free hands one block out twice, and both surface far from their cause.

Defences, from cheapest to strongest:

  • Poisoning. Fill freed blocks (after the link) with 0xDD and new ones with 0xCD. Stale reads show obvious values, and checking the pattern on allocation catches writes after free.
  • Canaries (guard words) before and after each payload, checked on free, catch overruns.
  • An in-use bit per block turns a double free into an immediate report instead of a corrupted list.
  • Pointer checks. On free, assert the pointer is inside a chunk and on a block boundary: (p - base) % block == 0.
  • ASan manual poisoning. <sanitizer/asan_interface.h> provides ASAN_POISON_MEMORY_REGION(addr, size) and ASAN_UNPOISON_MEMORY_REGION. Poison a block in deallocate (except while the pool itself touches the next pointer) and unpoison it in allocate. ASan then reports use-after-poison at the exact faulty access. The macros compile to nothing when ASan is off. The reading section has a pool that does this.
  • A pass-through switch. A build flag that sends every block to malloc/free lets ASan, Valgrind and heap profilers see everything.
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstring>
#include <new>

// Debug pool: poisons freed blocks and verifies the poison on reuse.
class DebugPool {
    struct Node { Node* next; };
    static constexpr std::size_t kBlock = 32, kCount = 4;
    static constexpr unsigned char kFreed = 0xDD;
    alignas(std::max_align_t) std::byte buf_[kBlock * kCount];
    Node* head_ = nullptr;

    static void poison(void* p) { std::memset(static_cast<std::byte*>(p) + sizeof(Node), kFreed, kBlock - sizeof(Node)); }
    static bool poison_intact(const void* p) {
        auto* b = static_cast<const unsigned char*>(p) + sizeof(Node);
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < kBlock - sizeof(Node); ++i) if (b[i] != kFreed) return false;
        return true;
    }
public:
    DebugPool() { for (std::size_t i = kCount; i-- > 0;) deallocate(buf_ + i * kBlock); }
    void* allocate() {
        Node* n = head_;
        if (!n) return nullptr;
        head_ = n->next;
        if (!poison_intact(n)) std::printf("pool: block %td was written after it was freed\n", (reinterpret_cast<std::byte*>(n) - buf_) / std::ptrdiff_t{kBlock});
        return n;
    }
    void deallocate(void* p) { poison(p); head_ = ::new (p) Node{head_}; }
};

int main() {
    DebugPool pool;
    auto* counters = static_cast<int*>(pool.allocate());
    counters[0] = 0;
    counters[3] = 0;
    pool.deallocate(counters);
    counters[3] = 42;              // bug: stale pointer written after free
    void* again = pool.allocate(); // LIFO: the same block comes back and the check fires
    pool.deallocate(again);
}
pool: block 0 was written after it was freed

The program is tagged ub because it writes to freed storage on purpose. The pool found the bug at the block's next allocation, not at the write; only ASan poisoning or the pass-through switch catches the write itself.

Measuring the benefit

Theory

Claims like "pools are 10 times faster" are only useful with the workload and the method attached. A sound allocator benchmark:

  1. Uses a realistic pattern. Allocate-then-free in a tight loop flatters every allocator (one block bounces in a thread cache); random churn over a live set of a few thousand objects is closer to real use.
  2. Touches the memory, so cache misses count and the compiler cannot elide the allocation ([expr.new] allows removing new/delete pairs).
  3. Repeats and reports the median plus the spread, as ratios against a baseline measured in the same process.
  4. Looks at the tail (p99, p99.9 of per-operation or per-batch times) when latency matters, since the median hides the spikes that pools remove.
#include <algorithm>
#include <chrono>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory_resource>
#include <new>
#include <vector>

class FixedPool {
    union Block { Block* next; alignas(std::max_align_t) unsigned char data[64]; };
    std::vector<Block> storage_;
    Block* head_ = nullptr;
public:
    explicit FixedPool(std::size_t n) : storage_(n) {
        for (auto& b : storage_) { b.next = head_; head_ = &b; }
    }
    void* allocate() { Block* b = head_; head_ = b->next; return b; }
    void deallocate(void* p) { auto* b = static_cast<Block*>(p); b->next = head_; head_ = b; }
};

constexpr int kSlots = 4096, kOps = 2'000'000, kReps = 7;

// Random churn: each step frees the object in a random slot, or allocates one if the slot is empty.
template <class Alloc, class Free>
static double churn(Alloc alloc, Free release) {
    std::vector<void*> live(kSlots, nullptr);
    std::uint32_t x = 12345;
    auto t0 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    for (int i = 0; i < kOps; ++i) {
        x = x * 1664525u + 1013904223u;
        void*& s = live[x >> 20];
        if (s) { release(s); s = nullptr; }
        else { s = alloc(); static_cast<char*>(s)[0] = 1; }
    }
    auto t1 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    for (void* p : live) if (p) release(p);
    return std::chrono::duration<double, std::nano>(t1 - t0).count() / kOps;
}

template <class F>
static double median_of(F f) {
    std::vector<double> v;
    for (int r = 0; r < kReps; ++r) v.push_back(f());
    std::sort(v.begin(), v.end());
    std::printf("    runs: min %.2f  max %.2f ns/op\n", v.front(), v.back());
    return v[v.size() / 2];
}

int main() {
    std::puts("malloc/free:");
    double m = median_of([] { return churn([] { return std::malloc(64); }, [](void* p) { std::free(p); }); });
    std::puts("fixed pool:");
    FixedPool pool(kSlots);
    double p = median_of([&] { return churn([&] { return pool.allocate(); }, [&](void* q) { pool.deallocate(q); }); });
    std::puts("pmr::unsynchronized_pool_resource:");
    std::pmr::unsynchronized_pool_resource upr;
    double u = median_of([&] { return churn([&] { return upr.allocate(64); }, [&](void* q) { upr.deallocate(q, 64); }); });
    std::puts("pmr::synchronized_pool_resource:");
    std::pmr::synchronized_pool_resource spr;
    double s = median_of([&] { return churn([&] { return spr.allocate(64); }, [&](void* q) { spr.deallocate(q, 64); }); });
    std::printf("median ns/op: malloc %.2f, pool %.2f, unsync pmr %.2f, sync pmr %.2f\n", m, p, u, s);
    std::printf("speed-up vs malloc: pool %.1fx, unsync pmr %.1fx, sync pmr %.1fx\n", m / p, m / u, m / s);
}

Representative results on an Apple M1 (macOS libmalloc, -O2, median of 7 runs of 2 million operations, 64-byte blocks). The program is tagged ub so timings are never compared.

Allocatorclang + libc++: ns/opratio vs mallocGCC + libstdc++: ns/opratio vs malloc
malloc/free28.21.0×28.41.0×
Fixed pool (free list)6.84.1× faster6.94.1× faster
unsynchronized_pool_resource12.42.3× faster36.60.8× (slower)
synchronized_pool_resource20.61.4× faster46.20.6× (slower)

What to take from it:

  • The hand-written pool is about 4 times faster than malloc with both compilers, and part of its 7 ns is the loop itself, so the pool operation is cheaper still.
  • The two standard libraries' pmr pools differ by about 3 times. libc++ keeps a plain free list per size class, so deallocate is a push. libstdc++ tracks blocks with a bitmap per chunk, so deallocate must first find the chunk that owns the pointer (a binary search over chunks sorted by address). A separate test on the same machine timed shuffled deallocations at about 5 ns on libc++ and 32 to 41 ns on libstdc++, rising with the number of chunks. "Use pmr" is not automatically a speed-up: measure it with your library.
  • Variance is real: the first GCC run after the build had malloc anywhere from 39.6 to 61.4 ns/op. Run the benchmark several times, and quote ratios with the platform (glibc's tcache is very quick for this pattern).

Concept and tricky questions

Drills

ConceptWhy is allocation from a fixed-size pool O(1), and why is it more predictable than malloc, not just faster on average?

Answer

Answer. Allocation pops the head of a singly linked free list and freeing pushes onto it: no search, no size lookup, no lock and no system call. The cost is the same on every call because there is no slow path, apart from a possible cache miss on the block itself.

Why. malloc's fast path is also tens of nanoseconds, so "faster" is only part of the answer. Its slow paths (refilling a thread cache, a lock, mmap or brk, first-touch page faults) cost microseconds at times the caller cannot control, and a pre-faulted pool has none. The common weak answer is "because the pool is in cache"; locality helps, but the structural reason is a constant number of loads and stores.

ConceptWhat does "intrusive" mean in "intrusive free list", and what is the per-block memory overhead of such a pool?

Answer

Answer. The list links are stored inside the elements themselves: each free block holds the pointer to the next free block in its own first bytes. The overhead per block is zero beyond rounding the block up to at least pointer size and to the alignment.

Why. A free block holds no user data, so its bytes can be the list node; once handed out, the user's object overwrites the link, which is no longer needed. malloc keeps a size header or page metadata so free(p) can find the size; a pool does not, because all blocks have one size. Wrong answer: "the list costs one pointer per block", which describes a non-intrusive list stored beside the blocks.

TrickyYou build a pool for char objects (or std::uint16_t). What is the smallest block size it can use on a 64-bit machine, and how would you get closer to the object size?

Answer

Answer. 8 bytes, because each free block must hold a void* for the free list. To approach 1 or 2 bytes per object, store the link as a small index (for example a 16-bit block number) instead of a pointer, or keep a separate bitmap of free blocks.

Why. The intrusive design reuses the block as a list node, so the block must be at least as big as the node and aligned for it. People answer "1 byte" and then write an 8-byte pointer into a 1-byte block, which overwrites the neighbouring blocks and runs off the end of the buffer (the reading section has this bug). With 16-bit indices the block must still be 2 bytes and the pool can hold at most 65,535 blocks. A bitmap costs one bit per block and makes allocation a "find first set bit" scan, which is O(n/64) words in the worst case.

TrickyA colleague writes a pool allocator whose pool is sized for sizeof(T) and uses it as std::list<int, PoolAlloc<int>>. The pool is built for 4-byte blocks. What actually happens?

Answer

Answer. std::list never allocates an int. It rebinds the allocator to its node type (two pointers plus the int, 24 bytes on 64-bit) through allocator_traits::rebind_alloc, which constructs PoolAlloc<Node> from PoolAlloc<int>. If the allocator's pool is keyed on the user's T instead of the type it is instantiated with, it hands out 4-byte blocks for 24-byte nodes and the list writes over neighbouring blocks.

Why. Node-based containers (list, map, set, unordered_*) all allocate internal types. The correct design picks the pool inside allocate from sizeof(value_type) of the rebound allocator, or keeps pools for several sizes behind a shared pointer. unordered_map also allocates a bucket array with n > 1, so multi-object requests must be handled too (usually by forwarding to operator new). The wrong answer is "the pool sees 4-byte requests"; it never sees one.

ConceptHow does a pool affect internal and external fragmentation?

Answer

Answer. Inside one pool there is no external fragmentation, because every free block fits every request. Internal fragmentation is the gap between the block size and the object size (plus rounding to alignment). Across the whole program, pools can increase memory use, because each pool keeps its peak footprint and free blocks of one size cannot serve another size.

Why. External fragmentation means "enough free bytes in total but no hole large enough", which needs holes of different sizes. Equal blocks remove that. Size-class designs trade internal fragmentation (a 65-byte request in a 128-byte class wastes 63 bytes) for the number of pools. The memory held by idle pools is sometimes called "stranded" memory. The wrong answer is "pools eliminate fragmentation": they remove the external kind inside one pool and add internal and cross-pool waste. Ch 10 covers the general theory.

Concept"Design a memory pool." What do you ask before writing code, and which decisions does the design come down to?

Answer

Answer. Ask: one object size or many; is the peak live count known; which threads allocate and which free (and can a block be freed by a different thread); is tail latency or throughput the goal; must memory go back to the OS; what happens on exhaustion. Then decide: block size round_up(max(size, sizeof(void*)), align); an intrusive LIFO free list; one pre-faulted buffer (fixed capacity) or a chain of chunks (growth that never moves blocks); the exhaustion policy (null, throw, or a counted fallback to malloc); thread safety (one pool per thread, a mutex, or a tagged lock-free list); the API (raw blocks, typed create/destroy, an STL or pmr adapter); and a debug mode (poisoning, in-use bits, ASan poisoning, a malloc pass-through).

Why. The interviewer grades the trade-offs more than the free list, which takes five minutes. Weak answers jump straight to code, forget the minimum block size and alignment, or use a std::vector<void*> free stack that itself allocates. Say the memory consequence too: freed blocks go back on the free list, not to the system, so the process's RSS stays at the peak until the pool is destroyed (a chunk can be returned only when all its blocks are free, which needs per-chunk counts).

ConceptExplain how std::pmr works. What does a std::pmr::vector<int> store, what happens when it grows, and why can one function accept vectors backed by different resources?

Answer

Answer. std::pmr::vector<int> is std::vector<int, std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<int>>, and that allocator is one pointer to a memory_resource. Growing calls allocator_traits::allocate, which calls resource->allocate(n * sizeof(int), alignof(int)), a non-virtual function that calls the private virtual do_allocate. The allocator type is the same whatever the resource, so the container type is too, and the choice of memory is made at run time by the pointer.

Why. A custom allocator type makes vector<int, PoolAlloc<int>> a different type from vector<int>, which spreads through every interface. pmr trades that for a virtual call per allocation, one extra pointer per container, and the propagation rules (a copy uses the default resource, assignment does not propagate). Nested pmr elements receive the same resource through uses-allocator construction. Two wrong answers: "pmr containers are a separate, faster implementation" (it is the same container code with a different allocator), and "the container owns its resource" (it holds only a pointer, so the resource must outlive it).

ConceptWhen would you choose std::pmr::unsynchronized_pool_resource over synchronized_pool_resource, and what happens if two threads share the unsynchronised one?

Answer

Answer. Use the unsynchronised one when a single thread owns the resource, for example a per-thread or per-request resource, or a single-threaded game loop. It avoids locking. Sharing it between threads without external locking is a data race, which is undefined behaviour and in practice corrupts the free lists (two threads get the same block).

Why. The synchronised version pays for thread safety: libc++ wraps an unsynchronised pool in one mutex, and libstdc++ keeps per-thread pools behind a shared_mutex. In the benchmark it cost about 1.7 times the unsynchronised one on libc++, with no contention at all. The wrong answer is "the race is harmless because blocks are all the same size": two threads popping the same free-list head get the same block.

Trickystd::pmr::vector<int> v(&pool); then auto w = v;. Which memory resource does w use? And auto m = std::move(v);?

Answer

Answer. w uses the default resource (get_default_resource(), normally new_delete_resource()), not pool. m uses pool, and it takes over v's buffer.

Why. Copy construction obtains the new allocator from allocator_traits::select_on_container_copy_construction, and polymorphic_allocator defines that to return a default-constructed allocator. The design reason is that a resource is often scoped to a request or a frame, and a copy may outlive it. Move construction always takes the source's allocator. To copy into the same pool, say so: std::pmr::vector<int> w(v, &pool);. Most candidates assume the copy shares the resource, which leads to silent heap allocation on a hot path.

TrickyExplain the ABA problem in a lock-free free list and give two ways to fix it.

Answer

Answer. Thread 1 reads head = A and next = B, then stalls. Thread 2 pops A, pops B, and pushes A back. Thread 1 resumes and its compare_exchange(head, A, B) succeeds because head is A again, so it installs B as the head even though B is in use. B is then handed out twice. Fixes: a version counter compared together with the pointer (tagged pointer or double-width CAS), or safe memory reclamation (hazard pointers, epochs) so A cannot be recycled while a thread is still reading it.

Why. CAS compares values, not history. Pools make ABA very likely because LIFO reuse returns the same address immediately. A packed 32-bit index plus 32-bit tag in one 64-bit atomic avoids needing a 128-bit CAS. The tag can wrap after 232 changes, which is accepted as practically impossible during one stall. Wrong answers: "use memory_order_seq_cst" (ordering does not detect reuse) and "ABA cannot happen because we never free memory" (never freeing prevents a crash on reading A->next, but not the stale CAS).

ConceptThread-local pools avoid locking. What is the hard case, and how do production allocators handle it?

Answer

Answer. A cross-thread free: an object allocated from thread A's pool is freed by thread B. Common designs either send the object back to its owner through a queue, or give each pool a lock-free "remote free" stack that other threads push onto and the owner drains in batches when its local list is empty.

Why. The tempting wrong answer is "B pushes it onto A's list", which is a data race on A's head. Putting the block on B's own list works only if all pools share one block size and never release chunks, and memory then migrates until one thread holds everything. mimalloc and snmalloc use remote free lists. Trading systems usually solve it architecturally: the thread that allocates an order also frees it.

TrickyYour code reads an object after returning it to a pool, but AddressSanitizer reports nothing. Why, and how do you make ASan see it?

Answer

Answer. ASan tracks allocations made through malloc/new. The pool's chunk was allocated once and is still live, so every byte in it is addressable as far as ASan knows. Use ASan's manual poisoning API (ASAN_POISON_MEMORY_REGION in deallocate, ASAN_UNPOISON_MEMORY_REGION in allocate) or a debug switch that sends every block to malloc.

Why. ASan poisons a heap chunk's shadow memory at free, and a pool never calls free for one block. Worse, LIFO reuse means the stale pointer usually reaches a new, live object; if that object has the same type and was created directly in the old storage, [basic.life] even makes the old pointer refer to it, so the access is defined and only logically wrong. The wrong answer is "ASan catches every use-after-free". Valgrind has the same blind spot (its mempool client requests fix it).

ConceptLIFO free lists are the default. What do they buy, and when would you deliberately make the free list FIFO?

Answer

Answer. LIFO returns the most recently freed block, which is probably still in cache, and it needs only a head pointer. FIFO (a queue with head and tail) delays reuse, which turns use-after-free bugs into reads of poisoned, unused blocks instead of reads of a live object, so debug builds sometimes use it.

Why. The cache argument is the main reason allocators default to LIFO: a hot loop that frees and allocates touches the same few cache lines. FIFO costs a tail pointer and spreads accesses over the whole pool. A "quarantine" (hold freed blocks for N frees before reuse) is the same idea, and ASan's own heap uses one. The wrong answer is that FIFO is "fairer" or reduces fragmentation; with equal-size blocks the order changes only cache behaviour and bug visibility.

TrickyTwo std::pmr::vector<int> objects use different pool resources. What does a = std::move(b); cost, and what about std::swap(a, b)?

Answer

Answer. The move assignment is O(n): the allocator does not propagate, the resources are unequal, so a cannot steal b's buffer and instead move-assigns the elements into storage from its own resource. swap with unequal allocators that do not propagate is undefined behaviour.

Why. propagate_on_container_move_assignment is false_type for polymorphic_allocator. The container may only steal the buffer when the allocators compare equal, which for pmr means a.resource()->is_equal(*b.resource()). The usual wrong answer is "moves are always O(1) pointer swaps". That is true for std::allocator (always equal), not for stateful allocators. Because it may allocate, it can throw, so vector's move assignment is noexcept only when the allocator propagates or is always equal.

ConceptWhen is a hand-written pool worse than plain malloc?

Answer

Answer. When sizes vary widely (one pool per size strands memory), when objects are freed by other threads (a shared pool needs a lock, while malloc already has per-thread caches), when memory must go back to the system after a burst, and when the allocation was never the bottleneck. A pool shared behind one mutex is often slower than a modern malloc's lock-free thread-cache fast path.

Why. jemalloc, tcmalloc, mimalloc and glibc's tcache are already size-class pools with per-thread caches, so a pool beats them only by removing what they must keep: the size lookup, the cross-thread handling and the slow paths. The pool also costs debuggability (ASan sees one big allocation). The wrong answer is "a pool is always faster": profile first, and the benchmark in this chapter shows a standard pool resource losing to malloc.

TrickyA class gives itself pooled allocation by defining static void* operator new(std::size_t) that returns a block from a pool sized for sizeof(Base). What breaks when someone derives from it?

Answer

Answer. Class-specific operator new is inherited, so new Derived calls it with sizeof(Derived), which may be larger than the block size. The derived object then overruns its block. The operator must check the size and forward other sizes to ::operator new, and the matching operator delete(void*, std::size_t) must do the same.

Why. The size parameter exists precisely for this case. Deleting through a base pointer is fine only if the base has a virtual destructor, because then the sized operator delete receives the dynamic type's size. Without a virtual destructor, delete base_ptr is undefined anyway. The common wrong answer is "nothing, operator new is not inherited"; it is, like any static member function. A safer design is to make the pooled class final, or to keep pooling outside the class (Ch 16).

Predict the output and find the bug

Drills

OutputWhat does this print?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>

class Pool {
    struct Node { Node* next; };
    alignas(16) std::byte buf_[16 * 4];
    Node* head_ = nullptr;
public:
    Pool() { for (int i = 3; i >= 0; --i) deallocate(buf_ + i * 16); }
    void* allocate() { if (!head_) return nullptr; Node* n = head_; head_ = n->next; return n; }
    void deallocate(void* p) { head_ = ::new (p) Node{head_}; }
    int index(const void* p) const { return static_cast<int>((static_cast<const std::byte*>(p) - buf_) / 16); }
};

int main() {
    Pool pool;
    void* a = pool.allocate();
    void* b = pool.allocate();
    void* c = pool.allocate();
    std::printf("%d %d %d\n", pool.index(a), pool.index(b), pool.index(c));
    pool.deallocate(a);
    pool.deallocate(b);
    void* x = pool.allocate();
    void* y = pool.allocate();
    void* z = pool.allocate();
    void* w = pool.allocate();
    std::printf("%d %d %d %s\n", pool.index(x), pool.index(y), pool.index(z), w ? "more" : "empty");
}
Answer
0 1 2
1 0 3 empty

Answer. The constructor pushes blocks 3, 2, 1, 0, so 0 is on top and the first three allocations get 0, 1, 2. Freeing a then b pushes 0 then 1, so the list is 1 → 0 → 3. The next three allocations return 1, 0, 3, and the fourth finds the list empty.

Why. The free list is a stack: last freed, first reused. Many people predict "0 1 3" because they expect blocks to come back in address order or in the order they were freed. That would need a FIFO queue or a sorted list, which a pool does not keep.

Find the bugA pool for small integers. The author used memcpy for the link to avoid alignment problems. What is wrong?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstring>

class IntPool {
    std::size_t n_;
    unsigned char* buf_;
    unsigned char* head_ = nullptr;
public:
    explicit IntPool(std::size_t n) : n_(n), buf_(new unsigned char[n * sizeof(int)]) {
        for (std::size_t i = n; i-- > 0;) {
            unsigned char* block = buf_ + i * sizeof(int);
            std::memcpy(block, &head_, sizeof head_);   // store the link
            head_ = block;
        }
    }
    ~IntPool() { delete[] buf_; }
    int* allocate() {
        if (!head_) return nullptr;
        unsigned char* b = head_;
        std::memcpy(&head_, b, sizeof head_);
        return reinterpret_cast<int*>(b);
    }
};

int main() {
    IntPool pool(8);
    int* p = pool.allocate();
    *p = 1;
    std::printf("%d\n", *p);
}
Answer

Answer. The block size is sizeof(int) (4 bytes), but each link is a pointer (8 bytes). Writing the link for the last block writes 4 bytes past the end of the buffer, and every other link overwrites half of the next block's link. ASan reports a heap-buffer-overflow in memcpy during construction.

Why. The minimum block size of an intrusive pool is max(sizeof(T), sizeof(void*)), rounded to alignment. memcpy fixes alignment, not size. Without ASan the program may even appear to work, because the first allocation reads the link written last, before anything clobbered it, and the overflow lands in malloc's padding; the corruption shows up later as a garbage pointer from a later allocation. Fix: block = std::max(sizeof(int), sizeof(void*)), or 16-bit indices as links.

Find the bugEach session gets its own counting resource. The author reasoned that "they all end up in new and delete anyway" when writing do_is_equal. What does this print, and what goes wrong with real pools?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory_resource>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class SessionResource : public std::pmr::memory_resource {
public:
    long live = 0;                       // bytes this session has outstanding
private:
    void* do_allocate(std::size_t n, std::size_t a) override {
        live += static_cast<long>(n);
        return std::pmr::new_delete_resource()->allocate(n, a);
    }
    void do_deallocate(void* p, std::size_t n, std::size_t a) override {
        live -= static_cast<long>(n);
        std::pmr::new_delete_resource()->deallocate(p, n, a);
    }
    bool do_is_equal(const memory_resource&) const noexcept override { return true; }
};

int main() {
    SessionResource a, b;
    {
        std::pmr::vector<int> va(&a), vb(&b);
        vb.assign(100, 7);
        va = std::move(vb);
        std::printf("va size %zu, vb size %zu\n", va.size(), vb.size());
    }
    std::printf("a live %ld bytes, b live %ld bytes\n", a.live, b.live);
}
Answer
va size 100, vb size 0
a live -400 bytes, b live 400 bytes

Answer. Because the allocators compare equal, the move assignment steals vb's 400-byte buffer, which came from b. When va dies it returns that buffer to a. Session a's books show minus 400 bytes and session b's show a 400-byte leak that never goes away. With two real pool resources, the block would be pushed onto the wrong pool's free list, and destroying b would free a chunk that a still hands out: a use-after-free.

Why. is_equal is a correctness contract ([mem.res.private]): return true only if memory allocated by one resource can be deallocated by the other. polymorphic_allocator's == calls it, and containers use that answer to decide whether a move assignment, a swap or a splice may hand a buffer from one allocator to the other. The usual wrong belief is that it is an optimisation hint. Fix: return this == &other;. The move assignment then becomes an element-wise move into memory from a (O(n)), and both counters end at 0.

Find the bugA block is read after release, in a pool that uses ASan's manual poisoning API. What does the sanitizer build report, and where?

#include <sanitizer/asan_interface.h>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>

class Pool {
    struct Node { Node* next; };
    static constexpr std::size_t kBlock = 16, kCount = 8;
    std::byte* buf_ = static_cast<std::byte*>(::operator new(kBlock * kCount));
    Node* head_ = nullptr;
public:
    Pool() { for (std::size_t i = kCount; i-- > 0;) deallocate(buf_ + i * kBlock); }
    ~Pool() { ASAN_UNPOISON_MEMORY_REGION(buf_, kBlock * kCount); ::operator delete(buf_); }
    void* allocate() {
        Node* n = head_;
        if (!n) return nullptr;
        ASAN_UNPOISON_MEMORY_REGION(n, kBlock);
        head_ = n->next;
        return n;
    }
    void deallocate(void* p) {
        head_ = ::new (p) Node{head_};
        ASAN_POISON_MEMORY_REGION(p, kBlock);   // nobody may touch a free block
    }
};

struct Order { int id; int qty; };

int main() {
    Pool pool;
    auto* o = ::new (pool.allocate()) Order{7, 100};
    pool.deallocate(o);
    std::printf("qty %d\n", o->qty);   // read after release
}
Answer

Answer. Under ASan the read o->qty is reported as use-after-poison at that exact line, with the poisoned region shown as f7 ("poisoned by user") in the shadow map. Without ASan the macros expand to nothing and the program prints whatever is in the block, which is undefined behaviour (the harness tags it ub).

Why. Poisoning in deallocate and unpoisoning in allocate gives the pool the heap's error detection. The pool must unpoison before reading n->next, and the destructor before handing the buffer back. ASan poisons in 8-byte granules, so blocks should be multiples of 8 and 8-aligned. The common wrong answer is "ASan is blind to pools", which is true only until the pool tells it. With LIFO reuse the next allocate unpoisons the block again, so debug builds pair this with a FIFO quarantine.

OutputThe default resource is set to null_memory_resource() to catch hidden heap use. What does this print?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory_resource>
#include <new>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::pmr::unsynchronized_pool_resource pool(std::pmr::new_delete_resource());
    std::pmr::set_default_resource(std::pmr::null_memory_resource());

    std::pmr::vector<int> prices(&pool);
    for (int i = 0; i < 100; ++i) prices.push_back(i);
    std::puts("filled from the pool");

    try {
        std::pmr::vector<int> copy = prices;
        std::printf("copy has %zu\n", copy.size());
    } catch (const std::bad_alloc&) {
        std::puts("copy threw bad_alloc");
    }

    std::pmr::vector<int> copy2(prices, &pool);
    std::printf("copy2 has %zu\n", copy2.size());
    std::pmr::set_default_resource(nullptr);   // restore new_delete_resource
}
Answer
filled from the pool
copy threw bad_alloc
copy2 has 100

Answer. Filling works because prices uses the pool, whose upstream was passed explicitly. The plain copy uses the default resource, which is now the null resource, so its allocation throws std::bad_alloc. The copy that names &pool succeeds.

Why. select_on_container_copy_construction for polymorphic_allocator returns a default-constructed allocator, which captures get_default_resource(). Setting the default to the null resource in tests is a cheap way to find every place that silently falls back to the heap. Two details: the pool was built with an explicit upstream before the default changed (a pool built with no argument would capture the default at construction), and set_default_resource(nullptr) restores new_delete_resource(). Most people predict "copy has 100", assuming the copy inherits the pool.

Find the bugWhy does this allocator fail to compile with std::list?

#include <cstddef>
#include <list>
#include <new>

template <class T>
struct PoolAlloc {
    using value_type = T;
    PoolAlloc() = default;
    T* allocate(std::size_t n) { return static_cast<T*>(::operator new(n * sizeof(T))); }
    void deallocate(T* p, std::size_t) noexcept { ::operator delete(p); }
    bool operator==(const PoolAlloc&) const noexcept { return true; }
};

int main() {
    PoolAlloc<int> alloc;
    std::list<int, PoolAlloc<int>> l(alloc);   // the list must build PoolAlloc<Node> from alloc
    l.push_back(1);
}
Answer

Answer. It has no converting constructor template <class U> PoolAlloc(const PoolAlloc<U>&). The list stores an allocator for its node type, PoolAlloc<Node>, and must construct it from the PoolAlloc<int> it was given. Both GCC and Clang reject the program. Interestingly, std::list<int, PoolAlloc<int>> l; alone compiles, because then the list default-constructs its node allocator and never converts; the error appears as soon as an allocator object is passed in, which is exactly what a stateful pool allocator needs.

Why. The Allocator requirements say A a(b) must work where b is an allocator for another type, and that the two must compare equal afterwards. allocator_traits::rebind_alloc names the type, but only the converting constructor can create the object. A defaulted constructor does not help, because the rebound allocator must share the original's state. The operator== here also only compares same-type allocators; making it a template over U is the usual, more general form.

Find the bugAn error path frees a block twice. What does the program print, and does ASan notice?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>

class Pool {
    struct Node { Node* next; };
    alignas(16) std::byte buf_[32 * 8];
    Node* head_ = nullptr;
public:
    Pool() { for (int i = 7; i >= 0; --i) deallocate(buf_ + i * 32); }
    void* allocate() { if (!head_) return nullptr; Node* n = head_; head_ = n->next; return n; }
    void deallocate(void* p) { head_ = ::new (p) Node{head_}; }
};

int main() {
    Pool pool;
    void* msg = pool.allocate();
    pool.deallocate(msg);   // normal release
    pool.deallocate(msg);   // error path releases it again
    void* a = pool.allocate();
    void* b = pool.allocate();
    std::printf("a == b: %s\n", a == b ? "yes" : "no");
    void* c = pool.allocate();
    std::printf("c == a: %s\n", c == a ? "yes" : "no");
}
Answer
a == b: yes
c == a: yes

Answer. The second deallocate pushes the block again, and its link now points to itself: the list is msg → msg → msg …. Every later allocation returns the same block, so a, b and c are all equal. Two live objects share memory, and the rest of the pool is lost. ASan says nothing: the harness runs this program under ASan and it is clean.

Why. After the first free, head = msg. The second free writes msg->next = head, which is msg itself, creating a cycle of length one. With malloc, ASan would report attempting double-free. A debug pool should keep an in-use bit per block and check it in deallocate, or check that the block being freed is not the current head (cheap, catches the immediate case only). The usual prediction is "a == b: yes, c == a: no", which assumes the list still continues past the duplicate; the self-loop means it never does.

OutputA power-of-two size-class table. What does it print?

#include <algorithm>
#include <bit>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>

constexpr std::size_t kMinClass = 8, kMaxClass = 4096;

static std::size_t class_size(std::size_t n) {
    if (n > kMaxClass) return 0;                 // 0 means: go upstream
    return std::max(kMinClass, std::bit_ceil(n));
}

int main() {
    for (std::size_t n : {1, 8, 9, 64, 65, 200, 4096, 5000}) {
        std::size_t c = class_size(n);
        if (c) std::printf("%4zu -> %4zu (waste %zu)\n", n, c, c - n);
        else std::printf("%4zu -> upstream\n", n);
    }
}
Answer
   1 ->    8 (waste 7)
   8 ->    8 (waste 0)
   9 ->   16 (waste 7)
  64 ->   64 (waste 0)
  65 ->  128 (waste 63)
 200 ->  256 (waste 56)
4096 -> 4096 (waste 0)
5000 -> upstream

Answer. Each request rounds up to the next power of two, with 8 as the smallest class (the free-list link needs 8 bytes). 65 bytes wastes 63 and 200 wastes 56, while exact powers of two waste nothing. Requests above 4096 bypass the pools.

Why. Power-of-two classes make the class index a bit operation (std::bit_width(n - 1)), but the worst-case internal fragmentation is just under 50 percent. That is why jemalloc and tcmalloc use four or more classes per power of two (for example 80, 96, 112, 128) above the small range. A common slip is mapping 64 to 128 (rounding n instead of n - 1), or 1 to 1, forgetting the 8-byte minimum.

Find the bugTwo worker threads share one pool. What goes wrong, and what does ThreadSanitizer say?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>
#include <thread>

class Pool {
    struct Node { Node* next; };
    alignas(16) std::byte buf_[64 * 256];
    Node* head_ = nullptr;
public:
    Pool() { for (int i = 255; i >= 0; --i) deallocate(buf_ + i * 64); }
    void* allocate() { if (!head_) return nullptr; Node* n = head_; head_ = n->next; return n; }
    void deallocate(void* p) { head_ = ::new (p) Node{head_}; }
};

static Pool pool;

static void worker() {
    for (int i = 0; i < 20000; ++i)
        if (void* p = pool.allocate()) pool.deallocate(p);
}

int main() {
    std::thread t1(worker), t2(worker);
    t1.join();
    t2.join();
    std::puts("done");
}
Answer

Answer. head_ is read and written by both threads with no synchronisation: a data race, so the behaviour is undefined. TSan reports WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race on head_ (and on the next fields). In practice both threads can pop the same block, or a push can be lost, so blocks are handed out twice or leak.

Why. Pop is a read-modify-write of head_ in three steps. If both threads read the same head before either writes, both return the same block. The fixes are a std::mutex around both operations, one pool per thread, or a lock-free list with ABA protection (the coding section builds one). The program may print "done" and look fine in a normal run, which is why it is tagged ub and checked with TSan.

Find the bugA pool of 24-byte blocks is reused for a SIMD-friendly vector type. What does the sanitizer build report?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>

struct alignas(16) Vec4 { float x, y, z, w; };

class Pool24 {
    struct Node { Node* next; };
    alignas(16) std::byte buf_[24 * 4];
    Node* head_ = nullptr;
public:
    Pool24() { for (int i = 3; i >= 0; --i) head_ = ::new (buf_ + i * 24) Node{head_}; }
    void* allocate() { Node* n = head_; head_ = n->next; return n; }
};

int main() {
    Pool24 pool;
    auto* a = ::new (pool.allocate()) Vec4{1, 2, 3, 4};
    auto* b = ::new (pool.allocate()) Vec4{5, 6, 7, 8};
    std::printf("%g %g\n", a->w, b->w);
}
Answer

Answer. Block 1 starts at offset 24, which is 8-aligned but not 16-aligned, so constructing a Vec4 there is undefined behaviour. UBSan (part of the harness's ASan build) reports constructor call on misaligned address … which requires 16 byte alignment (or "member access within misaligned address").

Why. The block size must be a multiple of the alignment of every type stored in it: round_up(24, 16) = 32. Sizing blocks by sizeof alone works only when sizeof is already a multiple of the alignment, which is true for complete types (a type's size is always a multiple of its alignment) but not for an arbitrary byte count like 24 chosen for a different type. On x86 a misaligned movaps faults; on ARM64 ordinary loads tolerate it, which is how this bug survives testing on one platform.

Write the code

Coding

CodeImplement a fixed-capacity pool FixedPool(object_size, object_align, capacity) with allocate() (returns nullptr when exhausted), deallocate(p), owns(p) and in_use(). Both operations must be O(1), every block must be aligned to object_align (which may exceed 16), and the pool must not be copyable.

Answer

Approach. Compute the block alignment as the larger of the requested alignment and a pointer's, and the block size as the object size (at least one pointer) rounded up to that alignment. Allocate one buffer with aligned operator new, then thread an intrusive free list through it in address order. owns is a range check plus a block-boundary check, which also makes a good assertion in deallocate.

#include <algorithm>
#include <cassert>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <functional>
#include <new>

class FixedPool {
    struct Node { Node* next; };
    std::size_t align_, block_, cap_, used_ = 0;
    std::byte* buf_;
    Node* head_ = nullptr;

    static std::size_t round_up(std::size_t n, std::size_t a) { return (n + a - 1) & ~(a - 1); }

public:
    FixedPool(std::size_t object_size, std::size_t object_align, std::size_t capacity)
        : align_(std::max(object_align, alignof(Node))),
          block_(round_up(std::max(object_size, sizeof(Node)), align_)),
          cap_(capacity),
          buf_(static_cast<std::byte*>(::operator new(block_ * cap_, std::align_val_t{align_}))) {
        for (std::size_t i = cap_; i-- > 0;) head_ = ::new (buf_ + i * block_) Node{head_};
    }
    ~FixedPool() { ::operator delete(buf_, std::align_val_t{align_}); }
    FixedPool(const FixedPool&) = delete;
    FixedPool& operator=(const FixedPool&) = delete;

    void* allocate() noexcept {
        if (!head_) return nullptr;
        Node* n = head_;
        head_ = n->next;
        ++used_;
        return n;
    }
    void deallocate(void* p) noexcept {
        assert(owns(p));
        head_ = ::new (p) Node{head_};
        --used_;
    }
    bool owns(const void* p) const noexcept {
        auto* b = static_cast<const std::byte*>(p);
        std::less<const std::byte*> lt;          // total order even for unrelated pointers
        if (lt(b, buf_) || !lt(b, buf_ + block_ * cap_)) return false;
        return static_cast<std::size_t>(b - buf_) % block_ == 0;
    }
    std::size_t in_use() const noexcept { return used_; }
    std::size_t block_size() const noexcept { return block_; }
};

struct alignas(32) Tile { float v[5]; };

int main() {
    FixedPool pool(sizeof(Tile), alignof(Tile), 3);
    std::printf("block %zu for a %zu-byte, %zu-aligned type\n", pool.block_size(), sizeof(Tile), alignof(Tile));
    void* p[3];
    bool aligned = true;
    for (auto& q : p) {
        q = pool.allocate();
        aligned = aligned && reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t>(q) % alignof(Tile) == 0;
    }
    std::printf("all aligned: %s, in use %zu, fourth: %s\n", aligned ? "yes" : "no", pool.in_use(),
                pool.allocate() ? "got one" : "nullptr");
    pool.deallocate(p[1]);
    std::printf("reuse: %s\n", pool.allocate() == p[1] ? "same block" : "other block");
    int local = 0;
    std::printf("owns a stack address: %s\n", pool.owns(&local) ? "yes" : "no");
    for (auto q : p) pool.deallocate(q);
    std::printf("in use at end: %zu\n", pool.in_use());
}
block 32 for a 32-byte, 32-aligned type
all aligned: yes, in use 3, fourth: nullptr
reuse: same block
owns a stack address: no
in use at end: 0

Complexity and pitfalls. Both operations are O(1); construction is O(capacity). The pitfalls are the ones this chapter keeps returning to: a block smaller than a pointer, a block size that is not a multiple of the alignment, and freeing the buffer with the unaligned operator delete (it must match the aligned new). Comparing unrelated pointers with < is unspecified, so owns uses std::less, which guarantees a total order. The pool does not run destructors: it serves raw memory.

Estimated rating: ~1400 · short code, but alignment rounding and the aligned new/delete pairing must be exact

CodeWrite TypedPool<T> with T* create(Args&&...) and void destroy(T*). It grows by chunks that double in size (16, 32, 64, ... blocks), never moves existing objects, and stays consistent if T's constructor throws. Report the number of chunks.

Answer

Approach. A block is a union of a free-list link and raw storage for a T, so its size and alignment are right by construction. When the list is empty, allocate a new chunk with std::make_unique<Slot[]>, keep it in a vector for cleanup, and push its blocks. create pops the block before constructing (the constructor will overwrite the link) and pushes it back if the constructor throws. destroy runs the destructor and re-creates a link object in the storage.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <new>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

template <class T>
class TypedPool {
    union Slot {
        Slot* next;
        alignas(T) unsigned char storage[sizeof(T)];
    };
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Slot[]>> chunks_;
    std::size_t next_chunk_ = 16;
    Slot* head_ = nullptr;
    std::size_t live_ = 0;

    void grow() {
        auto chunk = std::make_unique<Slot[]>(next_chunk_);
        for (std::size_t i = next_chunk_; i-- > 0;) { chunk[i].next = head_; head_ = &chunk[i]; }
        chunks_.push_back(std::move(chunk));
        next_chunk_ *= 2;
    }

public:
    TypedPool() = default;
    TypedPool(const TypedPool&) = delete;
    TypedPool& operator=(const TypedPool&) = delete;
    ~TypedPool() { if (live_) std::fprintf(stderr, "TypedPool: %zu objects leaked\n", live_); }

    template <class... Args>
    T* create(Args&&... args) {
        if (!head_) grow();
        Slot* s = head_;
        head_ = s->next;
        try {
            T* p = ::new (static_cast<void*>(s->storage)) T(std::forward<Args>(args)...);
            ++live_;
            return p;
        } catch (...) {
            s->next = head_;        // give the block back
            head_ = s;
            throw;
        }
    }
    void destroy(T* p) noexcept {
        p->~T();
        head_ = ::new (static_cast<void*>(p)) Slot{.next = head_};
        --live_;
    }
    std::size_t chunks() const noexcept { return chunks_.size(); }
    std::size_t live() const noexcept { return live_; }
};

struct Message {
    static inline int alive = 0;
    std::string text;
    explicit Message(std::string t, bool fail = false) : text(std::move(t)) {
        if (fail) throw std::runtime_error("bad message");
        ++alive;
    }
    ~Message() { --alive; }
};

int main() {
    TypedPool<Message> pool;
    std::vector<Message*> msgs;
    for (int i = 0; i < 100; ++i) msgs.push_back(pool.create("message number " + std::to_string(i)));
    Message* first = msgs.front();
    std::printf("100 live, %zu chunks, first: %s\n", pool.chunks(), first->text.c_str());

    try { pool.create("broken", true); } catch (const std::exception& e) { std::printf("caught: %s\n", e.what()); }
    std::printf("live after the throw: %zu, alive count %d\n", pool.live(), Message::alive);

    for (Message* m : msgs) pool.destroy(m);
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) pool.destroy(pool.create("x"));
    std::printf("after churn: live %zu, chunks %zu, alive %d\n", pool.live(), pool.chunks(), Message::alive);
}
100 live, 3 chunks, first: message number 0
caught: bad message
live after the throw: 100, alive count 100
after churn: live 0, chunks 3, alive 0

Complexity and pitfalls. create and destroy are O(1) amortised; growth is O(chunk size) but happens O(log n) times. 100 objects need chunks of 16 + 32 + 64 = 112 blocks, so 3 chunks, and the churn afterwards never grows. Pitfalls: reading s->next after constructing T (the constructor has already overwritten it), losing the block when the constructor throws, and destroying the pool while objects are alive (their destructors never run; this version reports it). destroy must only receive pointers from this pool; the next exercise in debug builds is to assert that with a chunk range check.

Estimated rating: ~1600 · union slot, exception safety in create and chunk growth are each easy to get slightly wrong

CodeWrite an allocator PoolAllocator<T> that makes std::list and std::map take their nodes from fixed-size pools. Single-object requests come from a pool for sizeof(T) and alignof(T) of the type the allocator is instantiated with; multi-object requests go to operator new. Show how many allocations the pools served.

Answer

Approach. Make the allocator stateless and keep one pool per (size, alignment) pair as a function-local static, so every rebound allocator for the same node type shares a pool and all instances compare equal. The rebind happens automatically through allocator_traits because PoolAllocator is a class template; we only supply the converting constructor. The pools grow by chunks so the containers have no size limit.

#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <list>
#include <map>
#include <memory>
#include <new>
#include <vector>

static std::size_t g_pool_allocs = 0;

template <std::size_t Size, std::size_t Align>
class SizedPool {
    struct Node { Node* next; };
    static constexpr std::size_t kAlign = std::max(Align, alignof(Node));
    static constexpr std::size_t kBlock = (std::max(Size, sizeof(Node)) + kAlign - 1) / kAlign * kAlign;
    static constexpr std::size_t kChunkBlocks = 256;
    std::vector<std::byte*> chunks_;
    Node* head_ = nullptr;

    SizedPool() = default;
    ~SizedPool() { for (auto* c : chunks_) ::operator delete(c, std::align_val_t{kAlign}); }
    void grow() {
        auto* c = static_cast<std::byte*>(::operator new(kBlock * kChunkBlocks, std::align_val_t{kAlign}));
        chunks_.push_back(c);
        for (std::size_t i = kChunkBlocks; i-- > 0;) head_ = ::new (c + i * kBlock) Node{head_};
    }
public:
    static SizedPool& instance() { static SizedPool pool; return pool; }
    void* allocate() {
        if (!head_) grow();
        Node* n = head_;
        head_ = n->next;
        ++g_pool_allocs;
        return n;
    }
    void deallocate(void* p) noexcept { head_ = ::new (p) Node{head_}; }
};

template <class T>
struct PoolAllocator {
    using value_type = T;
    using Pool = SizedPool<sizeof(T), alignof(T)>;

    PoolAllocator() noexcept = default;
    template <class U> PoolAllocator(const PoolAllocator<U>&) noexcept {}

    T* allocate(std::size_t n) {
        if (n == 1) return static_cast<T*>(Pool::instance().allocate());
        return static_cast<T*>(::operator new(n * sizeof(T), std::align_val_t{alignof(T)}));
    }
    void deallocate(T* p, std::size_t n) noexcept {
        if (n == 1) Pool::instance().deallocate(p);
        else ::operator delete(p, std::align_val_t{alignof(T)});
    }
    template <class U> bool operator==(const PoolAllocator<U>&) const noexcept { return true; }
};

int main() {
    std::list<int, PoolAllocator<int>> l;
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) l.push_back(i);
    std::printf("list: %zu pool allocations\n", g_pool_allocs);
    l.remove_if([](int x) { return x % 2 == 0; });
    long sum = 0;
    for (int x : l) sum += x;
    std::printf("sum of odd values: %ld\n", sum);
    for (int i = 0; i < 500; ++i) l.push_front(i);   // reuses the freed nodes
    std::printf("after refill: %zu pool allocations, size %zu\n", g_pool_allocs, l.size());

    g_pool_allocs = 0;
    std::map<int, int, std::less<int>, PoolAllocator<std::pair<const int, int>>> m;
    for (int i = 0; i < 300; ++i) m[i * 7 % 300] = i;
    std::printf("map: %zu entries, %zu pool allocations\n", m.size(), g_pool_allocs);
}
list: 1000 pool allocations
sum of odd values: 250000
after refill: 1500 pool allocations, size 1000
map: 300 entries, 300 pool allocations

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) per node. The list and map nodes get different SizedPool instantiations because their sizes differ. Pitfalls: keying the pool on the user's T instead of the rebound one; forgetting n > 1 requests (vector, unordered_map buckets); and static lifetime: a static container constructed before the pool's first use is destroyed after the pool, so its nodes are freed into a dead pool. The pools are process-wide, so this is not thread safe; a thread_local pool fixes that if nodes never cross threads. Boost's fast_pool_allocator uses this design.

Estimated rating: ~1800 · needs a working model of rebind, allocator equality and static lifetime, not just a free list

CodeBuild a small-object allocator with 16 size classes (16, 32, ..., 256 bytes). allocate(size) routes to the smallest class that fits, larger requests go to operator new, and deallocate(p, size) uses the size to find the class. Test it with many random sizes and verify that no two live allocations overlap.

Answer

Approach. Keep an array of 16 free-list heads and a list of chunks. The class index is (size + 15) / 16 - 1. An empty class takes a 4 KiB chunk and slices it into blocks of that class's size. Sized deallocation means no header is needed. The test fills every allocation with a byte unique to it and checks the pattern before freeing, which detects any overlap.

#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstring>
#include <new>
#include <vector>

class SmallObjectAllocator {
    struct Node { Node* next; };
    static constexpr std::size_t kStep = 16, kClasses = 16, kMax = kStep * kClasses, kChunk = 4096;
    std::array<Node*, kClasses> heads_{};
    std::vector<void*> chunks_;

    static std::size_t class_of(std::size_t n) { return (n + kStep - 1) / kStep - 1; }
    void refill(std::size_t c) {
        std::size_t block = (c + 1) * kStep;
        auto* chunk = static_cast<std::byte*>(::operator new(kChunk));
        chunks_.push_back(chunk);
        for (std::size_t off = kChunk / block * block; off >= block; off -= block)
            heads_[c] = ::new (chunk + off - block) Node{heads_[c]};
    }

public:
    SmallObjectAllocator() = default;
    SmallObjectAllocator(const SmallObjectAllocator&) = delete;
    SmallObjectAllocator& operator=(const SmallObjectAllocator&) = delete;
    ~SmallObjectAllocator() { for (void* c : chunks_) ::operator delete(c); }

    void* allocate(std::size_t n) {
        if (n == 0) n = 1;
        if (n > kMax) return ::operator new(n);
        std::size_t c = class_of(n);
        if (!heads_[c]) refill(c);
        Node* b = heads_[c];
        heads_[c] = b->next;
        return b;
    }
    void deallocate(void* p, std::size_t n) noexcept {
        if (n == 0) n = 1;
        if (n > kMax) { ::operator delete(p); return; }
        std::size_t c = class_of(n);
        heads_[c] = ::new (p) Node{heads_[c]};
    }
    std::size_t chunks() const { return chunks_.size(); }
};

struct Live { unsigned char* p; std::size_t n; unsigned char tag; };

int main() {
    SmallObjectAllocator alloc;
    std::vector<Live> live;
    std::uint32_t x = 7;
    auto rnd = [&] { x = x * 1103515245u + 12345u; return x >> 8; };
    int corrupt = 0;
    for (int step = 0; step < 20000; ++step) {
        if (live.size() < 500 && (live.empty() || rnd() % 3 != 0)) {
            std::size_t n = 1 + rnd() % 300;                  // some go above 256
            auto tag = static_cast<unsigned char>(rnd());
            auto* p = static_cast<unsigned char*>(alloc.allocate(n));
            std::memset(p, tag, n);
            live.push_back({p, n, tag});
        } else {
            std::size_t i = rnd() % live.size();
            Live v = live[i];
            for (std::size_t k = 0; k < v.n; ++k) corrupt += v.p[k] != v.tag;
            alloc.deallocate(v.p, v.n);
            live[i] = live.back();
            live.pop_back();
        }
    }
    for (Live v : live) alloc.deallocate(v.p, v.n);
    std::printf("corrupted bytes: %d\n", corrupt);
    std::printf("chunks used: %s\n", alloc.chunks() < 64 ? "fewer than 64" : "too many");
}
corrupted bytes: 0
chunks used: fewer than 64

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) per call, plus O(chunk / block) when a class refills. Worst-case internal fragmentation is 15 bytes per block. The classic bugs: computing the class differently in allocate and deallocate (for example, if the size passed back is not the size requested), not handling n == 0, and alignment: blocks of 48 bytes are only 16-aligned, which is fine for max_align_t but not for over-aligned types, so a real allocator also takes an alignment argument. Chunks are never returned until destruction; returning them needs a per-chunk count of live blocks.

Estimated rating: ~1700 · several free lists and an off-by-one-prone slicing loop, plus a randomised self-check

CodeWrite a lock-free fixed-size pool for 48-byte blocks that is safe for many threads and immune to ABA. Use only 64-bit atomics (no double-width CAS). Test it with 4 threads and prove that no block is ever handed to two threads at once.

Answer

Approach. Blocks live in an array, so a block can be named by a 32-bit index. The head is one std::atomic<std::uint64_t> that packs a 32-bit version tag with the 32-bit index of the top block, and every successful CAS increments the tag, so a stale head never matches. Each block's link is a separate std::atomic<std::uint32_t>, so a thread that reads a link while another thread uses the block's data is not a data race. Pop uses acquire and push uses release, which orders the data written by the previous owner before the next owner's writes.

#include <atomic>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

class LockFreePool {
    static constexpr std::uint32_t kNil = 0xFFFFFFFFu;
    struct Block {
        alignas(16) unsigned char data[48];
        std::atomic<std::uint32_t> next{kNil};
    };
    std::unique_ptr<Block[]> blocks_;
    std::uint32_t count_;
    std::atomic<std::uint64_t> head_;

    static std::uint64_t pack(std::uint64_t tag, std::uint32_t idx) { return tag << 32 | idx; }
    std::uint32_t index_of(void* p) const {
        auto* b = static_cast<unsigned char*>(p);
        return static_cast<std::uint32_t>((b - reinterpret_cast<unsigned char*>(blocks_.get())) / sizeof(Block));
    }

public:
    explicit LockFreePool(std::uint32_t n) : blocks_(std::make_unique<Block[]>(n)), count_(n), head_(pack(0, kNil)) {
        for (std::uint32_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) blocks_[i].next.store(i + 1 < n ? i + 1 : kNil, std::memory_order_relaxed);
        head_.store(pack(0, 0), std::memory_order_release);
    }
    void* allocate() noexcept {
        std::uint64_t old = head_.load(std::memory_order_acquire);
        for (;;) {
            auto idx = static_cast<std::uint32_t>(old);
            if (idx == kNil) return nullptr;
            std::uint32_t next = blocks_[idx].next.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
            if (head_.compare_exchange_weak(old, pack((old >> 32) + 1, next),
                                            std::memory_order_acquire, std::memory_order_acquire))
                return blocks_[idx].data;
        }
    }
    void deallocate(void* p) noexcept {
        std::uint32_t idx = index_of(p);
        std::uint64_t old = head_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        for (;;) {
            blocks_[idx].next.store(static_cast<std::uint32_t>(old), std::memory_order_relaxed);
            if (head_.compare_exchange_weak(old, pack((old >> 32) + 1, idx),
                                            std::memory_order_release, std::memory_order_relaxed))
                return;
        }
    }
    std::uint32_t capacity() const noexcept { return count_; }
};

int main() {
    constexpr std::uint32_t kBlocks = 64;
    LockFreePool pool(kBlocks);
    std::vector<std::atomic<int>> owner(kBlocks);
    std::atomic<int> clashes{0};
    auto base = static_cast<unsigned char*>(pool.allocate());   // block 0: learn the layout, then return it
    pool.deallocate(base);
    auto slot_of = [&](void* p) { return (static_cast<unsigned char*>(p) - base) / 64; };   // sizeof(Block) == 64

    auto worker = [&](int id) {
        void* held[4] = {};
        for (int i = 0; i < 20000; ++i) {
            void*& h = held[i % 4];
            if (h) {
                owner[slot_of(h)].store(0, std::memory_order_relaxed);
                pool.deallocate(h);
                h = nullptr;
            } else if ((h = pool.allocate())) {
                if (owner[slot_of(h)].exchange(1, std::memory_order_relaxed) != 0) ++clashes;
                static_cast<unsigned char*>(h)[0] = static_cast<unsigned char>(id);   // use the block
            }
        }
        for (void* h : held) if (h) { owner[slot_of(h)].store(0, std::memory_order_relaxed); pool.deallocate(h); }
    };
    std::vector<std::thread> ts;
    for (int t = 0; t < 4; ++t) ts.emplace_back(worker, t);
    for (auto& t : ts) t.join();

    std::uint32_t back = 0;
    while (pool.allocate()) ++back;
    std::printf("blocks handed to two threads at once: %d\n", clashes.load());
    std::printf("blocks recovered: %u of %u\n", back, pool.capacity());
}
blocks handed to two threads at once: 0
blocks recovered: 64 of 64

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) without contention, with retries under contention (lock-free, not wait-free). Pitfalls: a plain uint32_t link would race when a slow popper reads a link the block's new owner is writing, so the link is atomic and outside the user data; the tag must change on push as well as pop; and the tag wraps after 232 updates, which is accepted. A 128-bit pointer-plus-tag CAS also works, but GCC may route it through libatomic and report it as not lock-free. The test's owner checks are relaxed on purpose, so the happens-before edges TSan verifies come from the pool itself.

Estimated rating: ~2200 · correct memory orders, ABA tagging and a meaningful concurrent test are all required

CodeWrite a debugging std::pmr::memory_resource that wraps an upstream resource and detects buffer overruns (canaries before and after each block), size mismatches on deallocate, and leaks (live blocks when it is destroyed). It must work as the resource of ordinary pmr containers.

Answer

Approach. For each request, ask upstream for a 16-byte header, the user's bytes and an 8-byte tail. The header stores the size and a front canary; the tail canary is written with memcpy because it may be unaligned. On deallocate, check both canaries and compare the stored size with the one passed in, then free with the stored size. Alignments above 16 are forwarded unchecked to keep the layout simple.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstring>
#include <memory_resource>
#include <vector>
