class CheckingResource : public std::pmr::memory_resource {
    static constexpr std::uint64_t kFront = 0xF00DFACEF00DFACEull, kBack = 0xDEADC0DEDEADC0DEull;
    static constexpr std::size_t kHeader = 16, kTail = sizeof(std::uint64_t);
    struct Header { std::size_t size; std::uint64_t canary; };
    std::pmr::memory_resource* up_;
    std::size_t live_ = 0;

public:
    int errors = 0;
    explicit CheckingResource(std::pmr::memory_resource* up = std::pmr::new_delete_resource()) : up_(up) {}
    ~CheckingResource() override { if (live_) std::printf("leak: %zu block(s) never freed\n", live_); }

private:
    void* do_allocate(std::size_t n, std::size_t align) override {
        if (align > kHeader) return up_->allocate(n, align);
        auto* raw = static_cast<std::byte*>(up_->allocate(kHeader + n + kTail, kHeader));
        ::new (raw) Header{n, kFront};
        std::memcpy(raw + kHeader + n, &kBack, kTail);
        ++live_;
        return raw + kHeader;
    }
    void do_deallocate(void* p, std::size_t n, std::size_t align) override {
        if (align > kHeader) { up_->deallocate(p, n, align); return; }
        auto* raw = static_cast<std::byte*>(p) - kHeader;
        auto* h = reinterpret_cast<Header*>(raw);
        std::uint64_t back;
        std::memcpy(&back, raw + kHeader + h->size, kTail);
        if (h->canary != kFront) { ++errors; std::puts("error: front canary overwritten (underrun)"); }
        if (back != kBack) { ++errors; std::puts("error: back canary overwritten (overrun)"); }
        if (h->size != n) { ++errors; std::printf("error: freed with size %zu, allocated %zu\n", n, h->size); }
        --live_;
        up_->deallocate(raw, kHeader + h->size + kTail, kHeader);
    }
    bool do_is_equal(const memory_resource& o) const noexcept override { return this == &o; }
};

int main() {
    CheckingResource checker;
    {
        std::pmr::vector<int> v(&checker);
        for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) v.push_back(i);
    }
    std::printf("after a clean vector: %d errors\n", checker.errors);

    auto* buf = static_cast<char*>(checker.allocate(10, 1));
    std::memset(buf, 'x', 11);                   // one byte too many
    checker.deallocate(buf, 10, 1);

    void* q = checker.allocate(32);
    checker.deallocate(q, 16);                   // wrong size

    {
        CheckingResource scoped;
        [[maybe_unused]] void* forgotten = scoped.allocate(64);
    }
    std::printf("total errors: %d\n", checker.errors);
}
after a clean vector: 0 errors
error: back canary overwritten (overrun)
error: freed with size 16, allocated 32
leak: 1 block(s) never freed
total errors: 2

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) extra work and 24 extra bytes per allocation. The inner scope's block is deliberately leaked (the harness turns off LeakSanitizer). The off-by-one write lands in the tail canary, which is inside this resource's own allocation, so ASan sees nothing: exactly the class of bug canaries exist for. Pitfalls: keeping the user pointer aligned (the 16-byte header preserves 16-byte alignment), an unaligned load of the tail canary (use memcpy), and freeing upstream with the caller's size instead of the stored one.

Estimated rating: ~1700 · memory_resource plumbing plus careful header and tail layout arithmetic

Cheat sheet

Theory
  • A pool trades generality for O(1), constant-time allocation with no slow path, no external fragmentation and pre-faultable memory. The win that matters on hot paths is the tail latency.
  • Intrusive free list: free blocks store the next pointer. Block size = round_up(max(size, sizeof(void*)), align). LIFO reuse is cache-warm and hides use-after-free.
  • Fixed capacity (pre-sized, alarm on exhaustion) for HFT; chunked growth (doubling, never moving blocks) elsewhere. Freed blocks do not go back to the OS.
  • Size classes: an array of pools; deallocation needs the size (sized delete, deallocate(p, n)) or an address lookup. Power-of-two classes waste up to about 50 percent.
  • Thread safety: mutex (simple), thread-local pools (fast, cross-thread frees need a remote list), lock-free Treiber stack (needs ABA protection: tag counter or hazard pointers).
  • std::pmr: memory_resource, (un)synchronized_pool_resource, polymorphic_allocator; copies use the default resource, moves keep it, move-assign across resources is O(n), swap across resources is UB.
  • STL allocator: value_type, allocate, deallocate, converting constructor, ==. Node containers rebind to their node type.
  • Debug pools with poisoning, canaries, in-use bits, ASan manual poisoning or a malloc pass-through switch. Benchmark with realistic churn, medians plus spread, ratios, and the platform named (pmr pools were 2.3× faster than malloc on libc++ but slower on libstdc++ on an Apple M1).

Part E · Memory management · Chapter 16

Object pools

An object pool keeps fully constructed objects and lends them out, so the expensive part of creating an object (its buffers, its connection, its thread) happens once. This chapter covers acquire and release, reset semantics, RAII handles, exhaustion policies, the bugs pools invite (stale state, double release, use after release) and the generation-counter handles that catch them. Interviewers ask about object pools because they test lifetime reasoning more than allocation tricks.

TheoryDrillsCoding· about 4 hours· prerequisites: Ch 11, Ch 12, Ch 15

Object pools vs memory pools

Theory

Mental model. A memory pool (Ch 15) recycles raw blocks: you construct an object in a block, destroy it, and the block goes back. An object pool recycles live objects: they are constructed once, handed out, reset to a clean state when returned, and destroyed only when the pool dies. The destructor and constructor do not run per use.

That distinction decides when each one helps:

  • A memory pool helps when the allocation is the cost: many small objects of one size, created and destroyed often.
  • An object pool helps when construction is the cost: an object that owns a 64 KiB buffer, a TCP connection with a completed TLS handshake, a thread, a database statement handle, a game entity with components wired up. Resetting such an object (clear the buffer but keep its capacity, keep the socket open) is far cheaper than building a new one.
Key factsMemory poolObject pool
RecyclesRaw storageConstructed objects
Per-use cost savedmalloc/freeConstruction, destruction and their allocations
Per-use cost addedPlacement new and destructor callreset() on release (or on acquire)
Typical APIvoid* allocate(), deallocate(p)Handle acquire(), release via the handle's destructor
Main bug riskUse after free, wrong sizeStale state from the previous user, use after release
Objects areOne type or one size classOne type, often heavy (buffers, sockets, threads)
Memory heldPeak block countPeak object count, plus every buffer each object grew

The two combine: an object pool can store its objects in memory from a memory pool or an arena, and many systems call both of them "pools". In an interview, define which one you mean first.

Acquire, release and reset semantics

Theory

The interface has two operations. acquire() removes an idle object from the pool and gives the caller exclusive use. release(obj) gives it back. Between the two, the pool must not hand that object to anyone else, and after release the caller must not touch it.

What reset means

Reset returns the object to a state that is indistinguishable, for the next user, from a freshly constructed one, while keeping whatever made construction expensive. Examples:

  • A buffer: clear() (size 0) but keep the capacity. Do not shrink_to_fit(), or you lose the point of pooling.
  • A request object: clear every field, including the optional ones (authentication token, user id, error flags). Missing one field is the classic stale-state bug.
  • A connection: roll back any open transaction, reset session variables, keep the socket and TLS session.
  • A game entity: reset position, health and timers, unsubscribe it from events, keep its allocated component storage.

Reset on release or on acquire?

Both are used, and the trade-offs are real:

  • On release (most common): the previous user's data and resources are dropped as soon as they are done. Secrets do not linger in idle objects, references to other objects are cut early so they can be freed, and the acquire path stays fast. The releasing thread pays the cost.
  • On acquire: lazy, so objects that are never reused are never reset, and the cost lands on the thread that needs the object. Idle objects still hold the previous user's data, which is a security and memory concern.

Whichever you choose, also validate: a pool of connections typically checks on acquire that the connection is still alive (the server may have closed it while it sat idle) and discards it if not.

A basic object pool

This version owns every object through a std::vector<std::unique_ptr<T>> and keeps a stack of idle ones. The free stack is reserved up front, so release never allocates and can be noexcept.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <functional>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

template <class T>
class ObjectPool {
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<T>> all_;   // owns every object
    std::vector<T*> idle_;                  // objects ready to hand out
    std::function<void(T&)> reset_;
public:
    ObjectPool(std::size_t n, std::function<void(T&)> reset) : reset_(std::move(reset)) {
        all_.reserve(n);
        idle_.reserve(n);
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
            all_.push_back(std::make_unique<T>());
            idle_.push_back(all_.back().get());
        }
    }
    T* acquire() {
        if (idle_.empty()) return nullptr;
        T* obj = idle_.back();
        idle_.pop_back();
        return obj;
    }
    void release(T* obj) noexcept {
        reset_(*obj);
        idle_.push_back(obj);   // never reallocates: capacity is all_.size()
    }
    std::size_t idle() const { return idle_.size(); }
};

struct Packet { std::string payload; int retries = 0; };

int main() {
    ObjectPool<Packet> pool(2, [](Packet& p) { p.payload.clear(); p.retries = 0; });
    Packet* p = pool.acquire();
    p->payload.assign(1000, 'x');
    p->retries = 3;
    auto cap = p->payload.capacity();
    pool.release(p);
    Packet* q = pool.acquire();
    std::printf("same object: %s, size %zu, retries %d, capacity kept: %s\n",
                q == p ? "yes" : "no", q->payload.size(), q->retries, q->payload.capacity() == cap ? "yes" : "no");
    pool.release(q);
    std::printf("idle: %zu\n", pool.idle());
}
same object: yes, size 0, retries 0, capacity kept: yes
idle: 2

The raw T* interface is the weak point: nothing stops a caller from forgetting to release, releasing twice, or keeping the pointer after release. The next section fixes the first two with RAII, and generation handles fix the third.

RAII handles

Theory

A pooled object should be returned exactly once, on every path, including exceptions and early returns. That is what RAII is for (Ch 1). The standard tool is std::unique_ptr with a custom deleter (Ch 12) whose call operator returns the object to the pool instead of deleting it.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <vector>

struct Connection {
    int id;
    int queries = 0;
};

class ConnectionPool {
public:
    struct Return {
        ConnectionPool* pool;
        void operator()(Connection* c) const noexcept { pool->give_back(c); }
    };
    using Handle = std::unique_ptr<Connection, Return>;

    explicit ConnectionPool(int n) {
        for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) all_.push_back(std::make_unique<Connection>(Connection{i}));
        for (auto& c : all_) idle_.push_back(c.get());
    }
    Handle acquire() {
        if (idle_.empty()) throw std::runtime_error("no connection available");
        Connection* c = idle_.back();
        idle_.pop_back();
        return Handle(c, Return{this});
    }
    std::size_t idle() const { return idle_.size(); }

private:
    void give_back(Connection* c) noexcept {
        c->queries = 0;            // reset
        idle_.push_back(c);
    }
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Connection>> all_;
    std::vector<Connection*> idle_;
};

static void run_query(ConnectionPool& pool, bool fail) {
    auto conn = pool.acquire();
    ++conn->queries;
    if (fail) throw std::runtime_error("query failed");
}   // conn returns to the pool here, on both paths

int main() {
    ConnectionPool pool(2);
    run_query(pool, false);
    try { run_query(pool, true); } catch (const std::exception& e) { std::printf("caught: %s\n", e.what()); }
    std::printf("idle after both calls: %zu\n", pool.idle());
    {
        auto a = pool.acquire();
        auto b = std::move(a);     // ownership moves; still exactly one release
        std::printf("while held: idle %zu, a empty: %s\n", pool.idle(), a ? "no" : "yes");
    }
    std::printf("idle at the end: %zu\n", pool.idle());
}
caught: query failed
idle after both calls: 2
while held: idle 1, a empty: yes
idle at the end: 2

Design points:

  • Move-only handles make double release impossible by construction: copying is a compile error, and moving leaves the source empty, so its destructor does nothing.
  • Size. A deleter holding a pool pointer makes the handle 16 bytes on 64-bit instead of 8. A stateless deleter (for a global or thread_local pool) keeps it at 8, thanks to the empty-member optimisation inside unique_ptr.
  • The pool must outlive every handle. If the pool is destroyed first, the deleter calls into a dead object. Either guarantee the order (declare the pool before its users, destroy users first), or make handles hold a std::weak_ptr to shared pool state and delete the object if the pool is gone. The coding section builds the second design.
  • std::shared_ptr handles work too (std::shared_ptr<T>(raw, deleter)), and are thread-safe to copy, but each one allocates a control block, which puts an allocation back on the path the pool was meant to clear. Use std::allocate_shared with a pool allocator, or an intrusive reference count, if you need sharing.

Pool exhaustion policies

Theory

When every object is out, acquire has three choices. Pick one deliberately and document it.

PolicyHowGood forDanger
GrowConstruct a new object (maybe up to a hard limit)Buffers, general services where memory is cheapUnbounded memory under a load spike; the expensive construction happens on the hot path at the worst time
BlockWait on a condition variable until a release, usually with a timeoutConnection pools, worker pools: the limit protects a downstream resourceDeadlock if a thread holding one object waits for a second one; latency spikes
FailReturn an empty handle, std::optional, an error code, or throwTrading and real-time systems: shed load, reject the order, raise an alarmCallers that do not check the result

Blocking pools have one classic trap: a thread that already holds an object and asks for another can deadlock when every thread does the same (each holds one, all wait for a second). Database connection pools hit this when a request handler opens a nested transaction on a second connection. The fix is to never acquire a second object while holding one, or to size the pool for the nesting depth times the number of threads.

Always expose a high-water mark (the most objects ever in use) and a counter of exhaustion events. They tell you how to size the pool, and in a grow policy they show whether growth is a rare event or the normal case.

Stale state, double release and use after release

Theory

Object pools turn three kinds of bugs from crashes into silent data corruption, because the memory involved is always valid.

  • Stale state. reset() forgets a field, so the next user inherits it: a previous user's authentication token, a "cancelled" flag, a half-filled vector, a pending timer. The object looks valid, so nothing crashes. This is the most common object pool bug in production, and it can be a security hole (one customer's data in another customer's response).
  • Double release. The same object is pushed onto the idle list twice, so two later acquire calls return it to two different users, who then overwrite each other's data.
  • Use after release. A caller keeps a raw pointer or reference after releasing. The object is reset and handed to someone else, and the old caller now reads or writes the new user's object. No tool sees a problem: the pointer is to a live object of the right type.

Interview trap

"ASan will catch use after release." It will not. The object was never freed: it is a live T inside a live allocation. ASan, Valgrind and the debug heap only see allocator-level frees. The defences have to be in the pool's design: RAII handles for release, generation-checked handles for access, and a debug mode that poisons or cross-checks idle objects.

Defences that work:

  • Make reset() assign a freshly constructed object's state where possible (obj = T{}), but move the buffers you want to keep out first and back afterwards, because the assignment also throws away their capacity (the reading section shows it). Test that a reset object compares equal to a new one.
  • Keep an in_pool flag (or a state enum) per object and check it in both acquire and release. A double release becomes an assertion failure at the second call.
  • In debug builds, fill idle objects with a recognisable pattern after reset, or keep idle objects in a FIFO quarantine so a stale pointer does not immediately alias a new user.
  • Hand out handles rather than pointers, and check them on every access. That is the next section.

Generation counters and slot maps

Theory

Mental model. Instead of a pointer, the user holds a handle: a slot index plus a generation number. Each slot also stores a generation, and the pool increments it every time the slot is released. A lookup succeeds only when the handle's generation equals the slot's. A stale handle (one taken before the release) carries an old generation, so it fails cleanly instead of reaching the new occupant.

A generational pool

#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct Handle { std::uint32_t index; std::uint32_t gen; };

template <class T>
class GenPool {
    static constexpr std::uint32_t kNone = UINT32_MAX;
    struct Slot { T value{}; std::uint32_t gen = 0; bool live = false; std::uint32_t next_free = kNone; };
    std::vector<Slot> slots_;
    std::uint32_t free_head_ = kNone;
public:
    Handle acquire() {
        if (free_head_ == kNone) {
            slots_.push_back({});
            free_head_ = static_cast<std::uint32_t>(slots_.size() - 1);
        }
        std::uint32_t i = free_head_;
        Slot& s = slots_[i];
        free_head_ = s.next_free;
        s.live = true;
        return {i, s.gen};
    }
    T* get(Handle h) {
        if (h.index >= slots_.size()) return nullptr;
        Slot& s = slots_[h.index];
        return s.live && s.gen == h.gen ? &s.value : nullptr;
    }
    bool release(Handle h) {
        if (!get(h)) return false;          // stale or double release: refuse
        Slot& s = slots_[h.index];
        s.value = T{};                      // reset
        s.live = false;
        ++s.gen;                            // invalidates every outstanding handle
        s.next_free = free_head_;
        free_head_ = h.index;
        return true;
    }
};

int main() {
    GenPool<std::string> names;
    Handle player = names.acquire();
    *names.get(player) = "player";
    names.release(player);
    Handle enemy = names.acquire();         // reuses slot 0
    *names.get(enemy) = "enemy";
    std::printf("slot reused: %s\n", enemy.index == player.index ? "yes" : "no");
    std::printf("old handle: %s\n", names.get(player) ? names.get(player)->c_str() : "stale (null)");
    std::printf("new handle: %s\n", names.get(enemy)->c_str());
    std::printf("double release accepted: %s\n", names.release(player) ? "yes" : "no");
}
slot reused: yes
old handle: stale (null)
new handle: enemy
double release accepted: no

Slot maps

A slot map (the name comes from game engines; SG14's proposal for a std::slot_map, P0661, was never adopted, so you write or borrow one) adds one more idea: the values are kept in a dense array with no holes, and each slot stores the index of its value in that array. Erase moves the last value into the hole and patches the moved value's slot. Lookups cost one extra indirection, but iterating over all live values is a straight walk over contiguous memory, which is what a game loop that updates every entity each frame wants (see Ch 19 on cache-friendly layouts). The coding section builds one.

  • Handle size. 32-bit index plus 32-bit generation fits in 8 bytes, the same as a pointer, and can be serialised or sent between threads, which a pointer cannot do safely.
  • Wrap-around. After 232 reuses of one slot, the generation repeats and a very old handle would match again. At one reuse per millisecond of a single slot that takes about 50 days, at one per microsecond about 72 minutes. Either accept the risk because stale handles never live that long, or retire a slot permanently when its generation reaches the maximum. With 16-bit generations, wrap-around is a real risk and retiring is required.
  • Pointer stability. In the version above, get() returns a pointer that is valid only until the next acquire, because slots_ can reallocate. Users must re-resolve handles instead of caching pointers. A fixed-capacity pool, or chunked storage, keeps addresses stable.

Thread-safe object pools

Theory

Object pools are shared more often than memory pools, because the things they hold (connections, buffers) are used by many request threads. The options mirror Ch 15:

  • A mutex around the idle list. Acquire and release are short (a vector push or pop), so the critical section is tiny. Do the reset outside the lock, before taking it in release, so a slow reset does not serialise every thread.
  • A mutex plus a condition variable for the blocking policy: acquire waits with a predicate (!idle_.empty()) and a timeout; release notifies one waiter after pushing. Always use the predicate form of wait to handle spurious wake-ups (Ch 6).
  • Per-thread caches in front of a shared pool. Each thread keeps a few idle objects locally and moves them to or from the shared pool in batches, which takes the lock once per batch. This is how thread-caching allocators and high-throughput buffer pools work.
  • Lock-free stacks with ABA protection, as in Ch 15. Rarely needed for object pools: the work done with each object usually dwarfs the cost of a short lock.

RAII handles keep working across threads: a handle moved to another thread releases from that thread, so release must be thread safe even if acquire is always called from one thread. The deleter's call into the pool is the only shared access.

Tip

Releasing must never throw and should not allocate. Reserve the idle list's capacity for the pool's maximum size, so push_back in release never reallocates, and mark the deleter noexcept. A throwing deleter inside a destructor during stack unwinding calls std::terminate.

Typical uses

Theory
Pooled objectExpensive part keptReset doesUsual exhaustion policy
Database / HTTP connectionsTCP connect, TLS handshake, authenticationRoll back transaction, reset session state, health checkBlock with timeout (the limit protects the server)
Threads (a thread pool)Thread creation, stack, TLS setupNothing: the thread waits for the next taskQueue tasks instead of creating threads
I/O and message buffersLarge heap buffers, registered or pinned memory for DMA and kernel bypassclear(), keep capacity; drop buffers that grew too largeGrow, with a cap
Game entities, particles, bulletsComponent storage, loaded assets, registrationReset transforms and timers, deactivateFail (skip spawning) or recycle the oldest
Orders and messages in tradingPre-faulted memory, pre-sized fields, no allocation on the hot pathClear fields, bump a sequence numberFail and alarm; pool is sized for the worst day
Parsers, regex or compression contextsInternal tables and work buffersLibrary reset call (for example deflateReset)Grow

A thread pool is the object pool everybody already knows, with one difference: threads are not handed to the caller. The caller submits work and the pool's threads acquire tasks, so the pool, not the user, controls the lifetime.

When pools hurt

Theory

An object pool is a cache of objects, and it has the costs of any cache.

  • Memory held forever. Every idle object keeps whatever it grew. One request with a 50 MB payload leaves a 50 MB buffer in the pool for the life of the process. Cap the capacity an object may keep (shrink or discard on release if it exceeds the cap), and cap the number of idle objects.
  • Cache effects. Pooled objects allocated one by one are scattered on the heap, and a pool that cycles through many idle objects touches memory that has gone cold. A fresh allocation from a thread-caching malloc can be hotter. LIFO reuse (always hand out the most recently released object) mitigates this.
  • Complexity and bugs. Reset functions must be kept in sync with every field added to the class, and lifetime bugs become silent. A pool is a manual memory manager with all the risks that implies.
  • Hiding problems from tools. Leak checkers, ASan and heap profilers see one long-lived allocation instead of the real usage pattern.
  • Small objects gain little. For an object that is just a few fields with no owned resources, modern allocators already serve the memory in 10 to 30 ns. Pooling it adds code and saves almost nothing; a memory pool or an arena is a better fit.

What a pool saves, measured

This benchmark builds a message object with a 2 KiB payload and four heap-allocated header strings, either fresh each time or from a pool that resets with clear().

#include <algorithm>
#include <chrono>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct Message {
    std::vector<char> payload;
    std::vector<std::string> headers;
    void reset() { payload.clear(); headers.clear(); }
};

class MessagePool {
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Message>> free_;
public:
    std::unique_ptr<Message> acquire() {
        if (free_.empty()) return std::make_unique<Message>();
        auto m = std::move(free_.back());
        free_.pop_back();
        return m;
    }
    void release(std::unique_ptr<Message> m) { m->reset(); free_.push_back(std::move(m)); }
};

static void fill(Message& m, int i) {
    m.payload.resize(2048, static_cast<char>(i));
    for (int h = 0; h < 4; ++h) m.headers.emplace_back("x-header-with-a-long-name-" + std::to_string(h));
}

constexpr int kIters = 200000, kReps = 7;

template <class F>
static double median_ns(F f) {
    std::vector<double> v;
    for (int r = 0; r < kReps; ++r) {
        auto t0 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        f();
        auto t1 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        v.push_back(std::chrono::duration<double, std::nano>(t1 - t0).count() / kIters);
    }
    std::sort(v.begin(), v.end());
    std::printf("    min %.1f  max %.1f ns per message\n", v.front(), v.back());
    return v[v.size() / 2];
}

int main() {
    long sink = 0;
    std::puts("fresh object per message:");
    double fresh = median_ns([&] {
        for (int i = 0; i < kIters; ++i) { auto m = std::make_unique<Message>(); fill(*m, i); sink += m->payload[7]; }
    });
    std::puts("pooled object, reset on release:");
    MessagePool pool;
    double pooled = median_ns([&] {
        for (int i = 0; i < kIters; ++i) { auto m = pool.acquire(); fill(*m, i); sink += m->payload[7]; pool.release(std::move(m)); }
    });
    std::printf("median: fresh %.1f ns, pooled %.1f ns, ratio %.1fx (sink %ld)\n", fresh, pooled, fresh / pooled, sink & 1);
}

Representative numbers on an Apple M1 (macOS, -O2, median of 7 runs of 200,000 messages). The program is tagged ub so timings are never compared.

BuildFresh objectPooled objectRatio
GCC 16 + libstdc++336 ns158 ns2.1× faster pooled
Clang 22 + libc++484 to 548 ns294 to 322 ns1.6 to 1.7× faster pooled

The pool removes the payload allocation and the header vector's allocation, but not the four string allocations: headers.clear() destroys the strings, so their buffers are freed and reallocated on every message. Keeping them would need a reset that reuses the existing strings (assign into them instead of clearing the vector). The lesson for the interview: measure what the reset really keeps, and quote ratios with the platform; the two standard libraries differ by 1.5 times on the same machine.

Concept and tricky questions

Drills

ConceptWhat is the difference between an object pool and a memory pool, and how do you decide which one a problem needs?

Answer

Answer. A memory pool recycles raw storage, so the constructor and destructor still run on every use; it saves the malloc/free. An object pool recycles constructed objects and resets them instead, so it saves construction and destruction and everything they allocate or acquire. Profile first: if the time is in the allocator, use a memory pool or arena; if it is in constructors (buffer allocation, connecting, thread start), use an object pool.

Why. A pool of 32-byte trivially constructible structs gains nothing from an object pool, since the constructor is free. A pool of TLS connections gains nothing from a memory pool, since the cost is the handshake, not the 200 bytes of memory. Candidates who use the terms interchangeably usually get asked to clarify, so state the distinction first.

TrickyShould a pool reset an object when it is released or when it is next acquired? Give a case where the choice matters.

Answer

Answer. Usually on release. A request object that held a customer's authentication token or personal data should be wiped as soon as the request ends, not when some later request happens to pick it up. Release-time reset also drops references to other objects early (so they can be freed) and keeps acquire fast.

Why. Acquire-time reset is lazy and avoids resetting objects that are never reused, and it charges the cost to the thread that needs the object, which some designs prefer. But idle objects then hold the previous user's data and resources indefinitely: memory dumps, debugging tools and heap-inspection bugs can expose it, and an idle object may keep a large buffer or a lock alive. A common compromise is a cheap reset on release (drop secrets and references) and a validation on acquire (is the connection still alive?).

ConceptWhy return pooled objects through a std::unique_ptr with a custom deleter instead of a raw pointer and a release() function?

Answer

Answer. The handle releases the object exactly once on every path out of its scope, including exceptions and early returns, and its move-only type makes double release a compile error. Ownership transfer is explicit (std::move), and the moved-from handle is empty.

Why. A manual release() is skipped by any exception thrown between acquire and release, which leaks the object from the pool until it runs dry. The deleter's operator() receives the raw pointer and calls the pool instead of delete, which is a direct use of Ch 12's custom deleters. What the handle does not prevent is a raw pointer taken with get() and kept after the handle dies.

TrickyA ConnectionPool is a member of a server object, and handles are stored in a session cache that is also a member. The server's destructor crashes. What is the likely cause and the fix?

Answer

Answer. Members are destroyed in reverse declaration order. If the pool is declared after the session cache, the pool is destroyed first, and then the cache's handles run their deleters, which call give_back on a destroyed pool: use after free. Declare the pool first (so it dies last), or make handles hold a std::weak_ptr to the pool's shared state so a handle that outlives the pool just deletes its object.

Why. A deleter that stores Pool* silently assumes the pool outlives every handle. That holds for a pool in main and breaks for pools inside objects, static pools destroyed at exit while some other static still holds a handle, and pools destroyed during shutdown while another thread is still working. The weak-pointer design costs an atomic operation per release, which is usually acceptable. A debug-build check (the pool asserts that all objects are idle in its destructor) catches the order bug early.

TrickySomeone makes the pool return std::shared_ptr<T>(raw, [this](T* p) { release(p); }) so handles can be shared. What did that cost on the hot path?

Answer

Answer. Every acquire now allocates a control block on the heap (it holds the counts and the deleter), and every copy of the handle does an atomic increment and decrement. The pool was supposed to remove allocation from this path, and it has added one back.

Why. The shared_ptr(ptr, deleter) constructor must store the deleter somewhere, and for a type-erased deleter that is a separately allocated control block (make_shared cannot be used because the object already exists). Options: pass a pool allocator as the third argument so control blocks come from a pool (std::shared_ptr<T>(raw, deleter, alloc)), use an intrusive reference count inside T, or keep unique_ptr handles and share only borrowed references within a scope.

ConceptList the three exhaustion policies and choose one for a database connection pool and one for an order pool in a trading engine.

Answer

Answer. Grow (create another object), block (wait for a release, with a timeout), or fail (return an empty handle or error). A connection pool usually blocks with a timeout, because its size limit exists to protect the database from too many connections. An order pool fails: it rejects or throttles the new order and raises an alarm, because blocking or constructing objects on the hot path would add unpredictable latency.

Why. The policy follows from what the pool's limit protects. Grow is right when the limit is only a performance hint (buffer pools), and it should still have a hard cap. In every case expose a high-water mark and an exhaustion counter, so the pool can be sized from data rather than guesses.

TrickyA blocking connection pool has 10 connections and 10 worker threads. Under load the service hangs with every thread waiting in acquire(). No connection is leaked. What happened?

Answer

Answer. Each request acquires a connection and then, somewhere deeper (an audit log, a nested transaction), acquires a second one. With all 10 threads holding one connection and waiting for another, nobody can release: a resource deadlock with the hold-and-wait condition.

Why. This is the dining philosophers problem with a pool as the shared resource (Ch 6). It does not show up in light load, because a second connection is usually free. Fixes: pass the already-held connection down instead of acquiring another, size the pool as threads × maximum nesting depth, or use a timeout on acquire so the request fails instead of hanging forever. Many connection pool libraries detect it by logging when a thread that already holds a connection asks for another.

TrickyA slot map uses 16-bit generation counters to keep handles at 6 bytes. What can go wrong, and how do you prevent it?

Answer

Answer. After 65,536 reuses of one slot the generation wraps, and a stale handle from 65,536 reuses ago matches again and reaches the wrong object. A busy slot (a bullet in a shooter, an order slot in a trading system) can be reused that often within minutes. Prevent it by retiring a slot whose generation reaches the maximum (never put it back on the free list), or by using 32-bit generations.

Why. Generation checking is a probabilistic defence that is exact only until the counter wraps. With 32 bits, a slot reused once per microsecond wraps after about 72 minutes, so even 32 bits is not enough for the busiest slots in a long-running system if stale handles can live that long; retirement removes the problem entirely at the cost of a slowly shrinking pool. Spreading reuse across slots (FIFO free list) makes wrap-around much less likely for any single slot.

ConceptWhy do game engines identify entities with slot-map handles instead of raw pointers or an std::unordered_map<EntityId, Entity>?

Answer

Answer. Handles detect use of a destroyed entity (generation mismatch) instead of silently reaching a recycled one; the lookup is an array index, O(1) with no hashing; and the dense value array makes "update every entity" a linear, cache-friendly loop. Handles are also plain integers, so they can be saved, sent over the network and stored in other components safely.

Why. A raw pointer cannot tell a dead entity from a new one at the same address, and it is invalidated if storage moves. An unordered_map detects dead ids (lookup fails) but costs a hash and a pointer chase per lookup, scatters entities across nodes, and iterates slowly. The slot map costs one extra indirection per lookup and a swap on erase, which reorders the dense array.

TrickyA buffer pool resets buffers with clear(). After a week in production, the process uses 6 GB although typical messages are 4 KiB. Why?

Answer

Answer. clear() sets the size to zero and keeps the capacity. Every buffer that ever held a rare large message (say 50 MB) keeps that capacity forever, and over time most pooled buffers have seen one. The pool's memory converges to "number of buffers × largest message ever seen".

Why. Keeping capacity is the reason to pool buffers, so the reset is doing what it was asked. The fix is a cap: on release, if capacity() > limit, replace the buffer with a fresh one (std::vector<char>().swap(buf) or shrink_to_fit after clear, which is a non-binding request) or discard the object entirely. Separate pools by size class also help. This is the "memory held forever" cost of pools.

ConceptIn a mutex-protected object pool, should reset() run inside the lock in release?

Answer

Answer. No. Reset the object first, while the releasing thread still owns it exclusively, then take the lock only to push it onto the idle list. The critical section stays a few instructions long.

Why. The object is not shared until it is back on the list, so resetting it needs no synchronisation. Doing it inside the lock makes every acquire and release in the process wait for the slowest reset (clearing a large map, closing a cursor). The same reasoning applies to construction when a pool grows: construct outside the lock, then publish. If release notifies a condition variable, notifying after unlocking avoids waking a thread that immediately blocks on the mutex.

TrickyIs a thread pool an object pool? Explain what is the same and what is different.

Answer

Answer. Yes in purpose, no in interface. It keeps expensive objects (threads: kernel task, stack, thread-local state) alive and reuses them, exactly like an object pool. But callers do not acquire a thread; they submit tasks to a queue, and the pool's threads take tasks. Ownership and lifetime stay inside the pool.

Why. Handing out threads would let callers hold them indefinitely and would need the same exhaustion policies. Inverting the control (tasks go to threads) gives queueing for free and makes "block when exhausted" the natural behaviour. The reset step exists too, implicitly: a task must not leave thread-local state behind for the next task (a classic bug with thread_local caches in pooled threads).

TrickyA pooled Session holds a std::unique_lock<std::mutex> and a std::ofstream as members. The pool resets Session by clearing its string fields. What leaks while sessions are idle?

Answer

Answer. The lock stays held and the file stays open, possibly for hours, because the destructor (which would release them) does not run when an object returns to the pool. Other threads block on that mutex, and the process can run out of file descriptors.

Why. RAII members release resources in the destructor, and an object pool deliberately skips the destructor. Reset must therefore release every resource that should not outlive a use: lock.unlock() (or lock = {}), file.close(). A good habit is to write reset as "assign a default-constructed object", which runs the members' assignment operators and releases what they own, then add back only what you want to keep.

ConceptWould you put a 24-byte Point3 struct in an object pool? When is an object pool the wrong tool?

Answer

Answer. No. Its constructor costs nothing and the allocator serves 24 bytes in tens of nanoseconds; better still, keep such values in a std::vector or on the stack. Object pools are wrong when construction is cheap, when objects are small values, when the peak population is much larger than the steady state (the pool holds the peak forever), and when the extra lifetime bugs outweigh the measured gain.

Why. The benefit of an object pool is proportional to what reset keeps and construction would rebuild. For a value type that is nothing. A memory pool or an arena (Ch 17) helps with allocation cost, and value semantics in contiguous containers avoid the allocation entirely.

Predict the output and find the bug

Drills

Find the bugTwo HTTP requests reuse a pooled Request. What does the second request see?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <optional>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct Request {
    std::string path;
    std::vector<std::string> headers;
    std::optional<std::string> auth_user;
    void reset() { path.clear(); headers.clear(); }
};

class RequestPool {
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Request>> idle_;
public:
    std::unique_ptr<Request> acquire() {
        if (idle_.empty()) return std::make_unique<Request>();
        auto r = std::move(idle_.back());
        idle_.pop_back();
        return r;
    }
    void release(std::unique_ptr<Request> r) { r->reset(); idle_.push_back(std::move(r)); }
};

static void handle(const Request& r) {
    std::printf("%s as %s\n", r.path.c_str(), r.auth_user ? r.auth_user->c_str() : "anonymous");
}

int main() {
    RequestPool pool;
    auto a = pool.acquire();
    a->path = "/account";
    a->auth_user = "alice";
    handle(*a);
    pool.release(std::move(a));

    auto b = pool.acquire();     // an unauthenticated request
    b->path = "/account";
    handle(*b);
    pool.release(std::move(b));
}
Answer
/account as alice
/account as alice

Answer. The anonymous second request is treated as Alice. reset() clears path and headers but forgets auth_user, and the pool hands the same object back.

Why. Stale state is the signature bug of object pools, and here it is a security hole. Nothing crashes and no sanitizer can help: every access is to a live, valid object. Fix: reset every field (auth_user.reset()), or better, write reset() so that new fields cannot be forgotten, for example *this = Request{} followed by restoring the capacities you want to keep, and add a test that a reset object compares equal to a new one.

Find the bugThis pool stores its objects directly in a std::vector and grows it on demand. What does the sanitizer build report?

#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

struct Bullet { float x = 0, y = 0; bool active = false; };

class BulletPool {
    std::vector<Bullet> bullets_;
    std::vector<std::size_t> idle_;
public:
    Bullet* acquire() {
        if (idle_.empty()) {
            bullets_.push_back({});            // grow
            idle_.push_back(bullets_.size() - 1);
        }
        std::size_t i = idle_.back();
        idle_.pop_back();
        bullets_[i].active = true;
        return &bullets_[i];
    }
};

int main() {
    BulletPool pool;
    Bullet* first = pool.acquire();
    for (int i = 0; i < 10; ++i) pool.acquire();   // more bullets
    first->x = 5.0f;                               // move the first bullet
    std::printf("%g\n", first->x);
}
Answer

Answer. push_back reallocates the vector when it grows, so first points into the old, freed buffer. ASan reports heap-use-after-free on the write first->x = 5.0f.

Why. A pool that hands out pointers must never move its objects. A std::vector moves all elements on reallocation, invalidating every pointer and reference. Fixes: reserve the full capacity up front and never grow, store objects in chunks that are never moved (std::deque keeps element addresses stable on push_back, or a vector of unique_ptr<Bullet[]> chunks), or hand out indices / generation handles instead of pointers. This is one of the few object pool bugs ASan does catch, because the old buffer really was freed.

OutputWhat does this print on a 64-bit platform?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>

struct Widget { int v; };
struct Pool;                                         // only pointers to it are needed

struct EmptyReturn { void operator()(Widget*) const noexcept {} };
struct PoolReturn { Pool* pool; void operator()(Widget*) const noexcept {} };
using FnReturn = void (*)(Widget*);

int main() {
    std::printf("%zu %zu %zu %zu\n",
                sizeof(std::unique_ptr<Widget>) / sizeof(void*),
                sizeof(std::unique_ptr<Widget, EmptyReturn>) / sizeof(void*),
                sizeof(std::unique_ptr<Widget, PoolReturn>) / sizeof(void*),
                sizeof(std::unique_ptr<Widget, FnReturn>) / sizeof(void*));
}
Answer
1 1 2 2

Answer. In pointer-sized words: the default deleter and an empty deleter add nothing (1 word), while a deleter that stores the pool pointer and a function-pointer deleter both double the handle to 2 words (16 bytes).

Why. unique_ptr stores its deleter as a member, using the empty base optimisation or [[no_unique_address]], so a stateless deleter takes no space. A function pointer is state, even if every handle stores the same one. For a global or thread_local pool, a stateless deleter that finds the pool itself keeps handles pointer-sized, which matters when millions of handles are stored. Ch 12 covers deleter costs in detail.

Find the bugA handle outlives its pool. What does the sanitizer build report?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <vector>

struct Buffer { std::vector<char> bytes; };

class BufferPool {
public:
    struct Return { BufferPool* pool; void operator()(Buffer* b) const noexcept { pool->give_back(b); } };
    using Handle = std::unique_ptr<Buffer, Return>;
    BufferPool() { for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) idle_.push_back(new Buffer); }
    ~BufferPool() { for (Buffer* b : idle_) delete b; }
    Handle acquire() { Buffer* b = idle_.back(); idle_.pop_back(); return Handle(b, Return{this}); }
private:
    void give_back(Buffer* b) noexcept { b->bytes.clear(); idle_.push_back(b); }
    std::vector<Buffer*> idle_;
};

int main() {
    auto pool = std::make_unique<BufferPool>();
    BufferPool::Handle h = pool->acquire();
    h->bytes.assign(64, 'x');
    pool.reset();                 // shutdown order bug: pool first
    std::puts("pool destroyed");
}                                 // h's deleter runs here
Answer

Answer. When h is destroyed at the end of main, its deleter calls give_back on the deleted pool, which reads and writes the freed idle_ vector. ASan reports heap-use-after-free inside give_back. (The buffer that was out also leaks, since the pool's destructor only deletes idle buffers.)

Why. A deleter holding a raw Pool* silently requires the pool to outlive every handle. Fixes: destroy users before the pool (declaration order), have the pool's destructor assert that nothing is checked out, or let handles hold a std::weak_ptr to shared pool state and simply delete the object when the pool is gone. The coding section implements the last one.

Find the bugAfter the stale-state incident, the team rewrote reset() so that no field can ever be forgotten. What does this print, and what did the pool stop doing?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <vector>

struct Message {
    std::vector<char> payload;
    int retries = 0;
    void reset() { *this = Message{}; }   // every field back to its default
};

class MessagePool {
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Message>> idle_;
public:
    std::unique_ptr<Message> acquire() {
        if (idle_.empty()) return std::make_unique<Message>();
        auto m = std::move(idle_.back());
        idle_.pop_back();
        return m;
    }
    void release(std::unique_ptr<Message> m) { m->reset(); idle_.push_back(std::move(m)); }
};

int main() {
    MessagePool pool;
    const Message* first = nullptr;
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) {
        auto m = pool.acquire();
        if (!first) first = m.get();
        std::printf("request %d: same object %s, capacity %zu\n", i, m.get() == first ? "yes" : "no", m->payload.capacity());
        m->payload.resize(4096);
        m->retries = 1;
        pool.release(std::move(m));
    }
}
Answer
request 0: same object yes, capacity 0
request 1: same object yes, capacity 0
request 2: same object yes, capacity 0

Answer. The same Message comes back every time, but its buffer does not. *this = Message{} move-assigns from a temporary, and the vector's move assignment frees the 4 KiB buffer and adopts the temporary's empty one. Every request allocates the payload again, so the pool now saves one small new and nothing else. Most people predict capacity 4096 for requests 1 and 2, because "the pool keeps the object".

Why. Assignment from a fresh object gives fresh state, and fresh state includes capacity 0: with std::allocator (which propagates on move assignment) both standard libraries free the old buffer and take the source's. The safety idea is right and only needs to keep what the pool exists for: auto keep = std::move(payload); *this = Message{}; payload = std::move(keep); payload.clear(); resets every other field, including ones added later, and keeps the buffer. Test both properties: a reset object compares equal to a new one, and its capacity survives.

Find the bugWhy does this not compile, and is the compiler right?

#include <memory>
#include <vector>

struct Conn { int fd = -1; };
struct Return { void operator()(Conn* c) const noexcept { delete c; } };
using Handle = std::unique_ptr<Conn, Return>;

static Handle acquire() { return Handle(new Conn{3}); }

int main() {
    Handle h = acquire();
    std::vector<Handle> in_flight;
    in_flight.push_back(h);       // keep a copy for the retry logic
}
Answer

Answer. push_back(h) needs to copy the handle, and unique_ptr's copy constructor is deleted. Both compilers reject it. The compiler is right: two copies of the handle would both return the connection to the pool, which is a double release.

Why. Move-only handles turn the double-release bug into a compile error. If the vector should own the handle, write in_flight.push_back(std::move(h)) and stop using h. If the retry logic only needs to look at the connection, store a reference or the generation handle, not a second owner. Returning Handle by value from acquire compiles because a returned local is moved (or elided, Ch 23).

OutputTrace the generations. What does this print?

#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

struct Handle { std::uint32_t index, gen; };

class Slots {
    struct Slot { std::uint32_t gen = 0; bool live = false; };
    std::vector<Slot> slots_ = std::vector<Slot>(2);
public:
    Handle acquire() {
        for (std::uint32_t i = 0; i < slots_.size(); ++i)
            if (!slots_[i].live) { slots_[i].live = true; return {i, slots_[i].gen}; }
        return {UINT32_MAX, 0};
    }
    bool valid(Handle h) const { return h.index < slots_.size() && slots_[h.index].live && slots_[h.index].gen == h.gen; }
    void release(Handle h) { if (valid(h)) { slots_[h.index].live = false; ++slots_[h.index].gen; } }
};

int main() {
    Slots s;
    Handle a = s.acquire();
    Handle b = s.acquire();
    s.release(a);
    Handle c = s.acquire();
    s.release(c);
    Handle d = s.acquire();
    std::printf("a{%u,%u} b{%u,%u} c{%u,%u} d{%u,%u}\n", a.index, a.gen, b.index, b.gen, c.index, c.gen, d.index, d.gen);
    std::printf("valid: a=%d b=%d c=%d d=%d\n", s.valid(a), s.valid(b), s.valid(c), s.valid(d));
    s.release(a);   // stale: ignored
    std::printf("d still valid: %d\n", s.valid(d));
}
Answer
a{0,0} b{1,0} c{0,1} d{0,2}
valid: a=0 b=1 c=0 d=1
d still valid: 1

Answer. a and b take slots 0 and 1 at generation 0. Releasing a bumps slot 0 to generation 1, so c is {0, 1}; releasing c bumps it to 2, so d is {0, 2}. Only b and d are valid, and the stale release through a is rejected, so d survives.

Why. The generation is the number of times the slot has been released. Every handle created before a release carries a smaller number and can no longer read or release the slot. Without generations, s.release(a) would have freed d's slot: the classic use-after-release turned into a double use.

Find the bugA thread-safe pool locks in acquire. What does ThreadSanitizer report?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <mutex>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

struct Job { int payload = 0; };

class JobPool {
    std::mutex m_;
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Job>> all_;
    std::vector<Job*> idle_;
public:
    JobPool() {
        for (int i = 0; i < 64; ++i) { all_.push_back(std::make_unique<Job>()); idle_.push_back(all_.back().get()); }
        idle_.reserve(64);
    }
    Job* acquire() {
        std::lock_guard lock(m_);
        if (idle_.empty()) return nullptr;
        Job* j = idle_.back();
        idle_.pop_back();
        return j;
    }
    void release(Job* j) {        // "release is just a push, no lock needed"
        j->payload = 0;
        idle_.push_back(j);
    }
};

int main() {
    JobPool pool;
    auto work = [&] {
        for (int i = 0; i < 10000; ++i)
            if (Job* j = pool.acquire()) { j->payload = i; pool.release(j); }
    };
    std::thread t1(work), t2(work);
    t1.join();
    t2.join();
    std::puts("done");
}
Answer

Answer. TSan reports a data race on idle_: release modifies the vector without the mutex while the other thread reads and modifies it inside acquire. Even a push that never reallocates writes the vector's end pointer, and the pop in the other thread reads it.

Why. A mutex protects data only if every access to that data takes it. Locking one side of a producer/consumer pair is the most common way to get this wrong. The fix is std::lock_guard lock(m_); around the push, with the reset (j->payload = 0) left outside the lock because the releasing thread still owns the job at that point. The program usually prints "done" in a normal build, which is why it is tagged ub and checked with TSan.

OutputA pool hands out std::shared_ptr handles. When does the object return to the pool?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <vector>

struct Frame { int seq = 0; };

class FramePool {
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Frame>> all_;
    std::vector<Frame*> idle_;
public:
    FramePool() { all_.push_back(std::make_unique<Frame>()); idle_.push_back(all_.back().get()); }
    std::shared_ptr<Frame> acquire() {
        Frame* f = idle_.back();
        idle_.pop_back();
        return std::shared_ptr<Frame>(f, [this](Frame* p) { std::printf("  frame %d back in pool\n", p->seq); idle_.push_back(p); });
    }
    std::size_t idle() const { return idle_.size(); }
};

int main() {
    FramePool pool;
    auto f = pool.acquire();
    f->seq = 42;
    {
        auto encoder = f;
        auto network = f;
        std::printf("use_count %ld, idle %zu\n", f.use_count(), pool.idle());
        f.reset();
        std::puts("main dropped its copy");
    }
    std::printf("idle %zu\n", pool.idle());
}
Answer
use_count 3, idle 0
main dropped its copy
  frame 42 back in pool
idle 1

Answer. Three owners exist inside the block, so use_count is 3 and nothing is idle. Dropping f does not return the frame; the deleter runs when the last copy (network or encoder, whichever is destroyed last) goes away at the closing brace.

Why. A shared_ptr deleter runs when the strong count reaches zero, whichever copy that happens in. That is convenient for frames shared by several consumers, but remember the cost: constructing this shared_ptr allocated a control block, and copies do atomic count updates. The deleter captures this, so the same "pool must outlive handles" rule applies.

Find the bugA logger keeps a raw pointer obtained from a handle. What does it log?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct Quote { std::string symbol; double px = 0; };

class QuotePool {
public:
    struct Return { QuotePool* p; void operator()(Quote* q) const noexcept { q->symbol.clear(); q->px = 0; p->idle_.push_back(q); } };
    using Handle = std::unique_ptr<Quote, Return>;
    QuotePool() { for (int i = 0; i < 2; ++i) { all_.push_back(std::make_unique<Quote>()); idle_.push_back(all_.back().get()); } }
    Handle acquire() { Quote* q = idle_.back(); idle_.pop_back(); return Handle(q, Return{this}); }
private:
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Quote>> all_;
    std::vector<Quote*> idle_;
};

int main() {
    QuotePool pool;
    const Quote* last_logged = nullptr;
    {
        auto q = pool.acquire();
        q->symbol = "AAPL";
        q->px = 227.5;
        last_logged = q.get();             // keep it for the end-of-day report
    }
    auto next = pool.acquire();
    next->symbol = "MSFT";
    next->px = 512.25;
    std::printf("last logged: %s %.2f\n", last_logged->symbol.c_str(), last_logged->px);
}
Answer
last logged: MSFT 512.25

Answer. It logs MSFT at 512.25. The AAPL quote went back to the pool at the closing brace, the next acquire got the same object (LIFO), and last_logged now looks at the new quote. ASan is clean, and this program has no undefined behaviour at all: the object was never destroyed, only reset and reused.

Why. RAII handles fix release, not borrowing. A raw pointer from get() is a non-owning view and must not outlive the handle. If something needs the data later, copy the data (Quote copy = *q;), or keep a generation-checked handle that will report the reuse. This is the purest form of use-after-release: no tool can find it, only the pool's design.

OutputA fail-fast pool with capacity 2. What does this print?

#include <algorithm>
#include <cstdio>
#include <optional>
#include <vector>

class TicketPool {
    std::vector<int> idle_{1, 2};
    int high_water_ = 0, out_ = 0, rejected_ = 0;
public:
    std::optional<int> acquire() {
        if (idle_.empty()) { ++rejected_; return std::nullopt; }
        int t = idle_.back();
        idle_.pop_back();
        high_water_ = std::max(high_water_, ++out_);
        return t;
    }
    void release(int t) { idle_.push_back(t); --out_; }
    void stats() const { std::printf("high water %d, rejected %d\n", high_water_, rejected_); }
};

int main() {
    TicketPool pool;
    auto a = pool.acquire();
    auto b = pool.acquire();
    auto c = pool.acquire();
    std::printf("a=%d b=%d c=%s\n", *a, *b, c ? "got one" : "none");
    pool.release(*a);
    auto d = pool.acquire();
    std::printf("d=%d\n", d.value_or(-1));
    pool.stats();
}
Answer
a=2 b=1 c=none
d=2
high water 2, rejected 1

Answer. The idle list is a stack with 2 on top, so a gets 2 and b gets 1. The third request is rejected. Releasing ticket 2 puts it back on top, so d gets 2. At most two were ever out, and one request was rejected.

Why. The fail policy returns an empty std::optional and counts the event, which is what you want on a latency-critical path: the caller decides what to do (reject, retry later) and the counters tell operations how to size the pool. Note that *c on an empty optional would be undefined, which is why the code tests c first; value() would throw std::bad_optional_access instead.

Write the code

Coding

CodeImplement ObjectPool<T> with RAII handles. Requirements: ObjectPool(initial, max, reset) pre-constructs initial objects; acquire() returns a std::unique_ptr<T, Return>, growing up to max and returning an empty handle beyond that; release (through the handle) resets the object, never allocates and never throws; the pool reports its high-water mark and the number of failed acquires.

Answer

Approach. The pool owns every object in all_ and lists the idle ones in idle_; both vectors reserve max slots at construction, so a release is a reset plus a push_back that cannot reallocate. The deleter holds a pool pointer and calls a private release. Growth constructs a new object only when the idle list is empty and the limit allows it.

#include <algorithm>
#include <cassert>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <functional>
#include <memory>
#include <vector>

template <class T>
class ObjectPool {
public:
    class Return {
        ObjectPool* pool_ = nullptr;
    public:
        Return() = default;
        explicit Return(ObjectPool* p) noexcept : pool_(p) {}
        void operator()(T* obj) const noexcept { pool_->release(obj); }
    };
    using Handle = std::unique_ptr<T, Return>;

    ObjectPool(std::size_t initial, std::size_t max, std::function<void(T&)> reset)
        : max_(max), reset_(std::move(reset)) {
        all_.reserve(max_);
        idle_.reserve(max_);
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < initial && i < max_; ++i) {
            all_.push_back(std::make_unique<T>());
            idle_.push_back(all_.back().get());
        }
    }
    ~ObjectPool() { assert(idle_.size() == all_.size() && "objects still checked out"); }
    ObjectPool(const ObjectPool&) = delete;
    ObjectPool& operator=(const ObjectPool&) = delete;

    Handle acquire() {
        if (idle_.empty()) {
            if (all_.size() == max_) { ++failed_; return Handle(nullptr, Return(this)); }
            all_.push_back(std::make_unique<T>());          // grow (may throw: nothing changed yet)
            idle_.push_back(all_.back().get());
        }
        T* obj = idle_.back();
        idle_.pop_back();
        high_water_ = std::max(high_water_, all_.size() - idle_.size());
        return Handle(obj, Return(this));
    }
    std::size_t high_water() const { return high_water_; }
    std::size_t failed() const { return failed_; }
    std::size_t size() const { return all_.size(); }
    std::size_t idle() const { return idle_.size(); }

private:
    void release(T* obj) noexcept {
        reset_(*obj);
        idle_.push_back(obj);                               // capacity is max_: no reallocation
    }
    std::size_t max_, high_water_ = 0, failed_ = 0;
    std::function<void(T&)> reset_;
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<T>> all_;
    std::vector<T*> idle_;
};

struct Buffer { std::vector<char> data; };

int main() {
    ObjectPool<Buffer> pool(2, 3, [](Buffer& b) { b.data.clear(); });
    {
        auto a = pool.acquire();
        auto b = pool.acquire();
        auto c = pool.acquire();          // grows to 3
        auto d = pool.acquire();          // over the limit
        a->data.assign(4096, 'a');
        std::printf("size %zu, d is %s\n", pool.size(), d ? "valid" : "empty");
    }
    auto e = pool.acquire();
    std::printf("reused buffer: size %zu, capacity kept %s\n", e->data.size(), e->data.capacity() >= 4096 ? "yes" : "no");
    e.reset();
    std::printf("idle %zu, high water %zu, failed %zu\n", pool.idle(), pool.high_water(), pool.failed());
}
size 3, d is empty
reused buffer: size 0, capacity kept yes
idle 3, high water 3, failed 1

Complexity and pitfalls. Acquire and release are O(1); growth is one construction. The LIFO idle list hands the most recently released buffer (the one with 4 KiB of capacity) back first, which is why e gets it. Pitfalls: an empty handle still carries a deleter, but unique_ptr never calls the deleter on a null pointer, so that is safe; a reset_ that throws inside the noexcept release calls std::terminate; and the pool must outlive its handles (the destructor asserts in debug builds).

Estimated rating: ~1500 · straightforward structure, but no-allocation release, growth limits and the deleter design must all be right

CodeWrite a blocking pool: acquire_for(timeout) waits until an object is free or the timeout expires (then returns an empty handle). Test with 6 threads sharing 2 objects and check that at most 2 are ever in use at once.

Answer

Approach. A mutex protects the idle list and a condition variable signals releases. acquire_for uses wait_for with a predicate, which handles spurious wake-ups and returns false on timeout. release pushes under the lock and notifies one waiter after unlocking.

#include <atomic>
#include <chrono>
#include <condition_variable>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <mutex>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

struct Conn { int id = 0; int uses = 0; };

class BlockingPool {
public:
    struct Return { BlockingPool* p; void operator()(Conn* c) const noexcept { p->release(c); } };
    using Handle = std::unique_ptr<Conn, Return>;

    explicit BlockingPool(int n) {
        for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) all_.push_back(std::make_unique<Conn>(Conn{i}));
        for (auto& c : all_) idle_.push_back(c.get());
    }
    Handle acquire_for(std::chrono::milliseconds timeout) {
        std::unique_lock lock(m_);
        if (!cv_.wait_for(lock, timeout, [&] { return !idle_.empty(); }))
            return Handle(nullptr, Return{this});
        Conn* c = idle_.back();
        idle_.pop_back();
        return Handle(c, Return{this});
    }
    std::size_t idle() { std::lock_guard lock(m_); return idle_.size(); }

private:
    void release(Conn* c) noexcept {
        {
            std::lock_guard lock(m_);
            idle_.push_back(c);           // capacity never exceeds all_.size(): reserved by construction
        }
        cv_.notify_one();
    }
    std::mutex m_;
    std::condition_variable cv_;
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Conn>> all_;
    std::vector<Conn*> idle_;
};

int main() {
    BlockingPool pool(2);
    std::atomic<int> in_use{0}, max_in_use{0}, timeouts{0}, done{0};
    auto client = [&] {
        for (int i = 0; i < 20; ++i) {
            auto c = pool.acquire_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(500));
            if (!c) { ++timeouts; continue; }
            int now = ++in_use;
            int seen = max_in_use.load();
            while (now > seen && !max_in_use.compare_exchange_weak(seen, now)) {}
            ++c->uses;                                  // exclusive use: no race
            std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::microseconds(200));
            --in_use;
            ++done;
        }
    };
    std::vector<std::thread> ts;
    for (int t = 0; t < 6; ++t) ts.emplace_back(client);
    for (auto& t : ts) t.join();
    std::printf("completed %d, timeouts %d, max in use %d, idle %zu\n", done.load(), timeouts.load(), max_in_use.load(), pool.idle());
}
completed 120, timeouts 0, max in use 2, idle 2

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) per operation plus waiting time. The idle_ vector was filled to its full size at construction, so its capacity covers every release. Pitfalls: wait_for without a predicate (spurious wake-ups, and a missed notification if the release happened before the wait), notifying while holding the lock (correct, but the woken thread immediately blocks on the mutex), and the nested-acquire deadlock from the concept drills. The 500 ms timeout is generous so the test never times out under TSan's slowdown.

Estimated rating: ~1600 · standard condition-variable pattern, plus a concurrent test that actually checks the invariant

CodeImplement a slot map: Key insert(T), bool erase(Key), T* get(Key), size() and iteration over all live values in a dense, contiguous array. Stale keys must return null, and erase must be O(1).

Answer

Approach. Three arrays: slots_ (generation, live flag, and either the value's dense index or the next free slot), values_ (dense values) and owner_ (for each dense value, the slot that points to it). Erase moves the last value into the hole, updates the moved value's slot through owner_, bumps the erased slot's generation and pushes it on the free list.

#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

template <class T>
class SlotMap {
public:
    struct Key { std::uint32_t index, gen; };

    Key insert(T value) {
        std::uint32_t s;
        if (free_head_ != kNone) { s = free_head_; free_head_ = slots_[s].link; }
        else { s = static_cast<std::uint32_t>(slots_.size()); slots_.push_back({}); }
        slots_[s].link = static_cast<std::uint32_t>(values_.size());
        slots_[s].live = true;
        values_.push_back(std::move(value));
        owner_.push_back(s);
        return {s, slots_[s].gen};
    }
    T* get(Key k) {
        if (k.index >= slots_.size()) return nullptr;
        const Slot& s = slots_[k.index];
        return s.live && s.gen == k.gen ? &values_[s.link] : nullptr;
    }
    bool erase(Key k) {
        if (!get(k)) return false;
        Slot& s = slots_[k.index];
        std::uint32_t hole = s.link, last = static_cast<std::uint32_t>(values_.size() - 1);
        if (hole != last) {
            values_[hole] = std::move(values_[last]);
            owner_[hole] = owner_[last];
            slots_[owner_[hole]].link = hole;
        }
        values_.pop_back();
        owner_.pop_back();
        s.live = false;
        ++s.gen;
        s.link = free_head_;
        free_head_ = k.index;
        return true;
    }
    std::size_t size() const { return values_.size(); }
    auto begin() { return values_.begin(); }
    auto end() { return values_.end(); }

private:
    static constexpr std::uint32_t kNone = UINT32_MAX;
    struct Slot { std::uint32_t gen = 0; std::uint32_t link = kNone; bool live = false; };
    std::vector<Slot> slots_;
    std::vector<T> values_;
    std::vector<std::uint32_t> owner_;
    std::uint32_t free_head_ = kNone;
};

struct Entity { std::string name; int hp; };

int main() {
    SlotMap<Entity> world;
    auto hero = world.insert({"hero", 100});
    auto orc = world.insert({"orc", 30});
    auto bat = world.insert({"bat", 5});
    auto elf = world.insert({"elf", 60});

    world.erase(orc);                                  // elf moves into orc's dense position
    std::printf("orc: %s, elf: %s %d\n", world.get(orc) ? "alive" : "gone", world.get(elf)->name.c_str(), world.get(elf)->hp);

    auto troll = world.insert({"troll", 80});          // reuses orc's slot with a new generation
    std::printf("troll slot %u gen %u, orc slot %u gen %u, stale orc: %s\n",
                troll.index, troll.gen, orc.index, orc.gen, world.get(orc) ? "found" : "null");

    int total = 0;
    for (Entity& e : world) total += e.hp;             // dense iteration
    std::printf("%zu entities, total hp %d, double erase: %s\n", world.size(), total, world.erase(orc) ? "accepted" : "refused");
    world.erase(hero);
    world.erase(bat);
    std::printf("left: %zu, troll is %s\n", world.size(), world.get(troll)->name.c_str());
}
orc: gone, elf: elf 60
troll slot 1 gen 1, orc slot 1 gen 0, stale orc: null
4 entities, total hp 245, double erase: refused
left: 2, troll is troll

Complexity and pitfalls. Insert, get and erase are O(1) (insert amortised); iteration is a linear walk over contiguous values. Pitfalls: forgetting to update the moved element's slot (its key then points at the wrong value or out of range), erasing the last element (the move must be skipped, or the self-move leaves a moved-from value), and keeping T* across inserts, because values_ can reallocate and erase reorders it. Dense order is not insertion order. The generations can wrap after 232 reuses of a slot; production slot maps retire such slots.

Estimated rating: ~1800 · three arrays that must stay consistent through swap-and-pop, plus generation handling

CodeDesign an object pool whose handles may safely outlive the pool. If the pool still exists, releasing a handle returns the object; if the pool has been destroyed, releasing deletes the object. It must be safe to release from any thread.

Answer

Approach. Put the pool's state (mutex, idle list, reset function) in a std::shared_ptr<State> owned by the pool, and give each handle's deleter a std::weak_ptr<State>. On release, lock() the weak pointer: if it succeeds, the state is kept alive for the duration of the release and the object goes back; if it fails, the pool is gone and the deleter deletes the object. Checked-out objects are owned by their handle, idle ones by the state.

#include <cstdio>
#include <functional>
#include <memory>
#include <mutex>
#include <vector>

template <class T>
class SafePool {
    struct State {
        std::mutex m;
        std::vector<std::unique_ptr<T>> idle;
        std::function<void(T&)> reset;
    };
    std::shared_ptr<State> state_;

public:
    struct Return {
        std::weak_ptr<State> state;
        void operator()(T* obj) const noexcept {
            std::unique_ptr<T> owned(obj);              // deletes obj unless handed back
            if (auto s = state.lock()) {
                s->reset(*owned);
                std::lock_guard lock(s->m);
                s->idle.push_back(std::move(owned));
            }
        }
    };
    using Handle = std::unique_ptr<T, Return>;

    SafePool(std::size_t n, std::function<void(T&)> reset) : state_(std::make_shared<State>()) {
        state_->reset = std::move(reset);
        state_->idle.reserve(n);
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) state_->idle.push_back(std::make_unique<T>());
    }
    Handle acquire() {
        std::lock_guard lock(state_->m);
        if (state_->idle.empty()) return Handle(nullptr, Return{state_});
        T* obj = state_->idle.back().release();
        state_->idle.pop_back();
        return Handle(obj, Return{state_});
    }
    std::size_t idle() const { std::lock_guard lock(state_->m); return state_->idle.size(); }
};

struct Tracked {
    static inline int alive = 0;
    int value = 0;
    Tracked() { ++alive; }
    ~Tracked() { --alive; }
};

int main() {
    SafePool<Tracked>::Handle survivor;
    {
        SafePool<Tracked> pool(3, [](Tracked& t) { t.value = 0; });
        {
            auto a = pool.acquire();
            a->value = 7;
        }
        std::printf("after normal release: idle %zu, alive %d\n", pool.idle(), Tracked::alive);
        survivor = pool.acquire();
        survivor->value = 9;
    }   // pool destroyed while survivor is checked out
    std::printf("pool gone: alive %d, survivor value %d\n", Tracked::alive, survivor->value);
    survivor.reset();   // deleter finds no pool and deletes the object
    std::printf("after release: alive %d\n", Tracked::alive);
}
after normal release: idle 3, alive 3
pool gone: alive 1, survivor value 9
after release: alive 0

Complexity and pitfalls. Each handle stores a weak_ptr (16 bytes), so handles are 24 bytes, and each release does an atomic lock() plus the mutex. The object is wrapped in a unique_ptr at the top of the deleter so that every path either hands it back or deletes it. Pitfalls: push_back inside a noexcept deleter could throw bad_alloc if the idle vector had to grow (it cannot here, because only objects created by this pool come back and the vector reserved room for all of them); and calling reset outside the lock is deliberate, because the releasing thread still owns the object exclusively.

Estimated rating: ~1800 · ownership transfer between handle and pool and weak_ptr lifetime reasoning, with no leak on either destruction order

CodeBuild a buffer pool with size buckets (4 KiB, 16 KiB, 64 KiB). acquire(n) returns a handle to a std::vector<char> with capacity of at least n, taken from the smallest bucket that fits; larger requests get an unpooled buffer. On release, buffers that grew beyond twice their bucket size are discarded instead of kept, and each bucket keeps at most 4 idle buffers.

Answer

Approach. Each bucket is a stack of idle buffers. The handle's deleter knows the bucket index (or a sentinel for unpooled buffers). Release clears the buffer and keeps it only if its capacity is within the cap and the bucket has room; otherwise the buffer is freed. Counters show reuse and discards so the policy is observable.

#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <vector>

class BufferPool {
public:
    using Buffer = std::vector<char>;
    static constexpr std::array<std::size_t, 3> kSizes{4096, 16384, 65536};
    static constexpr std::size_t kMaxIdle = 4, kUnpooled = kSizes.size();

    struct Return {
        BufferPool* pool;
        std::size_t bucket;
        void operator()(Buffer* b) const noexcept { pool->release(b, bucket); }
    };
    using Handle = std::unique_ptr<Buffer, Return>;

    BufferPool() { for (auto& b : idle_) b.reserve(kMaxIdle); }

    Handle acquire(std::size_t n) {
        std::size_t k = 0;
        while (k < kSizes.size() && kSizes[k] < n) ++k;
        if (k == kUnpooled) {                                   // too large to pool
            auto* b = new Buffer;
            b->reserve(n);
            return Handle(b, Return{this, kUnpooled});
        }
        auto& stack = idle_[k];
        if (!stack.empty()) {
            ++reused_;
            Buffer* b = stack.back().release();
            stack.pop_back();
            return Handle(b, Return{this, k});
        }
        auto* b = new Buffer;
        b->reserve(kSizes[k]);
        return Handle(b, Return{this, k});
    }
    void stats() const {
        std::printf("reused %d, discarded %d, idle per bucket: %zu %zu %zu\n",
                    reused_, discarded_, idle_[0].size(), idle_[1].size(), idle_[2].size());
    }

private:
    void release(Buffer* b, std::size_t k) noexcept {
        std::unique_ptr<Buffer> owned(b);
        if (k == kUnpooled) return;                             // freed
        if (b->capacity() > 2 * kSizes[k] || idle_[k].size() == kMaxIdle) { ++discarded_; return; }
        b->clear();                                             // keep the capacity
        idle_[k].push_back(std::move(owned));
    }
    std::array<std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Buffer>>, 3> idle_;
    int reused_ = 0, discarded_ = 0;
};

int main() {
    BufferPool pool;
    {
        auto a = pool.acquire(1000);
        auto b = pool.acquire(10000);
        a->assign(1000, 'a');
        b->assign(200000, 'b');                // grows far past its 16 KiB bucket
        auto big = pool.acquire(1 << 20);      // unpooled
        std::printf("a cap >= 4096: %s, big cap >= 1 MiB: %s\n",
                    a->capacity() >= 4096 ? "yes" : "no", big->capacity() >= (1u << 20) ? "yes" : "no");
    }
    pool.stats();
    auto c = pool.acquire(3000);               // reuses a's buffer
    std::printf("c is empty: %s, cap >= 4096: %s\n", c->empty() ? "yes" : "no", c->capacity() >= 4096 ? "yes" : "no");
    c.reset();
    std::vector<BufferPool::Handle> many;
    for (int i = 0; i < 6; ++i) many.push_back(pool.acquire(100));
    many.clear();                              // only 4 may stay idle
    pool.stats();
}
a cap >= 4096: yes, big cap >= 1 MiB: yes
reused 0, discarded 1, idle per bucket: 1 0 0
c is empty: yes, cap >= 4096: yes
reused 2, discarded 3, idle per bucket: 4 0 0

Complexity and pitfalls. O(number of buckets) to pick a bucket, O(1) otherwise. The 200,000-byte buffer is discarded on release instead of pinning 200 KB in the 16 KiB bucket forever, which is the "memory held forever" fix from the theory. Pitfalls: the deleter's bucket must be the one the buffer came from, not recomputed from its current capacity (it may have grown); clear() keeps capacity but shrink_to_fit() would throw it away; and the idle stacks reserve kMaxIdle so release never allocates.

Estimated rating: ~1600 · a policy-heavy pool: bucket choice, capacity caps and idle limits must agree between acquire and release

CodePut a per-thread cache in front of a shared, mutex-protected pool.
