Each thread keeps up to 8 idle objects locally; when its cache is empty it takes a batch of 4 from the shared pool (constructing new objects if needed), and when the cache is over 8 it returns a batch of 4. A thread's cache must flush back when the thread exits. Test with 4 threads.

Answer

Approach. A global SharedPool holds idle objects under a mutex. A thread_local cache object serves acquire and release without locking and moves objects to and from the shared pool in batches of 4, so the lock is taken about once per four operations at most. The cache's destructor runs at thread exit and returns everything. Each object carries an atomic "owned" flag so the test can prove no object is ever held by two threads.

#include <atomic>
#include <cstdio>
#include <mutex>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

struct Msg {
    std::atomic<bool> owned{false};
    int payload = 0;
};

class SharedPool {
    std::mutex m_;
    std::vector<Msg*> idle_;
    std::vector<Msg*> all_;
public:
    ~SharedPool() { for (Msg* p : all_) delete p; }
    void take(std::vector<Msg*>& out, std::size_t n) {
        std::lock_guard lock(m_);
        while (n-- > 0) {
            if (idle_.empty()) { all_.push_back(new Msg); idle_.push_back(all_.back()); }
            out.push_back(idle_.back());
            idle_.pop_back();
        }
    }
    void give(std::vector<Msg*>& from, std::size_t n) {
        std::lock_guard lock(m_);
        while (n-- > 0 && !from.empty()) { idle_.push_back(from.back()); from.pop_back(); }
    }
    std::size_t total() { std::lock_guard lock(m_); return all_.size(); }
    std::size_t idle() { std::lock_guard lock(m_); return idle_.size(); }
};

static SharedPool g_pool;

class LocalCache {
    static constexpr std::size_t kHigh = 8, kBatch = 4;
    std::vector<Msg*> cache_;
public:
    ~LocalCache() { g_pool.give(cache_, cache_.size()); }   // thread exit
    Msg* acquire() {
        if (cache_.empty()) g_pool.take(cache_, kBatch);
        Msg* m = cache_.back();
        cache_.pop_back();
        return m;
    }
    void release(Msg* m) {
        m->payload = 0;                                       // reset
        cache_.push_back(m);
        if (cache_.size() > kHigh) g_pool.give(cache_, kBatch);
    }
};

static thread_local LocalCache t_cache;

int main() {
    std::atomic<int> clashes{0};
    auto worker = [&](int id) {
        std::vector<Msg*> held;
        for (int i = 0; i < 20000; ++i) {
            if (held.size() < 12 && (i % 3 != 2)) {
                Msg* m = t_cache.acquire();
                if (m->owned.exchange(true)) ++clashes;
                m->payload = id;
                held.push_back(m);
            } else if (!held.empty()) {
                Msg* m = held.back();
                held.pop_back();
                m->owned.store(false);
                t_cache.release(m);
            }
        }
        for (Msg* m : held) { m->owned.store(false); t_cache.release(m); }
    };
    std::vector<std::thread> ts;
    for (int t = 0; t < 4; ++t) ts.emplace_back(worker, t);
    for (auto& t : ts) t.join();
    std::printf("clashes: %d\n", clashes.load());
    std::printf("all objects back in the shared pool: %s\n", g_pool.idle() == g_pool.total() ? "yes" : "no");
    std::printf("objects created: %s\n", g_pool.total() <= 4 * 24 ? "bounded" : "too many");
}
clashes: 0
all objects back in the shared pool: yes
objects created: bounded

Complexity and pitfalls. Most operations touch only the thread's own vector; the mutex is taken once per batch. Each thread holds at most 12 objects plus a cache of at most 8 plus a batch of 4, so the total stays bounded. Pitfalls: a thread that exits without flushing its cache strands objects (the thread_local destructor prevents it); static destruction order (the global pool must outlive every thread-local cache, which holds because thread-local objects of a thread are destroyed before static objects, and worker threads are joined before main returns); and objects migrating between threads, which is fine here because the shared pool is the only meeting point and it is locked. The main thread's own cache is never used, so it is empty at exit.

Estimated rating: ~2000 · two-level design with batching, thread-exit flushing and destruction-order reasoning, verified under TSan

Cheat sheet

Theory
  • Object pool = reuse constructed objects (saves construction); memory pool = reuse raw blocks (saves allocation). Say which one you mean.
  • Reset must make the object indistinguishable from a new one while keeping the expensive parts (capacity, sockets). Reset on release by default; validate on acquire.
  • Hand out std::unique_ptr<T, Return>: exactly-once release on every path, move-only so no double release. Pool-pointer deleters make handles 16 bytes; the pool must outlive handles (or use weak_ptr state).
  • shared_ptr handles allocate a control block per acquire unless you supply an allocator.
  • Exhaustion: grow (buffers), block with timeout (connections, beware nested acquires), fail and alarm (trading). Track a high-water mark.
  • Stale state, double release and use after release are silent: ASan cannot see them. Use in-pool flags, debug poisoning and generation-checked handles.
  • Slot map: handle = (index, generation), dense values, O(1) insert/erase/get; watch generation wrap-around and pointer invalidation.
  • Pools hurt when objects are cheap to build, when peak population is far above normal (memory held forever), and when reset logic drifts from the class. Measure: a pooled message was 1.6 to 2.1 times faster on an Apple M1, not 10 times.

Part E · Memory management · Chapter 17

Arena allocation

An arena hands out memory by moving a pointer forward and frees everything at once by moving it back. It is the fastest allocator there is, and it works whenever a group of objects shares one lifetime: a request, a frame, a parse. This chapter covers the bump pointer and its alignment arithmetic, the lifetime discipline arenas demand, destructors, std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource, growing and scratch arenas, and the bugs that come with them.

TheoryDrillsCoding· about 4 hours· prerequisites: Ch 14, Ch 15

Bump-pointer arenas

Theory

Mental model. An arena (also called a region, a linear allocator or a bump allocator) owns one large buffer and an offset into it. Everything before the offset is in use, everything after is free. To allocate n bytes, round the offset up to the required alignment, return that address, and add n. There is no per-object bookkeeping and no way to free one object: the whole arena is freed, or reset, at once.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>
#include <type_traits>

class Arena {
    std::byte* base_;
    std::size_t cap_, offset_ = 0;
public:
    Arena(std::byte* buf, std::size_t cap) : base_(buf), cap_(cap) {}

    void* allocate(std::size_t n, std::size_t align) {
        auto addr = reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t>(base_) + offset_;
        auto aligned = (addr + align - 1) & ~(std::uintptr_t{align} - 1);   // align must be a power of two
        std::size_t start = aligned - reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t>(base_);
        if (start + n > cap_) throw std::bad_alloc();
        offset_ = start + n;
        return base_ + start;
    }
    template <class T, class... A> T* create(A&&... a) {
        static_assert(std::is_trivially_destructible_v<T>, "the arena never runs destructors");
        return ::new (allocate(sizeof(T), alignof(T))) T{static_cast<A&&>(a)...};
    }
    void reset() noexcept { offset_ = 0; }
    std::size_t used() const noexcept { return offset_; }
};

struct Token { int kind; int line; char text[16]; };          // 24 bytes, align 4
struct alignas(16) Node { Node* lhs; Node* rhs; int op; };    // 32 bytes, align 16

int main() {
    alignas(16) std::byte buffer[256];
    Arena arena(buffer, sizeof buffer);
    arena.create<Token>(1, 10);
    std::printf("after Token: %zu\n", arena.used());
    Node* n = arena.create<Node>(nullptr, nullptr, '+');
    std::printf("Node at offset %td, after Node: %zu\n", reinterpret_cast<std::byte*>(n) - buffer, arena.used());
    arena.allocate(13, 1);
    std::printf("after 13 chars: %zu\n", arena.used());
    arena.reset();
    std::printf("after reset: %zu\n", arena.used());
}
after Token: 24
Node at offset 32, after Node: 64
after 13 chars: 77
after reset: 0

Why this is fast: an allocation is an add, a mask, a compare and a store, all in registers, and the next allocation lands right after the previous one, so consecutive objects share cache lines and pages. There is no header before each object, so a 13-byte string costs 13 bytes, not 32.

Alignment rounding arithmetic

Theory

For a power-of-two alignment a, the next multiple of a at or above x is

round_up(x, a) = (x + a - 1) & ~(a - 1)

Adding a - 1 pushes x past the next boundary unless it is already on one, and the mask clears the low bits. For x = 24, a = 16: 24 + 15 = 39 = 0b100111, masked with ~0b1111 gives 32. For x = 32 it gives 32 again. The padding is round_up(x, a) - x, which is at most a - 1.

  • Align the address, not the offset. Rounding the offset only works if the buffer's base is itself aligned to the strictest alignment you serve. A char buf[1024] on the stack, or a sub-range of another buffer, may start at an odd address. The arena above adds the base before rounding, which is always correct. The reading section has the bug where it does not.
  • Check the alignment is a power of two (std::has_single_bit(a)). The mask trick gives garbage for 12 or 24. All alignments the language produces (alignof) are powers of two.
  • Check for overflow before adding: start + n > cap can wrap for a huge n. A robust check is n > cap - start after verifying start <= cap.
  • std::align(alignment, size, ptr, space) in <memory> does the same job: it adjusts ptr and space and returns null if the request does not fit.

Know this cold

Be ready to derive (x + a - 1) & ~(a - 1) on a whiteboard, explain why it needs a power of two, and compute a few cases. Interviewers at trading firms often ask for it directly, then ask what goes wrong if the arena's base buffer is not aligned.

Bulk free, reset, and why individual free is a no-op

Theory

An arena has no record of where one object ends and the next begins, and no free list. That is exactly why it is fast, and it means freeing a single object cannot be done in general: the hole in the middle could not be found again. So an arena's deallocate does nothing, and memory comes back only in bulk:

  • Reset sets the offset back to zero. The buffer is kept and reused, so a per-frame or per-request arena reaches a steady state with no allocation at all.
  • Destroying the arena returns its buffers to wherever they came from.
  • Rewinding to a mark frees everything allocated after the mark (see scratch arenas).

One optimisation is common: if the object being freed is the last one allocated, the arena can move the offset back by its size (an "undo last" free). It helps temporaries that are freed in reverse order of allocation, such as a buffer allocated and released inside one function. It does not help std::vector growth, because the vector allocates its new buffer before it frees the old one, so the old one is never on top. std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource does not do this; its deallocate is specified to have no effect.

The cost model follows: allocation is O(1), free is free, reset is O(1) (or O(number of chained blocks) if extra blocks are released). Memory use is the sum of everything allocated since the last reset, live or dead. An arena is the wrong tool when objects die at different times and the total over the arena's life is much bigger than what is live at any moment.

The lifetime discipline

Theory

An arena is safe when one rule holds: every object in the arena dies at or before the reset, and nothing outside the arena keeps a pointer into it past that point. Arena-friendly designs make that rule structural by tying each arena to a unit of work.

  • Per-request arenas. A server creates (or takes from a pool) an arena when a request arrives, puts the parsed request, temporary strings and the response in it, and resets it when the response is sent. Apache's APR pools and nginx's ngx_pool_t work like this. Nothing in the request may be stored in a cache that outlives it, unless it is copied out.
  • Per-frame arenas. A game allocates the frame's temporary data (visible object lists, draw commands, particle updates) from a frame arena and resets it at the start of the next frame. With double buffering, two arenas alternate, so data from the previous frame (for example for the renderer running one frame behind) stays valid for one extra frame.
  • Per-parse arenas. A parser allocates tokens and the AST in one arena; the AST lives until compilation finishes, then the whole tree is dropped in one step instead of walking it to delete each node.

Compilers and parsers as typical users

Compilers are the textbook arena users. An abstract syntax tree has millions of small nodes (expressions, declarations, types) that are created during parsing, linked by raw pointers in every direction, and all freed when the translation unit is done. Per-node delete would need a tree walk and an ownership structure for a graph that is not a tree. Clang allocates its AST from ASTContext, which uses LLVM's BumpPtrAllocator, and many AST node destructors are never run. Protocol Buffers offers google::protobuf::Arena for messages parsed per request. JSON parsers such as simdjson's DOM and RapidJSON's MemoryPoolAllocator use arenas for the same reason: the parse result is one unit with one lifetime.

Destructors in an arena

Theory

Resetting an arena reuses its bytes without running any destructor. Two policies keep that sound.

Policy 1: trivially destructible types only

Restrict the arena to types where skipping the destructor changes nothing: static_assert(std::is_trivially_destructible_v<T>) in create, as in the arena above. AST nodes and tokens are designed this way on purpose: they hold raw pointers into the same arena and string views of the source, never owning containers. The standard allows reusing storage without calling a destructor ([basic.life]/5), and for a trivially destructible type there is nothing to call anyway.

Policy 2: a destructor list

To allow types like std::string, the arena keeps a singly linked list of "finalisers": for every non-trivially-destructible object it allocates a small record (a pointer to the object, a function pointer that destroys it, and the link) from the arena itself. Reset walks the list and calls each destructor, newest first, then rewinds. Trivially destructible types skip the record, so they still cost nothing.

struct Finalizer { void (*destroy)(void*); void* object; Finalizer* next; };

template <class T, class... A>
T* create(A&&... args) {
    void* mem = allocate(sizeof(T), alignof(T));
    T* obj = ::new (mem) T(std::forward<A>(args)...);
    if constexpr (!std::is_trivially_destructible_v<T>) {
        auto* f = ::new (allocate(sizeof(Finalizer), alignof(Finalizer)))
            Finalizer{[](void* p) { static_cast<T*>(p)->~T(); }, obj, finalizers_};
        finalizers_ = f;                               // reset() runs them newest first
    }
    return obj;
}

Order matters in that code: the object is constructed before its finaliser record exists, so if the constructor throws, no record points at a half-built object (the arena bytes are simply wasted until reset). If allocating the record throws, the object is already constructed and must be destroyed before rethrowing; the coding section avoids the problem by reserving the record first. Protobuf's arena and LLVM's SpecificBumpPtrAllocator<T> (which destroys all objects of one type on reset) are real versions of this idea.

Interview trap

An arena-allocated std::vector<int> or std::string with the default allocator puts only its 24 or 32-byte header in the arena. Its elements are on the global heap, and if the destructor never runs, that heap memory leaks on every reset. Either run destructors (a finaliser list), or give the container an allocator that also uses the arena (a std::pmr container on the arena's memory resource), so its elements vanish with the arena and skipping the destructor is harmless.

std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource

Theory

The standard library's arena is std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource (C++17, <memory_resource>). It is a memory_resource (Ch 15), so any pmr container can use it.

  • Construction. monotonic_buffer_resource(void* buffer, size_t size, memory_resource* upstream) starts by bumping through buffer (often a stack array). Other constructors take only an initial size hint, or nothing. The upstream defaults to get_default_resource() at construction.
  • Growth. When the current buffer is full, it asks the upstream for a new one, each larger than the last by an implementation-defined geometric factor (libstdc++ multiplies by 1.5; libc++ doubles). The initial buffer is never freed by it, because it does not own it.
  • deallocate has no effect. Memory only grows until release() or the destructor, which return every upstream buffer. After release(), the resource starts over from the initial buffer.
  • Not thread safe, not copyable, and it must outlive every container using it.
  • Pair it with null_memory_resource() as upstream to guarantee that a hot path never touches the heap: if the stack buffer is too small, you get std::bad_alloc in testing instead of a silent heap allocation in production.
  • Stack it under a pool. unsynchronized_pool_resource pool(&monotonic) reuses freed blocks within the request while the monotonic resource supplies chunks and frees everything at the end.
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <functional>
#include <memory_resource>
#include <new>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

class CountingResource : public std::pmr::memory_resource {
    std::pmr::memory_resource* up_ = std::pmr::new_delete_resource();
public:
    std::size_t calls = 0, live = 0;
private:
    void* do_allocate(std::size_t n, std::size_t a) override { ++calls; live += n; return up_->allocate(n, a); }
    void do_deallocate(void* p, std::size_t n, std::size_t a) override { live -= n; up_->deallocate(p, n, a); }
    bool do_is_equal(const memory_resource& o) const noexcept override { return this == &o; }
};

int main() {
    alignas(std::max_align_t) std::array<std::byte, 2048> stack_buf;
    auto inside = [&](const void* p) {
        std::less<const void*> lt;
        return !lt(p, stack_buf.data()) && lt(p, stack_buf.data() + stack_buf.size());
    };

    {   // 1. a stack buffer with no heap fallback
        std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource arena(stack_buf.data(), stack_buf.size(), std::pmr::null_memory_resource());
        std::pmr::vector<std::pmr::string> words(&arena);
        words.reserve(4);
        for (const char* w : {"bid", "ask", "a symbol name long enough to need its own buffer", "fill"}) words.emplace_back(w);
        bool all_inside = true;
        for (auto& w : words) all_inside = all_inside && inside(w.data());
        std::printf("all strings in the stack buffer: %s\n", all_inside ? "yes" : "no");
        try {
            arena.allocate(4096);
        } catch (const std::bad_alloc&) {
            std::puts("over the stack buffer: bad_alloc");
        }
    }
    {   // 2. a small initial buffer with a counting upstream
        CountingResource upstream;
        std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource arena(stack_buf.data(), 256, &upstream);
        for (int i = 0; i < 100; ++i) {
            void* p = arena.allocate(64);
            arena.deallocate(p, 64);                 // no effect
        }
        std::printf("went upstream: %s, bytes held upstream >= 6400: %s\n",
                    upstream.calls > 0 ? "yes" : "no", upstream.live >= 6400 - 256 ? "yes" : "no");
        arena.release();
        std::printf("after release: %zu bytes held upstream\n", upstream.live);
    }
}
all strings in the stack buffer: yes
over the stack buffer: bad_alloc
went upstream: yes, bytes held upstream >= 6400: yes
after release: 0 bytes held upstream

The second block shows the defining behaviour: 100 allocate/deallocate pairs of 64 bytes consumed about 6.4 KB, because nothing freed was reused. A pool resource would have needed one block.

Growing arenas with chained blocks

Theory

A fixed buffer is ideal when the maximum size is known. Otherwise the arena grows by allocating a new block when the current one is full and linking it to the previous ones, so destruction can free them all. Each new block is usually twice the size of the last, so the number of blocks stays logarithmic in the total size.

Design decisions in a growing arena:

  • Where the block header lives. Putting {next, size} at the start of each block costs 16 bytes per block and no separate allocation. The usable region starts after the header.
  • Oversized requests. If a request is larger than the next block size, allocate a block of exactly that size (plus header). Some arenas put such blocks behind the current block in the chain so the current block keeps serving small requests.
  • What reset keeps. Freeing everything returns memory but makes the next cycle allocate again. Keeping the largest block means the steady state needs one block and no allocation. LLVM's BumpPtrAllocator::Reset keeps the first slab and frees the rest.
  • Wasted tail. When a request does not fit, the rest of the current block is abandoned. With doubling blocks this waste is bounded by the request size, and it is part of the trade.

Scratch arenas and save/restore marks

Theory

A mark is a saved position in the arena: the current block and offset. Rewinding to the mark frees everything allocated since, in O(1), without touching what was allocated before. This turns an arena into a stack-like allocator for temporary work:

struct Mark { std::size_t offset; };

class ScratchScope {                 // RAII: rewinds on every exit path
    Arena& arena_;
    Arena::Mark mark_;
public:
    explicit ScratchScope(Arena& a) : arena_(a), mark_(a.mark()) {}
    ~ScratchScope() { arena_.rewind(mark_); }
    ScratchScope(const ScratchScope&) = delete;
    ScratchScope& operator=(const ScratchScope&) = delete;
};

std::string_view longest_word(Arena& scratch, std::string_view text) {
    ScratchScope scope(scratch);               // temporaries below vanish at return
    auto* words = split_into(scratch, text);   // arena-allocated array of views
    return pick_longest(words);                // fine: the view points into text, not the arena
}

Rules that come with marks:

  • Marks nest like a stack. Rewinding to an outer mark invalidates inner marks. Rewinding to an inner mark after the outer one was restored is a bug (it moves the offset forward over freed memory).
  • Nothing allocated inside the scope may escape it. Returning a pointer to scratch memory from inside a ScratchScope is a dangling pointer the moment the scope ends. Results must be copied to a longer-lived arena or into the caller's memory.
  • Two scratch arenas solve the "result and temporaries in the same arena" problem: a function takes a persistent arena for its result and uses a separate scratch arena for its temporaries. Game engines and some compilers keep a pair of thread-local scratch arenas and pass the "other" one to callees so that callers' and callees' scratch data never collide.
  • In a growing arena, the mark must record the block as well as the offset, and rewinding frees blocks allocated after the mark (or keeps them for reuse).

Arena vs pool vs malloc

Theory
Key factsArena (bump)Pool (free list)malloc / new
Sizes servedAny size, any alignmentOne size (or a few classes)Any
AllocateBump a pointer: a few instructionsPop a list: a few instructionsFast path 10 to 30 ns, slow paths much longer
Free one objectNot possible (no-op)O(1) pushO(1) typical
Free everythingO(1) resetWalk or destroy the poolOne free per object
Per-object overheadAlignment padding onlyRounding to the block sizeHeader or size-class rounding
Memory reuseOnly after reset or rewindImmediately, per blockImmediately
DestructorsNot run unless a finaliser list existsRun by the user before freeingRun by delete
Fits whenObjects share one lifetime (request, frame, parse)Many same-size objects with individual lifetimesGeneral use, unknown lifetimes
Fails whenLifetimes differ, so dead objects pile upSizes vary widelyHot paths needing predictable latency
Standard versionmonotonic_buffer_resource(un)synchronized_pool_resourcenew_delete_resource

Measured

The benchmark builds a chain of 100,000 32-byte nodes (an AST-like workload), walks it, and drops it, with malloc per node and free per node, with a pre-sized bump arena and one reset, and with a default-constructed monotonic_buffer_resource and one release().

#include <algorithm>
#include <chrono>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory_resource>
#include <new>
#include <vector>

struct Node { Node* left; Node* right; long key; long pad; };   // 32 bytes, like an AST node

class Arena {
    std::byte* buf_;
    std::size_t cap_, used_ = 0;
public:
    explicit Arena(std::size_t cap) : buf_(static_cast<std::byte*>(::operator new(cap))), cap_(cap) {}
    ~Arena() { ::operator delete(buf_); }
    void* allocate(std::size_t n, std::size_t a) {
        std::size_t p = (used_ + a - 1) & ~(a - 1);
        if (p + n > cap_) throw std::bad_alloc();
        used_ = p + n;
        return buf_ + p;
    }
    void reset() { used_ = 0; }
};

constexpr int kNodes = 100000, kReps = 7;

// Build a chain of nodes (each points to the previous), sum the keys, then drop everything.
template <class Alloc, class FreeAll>
static double build(Alloc alloc, FreeAll free_all, long& sink) {
    auto t0 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    Node* prev = nullptr;
    for (int i = 0; i < kNodes; ++i) prev = ::new (alloc()) Node{prev, nullptr, i, 0};
    for (Node* n = prev; n; n = n->left) sink += n->key;
    free_all(prev);
    auto t1 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    return std::chrono::duration<double, std::nano>(t1 - t0).count() / kNodes;
}

template <class F>
static double median_of(F f) {
    std::vector<double> v;
    for (int r = 0; r < kReps; ++r) v.push_back(f());
    std::sort(v.begin(), v.end());
    std::printf("    min %.2f  max %.2f ns/node\n", v.front(), v.back());
    return v[v.size() / 2];
}

int main() {
    long sink = 0;
    std::puts("malloc per node, free each:");
    double m = median_of([&] {
        return build([] { return std::malloc(sizeof(Node)); },
                     [](Node* n) { while (n) { Node* l = n->left; std::free(n); n = l; } }, sink);
    });
    std::puts("bump arena, one reset:");
    Arena arena(kNodes * sizeof(Node));
    double a = median_of([&] {
        return build([&] { return arena.allocate(sizeof(Node), alignof(Node)); }, [&](Node*) { arena.reset(); }, sink);
    });
    std::puts("pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource, one release:");
    std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource mono;
    double p = median_of([&] {
        return build([&] { return mono.allocate(sizeof(Node), alignof(Node)); }, [&](Node*) { mono.release(); }, sink);
    });
    std::printf("median ns/node: malloc %.2f, arena %.2f, monotonic %.2f\n", m, a, p);
    std::printf("speed-up vs malloc: arena %.1fx, monotonic %.1fx (sink %ld)\n", m / a, m / p, sink & 1);
}

Representative results on an Apple M1 (macOS, -O2, median of 7 repetitions, two runs each). The program is tagged ub because its output is timing.

AllocatorGCC 16 + libstdc++Clang 22 + libc++
malloc + free per node32.2 ns/node (1.0×)32.4 ns/node (1.0×)
Pre-sized bump arena, one reset2.9 ns/node (about 11× faster)3.4 ns/node (about 9.5× faster)
monotonic_buffer_resource, one release7.1 ns/node (about 4.6× faster)8.1 ns/node (4.0 to 5.2× faster)

The arena's advantage is bigger here than a pool's was in Ch 15 (about 4×), because the arena also deletes the 100,000 free calls and its nodes are contiguous, so the walk streams through memory. The monotonic resource pays for a virtual call per allocation and for re-acquiring its growing buffers from the heap after every release(); giving it an initial buffer of the right size would close most of the gap. Individual runs varied by up to 2× (the max column), so trust medians, not single runs.

Pitfalls

Theory

Dangling pointers after reset

After a reset, every pointer into the arena dangles, but the memory is usually still mapped and owned by the arena, so reads return plausible stale data or a newer object's data. ASan does not see it (the buffer is one live allocation), unless the arena poisons its memory on reset with ASAN_POISON_MEMORY_REGION and unpoisons on allocation. Arenas that free extra blocks on reset turn some of these bugs into detectable heap-use-after-free; the reading section shows both cases.

Unbounded growth

An arena that is never reset is a memory leak with good performance. Typical causes: a per-connection arena on a WebSocket or database connection that lives for hours; a loop that reallocates a growing pmr::vector in a monotonic resource (each regrowth abandons the old buffer, so the arena holds about twice the final size); a "temporary" scratch arena used by a long-running background task. Cap arena size in debug builds and log the high-water mark.

Mixing arena objects with long-lived ones

The lifetime rule breaks the moment a long-lived structure points into the arena: a global cache storing a std::string_view of an arena string, a long-lived object holding an arena-allocated child, a callback registered with a pointer to per-request data. The opposite direction also bites: an arena object that owns heap memory (a std::vector with the default allocator) leaks it at reset. Keep a clear boundary: arena objects point only into the same arena or to longer-lived data, and anything that must survive is copied out.

Alignment bugs

Rounding the offset instead of the address with an unaligned base, a non-power-of-two alignment fed to the mask formula, ignoring alignof(T) for over-aligned types (alignas(64) cache-line-aligned structs, SIMD types), and assuming the arena's buffer from operator new is more than __STDCPP_DEFAULT_NEW_ALIGNMENT__-aligned. x86 tolerates most misaligned scalar accesses, so these bugs often appear only on ARM or with SIMD and under UBSan's alignment check.

Threads

A bump pointer is a shared mutable offset, so a shared arena needs a lock or an atomic fetch_add on the offset (which works for a fixed buffer but not for growth). The usual design is one arena per thread or per task. Reading arena data from many threads after it is built is fine, provided the hand-over is synchronised.

Concept and tricky questions

Drills

ConceptWhy is an arena faster than malloc, and what does it give up to get there?

Answer

Answer. Allocation is a round-up, an add and a bounds check on one offset, with no size classes, headers, free lists, locks or system calls, and freeing costs nothing because all objects go together at reset. It gives up individual frees: memory is only reclaimed in bulk, so it suits objects that share one lifetime.

Why. malloc must support any free order, so it keeps metadata to find, merge and reuse holes. An arena has no holes by design. Consecutive allocations are also adjacent, which improves cache and TLB locality. The measured gap in this chapter was about 10× for an AST-like build-and-drop workload on an Apple M1. Saying only "it avoids system calls" misses the point: malloc's fast path avoids them too.

TrickyAn arena's deallocate(p, n) is a no-op. Is there any case where an arena can usefully reclaim a single allocation?

Answer

Answer. Yes: if p is the most recent allocation, the arena can move the offset back to p (an "undo last" free). A temporary freed right after use, or a group of temporaries freed in reverse order, then costs nothing. Any other single free cannot be honoured, and that includes the old buffer of a growing std::vector: the vector allocates the new buffer before freeing the old one, so the old one is never the most recent.

Why. The arena knows only the current offset, so it can recognise "the block that ends exactly at the offset" and nothing else. LLVM's bump allocator and many game-engine linear allocators do this. std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource deliberately does not: the standard says its do_deallocate has no effect, so code can rely on the simpler behaviour. A related trick is a mark and rewind, which frees a whole stack-like group of recent allocations.

TrickyA monotonic_buffer_resource is built over a 4 KiB stack buffer with the default upstream. Request 1 uses 100 KiB, then the server calls release(); request 2 uses 3 KiB. Where does request 2's memory come from, and does it start with a large upstream buffer because request 1 needed one?

Answer

Answer. Request 2 is served entirely from the 4 KiB stack buffer, with no upstream call. release() frees every upstream buffer and returns the resource to its state at construction: the current buffer is the user's buffer again, and the size of the next upstream buffer is back to its initial value. So the next large request grows from small buffers again; nothing is remembered from request 1.

Why. The standard specifies that release() resets current_buffer and next_buffer_size to their initial values ([mem.res.monotonic.buffer.mem]), and the growth factor is implementation-defined. With an initial size of 1000 bytes and a counting upstream, libstdc++ here asked for 1024, 1536, 2304, 3392, 5120 bytes (factor 1.5) and libc++ for 2032, 4032, 8032 (about 2), and both started from the first size again after release(). Wrong answers: "release() frees the stack buffer" (the resource never owned it), and "it keeps the biggest block for next time" (that is what a hand-written arena that keeps blocks on reset does; the standard resource pays to re-acquire them instead). If every request is large, construct the resource with a bigger initial buffer or size hint.

ConceptDescribe the lifetime discipline that makes a per-frame arena safe in a game engine, and how double buffering changes it.

Answer

Answer. Everything allocated during frame N is used only during frame N, and nothing outside the arena keeps a pointer to it; the arena is reset at the start of frame N + 1. With two arenas alternating, data from frame N stays valid during frame N + 1 as well (for a renderer or a job system running one frame behind), and its arena is reset at the start of frame N + 2.

Why. The schedule enforces the lifetime, so no reference counting or per-object frees are needed. The rule is broken by caches and long-lived systems that remember pointers into frame data; anything that must persist (a spawned entity, a loaded asset) has to be allocated from a longer-lived allocator or copied out before the reset.

TrickyYou place a std::string in an arena with placement new and never call its destructor. Is that undefined behaviour? What leaks, and what changes if it is a std::pmr::string using the arena?

Answer

Answer. Not calling the destructor is not undefined by itself: [basic.life]/5 lets a program end an object's lifetime by reusing or releasing its storage. Up to C++20 the same paragraph also said that a program which depends on the destructor's side effects has undefined behaviour; CWG2523 removed that sentence as a defect report against C++23, so now the destructor simply does not run. But a std::string longer than its small-string buffer owns a heap block, and that block leaks on every reset. A std::pmr::string whose resource is the arena allocates its characters from the arena too, so skipping its destructor leaks nothing: the characters vanish with the arena.

Why. The skipped side effect here is operator delete on the character buffer, which is exactly what the program needs to avoid leaking. Common wrong answers: "it is always UB" (it is not), and "short strings are fine, so all strings are fine" (it depends on the length and the library's SSO capacity, 15 characters in libstdc++ and 22 in libc++ on 64-bit). The robust options are trivially destructible types, a finaliser list, or containers that allocate from the same arena.

ConceptWhat do deallocate, release() and the destructor of std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource each do?

Answer

Answer. deallocate does nothing. release() returns every buffer obtained from the upstream resource and resets the resource to its initial state (bumping through the user-supplied initial buffer again, if there was one). The destructor calls release().

Why. It is a pure arena, specified as such so that its behaviour does not depend on the implementation. The initial buffer is not owned, so it is never freed. Pmr containers still call deallocate (when they grow or are destroyed), which is why their destructors are cheap but not free: they still walk their elements. If the containers live in the arena too, you can skip their destruction entirely and just release(), provided nothing else they own lives elsewhere.

TrickyA std::pmr::vector<int> on a monotonic_buffer_resource gets 1,000,000 push_back calls without reserve. Roughly how much memory does the arena hold at the end, and why?

Answer

Answer. About 8 MiB, twice what the data needs. With the doubling growth of libstdc++ and libc++, the final capacity is 220 ints (4 MiB), and the abandoned buffers of 1, 2, 4, ..., 219 ints add up to almost another 4 MiB. With reserve(1'000'000) the arena holds 4 MB.

Why. Each time the vector grows it allocates a bigger buffer, moves the elements and deallocates the old one, which the monotonic resource ignores. The geometric series of old buffers sums to about the size of the last one. In a pool or malloc the old buffers would be reused; in an arena they are dead weight until release(). The reading section measures it: reserve exactly when the size is known, or build into a scratch structure and copy the final result into the arena once.

TrickyWhy would anyone construct a monotonic_buffer_resource over a stack buffer with std::pmr::null_memory_resource() as upstream?

Answer

Answer. To prove that a code path never touches the heap. All allocations come from the stack buffer, and if it ever runs out, the null upstream throws std::bad_alloc instead of silently calling operator new. In a latency-critical path, that turns a hidden heap allocation into a test failure.

Why. With the default upstream, overflowing the buffer works but is invisible, and the heap allocation it causes is exactly what a trading or audio thread must avoid. The same trick works for the default resource (set_default_resource(null_memory_resource()) in tests) to find containers that were not given a resource. The buffer must be big enough for the worst case, and the code must be tested with worst-case input.

ConceptWhen would you choose an arena over a pool, and when a pool over an arena?

Answer

Answer. Choose an arena when many objects of mixed sizes share one lifetime (a request, a frame, a parse result) and are dropped together. Choose a pool when objects of one size come and go individually over a long period (orders, connections, nodes in a long-lived structure), because a pool reuses each freed block immediately and an arena would grow without bound.

Why. An arena's memory is the sum of all allocations since reset; a pool's memory is the peak number of live blocks. They also compose: a pmr::unsynchronized_pool_resource on top of a monotonic_buffer_resource reuses blocks within a request (pool) and frees everything at the end (arena).

TrickyTwo threads allocate from one monotonic_buffer_resource. What goes wrong, and what are the fixes?

Answer

Answer. The resource is not thread safe: both threads read and update the same current pointer and remaining-space fields without synchronisation, which is a data race (undefined behaviour) and in practice hands out overlapping memory. Fixes: one arena per thread (the usual answer), a mutex around the shared resource, or, for a fixed buffer only, an atomic fetch_add on the offset.

Why. fetch_add works for a fixed-size buffer (each thread gets a disjoint range, alignment can be handled by over-allocating and rounding), but growing a chained arena needs a lock because installing a new block is a multi-step update. Reading arena-built data from many threads afterwards is fine once its construction happens-before the reads (for example, the builder joins or publishes with a release store).

ConceptWhat is a scratch arena with save/restore marks, and why do some codebases keep two scratch arenas per thread?

Answer

Answer. A scratch arena is a per-thread arena for temporaries. A function records a mark (the current offset), allocates freely, and rewinds to the mark when it returns, usually through an RAII guard, freeing all its temporaries in O(1). Two arenas are kept so that a function can put its result in one and its temporaries in the other: if both were in the same arena, rewinding the temporaries would also free the result allocated after the mark.

Why. Marks behave like a stack, so they need LIFO discipline. When a function calls another function that also uses scratch memory, passing the "other" arena to the callee guarantees the callee's rewind cannot destroy the caller's live temporaries. This gives stack-like allocation for variable-sized data without alloca (Ch 18).

TrickyA function opens a ScratchScope, builds a std::string_view into scratch memory, and returns the view. Tests pass. Why is it still a bug, and why do the tests pass?

Answer

Answer. The scope's destructor rewinds the arena at return, so the view points to freed scratch memory. Tests pass because rewinding does not erase anything: the bytes stay there until the next scratch allocation overwrites them, and a simple test reads the result before anything else allocates.

Why. It is a use-after-free that no tool sees, since the arena's buffer remains a live allocation. It fails later, when the caller allocates scratch memory before reading the view, and then the "string" contains someone else's data. Fixes: allocate the result in a longer-lived arena passed in by the caller, return an owning std::string, or make the arena poison rewound memory in debug builds (fill with a pattern or use ASan manual poisoning).

ConceptWhy do compilers allocate their AST nodes from arenas?

Answer

Answer. An AST has a huge number of small nodes created during parsing, connected by raw pointers in many directions (parents, types, declarations referenced from uses), and all of them are needed until the translation unit is done. An arena makes each allocation a bump, keeps related nodes adjacent in memory, and frees the whole graph in one step without walking it.

Why. Per-node ownership would need a tree of unique_ptrs (and the AST is a graph, not a tree) or reference counting, and freeing would walk millions of nodes. Clang's ASTContext uses LLVM's BumpPtrAllocator and designs most node types to be trivially destructible or to not need destruction. Many compilers even skip freeing the arena at exit, letting the OS reclaim the memory.

TrickyA per-request arena stores parsed headers as std::string_views into arena memory. A developer adds a global cache of "recently seen user agents" that stores those views. What happens, and how do you fix the design?

Answer

Answer. After the request ends and the arena is reset, the cached views dangle. The next request overwrites that memory, so the cache returns other requests' bytes, or garbage. The fix is to copy the data into storage owned by the cache (a std::string, or a separate long-lived arena for interned strings) at the moment it crosses from request lifetime to process lifetime.

Why. Mixing arena objects with long-lived ones breaks the arena's only safety rule. It is easy to miss because string_view looks like a value. Code review rule of thumb: any pointer, reference or view stored in something that outlives the arena is a bug unless it was copied.

TrickyA server resets its request arena after each request, but the process's RSS keeps the peak from a single huge request forever. Why, and what can you do?

Answer

Answer. Reset only moves the offset; the arena keeps its blocks (often deliberately, to avoid reallocating next time), so one 500 MB request leaves 500 MB of blocks attached to that arena. Options: on reset, free every block beyond a size limit and keep only a modest first block; cap the arena and reject oversized requests; or madvise(MADV_DONTNEED) the pages of a kept block so the kernel drops them while the address range stays reserved.

Why. "Reset is O(1)" and "reset returns memory" are different properties. Keeping blocks makes the steady state allocation-free, which is the point, but a high-water mark set by an outlier then becomes permanent. monotonic_buffer_resource::release() does free upstream buffers, so it does not have this problem, at the price of re-acquiring them on the next request.

Predict the output and find the bug

Drills

OutputEach allocation is placed at the next offset that satisfies its alignment. What does this print?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>

class Arena {
    std::byte* base_;
    std::size_t cap_, off_ = 0;
public:
    Arena(std::byte* b, std::size_t c) : base_(b), cap_(c) {}
    std::size_t alloc(std::size_t n, std::size_t a) {   // returns the offset, for the drill
        std::size_t start = (off_ + a - 1) & ~(a - 1);
        if (start + n > cap_) return SIZE_MAX;
        off_ = start + n;
        return start;
    }
};

int main() {
    alignas(64) std::byte buf[128];
    Arena a(buf, sizeof buf);
    std::size_t c = a.alloc(1, 1);
    std::size_t d = a.alloc(8, 8);
    std::size_t s = a.alloc(2, 2);
    std::size_t v = a.alloc(32, 32);
    std::size_t big = a.alloc(64, 16);
    std::printf("char %zu, double %zu, short %zu, vec %zu, big %s\n", c, d, s, v, big == SIZE_MAX ? "does not fit" : "fits");
}
Answer
char 0, double 8, short 16, vec 32, big fits

Answer. The char takes offset 0. The double needs a multiple of 8, so it starts at 8 (7 bytes of padding) and ends at 16. The short fits at 16. The 32-aligned block skips to 32 and ends at 64. The last request would start at 64 and end at 128, which is exactly the capacity, so it fits.

Why. Each start is round_up(previous end, alignment). People often add the padding to the wrong side (after the object) or forget that a request ending exactly at the capacity fits (start + n > cap is the failure test, not >=). The base is declared alignas(64), so aligning offsets is the same as aligning addresses here; see the bug drill below for when it is not.

Find the bugA request handler keeps a pointer across a reset. What does it print, and does ASan (the harness runs it under ASan) report it?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstring>
#include <new>

class Arena {
    std::byte* buf_ = static_cast<std::byte*>(::operator new(4096));
    std::size_t off_ = 0;
public:
    ~Arena() { ::operator delete(buf_); }
    char* copy(const char* s) {
        std::size_t n = std::strlen(s) + 1;
        char* p = reinterpret_cast<char*>(buf_ + off_);
        std::memcpy(p, s, n);
        off_ += n;
        return p;
    }
    void reset() { off_ = 0; }
};

int main() {
    Arena arena;
    const char* user = arena.copy("alice");      // request 1
    arena.reset();                                // request 1 done
    arena.copy("mallory");                        // request 2
    std::printf("audit log: request 1 was made by %s\n", user);
}
Answer
audit log: request 1 was made by mallory

Answer. In practice it logs "mallory": after the reset, request 2's string was copied to offset 0, exactly where user points. ASan reports nothing (the harness confirms a clean run), because the 4 KiB buffer is one live heap allocation.

Why. Reset invalidates every pointer into the arena, but the bytes stay mapped and owned by the arena, so stale reads see whatever was written next. The program is tagged ub because reading through a pointer to an object whose storage has been reused is undefined. Defences: copy anything that outlives the request out of the arena; in debug builds, poison the arena on reset (fill it with a pattern, or call ASAN_POISON_MEMORY_REGION(buf_, 4096) and unpoison on allocation) so the stale read fails loudly.

Find the bugThis growing arena frees its extra blocks on reset. What does the sanitizer build report?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>
#include <vector>

class GrowingArena {
    std::vector<std::byte*> blocks_;
    std::size_t block_size_ = 64, off_ = 0;
public:
    GrowingArena() { blocks_.push_back(static_cast<std::byte*>(::operator new(block_size_))); }
    ~GrowingArena() { for (auto* b : blocks_) ::operator delete(b); }
    void* allocate(std::size_t n) {
        n = (n + 15) & ~std::size_t{15};
        if (off_ + n > block_size_) {                     // new block (requests assumed smaller than a block)
            blocks_.push_back(static_cast<std::byte*>(::operator new(block_size_)));
            off_ = 0;
        }
        void* p = blocks_.back() + off_;
        off_ += n;
        return p;
    }
    void reset() {                                        // keep only the first block
        for (std::size_t i = 1; i < blocks_.size(); ++i) ::operator delete(blocks_[i]);
        blocks_.resize(1);
        off_ = 0;
    }
};

int main() {
    GrowingArena arena;
    int* counters[6];
    for (auto& c : counters) { c = static_cast<int*>(arena.allocate(32)); *c = 1; }
    arena.reset();
    std::printf("last counter: %d\n", *counters[5]);      // lives in the third block
}
Answer

Answer. Six 32-byte allocations fill three 64-byte blocks. Reset frees blocks 2 and 3, so reading *counters[5] touches freed heap memory: ASan reports heap-use-after-free on that read.

Why. This is the same bug as the previous drill (a pointer kept across reset), but here part of the arena really went back to the heap, so ASan can see it. Pointers into the first, kept block would still be silent. This asymmetry is worth saying in an interview: whether a dangling arena pointer is detectable depends on an implementation detail (which blocks reset keeps), so arena bugs need arena-aware tooling (poisoning on reset), not luck.

Find the bugAn arena is built on a sub-range of a bigger buffer. The alignment rounding looks correct. What does the sanitizer build report?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>

class Arena {
    unsigned char* base_;
    std::size_t cap_, off_ = 0;
public:
    Arena(unsigned char* b, std::size_t c) : base_(b), cap_(c) {}
    void* allocate(std::size_t n, std::size_t a) {
        std::size_t start = (off_ + a - 1) & ~(a - 1);     // aligns the offset only
        if (start + n > cap_) throw std::bad_alloc();
        off_ = start + n;
        return base_ + start;
    }
};

struct alignas(16) Quote { double bid, ask; };

int main() {
    alignas(16) static unsigned char storage[1 + 1024];
    storage[0] = 0x7F;                                       // a one-byte message header
    Arena arena(storage + 1, 1024);                          // payload area starts after it
    auto* q = ::new (arena.allocate(sizeof(Quote), alignof(Quote))) Quote{101.25, 101.5};
    std::printf("%.2f\n", q->ask - q->bid);
}
Answer

Answer. The arena's base is storage + 1, an odd address. Offset 0 is "aligned", so the Quote is constructed at an address that is 1 mod 16. UBSan (part of the harness's sanitizer build) reports a misaligned address for type Quote, which requires 16-byte alignment.

Why. Alignment is a property of the absolute address. Fix: round reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t>(base_) + off_ and convert back to an offset, as the arena in the theory section does, or align the base once in the constructor. On ARM64 and x86 a misaligned scalar double load usually works (slowly), which hides the bug; aligned SIMD loads (movaps) and atomic operations fault.

OutputAn arena with a destructor list. In what order do the destructors run?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>
#include <string>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>

class Arena {
    struct Finalizer { void (*destroy)(void*); void* obj; Finalizer* next; };
    alignas(std::max_align_t) std::byte buf_[1024];
    std::size_t off_ = 0;
    Finalizer* fin_ = nullptr;
    void* raw(std::size_t n, std::size_t a) {
        std::size_t s = (off_ + a - 1) & ~(a - 1);
        off_ = s + n;
        return buf_ + s;
    }
public:
    template <class T, class... A> T* make(A&&... args) {
        T* obj = ::new (raw(sizeof(T), alignof(T))) T(std::forward<A>(args)...);
        if constexpr (!std::is_trivially_destructible_v<T>)
            fin_ = ::new (raw(sizeof(Finalizer), alignof(Finalizer)))
                Finalizer{[](void* p) { static_cast<T*>(p)->~T(); }, obj, fin_};
        return obj;
    }
    void reset() {
        for (Finalizer* f = fin_; f; f = f->next) f->destroy(f->obj);
        fin_ = nullptr;
        off_ = 0;
    }
    ~Arena() { reset(); }
};

struct Noisy {
    std::string name;
    explicit Noisy(std::string n) : name(std::move(n)) { std::printf("make %s\n", name.c_str()); }
    ~Noisy() { std::printf("drop %s\n", name.c_str()); }
};

int main() {
    Arena arena;
    arena.make<Noisy>("lexer");
    arena.make<int>(42);                     // trivially destructible: no finalizer
    arena.make<Noisy>("parser");
    arena.make<Noisy>("ast");
    std::puts("reset:");
    arena.reset();
    arena.make<Noisy>("next request");
    std::puts("end of main");
}
Answer
make lexer
make parser
make ast
reset:
drop ast
drop parser
drop lexer
make next request
end of main
drop next request

Answer. Each finaliser is pushed on the front of a list, so reset runs them newest first: ast, parser, lexer. The int has no finaliser. The object made after the reset is destroyed by the arena's destructor at the end of main.

Why. Reverse order of construction matches what C++ does for locals and members, which matters when later objects refer to earlier ones (the parser holds a reference to the lexer). A queue would give construction order, which is usually wrong for exactly that reason.

Find the bugA parse tree is placed in a trivial arena, and each node owns a std::vector of children. What does this print, and what is the real damage?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>
#include <vector>

static int live_vectors = 0;

struct Children {
    std::vector<void*> items;
    Children() { ++live_vectors; }
    ~Children() { --live_vectors; }
};

struct Node { int kind; Children kids; };

class Arena {
    alignas(std::max_align_t) std::byte buf_[4096];
    std::size_t off_ = 0;
public:
    template <class T> T* make() {
        std::size_t s = (off_ + alignof(T) - 1) & ~(alignof(T) - 1);
        off_ = s + sizeof(T);
        return ::new (buf_ + s) T{};
    }
    void reset() { off_ = 0; }
};

int main() {
    Arena arena;
    for (int request = 0; request < 3; ++request) {
        Node* root = arena.make<Node>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 10; ++i) root->kids.items.push_back(arena.make<Node>());
        arena.reset();
    }
    std::printf("vectors never destroyed: %d\n", live_vectors);
}
Answer
vectors never destroyed: 33

Answer. 33 node objects were created (11 per request) and none was destroyed, so every Children constructor ran without its destructor. The real damage is the heap buffer of each root's std::vector: it was allocated with the global allocator and is leaked at every reset. (The harness disables LeakSanitizer, so this run is clean; with leak detection on, ASan reports the three buffers.)

Why. The arena only owns the bytes of the Node objects themselves. Anything a node owns elsewhere must be released by its destructor, which an arena reset does not run. Fixes: make nodes trivially destructible (children as an arena-allocated array plus a count, or an intrusive linked list of siblings), use std::pmr::vector on the arena's resource, or add a finaliser list. A static_assert(std::is_trivially_destructible_v<T>) in make would have rejected this code at compile time.

OutputMarks and rewinds. What does this print?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>

class Scratch {
    alignas(16) std::byte buf_[256];
    std::size_t off_ = 0;
public:
    struct Mark { std::size_t off; };
    void* alloc(std::size_t n) { std::size_t s = (off_ + 15) & ~std::size_t{15}; off_ = s + n; return buf_ + s; }
    Mark mark() const { return {off_}; }
    void rewind(Mark m) { off_ = m.off; }
    std::size_t used() const { return off_; }
};

int main() {
    Scratch s;
    void* keep = s.alloc(10);
    auto outer = s.mark();
    void* a = s.alloc(40);
    auto inner = s.mark();
    s.alloc(100);
    std::printf("used %zu\n", s.used());
    s.rewind(inner);
    std::printf("after inner rewind %zu\n", s.used());
    s.rewind(outer);
    void* b = s.alloc(24);
    std::printf("after outer rewind and alloc %zu, b reuses a: %s, keep intact: %s\n",
                s.used(), b == a ? "yes" : "no", keep != b ? "yes" : "no");
}
Answer
used 164
after inner rewind 56
after outer rewind and alloc 40, b reuses a: yes, keep intact: yes

Answer. keep occupies 0..10; a starts at 16 and ends at 56; the 100-byte block starts at 64 and ends at 164. Rewinding to inner returns to 56. Rewinding to outer returns to 10, and the next 24-byte allocation starts at 16, the address a had, ending at 40. keep is untouched because it was allocated before the outer mark.

Why. A mark is just a saved offset, so rewinding is O(1) and frees everything allocated after it, in stack order. Note the alignment: the mark stores the unaligned end (10, 56), and the next allocation re-rounds it. Rewinding to inner after rewinding to outer would have jumped the offset forward to 56, over memory that b now uses, which is the nesting bug.

Find the bugWhy does this not compile? Is the arena right to reject it?

#include <cstddef>
#include <new>
#include <string>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>

class Arena {
    alignas(std::max_align_t) std::byte buf_[1024];
    std::size_t off_ = 0;
public:
    template <class T, class... A> T* create(A&&... args) {
        static_assert(std::is_trivially_destructible_v<T>, "arena objects are never destroyed");
        std::size_t s = (off_ + alignof(T) - 1) & ~(alignof(T) - 1);
        off_ = s + sizeof(T);
        return ::new (buf_ + s) T(std::forward<A>(args)...);
    }
};

int main() {
    Arena arena;
    auto* symbol = arena.create<std::string>("a_rather_long_symbol_name_from_the_parser");
    (void)symbol;
}
Answer

Answer. std::string has a non-trivial destructor, so the static_assert fires and both compilers reject the program. The arena is right: it never runs destructors, and this 41-character string owns a heap buffer that would leak on every reset.

Why. Turning the lifetime rule into a compile-time check is the cheapest arena safety measure there is. Alternatives that compile and are correct: store a std::string_view into arena-copied characters, use std::pmr::string on the arena's memory resource, or give the arena a finaliser list. Note that the check must use is_trivially_destructible, not is_trivial: a type with a non-trivial constructor but a trivial destructor (most AST nodes) is perfectly fine.

Find the bugA parser function owns its arena and returns the result. What does the sanitizer build report?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <memory_resource>
#include <vector>

static std::pmr::vector<int> parse_numbers() {
    auto arena = std::make_unique<std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource>();
    std::pmr::vector<int> out(arena.get());
    for (int i = 1; i <= 100; ++i) out.push_back(i * 10);
    return out;                    // arena is destroyed here
}

int main() {
    auto nums = parse_numbers();
    std::printf("first %d, last %d\n", nums.front(), nums.back());
}
Answer

Answer. The vector is moved out, but its elements live in buffers owned by the arena, and the arena is destroyed when the function returns. Reading nums.front() is a heap-use-after-free, which ASan reports; later, nums's destructor would also call deallocate on the destroyed resource.

Why. A pmr container stores a raw pointer to its memory resource and never owns it. Moving the container moves the pointer, not the resource. The arena must outlive every container that uses it: create it in the caller and pass it in (parse_numbers(std::pmr::memory_resource& arena)), or return a struct that owns both the arena and the data, declared in that order so the data is destroyed first.

OutputHow many bytes does a pmr::vector request from its arena while growing to 1000 ints, with and without reserve?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory_resource>
#include <vector>

class Tally : public std::pmr::memory_resource {
    std::pmr::memory_resource* up_;
public:
    std::size_t requested = 0;
    explicit Tally(std::pmr::memory_resource* up) : up_(up) {}
private:
    void* do_allocate(std::size_t n, std::size_t a) override { requested += n; return up_->allocate(n, a); }
    void do_deallocate(void* p, std::size_t n, std::size_t a) override { up_->deallocate(p, n, a); }
    bool do_is_equal(const memory_resource& o) const noexcept override { return this == &o; }
};

int main() {
    std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource arena;
    Tally grow(&arena), reserved(&arena);
    {
        std::pmr::vector<int> v(&grow);
        for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) v.push_back(i);
        std::pmr::vector<int> w(&reserved);
        w.reserve(1000);
        for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) w.push_back(i);
    }
    std::printf("without reserve: %zu bytes, with reserve: %zu bytes\n", grow.requested, reserved.requested);
}
Answer
without reserve: 8188 bytes, with reserve: 4000 bytes

Answer. Without reserve, the vector requests capacities 1, 2, 4, ..., 1024 ints: 2047 ints, 8188 bytes, of which only the last 4096 are in use. With reserve(1000) it requests exactly 4000 bytes once.

Why. Both libstdc++ and libc++ double the capacity on growth (MSVC uses 1.5), so the abandoned buffers sum to just under the final one. With malloc or a pool those old buffers are reused; in a monotonic arena, deallocate is a no-op and they stay dead until release(). The output is the same for both libraries because both double; a library with a different growth factor would print a different first number.

Write the code

Coding

CodeImplement a fixed-buffer arena over caller-supplied memory: void* try_allocate(n, align) (null when full), allocate (throws std::bad_alloc), T* create<T>(args...) for trivially destructible types only, T* create_array<T>(count), reset() and used(). The base may be misaligned, alignments may be up to 4096, and huge sizes must not overflow the bounds check.

Answer

Approach. Work on absolute addresses: round base + offset up to the alignment, convert back to an offset, then check n <= cap - start (which cannot overflow once start <= cap is known). create enforces trivial destructibility with a static_assert, and create_array checks the multiplication for overflow.

#include <bit>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <limits>
#include <memory>
#include <new>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>

class FixedArena {
    std::byte* base_;
    std::size_t cap_, off_ = 0;
public:
    FixedArena(void* buf, std::size_t cap) : base_(static_cast<std::byte*>(buf)), cap_(cap) {}
    FixedArena(const FixedArena&) = delete;
    FixedArena& operator=(const FixedArena&) = delete;

    void* try_allocate(std::size_t n, std::size_t align = alignof(std::max_align_t)) noexcept {
        if (!std::has_single_bit(align)) return nullptr;
        auto b = reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t>(base_);
        auto aligned = (b + off_ + align - 1) & ~(std::uintptr_t{align} - 1);
        std::size_t start = aligned - b;
        if (start > cap_ || n > cap_ - start) return nullptr;
        off_ = start + n;
        return base_ + start;
    }
    void* allocate(std::size_t n, std::size_t align = alignof(std::max_align_t)) {
        if (void* p = try_allocate(n, align)) return p;
        throw std::bad_alloc();
    }
    template <class T, class... A> T* create(A&&... args) {
        static_assert(std::is_trivially_destructible_v<T>, "the arena never runs destructors");
        return ::new (allocate(sizeof(T), alignof(T))) T{std::forward<A>(args)...};
    }
    template <class T> T* create_array(std::size_t count) {
        static_assert(std::is_trivially_destructible_v<T>);
        if (count > std::numeric_limits<std::size_t>::max() / sizeof(T)) throw std::bad_alloc();
        T* p = static_cast<T*>(allocate(sizeof(T) * count, alignof(T)));
        std::uninitialized_value_construct_n(p, count);
        return p;
    }
    void reset() noexcept { off_ = 0; }
    std::size_t used() const noexcept { return off_; }
};

struct alignas(64) CacheLine { long counters[8]; };
struct Token { int kind; int start; int len; };

int main() {
    alignas(64) static std::byte storage[1 + 8192];
    FixedArena arena(storage + 1, 8192);                    // deliberately misaligned base

    auto* t = arena.create<Token>(1, 0, 5);
    auto* line = arena.create<CacheLine>();
    auto* page = arena.allocate(16, 4096);
    std::printf("token kind %d, cache line aligned: %s, page aligned: %s\n", t->kind,
                reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t>(line) % 64 == 0 ? "yes" : "no",
                reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t>(page) % 4096 == 0 ? "yes" : "no");

    int* zeros = arena.create_array<int>(100);
    int sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 100; ++i) sum += zeros[i];
    std::printf("array of 100 ints sums to %d\n", sum);

    std::printf("huge request: %s\n", arena.try_allocate(std::numeric_limits<std::size_t>::max() - 8) ? "granted" : "refused");
    std::printf("bad alignment: %s\n", arena.try_allocate(8, 24) ? "granted" : "refused");
    try { arena.create_array<double>(std::numeric_limits<std::size_t>::max() / 4); }
    catch (const std::bad_alloc&) { std::puts("overflowing array: bad_alloc"); }

    arena.reset();
    std::printf("used after reset: %zu\n", arena.used());
}
token kind 1, cache line aligned: yes, page aligned: yes
array of 100 ints sums to 0
huge request: refused
bad alignment: refused
overflowing array: bad_alloc
used after reset: 0

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) per allocation, plus O(count) to value-initialise arrays. The tests cover each classic bug: the misaligned base (the 64- and 4096-aligned requests would fail with offset-only rounding), the overflow in start + n for a huge n, a non-power-of-two alignment, and the overflow in sizeof(T) * count. The arena does not own its buffer, so destroying it frees nothing; that is the caller's job.

Estimated rating: ~1500 · short, but every line has an alignment or overflow edge case that interviewers probe

CodeExtend an arena with a destructor list so it accepts any type. make<T>(args...) registers a finaliser only for types that need one; reset() and the destructor run finalisers newest first. The arena must stay consistent if T's constructor throws or if the arena runs out of space while registering the finaliser.

Answer

Approach. Reserve the finaliser record before constructing the object, so that the only thing that can fail after construction is nothing. If the constructor throws, rewind the offset to where it was before both allocations, so the arena is exactly as before the call. The record stores a type-erased destroy function (a captureless lambda converted to a function pointer) and the object's address.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <string>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class Arena {
    struct Finalizer { void (*destroy)(void*); void* obj; Finalizer* next; };
    std::byte* buf_;
    std::size_t cap_, off_ = 0;
    Finalizer* fin_ = nullptr;

    void* raw(std::size_t n, std::size_t a) {
        std::size_t s = (off_ + a - 1) & ~(a - 1);
        if (s > cap_ || n > cap_ - s) throw std::bad_alloc();
        off_ = s + n;
        return buf_ + s;
    }
public:
    explicit Arena(std::size_t cap) : buf_(static_cast<std::byte*>(::operator new(cap))), cap_(cap) {}
    ~Arena() { reset(); ::operator delete(buf_); }
    Arena(const Arena&) = delete;
    Arena& operator=(const Arena&) = delete;

    template <class T, class... A> T* make(A&&... args) {
        static_assert(alignof(T) <= __STDCPP_DEFAULT_NEW_ALIGNMENT__, "buffer is only new-aligned");
        const std::size_t saved = off_;
        Finalizer* rec = nullptr;
        if constexpr (!std::is_trivially_destructible_v<T>)
            rec = static_cast<Finalizer*>(raw(sizeof(Finalizer), alignof(Finalizer)));   // may throw: nothing to undo
        void* mem;
        try {
            mem = raw(sizeof(T), alignof(T));
            T* obj = ::new (mem) T(std::forward<A>(args)...);
            if constexpr (!std::is_trivially_destructible_v<T>)
                fin_ = ::new (rec) Finalizer{[](void* p) { static_cast<T*>(p)->~T(); }, obj, fin_};
            return obj;
        } catch (...) {
            off_ = saved;                     // undo both allocations
            throw;
        }
    }
    void reset() noexcept {
        while (fin_) { Finalizer* f = fin_; fin_ = f->next; f->destroy(f->obj); }
        off_ = 0;
    }
    std::size_t used() const noexcept { return off_; }
};

struct Symbol {
    static inline int live = 0;
    std::string name;
    std::vector<int> uses;
    explicit Symbol(std::string n, bool fail = false) : name(std::move(n)) {
        if (fail) throw std::runtime_error("bad symbol");
        ++live;
    }
    ~Symbol() { --live; }
};

int main() {
    Arena arena(4096);
    arena.make<Symbol>("a_symbol_name_long_enough_for_the_heap")->uses.assign(50, 7);
    arena.make<double>(3.5);
    arena.make<Symbol>("another_long_symbol_name_on_the_heap");
    std::size_t before = arena.used();
    try { arena.make<Symbol>("broken", true); } catch (const std::exception& e) { std::printf("caught: %s\n", e.what()); }
    std::printf("live %d, offset restored: %s\n", Symbol::live, arena.used() == before ? "yes" : "no");
    try { for (;;) arena.make<Symbol>("filler"); } catch (const std::bad_alloc&) { std::puts("arena full: bad_alloc"); }
    std::printf("live before reset: %s\n", Symbol::live > 2 ? "many" : "few");
    arena.reset();
    std::printf("live after reset: %d, used %zu\n", Symbol::live, arena.used());
}
caught: bad symbol
live 2, offset restored: yes
arena full: bad_alloc
live before reset: many
live after reset: 0, used 0

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) per make, O(number of non-trivial objects) per reset. ASan runs this clean, which proves the strings' and vectors' heap buffers are freed by the finalisers. Pitfalls: registering the finaliser after construction (if that allocation throws, the constructed object is never destroyed); pushing a finaliser before the constructor succeeds (reset would destroy a half-built object); running finalisers oldest first; and finalisers that throw, which is why reset is noexcept and destructors must not throw. Rewinding on failure is only valid because nothing else allocated in between.

Estimated rating: ~1800 · type erasure with function pointers plus careful exception-safety ordering

CodeWrite a growing arena that chains blocks: the first block is 1 KiB, each new block doubles, requests larger than half the next block size get a dedicated block, and reset() keeps only the first block. Each block stores its header at its start. Report the number of blocks and the bytes reserved.

Answer

Approach. Each block begins with {next, size} and the usable area follows, so the arena needs one allocation per block. The arena tracks the current block's bump pointer and end. A request that does not fit allocates either a normal doubled block (which becomes current) or, for large requests, a dedicated block inserted behind the current one so the current block keeps serving small requests.

#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <new>

class GrowingArena {
    struct Block { Block* next; std::size_t size; };            // header; data follows
    static constexpr std::size_t kHeader = (sizeof(Block) + 15) & ~std::size_t{15};
    static constexpr std::size_t kFirst = 1024;

    Block* head_ = nullptr;          // current block, chain points to older blocks
    Block* first_ = nullptr;         // the 1 KiB block that reset() keeps
    std::byte* ptr_ = nullptr;
    std::byte* end_ = nullptr;
    std::size_t next_size_ = kFirst;

    static Block* new_block(std::size_t data_size, Block* next) {
        void* mem = ::operator new(kHeader + data_size);
        return ::new (mem) Block{next, data_size};
    }
    static std::byte* data(Block* b) { return reinterpret_cast<std::byte*>(b) + kHeader; }
    static std::byte* align_up(std::byte* p, std::size_t a) {
        auto v = reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t>(p);
        return p + (((v + a - 1) & ~(std::uintptr_t{a} - 1)) - v);
    }

public:
    GrowingArena() { first_ = head_ = new_block(kFirst, nullptr); ptr_ = data(head_); end_ = ptr_ + kFirst; next_size_ = 2 * kFirst; }
    ~GrowingArena() { release_all(head_); }
    GrowingArena(const GrowingArena&) = delete;
    GrowingArena& operator=(const GrowingArena&) = delete;

    void* allocate(std::size_t n, std::size_t align = 16) {     // align <= 16
        std::byte* p = align_up(ptr_, align);
        if (p <= end_ && n <= static_cast<std::size_t>(end_ - p)) { ptr_ = p + n; return p; }
        if (n > next_size_ / 2) {                                // dedicated block behind the current one
            head_->next = new_block(n, head_->next);
            return data(head_->next);
        }
        head_ = new_block(next_size_, head_);
        ptr_ = data(head_) + n;
        end_ = data(head_) + next_size_;
        next_size_ *= 2;
        return data(head_);
    }
    void reset() {
        for (Block* b = head_; b;) {                             // a dedicated block may sit behind first_
            Block* n = b->next;
            if (b != first_) ::operator delete(b);
            b = n;
        }
        first_->next = nullptr;
        head_ = first_;
        ptr_ = data(first_);
        end_ = ptr_ + first_->size;
        next_size_ = 2 * kFirst;
    }
    void stats(const char* when) const {
        std::size_t blocks = 0, bytes = 0;
        for (Block* b = head_; b; b = b->next) { ++blocks; bytes += b->size; }
        std::printf("%-14s %zu blocks, %zu bytes reserved\n", when, blocks, bytes);
    }

private:
    static void release_all(Block* b) { while (b) { Block* n = b->next; ::operator delete(b); b = n; } }
};

int main() {
    GrowingArena arena;
    arena.stats("start:");
    for (int i = 0; i < 100; ++i) static_cast<char*>(arena.allocate(40))[0] = 'x';   // 4000 bytes in 48-byte steps
    arena.stats("100 x 40 B:");
    auto* big = static_cast<char*>(arena.allocate(100000));
    big[99999] = 'y';
    void* small = arena.allocate(16);
    arena.stats("after 100 KB:");
    std::printf("small request still served from the current block: %s\n", small != nullptr ? "yes" : "no");
    arena.reset();
    arena.stats("after reset:");
    arena.allocate(5000);                                       // dedicated block behind the first one
    arena.reset();
    arena.stats("reset again:");
}
start:         1 blocks, 1024 bytes reserved
100 x 40 B:    3 blocks, 7168 bytes reserved
after 100 KB:  4 blocks, 107168 bytes reserved
small request still served from the current block: yes
after reset:   1 blocks, 1024 bytes reserved
reset again:   1 blocks, 1024 bytes reserved

Complexity and pitfalls. Allocation is O(1) amortised; reset is O(number of blocks). The header is rounded to 16 bytes so that block data stays 16-aligned (the header itself is 16 bytes on 64-bit, so this is free). Pitfalls: a large request that becomes the current block wastes the rest of the previous block and makes the next small request start a new block, which is why it is linked behind; reset must keep the first block, which is not always the tail of the chain (a large request made while the first block is current is linked behind it), so the arena remembers it; and the bounds test compares n with the remaining space rather than computing p + n, which could overflow past the end of the block.

Estimated rating: ~1800 · pointer arithmetic across a linked list of blocks, with a dedicated-block path and a selective reset

CodeImplement a scratch arena with mark(), rewind(mark) and an RAII ScratchScope. Use it in a recursive function that needs a temporary array at every level (a merge sort), and show that the peak memory stays far below the total requested. In debug builds, rewinding should fill freed memory with a pattern.

Answer

Approach. A mark is the current offset. The scope saves it in its constructor and rewinds in its destructor, so every exit path, including exceptions, frees the temporaries. Rewinding fills the released range with 0xCD so a stale pointer reads garbage at once. A merge sort that takes its merge buffer from the arena at every level shows the effect: the total requested is n log n per sort, but the high-water mark is a single buffer of n elements.

#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstring>
#include <new>

class ScratchArena {
    alignas(16) std::byte buf_[64 * 1024];
    std::size_t off_ = 0, high_ = 0;
public:
    struct Mark { std::size_t off; };
    void* allocate(std::size_t n) {
        std::size_t s = (off_ + 15) & ~std::size_t{15};
        if (s > sizeof buf_ || n > sizeof buf_ - s) throw std::bad_alloc();
        off_ = s + n;
        high_ = std::max(high_, off_);
        return buf_ + s;
    }
    template <class T> T* array(std::size_t n) { return ::new (allocate(n * sizeof(T))) T[n]{}; }
    Mark mark() const noexcept { return {off_}; }
    void rewind(Mark m) noexcept {
        std::memset(buf_ + m.off, 0xCD, off_ - m.off);      // debug poison
        off_ = m.off;
    }
    std::size_t used() const noexcept { return off_; }
    std::size_t high_water() const noexcept { return high_; }
};

class ScratchScope {
    ScratchArena& a_;
    ScratchArena::Mark m_;
public:
    explicit ScratchScope(ScratchArena& a) : a_(a), m_(a.mark()) {}
    ~ScratchScope() { a_.rewind(m_); }
    ScratchScope(const ScratchScope&) = delete;
    ScratchScope& operator=(const ScratchScope&) = delete;
};

// Merge sort that takes its merge buffer from the scratch arena at every level.
static void merge_sort(ScratchArena& s, int* a, std::size_t n, std::size_t& total_bytes) {
    if (n < 2) return;
    std::size_t half = n / 2;
    merge_sort(s, a, half, total_bytes);
    merge_sort(s, a + half, n - half, total_bytes);
    ScratchScope scope(s);                          // the buffer below is freed when this level returns
    int* tmp = s.array<int>(n);
    total_bytes += n * sizeof(int);
    std::merge(a, a + half, a + half, a + n, tmp);
    std::copy(tmp, tmp + n, a);
}

int main() {
    ScratchArena scratch;
    int data[1000];
    std::size_t total = 0;
    bool sorted = true;
    for (int round = 0; round < 100; ++round) {
        for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) data[i] = (i * 7919 + round * 31) % 1000;
        merge_sort(scratch, data, 1000, total);
        sorted = sorted && std::is_sorted(data, data + 1000);
    }
    std::printf("100 sorts correct: %s\n", sorted ? "yes" : "no");
    std::printf("scratch requested in total: %zu bytes\n", total);
