    std::printf("high-water mark: %zu bytes, used now: %zu\n", scratch.high_water(), scratch.used());

    auto outer = scratch.mark();
    int* stale = scratch.array<int>(4);
    stale[0] = 42;
    scratch.rewind(outer);
    std::printf("stale read after rewind: 0x%X\n", static_cast<unsigned>(stale[0]));
}
100 sorts correct: yes
scratch requested in total: 3990400 bytes
high-water mark: 4000 bytes, used now: 0
stale read after rewind: 0xCDCDCDCD

Complexity and pitfalls. Allocation and rewind are O(1) (the debug fill is O(bytes freed)). 100 sorts of 1000 ints requested almost 4 MB of scratch in total, yet the arena never held more than one 4000-byte buffer: each level opens its scope after its recursive calls have returned and rewound, so buffers never stack up. Opening the scope at the top of the function instead would still be correct but would hold buffers along the whole recursion path. Pitfalls: returning a pointer allocated inside the scope, rewinding marks out of order, and forgetting that the fill is a debugging aid only. The last lines read freed scratch memory on purpose to show the poison; it is safe here only because the bytes are still inside the arena's own buffer and are read as plain integers.

Estimated rating: ~1600 · RAII rewinding plus reasoning about high-water memory in recursion

CodeWrite a parser for integer expressions with +, *, parentheses and variable names (for example 2 * (price + 3) * qty) that builds an AST in a std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource over a stack buffer, with null_memory_resource() as upstream so it provably never touches the heap. Variable names are std::pmr::string. Evaluate the AST with a variable table.

Answer

Approach. A recursive-descent parser (expr := term ('+' term)*, term := factor ('*' factor)*, factor := number | name | '(' expr ')') creates nodes with std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<>::new_object, so every node and every name comes from the arena. Nodes are never destroyed individually: the whole tree disappears when the arena does. That is safe because everything a node owns (the name's characters) is in the same arena.

#include <array>
#include <cctype>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <map>
#include <memory_resource>
#include <new>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

struct Node {
    char op;                   // '+', '*', 'n' (number) or 'v' (variable)
    long value = 0;
    std::pmr::string name;
    Node* lhs = nullptr;
    Node* rhs = nullptr;
    Node(char o, std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<> a) : op(o), name(a) {}
};

class Parser {
    std::string_view src_;
    std::size_t pos_ = 0;
    std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<> alloc_;

    char peek() { while (pos_ < src_.size() && src_[pos_] == ' ') ++pos_; return pos_ < src_.size() ? src_[pos_] : '\0'; }
    Node* make(char op) { return alloc_.new_object<Node>(op, alloc_); }
    Node* binary(char op, Node* l, Node* r) { Node* n = make(op); n->lhs = l; n->rhs = r; return n; }

    Node* factor() {
        char c = peek();
        if (c == '(') { ++pos_; Node* e = expr(); if (peek() != ')') throw std::runtime_error("expected )"); ++pos_; return e; }
        if (std::isdigit(static_cast<unsigned char>(c))) {
            Node* n = make('n');
            while (pos_ < src_.size() && std::isdigit(static_cast<unsigned char>(src_[pos_]))) n->value = n->value * 10 + (src_[pos_++] - '0');
            return n;
        }
        if (std::isalpha(static_cast<unsigned char>(c)) || c == '_') {
            Node* n = make('v');
            std::size_t start = pos_;
            while (pos_ < src_.size() && (std::isalnum(static_cast<unsigned char>(src_[pos_])) || src_[pos_] == '_')) ++pos_;
            n->name.assign(src_.substr(start, pos_ - start));
            return n;
        }
        throw std::runtime_error("unexpected character");
    }
    Node* term() { Node* l = factor(); while (peek() == '*') { ++pos_; l = binary('*', l, factor()); } return l; }
    Node* expr() { Node* l = term(); while (peek() == '+') { ++pos_; l = binary('+', l, term()); } return l; }

public:
    Parser(std::string_view s, std::pmr::memory_resource* r) : src_(s), alloc_(r) {}
    Node* parse() { Node* e = expr(); if (peek() != '\0') throw std::runtime_error("trailing input"); return e; }
};

static long eval(const Node* n, const std::map<std::string, long, std::less<>>& vars) {
    switch (n->op) {
        case 'n': return n->value;
        case 'v': return vars.at(std::string(n->name));
        case '+': return eval(n->lhs, vars) + eval(n->rhs, vars);
        default:  return eval(n->lhs, vars) * eval(n->rhs, vars);
    }
}

static int count(const Node* n) { return n ? 1 + count(n->lhs) + count(n->rhs) : 0; }

int main() {
    const std::map<std::string, long, std::less<>> vars{{"price", 7}, {"qty", 5}, {"a_very_long_variable_name_for_the_heap", 2}};
    alignas(std::max_align_t) std::array<std::byte, 4096> stack_buf;
    for (const char* text : {"2 * (price + 3) * qty", "1 + 2 * 3 + a_very_long_variable_name_for_the_heap", "(1 + 2"}) {
        std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource arena(stack_buf.data(), stack_buf.size(), std::pmr::null_memory_resource());
        try {
            Node* ast = Parser(text, &arena).parse();
            std::printf("%-50s = %ld (%d nodes)\n", text, eval(ast, vars), count(ast));
        } catch (const std::exception& e) {
            std::printf("%-50s : error: %s\n", text, e.what());
        }
    }   // each arena (and its tree) vanishes here; the stack buffer is reused

    std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource tiny(stack_buf.data(), 64, std::pmr::null_memory_resource());
    try { Parser("1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6", &tiny).parse(); }
    catch (const std::bad_alloc&) { std::puts("64-byte arena: bad_alloc, never the heap"); }
}
2 * (price + 3) * qty                              = 100 (7 nodes)
1 + 2 * 3 + a_very_long_variable_name_for_the_heap = 9 (7 nodes)
(1 + 2                                             : error: expected )
64-byte arena: bad_alloc, never the heap

Complexity and pitfalls. Parsing is O(length); each node is one bump allocation. Nodes are not trivially destructible (they hold a pmr::string), yet skipping their destructors is safe because the string's buffer is in the same arena, so nothing is leaked (skipping a destructor is allowed by [basic.life]/5); ASan confirms it. The polymorphic_allocator passed to each Node makes the long variable name allocate from the arena too. Pitfalls: a name stored as std::string would leak at every reset; a tree that escapes the scope of its arena dangles; and the null upstream means the buffer must be sized for the largest input you accept, which is a feature for hot paths and a limit you must test.

Estimated rating: ~1900 · a working recursive-descent parser plus correct pmr allocator propagation and arena lifetime reasoning

CodeWrite ArenaAllocator<T>, an STL allocator over a bump arena, so that std::vector, std::map and std::basic_string can live in the arena. deallocate must reclaim the memory when it is the most recent allocation (so a temporary that is freed right away costs nothing), and two allocators must compare equal exactly when they share an arena.

Answer

Approach. The allocator is a handle holding an Arena*; the converting constructor copies that pointer so rebound allocators share the arena. The arena implements "undo last": if the block being freed ends exactly at the current offset, the offset moves back to its start. Equality compares arena pointers. Copy and move assignment propagate the allocator so containers can be swapped and assigned freely within one arena.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <map>
#include <new>
#include <string>
#include <type_traits>
#include <vector>

class Arena {
    alignas(std::max_align_t) std::byte buf_[64 * 1024];
    std::size_t off_ = 0;
public:
    void* allocate(std::size_t n, std::size_t a) {
        std::size_t s = (off_ + a - 1) & ~(a - 1);
        if (s > sizeof buf_ || n > sizeof buf_ - s) throw std::bad_alloc();
        off_ = s + n;
        return buf_ + s;
    }
    void deallocate(void* p, std::size_t n) noexcept {
        if (static_cast<std::byte*>(p) + n == buf_ + off_) off_ = static_cast<std::size_t>(static_cast<std::byte*>(p) - buf_);
    }
    std::size_t used() const noexcept { return off_; }
};

template <class T>
class ArenaAllocator {
    Arena* arena_;
    template <class U> friend class ArenaAllocator;
public:
    using value_type = T;
    using propagate_on_container_copy_assignment = std::true_type;
    using propagate_on_container_move_assignment = std::true_type;
    using propagate_on_container_swap = std::true_type;

    explicit ArenaAllocator(Arena& a) noexcept : arena_(&a) {}
    template <class U> ArenaAllocator(const ArenaAllocator<U>& o) noexcept : arena_(o.arena_) {}

    T* allocate(std::size_t n) {
        if (n > static_cast<std::size_t>(-1) / sizeof(T)) throw std::bad_alloc();
        return static_cast<T*>(arena_->allocate(n * sizeof(T), alignof(T)));
    }
    void deallocate(T* p, std::size_t n) noexcept { arena_->deallocate(p, n * sizeof(T)); }
    template <class U> bool operator==(const ArenaAllocator<U>& o) const noexcept { return arena_ == o.arena_; }
};

using AString = std::basic_string<char, std::char_traits<char>, ArenaAllocator<char>>;

int main() {
    Arena arena;
    {
        std::vector<int, ArenaAllocator<int>> v{ArenaAllocator<int>(arena)};
        for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) v.push_back(i);
        std::printf("vector of 1000 ints: arena holds %zu bytes\n", arena.used());
    }
    std::printf("after the vector died: %zu bytes\n", arena.used());
    {
        AString temp(200, 'x', ArenaAllocator<char>(arena));   // freed while still on top
    }
    std::printf("after a temporary string: %zu bytes\n", arena.used());

    ArenaAllocator<char> ca(arena);
    const std::size_t before_map = arena.used();
    std::map<AString, int, std::less<>, ArenaAllocator<std::pair<const AString, int>>> prices{ArenaAllocator<std::pair<const AString, int>>(arena)};
    for (const char* sym : {"AAPL", "MSFT", "a_long_instrument_identifier_on_the_arena"}) prices.emplace(AString(sym, ca), 100);
    std::printf("map entries %zu, nodes and keys in the arena: %s\n", prices.size(), arena.used() > before_map ? "yes" : "no");

    Arena other;
    ArenaAllocator<int> x(arena), y(arena), z(other);
    ArenaAllocator<long> rebound(x);
    std::printf("x == y: %d, x == z: %d, rebound == x: %d\n", x == y, x == z, rebound == x);
}
vector of 1000 ints: arena holds 8188 bytes
after the vector died: 4092 bytes
after a temporary string: 4092 bytes
map entries 3, nodes and keys in the arena: yes
x == y: 1, x == z: 0, rebound == x: 1

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) per allocation. The output shows what undo-last can and cannot do. While the vector grows it allocates the new buffer before freeing the old one, so the old buffer is never on top and is never reclaimed: the arena holds 8188 bytes, the same as a monotonic resource. When the vector dies, its final 4096-byte buffer is on top and comes back, leaving 4092 bytes of dead buffers. The temporary string is allocated and freed while on top, so it costs nothing. (std::vector has no way to ask an allocator to grow a block in place, which is why reserve matters so much in arenas.) The propagate_* traits are set to true so that assigning or swapping two arena containers never falls back to element-wise copies. Swapping containers on different arenas then swaps arenas, which is what you want only if the containers' lifetimes match their new arenas. The map's nodes and its long key string are both in the arena; short keys fit in the string's inline buffer. The Arena object is 64 KiB, which is fine on a desktop stack but should be heap-allocated or static on small-stack threads.

Estimated rating: ~1800 · allocator requirements, rebind, propagation traits and an undo-last arena working together

Cheat sheet

Theory
  • Arena = buffer + offset. Allocate: start = round_up(addr, a), offset = start + n. Free one: no-op (or undo-last). Free all: reset in O(1).
  • round_up(x, a) = (x + a - 1) & ~(a - 1) for power-of-two a; align the address, not just the offset; check n <= cap - start to avoid overflow.
  • Safe only under a lifetime discipline: per request, per frame (double buffered), per parse. Nothing outside may point in after reset.
  • Destructors are not run: allow only trivially destructible types (static_assert), or keep a finaliser list run newest first. Default-allocator containers inside arena objects leak.
  • std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource: optional initial buffer, geometric growth from upstream, no-op deallocate, release() frees upstream buffers, not thread safe; upstream null_memory_resource() proves no heap use.
  • Growing arenas chain doubling blocks, give huge requests their own block, and keep one block on reset. Marks give O(1) rewind for scratch memory; use RAII scopes and two scratch arenas.
  • Arena vs pool: one shared lifetime and mixed sizes → arena; one size with individual lifetimes → pool. Measured on an Apple M1: arena about 10× malloc, monotonic resource 4 to 5×.
  • Pitfalls: dangling pointers after reset (ASan silent unless blocks are freed or memory is poisoned), unbounded growth (vector regrowth doubles memory), mixing with long-lived objects, alignment bugs, sharing across threads.

Part E · Memory management · Chapter 18

Stack allocation optimisations

The cheapest allocation is the one that never reaches the allocator. This chapter explains why the stack is so cheap, how big it really is, and the techniques that keep small objects off the heap: small string optimisation, small-buffer optimisation, inline-storage vectors, stack buffers for pmr, and the compiler's own heap elision. Interviewers ask about it because it separates people who know std::string has SSO from people who can say how many bytes fit, why std::vector cannot do the same, and what happens when a thread runs out of stack.

TheoryDrillsCoding· about 5 hours· prerequisites: Ch 9, Ch 14, Ch 17

Why the stack is cheap

Theory

Mental model. The stack is a bump allocator that the hardware and the ABI give you for free. Each thread owns one contiguous region and one register (rsp on x86-64, sp on AArch64) that marks its top. Allocating every local of a function is a single subtraction from that register in the prologue, and freeing all of them is a single addition in the epilogue. There is no search for a free block, no header, no lock and no bookkeeping.

Under the hood. The compiler knows the size of every local at compile time, so it adds them up (plus spills and alignment) and emits one adjustment. A heap allocation is a call into operator new, which calls malloc, which picks a size class, pops a block from a thread cache or a shared free list, and may fall back to a system call (Ch 10). The matching delete has to find the size class again and push the block back. The generated code shows the difference:

// int local_sum() { int a[64]; fill(a); return sum(a); }      (AArch64, abridged)
local_sum:
    sub   sp, sp, #272           // all locals allocated: one instruction
    stp   x29, x30, [sp, #256]   // save frame pointer and link register
    ...
    ldp   x29, x30, [sp, #256]
    add   sp, sp, #272           // all locals freed: one instruction
    ret

// int heap_sum() { int* a = new int[64]; fill(a); int s = sum(a); delete[] a; return s; }
heap_sum:
    ...
    mov   x0, #256
    bl    operator new[](unsigned long)    // tens of instructions in the fast path
    ...
    bl    operator delete[](void*)         // and again on the way out

The stack also wins on locality. The top of the stack is touched constantly, so it is almost always in L1 cache and its pages are already mapped. A fresh heap block can come from anywhere in the address space and may share nothing with the data you are using.

Key facts

OperationTypical costWhy
Allocate all locals of a frame1 instruction, about 0 nsOne sub sp, sizes known at compile time
Free all locals1 instructionOne add sp (or mov sp, fp)
malloc/new fast path (thread cache hit)about 10 to 50 nsSize-class lookup, free-list pop, function calls
malloc slow pathhundreds of ns to microsecondsCentral lists, locks, mmap/brk, page faults
First touch of a new heap pageabout 0.1 to 1 µsMinor page fault, kernel zeroes the page
Default stack, Linux main thread8 MB (ulimit -s = 8192)RLIMIT_STACK soft limit
Default stack, macOS secondary thread512 KBpthread_attr default

Know this cold

The stack is fast for three reasons: allocation is a pointer bump that the compiler fuses for the whole frame, deallocation is free and implicit, and the memory is hot in cache. Its limits are just as important: the size is fixed and small, the lifetime ends with the function, and the size of each object must be known at compile time (unless you use alloca or VLAs, which are their own trouble).

The rest of the chapter is about using the stack, or storage inside an object, for things that would normally go to the heap, without hitting those limits.

Stack frame layout

Theory

Each call pushes a frame. The exact layout depends on the ABI (System V x86-64 on Linux, AAPCS64 on Linux arm64, Apple's arm64 variant on macOS), but every frame has the same parts: a way back to the caller, saved registers, locals, and space for arguments to the next call.

Two details matter in interviews. First, on x86-64 the call instruction pushes the return address, so a buffer overflow on a local array can overwrite it (the classic stack smashing attack, mitigated by stack canaries from -fstack-protector). On AArch64 the return address arrives in the link register x30 and is saved next to the frame pointer by stp x29, x30. Second, the stack pointer must stay aligned: 16 bytes at every call on both x86-64 SysV and AArch64.

Red zones

The System V x86-64 ABI promises that the 128 bytes below rsp will not be clobbered by signal handlers. A leaf function (one that calls nothing) can keep its locals there and skip the sub rsp entirely. Apple's arm64 ABI also has a 128-byte red zone, while the generic AAPCS64 used by Linux on arm64 has none, and Windows x64 has none. Kernel code is compiled with -mno-red-zone, because an interrupt arriving on the same stack would overwrite it.

Stack probes

If a function allocates a frame bigger than a page in one step, sp can jump straight over the guard page below the stack and land in some other mapping (the "stack clash" class of exploits, 2017). Stack probes fix this: the compiler touches each page of a large frame in order, so the guard page is always hit first. GCC and Clang emit them with -fstack-clash-protection, which many Linux distributions enable by default. Windows does the same through __chkstk for any frame over 4 KB. Probes cost a few instructions per page, only in functions with large frames.

Stack size limits and stack overflow

Theory

The stack is small and fixed, and that is the price of its speed. Know the defaults, because "why does this recursion crash only in a worker thread?" is a common interview and debugging question.

PlatformMain threadOther threadsHow to change
Linux, glibc8 MB soft limit, grows on demandDefaults to RLIMIT_STACK at startup (usually 8 MB), fixed sizeulimit -s, setrlimit before exec, pthread_attr_setstacksize
Linux, musl (Alpine)8 MB128 KBpthread_attr_setstacksize, linker flag -Wl,-z,stack-size=
macOS8 MB512 KBpthread_attr_setstacksize, linker -stack_size for main
Windows1 MB1 MBLinker /STACK, CreateThread parameter

On Linux the main thread's stack is a mapping that the kernel grows downward on page faults until it reaches RLIMIT_STACK. Thread stacks are allocated once by the thread library with mmap, with a guard page (or more) at the low end that is mapped with no access. Touching the guard page raises SIGSEGV. A stack overflow is not a C++ exception: no std::bad_alloc is thrown, no destructors run, and the process dies unless you installed a handler on an alternate signal stack (sigaltstack), which can only log and exit.

This program prints the limits it runs with. The values are platform-specific, so its output is not checked.

#include <pthread.h>
#include <sys/resource.h>
#include <cstdio>

int main() {
    rlimit r{};
    getrlimit(RLIMIT_STACK, &r);
    std::printf("RLIMIT_STACK soft: %llu KB\n", (unsigned long long)r.rlim_cur / 1024);

    pthread_attr_t attr;
    pthread_attr_init(&attr);
    std::size_t sz = 0;
    pthread_attr_getstacksize(&attr, &sz);
    std::printf("default new-thread stack: %zu KB\n", sz / 1024);
    pthread_attr_destroy(&attr);
}

On the Apple M1 used to test this guide it prints 8176 KB for the soft limit (8 MB less one 16 KB page) and 512 KB for new threads. A typical Linux x86-64 box prints 8192 KB for both.

Giving a thread a bigger stack

std::thread has no way to set the stack size. Use pthread_attr_setstacksize with pthread_create, boost::thread::attributes, or move the deep work onto the main thread. Better still, remove the depth: turn recursion over user-controlled data (trees, graphs, JSON nesting) into a loop with an explicit stack in a std::vector, which lives on the heap and grows as needed.

Interview trap

A recursive destructor is still recursion. A linked list built from std::unique_ptr<Node> next destroys node 1, which destroys node 2, and so on: one frame per node. A list of a million nodes overflows an 8 MB stack. The fix is an iterative destructor that unlinks nodes in a loop (see the drills).

Rules of thumb that interviewers like to hear: keep frames under a few KB, never put a buffer whose size depends on input on the stack, and treat any recursion whose depth depends on input as a bug waiting for a deep input.

Small string optimisation

Theory

Mental model. Most strings in real programs are short: names, keys, tokens, numbers. A std::string already needs a pointer, a size and a capacity, which is 24 bytes on a 64-bit target. SSO reuses those bytes (and sometimes a few more) as an inline character buffer when the string is short, so a short string needs no heap allocation at all.

Under the hood. The two major implementations use different layouts, and the numbers differ.

The program below measures it. It counts calls to operator new and assigns to a global string so the compiler cannot elide the allocation. The listed output is for GCC/libstdc++; the libc++ output follows it.

#include <atomic>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <new>
#include <string>

static std::atomic<int> g_allocs{0};   // atomic: see the elision section
void* operator new(std::size_t n) {
    g_allocs.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
    if (void* p = std::malloc(n ? n : 1)) return p;
    throw std::bad_alloc{};
}
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { std::free(p); }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { std::free(p); }

static std::string g;

int main() {
    std::printf("sizeof(std::string) = %zu, empty capacity = %zu\n", sizeof(std::string), g.capacity());
    for (std::size_t len : {15, 16, 22, 23}) {
        int before = g_allocs.load();
        g = std::string(len, 'x');
        std::printf("len %2zu: heap allocations %d\n", len, g_allocs.load() - before);
        g.clear();
        g.shrink_to_fit();
    }
}
sizeof(std::string) = 32, empty capacity = 15
len 15: heap allocations 0
len 16: heap allocations 1
len 22: heap allocations 1
len 23: heap allocations 1
// Clang with libc++ (same program)
sizeof(std::string) = 24, empty capacity = 22
len 15: heap allocations 0
len 16: heap allocations 0
len 22: heap allocations 0
len 23: heap allocations 1

MSVC's STL matches libstdc++ on these numbers (32 bytes, 15 characters) in x64 release builds; debug builds with iterator debugging add a pointer and make it 40 bytes. Everything here is implementation-defined: the standard does not require SSO at all. It does make it possible, because [string.require] allows swap and move to invalidate iterators and pointers into a string.

What SSO changes in practice

  • Moving a short string copies its characters. There is no heap pointer to steal. It is still cheap (a few dozen bytes), but a move is no longer "three pointer copies".
  • Pointers and views into a short string do not follow a move. After b = std::move(a), a string_view that pointed into a long a now points into b's heap buffer and still sees the text, while one that pointed into a short a still points at a's inline buffer, which is now empty. Code that "worked" with long strings breaks with short ones.
  • libstdc++ strings are not trivially relocatable. Because a short string points to itself, you cannot memcpy it to a new address. Containers must call the move constructor. libc++ strings have no self-pointer.
  • sizeof matters. A std::vector<std::string> of short keys is a contiguous array of 24 or 32 byte objects with the text inside, which is good for cache behaviour (Ch 19).
  • reserve and shrink_to_fit can move a string between modes. shrink_to_fit on a short string that has a heap buffer may bring it back inline.

Small-buffer optimisation in type-erased wrappers

Theory

The same trick generalises. Any wrapper that holds "some object of unknown type" (std::function, std::any, std::move_only_function, many Task or Callback classes) can keep a small inline buffer and place the object there with placement new (Ch 14) if it fits. Otherwise it allocates on the heap and stores a pointer.

// the shape of every SBO wrapper
class AnyCallable {
    alignas(std::max_align_t) unsigned char buf_[16];   // inline storage
    void* obj_;                                          // points into buf_ or to the heap
    const Ops* ops_;                                     // invoke, move, destroy for the real type
};

Whether an object goes inline depends on three conditions, all implementation-defined: it is small enough, its alignment fits the buffer, and it passes a type check. The check differs: std::any in both libraries requires a nothrow move constructor, libc++'s std::function requires a nothrow copy constructor, and libstdc++'s std::function requires the callable to be trivially copyable. The reason is the same in every case: moving the wrapper has to move or copy the inline object, and the wrapper's own move constructor is noexcept (heap-stored objects are moved by copying a pointer, which cannot throw).

Measured on GCC 16 with libstdc++ and Clang 22 with libc++ (escaping objects, so nothing is elided):

Wrappersizeof (libstdc++ / libc++)Inline if the stored object is at most
std::function<void()>32 / 3216 bytes on both (libstdc++ also requires it to be trivially copyable, libc++ requires a nothrow copy constructor)
std::any16 / 328 bytes (libstdc++) / 24 bytes (libc++), plus nothrow move
std::string32 / 2415 / 22 characters

A lambda that captures two pointers fits everywhere. A lambda that captures a std::string by value never fits libstdc++'s std::function (not trivially copyable) and always allocates. That is why hot callback paths often use a custom fixed-capacity function type (written in the coding drills) or std::function_ref (C++26), which never owns and never allocates.

Tip

To see whether a wrapper allocates, replace the global operator new with a counting version, as the programs in this chapter do. Make the object escape (store it in a global), and make the counter a std::atomic, or the optimiser may remove the allocation, or the count, and give you a false zero (details in the elision section below).

Inline-storage vectors and fixed arrays

Theory

Mental model. A small vector is a vector with SSO: it reserves room for N elements inside the object and uses the heap only when the size exceeds N. Real implementations are absl::InlinedVector<T, N>, llvm::SmallVector<T, N>, boost::container::small_vector<T, N> and folly::small_vector. A related type with no heap at all is the static or in-place vector: boost::container::static_vector, and std::inplace_vector<T, N> in C++26, which throws (or offers try_push_back) when full.

Designing one

  • Storage. alignas(T) unsigned char buf[N * sizeof(T)], never T buf[N], because that would default-construct N elements and require T to be default constructible. Elements are created with placement new and destroyed by hand (Ch 14).
  • Header. A T* begin that points either at the buffer or at a heap block, plus size and capacity. "Am I inline?" is begin == buffer. LLVM uses 32-bit size and capacity to keep the header at 16 bytes.
  • Growth. When full, allocate 2 × cap, construct the new element first (the argument may refer to an element of the vector itself), then move the old elements across with std::move_if_noexcept semantics, destroy them, and free the old block if it was on the heap.
  • Move is O(N) when inline. You cannot steal a buffer that lives inside the source object. Moving an inline small vector moves every element, can throw if T's move can throw, and invalidates pointers into the source. A heap-backed one can steal the pointer as std::vector does.
  • Copy must not copy the pointer. A copied inline small vector must point at its own buffer. Copying begin verbatim is the most common bug in hand-written versions (see the drills).
  • Choosing N. Use profiling data: pick N so that 90 to 99 percent of instances never spill. A huge N bloats every object and every frame that holds one. LLVM's default SmallVector<T> picks N so that the whole object is about 64 bytes.

Interview trap

"Why does std::vector not have SSO like std::string?" Because the standard forbids it. Container move construction must be constant time, and swap must not invalidate iterators, pointers or references to elements ([container.reqmts]). With inline elements both promises break: moving would be O(N) and the elements would change address. std::string is exempt because [string.require] explicitly allows those invalidations.

std::array vs C arrays vs std::vector

PropertyT a[N]std::array<T, N>std::vector<T>
Storageinline (stack or inside the object)inline, same layout as T[N]heap, 24-byte header
Sizecompile timecompile time, size() is constexprrun time
Copy and assignno assignment, decays to T* when passedvalue semantics, comparablevalue semantics, allocates
Return from a functionnot allowedby valueby value (moves)
Zero sizeill-formed (T a[0] is a GCC extension)allowed, sizeof is still at least 1allowed
Overheadnonenone (an aggregate wrapping T[N])allocation, indirection

Prefer std::array over a C array in new code: it does not decay, it knows its size, and it can be copied, compared and returned. Use std::to_array (C++20) to deduce N, and std::span to pass either one to a function without a template.

alloca and variable-length arrays

Theory

alloca(n) moves sp down by n bytes at run time and returns the address. A VLA (int buf[n]; with a run-time n) does the same with array syntax. Both free the memory when the function returns, and both are attractive because a run-time sized scratch buffer costs a subtraction.

Neither is standard C++. VLAs are standard in C99 and optional in C11; in C++ they are a GCC and Clang extension (rejected by MSVC, flagged by -Wvla, and by Clang's -Wvla-cxx-extension). alloca is a non-standard function from <alloca.h> (_alloca on Windows). A proposed std::dynarray was dropped before C++14.

void parse(std::size_t n) {
    char* scratch = static_cast<char*>(alloca(n));   // no failure report: a big n just crashes
    int counts[n];                                    // VLA: GCC/Clang extension in C++
    // ...
}

The dangers:

  • No failure path. alloca cannot return null or throw. Too large a request silently runs past the guard page, which crashes or, without stack probes, corrupts another mapping. An attacker who controls n controls your stack pointer.
  • Lifetime is the function, not the scope. alloca inside a loop allocates again on every iteration and frees nothing until return, so a loop of a million iterations can exhaust the stack.
  • Inlining changes behaviour. If a function that calls alloca is inlined into a loop, the caller's frame grows on every iteration. Compilers refuse to inline such functions in many cases, which is its own cost.
  • VLAs are not ordinary types. sizeof is evaluated at run time, they cannot be members or template arguments, and they cannot be initialised with = {} in older compilers.

The safe pattern gives the speed in the common case and a bound in the bad case: a fixed-size stack buffer for small inputs and the heap for large ones. That is absl::FixedArray, LLVM's SmallString, and the small vector above.

void parse(std::size_t n) {
    std::array<char, 256> local;
    std::unique_ptr<char[]> big;
    char* scratch = n <= local.size() ? local.data() : (big = std::make_unique_for_overwrite<char[]>(n)).get();
    // use scratch[0 .. n)
}

Heap allocation elision and escape analysis

Theory

The rule. Since C++14 (N3664), [expr.new] allows an implementation to omit a call to a replaceable global allocation function made by a new-expression, or to merge several allocations into one. The storage is then "provided by the implementation", which in practice means a register or a stack slot. This holds even if you replaced operator new with a function that has side effects, such as a counter. The permission covers new-expressions only: a direct call such as ::operator new(16) is an ordinary function call and is not elided by the rule.

What compilers do. Clang and GCC (version 10 onwards) run an escape analysis: if the pointer never leaves the function (it is not stored to memory that outlives the call, not passed to an opaque function, not returned) and the new is paired with a delete on every path, the pair is removed and the object becomes a local. Clang applies the same reasoning to library code that uses __builtin_operator_new, which libc++ does, so even temporary std::vectors and std::strings sometimes vanish.

#include <atomic>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <new>

static std::atomic<int> g_allocs{0};   // atomic: see the elision section
void* operator new(std::size_t n) {
    g_allocs.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
    if (void* p = std::malloc(n ? n : 1)) return p;
    throw std::bad_alloc{};
}
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { std::free(p); }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { std::free(p); }

int main() {
    int* p = new int(41);
    *p += 1;
    std::printf("value %d\n", *p);
    delete p;
    std::printf("operator new calls: %d\n", g_allocs.load());
}

Built with -O1, both GCC 16 and Clang 22 print operator new calls: 0: the allocation was folded into a constant. At -O0 they print 1. Both outputs are conforming, which is why the output is not checked.

GCC goes one step further. By default (-fassume-sane-operators-new-delete, added and enabled by default in GCC 15) it assumes that a replaced operator new does not read or modify any other global state of the program. With a plain static int counter, GCC may therefore read the counter before and after a new and fold the difference to zero, even when the allocation really happens. Every counting program in this chapter uses std::atomic<int> for the counter, which GCC cannot reason away; with a plain int, the SSO program above prints 0 allocations for every length under GCC 16.

Interview trap

"My allocation counter says zero, so my code does not allocate." Not necessarily: it only proves that this build, with this inlining, elided it. One more call to a function the optimiser cannot see (logging, a virtual call) and the object escapes, and the allocation comes back. Do not rely on elision for performance; use a type with inline storage when you need a guarantee.

Java's JIT and Go's compiler run this kind of escape analysis on every allocation. C++ compilers do it only for code the optimiser can see (one function after inlining, or across translation units with LTO), and no compiler moves an object that escapes onto the stack. The guarantee you can rely on is the one you write: a local object, a std::array, or an inline buffer.

Stack buffers for pmr, returning and passing

Theory

A pmr arena on a stack buffer

std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource (Ch 17) can start from a buffer you give it. Put that buffer on the stack and every pmr container in the function allocates by bumping a pointer through stack memory, with no delete calls at all: everything is released when the resource goes out of scope.

#include <cstddef>
#include <iostream>
#include <memory_resource>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    alignas(std::max_align_t) std::byte buf[4096];
    std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource arena(buf, sizeof buf, std::pmr::null_memory_resource());

    std::pmr::vector<std::pmr::string> words(&arena);   // the strings inherit the arena
    words.reserve(4);
    for (const char* w : {"stack", "buffers", "are", "fast, until they run out of room"})
        words.emplace_back(w);

    std::size_t total = 0;
    for (const auto& w : words) total += w.size();
    std::cout << words.size() << " words, " << total << " chars, no heap\n";
}
4 words, 47 chars, no heap

Two rules. First, choose the upstream deliberately: the default upstream is new_delete_resource(), so an overflowing buffer silently falls back to the heap. Passing null_memory_resource() makes overflow throw std::bad_alloc instead, which is what you want in a latency-critical path where a hidden heap call is a bug. Second, a monotonic resource never reuses memory, so a growing vector leaves every old block behind. Reserve up front.

Returning large objects

Returning a big object by value does not copy it onto the caller's stack and back. The caller reserves space for the result in its own frame and passes a hidden pointer to it; the callee constructs the result directly there. Since C++17 this is guaranteed for prvalues (return T{...};) and allowed, and usually done, for named locals (NRVO). See Ch 23 and Ch 24. So std::array<double, 512> make() costs no copy, but it does put 4 KB on the caller's stack.

Passing small types by value

Both the System V x86-64 ABI and AAPCS64 pass a trivially copyable struct of up to 16 bytes in two registers. So int, double, a pointer, std::string_view, std::span, std::pair<int, int> and a small Point should be passed by value: a const& forces the caller to put the object in memory, adds an indirection, and makes the optimiser worry that the reference aliases something the function writes.

The catch is "trivially copyable". The Itanium C++ ABI (used by GCC and Clang on Linux and macOS) passes any type with a non-trivial copy constructor, move constructor or destructor by invisible reference: the caller builds a temporary in its own frame and passes its address. That includes std::unique_ptr, so passing a unique_ptr by value costs more than passing a raw pointer, even though both hold one pointer. Large or non-trivial types (strings, vectors) are passed by const& when you only read them, and by value only when you would copy them anyway (the sink pattern, Ch 20).

Concept and tricky questions

Drills

ConceptWhy is allocating a local array faster than new-ing the same array? Give at least three reasons.

Answer

Answer. The stack allocation is a compile-time-sized pointer bump fused with the rest of the frame (one sub sp), it is freed by one add sp with no bookkeeping, it needs no synchronisation because each thread owns its stack, and the memory is almost always hot in L1 cache and already mapped.

Why. new calls operator new, which calls malloc: a size-class lookup, a free-list pop from a thread cache, and on a miss a trip to a shared arena with locks or a system call. delete repeats the lookup. A fresh heap block may also be cold in cache. The common incomplete answer is "the heap is slow because of system calls"; most allocations never make a system call, and the fast path still costs tens of nanoseconds against roughly zero for the stack.

ConceptWhat is the small string optimisation, and how many characters fit inline in libstdc++ and in libc++ on a 64-bit target?

Answer

Answer. SSO stores short strings inside the std::string object instead of on the heap. libstdc++ (GCC): sizeof 32, up to 15 characters inline. libc++ (Clang): sizeof 24, up to 22 characters inline. MSVC: 32 bytes, 15 characters.

Why. libstdc++ keeps a pointer, a size and a 16-byte union that holds either the characters (15 plus the terminating NUL) or the heap capacity. libc++ overlays the whole 24 bytes: one byte holds the size and a mode bit, the other 23 hold up to 22 characters and the NUL. The figures are measured in this chapter with a counting operator new. A common wrong answer is "SSO is required by the standard"; it is permitted, not required, and every number is implementation-defined.

TrickyWhy does std::vector not use a small-buffer optimisation, when std::string does?

Answer

Answer. The standard's container requirements forbid it. Moving a container must be constant time, and swap must not invalidate references, pointers or iterators to elements ([container.reqmts]). Inline elements would have to be moved one by one (O(N)) and would change address.

Why. With a heap buffer, std::vector's move steals the pointer, so an iterator into the source is now an iterator into the destination. Code relies on that, for example keeping pointers into a vector that is then moved into a member. std::string has an explicit exemption in [string.require]: passing a string to a library function that takes a non-const reference may invalidate its iterators. People often answer "because elements may be big"; size is a reason not to choose a large N, but the real blocker is the standard's guarantees. Libraries that want SSO for vectors provide separate types (SmallVector, InlinedVector).

TrickyA std::string_view points into string a. You then write std::string b = std::move(a);. Is the view still valid, and does the answer depend on the string's length?

Answer

Answer. Formally, the view must be treated as invalid. In practice it depends on the length: for a long string the heap buffer moves to b, so the view still points at the text (now owned by b); for a short string the characters were copied into b's own inline buffer and the view still points into a, which is now empty.

Why. [string.require] lets a move invalidate pointers into the source, precisely so that SSO is possible. Code tested only with long strings "works", then breaks for short names. The wrong answer is "moves steal the buffer, so pointers follow". They follow only when there is a heap buffer to steal.

TrickyCan delete new int(5); run without calling operator new at all, even if you replaced operator new with a function that increments a counter?

Answer

Answer. Yes. Since C++14, [expr.new] permits an implementation to omit calls to replaceable global allocation functions from new-expressions, or to merge them, and to provide the storage another way. GCC and Clang both do this at -O1 when the pointer does not escape.

Why. The rule (from paper N3664) exists so that compilers can turn short-lived heap objects into locals. Because the permission is explicit, the side effects inside your replacement function are not "observable behaviour" that must be preserved. The common wrong answer is "a replaced operator new has side effects, so the compiler must call it". Direct calls such as ::operator new(4) are ordinary function calls and are not covered.

ConceptWhat are the default stack sizes on Linux and macOS, for the main thread and for other threads, and how do you give a std::thread a bigger stack?

Answer

Answer. Linux (glibc): main thread 8 MB (the RLIMIT_STACK soft limit, ulimit -s shows 8192), other threads default to the same value read at startup, usually 8 MB. musl uses 128 KB for threads. macOS: 8 MB main, 512 KB for secondary threads. std::thread cannot set a stack size; use pthread_attr_setstacksize with pthread_create or boost::thread::attributes.

Why. The main thread's stack is grown by the kernel on demand up to the rlimit, while each thread stack is one fixed mmap with a guard page. That is why code that recurses happily in main can crash in a worker on macOS or Alpine. The standard library deliberately has no portable stack-size knob. A common wrong answer is "the stack grows until memory runs out"; it is capped by the rlimit and, for threads, by the fixed mapping.

TrickyDoes a stack overflow throw an exception you can catch, such as std::bad_alloc?

Answer

Answer. No. On Linux and macOS the overflowing access hits a guard page and the kernel delivers SIGSEGV (sometimes SIGBUS on macOS). No C++ exception is thrown, no destructors run, and the default action kills the process.

Why. The C++ standard says nothing about stack exhaustion; it is outside the abstract machine. A signal handler cannot run on the stack that just overflowed, so you need sigaltstack plus SA_ONSTACK even to log the crash, and you cannot safely resume. Windows raises a structured exception (EXCEPTION_STACK_OVERFLOW), which is still not a C++ exception. The fix is to bound depth, not to catch.

TrickyIs int n = read(); int buf[n]; valid C++?

Answer

Answer. No. Array bounds in C++ must be constant expressions. Variable-length arrays are a C99 feature (optional since C11) that GCC and Clang accept in C++ as an extension; MSVC rejects them, and -pedantic, -Wvla or Clang's -Wvla-cxx-extension flag them.

Why. VLAs break the type system (their sizeof is a run-time value, they cannot be members or template arguments), they have no failure path when n is too large, and an attacker-controlled n moves your stack pointer. A proposed std::dynarray was dropped. People say "it compiles, so it is legal"; it compiles because of an extension. Use std::array with a bound and a heap fallback, or a small vector.

TrickyMoving a std::vector is O(1) and noexcept. Is moving an llvm::SmallVector<T, 8> or absl::InlinedVector<T, 8> the same?

Answer

Answer. Only when the source has spilled to the heap. When the elements are inline, moving has to move-construct each element into the destination's inline buffer: O(N), and it can throw if T's move constructor can throw.

Why. You cannot transfer ownership of bytes that are physically inside another object. This also means pointers into an inline source are not valid in the destination. As a result, putting small vectors inside a std::vector makes reallocation more expensive, and if the move is not noexcept, std::vector will copy them instead (move_if_noexcept). The wrong answer assumes every move is a pointer steal.

ConceptWhen does std::function allocate, and how would you avoid it on a hot path?

Answer

Answer. It allocates when the callable does not fit its small buffer or does not meet the implementation's conditions for inline storage. Measured here: both libstdc++ and libc++ store up to 16 bytes inline; libstdc++ also needs the callable to be trivially copyable (the __stored_locally test in std_function.h), libc++ needs a nothrow copy constructor. A lambda that captures one 8-byte object with a user-written copy constructor therefore allocates in libstdc++ even though it is small. A lambda capturing a std::string therefore always allocates in libstdc++.

Why. std::function is a type-erased owner that must be copyable, so it either places the callable in its buffer with placement new or holds a pointer to a heap copy. Avoid the allocation by keeping captures small (capture a pointer to a context struct), by using a template parameter instead of type erasure, by using std::function_ref (C++26) for non-owning callbacks, or by writing a fixed-capacity function type that refuses at compile time to hold anything larger (see the coding drills).

ConceptWhat is a red zone, which platforms have one, and why does the Linux kernel disable it?

Answer

Answer. A red zone is a region just below the stack pointer that the ABI guarantees asynchronous code will not overwrite, so leaf functions can use it for locals without adjusting sp. System V x86-64 has 128 bytes, and so does Apple's arm64 ABI. Generic AAPCS64 (Linux on arm64) and Windows x64 have none. The Linux kernel builds with -mno-red-zone because interrupts and exceptions in kernel mode push state onto the current stack and would trash it.

Why. In user space, signal handlers are delivered below the red zone, which is how the ABI keeps its promise. In the kernel there is no such adjustment. The saving is small (one sub and one add in a leaf), which is why some ABIs do without it.

ConceptWhat problem do stack probes and -fstack-clash-protection solve?

Answer

Answer. They stop a large frame, alloca or VLA from moving sp past the guard page in one jump. The compiler touches every page of a big allocation in order, so the guard page is always hit and the program faults safely.

Why. A guard page only works if something touches it. A 64 KB frame on a stack with a 4 KB guard can skip straight over it into the heap or another thread's stack, and later writes corrupt that memory silently (the 2017 "stack clash" exploits). Windows has always done this through __chkstk. The cost is a few instructions per page in functions with large frames. Mentioning the Linux kernel's enlarged stack guard gap (256 pages since 2017) earns extra credit.

TrickyA colleague changes void f(int x) to void f(const int& x) "to avoid a copy". Faster or slower? And is passing std::unique_ptr<T> by value as cheap as passing T*?

Answer

Answer. Slower or equal. An int by value travels in a register; by const& the caller must store it in memory, pass its address, and the callee must load it, and the optimiser must assume the reference may alias memory the function writes. And no: unique_ptr by value is more expensive than a raw pointer under the Itanium ABI.

Why. System V x86-64 and AAPCS64 pass trivially copyable objects of up to 16 bytes in registers, so int, string_view, span and small structs belong by value. A type with a non-trivial destructor or copy/move constructor, such as unique_ptr, is passed by invisible reference: the caller materialises a temporary in its frame and passes its address, and the caller (not the callee) destroys it. "References are always cheaper" is the wrong instinct carried over from large objects.

ConceptWhy is std::array<int, 4> faster than a std::vector<int> holding 4 elements, when indexing either one is the same pointer arithmetic? When does the vector win?

Answer

Answer. The array has no allocation, no deallocation and no indirection, and its size is a compile-time constant. The vector pays a call to operator new on construction and operator delete on destruction (tens of nanoseconds, against nothing), keeps its elements in a separate heap block reached through a pointer, and carries its size at run time. The vector wins when the size is large or unknown (the array would blow the stack or need a worst-case bound) and when you move it: moving a vector steals one pointer, moving an array copies every element.

Why. With std::array the 16 bytes live inside the enclosing object or frame, usually in an L1-hot cache line, and often entirely in registers after optimisation. Because N is in the type, the compiler can fully unroll and vectorise loops over it, and copying is a 16-byte memcpy. A std::vector<std::array<int, 4>> is one contiguous block; a std::vector<std::vector<int>> is one allocation per row and a pointer chase per row. The common wrong answer is "vector::operator[] is slower"; it is not, once the data pointer is loaded. The cost is in creating, destroying and reaching the storage.

ConceptWhy prefer std::array<T, N> over T[N]? Is there any run-time cost?

Answer

Answer. No run-time cost: std::array is an aggregate wrapping T[N] with the same layout. It gains value semantics (copy, assign, compare, return from functions), it never decays to a pointer, and it carries its size in the type (size() is constexpr).

Why. C arrays decay to T* when passed, so sizeof inside the callee gives the pointer size and bounds information is lost; they cannot be assigned or returned. std::array also supports at() with bounds checking, structured bindings, and zero size. Pass it as std::span<const T> to accept arrays of any length. Someone usually claims "std::array adds overhead like vector"; it has no heap, no header and no indirection.

Predict the output and find the bug

Drills

OutputWhat does this print on a 64-bit target?

#include <array>
#include <cstdio>

static void f(int a[10]) { std::printf("%zu\n", sizeof(a)); }

int main() {
    int a[10] = {};
    std::array<int, 10> b{};
    std::printf("%zu %zu\n", sizeof a, sizeof b);
    f(a);
    std::printf("%zu\n", sizeof a / sizeof a[0]);
}
Answer
40 40
8
10

Why. int a[10] and std::array<int, 10> have the same 40-byte layout: std::array is an aggregate around a C array with no extra members. Inside f, the parameter int a[10] is adjusted to int* a ([dcl.fct]), so sizeof gives the pointer size, 8, and the 10 is ignored. Both compilers warn (-Wsizeof-array-argument). The usual wrong answer is 40 for the call. The sizeof a / sizeof a[0] idiom only works where a is still an array; std::size(a) refuses to compile on a pointer, which is why it is safer.

OutputHow many heap allocations does each assignment to std::function make?

#include <atomic>
#include <array>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <functional>
#include <new>

static std::atomic<int> g_allocs{0};   // atomic: see the elision section
void* operator new(std::size_t n) {
    g_allocs.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
    if (void* p = std::malloc(n ? n : 1)) return p;
    throw std::bad_alloc{};
}
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { std::free(p); }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { std::free(p); }

static std::function<int()> g_fn;   // global, so the callable escapes

template <std::size_t N>
static void store() {
    std::array<char, N> capture{};
    int before = g_allocs.load();
    g_fn = [capture] { return int(capture[0]); };
    std::printf("capture of %2zu bytes: %d\n", N, g_allocs.load() - before);
}

int main() {
    store<8>();
    store<16>();
    store<24>();
}
Answer
capture of  8 bytes: 0
capture of 16 bytes: 0
capture of 24 bytes: 1

Why. Both libstdc++ and libc++ have a 32-byte std::function whose small buffer holds a callable of up to 16 bytes. libstdc++ uses a 16-byte buffer next to two function pointers. libc++ uses a 24-byte buffer, but it stores a small object that has its own vtable pointer, which leaves 16 bytes for the lambda. A lambda capturing a std::array<char, N> by value is trivially copyable and nothrow copyable, so only size decides. The global target matters: with a local std::function the optimiser can remove the heap allocation entirely and print 0 for all three, which is legal under [expr.new]. The exact threshold is implementation-defined; MSVC's buffer is larger.

OutputThis uses a GCC/Clang extension. What does it print when run with no arguments?

#include <cstdio>

int main(int argc, char**) {
    int n = argc + 2;
    int v[n];                      // VLA: not standard C++
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) v[i] = i * i;
    std::printf("%zu %d\n", sizeof v, v[n - 1]);
}
Answer
12 4

Why. With no arguments argc is 1, so n is 3. For a VLA, sizeof is evaluated at run time, giving 3 × 4 = 12, and the last element is 2 × 2 = 4. In standard C++ sizeof is always a compile-time constant, which is one reason VLAs do not fit the language. GCC accepts this silently unless you pass -Wvla or -pedantic; Clang warns by default with -Wvla-cxx-extension. MSVC refuses to compile it.

OutputWhich of these std::any assignments allocate?

#include <atomic>
#include <any>
#include <array>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <new>

static std::atomic<int> g_allocs{0};   // atomic: see the elision section
void* operator new(std::size_t n) {
    g_allocs.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
    if (void* p = std::malloc(n ? n : 1)) return p;
    throw std::bad_alloc{};
}
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { std::free(p); }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { std::free(p); }

static std::any g_any;

template <std::size_t N>
static void store() {
    int before = g_allocs.load();
    g_any = std::array<char, N>{};
    std::printf("any holding %2zu bytes: %d allocation(s)\n", N, g_allocs.load() - before);
}

int main() {
    store<8>();
    store<32>();
}
Answer
any holding  8 bytes: 0 allocation(s)
any holding 32 bytes: 1 allocation(s)

Why. std::any keeps small, nothrow-movable objects in an internal buffer. The buffer size is where the libraries differ: libstdc++'s std::any is 16 bytes and stores inline only objects of at most one pointer (8 bytes); libc++'s is 32 bytes and stores up to 24 bytes inline. The program prints only the cases where they agree. A 16-byte object would allocate on libstdc++ and not on libc++. The standard only "encourages" implementations to avoid allocation for small objects such as int ([any.class]).

Find the bugThis passes every test with long names and fails for short ones. Why?

#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Registry {
    std::vector<std::string> names;
    std::vector<std::string_view> index;
    void add(std::string name) {
        index.push_back(name);              // view into the parameter
        names.push_back(std::move(name));   // ...which is then moved from
    }
};

int main() {
    Registry r;
    r.names.reserve(8);
    r.add("a-rather-long-name-that-lives-on-the-heap");
    r.add("bob");
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < r.index.size(); ++i)
        std::cout << "view " << i << (r.index[i] == r.names[i] ? " ok\n" : " broken\n");
}
Answer

Answer. The view is taken from name before it is moved. For the long name, the move transfers the heap buffer into the vector, so the view happens to point at live text owned by names.back(). For "bob", SSO copies the three characters into the vector element's inline buffer; the view still points into the parameter name, which is moved-from and then destroyed when add returns. Reading it is undefined behaviour. On the test machine the Clang build printed view 1 broken, while the GCC build printed ok because the dead parameter's bytes had not been overwritten yet: the worst kind of bug, one that passes tests.

Fix. Take the view from the stored string: names.push_back(std::move(name)); index.push_back(names.back());, and make sure names never reallocates (reserve, or use std::deque), or store indices instead of views. The lesson: a move does not promise that pointers into the source follow the data, and with SSO they visibly do not.

Find the bugA tiny inline-buffer name type. What is wrong, and which tool catches it?

#include <cstdio>
#include <cstring>

struct Name {
    char buf[16];
    char* data;   // points at buf
    explicit Name(const char* s) : data(buf) {
        std::strncpy(buf, s, sizeof buf - 1);
        buf[sizeof buf - 1] = '\0';
    }
};

int main() {
    Name kept("placeholder");
    {
        Name temp("alice");
        kept = temp;               // implicit copy assignment
    }
    std::puts(std::strcmp(kept.data, "alice") == 0 ? "alice" : "corrupted");
}
Answer

Answer. The implicit copy assignment copies data verbatim, so kept.data points into temp.buf. When the inner scope ends, temp is gone and the strcmp reads dead stack memory. AddressSanitizer reports stack-use-after-scope.

Why. Any type with inline storage and a pointer to it is self-referential, so the compiler-generated copy and move operations are wrong for it (rule of three/five, Ch 1). Fix it by writing copy operations that set data = buf and copy the characters, or better, by not storing the pointer at all: compute it (const char* c_str() const { return buf; }). This is exactly the bug libstdc++'s std::string has to avoid in its move constructor, and the classic bug in hand-written small vectors.

Find the bugWhy does this crash with GCC, while the Clang build seems to work?

#include <cstdio>

static const char* greeting(int id) {
    char buf[32];
    std::snprintf(buf, sizeof buf, "hello %d", id);
    return buf;
}

int main() {
    const char* g = greeting(7);
    std::printf("%c\n", g[0]);
}
Answer

Answer. buf lives in greeting's frame, which is released by the epilogue's add sp. The returned pointer dangles, and the next call (printf) reuses that stack. Both compilers warn (-Wreturn-local-addr in GCC, -Wreturn-stack-address in Clang). GCC goes further: because the result is undefined anyway, it returns a null pointer, so g[0] crashes immediately. Clang returns the stale address; on the test machine it even printed the expected h, because nothing had overwritten the dead frame yet. Both behaviours are allowed, since the program has undefined behaviour.

Fix. Return a value: std::string (likely within SSO, so no allocation), or std::array<char, 32>, which is returned in place by copy elision. Stack memory never outlives its function; the same applies to alloca.

Find the bugThis builds a list of a million nodes and crashes when it is destroyed. Why, given that there is no recursion in the source?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>

struct Node {
    int value;
    std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
};

int main() {
    std::unique_ptr<Node> head;
    for (int i = 0; i < 1'000'000; ++i)
        head = std::make_unique<Node>(Node{i, std::move(head)});
    std::puts("built");
    head.reset();
    std::puts("destroyed");
}
Answer

Answer. The recursion is in the generated destructors. Destroying node 0 destroys its member next, whose deleter destroys node 1, and so on: one or more stack frames per node, a million deep. That exceeds the 8 MB main-thread stack, and the process dies with SIGSEGV; ASan reports stack-overflow in ~unique_ptr. It is not a tail call, because operator delete runs after the destructor returns.

Fix. Give the list an iterative destructor that detaches each node before it dies:

~List() {
    while (head) head = std::move(head->next);   // old head is destroyed with next already null
}

The same issue hits trees built from unique_ptr children, recursive JSON values and deep expression trees. Interviewers like it because the source contains no recursive call.

Find the bugWhy does this not compile, and what is the smallest fix?

#include <cstdio>

static int (make())[3] {
    int r[3] = {1, 2, 3};
    return r;
}

int main() {
    int a[3] = {1, 2, 3};
    int b[3];
    b = a;
    std::printf("%d\n", b[2]);
}
Answer

Answer. Two errors. A function cannot return an array type ([dcl.fct]), and arrays are not assignable: in b = a the left side is an array lvalue, which is not modifiable, and the right side decays to int*.

Fix. Use std::array<int, 3>: it is an aggregate class, so the implicit copy assignment copies all three elements, and it can be returned by value (constructed in the caller's frame by copy elision). C arrays inside a struct are copied with the struct, which is the only reason std::array works at all: it is a struct with an array member.

Find the bugThe author wanted parsing to stay off the heap entirely. Does it?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory_resource>
#include <vector>

// Counts what reaches the default resource, standing in for "the heap".
struct CountingResource : std::pmr::memory_resource {
    int calls = 0;
    void* do_allocate(std::size_t n, std::size_t a) override {
        ++calls;
        return std::pmr::new_delete_resource()->allocate(n, a);
    }
    void do_deallocate(void* p, std::size_t n, std::size_t a) override {
        std::pmr::new_delete_resource()->deallocate(p, n, a);
    }
    bool do_is_equal(const memory_resource& o) const noexcept override { return this == &o; }
};

static std::size_t parse(int n) {
    alignas(std::max_align_t) std::byte buf[256];
    std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource arena(buf, sizeof buf);
    std::pmr::vector<int> tokens(&arena);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) tokens.push_back(i);
    return tokens.size();
}

int main() {
    CountingResource heap;
    std::pmr::set_default_resource(&heap);
    std::size_t n = parse(100);
    std::printf("tokens %zu, heap used: %s\n", n, heap.calls > 0 ? "yes" : "no");
    std::pmr::set_default_resource(nullptr);
}
Answer
tokens 100, heap used: yes

Answer. No. 100 ints need a 512-byte block at the last growth, and the earlier blocks (4 + 8 + ... + 256 bytes) are never reused, so the 256-byte buffer runs out early. The resource then asks its upstream. The constructor without an upstream argument uses get_default_resource(), which is normally new_delete_resource() and calls operator new. The program installs a counting default resource to make that visible. (Counting with a replaced global operator new is not reliable for this one: on macOS, GCC's libstdc++ dylib calls its own operator new internally.)

Fix. Decide what overflow should mean. If the heap is forbidden, pass std::pmr::null_memory_resource() as the upstream so overflow throws bad_alloc and tests catch it. Either way, call tokens.reserve(n) so the monotonic arena is not wasted on abandoned blocks, and size the buffer from measurements.

Coding

CodeImplement SmallVector<T, N>: a vector that stores up to N elements inside the object and spills to the heap beyond that. Support push_back (copy and move), emplace_back, pop_back, operator[], size, capacity, iteration, is_inline(), and correct copy, move and destruction. T need not be default constructible. v.push_back(v[0]) must work even when it triggers growth.

Answer

Approach. Keep raw, aligned storage for N elements (alignas(T) unsigned char[N * sizeof(T)]) and a T* that points either at it or at a heap block. Construct elements with placement new and destroy them with std::destroy. On growth, allocate double the capacity, construct the new element in the new block first (so an argument that refers to an existing element is still alive), then move the old elements across and free the old block if it was on the heap. Moving steals the pointer only when the source is on the heap; an inline source must have its elements moved one by one.

#include <cstddef>
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <new>
#include <string>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>

template <class T, std::size_t N>
class SmallVector {
    static_assert(N > 0, "use std::vector when N == 0");
    static_assert(alignof(T) <= __STDCPP_DEFAULT_NEW_ALIGNMENT__, "over-aligned T needs aligned new");

    alignas(T) unsigned char buf_[N * sizeof(T)];
    T* data_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    std::size_t cap_ = N;

    T* inline_data() { return reinterpret_cast<T*>(buf_); }
    void release_heap() {
        if (!is_inline()) ::operator delete(data_);
        data_ = inline_data();
        cap_ = N;
    }
    void steal(SmallVector& o) {
        if (o.is_inline()) {   // elements live inside o: move them one by one
            std::uninitialized_move(o.data_, o.data_ + o.size_, data_);
            size_ = o.size_;
            o.clear();
        } else {               // heap block: take the pointer
            data_ = o.data_; size_ = o.size_; cap_ = o.cap_;
            o.data_ = o.inline_data(); o.size_ = 0; o.cap_ = N;
        }
    }

public:
    SmallVector() : data_(inline_data()) {}
    SmallVector(const SmallVector& o) : SmallVector() {
        reserve(o.size_);
        std::uninitialized_copy(o.data_, o.data_ + o.size_, data_);
        size_ = o.size_;
    }
    SmallVector(SmallVector&& o) noexcept(std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<T>) : SmallVector() { steal(o); }
    SmallVector& operator=(const SmallVector& o) {
        if (this != &o) {
            clear();
            reserve(o.size_);
            std::uninitialized_copy(o.data_, o.data_ + o.size_, data_);
            size_ = o.size_;
        }
        return *this;
    }
    SmallVector& operator=(SmallVector&& o) noexcept(std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<T>) {
        if (this != &o) { clear(); release_heap(); steal(o); }
        return *this;
    }
    ~SmallVector() { clear(); release_heap(); }

    bool is_inline() const { return static_cast<const void*>(data_) == static_cast<const void*>(buf_); }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::size_t capacity() const { return cap_; }
    T& operator[](std::size_t i) { return data_[i]; }
    const T& operator[](std::size_t i) const { return data_[i]; }
    T* begin() { return data_; }
    T* end() { return data_ + size_; }
    const T* begin() const { return data_; }
    const T* end() const { return data_ + size_; }

    void clear() { std::destroy(data_, data_ + size_); size_ = 0; }
    void pop_back() { std::destroy_at(data_ + --size_); }

    void reserve(std::size_t n) {
        if (n <= cap_) return;
        T* nd = static_cast<T*>(::operator new(n * sizeof(T)));
        std::uninitialized_move(data_, data_ + size_, nd);   // assumes T's move does not throw
        std::destroy(data_, data_ + size_);
        if (!is_inline()) ::operator delete(data_);
        data_ = nd;
        cap_ = n;
    }

    template <class... A>
    T& emplace_back(A&&... args) {
        if (size_ < cap_) {
            T* p = ::new (static_cast<void*>(data_ + size_)) T(std::forward<A>(args)...);
            ++size_;
            return *p;
        }
        std::size_t ncap = cap_ * 2;
        T* nd = static_cast<T*>(::operator new(ncap * sizeof(T)));
        T* p;
        try {   // build the new element first: args may refer to an element of *this
            p = ::new (static_cast<void*>(nd + size_)) T(std::forward<A>(args)...);
        } catch (...) {
            ::operator delete(nd);
            throw;
        }
        std::uninitialized_move(data_, data_ + size_, nd);
        std::destroy(data_, data_ + size_);
        if (!is_inline()) ::operator delete(data_);
        data_ = nd;
        cap_ = ncap;
        ++size_;
        return *p;
    }
    void push_back(const T& v) { emplace_back(v); }
    void push_back(T&& v) { emplace_back(std::move(v)); }
};

template <class V>
static void show(const char* label, const V& v) {
    std::cout << label << ':';
    for (const auto& x : v) std::cout << ' ' << x;
    std::cout << " (size " << v.size() << ", " << (v.is_inline() ? "inline" : "heap") << ")\n";
}

int main() {
    SmallVector<std::string, 2> v;
    v.push_back("a");
    v.push_back("b");
    show("two", v);
    v.push_back("c");
    v.push_back(v[0]);   // aliasing an element during growth
    show("four", v);

    SmallVector<std::string, 2> copy = v;
    show("copy", copy);
    SmallVector<std::string, 2> moved = std::move(v);
    show("moved", moved);
    std::cout << "source after move: size " << v.size() << '\n';

    SmallVector<std::string, 2> s1;
    s1.push_back("x");
    SmallVector<std::string, 2> s2 = std::move(s1);
    show("small move", s2);
    s2 = copy;
    s2.pop_back();
    show("assigned", s2);
}
two: a b (size 2, inline)
four: a b c a (size 4, heap)
copy: a b c a (size 4, heap)
moved: a b c a (size 4, heap)
source after move: size 0
small move: x (size 1, inline)
assigned: a b c (size 3, heap)

Complexity and pitfalls. Amortised O(1) push_back; move is O(1) for a heap-backed source and O(size) for an inline one. Pitfalls: copying data_ verbatim in the copy constructor (the copy would point into the source's buffer), declaring T buf[N] (constructs N elements), forgetting to reset a moved-from heap source to its own inline buffer, and growing before constructing the new element, which makes v.push_back(v[0]) read a destroyed object. A production version also uses std::move_if_noexcept during growth for the strong guarantee, supports over-aligned T with std::align_val_t, and adds insert, erase and resize.

Estimated rating: ~1900 · manual lifetimes, aliasing during growth and two different move paths

CodeWrite a string class with a small string optimisation in the libstdc++ style: a pointer, a size, and a 16-byte union holding either up to 15 characters plus NUL or the heap capacity. Provide construction from const char*, copy and move (constructor and assignment), append (which must work when the argument points into the string itself), c_str, size, capacity and is_small.

Answer

Approach. The pointer always points at the characters, so c_str() needs no branch; "small" means ptr_ == local_. The move constructor is where SSO bites: for a small source you must copy the characters and point at your own buffer, never copy o.ptr_. For a heap source you steal the pointer and reset the source to its empty inline state. append grows geometrically and copies the new characters into the new block before freeing the old one, because the argument may live in the old block.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstring>
#include <iostream>
#include <utility>

class SsoString {
    static constexpr std::size_t kInline = 15;   // plus the NUL
    char* ptr_;                 // points at local_ or at a heap block
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    union {
        char local_[kInline + 1];
        std::size_t cap_;       // heap capacity, valid only when !is_small()
    };

    void init(const char* s, std::size_t n) {
        if (n <= kInline) {
            ptr_ = local_;
        } else {
            ptr_ = new char[n + 1];
            cap_ = n;
        }
        std::memcpy(ptr_, s, n);
        ptr_[n] = '\0';
        size_ = n;
    }

    void take(SsoString& o) noexcept {
        size_ = o.size_;
        if (o.is_small()) {
            ptr_ = local_;                              // never copy o.ptr_ here
            std::memcpy(local_, o.local_, o.size_ + 1);
        } else {
            ptr_ = o.ptr_;
            cap_ = o.cap_;
            o.ptr_ = o.local_;
        }
        o.size_ = 0;
        o.local_[0] = '\0';
    }

public:
    SsoString() : ptr_(local_) { local_[0] = '\0'; }
    SsoString(const char* s) { init(s, std::strlen(s)); }
    SsoString(const SsoString& o) { init(o.ptr_, o.size_); }
    SsoString(SsoString&& o) noexcept { take(o); }
    SsoString& operator=(SsoString&& o) noexcept {
        if (this != &o) {
            if (!is_small()) delete[] ptr_;
            take(o);
        }
        return *this;
    }
    SsoString& operator=(const SsoString& o) {
        if (this != &o) *this = SsoString(o);   // copy, then move-assign
        return *this;
    }
    ~SsoString() { if (!is_small()) delete[] ptr_; }

    bool is_small() const { return ptr_ == local_; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::size_t capacity() const { return is_small() ? kInline : cap_; }
    const char* c_str() const { return ptr_; }

    void append(const char* s, std::size_t n) {
        std::size_t need = size_ + n;
        if (need > capacity()) {
            std::size_t ncap = need > 2 * capacity() ? need : 2 * capacity();
            char* p = new char[ncap + 1];
            std::memcpy(p, ptr_, size_);
            std::memcpy(p + size_, s, n);   // s may point into the old buffer: copy before freeing
            if (!is_small()) delete[] ptr_;
            ptr_ = p;
            cap_ = ncap;                    // overwrites local_, which is no longer in use
        } else {
            std::memmove(ptr_ + size_, s, n);
        }
        size_ = need;
        ptr_[size_] = '\0';
    }
    SsoString& operator+=(const char* s) { append(s, std::strlen(s)); return *this; }
};

static void show(const SsoString& s) {
    std::cout << '"' << s.c_str() << "\" size " << s.size() << " cap " << s.capacity()
              << (s.is_small() ? " inline\n" : " heap\n");
}

int main() {
    SsoString a = "hello";
    show(a);
    a += ", world!!!";       // 15 chars: still inline
    show(a);
    a += " and more";        // spills to the heap
    show(a);

    SsoString small = "tiny";
    SsoString moved = std::move(small);
    show(moved);
    show(small);

    SsoString big = moved;
    big = a;                 // copy assignment
    show(big);
    a.append(a.c_str(), a.size());   // self-append that reallocates
    show(a);
}
"hello" size 5 cap 15 inline
"hello, world!!!" size 15 cap 15 inline
"hello, world!!! and more" size 24 cap 30 heap
"tiny" size 4 cap 15 inline
"" size 0 cap 15 inline
"hello, world!!! and more" size 24 cap 24 heap
"hello, world!!! and morehello, world!!! and more" size 48 cap 60 heap

Complexity and pitfalls. Amortised O(1) per appended character, O(n) copy, O(1) move (copying at most 16 bytes). Pitfalls: copying the self-pointer in a move or copy (the dangling-buffer bug from the reading drills), freeing the old buffer before copying a self-referencing argument, reading cap_ while the union holds characters (only read it when !is_small()), and forgetting the NUL. The copy assignment reuses the move assignment through a temporary, which gives the strong exception guarantee.
