CodeImplement InplaceFunction<R(Args...), Cap>: a move-only, type-erased callable that never allocates. A callable that is larger than Cap, over-aligned, or not nothrow movable must be rejected at compile time. Calling an empty one throws std::bad_function_call. It must accept move-only lambdas.

Answer

Approach. Store the callable in an aligned byte buffer with placement new, and keep a pointer to a static table of three function pointers (invoke, move, destroy) instantiated once per callable type. That table is a hand-written vtable, so the object is Cap + 8 bytes with no heap and no virtual functions. All checks are static_asserts in the converting constructor, so an oversized capture is a compile error rather than a hidden allocation. Being move-only removes the need for a copy operation, which is what makes move-only captures possible (the same reason std::move_only_function exists in C++23).

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <functional>
#include <memory>
#include <new>
#include <string>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>

template <class Sig, std::size_t Cap = 32>
class InplaceFunction;

template <class R, class... Args, std::size_t Cap>
class InplaceFunction<R(Args...), Cap> {
    struct Ops {
        R (*invoke)(void*, Args&&...);
        void (*move)(void* dst, void* src) noexcept;   // move-construct into dst, destroy src
        void (*destroy)(void*) noexcept;
    };
    template <class F>
    static constexpr Ops ops_for{
        [](void* p, Args&&... a) -> R { return (*static_cast<F*>(p))(std::forward<Args>(a)...); },
        [](void* dst, void* src) noexcept {
            ::new (dst) F(std::move(*static_cast<F*>(src)));
            static_cast<F*>(src)->~F();
        },
        [](void* p) noexcept { static_cast<F*>(p)->~F(); },
    };

    alignas(std::max_align_t) unsigned char buf_[Cap];
    const Ops* ops_ = nullptr;

public:
    InplaceFunction() = default;

    template <class F, class D = std::decay_t<F>,
              class = std::enable_if_t<!std::is_same_v<D, InplaceFunction>>>
    InplaceFunction(F&& f) {
        static_assert(sizeof(D) <= Cap, "callable too large for InplaceFunction");
        static_assert(alignof(D) <= alignof(std::max_align_t), "callable over-aligned");
        static_assert(std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<D>, "callable must be nothrow movable");
        static_assert(std::is_invocable_r_v<R, D&, Args...>, "wrong signature");
        ::new (static_cast<void*>(buf_)) D(std::forward<F>(f));
        ops_ = &ops_for<D>;
    }
    InplaceFunction(InplaceFunction&& o) noexcept : ops_(o.ops_) {
        if (ops_) { ops_->move(buf_, o.buf_); o.ops_ = nullptr; }
    }
    InplaceFunction& operator=(InplaceFunction&& o) noexcept {
        if (this != &o) {
            reset();
            if (o.ops_) { o.ops_->move(buf_, o.buf_); ops_ = o.ops_; o.ops_ = nullptr; }
        }
        return *this;
    }
    InplaceFunction(const InplaceFunction&) = delete;
    InplaceFunction& operator=(const InplaceFunction&) = delete;
    ~InplaceFunction() { reset(); }

    void reset() noexcept {
        if (ops_) { ops_->destroy(buf_); ops_ = nullptr; }
    }
    explicit operator bool() const noexcept { return ops_ != nullptr; }
    R operator()(Args... a) {
        if (!ops_) throw std::bad_function_call();
        return ops_->invoke(buf_, std::forward<Args>(a)...);
    }
};

int main() {
    int base = 10;
    InplaceFunction<int(int)> add = [base](int x) { return base + x; };
    std::printf("add(5) = %d\n", add(5));

    auto owner = std::make_unique<std::string>("owned by the lambda");
    InplaceFunction<std::size_t()> len = [p = std::move(owner)] { return p->size(); };   // move-only capture
    InplaceFunction<std::size_t()> len2 = std::move(len);
    std::printf("len2() = %zu, len empty: %s\n", len2(), len ? "no" : "yes");

    InplaceFunction<void(), 64> hello = [s = std::string("captured string")] { std::printf("%s\n", s.c_str()); };
    hello();
    hello = [] { std::puts("reassigned"); };
    hello();

    InplaceFunction<int(int)> empty;
    try { empty(1); } catch (const std::bad_function_call&) { std::puts("empty call throws"); }
    // InplaceFunction<void(), 8> tooBig = [s = std::string()] {};   // static_assert fires
}
add(5) = 15
len2() = 19, len empty: yes
captured string
reassigned
empty call throws

Complexity and pitfalls. One indirect call per invocation, like std::function. Pitfalls: the converting constructor template hijacking the move constructor (excluded with the is_same constraint), forgetting to destroy the source after moving it (the move op does both), and forgetting reset() before move-assigning into a non-empty object. Inline-only wrappers like this are common in trading systems, where a hidden allocation on the order path is a latency bug.

CodeWrite StackFirstResource<N>, a std::pmr::memory_resource that serves allocations from an N-byte buffer inside the object (so it is on the stack when the resource is a local), falls back to an upstream resource when the buffer cannot satisfy a request, counts fallbacks, and reclaims space when the most recently allocated block is freed (LIFO).

Answer

Approach. Override the three virtuals. do_allocate rounds the bump offset up to the requested alignment (always a power of two in pmr) and returns the next slice if it fits, otherwise counts a fallback and forwards to the upstream. do_deallocate forwards pointers it does not own; for its own blocks it rolls the offset back only if the block is the last one handed out, which makes stack-like usage (scoped containers) reuse the buffer. Identity is the only meaningful equality.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory_resource>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

template <std::size_t N>
class StackFirstResource : public std::pmr::memory_resource {
    alignas(std::max_align_t) std::byte buf_[N];
    std::size_t used_ = 0;
    std::pmr::memory_resource* upstream_;
    int fallbacks_ = 0;

    bool owns(const void* p) const {
        auto a = reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t>(p), b = reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t>(buf_);
        return a >= b && a < b + N;
    }
    void* do_allocate(std::size_t bytes, std::size_t align) override {
        std::size_t start = (used_ + align - 1) & ~(align - 1);   // align is a power of two
        if (align <= alignof(std::max_align_t) && start <= N && bytes <= N - start) {
            used_ = start + bytes;
            return buf_ + start;
        }
        ++fallbacks_;
        return upstream_->allocate(bytes, align);
    }
    void do_deallocate(void* p, std::size_t bytes, std::size_t align) override {
        if (!owns(p)) { upstream_->deallocate(p, bytes, align); return; }
        if (static_cast<std::byte*>(p) + bytes == buf_ + used_)   // most recent block: roll back
            used_ = static_cast<std::size_t>(static_cast<std::byte*>(p) - buf_);
    }
    bool do_is_equal(const std::pmr::memory_resource& o) const noexcept override { return this == &o; }

public:
    explicit StackFirstResource(std::pmr::memory_resource* up = std::pmr::new_delete_resource()) : upstream_(up) {}
    StackFirstResource(const StackFirstResource&) = delete;
    StackFirstResource& operator=(const StackFirstResource&) = delete;
    std::size_t used() const { return used_; }
    int fallbacks() const { return fallbacks_; }
};

int main() {
    StackFirstResource<1024> res;
    {
        std::pmr::vector<int> v(&res);
        v.reserve(64);                       // 256 bytes from the buffer
        for (int i = 0; i < 64; ++i) v.push_back(i);
        std::printf("after 64 ints: used %zu, fallbacks %d\n", res.used(), res.fallbacks());
    }
    std::printf("after vector freed: used %zu\n", res.used());   // LIFO free rolled back

    std::pmr::vector<std::pmr::string> words(&res);
    words.reserve(3);
    words.emplace_back("a long string that does not fit in the SSO buffer");
    words.emplace_back("short");
    std::printf("strings: fallbacks %d\n", res.fallbacks());

    std::pmr::vector<char> big(&res);
    big.resize(2000);                        // larger than the whole buffer: goes upstream
    std::printf("big: fallbacks %d, size %zu\n", res.fallbacks(), big.size());
}
after 64 ints: used 256, fallbacks 0
after vector freed: used 0
strings: fallbacks 0
big: fallbacks 1, size 2000

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) allocate and deallocate. Pitfalls: alignment rounding that overflows (check bytes <= N - start rather than start + bytes <= N), forwarding a buffer pointer to the upstream (instant heap corruption), copying the resource (containers hold a pointer to it, so it must be non-copyable and outlive them), and expecting non-LIFO frees to reclaim space. Compared with monotonic_buffer_resource, this adds LIFO reuse and makes fallbacks observable, which is useful in tests that assert "no heap on the hot path".

CodeA singly linked list built from std::unique_ptr<Node> and a binary tree with unique_ptr children both crash with a stack overflow on deep inputs (a million nodes), in their destructors and in a recursive max_depth. Rewrite them so that no operation uses stack space proportional to the input, and prove it on a thread with a 512 KB stack.

Answer

Approach. For the list, destroy nodes in a loop, detaching each node's next before the node dies: head_ = std::move(head_->next) releases the successor into head_ first and then deletes the old head, whose next is already null. For the tree, replace recursion with an explicit stack held in a std::vector (heap memory that grows as needed): push children with their depth for max_depth, and for destruction move each node's children onto the stack before the node goes out of scope.

#include <algorithm>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class List {
    struct Node {
        int value;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
    };
    std::unique_ptr<Node> head_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;

public:
    List() = default;
    List(List&&) noexcept = default;
    List& operator=(List&& o) noexcept {
        clear();
        head_ = std::move(o.head_);
        size_ = std::exchange(o.size_, 0);
        return *this;
    }
    ~List() { clear(); }
    void clear() {
        while (head_) head_ = std::move(head_->next);   // each node dies with next == nullptr
        size_ = 0;
    }
    void push_front(int v) {
        head_ = std::make_unique<Node>(Node{v, std::move(head_)});
        ++size_;
    }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
};

struct TreeNode {
    int value = 0;
    std::unique_ptr<TreeNode> left, right;
};

static std::size_t max_depth(const TreeNode* root) {
    std::vector<std::pair<const TreeNode*, std::size_t>> stack;   // heap, grows as needed
    if (root) stack.push_back({root, 1});
    std::size_t best = 0;
    while (!stack.empty()) {
        auto [n, d] = stack.back();
        stack.pop_back();
        best = std::max(best, d);
        if (n->left) stack.push_back({n->left.get(), d + 1});
        if (n->right) stack.push_back({n->right.get(), d + 1});
    }
    return best;
}

static void destroy_tree(std::unique_ptr<TreeNode> root) {
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<TreeNode>> stack;
    if (root) stack.push_back(std::move(root));
    while (!stack.empty()) {
        std::unique_ptr<TreeNode> n = std::move(stack.back());
        stack.pop_back();
        if (n->left) stack.push_back(std::move(n->left));
        if (n->right) stack.push_back(std::move(n->right));
    }   // n is destroyed here with both children already detached
}

static void* work(void*) {
    List list;
    for (int i = 0; i < 1'000'000; ++i) list.push_front(i);
    std::printf("list size %zu\n", list.size());
    list.clear();
    std::printf("list cleared\n");

    auto root = std::make_unique<TreeNode>();
    TreeNode* cur = root.get();
    for (int i = 0; i < 999'999; ++i) {           // degenerate tree: a left spine
        cur->left = std::make_unique<TreeNode>();
        cur = cur->left.get();
    }
    cur->right = std::make_unique<TreeNode>();
    std::printf("depth %zu\n", max_depth(root.get()));
    destroy_tree(std::move(root));
    std::printf("tree destroyed\n");
    return nullptr;
}

int main() {
    // std::thread cannot set a stack size, so use pthreads: 512 KB on every platform.
    pthread_attr_t attr;
    pthread_attr_init(&attr);
    pthread_attr_setstacksize(&attr, 512 * 1024);
    pthread_t t;
    if (pthread_create(&t, &attr, work, nullptr) != 0) return 1;
    pthread_join(t, nullptr);
    pthread_attr_destroy(&attr);
}
list size 1000000
list cleared
depth 1000001
tree destroyed

Complexity and pitfalls. O(n) time for everything; O(1) extra space for the list and O(height) heap space (not stack) for the tree. Pitfalls: writing head_.reset(head_->next.release()) in the wrong order and leaking, forgetting that the defaulted move assignment would destroy the old list recursively (hence the custom one), and forgetting that the tree's own ~TreeNode is still recursive if a node is destroyed while it still owns children. Tail recursion does not save you: destructors run before operator delete, so the recursive call is not in tail position.

Estimated rating: ~1400 · standard recursion-to-iteration, with the destructor twist

CodeWrite a FixedString<N> that holds a string literal by value with no heap, can be used as a C++20 class-type template argument (Counter<"cache.miss">), compares equal across lengths, and supports compile-time concatenation.

Answer

Approach. A C++20 non-type template parameter may be a structural class type: a literal type whose bases and non-static members are all public and non-mutable. So the class is a public char data[N] plus a constexpr constructor from const char (&)[N], which lets class template argument deduction pick N from the literal (including the NUL). Each distinct literal makes a distinct Counter type with its own static. Concatenation is a constexpr function that computes the new size from the arguments' sizes.

#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <string_view>

template <std::size_t N>
struct FixedString {
    char data[N] {};                                 // includes the terminating NUL
    constexpr FixedString(const char (&s)[N]) { std::copy_n(s, N, data); }
    constexpr std::size_t size() const { return N - 1; }
    constexpr std::string_view view() const { return {data, N - 1}; }
    constexpr const char* c_str() const { return data; }
    template <std::size_t M>
    constexpr bool operator==(const FixedString<M>& o) const { return view() == o.view(); }
};

// C++20: a literal class type with public members can be a template argument.
template <FixedString Name>
struct Counter {
    static inline int hits = 0;
    static void hit() { ++hits; }
    static constexpr std::string_view name() { return Name.view(); }
};

template <FixedString A, FixedString B>
constexpr auto concat() {
    constexpr std::size_t n = A.size() + B.size() + 1;
    char buf[n] {};
    std::copy_n(A.data, A.size(), buf);
    std::copy_n(B.data, B.size() + 1, buf + A.size());
    return FixedString<n>(buf);
}

int main() {
    Counter<"cache.miss">::hit();
    Counter<"cache.miss">::hit();
    Counter<"cache.hit">::hit();
    std::printf("%s = %d\n", Counter<"cache.miss">::name().data(), Counter<"cache.miss">::hits);
    std::printf("%s = %d\n", Counter<"cache.hit">::name().data(), Counter<"cache.hit">::hits);

    constexpr auto full = concat<"order.", "filled">();
    static_assert(full.size() == 12 && full == FixedString("order.filled"));
    std::printf("%s (%zu chars, sizeof %zu)\n", full.c_str(), full.size(), sizeof full);
}
cache.miss = 2
cache.hit = 1
order.filled (12 chars, sizeof 13)

Complexity and pitfalls. Everything happens at compile time; at run time the object is exactly N bytes. Pitfalls: making data private (the type stops being structural and the template argument is rejected), forgetting that N counts the NUL, and comparing raw arrays with == (compares addresses, and is deprecated in C++20). This is the building block of compile-time format strings and string-keyed metrics registries.

Estimated rating: ~1600 · C++20 structural types and CTAD from array references

Cheat sheet

Theory
  • Stack allocation is one sub sp per frame and free on return; new is a function call into a size-class allocator, tens of nanoseconds on the fast path.
  • Stack sizes: Linux main 8 MB (ulimit -s), glibc threads the same by default, musl threads 128 KB, macOS threads 512 KB, Windows 1 MB. Overflow is SIGSEGV on the guard page, never an exception. std::thread cannot set the size.
  • SSO: libstdc++ 32 bytes and 15 chars, libc++ 24 bytes and 22 chars, MSVC 32 and 15. Moving a short string copies; views into a short string do not follow a move.
  • SBO: std::function keeps callables of up to 16 bytes inline on both libraries (libstdc++ also needs trivially copyable); std::any 8 bytes (libstdc++) or 24 (libc++). Count allocations with an escaping object and an atomic counter.
  • Small vectors (SmallVector, InlinedVector, C++26 inplace_vector): raw aligned storage, placement new, O(N) move when inline. std::vector cannot do SSO because moves and swaps must not invalidate element pointers.
  • alloca and VLAs are non-standard in C++, have no failure path and live until the function returns. Use a fixed stack buffer with a heap fallback instead.
  • [expr.new] lets compilers elide or merge new-expressions even with a replaced operator new; GCC and Clang do it at -O1 for non-escaping pointers. Never rely on it.
  • Pass by value trivially copyable types up to 16 bytes (int, string_view, span); non-trivial types such as unique_ptr go by invisible reference under the Itanium ABI. Return large objects by value: elision builds them in the caller's frame.

Part E · Memory management · Chapter 19

Cache-friendly allocation

A cache miss to DRAM costs as much as hundreds of simple instructions, so where your objects live in memory often matters more than how many instructions touch them. This chapter covers the memory hierarchy, cache lines, locality, data layout (AoS vs SoA, padding, hot/cold splitting), false sharing, prefetching and the allocation patterns that keep related data together, with benchmarks measured on an Apple M1. Low-latency and systems interviews ask about it because it is where "big-O equal" designs differ by 10x or more.

TheoryDrillsCoding· about 5 hours· prerequisites: Ch 10, Ch 15, Ch 17, Ch 18

The memory hierarchy and latency numbers

Theory

Mental model. The CPU can only work on data in registers. Everything else is a ladder of caches, each larger and slower than the one above: L1 (per core, tens of KB), L2 (per core or per cluster, hundreds of KB to a few MB), often a shared L3 or system-level cache (several MB to tens of MB), then DRAM (GB). A load that hits L1 completes in a few cycles. A load that has to go to DRAM stalls for hundreds of cycles, and if the next load depends on it (pointer chasing), nothing hides that stall.

Key facts

LevelTypical latencyTypical sizeMeasured here (M1, pointer chase)
Register0 cycles16 to 32 general registers
L1 data cache3 to 5 cycles, about 1 ns32 to 48 KB (x86), 128 KB (M1 performance core)about 2 ns at 16 to 64 KB (includes loop overhead)
L212 to 18 cycles, about 3 to 5 ns256 KB to 2 MB per core (x86), 12 MB per performance cluster (M1)6 to 11 ns at 256 KB to 4 MB
L3 / system cache30 to 70 cycles, about 10 to 20 ns8 to 100+ MB, sharedM1 has an 8 MB system level cache instead of an L3
DRAMabout 60 to 120 nsGBabout 115 ns at 64 MB (includes TLB misses)
TLB miss (page walk)tens of cycles if the page tables are cached, a DRAM access each if notabout 64 L1 and 1 to 3 K L2 TLB entries
NVMe SSD readabout 10 to 100 µsTB

These numbers vary by a factor of two or more between CPU generations, clock speeds and load, so quote ranges in interviews and say so. What does not vary is the shape: each step down costs roughly 3 to 10 times more, and DRAM is roughly 100 times slower than L1.

The program below measures load latency the standard way: it builds a random cyclic permutation inside an array of a given size and follows it, so every load depends on the previous one and the hardware cannot overlap or prefetch them. The output is a timing, so it is not checked.

#include <algorithm>
#include <chrono>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <numeric>
#include <random>
#include <vector>

// Pointer chasing: each load depends on the previous one, so prefetchers cannot help
// and the time per step approximates the load latency of the level the array fits in.
static double ns_per_load(std::size_t bytes) {
    std::size_t n = bytes / sizeof(std::size_t);
    std::vector<std::size_t> order(n), next(n);
    std::iota(order.begin(), order.end(), 0);
    std::shuffle(order.begin() + 1, order.end(), std::mt19937_64{42});
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) next[order[i]] = order[(i + 1) % n];   // one random cycle
    const std::size_t steps = 5'000'000;
    std::size_t p = 0;
    auto t0 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < steps; ++i) p = next[p];
    auto t1 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    if (p == n) std::puts("");   // keep p alive
    return std::chrono::duration<double, std::nano>(t1 - t0).count() / steps;
}

int main() {
    for (std::size_t kb : {16, 64, 256, 1024, 4096, 16384, 65536})
        std::printf("%7zu KB: %6.1f ns per dependent load\n", kb, ns_per_load(kb * 1024));
}

On the Apple M1 used for this guide (GCC 16 and Clang 22, -O1) it printed about 2 ns up to 64 KB, 6 to 11 ns from 256 KB to 4 MB (L2), between 28 and 66 ns at 16 MB depending on the run (the system cache catches part of it), and about 115 ns at 64 MB. The jump points are where the working set stops fitting in a cache level.

Know this cold

L1 about 1 ns, L2 about 4 ns, L3 about 15 ns, DRAM about 100 ns. A cache miss to DRAM costs as much as a few hundred simple instructions. Independent misses can overlap (a core can keep 10 to 20 or more misses in flight), dependent misses cannot. That is why arrays beat linked structures even when both touch "the same amount" of memory.

Cache lines and locality

Theory

Caches do not move bytes, they move cache lines: aligned blocks of 64 bytes on every current x86 core and on most Arm cores. Apple silicon reports 128 bytes (sysctl hw.cachelinesize prints 128 on this M1), and 128 is the value to pad for there. Reading one byte brings the whole line in; writing one byte requires the core to own the whole line.

The address splits into three fields: the low 6 bits (for 64-byte lines) are the offset inside the line, the next bits pick the set, and the rest is the tag that identifies which line occupies a slot of that set. A cache with 8 or 12 ways can hold only that many lines with the same set index. Addresses that differ by a large power of two (4 KB, 8 KB, 16 KB) land in the same set, so walking a matrix whose row length is a power of two can thrash a cache that is mostly empty (the transpose measurements below show this).

Spatial and temporal locality

  • Spatial locality: if you touch an address, you will soon touch its neighbours. Contiguous arrays and sequential scans exploit it: one miss brings 16 ints.
  • Temporal locality: if you touch something, you will soon touch it again. Tiling (blocking) a loop so that it reuses a small working set before moving on exploits it.

Cache-friendly design means maximising the fraction of each fetched line that you use, and the number of times you use it before it is evicted.

std::hardware_destructive_interference_size

C++17 added two constants in <new>: hardware_destructive_interference_size (the minimum distance between two objects to avoid false sharing) and hardware_constructive_interference_size (the maximum size of data that is guaranteed to share a line). Measured with both compilers in this guide's harness:

#include <cstdio>
#include <new>

int main() {
    std::printf("destructive %zu, constructive %zu\n",
                std::hardware_destructive_interference_size,
                std::hardware_constructive_interference_size);
}
destructive 256, constructive 64

That is the output for the arm64 target used here, with both GCC 16 and Clang 22. On x86-64 both compilers print 64 and 64. The arm64 value of 256 is deliberately conservative, chosen to cover Arm designs with large lines or pair-wise prefetching. Two warnings come with these constants. They are compile-time values for a target, not a property of the machine the program runs on. And they become part of any struct layout that uses them, so a header that uses them can produce an ABI mismatch between translation units compiled with different flags; GCC has -Winterference-size for exactly that: it is on by default and fires when the constant is used in a header (a use in the main source file, like the program above, is not flagged), and it goes quiet once you pin the value with --param destructive-interference-size=N. Many projects simply hard-code 64 (x86) or 128 (to also cover Apple silicon and Intel's adjacent-line prefetcher).

Contiguous containers vs node-based containers

Theory

A std::vector<int> of a million elements is 4 MB in one block: a scan touches 62,500 lines in order, and the hardware prefetcher sees the stream and fetches ahead. A std::list<int> of the same elements is a million separate nodes of 24 bytes plus allocator overhead, each found by loading the previous node's next pointer. Every step is a dependent load, and if the nodes are scattered, every step is a cache miss.

#include <algorithm>
#include <chrono>
#include <cstdio>
#include <list>
#include <numeric>
#include <random>
#include <vector>

template <class F>
static double best_ms(F f) {
    double best = 1e30;
    for (int r = 0; r < 3; ++r) {
        auto t0 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        f();
        auto t1 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        best = std::min(best, std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>(t1 - t0).count());
    }
    return best;
}

int main() {
    const int n = 2'000'000;
    std::vector<int> v(n);
    std::iota(v.begin(), v.end(), 0);
    std::list<int> fresh(v.begin(), v.end());          // nodes allocated back to back

    std::vector<int> keys(n);
    std::iota(keys.begin(), keys.end(), 0);
    std::shuffle(keys.begin(), keys.end(), std::mt19937{1});
    std::list<std::pair<int, int>> scattered;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) scattered.push_back({keys[i], i});
    scattered.sort();   // relinks the nodes: list order no longer matches memory order
    long long s1 = 0, s2 = 0, s3 = 0;
    double tv = best_ms([&] { s1 = std::accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0LL); });
    double tf = best_ms([&] { s2 = std::accumulate(fresh.begin(), fresh.end(), 0LL); });
    double ts = best_ms([&] { long long s = 0; for (auto& p : scattered) s += p.second; s3 = s; });
    std::printf("vector %.2f ms, list (allocation order) %.2f ms, list (scattered) %.2f ms\n", tv, tf, ts);
    std::printf("ratios: %.1fx and %.1fx  [%lld %lld %lld]\n", tf / tv, ts / tv, s1, s2, s3);
}

Measured on the M1: the list in allocation order is about 3 times slower than the vector (the allocator happened to place nodes nearly back to back, so this is the list's best case). After sorting by a random key, which relinks the nodes so that list order no longer matches memory order, the list is about 170 to 200 times slower than the vector for the same 2 million elements. Long-running programs look like the second case: nodes are allocated and freed over time, and neighbours in the list end up far apart in memory.

Interview trap

"Linked lists have O(1) insertion, so they are better for frequent inserts in the middle." Only if you already hold an iterator to the position. Finding the position is an O(n) walk of cache misses, while a vector finds it with a fast scan or binary search and shifts the tail with memmove, which runs at memory bandwidth. Bjarne Stroustrup's well-known benchmark showed vector beating list for "insert at a random sorted position" at every size he tried. Big-O hides the constant, and the constant is the memory system.

Row-major traversal

C and C++ arrays are row-major: m[r][c] and m[r][c + 1] are adjacent. Walking along a row uses every byte of every line. Walking down a column jumps a whole row each step, uses 4 bytes of each 64- or 128-byte line, and, for large matrices, evicts the line before the next column would have used the rest of it.

#include <chrono>
#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    const int n = 4096;                        // 4096 × 4096 ints = 64 MB, far beyond every cache
    std::vector<int> m(static_cast<std::size_t>(n) * n, 1);
    auto time = [&](bool by_rows) {
        auto t0 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        long long s = 0;
        for (int a = 0; a < n; ++a)
            for (int b = 0; b < n; ++b)
                s += by_rows ? m[static_cast<std::size_t>(a) * n + b] : m[static_cast<std::size_t>(b) * n + a];
        auto t1 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        std::printf("%s: %.1f ms (sum %lld)\n", by_rows ? "row order   " : "column order",
                    std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>(t1 - t0).count(), s);
        return std::chrono::duration<double>(t1 - t0).count();
    };
    double r = time(true), c = time(false);
    std::printf("column / row = %.1fx\n", c / r);
}

On the M1 the column-order walk of a 64 MB matrix was 5 times (GCC) to 9 times (Clang) slower than the row-order walk. On many x86 machines the gap is larger. Loop interchange (swapping the loops) is the cheapest optimisation in this chapter.

AoS vs SoA, and hot/cold splitting

Theory

Array of structures (AoS) stores whole objects one after another: std::vector<Particle>. Structure of arrays (SoA) stores one array per field: std::vector<float> x, y, z, vx, .... The data is the same; what changes is which bytes share a cache line.

#include <algorithm>
#include <chrono>
#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

struct ParticleAoS {            // 64 bytes: one particle per cache line on x86
    float x, y, z;
    float vx, vy, vz;
    float mass, charge;
    int id, flags;
    double created, updated;
    float pad[2];
};
static_assert(sizeof(ParticleAoS) == 64);

struct ParticlesSoA {
    std::vector<float> x, y, z, vx, vy, vz, mass, charge;
    std::vector<int> id, flags;
    std::vector<double> created, updated;
};

int main() {
    const std::size_t n = 4'000'000;
    std::vector<ParticleAoS> aos(n, ParticleAoS{1, 2, 3, 0.5f, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, {}});
    ParticlesSoA soa;
    soa.x.assign(n, 1); soa.vx.assign(n, 0.5f);
    soa.y.assign(n, 2); soa.z.assign(n, 3); soa.vy.assign(n, 0); soa.vz.assign(n, 0);
    auto ms = [](auto t0, auto t1) { return std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>(t1 - t0).count(); };
    double ta = 1e30, ts = 1e30;
    for (int r = 0; r < 5; ++r) {
        auto t0 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        for (auto& p : aos) p.x += p.vx;                       // touches 8 of every 64 bytes
        auto t1 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) soa.x[i] += soa.vx[i];   // touches only what it uses
        auto t2 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        ta = std::min(ta, ms(t0, t1));
        ts = std::min(ts, ms(t1, t2));
    }
    std::printf("AoS %.2f ms, SoA %.2f ms, AoS / SoA = %.1fx (x[7] %.1f %.1f)\n", ta, ts, ta / ts, aos[7].x, soa.x[7]);
}

Measured on the M1 with 4 million particles: SoA was 3.1 times faster with GCC and 2.4 times faster with Clang for x += vx. The theoretical ratio is 8 (8 bytes used out of 64 in AoS, all of them in SoA); the M1's very high memory bandwidth and the loop's arithmetic eat into it.

SoA is not always better. If the code usually works on one whole entity at a time (look up a particle by id and read all its fields), AoS fetches one or two lines while SoA fetches one line per field. Many engines use a hybrid, AoSoA: blocks of, say, 8 entities stored SoA-style inside each block, which keeps SIMD-friendly runs and entity locality. Entity-component systems in games are SoA at heart.

Hot/cold splitting

A gentler version of the same idea: keep the fields that the hot loop touches in a compact struct, and move rarely used fields (names, debug info, audit timestamps, large buffers) into a separate "cold" struct reached by index or pointer.

struct OrderHot {             // 32 bytes: two per 64-byte line, scanned by the matching engine
    std::int64_t price;
    std::int64_t qty;
    std::uint32_t id;
    std::uint32_t cold_index;  // where the rest lives
    std::uint8_t side, flags;
};
struct OrderCold {            // touched on fills, cancels and reports only
    std::string client_ref;
    std::chrono::system_clock::time_point created;
    std::array<char, 64> notes;
};
std::vector<OrderHot> hot;    // the loop streams through this
std::vector<OrderCold> cold;  // indexed by cold_index

Profile first: the split only pays off when the hot loop is memory bound and the cold fields are a large share of the object.

Alignment, padding and member order

Theory

Every type has an alignment (a power of two) and objects must start at a multiple of it. The compiler lays out members at increasing addresses in declaration order (required by the standard; before C++23 only among members with the same access control), inserts padding before any member that would be misaligned, and pads the end so that sizeof is a multiple of the struct's alignment, which keeps every element of an array aligned.

The practical rule: declare members in decreasing order of alignment (8-byte types, then 4, 2, 1). It is optimal for the common case where all sizes are multiples of their alignment, and it is what the coding drill below automates. Group fields that are used together, too: reordering for size should not split the hot fields across two lines.

alignas, over-aligned types and packing

  • alignas(N) on a type raises its alignment and therefore rounds its size up to a multiple of N. struct alignas(64) Slot { long v; }; is 64 bytes, so an array of Slot puts each element on its own line.
  • alignas(N) on a variable aligns that variable only. alignas(64) long counters[4]; aligns the start of the array; the four elements are still 8 bytes apart (a reading drill below).
  • Since C++17, new honours over-alignment (it calls operator new(size_t, std::align_val_t)), and so does std::allocator, so std::vector<Slot> works. Before C++17, over-aligned heap objects were silently under-aligned.
  • [[no_unique_address]] (C++20) lets an empty member, such as a stateless allocator, comparator or deleter, take no space. GCC and Clang honour it; MSVC needs [[msvc::no_unique_address]].
  • #pragma pack(1) or __attribute__((packed)) removes padding to match a wire or file format. The members are then misaligned: accessing them by name is fine (the compiler emits safe loads), but taking their address and using the pointer is undefined behaviour, can be slow, and on some architectures traps. Atomics on packed members do not work. Prefer copying wire bytes with std::memcpy into a normal struct.

False sharing

Theory

Mental model. Coherence is tracked per cache line, not per variable. To write to a line, a core must hold it exclusively (the M state in MESI-style protocols), which invalidates every other core's copy. If two threads write to two different variables that happen to share a line, each write steals the line from the other core. Nothing is logically shared, but the hardware behaves as if everything were.

#include <atomic>
#include <algorithm>
#include <chrono>
#include <cstdio>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

struct Packed {
    std::atomic<long> value{0};                 // 8 bytes: four counters share one line
};
struct alignas(128) Padded {                    // 128: the line size macOS reports on Apple silicon
    std::atomic<long> value{0};
};

template <class Counter>
static double run_ms(int threads, long iters) {
    std::vector<Counter> counters(threads);
    auto t0 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    std::vector<std::thread> pool;
    for (int t = 0; t < threads; ++t)
        pool.emplace_back([&counters, t, iters] {
            for (long i = 0; i < iters; ++i) counters[t].value.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
        });
    for (auto& th : pool) th.join();
    auto t1 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    long total = 0;
    for (auto& c : counters) total += c.value.load();
    if (total != threads * iters) std::puts("lost updates?");
    return std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>(t1 - t0).count();
}

int main() {
    const int threads = 4;
    const long iters = 2'000'000;
    double best_packed = 1e30, best_padded = 1e30;
    for (int r = 0; r < 3; ++r) {
        best_packed = std::min(best_packed, run_ms<Packed>(threads, iters));
        best_padded = std::min(best_padded, run_ms<Padded>(threads, iters));
    }
    std::printf("sizeof Packed %zu, Padded %zu\n", sizeof(Packed), sizeof(Padded));
    std::printf("adjacent counters %.1f ms, padded counters %.1f ms, ratio %.1fx\n",
                best_packed, best_padded, best_packed / best_padded);
}

Measured on the M1 with 4 threads: adjacent counters took about 155 ms, padded counters about 7 ms, a ratio of about 22 with both compilers. The program is race free (each thread owns one atomic), so it also runs clean under ThreadSanitizer; only the timings are unchecked.

Where false sharing hides: arrays of per-thread counters or statistics, a lock and the data it protects in the same line (waiters spinning on the lock slow down the owner), the head and tail indices of a single-producer single-consumer queue, and small heap objects allocated back to back for different threads. The fixes are padding and alignment, per-thread accumulation in locals with one write at the end, and per-thread arenas.

Tip

On Linux, perf c2c record followed by perf c2c report finds false sharing directly: it lists cache lines with many HITM events (loads that hit a line modified in another core's cache) and the offsets inside the line that each thread touches.

Prefetching and blocking

Theory

Hardware prefetchers watch the stream of misses and fetch ahead. Every modern core has a next-line prefetcher and a stride prefetcher that recognises constant strides (forwards or backwards, per instruction), and Intel cores also fetch the adjacent line of each 128-byte pair. They are why sequential and strided scans run near memory bandwidth. They cannot predict pointer chasing or random indices.

__builtin_prefetch(addr, rw, locality) (GCC and Clang) emits a prefetch instruction: a hint to start loading a line that you will need soon. It helps only when you know a future address well in advance, the access is not predictable by hardware, and the core is not already overlapping those misses. The benchmark below gathers from random indices, with and without a prefetch 16 iterations ahead.

#include <algorithm>
#include <chrono>
#include <cstdio>
#include <numeric>
#include <random>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    const std::size_t n = 1u << 24;                  // 16M ints (64 MB) of data
    std::vector<int> data(n, 1);
    std::vector<unsigned> seq(n), rnd(n);
    std::iota(seq.begin(), seq.end(), 0u);
    rnd = seq;
    std::shuffle(rnd.begin(), rnd.end(), std::mt19937{7});

    auto gather = [&](const std::vector<unsigned>& idx, int distance) {
        long long s = 0;
        auto t0 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
            if (distance && i + distance < n) __builtin_prefetch(&data[idx[i + distance]]);
            s += data[idx[i]];
        }
        auto t1 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        return std::pair{std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>(t1 - t0).count(), s};
    };
    auto [ts, s1] = gather(seq, 0);
    auto [tr, s2] = gather(rnd, 0);
    auto [tp, s3] = gather(rnd, 16);
    std::printf("sequential %.0f ms, random %.0f ms, random + prefetch %.0f ms\n", ts, tr, tp);
    std::printf("random / sequential %.1fx, prefetch speedup %.1fx [%lld %lld %lld]\n", tr / ts, tr / tp, s1, s2, s3);
}

Measured on the M1: the random gather was 4.6 to 6.7 times slower than the sequential one, and the software prefetch gave no gain (0.9 to 1.0 times, so slightly worse). The loads in this loop are independent, so the out-of-order core already has many misses in flight, and the prefetch only adds instructions. Software prefetching pays off in loops with long dependency chains per element, such as hash-table probes or tree descents processed in batches. Measure every prefetch you add; a prefetch distance that is wrong for one machine is often wrong for the next.

Blocking (tiling)

When a loop nest touches one array along rows and another along columns, as in a matrix transpose or a naive matrix multiply, one of them is always strided. Blocking processes the matrix in tiles small enough that every line of the tile stays in L1 until it is fully used. The coding drill implements a blocked transpose. Timings on the M1 (milliseconds, best of 3, GCC -O1):

n × n floatsnaiveblocked, tile 16blocked, tile 64observation
20003.23.73.7no gain: the stride prefetcher handles the column writes
2048324.722power-of-two rows collide in the same cache sets; small tiles avoid it
40001022016.5about 6 times faster with blocking
4096167 to 200124121set conflicts and TLB misses dominate

The lesson is the interview answer: blocking is a large win when the working set exceeds the cache, but power-of-two strides can cause conflict misses that tiling alone does not cure. Padding each row by one line (allocate n + 16 floats per row) is the classic fix. And always measure on the target machine: the 2000 × 2000 case shows that a strong prefetcher can make the naive version good enough.

Allocation patterns that keep data together

Theory

Layout inside an object is half the story. The other half is where the allocator puts objects relative to each other. A general-purpose malloc serves requests of the same size class from the same pages in roughly allocation order, but after a while of mixed allocations and frees, related objects end up scattered (Ch 10).

  • Contiguous containers first. std::vector, std::array, std::deque (contiguous blocks), and sorted vectors in place of std::set/std::map when reads dominate (std::flat_map and std::flat_set in C++23, boost::container::flat_map before that).
  • reserve when the size is known or bounded. Besides avoiding reallocation copies, it keeps the final buffer in one place instead of leaving freed buffers of 1, 2, 4 ... elements scattered in the heap.
  • Open-addressing hash tables. std::unordered_map must keep references stable and expose buckets, so every mainstream implementation uses a bucket array of pointers to separately allocated nodes: a lookup is at least two dependent misses. absl::flat_hash_map, boost::unordered_flat_map and similar tables store entries in one array and probe neighbouring slots, so a lookup usually touches one or two lines. The cost: references are invalidated on rehash.
  • Pools and arenas (Ch 15, Ch 17). Allocate the nodes of one tree, graph or message from one arena and they sit next to each other in allocation order, which is usually traversal order. Freeing is one operation, and there is no per-node header.
  • Indices instead of pointers. Store nodes in a std::vector and link them with 32-bit indices. Nodes are contiguous, links are half the size of pointers, the structure can be copied or serialised with memcpy, and reallocation does not invalidate links.
  • Per-thread allocation. Objects used by one thread should come from that thread's arena or cache, which also prevents false sharing between neighbouring small objects owned by different threads.

TLB and huge pages

Every access also needs a virtual-to-physical translation. The TLB caches translations: typically about 64 entries in the first level and 1 to 3 thousand in the second. With 4 KB pages, 1,536 entries cover only 6 MB, so a random walk over a 1 GB working set misses the TLB on nearly every access and pays a page walk on top of the cache miss. Huge pages (2 MB or 1 GB on x86-64) make each entry cover 512 or 262,144 times more memory.

  • Linux: transparent huge pages (/sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled set to always or madvise; opt in per region with madvise(addr, len, MADV_HUGEPAGE)), or explicit huge pages with mmap(MAP_HUGETLB) or hugetlbfs, reserved in advance. Low-latency systems often pre-fault and lock huge pages at startup to avoid page faults later.
  • Costs: THP can increase memory use (a 2 MB page for a few KB of data) and background compaction can cause latency spikes, which is why some databases recommend madvise mode rather than always.
  • Apple silicon uses 16 KB base pages (hw.pagesize is 16384 on this M1), which quadruples TLB reach compared with 4 KB pages. Linux on arm64 can be built with 4, 16 or 64 KB pages.

How to measure cache behaviour

Theory

Never optimise layout on intuition alone. Measure the miss rates, change one thing, and measure again.

# Linux: hardware counters for the whole run
perf stat -e cycles,instructions,cache-references,cache-misses,L1-dcache-load-misses,LLC-load-misses,dTLB-load-misses ./app

# where the misses happen, per function and per source line
perf record -e cache-misses -g ./app
perf report

# false sharing: lines with HITM events and the offsets each thread touches
perf c2c record ./app
perf c2c report

# simulated caches, deterministic and exact per line (slow: 20 to 100 times)
valgrind --tool=cachegrind --cache-sim=yes ./app
cg_annotate cachegrind.out.<pid>

# cache geometry
lscpu --caches
getconf LEVEL1_DCACHE_LINESIZE
cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cache/index0/coherency_line_size

# macOS
sysctl hw.cachelinesize hw.l1dcachesize hw.l2cachesize hw.pagesize

Read perf stat with care. Instructions per cycle (IPC) below about 1 on a modern core usually means the program is stalled on memory. The generic cache-misses event usually means last-level cache misses, which is what costs DRAM time. Cachegrind simulates a simple cache model rather than your real CPU, and since Valgrind 3.21 (2023) its cache simulation is off unless you pass --cache-sim=yes; it is still the best tool for exact, repeatable per-line counts.

On macOS there is no perf, and Valgrind does not support Apple silicon. Use Instruments: the CPU Counters template records hardware events such as L1D and L2 misses per function, and the Time Profiler finds hot loops. The stock template records little until you choose the events, so configure them in Instruments, save the result as your own template, and record from the command line with xcrun xctrace record --template 'My Counters' --launch -- ./app. Combine counters with micro-benchmarks like the ones in this chapter, run several times and on a quiet machine, and always report the machine and compiler next to the numbers.

Concept and tricky questions

Drills

ConceptGive rough latencies for an L1 hit, an L2 hit, an L3 hit and a DRAM access, and explain why the ratio matters more than the exact values.

Answer

Answer. L1 about 1 ns (3 to 5 cycles), L2 about 3 to 5 ns, L3 about 10 to 20 ns, DRAM about 60 to 120 ns. On the M1 used here, a pointer chase measured about 2 ns, 6 to 11 ns, and about 115 ns for the L1, L2 and DRAM ranges.

Why. Each level is roughly 3 to 10 times slower than the one above, and DRAM is roughly 100 times slower than L1, on every machine of the last two decades. A DRAM miss costs as much as a few hundred simple instructions, so an algorithm that does twice the arithmetic but misses half as often usually wins. Quoting a single exact number is a weak answer, because latencies differ by generation, clock and load; quoting the ladder and the ratios is the strong one.

ConceptWhat is a cache line, how big is it, and what happens when you read a single byte from memory that is not cached?

Answer

Answer. A cache line is the aligned block that caches move and track as a unit: 64 bytes on x86 and most Arm cores, 128 bytes on Apple silicon (sysctl hw.cachelinesize prints 128 on the M1). Reading one byte fetches the whole line containing it into L1 (and usually the levels below), so the next 63 bytes are free to read.

Why. DRAM delivers data in bursts, and tags cost silicon, so tracking larger blocks is cheaper per byte. The consequences: a value that straddles two lines costs two fetches, an access pattern that uses 4 bytes per line wastes 94 percent of the bandwidth, and coherence (and therefore false sharing) operates on whole lines. The common wrong answer is that the cache loads "the variable".

TrickyYou need to keep a sequence sorted while inserting 100,000 random values. A colleague picks std::list because "insertion is O(1)". Is that a good choice?

Answer

Answer. No. std::vector with lower_bound and insert is much faster in practice, even though the insert shifts O(n) elements.

Why. The list's O(1) insertion assumes you already have the position. Finding it is an O(n) walk of dependent loads, each likely a cache miss once the nodes are scattered (the scattered list in this chapter was about 200 times slower to traverse than a vector on the M1). The vector finds the position by binary search in O(log n) and shifts the tail with a memmove at memory bandwidth, which the prefetcher handles perfectly. This is Stroustrup's well-known "vector vs list" demonstration. Lists still win when you hold iterators and splice, or need iterator stability, but rarely for search-then-insert.

TrickyA colleague says: "Linked lists are only slow because the nodes are scattered. Allocate them from an arena and a list traversal is as fast as a vector." Is that right?

Answer

Answer. Only partly. An arena (or a freshly built list) puts nodes in allocation order, which removes the random misses, but the traversal is still a chain of dependent loads over fat nodes. In this chapter's benchmark the list in allocation order was still about 3 times slower than the vector, and the gap returns as soon as inserts, splices or a sort make list order differ from memory order (about 200 times after a sort).

Why. Three costs remain. Each step must load next before it knows the next address, so the core cannot run ahead and the loop cannot be vectorised. A std::list<int> node is 24 bytes for 4 bytes of payload, so the scan moves six times the data. And the arena only fixes the layout at creation: a list that is edited over time drifts back to random order. The common wrong answer is that locality is the whole story; the dependency chain and the per-node overhead are the rest. If the data is iterated far more often than it is spliced, a vector (or indices into one) is still the better structure.

TrickyTo avoid false sharing, a per-thread counter type is declared struct alignas(64) Counter { std::atomic<long> v; };. Is that enough on every machine?

Answer

Answer. Not everywhere. It is enough on most x86 and Arm cores with 64-byte lines, but Apple silicon uses 128-byte lines, so two 64-byte counters can still share one line there. Intel's L2 spatial prefetcher also pulls 64-byte lines in 128-byte pairs, which causes milder interference between neighbours. 128 is the safer portable choice.

Why. Correctness also needs two other things that this declaration does get right: the alignment is on the type, so sizeof(Counter) becomes 64 and array elements are 64 bytes apart (with alignas on an array variable they would not be), and since C++17 new and std::vector honour the over-alignment. std::hardware_destructive_interference_size is 256 on arm64 builds and 64 on x86-64 builds with GCC and Clang, which shows that the "right" value depends on the target.

TrickyEight threads read the same configuration struct in a tight loop, and nobody writes it. Is there false sharing, or any coherence traffic?

Answer

Answer. No. Every core can hold a copy of the line in the Shared state at the same time, and reads hit in each core's own cache after the first miss.

Why. False sharing needs at least one writer: a write requires exclusive ownership, which invalidates the other copies. The trap is a read-mostly struct that sits on the same line as a frequently written field (a hit counter, a lock, a sequence number); then every write invalidates all the readers' copies. Keep read-mostly data and written data on separate lines. Read sharing is how lock-free readers in RCU and seqlocks stay fast.

TrickyWhy do some engineers avoid std::hardware_destructive_interference_size in public headers, even though it is standard C++17?

Answer

Answer. Because it is a compile-time constant chosen by the compiler for a target, and anything that uses it in a layout bakes that value into the ABI. Two translation units, or a library and its user, compiled with different flags or compiler versions can disagree on sizeof of the same struct.

Why. GCC warns about this with -Winterference-size and lets you fix the value with --param destructive-interference-size=N. The value also need not match the machine at run time: one arm64 binary runs on cores with 64-byte and 128-byte lines, and GCC and Clang both choose a conservative 256 for arm64. Many codebases define their own constant (64 or 128) for that reason. The constant is still fine inside a single program built in one go.

TrickyIs structure of arrays always faster than array of structures?

Answer

Answer. No. SoA wins for loops that touch a few fields of many objects (it was 2.4 to 3.1 times faster for x += vx in this chapter); AoS wins when code accesses whole objects one at a time, especially at random.

Why. Fetching all fields of entity i from an SoA layout costs one line per field (eight lines for eight fields), against one or two lines for an AoS object. SoA also makes insertion and deletion touch many arrays, and it complicates passing "an object" around. The usual compromises are hot/cold splitting and AoSoA (small SoA blocks inside an array), which many game engines and SIMD libraries use. The right layout follows the dominant access pattern, which you find by profiling.

TrickyA teammate adds #pragma pack(1) to all structs "to make them smaller and more cache friendly". What can go wrong?

Answer

Answer. Members become misaligned. Taking a member's address and using the pointer is undefined behaviour (UBSan reports "misaligned address"), atomics on packed members are not atomic or not allowed, some architectures trap or split the access, and the ABI of every struct changes, so it breaks interoperation with code compiled without the pragma.

Why. Accessing a packed member by name is safe, because the compiler knows it is packed and emits byte-wise or unaligned loads. Once you pass &s.field as an ordinary T*, that knowledge is lost. Reordering members by decreasing alignment gets almost all of the size benefit with none of the risk. Packing belongs only on structs that mirror an external byte format, and even there std::memcpy into a normal struct is cleaner.

TrickyWhy is std::unordered_map often several times slower than absl::flat_hash_map or boost::unordered_flat_map, when both are O(1) on average?

Answer

Answer. The standard's interface forces a node-based design: references to elements must stay valid across rehashing, and the bucket API (bucket, begin(n), local_iterator) must be supported. So every mainstream implementation allocates each element in its own node and chains nodes from a bucket array, and a lookup costs at least two dependent cache misses.

Why. Open-addressing tables store elements (or small metadata bytes plus elements) in one contiguous array and probe neighbouring slots, so a lookup usually touches one or two lines, and SIMD can check 16 metadata bytes at once (Swiss tables). The price is that a rehash moves elements, invalidating references and pointers. The common wrong answer is "a better hash function"; the hash is rarely the bottleneck.

ConceptExplain spatial and temporal locality with one example of code that has each, and one that has neither.

Answer

Answer. Spatial: a sequential scan of a std::vector uses every byte of each fetched line. Temporal: a blocked matrix multiply reuses each tile many times while it is in L1. Neither: following random pointers through a large linked structure, where each node is used once and its neighbours are unrelated.

Why. Caches bet on both kinds of locality: they fetch whole lines (spatial) and keep recently used lines (temporal). Code that defeats both pays the full memory latency on almost every access. Improving locality is usually about layout (what is next to what) and loop order (when data is reused), not about doing less work.

ConceptWhat is hot/cold splitting, and when is it worth doing?

Answer

Answer. Moving the fields that hot loops use into a compact struct and the rarely used fields into a separate struct (reached by index or pointer), so each cache line carries more useful data in the hot path.

Why. If an order object is 200 bytes but the matching loop reads 24 of them, the loop streams 200 bytes per order through the cache. Splitting makes the hot struct small enough for several per line. It pays when the loop is memory bound (profile: low IPC, high cache-miss rate) and the cold part is large; it costs an extra indirection when cold data is needed, and more complex code. Compilers can do a version of this for code (hot/cold function splitting with profile-guided optimisation), but not for your data.

ConceptWhat do hardware prefetchers detect, and when does __builtin_prefetch actually help?

Answer

Answer. Hardware prefetchers detect sequential streams and constant strides (per load instruction, forwards and backwards), plus adjacent lines on some Intel cores. Software prefetch helps only when the future address is known early, is not predictable by the hardware, and the core is not already overlapping the misses, for example batched hash-table lookups or tree descents.

Why. In this chapter's random gather benchmark on the M1, a prefetch 16 iterations ahead gave no speedup (0.9 to 1.0 times), because the loads were independent and the out-of-order core already had many in flight. Too short a distance arrives late, too long evicts useful data, and the right distance changes with the machine. Treat software prefetch as a measured, last-step optimisation.

ConceptWhat is the TLB, why can a program with a large random-access working set be slow even when cache misses look normal, and what do huge pages change?

Answer

Answer. The TLB caches virtual-to-physical translations. With 4 KB pages and about 1,500 second-level entries, it covers about 6 MB. Random access over gigabytes misses the TLB on most accesses, and each miss needs a page-table walk (up to four or five dependent loads) before the data access can even start. Huge pages (2 MB or 1 GB on x86-64) cover 512 or 262,144 times more per entry.

Why. perf stat -e dTLB-load-misses shows the problem. On Linux, enable transparent huge pages for the region with madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE) or use MAP_HUGETLB; low-latency systems often pre-fault huge pages at startup. Apple silicon's 16 KB base pages give four times the reach of 4 KB pages, one reason TLB effects show up later there.

ConceptHow do you measure cache behaviour on Linux and on macOS?

Answer

Answer. Linux: perf stat -e cycles,instructions,cache-misses,L1-dcache-load-misses,LLC-load-misses,dTLB-load-misses for totals, perf record/perf report to attribute misses to code, perf c2c for false sharing, and valgrind --tool=cachegrind --cache-sim=yes for exact simulated per-line counts. macOS: Instruments with the CPU Counters template (or xctrace), since perf does not exist there and Valgrind does not run on Apple silicon.

Why. Counters tell you whether a program is memory bound (low IPC, high LLC misses) before you change any layout. Micro-benchmarks need repeated runs, a quiet machine, a result that is used (so the optimiser cannot delete the loop), and the machine and compiler named next to every number, as in this chapter.

ConceptHow do pools, arenas and reserve improve locality, beyond saving allocation time?

Answer

Answer. They control where objects land. An arena places the nodes of one structure consecutively, in allocation order, which is usually the order they are traversed, with no headers in between. A per-type pool packs objects of one kind densely. reserve gives a vector its final buffer at once instead of leaving abandoned 1, 2, 4 ... element buffers scattered in the heap.

Why. A general-purpose allocator interleaves objects from unrelated code paths and, after churn, hands out blocks wherever there is space, so logically adjacent nodes end up on different lines and pages. Grouping related data improves both cache and TLB hit rates. Index-based links (32-bit indices into a vector) push this further by halving link size. See Ch 15 and Ch 17 for the allocators themselves.

Predict the output and find the bug

Drills

OutputSame three members, two orders. What are the sizes?

#include <cstdio>

struct A { char a; int b; char c; };
struct B { int b; char a; char c; };

int main() {
    std::printf("%zu %zu\n", sizeof(A), sizeof(B));
    std::printf("%zu %zu\n", alignof(A), sizeof(A[4]));
}
Answer
12 8
4 48

Why. In A, b must start at a multiple of 4, so 3 padding bytes follow a; c sits at offset 8, and 3 tail bytes round the size up to 12, a multiple of the struct's alignment (4). In B, a and c pack after b and only 2 tail bytes are needed: 8. An array of four A is exactly 4 × 12 = 48: arrays never add padding between elements, which is why the tail padding exists. The common wrong answer is 6 for A (summing the members).

OutputDoes putting the double last save space?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>

struct C { char c; double d; };
struct D { double d; char c; };

int main() {
    std::printf("%zu %zu\n", sizeof(C), sizeof(D));
    std::printf("%zu %zu\n", offsetof(C, d), offsetof(D, c));
}
Answer
16 16
8 8

Why. Both are 16. In C the padding is 7 bytes between c and d (so offsetof(C, d) is 8); in D the same 7 bytes move to the tail, after c at offset 8, because an array of D must keep every d 8-byte aligned. Reordering only helps when several small members can share the space that one of them would waste. People often expect D to be 9.

OutputHow big are an empty struct, a member of it, a [[no_unique_address]] member of it, and an empty base?

#include <cstdio>

struct Empty {};
struct F { int x; Empty e; };
struct G { int x; [[no_unique_address]] Empty e; };
struct H : Empty { int x; };

int main() {
    std::printf("%zu %zu %zu %zu\n", sizeof(Empty), sizeof(F), sizeof(G), sizeof(H));
}
Answer
1 8 4 4

Why. Every complete object has a size of at least 1 so that distinct objects have distinct addresses, so sizeof(Empty) is 1. As an ordinary member it occupies a byte, and alignment rounds F to 8. [[no_unique_address]] (C++20) lets the member overlap other members, so G is 4, and the empty base optimisation does the same for a base class in H. This is how std::unique_ptr<T> with the default deleter stays the size of a raw pointer (Ch 12). MSVC ignores the standard attribute and needs [[msvc::no_unique_address]].

OutputWhat do alignas on a type and alignas on a member do to size and offsets?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>

struct alignas(16) Vec3 { float x, y, z; };
struct Mixed {
    char tag;
    alignas(64) int counter;
};

int main() {
    std::printf("%zu %zu %zu\n", sizeof(Vec3), alignof(Vec3), sizeof(Vec3[3]));
    std::printf("%zu %zu\n", sizeof(Mixed), offsetof(Mixed, counter));
}
Answer
16 16 48
128 64

Why. Vec3 holds 12 bytes of data, but alignas(16) makes its alignment 16 and rounds its size to 16 (useful for SIMD loads), so three of them take 48 bytes. In Mixed, the member counter must start at a multiple of 64, which puts it at offset 64 after 63 bytes of padding, and the struct's alignment becomes 64, so its size rounds up from 68 to 128. Aligning a member is an easy way to waste a line by accident.

OutputBit-fields: what are the sizes with GCC and Clang on a 64-bit target?

#include <cstdio>

struct Flags { unsigned a : 3; unsigned b : 5; unsigned c : 24; };
struct Wide  { unsigned a : 3; unsigned long long b : 40; };
struct Split { char a; unsigned b : 4; char c; };

int main() {
    std::printf("%zu %zu %zu\n", sizeof(Flags), sizeof(Wide), sizeof(Split));
}
Answer
4 8 4

Why. Flags packs 3 + 5 + 24 = 32 bits into one unsigned. Wide packs 43 bits into one 8-byte unit. In Split, the Itanium ABI used by GCC and Clang places the 4-bit field in the byte after a, because it still fits within an aligned unsigned unit, then c, and rounds the size to the 4-byte alignment of unsigned. Bit-field layout is implementation-defined: MSVC allocates a whole unsigned for b and gives Split a size of 12. Never use bit-fields to match an external format across compilers.

OutputA market data quote, as written and after reordering. How many fit in a 64-byte line?

#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>

struct Quote {
    bool valid;
    std::int64_t price;
    bool is_bid;
    std::int32_t size;
    bool stale;
};

struct QuoteSorted {
    std::int64_t price;
    std::int32_t size;
    bool valid, is_bid, stale;
};

int main() {
    std::printf("%zu %zu\n", sizeof(Quote), sizeof(QuoteSorted));
    std::printf("quotes per 64-byte line: %zu vs %zu\n", 64 / sizeof(Quote), 64 / sizeof(QuoteSorted));
}
Answer
32 16
quotes per 64-byte line: 2 vs 4

Why. In Quote, each bool in front of a wider member wastes up to 7 bytes: valid (1 + 7 padding), price (8), is_bid (1 + 3), size (4), stale (1 + 7 tail) = 32. Sorted by decreasing alignment the data is 8 + 4 + 3 = 15 bytes, rounded to 16. Halving the struct doubles the quotes per line and halves the memory traffic of a scan over a book, with no code change.

OutputThis guide's harness targets arm64 (Apple M1). What does it print?

#include <cstdio>
#include <new>

struct Poly { virtual ~Poly() = default; char tag; };
struct alignas(std::hardware_destructive_interference_size) Slot { long value; };

int main() {
    std::printf("%zu\n", sizeof(Poly));
    std::printf("%zu %zu\n", std::hardware_destructive_interference_size, std::hardware_constructive_interference_size);
    std::printf("%zu\n", sizeof(Slot));
}
Answer
16
256 64
256

Why. Poly has a vptr (8 bytes) because of the virtual destructor, then tag, rounded to 16 by the pointer's alignment (Ch 2). GCC 16 and Clang 22 both report 256 and 64 for the interference sizes on arm64, so Slot becomes 256 bytes for one long. Compiled for x86-64, the same program prints 64 and 64, and Slot is 64. That difference is the reason the constants are risky in headers: the layout depends on the target the header was compiled for.

Find the bugThis parser works on x86 and on the M1. Which tool objects, and why?

#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>

#pragma pack(push, 1)
struct WireHeader {          // matches a network message byte for byte
    std::uint8_t type;
    std::uint32_t length;
    std::uint16_t flags;
};
#pragma pack(pop)

static std::uint32_t read_u32(const std::uint32_t* p) { return *p; }

int main() {
    WireHeader h[2] = {{1, 100, 0}, {2, 200, 0}};
    std::uint32_t total = 0;
    for (const WireHeader& w : h) total += read_u32(&w.length);
    std::printf("sizeof %zu, total %u\n", sizeof(WireHeader), total);
}
Answer
sizeof 7, total 300

Answer. &w.length is a uint32_t* to an address that is not a multiple of 4 (byte offset 1 inside the first element). Dereferencing it in read_u32 is undefined behaviour, and UBSan reports "load of misaligned address ... which requires 4 byte alignment".

Why. Inside the packed struct the compiler knows the member is misaligned and uses safe loads. Through a plain uint32_t* it assumes 4-byte alignment and may use instructions that fault on misaligned addresses (some Arm and older architectures, or SIMD loads on x86). It "works" here only because both test CPUs tolerate misaligned scalar loads. Fix: read the field by value (std::uint32_t len = w.length;) or std::memcpy the bytes into a normal, aligned struct. GCC's -Waddress-of-packed-member catches some of these at compile time, but not this one.

Find the bugThe result is correct and there is no data race. Why does this scale badly when the loop body is real work?

#include <cstdio>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    const int threads = 4;
    long hits[threads] = {};                 // one slot per thread: no data race
    std::vector<std::thread> pool;
    for (int t = 0; t < threads; ++t)
        pool.emplace_back([&hits, t] {
            for (int i = 0; i < 1'000'000; ++i)
                if (i % 3 == 0) ++hits[t];
        });
    for (auto& th : pool) th.join();
    long total = 0;
    for (long h : hits) total += h;
    std::printf("total %ld\n", total);
}
Answer
total 1333336

Answer. False sharing. The four longs occupy 32 contiguous bytes, one cache line, so every increment by one thread invalidates the line in the other three cores. With real work in the loop (function calls, memory accesses the compiler cannot see through), each ++hits[t] is a store to that shared line.

Why. At -O1 and above the compiler may keep hits[t] in a register for this simple loop and store it once at the end, which hides the problem in a micro-test. Do that explicitly: accumulate into a local long local = 0; and write hits[t] = local; once, or give each slot its own line with struct alignas(128) Slot { long v; };. This chapter's benchmark measured about 22 times between packed and padded atomic counters on the M1.

Find the bugThe comment claims the counters are on separate cache lines. Are they?

#include <atomic>
#include <cstdio>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

alignas(64) std::atomic<long> counters[4];   // "aligned to a cache line, so no false sharing"

int main() {
    std::vector<std::thread> pool;
    for (int t = 0; t < 4; ++t)
        pool.emplace_back([t] { for (int i = 0; i < 100'000; ++i) counters[t].fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed); });
    for (auto& th : pool) th.join();
    std::printf("sum %ld, distance between counters %td bytes\n",
                counters[0] + counters[1] + counters[2] + counters[3],
                reinterpret_cast<char*>(&counters[1]) - reinterpret_cast<char*>(&counters[0]));
}
Answer
sum 400000, distance between counters 8 bytes

Answer. No. alignas(64) on an array variable aligns the array's first byte. The elements keep their natural size, 8 bytes, so all four counters share one line, exactly the false sharing the comment claims to prevent.

Fix. Put the alignment on the element type, which also rounds its size: struct alignas(128) Counter { std::atomic<long> v{0}; }; Counter counters[4];. Then &counters[1] - &counters[0] is 128 bytes. Add a static_assert(sizeof(Counter) == 128) so the intent is checked. This is one of the most common false-sharing "fixes" that does nothing.

Find the bugThe answer is right. What makes it several times slower than it needs to be, and what is a second, smaller problem with the data structure?

#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

static long long sum_grid(const std::vector<std::vector<int>>& g) {
    long long s = 0;
    for (std::size_t col = 0; col < g[0].size(); ++col)
        for (std::size_t row = 0; row < g.size(); ++row)
            s += g[row][col];
    return s;
}

int main() {
    std::vector<std::vector<int>> grid(2000, std::vector<int>(2000, 1));
    std::printf("%lld\n", sum_grid(grid));
}
Answer
4000000

Answer. The loops are in column-major order over row-major data: the inner loop jumps to a different row (a different heap block) on every iteration, using 4 bytes of each fetched line. Swap the loops so the inner loop walks along g[row]. The second problem is vector<vector<int>> itself: 2,000 separate allocations, an extra indirection per row, and no guarantee that rows are adjacent.

Why. This chapter's row/column benchmark measured 5 to 9 times on the M1 for a 64 MB matrix. A single std::vector<int> of rows * cols elements indexed as v[r * cols + c] (or std::mdspan in C++23) is contiguous, has one allocation, and lets the compiler vectorise the row loop.

Write the code

Coding

CodeConvert an array-of-structures particle system to structure-of-arrays. Given std::vector<Particle> with position, velocity, mass and id, write a ParticleSystem class with one vector per field, a constructor from the AoS vector, an integrate(dt) that updates positions, total_mass(), and get(i) that reassembles one particle. Show that both layouts give identical results.

Answer

Approach. One std::vector per field, all with the same length, filled in one pass with reserve first. Write the update as separate tight loops over two arrays each, so every loop streams through exactly the bytes it needs and the compiler can vectorise it. total_mass reads one array. get(i) shows the cost of SoA: one load per field from a different array.

#include <cmath>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

struct Particle {            // AoS: what the code base had
    float x, y, z;
    float vx, vy, vz;
    float mass;
    int id;
};

class ParticleSystem {       // SoA: one array per field
public:
    std::vector<float> x, y, z, vx, vy, vz, mass;
    std::vector<int> id;

    explicit ParticleSystem(const std::vector<Particle>& in) {
        const std::size_t n = in.size();
        for (auto* v : {&x, &y, &z, &vx, &vy, &vz, &mass}) v->reserve(n);
        id.reserve(n);
        for (const Particle& p : in) {
            x.push_back(p.x); y.push_back(p.y); z.push_back(p.z);
            vx.push_back(p.vx); vy.push_back(p.vy); vz.push_back(p.vz);
            mass.push_back(p.mass); id.push_back(p.id);
        }
    }
    std::size_t size() const { return x.size(); }

    void integrate(float dt) {                       // reads 6 streams, writes 3: all sequential
        const std::size_t n = size();
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) x[i] += vx[i] * dt;
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) y[i] += vy[i] * dt;
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) z[i] += vz[i] * dt;
    }
    double total_mass() const {                      // touches only one array
        double s = 0;
        for (float m : mass) s += m;
        return s;
    }
    Particle get(std::size_t i) const {              // gathering one entity costs 8 loads
        return {x[i], y[i], z[i], vx[i], vy[i], vz[i], mass[i], id[i]};
    }
};

static void integrate_aos(std::vector<Particle>& ps, float dt) {
    for (Particle& p : ps) { p.x += p.vx * dt; p.y += p.vy * dt; p.z += p.vz * dt; }
}

int main() {
    std::vector<Particle> aos;
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i)
        aos.push_back({float(i), 0, 0, 1.0f, 0.5f, -0.25f, 1.0f + float(i % 3), i});
    ParticleSystem soa(aos);

    for (int step = 0; step < 10; ++step) { integrate_aos(aos, 0.1f); soa.integrate(0.1f); }

    bool same = true;
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < aos.size(); ++i) {
        Particle s = soa.get(i);
        same = same && s.x == aos[i].x && s.y == aos[i].y && s.z == aos[i].z && s.id == aos[i].id;
    }
    std::printf("same results: %s\n", same ? "yes" : "no");
    std::printf("particle 3: (%.2f, %.2f, %.2f)\n", soa.get(3).x, soa.get(3).y, soa.get(3).z);
    std::printf("total mass %.0f\n", soa.total_mass());
}
same results: yes
particle 3: (4.00, 0.50, -0.25)
total mass 1999

Complexity and pitfalls. O(n) per step either way; the gain is bandwidth (only used bytes cross the memory bus) and SIMD. Pitfalls: letting the field vectors get out of sync in length (wrap them in one class and never expose push_back on a single field), erasing from the middle (every array must shift; use swap-with-last if order does not matter), and expecting SoA to help code that reads whole particles at random. Floating-point results match here because both versions perform the same operations in the same order.
