CodeWrite a layout calculator: given a list of fields with size and alignment, compute each field's offset, the padding and the struct's sizeof under the usual C/Itanium rules, then compute the order that minimises the size. Check your numbers against the compiler's sizeof for the real structs.

Answer

Approach. Walk the fields keeping a running offset: round the offset up to the field's alignment, place the field, add its size. The struct's alignment is the maximum field alignment, and the final size is the offset rounded up to it. For fundamental types (size a multiple of alignment), sorting by decreasing alignment gives the minimum size, and a stable sort keeps related fields together within each alignment class.

#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

struct Field { const char* name; std::size_t size, align; };

// The C/Itanium layout rule: each member goes at the next offset that is a multiple of
// its alignment; the struct's alignment is the largest member alignment, and its size
// is rounded up to that so that arrays keep every element aligned.
static std::size_t layout_size(const std::vector<Field>& fs, bool print) {
    std::size_t off = 0, max_align = 1;
    for (const Field& f : fs) {
        std::size_t at = (off + f.align - 1) / f.align * f.align;
        if (print && at != off) std::printf("  [%zu bytes padding]\n", at - off);
        if (print) std::printf("  %-8s offset %2zu size %zu\n", f.name, at, f.size);
        off = at + f.size;
        max_align = std::max(max_align, f.align);
    }
    std::size_t total = (off + max_align - 1) / max_align * max_align;
    if (print && total != off) std::printf("  [%zu bytes tail padding]\n", total - off);
    return total;
}

static std::vector<Field> best_order(std::vector<Field> fs) {
    std::stable_sort(fs.begin(), fs.end(), [](const Field& a, const Field& b) { return a.align > b.align; });
    return fs;
}

struct Order {                         // as written by the original author
    bool active;
    double price;
    std::int16_t venue;
    std::int64_t qty;
    char side;
    std::int32_t trader;
    bool hidden;
};
struct OrderSorted {                   // largest alignment first
    double price;
    std::int64_t qty;
    std::int32_t trader;
    std::int16_t venue;
    bool active;
    char side;
    bool hidden;
};

int main() {
    std::vector<Field> fs = {{"active", 1, 1}, {"price", 8, 8}, {"venue", 2, 2}, {"qty", 8, 8},
                             {"side", 1, 1}, {"trader", 4, 4}, {"hidden", 1, 1}};
    std::printf("declared order:\n");
    std::size_t a = layout_size(fs, true);
    std::printf("computed %zu, compiler says %zu\n", a, sizeof(Order));
    std::printf("sorted by alignment:\n");
    std::size_t b = layout_size(best_order(fs), true);
    std::printf("computed %zu, compiler says %zu\n", b, sizeof(OrderSorted));
    std::printf("saved per million orders: %zu KB\n", (a - b) * 1'000'000 / 1000);
}
declared order:
  active   offset  0 size 1
  [7 bytes padding]
  price    offset  8 size 8
  venue    offset 16 size 2
  [6 bytes padding]
  qty      offset 24 size 8
  side     offset 32 size 1
  [3 bytes padding]
  trader   offset 36 size 4
  hidden   offset 40 size 1
  [7 bytes tail padding]
computed 48, compiler says 48
sorted by alignment:
  price    offset  0 size 8
  qty      offset  8 size 8
  trader   offset 16 size 4
  venue    offset 20 size 2
  active   offset 22 size 1
  side     offset 23 size 1
  hidden   offset 24 size 1
  [7 bytes tail padding]
computed 32, compiler says 32
saved per million orders: 16000 KB

Complexity and pitfalls. O(n log n) for the sort. Pitfalls: forgetting tail padding (the most common error in interviews), rounding with % on non-power-of-two values incorrectly, and assuming the rule holds for bit-fields, empty members with [[no_unique_address]], virtual bases or #pragma pack, which all change it. The 25 bytes of data cannot fit in less than 32 with 8-byte alignment, so the sorted order is optimal. In real code, also check that the hot fields still share a line after reordering.

Estimated rating: ~1300 · simple simulation, but you must know the alignment and tail-padding rules exactly

CodeImplement a sharded counter for many threads: add(shard, v) must not suffer false sharing, total() may be called concurrently with writers, and the slots must be on separate cache lines on both x86 and Apple silicon, including when allocated on the heap. Verify the slot spacing and alignment at run time.

Answer

Approach. Put the alignment on the slot type, struct alignas(128) Slot, so its size rounds up to 128 and array elements are 128 bytes apart. Allocate the array with new Slot[n], which since C++17 calls the aligned operator new. Each thread updates only its own slot with a relaxed atomic add (no ordering is needed for a statistic), and total() sums relaxed loads, which gives a value that was true at some point during the summation for each slot.

#include <atomic>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <new>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

// 128 covers Apple silicon's 128-byte lines and Intel's adjacent-line prefetcher, which
// pulls 64-byte lines in pairs. std::hardware_destructive_interference_size is an
// alternative, but it is a compile-time guess that can differ from the machine.
inline constexpr std::size_t kLine = 128;

class ShardedCounter {
    struct alignas(kLine) Slot {
        std::atomic<long> value{0};
    };
    static_assert(sizeof(Slot) == kLine && alignof(Slot) == kLine);
    std::unique_ptr<Slot[]> slots_;   // C++17 aligned new honours alignas(128)
    std::size_t n_;

public:
    explicit ShardedCounter(std::size_t shards) : slots_(new Slot[shards]), n_(shards) {}
    void add(std::size_t shard, long v) { slots_[shard % n_].value.fetch_add(v, std::memory_order_relaxed); }
    long total() const {                     // a racy-but-safe snapshot while writers run
        long s = 0;
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n_; ++i) s += slots_[i].value.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        return s;
    }
    std::size_t distance_bytes() const {
        return static_cast<std::size_t>(reinterpret_cast<const char*>(&slots_[1]) - reinterpret_cast<const char*>(&slots_[0]));
    }
    bool aligned() const { return reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t>(slots_.get()) % kLine == 0; }
};

int main() {
    const int threads = 4;
    const long per_thread = 200'000;
    ShardedCounter c(threads);
    std::vector<std::thread> pool;
    for (int t = 0; t < threads; ++t)
        pool.emplace_back([&c, t] { for (long i = 0; i < per_thread; ++i) c.add(t, 1); });
    for (auto& th : pool) th.join();
    std::printf("total %ld\n", c.total());
    std::printf("slot distance %zu bytes, base aligned: %s\n", c.distance_bytes(), c.aligned() ? "yes" : "no");
}
total 800000
slot distance 128 bytes, base aligned: yes

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) add, O(shards) total; memory 128 bytes per shard. Pitfalls: alignas on an array variable (aligns only the start), 64-byte padding on Apple silicon, using a plain long instead of an atomic when total() runs concurrently (a data race that TSan reports), and choosing the shard by thread id hash with too few shards, which reintroduces contention on the atomic itself. Production versions (for example in Folly or the Linux kernel's per-CPU counters) shard by CPU rather than thread.

Estimated rating: ~1300 · small code, but it tests alignment rules, C++17 aligned new and memory orders

CodeWrite a cache-friendly (blocked) transpose of a row-major rows × cols float matrix into a cols × rows matrix. It must handle sizes that are not multiples of the tile size and non-square matrices, and you must test it against a naive version.

Answer

Approach. The naive transpose reads along rows but writes down columns, so one side is always strided. Process the matrix in B × B tiles: within a tile, the B source lines and B destination lines all fit in L1 (32 × 32 floats is 4 KB each side), so each fetched line is used fully before eviction. Clamp each tile's end with std::min for the edges.

#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// out = transpose(in), where in is rows × cols, row-major, and out is cols × rows.
static void transpose_naive(const float* in, float* out, std::size_t rows, std::size_t cols) {
    for (std::size_t r = 0; r < rows; ++r)
        for (std::size_t c = 0; c < cols; ++c)
            out[c * rows + r] = in[r * cols + c];          // writes stride through memory
}

template <std::size_t B = 32>
static void transpose_blocked(const float* in, float* out, std::size_t rows, std::size_t cols) {
    for (std::size_t r0 = 0; r0 < rows; r0 += B)
        for (std::size_t c0 = 0; c0 < cols; c0 += B) {
            const std::size_t r1 = std::min(r0 + B, rows), c1 = std::min(c0 + B, cols);
            for (std::size_t r = r0; r < r1; ++r)           // one B × B tile: B lines read,
                for (std::size_t c = c0; c < c1; ++c)       // B lines written, all stay in L1
                    out[c * rows + r] = in[r * cols + c];
        }
}

int main() {
    bool all_ok = true;
    for (auto [rows, cols] : {std::pair<std::size_t, std::size_t>{1000, 1000}, {37, 1029}, {1, 5}, {64, 64}}) {
        std::vector<float> in(rows * cols), a(rows * cols), b(rows * cols);
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < in.size(); ++i) in[i] = float(i);
        transpose_naive(in.data(), a.data(), rows, cols);
        transpose_blocked(in.data(), b.data(), rows, cols);
        bool ok = a == b && (rows < 2 || b[1] == in[cols]);  // out[0][1] == in[1][0]
        std::printf("%zu x %zu: %s\n", rows, cols, ok ? "match" : "MISMATCH");
        all_ok = all_ok && ok;
    }
    std::printf("%s\n", all_ok ? "all tests passed" : "failure");
}
1000 x 1000: match
37 x 1029: match
1 x 5: match
64 x 64: match
all tests passed

Complexity and pitfalls. O(rows × cols) for both versions; the blocked one reduces cache misses from about one per element to about two per line. Measured on the M1 (see the prefetching section): about 6 times faster at 4000 × 4000, no gain at 2000 × 2000, and only modest gains at 4096 × 4096, where power-of-two rows map to the same cache sets. Pitfalls: integer overflow in r * cols with int indices on large matrices (use std::size_t), wrong edge handling, and tuning B on one machine only. Further steps are padding rows away from powers of two, transposing 4 × 4 or 8 × 8 micro-tiles in SIMD registers, and recursive (cache-oblivious) splitting.

Estimated rating: ~1400 · classic loop tiling; the edge cases and the explanation matter more than the code

CodeImplement an open-addressing hash map from uint64_t keys to values with linear probing, power-of-two capacity, a maximum load factor of 7/8, insert_or_assign, find and erase without tombstones. Test it against std::unordered_map with random operations.

Answer

Approach. Store entries in one contiguous array and keep occupancy in a dense byte array. Hash with a strong mixer (splitmix64) and mask with capacity - 1. Probe forwards until the key or an empty slot. For erase, use backward-shift deletion: after emptying slot i, scan forward through the cluster and move back any entry whose home position means its probe sequence passes through i; stop at the first empty slot. That keeps the invariant "no empty slot between an entry and its home", so lookups can stop at the first empty slot and no tombstones are needed.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <random>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// Open addressing with linear probing: one contiguous array, so a lookup usually
// touches one or two cache lines instead of chasing a bucket's linked list.
template <class V>
class FlatHashMap {
    struct Slot { std::uint64_t key; V value; };
    std::vector<Slot> slots_;
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> full_;   // 1 = occupied: dense metadata, like a Swiss table's control bytes
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    std::size_t mask_ = 0;

    static std::uint64_t mix(std::uint64_t k) {   // splitmix64 finaliser: spreads nearby keys
        k ^= k >> 30; k *= 0xbf58476d1ce4e5b9ULL;
        k ^= k >> 27; k *= 0x94d049bb133111ebULL;
        return k ^ (k >> 31);
    }
    std::size_t home(std::uint64_t k) const { return static_cast<std::size_t>(mix(k)) & mask_; }

    void rehash(std::size_t cap) {
        std::vector<Slot> old_slots = std::move(slots_);
        std::vector<std::uint8_t> old_full = std::move(full_);
        slots_.assign(cap, Slot{});
        full_.assign(cap, 0);
        mask_ = cap - 1;
        size_ = 0;
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < old_slots.size(); ++i)
            if (old_full[i]) insert_or_assign(old_slots[i].key, std::move(old_slots[i].value));
    }

public:
    FlatHashMap() { rehash(16); }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }

    void insert_or_assign(std::uint64_t key, V value) {
        if ((size_ + 1) * 8 > slots_.size() * 7) rehash(slots_.size() * 2);   // max load 7/8
        for (std::size_t i = home(key);; i = (i + 1) & mask_) {
            if (!full_[i]) { slots_[i] = Slot{key, std::move(value)}; full_[i] = 1; ++size_; return; }
            if (slots_[i].key == key) { slots_[i].value = std::move(value); return; }
        }
    }
    V* find(std::uint64_t key) {
        for (std::size_t i = home(key); full_[i]; i = (i + 1) & mask_)
            if (slots_[i].key == key) return &slots_[i].value;
        return nullptr;
    }
    bool erase(std::uint64_t key) {
        std::size_t i = home(key);
        while (full_[i] && slots_[i].key != key) i = (i + 1) & mask_;
        if (!full_[i]) return false;
        // Backward-shift deletion: pull later members of the cluster into the hole, so no
        // tombstones are needed and lookups can stop at the first empty slot.
        for (std::size_t j = (i + 1) & mask_; full_[j]; j = (j + 1) & mask_) {
            std::size_t h = home(slots_[j].key);
            if (((j - h) & mask_) >= ((j - i) & mask_)) {   // slot j may legally move back to i
                slots_[i] = std::move(slots_[j]);
                i = j;
            }
        }
        full_[i] = 0;
        slots_[i] = Slot{};
        --size_;
        return true;
    }
};

int main() {
    FlatHashMap<int> m;
    std::unordered_map<std::uint64_t, int> ref;
    std::mt19937_64 rng(2026);
    int mismatches = 0;
    for (int step = 0; step < 200'000; ++step) {
        std::uint64_t k = rng() % 5000;                 // small key space forces collisions and erasures
        switch (rng() % 3) {
        case 0: m.insert_or_assign(k, step); ref[k] = step; break;
        case 1: mismatches += m.erase(k) != (ref.erase(k) == 1); break;
        default: {
            int* v = m.find(k);
            auto it = ref.find(k);
            mismatches += (v == nullptr) != (it == ref.end()) || (v && *v != it->second);
        }
        }
    }
    std::printf("size %zu vs %zu, mismatches %d\n", m.size(), ref.size(), mismatches);
}
size 2485 vs 2485, mismatches 0

Complexity and pitfalls. Expected O(1) for all operations at a bounded load factor; a lookup usually touches one or two cache lines, against at least two dependent misses in a node-based table. Pitfalls: a weak hash with power-of-two masking (sequential keys collide into long clusters; identity hashing is the classic mistake), the wrap-around arithmetic in the backward-shift condition (do it modulo the capacity), forgetting that rehash invalidates pointers returned by find, and letting the load factor approach 1, where linear probing degrades sharply. This version requires V to be default constructible; production tables (Swiss tables) keep control bytes separately, use SIMD to test 16 slots at once, and construct values in raw storage.

Estimated rating: ~1800 · backward-shift deletion and the probe-distance condition are easy to get subtly wrong

CodeImplement FlatMap<K, V>, an ordered map stored as a sorted std::vector<std::pair<K, V>>, with insert_or_assign, find, erase, ordered iteration, and a bulk assign_unsorted that sorts once and keeps the last value for duplicate keys. Test it against std::map.

Answer

Approach. Every operation starts with std::lower_bound on the key, a binary search over contiguous memory. Insert and erase use vector::insert and vector::erase, which shift the tail. For bulk loading, appending everything and sorting once is O(n log n), against O(n²) for repeated sorted inserts; a stable sort followed by an in-place deduplication pass gives "last write wins".

#include <algorithm>
#include <cstdio>
#include <map>
#include <random>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// A sorted vector of pairs: lookups are a binary search over contiguous memory,
// iteration is a linear scan. Insertion is O(n) (a memmove), so it suits
// "build once, read many" data such as configuration, symbol tables or order-book levels.
template <class K, class V>
class FlatMap {
    std::vector<std::pair<K, V>> data_;
    auto lower(const K& k) {
        return std::lower_bound(data_.begin(), data_.end(), k, [](const auto& p, const K& key) { return p.first < key; });
    }
    auto lower(const K& k) const {
        return std::lower_bound(data_.begin(), data_.end(), k, [](const auto& p, const K& key) { return p.first < key; });
    }

public:
    void reserve(std::size_t n) { data_.reserve(n); }
    std::size_t size() const { return data_.size(); }
    bool insert_or_assign(const K& k, V v) {           // true if a new key was inserted
        auto it = lower(k);
        if (it != data_.end() && it->first == k) { it->second = std::move(v); return false; }
        data_.insert(it, {k, std::move(v)});
        return true;
    }
    const V* find(const K& k) const {
        auto it = lower(k);
        return it != data_.end() && it->first == k ? &it->second : nullptr;
    }
    bool erase(const K& k) {
        auto it = lower(k);
        if (it == data_.end() || it->first != k) return false;
        data_.erase(it);
        return true;
    }
    // Bulk build: append unsorted, then sort and deduplicate once (last write wins).
    template <class It>
    void assign_unsorted(It first, It last) {
        data_.assign(first, last);
        std::stable_sort(data_.begin(), data_.end(), [](const auto& a, const auto& b) { return a.first < b.first; });
        auto out = data_.begin();
        for (auto it = data_.begin(); it != data_.end(); ++it) {
            if (out != data_.begin() && std::prev(out)->first == it->first) *std::prev(out) = std::move(*it);
            else {
                if (out != it) *out = std::move(*it);   // never self-move-assign
                ++out;
            }
        }
        data_.erase(out, data_.end());
    }
    auto begin() const { return data_.begin(); }
    auto end() const { return data_.end(); }
};

int main() {
    FlatMap<int, std::string> fm;
    std::map<int, std::string> ref;
    std::mt19937 rng(19);
    int mismatches = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 20'000; ++i) {
        int k = static_cast<int>(rng() % 500);
        std::string v = "v" + std::to_string(i);
        if (rng() % 4 == 0) mismatches += fm.erase(k) != (ref.erase(k) == 1);
        else { fm.insert_or_assign(k, v); ref[k] = v; }
    }
    for (const auto& [k, v] : ref) {
        const std::string* got = fm.find(k);
        mismatches += !got || *got != v;
    }
    std::printf("size %zu vs %zu, mismatches %d, ordered: %s\n", fm.size(), ref.size(), mismatches,
                std::is_sorted(fm.begin(), fm.end()) ? "yes" : "no");

    std::vector<std::pair<int, std::string>> raw = {{3, "c"}, {1, "a"}, {3, "C"}, {2, "b"}};
    FlatMap<int, std::string> bulk;
    bulk.assign_unsorted(raw.begin(), raw.end());
    for (const auto& [k, v] : bulk) std::printf("%d=%s ", k, v.c_str());
    std::printf("\n");
}
size 374 vs 374, mismatches 0, ordered: yes
1=a 2=b 3=C

Complexity and pitfalls. Lookup O(log n) with excellent constants (the last few probes of the binary search share lines), iteration at memory bandwidth, insert and erase O(n). It beats std::map for read-heavy maps up to large sizes, and C++23 standardises the idea as std::flat_map (with keys and values in separate containers, which is even more cache friendly for key searches). Pitfalls: insert and erase invalidate all iterators and references, unlike std::map, and a self-move-assignment in the deduplication loop (*out = std::move(*it) when out == it) can leave a std::string value empty (a self-moved object is only "valid but unspecified"), which is why the code checks out != it. The bulk-load test with a duplicate key is what catches it.

Estimated rating: ~1400 · simple container, with an in-place dedupe that hides a self-move bug

Cheat sheet

Theory
  • Latency ladder: L1 about 1 ns, L2 about 4 ns, L3 about 15 ns, DRAM about 100 ns; numbers vary by machine, ratios do not. Dependent misses serialise, independent ones overlap.
  • Lines: 64 bytes on x86 and most Arm cores, 128 on Apple silicon. hardware_destructive_interference_size is 64 on x86-64 and 256 on arm64 with GCC and Clang, and it is a compile-time guess.
  • Contiguous beats node-based: vector over list (3 times faster in allocation order, about 200 times when scattered, on the M1), flat or open-addressing maps over std::map/unordered_map for read-heavy work.
  • Layout: order members by decreasing alignment, split hot from cold fields, choose SoA for field-wise loops and AoS for entity-wise access.
  • False sharing: threads writing different variables on one line; fix with alignas(128) types (not alignas on an array) or thread-local accumulation. About 22 times on the M1 with 4 threads.
  • Prefetch: hardware handles sequential and strided access; software prefetch only for unpredictable addresses known early, and it gave nothing here. Block (tile) loops whose working set exceeds the cache, and avoid power-of-two strides.
  • TLB: 4 KB pages cover a few MB of TLB reach; huge pages (2 MB, THP or MAP_HUGETLB) fix random access over large heaps.
  • Measure: perf stat, perf c2c, cachegrind on Linux; Instruments CPU Counters on macOS. Name the machine with every number.

Part F · Move semantics and value passing · Chapter 20

Move semantics

Moves let an object hand its resources to another object instead of duplicating them. This chapter covers value categories, rvalue references, what std::move really does, how to write the move constructor and move assignment operator, and why noexcept decides whether std::vector moves or copies. Interviewers use this topic to separate people who memorised "move is faster" from people who can predict which special member runs.

TheoryDrillsCoding· about 4 hours· prerequisites: Ch 1 (rule of 3/5/0), Ch 11 (unique_ptr)

Why moves exist

Theory

Mental model. A resource-owning type (a string, a vector, a buffer, a file handle) is a small "header" object that points at something expensive: heap memory, a kernel descriptor, a thread. Copying such an object means duplicating the expensive part. When the source is about to die anyway (a temporary, or a local you will never touch again), that duplication is wasted work. A move copies only the header and leaves the source in an empty but valid state, so its destructor frees nothing.

Before C++11 the language had no way to tell "an object you may plunder" from "an object you must preserve". Functions returning a std::vector by value relied on the optimiser eliding copies, and code like v.push_back(std::string(1000, 'x')) allocated twice. C++11 added a new reference type, T&&, which binds only to expressions the program has marked as expendable, plus two new special members that overload on it.

A move only pays off when the type owns something indirectly. For an int, a double, a plain struct of numbers or a std::array<int, 1000>, moving is exactly copying: there is no pointer to steal, so all the bytes must be transferred either way.

Know this cold

Move semantics is an optimisation of copying for the case where the source will not be used again. It is also the only way to transfer ownership of types that cannot be copied at all, such as std::unique_ptr, std::thread and std::fstream. (Some types, like std::mutex, can be neither copied nor moved.)

Value categories

Theory

Every expression in C++ has a type and a value category. The category decides which references can bind to it, and therefore which overload (copy or move) is chosen. C++11 defines three primary categories and two mixed ones, built from two properties:

  • Has identity: the expression refers to an object with an address you could take (a variable, *p, a[i]).
  • Can be moved from: the program has said the object's resources may be taken (a temporary, or the result of std::move).

Which category is this expression?

The rule that trips people up is the first one: the category is a property of the expression, not of the variable's declared type. A variable declared int&& r is an rvalue reference, but the expression r is an lvalue, because it has a name and you can take its address.

ExpressionCategoryWhy
x (any named variable, including T&& r)lvalueA name always denotes an object with identity
42, true, nullptrprvalueLiteral with no object behind it
"hello"lvalueString literals are arrays with static storage
x + 1, x++, &xprvalueBuilt-in operators producing a new value
++x, *p, a[i], x = ylvalueThey return the object itself
f() returning TprvalueReturn by value
f() returning T&lvalueReturn by lvalue reference
f() returning T&&, std::move(x), static_cast<T&&>(x)xvalueReturns an rvalue reference to an existing object
S{}.m (member of a prvalue)xvalueTemporary materialisation creates the object, then .m refers into it
[]{ }, S{}, thisprvaluePure values

You can make the compiler tell you. decltype((e)) with double parentheses yields T& for an lvalue, T&& for an xvalue and plain T for a prvalue:

#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>

template <class T> struct cat      { static constexpr const char* v = "prvalue"; };
template <class T> struct cat<T&>  { static constexpr const char* v = "lvalue"; };
template <class T> struct cat<T&&> { static constexpr const char* v = "xvalue"; };
#define CAT(...) std::printf("%s: %s\n", #__VA_ARGS__, cat<decltype((__VA_ARGS__))>::v)

struct S { int m; };
static int g = 0;
static int& ref() { return g; }
static int&& rref() { return std::move(g); }

int main() {
    int x = 1;
    int&& r = 5;
    CAT(x);
    CAT(42);
    CAT(x + 1);
    CAT(++x);
    CAT(x++);
    CAT("hi");
    CAT(r);
    CAT(std::move(x));
    CAT(S{});
    CAT(S{}.m);
    CAT(ref());
    CAT(rref());
}
x: lvalue
42: prvalue
x + 1: prvalue
++x: lvalue
x++: prvalue
"hi": lvalue
r: lvalue
std::move(x): xvalue
S{}: prvalue
S{}.m: xvalue
ref(): lvalue
rref(): xvalue

What binds to what

Parameterlvalueconst lvaluervalue (xvalue or prvalue)const rvalue
T&yesnonono
const T&yesyesyes (lifetime extended for prvalues)yes
T&&nonoyesno
const T&&nonoyesyes
T (by value)copycopymove (or elided for prvalues)copy

When both const T& and T&& overloads are viable for an rvalue, the rvalue reference wins (a better reference binding, [over.ics.rank]). That single rule is what makes moves happen automatically for temporaries.

#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>

static void f(int&)  { std::puts("f(int&)"); }
static void f(int&&) { std::puts("f(int&&)"); }

int main() {
    int x = 1;
    int&& r = std::move(x);   // r is an rvalue reference variable...
    f(x);
    f(r);                     // ...but the expression r is an lvalue
    f(std::move(r));
    f(2);
    f(static_cast<int&&>(x));
}
f(int&)
f(int&)
f(int&&)
f(int&&)
f(int&&)

Interview trap

"Inside void g(Widget&& w), is w an rvalue?" No. w has a name, so it is an lvalue. Passing it on as h(w) copies. You must write h(std::move(w)). The design is deliberate: a named object may be used several times in the body, and an implicit move on the first use would leave later uses looking at a gutted object.

std::move is only a cast

Theory

std::move moves nothing. It is an unconditional cast to an rvalue reference, which turns its argument into an xvalue. The actual move happens later, if and when overload resolution picks a function taking T&& (usually a move constructor or move assignment operator). If no such function exists, the cast is harmless and the copy runs.

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <type_traits>

namespace my {
template <class T>
constexpr std::remove_reference_t<T>&& move(T&& t) noexcept {
    return static_cast<std::remove_reference_t<T>&&>(t);
}
}

int main() {
    std::string a = "payload";
    static_assert(std::is_same_v<decltype(my::move(a)), std::string&&>);
    std::string b = my::move(a);         // the move constructor does the work
    std::printf("b=%s a.size()=%zu\n", b.c_str(), a.size());

    const std::string c = "const";
    static_assert(std::is_same_v<decltype(my::move(c)), const std::string&&>);
    std::string d = my::move(c);         // const string&& binds to const string&: a copy
    std::printf("d=%s c=%s\n", d.c_str(), c.c_str());
}
b=payload a.size()=0
d=const c=const

The parameter is a forwarding reference (T&& in a deduced context, see Ch 21), so move accepts lvalues and rvalues. remove_reference_t is needed because for an lvalue argument T is deduced as std::string&, and T&& would collapse back to std::string&. The printed a.size()=0 is what libstdc++ and libc++ do; the standard only promises a valid, unspecified state.

Moving a const object silently copies

std::move(c) on a const object yields const T&&. The move constructor takes T&& and cannot bind to it, but the copy constructor's const T& can. The code compiles, runs and copies, with no warning from either compiler at -Wall -Wextra. The same happens for const data members (moving the enclosing object copies the member) and for const locals you return: const std::string s = ...; return s; can still use NRVO, but if NRVO does not apply, the implicit move becomes a copy.

#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>

struct T {
    T() = default;
    T(const T&) { std::puts("copy"); }
    T(T&&) noexcept { std::puts("move"); }
};

int main() {
    const T a{};
    T b = std::move(a);   // const T&& -> picks T(const T&)
    T c = std::move(b);
}
copy
move

Writing the move constructor and move assignment

Theory

The move constructor has the signature T(T&& other) noexcept; move assignment is T& operator=(T&& other) noexcept. Each one does three things: take the source's resources, leave the source in a state its destructor (and assignment) can cope with, and for assignment, release what *this owned before.

A full Buffer with all five special members

#include <cstdio>
#include <cstring>
#include <utility>

class Buffer {
public:
    explicit Buffer(std::size_t n) : size_(n), data_(new char[n]()) { std::printf("ctor(%zu)\n", n); }
    ~Buffer() { std::printf("dtor(%zu)\n", size_); delete[] data_; }

    Buffer(const Buffer& o) : size_(o.size_), data_(new char[o.size_]) {
        std::memcpy(data_, o.data_, size_);
        std::printf("copy(%zu)\n", size_);
    }
    Buffer(Buffer&& o) noexcept
        : size_(std::exchange(o.size_, 0)), data_(std::exchange(o.data_, nullptr)) {
        std::printf("move(%zu)\n", size_);
    }
    Buffer& operator=(const Buffer& o) {
        if (this != &o) {
            char* p = new char[o.size_];      // allocate first: strong guarantee
            std::memcpy(p, o.data_, o.size_);
            delete[] data_;
            data_ = p;
            size_ = o.size_;
        }
        std::printf("copy=(%zu)\n", size_);
        return *this;
    }
    Buffer& operator=(Buffer&& o) noexcept {
        if (this != &o) {
            delete[] data_;
            data_ = std::exchange(o.data_, nullptr);
            size_ = std::exchange(o.size_, 0);
        }
        std::printf("move=(%zu)\n", size_);
        return *this;
    }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }

private:
    std::size_t size_;
    char* data_;
};

int main() {
    Buffer a(100);
    Buffer b = a;
    Buffer c = std::move(a);
    std::printf("a=%zu b=%zu c=%zu\n", a.size(), b.size(), c.size());
    b = std::move(c);
    std::printf("b=%zu c=%zu\n", b.size(), c.size());
}
ctor(100)
copy(100)
move(100)
a=0 b=100 c=100
move=(100)
b=100 c=0
dtor(0)
dtor(100)
dtor(0)

Destruction runs in reverse order of construction: c (empty), b, then a (empty). Both moved-from objects print dtor(0) and call delete[] nullptr, which is a no-op.

std::exchange: "take the value and leave this behind"

std::exchange(obj, new_value) (header <utility>, C++14) assigns new_value to obj and returns the old value. It turns the two-step "copy the pointer, then null the source" into one expression, which is why it is idiomatic in move constructors' member initialiser lists. It is also constexpr since C++20 and conditionally noexcept since C++23.

Alternatives: swap-based move, copy-and-swap, unified assignment

Three common shapes of move assignment:

  • Release then steal (as above). Needs a self-check, otherwise x = std::move(x) deletes the buffer and then steals the dangling pointer from itself.
  • Swap: swap(*this, o); return *this;. Self-safe without a check. The old resources are released later, when o dies, which may surprise people who expect a lock or file to close at the assignment.
  • Unified assignment: T& operator=(T o) noexcept { swap(*this, o); return *this; }. One function serves both copy and move assignment (the parameter is copy- or move-constructed by the caller). It costs an extra move for rvalues and loses the chance to reuse the existing buffer on copy (std::vector's copy assignment reuses capacity, copy-and-swap never does).

Self-move-assignment

The standard library's rule ([res.on.arguments]) is that a function taking an rvalue reference may assume it is the only reference to that argument. Self-move-assignment of a standard type therefore only promises a valid but unspecified result. For your own types, either check this != &o or use swap so that x = std::move(x) leaves x usable. It happens in real code through aliasing, for example v[i] = std::move(v[j]) with i == j inside a generic algorithm. GCC's -Wself-move (in -Wall since GCC 13) catches the literal spelling.

The moved-from state

Theory

After a move, the source is a live object: its destructor will run, and you may assign to it. The standard's wording for library types ([lib.types.movedfrom]) is that a moved-from object is in a valid but unspecified state. Valid means every operation without preconditions works: size(), clear(), assignment, destruction. Unspecified means you cannot assume its value. Calling front() on a moved-from vector is wrong because front() has the precondition "not empty", which you cannot know holds.

TypeState after move construction from itGuaranteed?
std::unique_ptrnullyes, specified
std::shared_ptr, std::weak_ptremptyyes, specified
std::thread, std::jthreadnot joinableyes, specified
std::unique_lockno mutex, not owningyes, specified
std::vector, std::stringempty in libstdc++, libc++ and MSVCno, only "valid but unspecified"
std::optional<T>still engaged, holding a moved-from Tyes, has_value() is unchanged
int, raw pointers, trivially copyable typesunchanged (move is a copy)yes

For your own types, make the moved-from state the cheapest valid state, usually the same as default-constructed. Keep the class invariants: if the class promises "data_ is never null", the move constructor must either allocate (and then it cannot be noexcept) or you must weaken the invariant to allow a null state. This is why std::list in some implementations had a throwing move constructor (it allocated a sentinel node), and why "never empty" designs fight with moves.

Tip

The safe rule for any type: after std::move(x), only destroy x or assign a new value to it. Reusing a moved-from std::string after s.clear() or s = "new" is fine and common in loops.

noexcept on moves and vector reallocation

Theory

The problem. std::vector::push_back gives the strong exception guarantee: if it throws, the vector is unchanged. When the vector is full it allocates a bigger buffer and must transfer the old elements. If it moves them and the third move throws, the first two elements are already gutted in the old buffer, and the original state cannot be restored (moving them back could throw too). Copying keeps the old buffer intact, so a throw just discards the new buffer.

The rule. The library uses std::move_if_noexcept for relocation: it moves when the move constructor is noexcept (or the type is not copyable at all), and copies otherwise. A move constructor that is not marked noexcept, even one that never throws in practice, turns every reallocation into a full deep copy.

#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

template <bool NoThrow>
struct Item {
    Item() = default;
    Item(const Item&) { ++copies; }
    Item(Item&&) noexcept(NoThrow) { ++moves; }
    static inline int copies = 0;
    static inline int moves = 0;
};

template <bool NoThrow>
static void run(const char* label) {
    std::vector<Item<NoThrow>> v;
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) v.emplace_back();
    std::printf("%-18s copies=%d moves=%d\n", label, Item<NoThrow>::copies, Item<NoThrow>::moves);
}

int main() {
    run<true>("noexcept move:");
    run<false>("throwing move:");
}
noexcept move:     copies=0 moves=1023
throwing move:     copies=1023 moves=0

Both libstdc++ and libc++ grow capacity 1, 2, 4, ..., 1024 when appending one element at a time from empty, so 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 512 = 1023 elements are relocated. MSVC grows by 1.5x and would print a different count, but the pattern is the same: all moves in the first line, all copies in the second.

std::move_if_noexcept

The helper (header <utility>) returns const T& when T has a potentially throwing move constructor and is copy constructible, and T&& otherwise. A move-only type with a throwing move (rare) still gets moved, and vector falls back to the basic guarantee for it.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>

struct Risky {
    Risky() = default;
    Risky(const Risky&) { std::puts("Risky copy"); }
    Risky(Risky&&) { std::puts("Risky move"); }      // not noexcept
};
struct Safe {
    Safe() = default;
    Safe(const Safe&) { std::puts("Safe copy"); }
    Safe(Safe&&) noexcept { std::puts("Safe move"); }
};

int main() {
    Risky r;
    Safe s;
    Risky r2 = std::move_if_noexcept(r);
    Safe s2 = std::move_if_noexcept(s);
    static_assert(std::is_same_v<decltype(std::move_if_noexcept(r)), const Risky&>);
    static_assert(std::is_same_v<decltype(std::move_if_noexcept(s)), Safe&&>);
    auto p = std::make_unique<int>(1);
    static_assert(std::is_same_v<decltype(std::move_if_noexcept(p)), std::unique_ptr<int>&&>);
}
Risky copy
Safe move

Know this cold

Mark move constructors, move assignment operators and swap noexcept whenever they cannot throw. Implicitly generated and = default moves are noexcept automatically when every member's move is. Check with static_assert(std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<T>).

Implicit moves, the rule of five and the rule of zero

Theory

The compiler declares an implicit move constructor and move assignment operator only if the class has no user-declared copy constructor, copy assignment operator, move operation (of the other kind) or destructor ([class.copy.ctor]/8). "User-declared" includes = default and = delete. The implicit move moves each base and member in declaration order (memberwise std::move).

You declaredefault ctordestructorcopy ctor / copy =move ctor / move =
nothingimplicitimplicitimplicitimplicit
any constructornot declaredimplicitimplicitimplicit
destructorimplicityoursimplicit (deprecated)not declared: moves copy
copy ctor or copy =(not declared if copy ctor)implicityours / implicit (deprecated)not declared: moves copy
move ctor or move =(not declared if move ctor)implicitdeletedyours / not declared

"Not declared" and "deleted" differ in an important way. A not-declared move constructor does not take part in overload resolution, so T b = std::move(a) quietly falls back to the copy constructor. A deleted function does take part, and choosing it is a compile error. A move constructor that is = default but would be ill-formed (for example a member that cannot be moved) is defined as deleted and then ignored by overload resolution ([class.copy.ctor]/10), again falling back to copy.

#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>

struct Tracer {
    Tracer() = default;
    Tracer(const Tracer&) { std::puts("  copy"); }
    Tracer(Tracer&&) noexcept { std::puts("  move"); }
};

struct Plain    { Tracer t; };                                // rule of zero
struct WithDtor { Tracer t; ~WithDtor() {} };                 // move not declared
struct Fixed    { Tracer t; ~Fixed() {}
                  Fixed() = default;
                  Fixed(Fixed&&) = default;                   // brings the move back
                  Fixed(const Fixed&) = default; };           // and keeps the copy

int main() {
    std::puts("Plain:");    Plain a;    Plain b = std::move(a);
    std::puts("WithDtor:"); WithDtor c; WithDtor d = std::move(c);
    std::puts("Fixed:");    Fixed e;    Fixed f = std::move(e);
}
Plain:
  move
WithDtor:
  copy
Fixed:
  move

Interview trap

Adding a destructor "just to log something" or virtual ~Base() = default; to a class silently disables its moves. Every std::move on it becomes a copy and every vector reallocation deep-copies. For a polymorphic base, declare all five: virtual ~Base() = default; plus defaulted copy and move operations (or delete them to prevent slicing).

Rule of zero, rule of five

  • Rule of zero: classes that do not manage a resource directly declare none of the five. They hold members that manage themselves (std::string, std::vector, std::unique_ptr), and the implicit members do the right thing, including noexcept moves.
  • Rule of five: a class that does manage a resource (a raw pointer, a descriptor) declares the destructor, both copy operations and both move operations, or explicitly deletes the ones it does not support. Declaring only some of them changes the others in the ways the table shows.
  • A move-only type is the rule of five with the copies deleted: T(const T&) = delete; T& operator=(const T&) = delete; plus real moves.

A template constructor is never a move constructor. template <class U> T(U&&) does not suppress the implicit copy or move constructors, and the reverse trap (it hijacks copies of non-const lvalues) is covered in Ch 21. A constructor T(const T&&) technically is a move constructor by the standard's definition, but it cannot modify the source and so it cannot steal anything.

Moves in interfaces: returning, sinks, move-only types and ref-qualifiers

Theory

Do not write return std::move(local)

Returning a local by name already does the best possible thing. The compiler may construct the local directly in the caller's slot (NRVO), and when it cannot, the return statement treats the local as an rvalue automatically (the "implicit move", widened in C++20 by P1825 and again in C++23 by P2266). Writing return std::move(local); changes the returned expression from a name to an xvalue, which disables NRVO, so you get a guaranteed move instead of a free elision. GCC and Clang both warn with -Wpessimizing-move. Ch 24 covers NRVO in depth and Ch 23 covers guaranteed elision for prvalues.

#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>

struct T {
    T() { std::puts("ctor"); }
    T(const T&) { std::puts("copy"); }
    T(T&&) noexcept { std::puts("move"); }
    ~T() { std::puts("dtor"); }
};

static T good() { T t; return t; }
static T bad()  { T t; return std::move(t); }   // pessimising move

int main() {
    std::puts("-- good");
    T a = good();
    std::puts("-- bad");
    T b = bad();
    std::puts("-- end");
}
-- good
ctor
-- bad
ctor
move
dtor
-- end
dtor
dtor

NRVO in good() is not guaranteed by the standard, but GCC and Clang apply it to this simple shape at every optimisation level. When std::move on return is right: returning a data member from an rvalue-qualified function (return std::move(member_);), returning a member of a local (return std::move(local.field);, since local.field is not a plain name and gets no implicit move; structured bindings are a murkier case where GCC and Clang disagree, see Ch 24), or, in pre-C++20 code, returning an rvalue-reference parameter or a local whose type differs from the return type in ways the old rule did not cover (for example a Derived local returned as Base).

Sink arguments: pass by value and move

A "sink" function stores its argument (a constructor that keeps a string, a setter, push). Three ways to write it:

SignatureCaller passes lvalueCaller passes rvalueCost to write
void set(const std::string& s) { s_ = s; }1 copy1 copy (wasted)1 function
set(const std::string&) + set(std::string&&)1 copy1 move2 functions (2n for n params)
void set(std::string s) { s_ = std::move(s); }1 copy + 1 move2 moves (1 for a prvalue)1 function
template <class S> void set(S&& s) { s_ = std::forward<S>(s); }1 copy1 movetemplate, see Ch 21

Pass-by-value is the usual recommendation for constructors that always store the argument: one extra cheap move, one function. It is a poor choice for setters called repeatedly with lvalues on long strings, because s_ = s (const& version) reuses s_'s existing capacity, while by-value always allocates a fresh copy for the parameter. It is also wrong for types that are expensive to move (std::array, large aggregates).

#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>

struct Tracer {
    Tracer() = default;
    Tracer(const Tracer&) { std::puts("  copy"); }
    Tracer(Tracer&&) noexcept { std::puts("  move"); }
};

struct ByValue {
    Tracer t;
    explicit ByValue(Tracer x) : t(std::move(x)) {}
};
struct Overloads {
    Tracer t;
    explicit Overloads(const Tracer& x) : t(x) {}
    explicit Overloads(Tracer&& x) : t(std::move(x)) {}
};

int main() {
    Tracer a;
    std::puts("by value, lvalue:");   ByValue v1(a);
    std::puts("by value, xvalue:");   ByValue v2(std::move(a));
    std::puts("by value, prvalue:");  ByValue v3(Tracer{});
    std::puts("overloads, lvalue:");  Overloads o1(a);
    std::puts("overloads, xvalue:");  Overloads o2(std::move(a));
}
by value, lvalue:
  copy
  move
by value, xvalue:
  move
  move
by value, prvalue:
  move
overloads, lvalue:
  copy
overloads, xvalue:
  move

The prvalue case shows C++17 guaranteed elision: Tracer{} initialises the parameter directly, so only the move into the member remains.

Move-only types

std::unique_ptr, std::thread, std::jthread, the file and string streams (std::fstream, std::stringstream), std::unique_lock, std::promise, std::future and std::move_only_function (C++23) are movable but not copyable. They can live in containers, be returned from functions and be passed by value, but each transfer must be from an rvalue. std::mutex, std::atomic and std::condition_variable are neither copyable nor movable, because other threads may hold their address.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

static std::unique_ptr<int> make(int v) { return std::make_unique<int>(v); }  // implicit move

int main() {
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<int>> v;
    v.push_back(make(1));
    auto p = make(2);
    v.push_back(std::move(p));                 // v.push_back(p) does not compile
    std::printf("p is %s, v = {%d, %d}\n", p ? "set" : "null", *v[0], *v[1]);

    std::thread t([] {});
    std::thread u = std::move(t);
    std::printf("t joinable=%d u joinable=%d\n", t.joinable(), u.joinable());
    u.join();
}
p is null, v = {1, 2}
t joinable=0 u joinable=1
#include <memory>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<int>> v;
    auto p = std::make_unique<int>(1);
    v.push_back(p);                                 // error: copy constructor is deleted
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<int>> w = v;        // error: copying the vector copies elements
}

Ref-qualified member functions

A member function can overload on the value category of *this by adding & or && after the parameter list (and after const). The && overload runs on temporaries and on std::move(obj), so it may steal from the object. std::optional::value(), std::move_only_function::operator() and std::basic_stringbuf::str() (C++20) use this. If one overload of a name is ref-qualified, all overloads with the same parameter list must be.

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>
#include <utility>

class Builder {
public:
    Builder& add(std::string_view x) & { s_ += x; return *this; }
    Builder&& add(std::string_view x) && { s_ += x; return std::move(*this); }
    std::string build() const& { std::puts("build: copy out"); return s_; }
    std::string build() && { std::puts("build: move out"); return std::move(s_); }
private:
    std::string s_;
};

int main() {
    Builder b;
    b.add("a").add("b");
    std::string s1 = b.build();                          // b is an lvalue
    std::string s2 = Builder{}.add("x").add("y").build(); // chain of xvalues
    std::string s3 = std::move(b).build();
    std::printf("%s %s %s\n", s1.c_str(), s2.c_str(), s3.c_str());
}
build: copy out
build: move out
build: move out
ab xy ab

The && overload of add returns Builder&&, so the chain stays an xvalue and the final build() also picks the && overload. Returning a reference into a temporary is safe here because the temporary lives until the end of the full expression.

Concept and tricky questions

Drills

ConceptWhat does std::move do at run time?

Answer

Answer. Nothing. It is static_cast<std::remove_reference_t<T>&&>(t), a compile-time cast that changes the expression's value category to xvalue.

Why. The cast only affects overload resolution: an xvalue binds to T&& parameters, so a move constructor or move assignment (if one exists and is accessible) wins over the copy. The resource transfer happens inside that function. The common wrong answer is "it moves the object" or "it makes the source empty"; std::move(x); as a statement on its own leaves x completely untouched. A better name would have been rvalue_cast.

TrickyInside void store(std::string&& s) { member_ = s; }, does the assignment move or copy?

Answer

Answer. It copies. Write member_ = std::move(s);.

Why. The parameter's type is rvalue reference, but the expression s is a named variable and therefore an lvalue. Value category belongs to expressions, not declarations. The rule exists so that a function can use the parameter several times safely; the move must be the explicit last use. People answer "it moves because s is an rvalue reference", which confuses the type with the category.

Trickyconst std::vector<int> big(1'000'000); auto v = std::move(big); How expensive is the second statement, and is big empty afterwards?

Answer

Answer. It is a full copy of a million ints (one allocation and a 4 MB memcpy), and big still holds all its elements.

Why. std::move(big) yields const std::vector<int>&&. The move constructor takes a non-const vector&& and cannot bind to it; the copy constructor's const vector& can. Overload resolution silently chooses the copy, and no compiler warns at -Wall -Wextra (clang-tidy has performance-move-const-arg). The same happens for const data members, which is why const members make a class effectively non-movable.

ConceptName the five value categories and give an example of each primary one.

Answer

Answer. Primary: lvalue (x, *p, "lit"), xvalue (std::move(x), S{}.m, a call returning T&&), prvalue (42, x + 1, a call returning T). Mixed: glvalue = lvalue or xvalue (has identity), rvalue = xvalue or prvalue (movable).

Why. The two properties "has identity" and "may be moved from" give three useful combinations, and the mixed categories name the overlaps. Since C++17, a prvalue is not an object at all: it is a recipe that initialises a result object, and it is turned into an xvalue only when it must be (temporary materialisation, [conv.rval]). A frequent mistake is to call string literals rvalues; they are lvalue arrays with static storage duration.

ConceptWhy does std::vector copy its elements on reallocation when the element's move constructor is not noexcept?

Answer

Answer. To keep the strong exception guarantee of push_back, reserve and friends: if relocation fails, the vector must be unchanged.

Why. With copies, a throw half-way leaves the old buffer intact, so the new buffer is destroyed and the exception propagates. With moves, the old elements before the failure point are already gutted, and moving them back could throw again. The library therefore uses std::move_if_noexcept, which moves only when the move is noexcept or the type is not copyable. "The compiler adds noexcept for you" is wrong for user-written moves; only implicit and defaulted ones get an inferred exception specification.

TrickyA class has a std::string member and a user-written ~Logger() { std::puts("bye"); }. Does Logger b = std::move(a); move the string?

Answer

Answer. No. It copies the string.

Why. A user-declared destructor prevents the implicit declaration of the move constructor and move assignment ([class.copy.ctor]/8). The implicit copy constructor is still generated (deprecated but legal), and const Logger& binds to the xvalue, so the copy runs. ~Logger() = default; also counts as user-declared. Fix it with Logger(Logger&&) = default; Logger& operator=(Logger&&) = default; plus defaulted copies, or remove the destructor. The wrong answer "only the copy operations suppress moves" misses the destructor rule.

TrickyAfter std::optional<std::string> a = "hi"; auto b = std::move(a);, what does a.has_value() return?

Answer

Answer. true. a still contains a string, which is itself in a moved-from state (empty in practice).

Why. optional's move constructor is specified to move-construct the contained value and leave the source's engaged flag unchanged ([optional.ctor]). Resetting it would cost an extra destructor call and branch. People assume it behaves like unique_ptr, which is specified to become null. The lesson: "moved-from" means whatever that type documents, and for most types only "valid but unspecified".

ConceptAfter std::vector<int> b = std::move(a);, which of these are allowed on a: a.size(), a.clear(), a.push_back(1), a = {1, 2}, a[0], a.front(), letting a go out of scope?

Answer

Answer. Everything except a[0] and a.front(). Those two have the precondition "not empty", which you cannot know holds. In practice a is empty in every mainstream library, but you should call a.clear() or assign before relying on its contents.

Why. [lib.types.movedfrom] says a moved-from library object is in a "valid but unspecified state": every operation without preconditions works, and the destructor runs normally. So a moved-from object is usable, and reusing it after clear() or assignment is idiomatic (a buffer reused across loop iterations). The two common wrong answers are opposite extremes: "a moved-from object must not be touched at all except to destroy it" (too strict: size() and assignment are fine) and "it is guaranteed empty" (too loose for std::vector and std::string, although std::unique_ptr really is guaranteed null).

ConceptState the rule of five and the rule of zero. Which should a typical class follow?

Answer

Answer. Rule of five: a class that manages a resource declares (or deletes) the destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, move constructor and move assignment together. Rule of zero: every other class declares none of them and lets members like std::vector and std::unique_ptr manage resources. Most classes should follow the rule of zero.

Why. Declaring any one of the five changes what the compiler generates for the others (a destructor suppresses moves, a move deletes copies), so partial declarations cause silent copies or surprising compile errors. Pushing ownership into a single-purpose RAII member means only that member needs the five, and the outer class gets correct, noexcept moves for free. See Ch 1 for the copy side.

TrickyIs moving a std::array<int, 1000> cheaper than copying it? What about a std::string holding "hi"?

Answer

Answer. No for the array: move and copy both transfer all 4000 bytes. For a short string, a move is about as cheap as a copy too, because of the small string optimisation.

Why. A move is faster only when there is an indirection to steal. std::array stores its elements inline, so "moving" each int is copying it. A short std::string stores its characters inside the object (SSO, see Ch 18), so the move constructor copies the inline bytes and resets the source; there is no heap pointer to steal. Interviewers ask this to catch the belief that std::move always makes things O(1).

ConceptWhy is std::exchange popular in move constructors? Write the move constructor for a class holding int fd_ where -1 means "no descriptor".

Handle(Handle&& o) noexcept : fd_(std::exchange(o.fd_, -1)) {}
Answer

Answer. It reads the old value and writes the empty value in one expression, so it fits in the member initialiser list and you cannot forget to reset the source.

Why. Forgetting to reset the source is the classic move bug: two objects then own the same descriptor or pointer and both release it (double close or double free). std::exchange(obj, v) is defined as T old = std::move(obj); obj = std::forward<U>(v); return old;. For int and pointers this compiles to two moves of registers. It also makes move assignment short: reset(); fd_ = std::exchange(o.fd_, -1);.

TrickyIs template <class U> Widget(U&& u); a move constructor? Does declaring it stop the compiler from generating one?

Answer

Answer. No and no. A constructor template is never a copy or move constructor, so the implicit copy and move constructors are still declared.

Why. [class.copy.ctor]/1 defines a copy or move constructor as a non-template constructor whose first parameter is X&, const X&, X&& and so on. The template still competes in overload resolution, and for a non-const lvalue Widget it deduces U = Widget&, which is a better match than the implicit const Widget& copy constructor. That greedy-template problem is the subject of Ch 21. Conversely, Widget(const Widget&&) is formally a move constructor, but useless.

ConceptWhen should a constructor take a std::string by value and move it, and when is const std::string& better?

Answer

Answer. By value plus std::move for constructors and other sinks that always keep a copy: callers pay one copy plus one move for lvalues and two moves for rvalues, with a single function. const& is better when the function only reads the argument, when the storage may not happen, or for assignment-style setters called with lvalues, where reusing the member's existing buffer avoids an allocation.

Why. The overload pair const T& + T&& is optimal but doubles per parameter (2n overloads). A forwarding-reference template is also optimal but must be constrained and lives in a header. The by-value version is the simplest good default for constructors, and it is what clang-tidy's modernize-pass-by-value check rewrites to. The C++ Core Guidelines are more conservative: F.16 says const& for "in" parameters, and F.15/F.18 add a T&& overload only when the optimisation matters. People who answer "always pass by value now" miss the setter case.

Predict the output and find the bug

#include <cstdio>

struct T {
    T() { std::puts("ctor"); }
    T(const T&) { std::puts("copy"); }
    T(T&&) noexcept { std::puts("move"); }
    T& operator=(const T&) { std::puts("copy="); return *this; }

int main() {

    T b = a;

Answer. As above: 2 constructions by default ctor, one copy, one move, one of each assignment, four destructors.

Why. T b = a is initialisation, not assignment, so it calls the copy constructor. b = c and c = std::move(b) assign to existing objects. T d = T{}; prints only ctor: since C++17 the prvalue T{} initialises d directly, with no temporary and no move (Ch 23). People often add a "move" and an extra "dtor" there, which was the possible C++14 behaviour without elision.

OutputTwo push_back calls on an empty vector with a noexcept move. What is printed?

#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

struct T {
    T() { std::puts("ctor"); }
    T(const T&) { std::puts("copy"); }
    T(T&&) noexcept { std::puts("move"); }
    ~T() { std::puts("dtor"); }
};

int main() {
    std::vector<T> v;
    std::puts("-- push 1");
    v.push_back(T{});
    std::puts("-- push 2");
    v.push_back(T{});
    std::puts("-- end");
}
Answer
-- push 1
ctor
move
dtor
-- push 2
ctor
move
move
dtor
dtor
-- end
dtor
dtor

Answer. Push 1: the temporary is built, moved into the buffer, then destroyed at the end of the statement. Push 2: capacity is 1, so the vector reallocates to capacity 2. It first move-constructs the new element from the temporary into the new buffer, then moves the old element across, destroys the old element, and finally the temporary is destroyed.

Why. Both libstdc++ and libc++ construct the new element before relocating the old ones, so that an argument referring into the vector itself (v.push_back(v[0])) is still valid when it is read. A temporary bound to push_back(T&&) cannot be elided into the buffer: it must exist so the reference can bind to it. That is the cost emplace_back avoids (Ch 22).

OutputThe same program, but the move constructor is no longer noexcept. What changes?

#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

struct T {

    T(const T&) { std::puts("copy"); }
    T(T&&) { std::puts("move"); }
    ~T() { std::puts("dtor"); }
};

int main() {

    v.push_back(T{});

ctor
move

-- push 2
ctor
move
copy
dtor

-- end
dtor
dtor

Answer. The new element is still moved in from the temporary, but the existing element is now copied into the new buffer.

Why. Placing the new element uses plain T&& overload resolution, because if it throws nothing old has been touched. Relocating the existing elements uses std::move_if_noexcept, which returns const T& for a copyable type whose move may throw. With real resource-owning types, this one missing keyword turns every growth step into deep copies.

OutputA function takes an rvalue reference and forwards it on. What is printed?

#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>

struct T {
    T() = default;
    T(const T&) { std::puts("copy"); }
    T(T&&) noexcept { std::puts("move"); }
};

static void keep(T&& t) {
    T a = t;
    T b = std::move(t);
    T c = std::move(t);

int main() {
    keep(T{});
    const T k;
    T d = std::move(k);
