Answer
copy
move
move
copy

Answer. copy, move, move, copy.

Why. t is a named rvalue reference, so T a = t copies. Each std::move(t) is just a cast, so moving twice from the same object compiles and calls the move constructor twice (with real resources, c would get an empty object, which is a logic bug the compiler will not catch). std::move(k) on a const object yields const T&&, which only the copy constructor accepts. A side note: const T k; compiles even though the default constructor is defaulted, because T has no data members that would be left uninitialised, which makes it const-default-constructible ([dcl.init.general]; the paragraph number differs between C++20, C++23 and the current draft).

OutputTwo wrapper classes differ only in a destructor. What is printed?

#include <cstdio>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Res {
    Res() = default;
    Res(const Res&) { std::puts("Res copy"); }
    Res(Res&&) noexcept { std::puts("Res move"); }
};
struct A { Res r; };
struct B { Res r; virtual ~B() = default; };

int main() {
    A a1; A a2 = std::move(a1);
    B b1; B b2 = std::move(b1);
    std::printf("%d %d\n", std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<A>,
                           std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<B>);
}
Answer
Res move
Res copy
1 0

Answer. A moves; B copies; the traits print 1 0.

Why. virtual ~B() = default; is user-declared, so B gets no implicit move constructor. std::move(b1) binds to the implicit copy constructor, which copies Res. is_nothrow_move_constructible<B> asks whether B(B&&) is a valid non-throwing expression; it is valid (via the copy constructor), but Res's copy constructor is not noexcept, so the answer is false. A std::vector<B> would copy on every reallocation. The usual wrong answer is that = default on the destructor "doesn't count".

Find the bugThis string class crashes at the end of main. Why?

#include <cstdio>
#include <cstring>

class Str {
public:
    explicit Str(const char* s) : len_(std::strlen(s)), p_(new char[len_ + 1]) {
        std::memcpy(p_, s, len_ + 1);
    }
    ~Str() { delete[] p_; }
    Str(const Str&) = delete;
    Str& operator=(const Str&) = delete;
    Str(Str&& o) noexcept : len_(o.len_), p_(o.p_) {}
    const char* c_str() const { return p_; }
private:
    std::size_t len_;
    char* p_;
};

int main() {
    Str a("hello");
    Str b(static_cast<Str&&>(a));
    std::puts(b.c_str());
}
Answer

Answer. The move constructor copies the pointer but does not reset o.p_. Both a and b own the same buffer, and both destructors call delete[] on it: a double free, which ASan reports as attempting double-free.

Why. A move is "shallow copy plus disarm the source". Without the second half, it is just a shallow copy, the exact bug the rule of three was invented to prevent. Fix: Str(Str&& o) noexcept : len_(std::exchange(o.len_, 0)), p_(std::exchange(o.p_, nullptr)) {}. Then also make c_str() cope with a null p_ (return ""), because the moved-from state must keep the class usable. The output is marked as undefined behaviour: without a sanitizer, a double free may abort, corrupt the heap silently or appear to work.

Find the bugThe author expected this move constructor to be cheap. The trace says otherwise. Fix it.

#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>

struct Blob {
    Blob() = default;
    Blob(const Blob&) { std::puts("Blob copy"); }
    Blob(Blob&&) noexcept { std::puts("Blob move"); }
};

struct Doc {
    Blob body;
    Blob meta;
    Doc() = default;
    Doc(Doc&& o) noexcept : body(o.body), meta(std::move(o.meta)) {}
};

int main() {
    Doc a;
    Doc b = std::move(a);
}
Answer
Blob copy
Blob move

Answer. body(o.body) copies: o is a named rvalue reference, so o.body is an lvalue. Write body(std::move(o.body)), or better, delete the hand-written constructor and let the compiler generate Doc(Doc&&) = default;.

Why. Member access on an lvalue gives an lvalue. Only std::move(o).body or std::move(o.body) gives an xvalue. Hand-written move constructors are a common source of accidental copies, and a missed member compiles silently. The defaulted version moves every base and member in declaration order and gets the right noexcept automatically.

Find the bugWhy does moving a Person copy its name?

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

struct Name {
    std::string s;
    explicit Name(std::string v) : s(std::move(v)) {}
    Name(const Name& o) : s(o.s) { std::puts("Name copy"); }
    Name(Name&& o) noexcept : s(std::move(o.s)) { std::puts("Name move"); }
};

struct Person {
    const Name name;
    int age;
};

int main() {
    Person a{Name("Ada"), 36};
    Person b = std::move(a);
    std::printf("%s %d\n", b.name.s.c_str(), b.age);
}
Answer
Name copy
Ada 36

Answer. name is a const member, so Person's implicit move constructor initialises it from std::move(o).name, a const Name&&, which binds only to the copy constructor. That is the single Name copy line. (The aggregate initialisation prints nothing: the prvalue Name("Ada") initialises the member directly.)

Why. The wrong answer is "the implicit move constructor moves every member". It does, but moving a const member is a copy. Drop the const and enforce immutability through the interface (private member plus a getter). const data members also delete the implicit copy and move assignment, so Person cannot be assigned or sorted in a vector. This is one of the most common accidental-copy sources in real codebases.

Find the bugThe program crashes. Which line is wrong, and why does it compile?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <vector>

struct Job { int id; };

int main() {
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Job>> queue;
    auto job = std::make_unique<Job>(Job{7});
    queue.push_back(std::move(job));
    std::printf("queued job %d\n", job->id);
}
Answer

Answer. job->id after std::move(job). unique_ptr's move constructor is specified to leave the source null, so this dereferences a null pointer (UBSan/ASan report it; a normal build segfaults).

Why. The compiler does not track moved-from state, so use-after-move compiles cleanly. clang-tidy's bugprone-use-after-move catches it. Fix by reading what you need before the move (int id = job->id;) or through the container (queue.back()->id). The output is marked undefined behaviour because a null dereference has no defined result.

Write the code

Coding

CodeImplement Buffer, a heap byte buffer with the rule of five. Requirements: explicit Buffer(std::size_t n) zero-fills; size(), data(), operator[]; deep copy; noexcept moves that leave the source with size 0 and null data; copy assignment with the strong exception guarantee; self-assignment and self-move safe; a noexcept member and free swap. Show with static_assert that a vector of Buffers will move on reallocation.

Answer

Approach. Own a char* and a size. The copy constructor allocates and copies. Moves use std::exchange to steal and reset. Copy assignment uses copy-and-swap (construct a temporary copy, which may throw, then swap, which cannot), giving the strong guarantee and self-assignment safety. Move assignment uses swap, which is self-safe without a branch, and the old buffer is freed by the source's destructor.

#include <cassert>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstring>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class Buffer {
public:
    Buffer() noexcept = default;
    explicit Buffer(std::size_t n) : size_(n), data_(n ? new char[n]() : nullptr) {}
    ~Buffer() { delete[] data_; }

    Buffer(const Buffer& o) : size_(o.size_), data_(o.size_ ? new char[o.size_] : nullptr) {
        if (size_) std::memcpy(data_, o.data_, size_);
    }
    Buffer(Buffer&& o) noexcept
        : size_(std::exchange(o.size_, 0)), data_(std::exchange(o.data_, nullptr)) {}

    Buffer& operator=(const Buffer& o) {
        Buffer tmp(o);          // may throw; *this untouched
        swap(tmp);
        return *this;
    }
    Buffer& operator=(Buffer&& o) noexcept {
        Buffer tmp(std::move(o));   // o is now empty, even when &o == this
        swap(tmp);                  // old contents die with tmp
        return *this;
    }

    void swap(Buffer& o) noexcept {
        std::swap(size_, o.size_);
        std::swap(data_, o.data_);
    }
    friend void swap(Buffer& a, Buffer& b) noexcept { a.swap(b); }

    std::size_t size() const noexcept { return size_; }
    char* data() noexcept { return data_; }
    const char* data() const noexcept { return data_; }
    char& operator[](std::size_t i) { return data_[i]; }
    const char& operator[](std::size_t i) const { return data_[i]; }

private:
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    char* data_ = nullptr;
};

static_assert(std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<Buffer>);
static_assert(std::is_nothrow_move_assignable_v<Buffer>);

int main() {
    Buffer a(4);
    std::memcpy(a.data(), "abc", 4);
    Buffer b = a;                      // deep copy
    b[0] = 'X';
    assert(a[0] == 'a');
    Buffer c = std::move(a);
    assert(a.size() == 0 && a.data() == nullptr && c.size() == 4);
    b = b;                             // self copy-assign
    assert(std::strcmp(b.data(), "Xbc") == 0);
    Buffer& alias = c;
    c = std::move(alias);              // self move-assign keeps the value
    assert(std::strcmp(c.data(), "abc") == 0);
    a = c;                             // reuse a moved-from object
    std::vector<Buffer> v;
    for (int i = 0; i < 100; ++i) v.emplace_back(16);
    std::printf("a=%s b=%s c=%s v=%zu\n", a.data(), b.data(), c.data(), v.size());
}
a=abc b=Xbc c=abc v=100

Complexity and pitfalls. Copy O(n), move O(1), swap O(1). Pitfalls: forgetting to reset the source in the move constructor (double free); forgetting noexcept (vector copies); calling memcpy with a null pointer even for size 0 (undefined behaviour under the C rules that C++20 inherits, so guard it); declaring data_ before size_ and then reading size_ in data_'s initialiser (members initialise in declaration order). The b = b line triggers -Wself-assign-overloaded on Clang, which is expected in a test. The swap-based move assignment frees the old buffer immediately here because tmp dies at the end of the function.

Estimated rating: ~1500 · standard rule-of-five boilerplate, but four special members each have a distinct trap

CodeWrite a move-only UniqueHandle that owns an integer descriptor (-1 means empty) and closes it with a given function. Interface: explicit UniqueHandle(int fd), get(), release(), reset(int = -1), explicit operator bool. Copies must not compile. Use a fake close that records calls so the test can check that every descriptor is closed exactly once.

Answer

Approach. Delete both copy operations. The move constructor takes the descriptor with std::exchange(o.fd_, -1). Move assignment is reset(o.release()), which is self-safe: on self-move, release() first sets our own fd to -1 and returns it, so reset finds nothing old to close and simply takes the fd back. The old != fd check in reset covers the separate case h.reset(h.get()). The destructor calls reset().

#include <cassert>
#include <cstdio>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

static std::vector<int> closed;                 // fake ::close for the test
static void fake_close(int fd) { closed.push_back(fd); }

class UniqueHandle {
public:
    UniqueHandle() noexcept = default;
    explicit UniqueHandle(int fd) noexcept : fd_(fd) {}
    ~UniqueHandle() { reset(); }

    UniqueHandle(const UniqueHandle&) = delete;
    UniqueHandle& operator=(const UniqueHandle&) = delete;

    UniqueHandle(UniqueHandle&& o) noexcept : fd_(std::exchange(o.fd_, -1)) {}
    UniqueHandle& operator=(UniqueHandle&& o) noexcept {
        reset(o.release());
        return *this;
    }

    int get() const noexcept { return fd_; }
    explicit operator bool() const noexcept { return fd_ != -1; }
    [[nodiscard]] int release() noexcept { return std::exchange(fd_, -1); }
    void reset(int fd = -1) noexcept {
        int old = std::exchange(fd_, fd);
        if (old != -1 && old != fd) fake_close(old);
    }

private:
    int fd_ = -1;
};

static_assert(!std::is_copy_constructible_v<UniqueHandle>);
static_assert(std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<UniqueHandle>);

static UniqueHandle open_fake(int fd) { return UniqueHandle(fd); }

int main() {
    {
        UniqueHandle a = open_fake(3);
        UniqueHandle b = std::move(a);
        assert(!a && b.get() == 3);
        UniqueHandle c(4);
        c = std::move(b);              // closes 4, takes 3
        UniqueHandle& alias = c;
        c = std::move(alias);          // self-move: no close
        assert(c.get() == 3);
        std::vector<UniqueHandle> v;
        v.push_back(UniqueHandle(5));
        v.push_back(open_fake(6));
        int raw = v[0].release();      // caller now owns 5
        fake_close(raw);
    }                                  // closes 6, then 3
    for (int fd : closed) std::printf("%d ", fd);
    std::printf("\n");
}
4 5 6 3

Complexity and pitfalls. Every operation is O(1). Destruction order at the closing brace is reverse declaration: v (closes 6, element 0 is empty), then c (closes 3), then the empty b and a. Pitfalls: a move assignment written as reset(); fd_ = o.fd_; o.fd_ = -1; closes our own descriptor on self-move; forgetting [[nodiscard]] on release() lets callers leak; using 0 as the empty value is wrong because descriptor 0 (stdin) is valid. In production, prefer std::unique_ptr with a custom deleter only if the handle is a pointer; for int descriptors a small class like this is the norm (Ch 12).

Estimated rating: ~1400 · move-only RAII is short but the self-move and release semantics are easy to get wrong

CodeImplement my::move and my::move_if_noexcept without using the standard versions. Prove with static_assert that they return the same types as std::move and std::move_if_noexcept for: a non-const lvalue, a const lvalue, an rvalue, a type with a throwing move, and a move-only type with a throwing move.

Answer

Approach. move takes a forwarding reference and casts to remove_reference_t<T>&&. move_if_noexcept picks its return type with std::conditional_t: const T& when the move may throw and a copy is possible, T&& otherwise. Both are constexpr and noexcept because they are pure casts.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>

namespace my {
template <class T>
[[nodiscard]] constexpr std::remove_reference_t<T>&& move(T&& t) noexcept {
    return static_cast<std::remove_reference_t<T>&&>(t);
}

template <class T>
using move_if_noexcept_t = std::conditional_t<
    !std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<T> && std::is_copy_constructible_v<T>,
    const T&, T&&>;

template <class T>
[[nodiscard]] constexpr move_if_noexcept_t<T> move_if_noexcept(T& x) noexcept {
    return static_cast<move_if_noexcept_t<T>>(x);
}
}

struct Throwing { Throwing() = default; Throwing(const Throwing&) {} Throwing(Throwing&&) {} };
struct ThrowingMoveOnly { ThrowingMoveOnly() = default; ThrowingMoveOnly(ThrowingMoveOnly&&) {} };

#define SAME(a, b) static_assert(std::is_same_v<decltype(a), decltype(b)>)

int main() {
    std::string s = "x";
    const std::string cs = "y";
    Throwing t;
    ThrowingMoveOnly m;
    auto u = std::make_unique<int>(1);

    SAME(my::move(s), std::move(s));
    SAME(my::move(cs), std::move(cs));
    SAME(my::move(std::string{}), std::move(std::string{}));
    SAME(my::move_if_noexcept(s), std::move_if_noexcept(s));
    SAME(my::move_if_noexcept(t), std::move_if_noexcept(t));
    SAME(my::move_if_noexcept(m), std::move_if_noexcept(m));
    SAME(my::move_if_noexcept(u), std::move_if_noexcept(u));
    static_assert(std::is_same_v<decltype(my::move_if_noexcept(t)), const Throwing&>);
    static_assert(std::is_same_v<decltype(my::move_if_noexcept(m)), ThrowingMoveOnly&&>);

    std::string moved = my::move(s);
    std::printf("moved=%s source_size=%zu\n", moved.c_str(), s.size());
}
moved=x source_size=0

Complexity and pitfalls. Zero run-time cost. Pitfalls: returning T&& instead of remove_reference_t<T>&& (for an lvalue argument, T = std::string& and T&& collapses to std::string&, so nothing would move); taking the parameter by T& only (then move(std::string{}) fails); forgetting is_copy_constructible in move_if_noexcept, which would try to copy a move-only type. The source size 0 is what both standard libraries do; it is not guaranteed.

Estimated rating: ~1300 · tiny code, but needs reference collapsing and the exact move_if_noexcept condition

CodeWrite a numeric Vec (heap array of doubles, rule of five with noexcept moves) and overload operator+ so that Vec s = a + b + c + d; performs exactly one heap allocation. Count allocations to prove it, and explain how many a single const Vec&, const Vec& overload would make.

Answer

Approach. a + b + c + d parses as ((a + b) + c) + d. Only the first addition sees two lvalues; every later one has a temporary on the left. Overload on the value category of the operands: when an operand is an rvalue, add into its buffer with += and move it out as the result. Four overloads are needed, because with only (Vec&&, const Vec&) and (const Vec&, Vec&&) the call with two temporaries would be ambiguous. This is the same trick std::string's operator+ uses.

#include <cstdio>
#include <cstddef>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>

class Vec {
public:
    explicit Vec(std::size_t n, double x = 0) : n_(n), d_(alloc(n)) {
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n_; ++i) d_[i] = x;
    }
    Vec(const Vec& o) : n_(o.n_), d_(alloc(o.n_)) {
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n_; ++i) d_[i] = o.d_[i];
    }
    Vec(Vec&&) noexcept = default;
    Vec& operator=(const Vec& o) { Vec t(o); return *this = std::move(t); }
    Vec& operator=(Vec&&) noexcept = default;
    ~Vec() = default;

    Vec& operator+=(const Vec& o) {
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n_; ++i) d_[i] += o.d_[i];
        return *this;
    }
    double operator[](std::size_t i) const { return d_[i]; }
    static inline int allocations = 0;

private:
    static std::unique_ptr<double[]> alloc(std::size_t n) {
        ++allocations;
        return std::make_unique<double[]>(n);
    }
    std::size_t n_;
    std::unique_ptr<double[]> d_;
};

// Both operands are lvalues: the result needs a new buffer.
inline Vec operator+(const Vec& a, const Vec& b) { Vec r(a); r += b; return r; }
// The left operand is a temporary: reuse its buffer.
inline Vec operator+(Vec&& a, const Vec& b) { a += b; return std::move(a); }
// The right operand is a temporary: addition commutes, so reuse it.
inline Vec operator+(const Vec& a, Vec&& b) { b += a; return std::move(b); }
// Both temporaries: needed, otherwise the two overloads above are ambiguous.
inline Vec operator+(Vec&& a, Vec&& b) { a += b; return std::move(a); }

int main() {
    Vec a(1000, 1), b(1000, 2), c(1000, 3), d(1000, 4);
    Vec::allocations = 0;
    Vec s = a + b + c + d;
    std::printf("a+b+c+d: allocations=%d s[0]=%g\n", Vec::allocations, s[0]);
    Vec::allocations = 0;
    Vec t = (a + b) + (c + d);
    std::printf("(a+b)+(c+d): allocations=%d t[0]=%g\n", Vec::allocations, t[0]);
    Vec::allocations = 0;
    Vec u = a + (b + (c + d));
    std::printf("a+(b+(c+d)): allocations=%d u[0]=%g\n", Vec::allocations, u[0]);
}
a+b+c+d: allocations=1 s[0]=10
(a+b)+(c+d): allocations=2 t[0]=10
a+(b+(c+d)): allocations=1 u[0]=10

Complexity and pitfalls. Each addition is O(n); the chain does one allocation instead of three, which is what a lone operator+(const Vec&, const Vec&) makes (each temporary result binds to const Vec& and a new buffer is allocated for the next result). (a+b)+(c+d) needs two, because two independent sums exist at the same time. Pitfalls: returning Vec&& instead of Vec from the rvalue overloads (const Vec& r = a + b + c; would then dangle, since the result refers to a temporary that dies at the semicolon); forgetting the (Vec&&, Vec&&) overload (ambiguity); reusing the right operand for a non-commutative operation such as -. In C++20, return a; would also move the rvalue-reference parameter implicitly (P1825); std::move keeps the code correct in C++17.

Estimated rating: ~1600 · needs value-category overloading of a free operator and the ambiguity case, not just a move constructor

CodeWrite a minimal Stack<T> over raw storage with push(const T&), push(T&&), pop(), top() and size(). When it grows (doubling), it must relocate elements with std::move_if_noexcept and keep the strong exception guarantee. Test with a type whose copy constructor throws on the third copy, and show the stack is unchanged after the failed push.

Answer

Approach. Allocate raw memory with std::allocator<T>. On growth, allocate the new block, construct the new element at index size first (the argument may alias an existing element), then relocate old elements with std::construct_at(dst, std::move_if_noexcept(src)). If any construction throws, destroy what was built in the new block, free it and rethrow; the old block is untouched. Only after full success destroy the old elements and swap in the new block.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <utility>

template <class T>
class Stack {
public:
    Stack() = default;
    Stack(const Stack&) = delete;
    Stack& operator=(const Stack&) = delete;
    ~Stack() { std::destroy_n(data_, size_); alloc_.deallocate(data_, cap_); }

    void push(const T& v) { emplace(v); }
    void push(T&& v) { emplace(std::move(v)); }
    void pop() { std::destroy_at(data_ + --size_); }
    T& top() { return data_[size_ - 1]; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }

private:
    template <class U>
    void emplace(U&& v) {
        if (size_ < cap_) { std::construct_at(data_ + size_, std::forward<U>(v)); ++size_; return; }
        std::size_t ncap = cap_ ? 2 * cap_ : 1;
        T* nd = alloc_.allocate(ncap);
        std::size_t built = 0;
        bool placed = false;
        try {
            std::construct_at(nd + size_, std::forward<U>(v));   // new element first
            placed = true;
            for (; built < size_; ++built)
                std::construct_at(nd + built, std::move_if_noexcept(data_[built]));
        } catch (...) {
            std::destroy_n(nd, built);
            if (placed) std::destroy_at(nd + size_);
            alloc_.deallocate(nd, ncap);
            throw;
        }
        std::destroy_n(data_, size_);
        alloc_.deallocate(data_, cap_);
        data_ = nd; cap_ = ncap; ++size_;
    }

    std::allocator<T> alloc_;
    T* data_ = nullptr;
    std::size_t size_ = 0, cap_ = 0;
};

struct Fragile {
    int v;
    static inline int copies = 0;
    explicit Fragile(int x) : v(x) {}
    Fragile(const Fragile& o) : v(o.v) {
        if (++copies == 3) throw std::runtime_error("copy failed");
    }
    Fragile(Fragile&& o) : v(o.v) { o.v = -1; }   // may throw, so Stack copies on growth
};

int main() {
    Stack<Fragile> s;
    s.push(Fragile(1));                 // cap 1
    s.push(Fragile(2));                 // grow to 2: copy #1
    try {
        s.push(Fragile(3));             // grow to 4: copy #2 ok, copy #3 throws
    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        std::printf("caught: %s\n", e.what());
    }
    std::printf("size=%zu top=%d\n", s.size(), s.top().v);
    s.pop();
    std::printf("size=%zu top=%d\n", s.size(), s.top().v);
}
caught: copy failed
size=2 top=2
size=1 top=1

Complexity and pitfalls. Amortised O(1) push. Pitfalls: relocating with std::move instead of move_if_noexcept (a throwing move half-way corrupts the old buffer); constructing the new element after relocation, which breaks s.push(s.top()) because the reference points into the old buffer only until it is destroyed; leaking the new block on exception; destroying the old elements before the new ones are complete. The values are intact after the failure (top=2, then 1), which proves no element was moved from.

Estimated rating: ~1900 · raw storage, exception safety and move_if_noexcept together, where most candidates leak or corrupt on the failure path

CodeImplement move_remove_if(first, last, pred) with the semantics of std::remove_if: keep the elements that do not satisfy pred, in order, at the front, and return the new logical end. It must move (never copy) elements, so it works for std::unique_ptr. Show what is left in the tail and why erase must follow.

Answer

Approach. Find the first element to remove; that slot becomes the write position. Walk the rest with a read iterator and move-assign every kept element into the write position, advancing it. Elements already in the right place are never touched, so the cost is one move assignment per kept element after the first removal. The range [result, last) then holds moved-from or leftover objects, which the caller erases (the erase-remove idiom, or C++20's std::erase_if).

#include <algorithm>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

template <class It, class Pred>
It move_remove_if(It first, It last, Pred pred) {
    first = std::find_if(first, last, pred);
    if (first == last) return last;
    for (It it = std::next(first); it != last; ++it)
        if (!pred(*it)) *first++ = std::move(*it);
    return first;
}

struct Tr {
    int v;
    static inline int copies = 0, moves = 0;
    Tr(int x) : v(x) {}
    Tr(const Tr& o) : v(o.v) { ++copies; }
    Tr(Tr&& o) noexcept : v(o.v) { ++moves; }
    Tr& operator=(const Tr& o) { v = o.v; ++copies; return *this; }
    Tr& operator=(Tr&& o) noexcept { v = o.v; ++moves; return *this; }
};

int main() {
    std::vector<Tr> t{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6};
    Tr::copies = Tr::moves = 0;
    auto mid = move_remove_if(t.begin(), t.end(), [](const Tr& x) { return x.v % 2 == 0; });
    std::printf("kept=%td copies=%d moves=%d\n", mid - t.begin(), Tr::copies, Tr::moves);
    t.erase(mid, t.end());
    for (const Tr& x : t) std::printf("%d ", x.v);
    std::printf("\n");

    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<int>> p;
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; ++i) p.push_back(std::make_unique<int>(i));
    auto pend = move_remove_if(p.begin(), p.end(), [](const auto& q) { return *q < 2; });
    std::printf("tail after remove: %td elements, first tail is %s\n", p.end() - pend,
                *pend ? "non-null" : "null");
    p.erase(pend, p.end());
    for (const auto& q : p) std::printf("%d ", *q);
    std::printf("\n");
}
kept=3 copies=0 moves=2
1 3 5
tail after remove: 2 elements, first tail is null
2 3 4

Complexity and pitfalls. O(n) predicate calls and at most n move assignments, no allocation. The tail is the lesson: after std::remove_if the elements in [new_end, end) are valid but unspecified (here the first tail unique_ptr is null because it was moved from, but the standard algorithm promises nothing about which values remain), so reading them is a logic error and forgetting erase leaves them in the container. Pitfalls: writing *first++ = *it (copies, and does not compile for unique_ptr); swapping instead of moving (correct but slower, and it changes what the tail holds); calling pred on an element after it has been moved from.

Estimated rating: ~1300 · short loop, but it forces you to reason about moved-from elements left behind by a standard algorithm

Cheat sheet

Theory
  • Categories: lvalue (has a name or identity), prvalue (pure value), xvalue (std::move(x), S{}.m). A named T&& variable is an lvalue.
  • std::move is static_cast<remove_reference_t<T>&&>. It moves nothing; the move constructor or assignment does. On a const object it silently copies.
  • Move members: steal with std::exchange(o.p_, nullptr), leave the source destructible and assignable, mark them noexcept, handle self-move (check or swap).
  • noexcept: vector relocation uses std::move_if_noexcept; a throwing move means copies on every growth.
  • Suppression: a user-declared destructor or copy operation (even = default) stops implicit moves, and std::move then copies. Declaring a move deletes the copies.
  • Rule of zero for normal classes, rule of five for resource owners, copies deleted for move-only types.
  • Interfaces: never return std::move(local) (Ch 24); sinks take by value then move; ref-qualify members to steal from temporaries.
  • Moved-from: valid but unspecified; only unique_ptr, shared_ptr, thread and a few others specify empty. Moved-from optional stays engaged.
