Part F · Move semantics and value passing · Chapter 21

Perfect forwarding

Perfect forwarding lets a template pass its arguments on to another function exactly as the caller supplied them: lvalues stay lvalues, rvalues stay rvalues, const stays const. It is how std::make_unique, emplace_back, std::invoke and every logging or timing wrapper avoid extra copies. Interviewers ask about it because it combines template deduction, reference collapsing and value categories, and because the failure cases are well known.

TheoryDrillsCoding· about 4 hours· prerequisites: Ch 20 (value categories, std::move), basic templates

The forwarding problem

Theory

Mental model. A wrapper sits between a caller and a target. Whatever the caller passes, the target should see the same thing it would have seen without the wrapper. If the caller passes a temporary, the target should be able to move from it; if the caller passes a named object, the target must copy (or modify it, if it takes a non-const reference).

Before C++11 there was no good way to write such a wrapper. Each obvious parameter type loses something:

  • template <class A> void wrap(A& a) rejects rvalues: wrap(T{}) does not compile.
  • template <class A> void wrap(const A& a) accepts everything but adds const, so the target can never move from a temporary and cannot take a non-const reference.
  • Overloading on both A& and const A& for each parameter needs 2n overloads for n parameters, and still cannot express "rvalue".

C++11 solved it with two pieces: a special deduction rule for T&& in a template, and std::forward, which restores the original value category inside the wrapper.

#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>

struct T {
    T() = default;
    T(const T&) { std::puts("  copy"); }
    T(T&&) noexcept { std::puts("  move"); }
};

static void target(T) {}

template <class A> void by_cref(const A& a) { target(a); }               // always copies
template <class A> void perfect(A&& a) { target(std::forward<A>(a)); }   // copies or moves

int main() {
    T t;
    std::puts("by_cref(lvalue):");  by_cref(t);
    std::puts("by_cref(rvalue):");  by_cref(T{});
    std::puts("perfect(lvalue):");  perfect(t);
    std::puts("perfect(rvalue):");  perfect(T{});
}
by_cref(lvalue):
  copy
by_cref(rvalue):
  copy
perfect(lvalue):
  copy
perfect(rvalue):
  move

Calling target(T{}) directly would print nothing at all (the prvalue initialises the parameter in place, Ch 23). Perfect forwarding gets as close as a reference parameter can: the temporary has to be materialised to bind to a, so one move remains. That residual move is the reason emplace_back takes constructor arguments rather than an object (Ch 22).

Forwarding references vs rvalue references

Theory

The syntax && means two different things. In void f(Widget&& w) it is an rvalue reference: only rvalues bind. In template <class T> void f(T&& x), where T is deduced from this very argument, it is a forwarding reference (Scott Meyers' older name: "universal reference"), and it binds to everything. The standard defines it in [temp.deduct.call]/3: "an rvalue reference to a cv-unqualified template parameter that does not represent a template parameter of a class template (during class template argument deduction)". The parenthesised clause only matters for CTAD. A member function of a class template such as V<T>::push(T&&) is excluded for a simpler reason: its T is already fixed, so no deduction happens at the call.

The conditions are strict. All of them must hold:

  1. the form is exactly T&&, with no const and no wrapping template;
  2. T is a template parameter of the function template itself (or auto);
  3. deduction happens for that call.
DeclarationForwarding reference?Reason
template <class T> void f(T&& x)yesthe canonical form
auto&& x = expr;yesauto uses template deduction rules
[](auto&& x) { }yesa generic lambda is a template operator()
template <class... A> void f(A&&... a)yes, each onea pack of forwarding references
void f(Widget&& w)nono deduction
template <class T> void f(const T&& x)noconst breaks the special rule: binds only rvalues
template <class T> void f(std::vector<T>&& v)nothe reference is to vector<T>, not to T
template <class T> struct V { void push(T&& x); };noT was fixed when V<int> was instantiated
template <class T> struct V { template <class U> void emplace(U&& x); };yesU is deduced per call

This is why std::vector<T>::push_back needs two overloads (const T& and T&&, the second being a real rvalue reference), while emplace_back is a single variadic template with forwarding references.

Interview trap

"template <class T> void f(const T&& x) is a universal reference that accepts const objects." It is not. It is an rvalue reference to const and rejects every lvalue: int i; f(i); does not compile. The forwarding rule applies only to the exact form T&&.

Deduction and reference collapsing

Theory

For a parameter T&& where T is deduced, the language adds one special rule ([temp.deduct.call]/3): if the argument is an lvalue of type U, T is deduced as U&. If the argument is an rvalue, T is deduced as plain U. The parameter type is then T&& with T substituted, which can produce a "reference to reference". C++ never lets you write that directly, but it can arise through templates and aliases, and the reference collapsing rules turn it back into a single reference.

T isT& becomesT&& becomes
UU&U&&
U&U& (& & → &)U& (& && → &)
U&&U& (&& & → &)U&& (&& && → &&)

One sentence covers it: if either reference is an lvalue reference, the result is an lvalue reference; only && && gives &&. Collapsing applies in four places: template instantiation, auto deduction, typedef/using aliases and decltype.

#include <cstdio>
#include <type_traits>

using L = int&;
using R = int&&;

template <class T> constexpr bool param_is_lref(T&&) { return std::is_lvalue_reference_v<T&&>; }

int main() {
    static_assert(std::is_same_v<L&, int&>);
    static_assert(std::is_same_v<L&&, int&>);
    static_assert(std::is_same_v<R&, int&>);
    static_assert(std::is_same_v<R&&, int&&>);
    static_assert(std::is_same_v<const L, int&>);      // const on a reference is ignored
    int i = 0;
    std::printf("lvalue arg -> lref param: %d\n", param_is_lref(i));
    std::printf("rvalue arg -> lref param: %d\n", param_is_lref(42));
}
lvalue arg -> lref param: 1
rvalue arg -> lref param: 0

The line const L shows a related rule: const applied to a reference type through an alias is silently dropped (references cannot be reseated anyway), so it stays int&, not const int&. This matters when people write const T& in a template where T may already be a reference.

A const lvalue deduces T = const U&, so constness is part of what is forwarded. The forwarding reference never strips const; it just carries it along, which is why a target can never move from a const argument.

std::forward and why it needs the template argument

Theory

Inside the wrapper the parameter has a name, so it is an lvalue, whatever was passed. std::forward<T>(x) is a conditional cast: it casts x to T&&. By reference collapsing, that is U& when T = U& (the caller passed an lvalue) and U&& when T = U (the caller passed an rvalue).

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>

namespace my {
template <class T>
constexpr T&& forward(std::remove_reference_t<T>& t) noexcept {
    return static_cast<T&&>(t);
}
template <class T>
constexpr T&& forward(std::remove_reference_t<T>&& t) noexcept {
    static_assert(!std::is_lvalue_reference_v<T>, "cannot forward an rvalue as an lvalue");
    return static_cast<T&&>(t);
}
}

static void g(const std::string&) { std::puts("g(const string&)"); }
static void g(std::string&&) { std::puts("g(string&&)"); }

template <class T>
void wrap(T&& x) { g(my::forward<T>(x)); }

int main() {
    std::string s = "abc";
    wrap(s);
    wrap(std::string{"tmp"});
    wrap(std::as_const(s));
    wrap(std::move(s));
}
g(const string&)
g(string&&)
g(const string&)
g(string&&)

Why the explicit template argument. The parameter of forward is std::remove_reference_t<T>&. A T that appears only inside a nested type like remove_reference_t<T> (formally, to the left of ::type) is a non-deduced context ([temp.deduct.type]/5), so std::forward(x) fails to compile. That is deliberate: the argument x is always an lvalue, so deduction from it would always produce the "lvalue" answer and lose the information. The caller's category lives only in the wrapper's T, so you must pass it in by hand.

#include <utility>

template <class T>
void wrap(T&& x) {
    auto y = std::forward(x);   // error: couldn't deduce template parameter
    (void)y;
}

int main() { wrap(1); }

The second overload (taking an rvalue) exists for expressions like std::forward<T>(get_member(x)) where the inner expression is an rvalue. Its static_assert catches the nonsense request "forward this rvalue as an lvalue reference", which would create a dangling reference.

std::move vs std::forward

std::move(x)std::forward<T>(x)
Castalways to remove_reference_t<T>&&to T&&: lvalue or rvalue depending on T
Use ona value you own and will not use again (locals, rvalue reference parameters, members in && functions)forwarding references only
Template argumentdeducedmust be written
Wrong useon a forwarding reference: steals from the caller's lvalueon a non-forwarding parameter: forward<int>(x) just moves, which works but misleads readers

Rule of thumb from Effective Modern C++ (Items 24 and 25): std::move on rvalue references, std::forward on forwarding references, each applied once, at the last use.

Variadic forwarding: make_unique and emplace

Theory

Forwarding references combine with parameter packs. Args&&... args declares one forwarding reference per argument, each with its own deduced type, and std::forward<Args>(args)... expands pairwise into std::forward<A1>(a1), std::forward<A2>(a2), .... This is the whole implementation of std::make_unique for single objects:

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>

namespace my {
template <class T, class... Args>
std::unique_ptr<T> make_unique(Args&&... args) {
    return std::unique_ptr<T>(new T(std::forward<Args>(args)...));
}
}

struct Tracer {
    Tracer() = default;
    Tracer(const Tracer&) { std::puts("  copy"); }
    Tracer(Tracer&&) noexcept { std::puts("  move"); }
};

struct Widget {
    Tracer a, b;
    int n;
    Widget(const Tracer& x, Tracer&& y, int k) : a(x), b(std::move(y)), n(k) {}
};

int main() {
    Tracer t;
    std::puts("make_unique<Widget>(t, Tracer{}, 3):");
    auto w = my::make_unique<Widget>(t, Tracer{}, 3);
    auto p = my::make_unique<std::unique_ptr<int>>(std::make_unique<int>(7));   // move-only argument
    std::printf("n=%d **p=%d\n", w->n, **p);
}
make_unique<Widget>(t, Tracer{}, 3):
  copy
  move
n=3 **p=7

Note the parentheses in new T(...). Before C++20 that meant aggregates could not be created with make_unique (no constructor to call); C++20's parenthesised aggregate initialisation (P0960) fixed it. Another detail: the order in which a constructor's by-value parameters are initialised is unspecified, so tracing programs that print from several by-value parameters can differ between GCC and Clang. The Widget above takes references and initialises members, which always happens in declaration order.

The container version is the same idea with placement construction into already allocated storage: std::allocator_traits<A>::construct(alloc, p, std::forward<Args>(args)...). Ch 22 traces it in detail.

Two other patterns appear often. sizeof...(Args) gives the pack size. And forwarding into several calls means each argument is forwarded at most once: if you pass the same pack to two functions, only the last use may forward; earlier uses must pass the plain names (lvalues).

When perfect forwarding fails

Theory

"Perfect" forwarding is not perfect. Forwarding fails when calling the target directly would work but going through a template does not. There are five classic cases (Effective Modern C++, Item 30), plus the logic error of forwarding twice.

ArgumentWhy it failsFix
Braced initialiser {1, 2, 3}A braced-init-list has no type, so T cannot be deduced ([temp.deduct.call]/1)auto il = {1, 2, 3}; fwd(il); or name the type: fwd(std::vector{1, 2, 3})
0 or NULL as a null pointerDeduced as int (or long); an int variable does not convert to a pointernullptr
Name of an overloaded function or a function templateNo single type to deducestatic_cast<void(*)(int)>(f) or a lambda
Bit-field h.ihlA non-const reference cannot bind to a bit-fieldCopy it first: fwd(static_cast<unsigned>(h.ihl))
static const int N = 28; declared but not definedBinding a reference odr-uses N, which then needs a definition; link errorstatic constexpr (implicitly inline since C++17) or an out-of-class definition
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

static void take(const std::vector<int>&) {}

template <class T>
void fwd(T&& x) { take(std::forward<T>(x)); }

int main() {
    take({1, 2, 3});   // fine: the parameter type is known
    fwd({1, 2, 3});    // error: cannot deduce T from a braced-init-list
}
#include <utility>

static void take(int*) {}

template <class T>
void fwd(T&& x) { take(std::forward<T>(x)); }

int main() {
    take(0);     // fine: the literal 0 is a null pointer constant
    fwd(0);      // error: T = int, and an int expression does not convert to int*
}

All five fixes in one program, using a generic forwarder that calls any callable:

#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

template <class F, class... A>
void fwd(F&& f, A&&... a) { std::forward<F>(f)(std::forward<A>(a)...); }

static void take_vec(const std::vector<int>& v) { std::printf("vector of %zu\n", v.size()); }
static void take_ptr(int* p) { std::printf("pointer is %s\n", p ? "set" : "null"); }
static void process(int x) { std::printf("process(int %d)\n", x); }
static void process(double x) { std::printf("process(double %g)\n", x); }
struct Header { unsigned version : 4, ihl : 4; };
static void take_u(unsigned u) { std::printf("ihl %u\n", u); }
struct Limits { static constexpr int N = 28; };   // implicitly inline: has a definition
static void take_n(const int& n) { std::printf("N %d\n", n); }

int main() {
    auto il = {1, 2, 3};                           // std::initializer_list<int>
    fwd(take_vec, il);
    fwd(take_ptr, nullptr);
    fwd(static_cast<void (*)(int)>(process), 1);
    fwd([](double d) { process(d); }, 2.5);
    Header h{4, 5};
    fwd(take_u, static_cast<unsigned>(h.ihl));
    fwd(take_n, Limits::N);
}
vector of 3
pointer is null
process(int 1)
process(double 2.5)
ihl 5
N 28

Interview trap

The "static const without definition" case often links fine at -O2 (the optimiser inlines the call, folds the value and never emits a reference to the symbol) and fails at -O0 with "undefined reference" / "Undefined symbols". On GCC 16 and Clang 22 the program in the table fails at -O0 and links at -O2; at -O1 GCC fails while Clang links. The standard calls it ill-formed, no diagnostic required, so either outcome is "allowed". A bug that depends on the optimisation level is the worst kind. Since C++17, prefer static constexpr data members, which are implicitly inline and so are always defined.

Forwarding the same argument twice

std::forward may hand the object to a function that moves from it. Any later use of the same parameter then sees a moved-from object. This compiles, and for lvalue arguments it even works, so tests that only pass lvalues never catch it. Forward only at the last use; earlier uses pass the plain name.

Overloading on forwarding references is greedy

Theory

A function template with a T&& parameter produces an exact match for almost any argument. Overload resolution prefers a non-template only when the two are otherwise equally good. The classic victim is a class with a forwarding constructor:

#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>

struct W {
    W() = default;
    template <class T> W(T&&) { std::puts("template ctor"); }
    W(const W&) { std::puts("copy ctor"); }
    W(W&&) noexcept { std::puts("move ctor"); }
};

int main() {
    W a;
    const W ca;
    W b(a);              // T = W&: exact match beats adding const
    W c(ca);             // T = const W&: tie, the non-template wins
    W d(std::move(a));   // T = W: tie, the non-template wins
    W e(std::move(ca));  // T = const W: const W&& beats const W&
}
template ctor
copy ctor
move ctor
template ctor

Copying a non-const W calls the template. If the template's body does something like name_(std::forward<T>(x)) with a std::string member, that is a compile error deep inside the class ("no conversion from W to string"), which confuses everyone. Derived classes hit the same problem: a hand-written derived copy constructor Derived(const Derived& o) : Base(o) calls Base with a const Derived&, and the template (with T = const Derived&) beats Base(const Base&), which needs a derived-to-base conversion. (The implicit copy constructor of Derived passes the Base subobject, so it is safe.)

Constraining the template

Remove the template from overload resolution for the types it should not handle. In C++20 use a requires clause; in C++11/14/17 use std::enable_if_t as a defaulted template parameter.

#include <concepts>
#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

class Person {
public:
    template <class S>
        requires std::constructible_from<std::string, S&&>
    explicit Person(S&& s) : name_(std::forward<S>(s)) { std::puts("forwarding ctor"); }
    Person(const Person& o) : name_(o.name_) { std::puts("copy ctor"); }
    Person(Person&& o) noexcept : name_(std::move(o.name_)) { std::puts("move ctor"); }
    const std::string& name() const { return name_; }
private:
    std::string name_;
};

int main() {
    Person a("Ada");
    std::string bob = "Bob";
    Person b(bob);
    Person c(a);              // the template is no longer viable for Person&
    Person d(std::move(b));
    std::printf("%s %s %s %s\n", a.name().c_str(), bob.c_str(), c.name().c_str(), d.name().c_str());
}
forwarding ctor
forwarding ctor
copy ctor
move ctor
Ada Bob Ada Bob

The C++17 spelling of the same constraint:

template <class S,
          class = std::enable_if_t<!std::is_base_of_v<Person, std::decay_t<S>>>>
explicit Person(S&& s);

Use is_base_of (or std::derived_from) with decay_t/remove_cvref_t when the class itself might be convertible to the target, so that derived classes are excluded too. Tag dispatch (forward to an implementation function overloaded on std::true_type/std::false_type from a trait such as std::is_integral) is the other classic C++11 technique (Effective Modern C++, Item 27). It works for ordinary function templates but not for constructors, which is why constructors use constraints.

Perfect returning and forwarding lambdas

Theory

decltype(auto)

A wrapper should also return exactly what the target returns. auto as a return type uses template deduction and strips references, so a wrapper around a function returning int& would return a copy. decltype(auto) (C++14) deduces the return type with decltype rules instead, preserving references and value category.

#include <cstdio>
#include <functional>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

template <class F, class... A>
decltype(auto) call(F&& f, A&&... a) {
    return std::invoke(std::forward<F>(f), std::forward<A>(a)...);
}
template <class F, class... A>
auto call_auto(F&& f, A&&... a) {
    return std::invoke(std::forward<F>(f), std::forward<A>(a)...);
}

int main() {
    std::vector<int> v{1, 2, 3};
    auto at = [&v](std::size_t i) -> int& { return v[i]; };
    static_assert(std::is_same_v<decltype(call(at, 0)), int&>);
    static_assert(std::is_same_v<decltype(call_auto(at, 0)), int>);
    call(at, 0) = 10;             // writes through the returned reference
    // call_auto(at, 1) = 20;     // error: cannot assign to a prvalue int
    std::printf("v[0]=%d\n", v[0]);
}
v[0]=10

Interview trap

With decltype(auto), parentheses change the type. decltype(x) is the declared type of x, but decltype((x)) is int& for an lvalue x. So decltype(auto) f() { int x = 1; return (x); } returns a dangling int&. Never parenthesise a local in a decltype(auto) return.

Forwarding in generic lambdas

A generic lambda parameter declared auto&& x is a forwarding reference, but there is no named T to pass to std::forward. The idiom is std::forward<decltype(x)>(x). For an lvalue argument decltype(x) is U&, which forwards as an lvalue. For an rvalue it is U&& rather than U, but forward<U&&> returns U&& &&, which collapses to U&&, the same result as forward<U>. C++20 template lambdas let you write the usual form directly.

auto log_call = [](auto&& f, auto&&... args) -> decltype(auto) {
    return std::invoke(std::forward<decltype(f)>(f), std::forward<decltype(args)>(args)...);
};
auto log_call20 = []<class F, class... A>(F&& f, A&&... args) -> decltype(auto) {
    return std::invoke(std::forward<F>(f), std::forward<A>(args)...);
};

auto&& also appears outside templates. for (auto&& e : range) binds to whatever the iterator yields, including proxy prvalues like std::vector<bool>::reference, where auto& would not compile. auto&& r = f(); on a function returning by value binds to a temporary whose lifetime is extended to that of r, so it does not dangle.

C++23 adds std::forward_like<Self>(member), which forwards a member with the value category and constness of the enclosing object. It pairs with "deducing this" (this auto&& self) to write one function instead of four ref-qualified overloads.

Concept and tricky questions

Drills

ConceptWhat is the forwarding problem, and which two language features solve it?

Answer

Answer. Writing a wrapper that passes its arguments to another function with their original value category and constness, so the target copies when the caller passed an lvalue and can move when the caller passed an rvalue. C++11 solves it with forwarding references (T&& with the special deduction rule plus reference collapsing) and std::forward<T>.

Why. const A& loses "rvalue-ness" (and adds const), A& rejects rvalues, and overloading every combination needs 2n functions. Forwarding references record the category in the deduced T; std::forward reads it back. A common incomplete answer mentions only std::forward, but without the deduction rule there would be nothing for it to read.

TrickyWhich of these parameters are forwarding references?

template <class T> void a(T&& x);
template <class T> void b(const T&& x);
template <class T> void c(std::vector<T>&& v);
void d(std::string&& s);
template <class T> struct Box { void e(T&& x); template <class U> void f(U&& y); };
auto&& g = compute();
auto h = [](auto&& z) {};
Answer

Answer. a, Box::f, g and the lambda's z. Not b, c, d or Box::e.

Why. The rule needs the exact form T&& (or auto&&) where T is deduced from that argument in that call. b has const, c wraps T inside vector, d has no template, and in Box::e the T belongs to the class and was fixed at instantiation (Box<int>::e takes int&&). All four only accept rvalues. Candidates often say Box::e is forwarding because "it's in a template", which is the most common error.

ConceptState the reference collapsing rules. Where do they apply?

Answer

Answer. & &, & && and && & all collapse to &; only && && collapses to &&. In words: lvalue reference wins. They apply during template instantiation, auto deduction, typedef/using aliases and decltype.

Why. You cannot write int& && in source code, but substituting T = int& into T&& produces it, and the rules define the result. Combined with "an lvalue argument deduces T = U&", they make a T&& parameter become U& for lvalues and U&& for rvalues, which is the whole forwarding-reference mechanism.

TrickyWhy does std::forward require an explicit template argument while std::move does not?

Answer

Answer. forward takes remove_reference_t<T>&, a non-deduced context, on purpose: the information it needs (the caller's category) is in the wrapper's T, not in the argument expression, which is always an lvalue.

Why. If forward deduced from its argument, it would always see an lvalue and always deduce "lvalue", making it useless. std::move needs no outside information: it casts to rvalue unconditionally, so deducing from the argument is fine. People sometimes answer "because of overloading" or "for readability"; the real reason is that the needed information is not present in the argument.

ConceptWhat do T, the parameter type and the category of the expression x become for template <class T> void f(T&& x) called as f(42), f(i) and f(ci), where int i; const int ci = 0;?

Answer

Answer. f(42): T = int, parameter int&&. f(i): T = int&, parameter int&. f(ci): T = const int&, parameter const int&. In all three, the expression x inside the body is an lvalue.

Why. Rvalues deduce the plain type; lvalues trigger the special rule that adds & to T, and collapsing then makes the parameter an lvalue reference. Constness is kept as part of T. The body sees a named variable either way, which is why it must call std::forward<T>(x) to restore the category.

TrickyFor std::vector<int*> v;, which of these compile: v.push_back(0), v.push_back(NULL), v.emplace_back(0), v.emplace_back(NULL), v.emplace_back(nullptr)?

Answer

Answer. Both push_back calls and emplace_back(nullptr) compile. emplace_back(0) and emplace_back(NULL) do not, on GCC 16 or Clang 22.

Why. push_back takes int* const& or int*&&, so the literal 0 converts directly: an integer literal with value zero is a null pointer constant. emplace_back deduces Args = int (or long for NULL, which both compilers define as __null), and inside the library the argument is an int&& expression, which is no longer a literal and does not convert to a pointer. This is forwarding failure case 2 from the table, hiding inside a standard container. The common wrong answer is "emplace accepts everything push_back accepts"; it does not, because forwarding throws away the "this is a literal 0" property along with braced lists.

Trickyv.emplace_back({1, 2}) fails to compile for std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>, but v.push_back({1, 2}) works. Why?

Answer

Answer. emplace_back takes Args&&..., and a braced-init-list has no type, so Args cannot be deduced. push_back is not a template on its argument: its parameter is const value_type& or value_type&&, so the braces initialise a pair<int, int> directly.

Why. [temp.deduct.call]/1: a braced-init-list argument makes the parameter a non-deduced context unless the parameter is std::initializer_list<P> or an array. This is the first of the classic perfect-forwarding failures. Write v.emplace_back(1, 2) instead, which forwards the two ints to pair's constructor.

ConceptWhen would you use decltype(auto) as a return type instead of auto?

Answer

Answer. In forwarding wrappers that must return exactly what the wrapped call returns, including references: decltype(auto) call(F&& f, A&&... a) { return std::invoke(...); }. Also for accessors that should return a reference when the underlying expression yields one.

Why. auto deduces like a by-value template parameter and drops references and top-level const, so a wrapper around vector::operator[] would return a copy. decltype(auto) applies decltype to the return expression. The cost: return (local); or returning a member access of a local can deduce a reference to a local, which dangles.

TrickyInside template <class T> class Stack { void push(T&& x) { ... } };, a colleague writes data_.push_back(std::forward<T>(x));. Is it a bug?

Answer

Answer. It is not a bug in behaviour, but it is wrong in intent. x is an rvalue reference (not forwarding, because T belongs to the class), and for a non-reference T, std::forward<T>(x) is exactly std::move(x). Write std::move(x).

Why. The two differ only if someone instantiates the class with an lvalue reference type, say Stack<std::string&>: then T&& collapses to std::string&, forward copies, and move would steal from the caller's object. The convention (move for rvalue references, forward for forwarding references) exists so that readers can tell which kind of parameter they are looking at.

ConceptHow do you perfectly forward a parameter in a generic lambda [](auto&& x) { g(???); }, and why does it work?

Answer

Answer. g(std::forward<decltype(x)>(x));. In C++20 you can also write []<class T>(T&& x) { g(std::forward<T>(x)); }.

Why. decltype(x) is the declared type of the parameter: U& for an lvalue argument and U&& for an rvalue. For an rvalue, forward<U&&> returns U&& &&, which collapses to U&&, identical to forward<U>. So the "wrong" template argument for rvalues gives the right answer. Writing std::forward<decltype(x)> without understanding this is fine in practice, but interviewers like to ask why it works.

TrickyIs auto&& r = make_string(); (returning std::string by value) a dangling reference? What about auto&& c = make_string().c_str(); and auto&& f = Builder{}.self(); where self() returns Builder&?

Answer

Answer. The first is safe: r binds directly to the temporary, whose lifetime is extended to r's. The second is a const char* pointing into a temporary string that dies at the end of the statement: dangling. The third is a reference returned by a function: no extension, dangling.

Why. Lifetime extension ([class.temporary]/6) applies only when a reference binds directly to a temporary (or a subobject of it via member access). A reference or pointer returned from a function call is not a temporary, so it never extends anything. auto&& is not special here; it just picks the reference type. People assume "auto&& always keeps things alive".

ConceptWhat does a const lvalue argument do to a forwarding reference parameter? Can the target move from it?

Answer

Answer. T is deduced as const U&, the parameter is const U&, and std::forward<T>(x) yields const U&. The target receives a const lvalue and can only copy.

Why. Forwarding preserves every property, constness included. A const rvalue (std::move(ci)) deduces T = const U and forwards as const U&&, which still binds only to copy constructors. That is correct behaviour: forwarding must not grant permissions the caller did not have.

Predict the output and find the bug

Drills

OutputWhat does each call deduce?

#include <cstdio>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>

template <class T>
constexpr const char* tn() {
    using std::is_same_v;
    if constexpr (is_same_v<T, int>) return "int";
    else if constexpr (is_same_v<T, int&>) return "int&";
    else if constexpr (is_same_v<T, int&&>) return "int&&";
    else if constexpr (is_same_v<T, const int>) return "const int";
    else if constexpr (is_same_v<T, const int&>) return "const int&";
    else if constexpr (is_same_v<T, const int&&>) return "const int&&";
    else return "?";
}

template <class T>
void f(T&&) { std::printf("T=%s param=%s\n", tn<T>(), tn<T&&>()); }

int main() {
    int x = 0;
    const int cx = 0;
    int&& rr = 5;
    f(x);
    f(cx);
    f(rr);
    f(0);
    f(std::move(x));
    f(std::move(cx));
}
Answer
T=int& param=int&
T=const int& param=const int&
T=int& param=int&
T=int param=int&&
T=int param=int&&
T=const int param=const int&&

Answer. As shown. The interesting line is the third: rr is declared int&&, but as an expression it is an lvalue, so T = int&.

Why. Deduction looks at the argument expression's type and category, never at how a variable was declared. Lvalues deduce U&, rvalues deduce U, and const stays part of U. The last line shows that a const rvalue forwards as const int&&, which a move constructor cannot accept.

OutputThe author wanted relay to make a local copy of its argument. What is printed?

#include <cstdio>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>

struct Tr {
    Tr() = default;
    Tr(const Tr&) { std::puts("  copy"); }
    Tr(Tr&&) noexcept { std::puts("  move"); }
};

template <class T>
void relay(T&& x) {
    T local = std::forward<T>(x);
    (void)local;
    std::printf("  local is %s\n", std::is_reference_v<T> ? "a reference" : "an object");
}

int main() {
    Tr t;
    const Tr ct;
    std::puts("lvalue:");        relay(t);
    std::puts("const lvalue:");  relay(ct);
    std::puts("rvalue:");        relay(Tr{});
}
Answer
lvalue:
  local is a reference
const lvalue:
  local is a reference
rvalue:
  move
  local is an object

Answer. No copy is ever printed. For lvalues, T is a reference type, so T local declares a reference that aliases the caller's object. Only the rvalue case creates an object, by moving.

Why. T is Tr& or const Tr& for lvalue arguments. Code that uses T as "the value type" inside a forwarding function is a classic bug: modifying local would modify the caller's object. Use std::remove_cvref_t<T> local = std::forward<T>(x); or simply auto local = std::forward<T>(x); to get a real copy or move.

OutputThree lambdas, two arguments each. What is printed?

#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>

struct Tr {
    Tr() = default;
    Tr(const Tr&) { std::puts("  copy"); }
    Tr(Tr&&) noexcept { std::puts("  move"); }
};

static void sink(Tr) {}

int main() {
    auto plain = [](auto&& x) { sink(x); };
    auto fwd = [](auto&& x) { sink(std::forward<decltype(x)>(x)); };
    auto fwd20 = []<class U>(U&& x) { sink(std::forward<U>(x)); };
    Tr t;
    std::puts("plain:"); plain(t); plain(Tr{});
    std::puts("fwd:");   fwd(t);   fwd(Tr{});
    std::puts("fwd20:"); fwd20(t); fwd20(Tr{});
}
Answer
plain:
  copy
  copy
fwd:
  copy
  move
fwd20:
  copy
  move

Answer. Without std::forward both calls copy; with it, the lvalue copies and the temporary moves.

Why. auto&& x is a forwarding reference, but inside the body x is a named lvalue, so sink(x) always copies. decltype(x) is Tr& or Tr&&; forwarding with either gives the right category thanks to collapsing. The C++20 template-lambda form is identical in effect.

OutputA class with an unconstrained forwarding constructor. Which constructor does each line call?

#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>

struct Base {
    Base() = default;
    template <class T> Base(T&&) { std::puts("Base template"); }
    Base(const Base&) { std::puts("Base copy"); }
    Base(Base&&) noexcept { std::puts("Base move"); }
};

struct Derived : Base {
    Derived() = default;
    Derived(const Derived& o) : Base(o) {}               // passes a Derived, not a Base
    Derived(Derived&& o) noexcept : Base(std::move(o)) {}
};

int main() {
    Derived d;
    const Derived cd;
    Derived d2(d);
    Derived d3(cd);
    Derived d4(std::move(d));
    Base b(cd);
}
Answer
Base template
Base template
Base template
Base template

Answer. All four lines call the template.

Why. Derived's hand-written copy constructor calls Base(o) with o of type const Derived&. The template deduces T = const Derived&, an exact match, while Base(const Base&) needs a derived-to-base conversion, which ranks worse. The move constructor passes Derived&&, and again the template wins over Base(Base&&). Base b(cd) goes through the template for the same reason. Had Derived used the implicit copy and move constructors, they would pass the Base subobject itself and the real constructors would run; hand-written ones that pass the whole object are the trap. Constraining with requires (!std::derived_from<std::remove_cvref_t<T>, Base>) makes all four use the copy or move constructors.

Find the bugA helper stores a string. After calling it, the caller's variable is empty. Why?

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

static std::vector<std::string> saved;

template <class S>
void remember(S&& s) {
    saved.push_back(std::move(s));
}

int main() {
    std::string name = "Ada Lovelace, first programmer";
    remember(name);
    std::printf("name='%s' saved='%s'\n", name.c_str(), saved[0].c_str());
}
Answer
name='' saved='Ada Lovelace, first programmer'

Answer. std::move on a forwarding reference moves unconditionally. For the lvalue name, S = std::string&, and std::move(s) steals the caller's string. Use std::forward<S>(s).

Why. The caller passed an lvalue and expects it to be untouched; only forward respects that. The printed empty string is what both libstdc++ and libc++ leave behind; the standard only says "valid but unspecified", which is worse: the program might print the old value on another library, hiding the bug in testing.

Find the bugThe second log line is wrong for rvalue arguments. Why?

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

static std::vector<std::string> store, audit;

template <class S>
void record(S&& s) {
    store.push_back(std::forward<S>(s));
    audit.push_back(std::forward<S>(s));
}

int main() {
    std::string a = "alpha-alpha-alpha-alpha";
    record(a);
    record(std::string("bravo-bravo-bravo-bravo"));
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < store.size(); ++i)
        std::printf("store='%s' audit='%s'\n", store[i].c_str(), audit[i].c_str());
}
Answer
store='alpha-alpha-alpha-alpha' audit='alpha-alpha-alpha-alpha'
store='bravo-bravo-bravo-bravo' audit=''

Answer. The argument is forwarded twice. For an rvalue, the first forward lets push_back move the string into store, and the second pushes the moved-from (empty) husk into audit.

Why. Forward only on the last use. Fix: audit.push_back(s); store.push_back(std::forward<S>(s));, copying first and forwarding last. The lvalue call works either way, so tests that only use named variables pass, which is why this bug survives code review. The empty output is the libstdc++ and libc++ behaviour for a moved-from string.

Find the bugThis factory takes forwarding references but still copies. Find the problem.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>

struct Tr {
    Tr() = default;
    Tr(const Tr&) { std::puts("copy"); }
    Tr(Tr&&) noexcept { std::puts("move"); }
};

struct Job {
    Tr payload;
    explicit Job(Tr p) : payload(std::move(p)) {}
};

template <class... Args>
std::unique_ptr<Job> make_job(Args&&... args) {
    return std::make_unique<Job>(args...);
}

int main() {
    auto j = make_job(Tr{});
}
Answer
copy
move

Answer. args... expands to named lvalues, so make_unique receives lvalues and the Job parameter is copy-constructed. Write std::make_unique<Job>(std::forward<Args>(args)...); the output then becomes move, move.

Why. Declaring a forwarding reference only captures the category in Args; nothing uses it unless std::forward is called. With move-only arguments (a unique_ptr) the same bug becomes a compile error deep inside make_unique, which is easier to notice than a silent copy.

Find the bugWhy does this not compile, and what are two fixes?

#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>

static void handler(int x) { std::printf("int %d\n", x); }
static void handler(const char* s) { std::printf("str %s\n", s); }

template <class F, class... A>
void dispatch(F&& f, A&&... a) { std::forward<F>(f)(std::forward<A>(a)...); }

int main() {
    dispatch(handler, 42);
}
Answer

Answer. handler names an overload set, which has no single type, so F cannot be deduced. Fixes: dispatch(static_cast<void (*)(int)>(handler), 42); or wrap it: dispatch([](auto&& x) { handler(std::forward<decltype(x)>(x)); }, 42);.

Why. Calling handler(42) directly works because overload resolution sees the argument. Passing the name to a template asks the compiler to pick a type before any call happens. The same failure occurs for a function template name, even with explicit template arguments: dispatch(std::max<int>, 1, 2) does not compile on GCC or Clang, because std::max<int> still names several overloads (two arguments, two arguments plus a comparator, an initializer list). People often assume the <int> picks one function. The lambda fix is the robust one: it defers overload resolution to the call.

Find the bugA bit-field passed through a forwarding wrapper. Why the compile error?

#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>

struct IPv4Header {
    std::uint32_t version : 4, ihl : 4, dscp : 6, ecn : 2, total_length : 16;
};

static void show(std::uint32_t v) { std::printf("%u\n", v); }

template <class T>
void log_and_show(T&& x) { show(std::forward<T>(x)); }

int main() {
    IPv4Header h{4, 5, 0, 0, 20};
    show(h.ihl);           // fine
    log_and_show(h.ihl);   // error
}
Answer

Answer. h.ihl is an lvalue, so T = std::uint32_t&, and a non-const reference cannot bind to a bit-field ([class.bit]/3): bit-fields are not addressable. Fix: pass a copy, log_and_show(static_cast<std::uint32_t>(h.ihl)) or auto v = h.ihl; log_and_show(v);.

Why. A function that takes the bit-field by value or by const& works, because the compiler can make a temporary copy. A forwarding reference deduced from an lvalue is a non-const lvalue reference, which must refer to the actual bits. This comes up in networking code that parses packed headers.

Find the bugA helper captures a call to run later. ASan reports a stack-use-after-scope. Why, and how do you fix it while keeping perfect forwarding?

#include <algorithm>
#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

static long count_a(const std::string& s) { return std::count(s.begin(), s.end(), 'a'); }

template <class F, class... A>
auto defer(F f, A&&... a) {
    return [f, &a...] { return f(std::forward<A>(a)...); };
}

int main() {
    auto job = defer(count_a, std::string("banana, papaya and a long tail of text"));
    std::printf("a count: %ld\n", job());
}
Answer

Answer. [f, &a...] captures the forwarding references by reference. For the rvalue argument, a refers to the temporary std::string, which dies at the end of the statement that creates job. Calling job() then reads a dead object. Fix by capturing the pack by value with a C++20 init-capture pack: [f, ...a = std::forward<A>(a)]() mutable { return f(std::move(a)...); }. Lvalue arguments are then copied into the closure and rvalues are moved in.

Why. A forwarding reference is still a reference: perfect forwarding is only safe within the call that received the arguments. Anything that outlives the call (a closure, a stored task, a thread) must decay-copy the arguments, as std::thread, std::bind and std::async do. Before C++20, use std::make_tuple(std::forward<A>(a)...) captured by value and std::apply. A tempting half-fix is [=] with std::forward<A>(a) left in the body: the copies are then const members of a non-mutable closure, std::forward cannot bind them, and the code stops compiling. The captured copies belong to the closure, so the body should std::move them, which needs mutable. Without ASan this program often prints the right count, because the dead string's buffer has not been reused yet.

Write the code

Coding

CodeImplement my::move and my::forward (both overloads of forward) and show, with an overload probe, that a forwarding wrapper built on them preserves all four combinations of const and value category. Show that forwarding an rvalue as an lvalue is rejected at compile time.

Answer

Approach. move casts to remove_reference_t<T>&&. forward has two overloads taking remove_reference_t<T>& and &&, both returning static_cast<T&&>(t); the second asserts that T is not an lvalue reference. A probe with four overloads reports what the wrapper delivered.

#include <cstdio>
#include <type_traits>

namespace my {
template <class T>
constexpr std::remove_reference_t<T>&& move(T&& t) noexcept {
    return static_cast<std::remove_reference_t<T>&&>(t);
}
template <class T>
constexpr T&& forward(std::remove_reference_t<T>& t) noexcept {
    return static_cast<T&&>(t);
}
template <class T>
constexpr T&& forward(std::remove_reference_t<T>&& t) noexcept {
    static_assert(!std::is_lvalue_reference_v<T>, "cannot forward an rvalue as an lvalue");
    return static_cast<T&&>(t);
}
}

static const char* probe(int&) { return "int&"; }
static const char* probe(const int&) { return "const int&"; }
static const char* probe(int&&) { return "int&&"; }
static const char* probe(const int&&) { return "const int&&"; }

template <class T>
const char* relay(T&& x) { return probe(my::forward<T>(x)); }

static int value() { return 3; }

int main() {
    int x = 1;
    const int cx = 2;
    std::printf("%s\n", relay(x));
    std::printf("%s\n", relay(cx));
    std::printf("%s\n", relay(7));
    std::printf("%s\n", relay(my::move(cx)));
    std::printf("%s\n", probe(my::forward<int>(value())));   // the rvalue overload
    static_assert(std::is_same_v<decltype(my::forward<int&>(x)), int&>);
    static_assert(std::is_same_v<decltype(my::forward<int>(x)), int&&>);
    static_assert(std::is_same_v<decltype(my::move(x)), int&&>);
}
int&
const int&
int&&
const int&&
int&&
#include <type_traits>

namespace my {
template <class T>
constexpr T&& forward(std::remove_reference_t<T>& t) noexcept { return static_cast<T&&>(t); }
template <class T>
constexpr T&& forward(std::remove_reference_t<T>&& t) noexcept {
    static_assert(!std::is_lvalue_reference_v<T>, "cannot forward an rvalue as an lvalue");
    return static_cast<T&&>(t);
}
}

int main() {
    int& r = my::forward<int&>(42);   // static_assert fires: would dangle
    (void)r;
}

Complexity and pitfalls. No run-time cost; both are casts. Pitfalls: writing forward(T&& t) with a deducible parameter (callers could omit the template argument and always get the lvalue answer); returning remove_reference_t<T>&& from forward (that is move); omitting the rvalue overload, which makes forward<int>(value()) fail to compile. The standard versions are also [[nodiscard]] in recent libraries.

Estimated rating: ~1500 · two lines each, but you must explain non-deduced contexts and collapsing to justify them

CodeImplement my::make_unique with the standard's three forms: make_unique<T>(args...) for single objects, make_unique<T[]>(n) for unbounded arrays (value-initialised), and a deleted overload for bounded arrays T[N]. Test with a move-only argument, an aggregate (C++20) and an array.

Answer

Approach. Three overloads selected by constraints on T. The single-object form forwards the pack into new T(...). The array form computes the element type with remove_extent_t and uses new E[n](), where the () value-initialises (zeroes ints). The bounded-array form is = delete so that make_unique<int[3]>() is a clear "use of deleted function" error instead of a confusing one.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>

namespace my {
template <class T, class... Args>
    requires (!std::is_array_v<T>)
std::unique_ptr<T> make_unique(Args&&... args) {
    return std::unique_ptr<T>(new T(std::forward<Args>(args)...));
}
template <class T>
    requires std::is_unbounded_array_v<T>
std::unique_ptr<T> make_unique(std::size_t n) {
    return std::unique_ptr<T>(new std::remove_extent_t<T>[n]());
}
template <class T, class... Args>
    requires std::is_bounded_array_v<T>
void make_unique(Args&&...) = delete;
}

struct Point { int x, y; };                      // aggregate: no constructor
struct Owner {
    std::unique_ptr<int> p;
    explicit Owner(std::unique_ptr<int> q) : p(std::move(q)) {}
};

int main() {
    auto s = my::make_unique<std::string>(3, 'z');
    auto pt = my::make_unique<Point>(1, 2);       // C++20 parenthesised aggregate init
    auto o = my::make_unique<Owner>(std::make_unique<int>(42));
    auto arr = my::make_unique<int[]>(4);
    arr[2] = 9;
    std::printf("%s (%d,%d) %d [%d %d %d %d]\n", s->c_str(), pt->x, pt->y, *o->p,
                arr[0], arr[1], arr[2], arr[3]);
}
zzz (1,2) 42 [0 0 9 0]

Complexity and pitfalls. One allocation per call. Pitfalls: using braces new T{...}, which changes meaning for types with initializer-list constructors (make_unique<std::vector<int>>(3, 1) must make three ones, not the list {3, 1}); forgetting the () in the array form, which leaves ints uninitialised (C++20's make_unique_for_overwrite does that on purpose); not forwarding, which breaks move-only arguments. Why make_unique exists at all: before C++17, f(std::unique_ptr<A>(new A), g()) could leak if the compiler evaluated new A, then g() threw (see Ch 11).

Estimated rating: ~1600 · variadic forwarding plus array specialisation via constraints, with a few value-initialisation details

CodeWrite logged(name, f, args...), a wrapper that prints -> name(N args) before the call and <- name after it, perfectly forwards the callable and arguments through std::invoke, and perfectly returns the result (value, reference or void). It must work with member function pointers and move-only return types.

Answer

Approach. The return type is decltype(auto) and the body returns the std::invoke call directly, which preserves references and works for void (returning a void expression is allowed). The "after" message is printed by a local object's destructor, which runs after the return value has been constructed. That avoids storing the result in a variable, which would break perfect returning.

#include <cstdio>
#include <functional>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

template <class F, class... A>
decltype(auto) logged(const char* name, F&& f, A&&... a) {
    std::printf("-> %s(%zu args)\n", name, sizeof...(A));
    struct Exit {
        const char* n;
        ~Exit() { std::printf("<- %s\n", n); }
    } exit_log{name};
    return std::invoke(std::forward<F>(f), std::forward<A>(a)...);
}

struct Account {
    int balance = 0;
    void deposit(int x) { balance += x; }
    int& ref() { return balance; }
};

static std::unique_ptr<std::string> make_name(std::string s) {
    return std::make_unique<std::string>(std::move(s));
}

int main() {
    Account acc;
    logged("deposit", &Account::deposit, acc, 50);              // member pointer, void
    logged("ref", &Account::ref, acc) += 5;                      // returns int&
    static_assert(std::is_same_v<decltype(logged("r", &Account::ref, acc)), int&>);
    auto name = logged("make_name", make_name, std::string("Ada")); // move-only result
    std::vector<int> v{3, 1, 2};
    auto sum = logged("sum", [](const std::vector<int>& xs) { int s = 0; for (int x : xs) s += x; return s; }, v);
    std::printf("balance=%d name=%s sum=%d\n", acc.balance, name->c_str(), sum);
}
-> deposit(2 args)
<- deposit
-> ref(1 args)
<- ref
-> make_name(1 args)
<- make_name
-> sum(1 args)
<- sum
balance=55 name=Ada sum=6

Complexity and pitfalls. No overhead beyond the two prints. Pitfalls: writing auto result = std::invoke(...); log(); return result; loses references and adds a move (and needs a special case for void); writing decltype(auto) r = ...; return r; keeps references but returning a named T&& variable needs C++23's implicit-move rules; forgetting std::invoke breaks member pointers. Note that <- ref prints before the += 5 runs, because the destructor fires when logged returns.

Estimated rating: ~1800 · perfect returning with a post-call hook is a known trick that most candidates do not reach unaided

CodeWrite a class Label holding a std::string, with a forwarding constructor that accepts anything a std::string can be constructed from. Label also has an implicit operator std::string(). Copying and moving a Label, and copying a class derived from it, must use the real copy and move constructors. Prove it with a trace.

Answer

Approach. A positive constraint (constructible_from<std::string, S>) is not enough here, because Label converts to std::string, so a Label& argument would satisfy it and the template would hijack copies. Add a negative constraint that removes Label and anything derived from it: !std::derived_from<std::remove_cvref_t<S>, Label>.

#include <concepts>
#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>

class Label {
public:
    template <class S>
        requires std::constructible_from<std::string, S&&> &&
                 (!std::derived_from<std::remove_cvref_t<S>, Label>)
    explicit Label(S&& s) : text_(std::forward<S>(s)) { std::puts("  forwarding"); }
    Label(const Label& o) : text_(o.text_) { std::puts("  copy"); }
    Label(Label&& o) noexcept : text_(std::move(o.text_)) { std::puts("  move"); }
    operator std::string() const { return text_; }
    const std::string& text() const { return text_; }
private:
    std::string text_;
};

struct Badge : Label {
    int level;
    Badge(std::string s, int l) : Label(std::move(s)), level(l) {}
    Badge(const Badge& o) : Label(o), level(o.level) {}   // passes a Badge to Label
};

int main() {
    std::puts("from literal, string, string_view:");
    Label a("alpha");
    std::string s = "beta";
    Label b(s);
    Label c(std::string_view("gamma"));
    std::puts("copy and move:");
    Label d(a);
    Label e(std::move(b));
    std::puts("derived:");
    Badge x("delta", 3);
    Badge y(x);
    std::printf("%s %s %s %s %d\n", a.text().c_str(), d.text().c_str(), e.text().c_str(),
                y.text().c_str(), y.level);
}
from literal, string, string_view:
  forwarding
  forwarding
  forwarding
copy and move:
  copy
  move
derived:
  forwarding
  copy
alpha alpha beta delta 3

Complexity and pitfalls. Construction is linear in the string length. Without the derived_from constraint, Label d(a) would run the template (Label& converts to std::string through the conversion operator, an extra copy) and so would Badge y(x), because Badge's copy constructor passes a whole const Badge& to Label. The constraint uses remove_cvref_t because S is a reference type for lvalues. Explicit is kept on the forwarding constructor so that strings do not silently convert to Label.

Estimated rating: ~1700 · requires seeing that a positive constraint is defeated by the conversion operator

CodeWrite make_scope_guard(f), returning a move-only ScopeGuard that runs f on destruction unless dismiss() was called. It must store the callable by value (decayed), copying lvalue callables and moving rvalue ones, and accept function names, lambdas and function objects. Trace the copies and moves of a function object.

Answer

Approach. ScopeGuard<F> holds an F and an active flag. The factory deduces the guard's type as ScopeGuard<std::decay_t<F>> (so a function name becomes a function pointer and a reference becomes a value) and forwards the callable into the guard's constructor. The guard is returned as a prvalue, so no move of the guard happens in C++17 and later; a move constructor is still provided for users who want to transfer it.

#include <cstdio>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>

template <class F>
class ScopeGuard {
public:
    template <class G>
    explicit ScopeGuard(G&& g) : f_(std::forward<G>(g)) {}
    ScopeGuard(ScopeGuard&& o) noexcept(std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<F>)
        : f_(std::move(o.f_)), active_(std::exchange(o.active_, false)) {}
    ScopeGuard(const ScopeGuard&) = delete;
    ScopeGuard& operator=(const ScopeGuard&) = delete;
    ScopeGuard& operator=(ScopeGuard&&) = delete;
    ~ScopeGuard() { if (active_) f_(); }
    void dismiss() noexcept { active_ = false; }
private:
    F f_;
    bool active_ = true;
};

template <class F>
[[nodiscard]] ScopeGuard<std::decay_t<F>> make_scope_guard(F&& f) {
    return ScopeGuard<std::decay_t<F>>(std::forward<F>(f));
}

struct Action {
    const char* msg;
    Action(const char* m) : msg(m) {}
    Action(const Action& o) : msg(o.msg) { std::puts("  Action copy"); }
    Action(Action&& o) noexcept : msg(o.msg) { std::puts("  Action move"); }
    void operator()() const { std::printf("  run: %s\n", msg); }
};

static void cleanup() { std::puts("  run: cleanup()"); }

int main() {
    Action named("named");
    {
        std::puts("lvalue functor:");
        auto g1 = make_scope_guard(named);
        std::puts("rvalue functor:");
        auto g2 = make_scope_guard(Action("temp"));
        std::puts("function name and lambda:");
        auto g3 = make_scope_guard(cleanup);
        auto g4 = make_scope_guard([] { std::puts("  run: lambda"); });
        g4.dismiss();
        static_assert(std::is_same_v<decltype(g3), ScopeGuard<void (*)()>>);
        std::puts("leaving scope:");
    }
}
lvalue functor:
  Action copy
rvalue functor:
  Action move
function name and lambda:
leaving scope:
  run: cleanup()
  run: temp
  run: named

Complexity and pitfalls. Zero overhead beyond the stored callable and a bool. Guards run in reverse order of creation (g4 is dismissed). Pitfalls: storing F instead of decay_t<F> makes the guard hold a reference to the caller's functor (dangling if the functor is a temporary) or fail to compile for function types; letting an exception escape the destructor terminates the program, so production guards wrap the call in try or require noexcept callables; the unconstrained template constructor is safe here only because copying is deleted and the class is never constructed from itself through it (the move constructor wins the tie for rvalues). C++ has std::experimental::scope_exit in the Library Fundamentals TS v3 with the same design.

Estimated rating: ~1600 · decay plus forwarding into a stored member, with move-only semantics and destructor ordering

CodeImplement my::forward_like<T>(x) (the C++23 utility): it returns x with the value category and constness of T, so that a function taking Self&& self can forward self.member correctly. Test all four combinations of const and value category on the owner.

Answer

Approach. Read two facts from T: is T&& an lvalue reference, and is remove_reference_t<T> const. Then return x as an lvalue or an xvalue, adding const with std::as_const when the owner was const. The return type is auto&&, so each if constexpr branch produces its own reference type.

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>

namespace my {
template <class T, class U>
constexpr auto&& forward_like(U&& x) noexcept {
    constexpr bool add_const = std::is_const_v<std::remove_reference_t<T>>;
    if constexpr (std::is_lvalue_reference_v<T&&>) {
        if constexpr (add_const) return std::as_const(x);
        else return static_cast<U&>(x);
    } else {
        if constexpr (add_const) return std::move(std::as_const(x));
        else return std::move(x);
    }
}
}

static const char* probe(std::string&) { return "string&"; }
static const char* probe(const std::string&) { return "const string&"; }
static const char* probe(std::string&&) { return "string&&"; }
static const char* probe(const std::string&&) { return "const string&&"; }

struct Holder { std::string s = "payload"; };

template <class Self>
const char* get(Self&& self) { return probe(my::forward_like<Self>(self.s)); }

int main() {
    Holder h;
    const Holder ch;
    std::printf("%s\n", get(h));
    std::printf("%s\n", get(ch));
    std::printf("%s\n", get(Holder{}));
    std::printf("%s\n", get(std::move(ch)));
    std::string taken = my::forward_like<Holder>(h.s);   // owner treated as rvalue: moves
    std::printf("taken=%s left=%zu\n", taken.c_str(), h.s.size());
}
string&
const string&
string&&
const string&&
taken=payload left=0

Complexity and pitfalls. Compile-time only. Why not just std::forward<Self>(self).s? That also works for data members (member access on an xvalue is an xvalue), but not for things reached through a pointer or a getter, such as *self.ptr_ in an optional-like class; forward_like handles those. Pitfall: for a const owner, the result must be const even if the member is not, otherwise a const object's internals could be moved from. The left=0 line reflects both standard libraries' moved-from strings.

Estimated rating: ~1900 · four-way category and constness propagation with if constexpr and auto&& returns

Cheat sheet

Theory
  • Forwarding reference: exactly T&& (or auto&&) with T deduced in this call. const T&&, vector<T>&& and a class template's T&& are plain rvalue references.
  • Deduction: lvalue argument gives T = U&, rvalue gives T = U; const is kept. Collapsing: any & wins; only && && gives &&.
  • std::forward<T>(x) = static_cast<T&&>(x); the template argument is mandatory because the argument is always an lvalue. Forward once, at the last use.
  • move vs forward: std::move for rvalue references and values you own; std::forward for forwarding references. Moving a forwarding reference steals from callers' lvalues.
  • Variadic: template <class... A> f(A&&... a) with std::forward<A>(a)...; that is all of make_unique and emplace.
  • Failures: braced lists, 0/NULL, overloaded names, bit-fields, undefined static const members.
  • Greedy templates: T&& constructors beat the copy constructor for non-const lvalues and derived classes; constrain with requires or enable_if.
  • Returning: decltype(auto) for perfect returning, never return (local);. In generic lambdas use std::forward<decltype(x)>(x).
