Part F · Move semantics and value passing · Chapter 22

emplace vs push_back

push_back inserts an object you already have; emplace_back builds the object inside the container from constructor arguments. The difference is one move at most, but emplace also calls explicit constructors and allows narrowing, so it can turn a compile error into a leak or a silent bug. Interviewers like this topic because "always use emplace" is a popular wrong answer.

TheoryDrillsCoding· about 3 hours· prerequisites: Ch 20 (moves), Ch 21 (perfect forwarding), Ch 14 (placement new)

What each function does

Theory

Mental model. A vector's spare capacity is raw memory. Something has to construct a T in the next free slot. push_back receives a finished T (by reference) and copy- or move-constructs the slot from it. emplace_back receives the ingredients and runs T's constructor directly in the slot, so no intermediate T ever exists.

void push_back(const T& value);                 // copy-constructs the slot from value
void push_back(T&& value);                      // move-constructs the slot from value
template <class... Args>
T& emplace_back(Args&&... args);                // constructs the slot from args (returns T& since C++17)

Under the hood all three end in the same call: std::allocator_traits<A>::construct(alloc, slot, args...). For std::allocator that is std::construct_at(slot, std::forward<Args>(args)...), which is placement new with parentheses: ::new (static_cast<void*>(slot)) T(std::forward<Args>(args)...). push_back(x) is simply the case where the argument list is one T.

The same pairs exist across the library: push_front/emplace_front (deque, list, forward_list), insert/emplace (every standard container except std::array, at a position for sequences), push/emplace (stack, queue, priority_queue adaptors) and insert/emplace/try_emplace for associative containers.

Tracing every combination

Theory

A type that prints each special member call, a vector with enough capacity reserved so no reallocation interferes, and the eight interesting calls:

#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

static bool tracing = true;

struct T {
    int v;
    T(int x) : v(x) { if (tracing) std::printf("  ctor(%d)\n", v); }
    T(const T& o) : v(o.v) { if (tracing) std::printf("  copy(%d)\n", v); }
    T(T&& o) noexcept : v(o.v) { if (tracing) std::printf("  move(%d)\n", v); }
    ~T() { if (tracing) std::printf("  dtor(%d)\n", v); }
};

int main() {
    std::vector<T> v;
    v.reserve(16);              // no reallocation noise
    T t(0);
    std::puts("push_back(t):");               v.push_back(t);
    std::puts("push_back(std::move(t)):");    v.push_back(std::move(t));
    std::puts("push_back(T(3)):");            v.push_back(T(3));
    std::puts("push_back(4):");               v.push_back(4);
    std::puts("emplace_back(t):");            v.emplace_back(t);
    std::puts("emplace_back(std::move(t)):"); v.emplace_back(std::move(t));
    std::puts("emplace_back(T(7)):");         v.emplace_back(T(7));
    std::puts("emplace_back(8):");            v.emplace_back(8);
    tracing = false;            // element destruction order differs by library
}
  ctor(0)
push_back(t):
  copy(0)
push_back(std::move(t)):
  move(0)
push_back(T(3)):
  ctor(3)
  move(3)
  dtor(3)
push_back(4):
  ctor(4)
  move(4)
  dtor(4)
emplace_back(t):
  copy(0)
emplace_back(std::move(t)):
  move(0)
emplace_back(T(7)):
  ctor(7)
  move(7)
  dtor(7)
emplace_back(8):
  ctor(8)

Key facts

CallSpecial membersNotes
push_back(lvalue)copyidentical to emplace_back(lvalue)
push_back(std::move(x))moveidentical to emplace_back(std::move(x))
push_back(T(args))ctor + move + dtorthe prvalue must be materialised to bind to T&&
push_back(arg), implicit conversionctor + move + dtoronly works if the converting constructor is not explicit
emplace_back(T(args))ctor + move + dtorno better than push_back: you built the temporary yourself
emplace_back(args)ctorthe only case where emplace wins; calls explicit constructors too
Return typepush_back: voidemplace_back: T& since C++17, void in C++11/14
Braced argument {1, 2}push_back worksemplace_back does not compile (no type to deduce, Ch 21)

Know this cold

Copy elision cannot reach into a container. A prvalue argument to push_back or emplace_back is always materialised as a temporary, because a reference parameter has to bind to an object. Only emplace_back(ctor args) avoids that object.

emplace_back returns a reference (C++17)

Theory

Since C++17, emplace_back and emplace_front on vector, deque, list and forward_list (which has only emplace_front), and emplace on the queue and stack adaptors, return a reference to the inserted element (P0084, "Emplace Return Type"). priority_queue::emplace still returns void, because the new element is not at a known position. Before that you wrote v.emplace_back(...); auto& x = v.back();. The reference is valid until the next operation that invalidates references (any reallocation for vector).

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct Order { std::string sym; int qty; Order(std::string s, int q) : sym(std::move(s)), qty(q) {} };

int main() {
    std::vector<Order> book;
    Order& o = book.emplace_back("AAPL", 100);
    o.qty += 50;
    book.emplace_back("MSFT", 10).qty *= 3;
    for (const Order& x : book) std::printf("%s %d\n", x.sym.c_str(), x.qty);
}
AAPL 150
MSFT 30
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<int> v;
    int& r = v.emplace_back(1);   // C++14: emplace_back returns void
    (void)r;
}

The returned reference is the safe way to touch the new element. Taking o above and then emplacing more elements is the bug: o refers into the old buffer once the vector grows (see the reallocation section below).

When emplace is no better, and when it is worse

Theory

No better

  • Passing an existing object: emplace_back(x) copies and emplace_back(std::move(x)) moves, exactly like push_back.
  • Passing a temporary you built yourself: emplace_back(T{...}) is the same as push_back(T{...}).
  • Types that are cheap to move (int, small structs, std::string under SSO): the saved move costs nothing measurable.
  • Associative containers when the key is often already present: emplace may build a node and throw it away (see the maps section below).

Explicit constructors are bypassed

push_back(arg) uses copy-initialisation of a T parameter, which respects explicit. emplace_back(arg) uses direct-initialisation inside the container, which calls explicit constructors happily. That removes a safety net the class author put there on purpose.

#include <memory>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<int>> v;
    v.push_back(new int(1));     // error: unique_ptr(pointer) is explicit
}

The emplace version compiles, and leaks if the vector has to grow and the allocation fails. The raw pointer is created as an argument; if emplace_back throws before the unique_ptr is constructed in the slot, nothing owns it:

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <new>
#include <vector>

static bool fail_next = false;

template <class T>
struct FlakyAlloc {
    using value_type = T;
    FlakyAlloc() = default;
    template <class U> FlakyAlloc(const FlakyAlloc<U>&) noexcept {}
    T* allocate(std::size_t n) {
        if (fail_next) throw std::bad_alloc();
        return std::allocator<T>{}.allocate(n);
    }
    void deallocate(T* p, std::size_t n) noexcept { std::allocator<T>{}.deallocate(p, n); }
    friend bool operator==(const FlakyAlloc&, const FlakyAlloc&) { return true; }
};

struct Obj {
    static inline int live = 0;
    Obj() { ++live; }
    ~Obj() { --live; }
};

int main() {
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Obj>, FlakyAlloc<std::unique_ptr<Obj>>> v;
    v.emplace_back(new Obj);                       // capacity 1
    fail_next = true;
    try { v.emplace_back(new Obj); }               // growth fails before any unique_ptr owns it
    catch (const std::bad_alloc&) { std::puts("emplace_back(new Obj): bad_alloc"); }
    try { v.push_back(std::make_unique<Obj>()); }  // the temporary unique_ptr cleans up
    catch (const std::bad_alloc&) { std::puts("push_back(make_unique): bad_alloc"); }
    fail_next = false;
    v.clear();
    std::printf("live objects after clear: %d\n", Obj::live);
}
emplace_back(new Obj): bad_alloc
push_back(make_unique): bad_alloc
live objects after clear: 1

The one surviving Obj is the leak. The rule: never pass a raw owning new as an argument; create the owner first with std::make_unique, then push or emplace it.

vector<vector<int>>: braces vs parentheses

push_back({10}) copy-list-initialises an std::vector<int> from {10}, which picks the initializer-list constructor: one element, value 10. emplace_back(10) direct-initialises with parentheses, std::vector<int>(10), which is the explicit size constructor: ten zeros. push_back(10) does not compile because that constructor is explicit.

#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<std::vector<int>> vv;
    vv.push_back({10});        // {10}
    vv.emplace_back(10);       // ten zeros
    vv.emplace_back(3, 7);     // {7, 7, 7}
    for (const auto& x : vv) std::printf("size %zu, first %d\n", x.size(), x[0]);
}
size 1, first 10
size 10, first 0
size 3, first 7

A nastier example: std::vector<std::regex> rs; rs.emplace_back(nullptr); compiles (it calls the explicit regex(const char*) with a null pointer, undefined behaviour), while rs.push_back(nullptr) is rejected.

Narrowing goes unnoticed

Placement new with parentheses allows narrowing conversions; a braced push_back does not.

#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> bytes;
    bytes.emplace_back(300);           // compiles: 300 mod 256
    std::vector<int> ints;
    ints.emplace_back(3.99);           // compiles: truncates to 3
    std::printf("%d %d\n", bytes[0], ints[0]);
}
44 3
#include <cstdint>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> bytes;
    bytes.push_back({300});            // error: narrowing conversion inside braces
}

Aggregates: emplace before and after C++20

For struct Point { int x, y; };, v.emplace_back(1, 2) becomes ::new (p) Point(1, 2). Before C++20 aggregates could only be initialised with braces, so this failed to compile and people wrote v.push_back({1, 2}). C++20 added parenthesised aggregate initialisation (P0960), so it now works. Parenthesised aggregate init allows narrowing and does not extend lifetimes of temporaries bound to reference members, unlike braces.

#include <vector>

struct Point { int x, y; };

int main() {
    std::vector<Point> v;
    v.push_back({1, 2});      // fine in every standard
    v.emplace_back(1, 2);     // C++17: no constructor Point(int, int)
}
#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

struct Point { int x, y; };

int main() {
    std::vector<Point> v;
    v.emplace_back(1, 2);     // C++20: parenthesised aggregate initialisation
    v.emplace_back(3);        // y is value-initialised to 0
    std::printf("(%d,%d) (%d,%d)\n", v[0].x, v[0].y, v[1].x, v[1].y);
}
(1,2) (3,0)

Interview trap

"Always prefer emplace_back because it is never slower." Abseil's Tip of the Week #112 recommends the opposite for the common case: use push_back when it works (you already have a T, or a braced initialiser), and emplace_back only when you are passing constructor arguments that push_back cannot take. Effective Modern C++ Item 42 ("consider emplacement") lists the same dangers. Emplace trades type safety for one avoided move.

Associative containers: emplace, try_emplace, insert_or_assign

Theory

Map insertion functions differ in when they construct the value, and what happens if the key is already present.

FunctionKey absentKey presentRequirements
insert(value_type)moves or copies the pair into a nodenothing; you built the pair for nothinga whole pair
emplace(args...)constructs the pair in a nodenothing inserted, but the node may be built and destroyed, and rvalue arguments may be moved frompair constructible from args
try_emplace(k, args...) (C++17)constructs the value from argsguaranteed not to touch argskey separate from value args
insert_or_assign(k, v) (C++17)constructs the value from vassigns v to the existing valuevalue assignable
operator[](k)value-initialises the value (default constructor, or zero for int), returns a referencereturns a referencevalue default-constructible
#include <cstdio>
#include <map>
#include <tuple>
#include <utility>

struct V {
    int v;
    V() : v(0) { std::puts("  V()"); }
    V(int x) : v(x) { std::printf("  V(%d)\n", v); }
    V(int a, int b) : v(a * b) { std::printf("  V(%d,%d)\n", a, b); }
    V(const V& o) : v(o.v) { std::puts("  copy"); }
    V(V&& o) noexcept : v(o.v) { std::puts("  move"); }
    V& operator=(const V& o) { v = o.v; std::puts("  copy="); return *this; }
    V& operator=(V&& o) noexcept { v = o.v; std::puts("  move="); return *this; }
};

int main() {
    std::map<int, V> m;
    std::puts("insert({1, V(10)}):");      m.insert({1, V(10)});
    std::puts("emplace(2, 20):");          m.emplace(2, 20);
    std::puts("emplace(piecewise, 3, (4,5)):");
    m.emplace(std::piecewise_construct, std::forward_as_tuple(3), std::forward_as_tuple(4, 5));
    std::puts("try_emplace(4, 6, 7):");    m.try_emplace(4, 6, 7);
    std::puts("m[5] = 50:");               m[5] = 50;
    std::puts("insert_or_assign(5, 55):"); m.insert_or_assign(5, 55);
    std::puts("insert_or_assign(6, 60):"); m.insert_or_assign(6, 60);
    std::puts("emplace(1, 99) existing:"); auto [it1, ok1] = m.emplace(1, 99);
    std::puts("try_emplace(1, 99) existing:"); auto [it2, ok2] = m.try_emplace(1, 99);
    std::printf("ok1=%d ok2=%d m[1]=%d m[3]=%d m[5]=%d\n", ok1, ok2, it1->second.v, m.at(3).v, m.at(5).v);
}
insert({1, V(10)}):
  V(10)
  move
  move
emplace(2, 20):
  V(20)
emplace(piecewise, 3, (4,5)):
  V(4,5)
try_emplace(4, 6, 7):
  V(6,7)
m[5] = 50:
  V(50)
  V()
  move=
insert_or_assign(5, 55):
  V(55)
  move=
insert_or_assign(6, 60):
  V(60)
emplace(1, 99) existing:
try_emplace(1, 99) existing:
ok1=0 ok2=0 m[1]=10 m[3]=20 m[5]=55

Reading the trace:

  • insert({1, V(10)}) builds V(10), moves it into a temporary pair<const int, V>, then moves that pair's value into the node: two moves.
  • emplace(2, 20) and try_emplace construct the value once, in the node.
  • m[5] = 50 constructs V(50) first (C++17 sequences the right operand of = before the left), then operator[] default-constructs the value, then move-assigns.
  • insert_or_assign(5, 55) on an existing key converts 55 to a V (its parameter is M&& with M = int, assigned through V's converting constructor) and move-assigns.
  • emplace(1, 99) on an existing key built nothing here: both libstdc++ and libc++ look the key up first when the first argument already has the key type. That is an optimisation, not a promise.

emplace can steal your argument even when it inserts nothing

When the key argument is not exactly the key type, the libraries must construct the node to learn the key. If the key is already present the node is destroyed, and anything you moved into it is gone.

#include <cstdio>
#include <map>
#include <memory>
#include <string>

int main() {
    std::map<std::string, std::unique_ptr<int>> m;
    m.emplace("a", std::make_unique<int>(1));

    auto p = std::make_unique<int>(2);
    m.emplace("a", std::move(p));                  // const char* key: node built, then destroyed
    std::printf("emplace with \"a\": p is %s\n", p ? "intact" : "gone");

    auto q = std::make_unique<int>(3);
    m.try_emplace("a", std::move(q));              // guaranteed: q untouched when the key exists
    std::printf("try_emplace with \"a\": q is %s\n", q ? "intact" : "gone");
}
emplace with "a": p is gone
try_emplace with "a": q is intact

The standard says emplace inserts "if and only if there is no element with an equivalent key"; it does not say the arguments are left alone. try_emplace was added in C++17 (N4279) exactly to make that guarantee, and also to allow a value that is not movable at all, since the key and the value arguments are separate.

std::piecewise_construct

std::pair has a constructor pair(std::piecewise_construct_t, std::tuple<A...>, std::tuple<B...>) that constructs first from the first tuple's elements and second from the second's. It is how you emplace into a map when the key or the value needs several constructor arguments, or when the value is neither copyable nor movable. std::forward_as_tuple builds a tuple of references, so nothing is copied on the way. Since C++17, try_emplace(key, args...) covers the common case (single-argument key) with less noise.

emplace_hint and insert with a hint

m.emplace_hint(pos, args...) inserts the element as close as possible to the position just before pos. If the hint is right (the new key belongs immediately before pos), insertion is amortised O(1) instead of O(log n). Inserting already-sorted data with m.emplace_hint(m.end(), ...) is the standard idiom. A wrong hint costs nothing beyond the normal lookup. Unordered containers accept hints too, but implementations mostly ignore them except for equivalent keys in multi-containers.

#include <cstdio>
#include <map>

int main() {
    std::map<int, int> squares;
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; ++i)
        squares.emplace_hint(squares.end(), i, i * i);    // sorted input: O(1) each
    auto it = squares.emplace_hint(squares.find(3), 2, -1); // key exists: returns it
    std::printf("existing key 2 -> %d, size %zu\n", it->second, squares.size());
    for (auto [k, v] : squares) std::printf("%d:%d ", k, v);
    std::printf("\n");
}
existing key 2 -> 4, size 5
0:0 1:1 2:4 3:9 4:16

Note the return type: emplace_hint returns an iterator only (not a pair), so you cannot tell from it whether insertion happened; compare the size before and after. try_emplace(hint, k, args...) has the same limitation; use the non-hint try_emplace when you need the bool.

Reallocation, invalidation and reserve

Theory

When size() == capacity(), any vector insertion allocates a larger buffer (both libstdc++ and libc++ double it, starting from 1; MSVC grows by 1.5x), constructs the new element there, relocates the old elements with std::move_if_noexcept (Ch 20) and frees the old buffer. After that, every pointer, reference and iterator into the vector is invalid, including references you got from emplace_back earlier and v.back().

#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

struct T {
    int v;
    T(int x) : v(x) { std::printf("  ctor(%d)\n", v); }
    T(const T& o) : v(o.v) { std::printf("  copy(%d)\n", v); }
    T(T&& o) noexcept : v(o.v) { std::printf("  move(%d)\n", v); }
    ~T() { std::puts("  dtor"); }
};

int main() {
    std::vector<T> v;
    for (int i = 1; i <= 3; ++i) {
        std::printf("emplace_back(%d), capacity %zu:\n", i, v.capacity());
        v.emplace_back(i);
    }
    std::puts("emplace_back(v[0]) with spare capacity:");
    v.emplace_back(v[0]);
    std::puts("end");
    v.clear();
}
emplace_back(1), capacity 0:
  ctor(1)
emplace_back(2), capacity 1:
  ctor(2)
  move(1)
  dtor
emplace_back(3), capacity 2:
  ctor(3)
  move(1)
  dtor
  move(2)
  dtor
emplace_back(v[0]) with spare capacity:
  copy(1)
end
  dtor
  dtor
  dtor
  dtor

This output is for GCC/libstdc++. Two things are the same in libc++: the new element is constructed before the old ones are relocated (so v.emplace_back(v[0]) is safe even when the vector grows, and the standard requires it), and the growth sequence is 1, 2, 4. One thing differs: libstdc++ relocates element by element (move, destroy, move, destroy), while libc++ moves all elements first and then destroys the old ones, so its third step prints move(1) move(2) dtor dtor.

reserve and the invalidation rules

  • v.reserve(n) with n > capacity() reallocates once and invalidates everything. With n <= capacity() it does nothing. It never shrinks. shrink_to_fit() is a non-binding request.
  • After reserve(n), insertions at the end do not invalidate references as long as size() <= n. Insertions in the middle still invalidate everything at and after the insertion point.
  • Calling reserve(size() + 1) before each push in a loop defeats geometric growth and makes the loop O(n²) on libraries that allocate exactly what you ask for. Reserve once, with the final size.
  • std::deque::emplace_back invalidates iterators but not references to existing elements, and it never relocates them. That is why a deque can hold non-movable types, and a vector cannot grow with them.
  • std::list and node-based maps never invalidate references on insertion.

Concept and tricky questions

Drills

ConceptWhat is the difference between push_back and emplace_back?

Answer

Answer. push_back takes a T (by const T& or T&&) and copy- or move-constructs the new element from it. emplace_back takes constructor arguments by forwarding reference and constructs the element in place with allocator_traits::construct, using direct-initialisation with parentheses.

Why. The practical difference is only visible when the argument is not already a T: emplace_back(args) skips the temporary and its move and destructor. Two side effects follow from direct-initialisation: explicit constructors are callable and narrowing is allowed. People often say "emplace avoids a copy"; it avoids a temporary, and when you pass an existing object it copies just the same.

TrickyIs v.emplace_back(std::move(s)) faster than v.push_back(std::move(s)) for a std::string s?

Answer

Answer. No. Both perform exactly one move construction into the slot.

Why. emplace_back forwards a std::string&& to std::string(std::string&&); push_back(T&&) calls the same constructor. After inlining the generated code is identical. Emplace only helps when the arguments differ from T itself, such as v.emplace_back(10, 'x') or v.emplace_back("literal").

Trickystd::vector<std::unique_ptr<Widget>> v; v.emplace_back(new Widget); compiles while push_back(new Widget) does not. What can go wrong with the emplace version?

Answer

Answer. A leak. If the vector is full, emplace_back allocates a new buffer before constructing the unique_ptr. If that allocation throws, the raw Widget* has no owner and is never deleted.

Why. unique_ptr's pointer constructor is explicit precisely to stop implicit ownership transfer from raw pointers; emplace's direct-initialisation bypasses it. With v.push_back(std::make_unique<Widget>()) (or emplace_back of that), the owner exists before the container does anything that can throw, so a failure destroys the temporary unique_ptr and the object. This is Item 42 of Effective Modern C++.

TrickyFor std::vector<std::vector<int>> vv;, what do vv.push_back({10}), vv.emplace_back(10) and vv.push_back(10) do?

Answer

Answer. push_back({10}) appends a vector holding the single value 10. emplace_back(10) appends a vector of ten zeros. push_back(10) does not compile.

Why. Braces initialise the parameter with list-initialisation, which strongly prefers the initializer_list constructor. Emplace constructs with parentheses, vector<int>(10), which is the size constructor. That constructor is explicit, so the implicit conversion push_back(10) would need is not allowed. Same tokens, three different outcomes.

ConceptWhat does emplace_back return, and since when?

Answer

Answer. A reference to the inserted element (T&) since C++17 for vector, deque and list (also emplace_front). In C++11 and C++14 it returned void.

Why. P0084 changed it so that auto& x = v.emplace_back(...); replaces the two-step emplace_back plus back(). push_back still returns void. The reference has the same lifetime rules as any element reference: the next reallocation invalidates it. Associative emplace returns pair<iterator, bool>, and emplace_hint returns just an iterator.

TrickyAfter std::vector<int> v; v.emplace_back();, what is v.back()? And for struct Raw { int x; }; std::vector<Raw> r; r.emplace_back();, what is r.back().x?

Answer

Answer. Both are 0. An empty argument list value-initialises the element.

Why. emplace_back() ends in std::construct_at(p), which is ::new (p) T(), with empty parentheses. T() is value-initialisation, which zero-initialises an int and an aggregate like Raw (a class with no user-provided default constructor is zeroed first). The usual wrong answer is "indeterminate, like int x;" or new int, which are default-initialisation. The same rule makes std::vector<int> v(n) and resize(n) write n zeros; avoiding that cost needs C++23's resize_and_overwrite (strings only) or an allocator whose construct default-initialises. A type with a user-provided constructor that leaves members uninitialised (Ctor() {}) is not zeroed: value-initialisation just calls that constructor.

ConceptWhat is std::piecewise_construct for? Give an example.

std::map<std::string, std::vector<int>> m;
m.emplace(std::piecewise_construct,
          std::forward_as_tuple("primes"),
          std::forward_as_tuple(5, 0));     // key "primes", value: five zeros
Answer

Answer. It selects pair's constructor that builds first and second each from their own argument tuple, so a map element can be constructed in place when the key or the value needs several constructor arguments (or none).

Why. Without it, m.emplace("primes", 5, 0) would try pair(const char*, int, int), which does not exist. forward_as_tuple makes tuples of references, so the arguments are forwarded, not copied. It is also how you insert a value that cannot be moved, such as a std::mutex: m.emplace(std::piecewise_construct, std::forward_as_tuple(k), std::tuple<>()). Since C++17 try_emplace(k, args...) does the same job more readably.

ConceptWhen does emplace_back give a real, measurable improvement over push_back?

Answer

Answer. When you pass constructor arguments for a type whose temporary is expensive to create, move or destroy, or for a type that cannot be moved at all (in a deque, list or map). Examples: v.emplace_back(1024, '\0') for strings, a type with a large inline array, a type holding a mutex.

Why. The saved work is one temporary construction's worth of move plus destructor. For a std::string built from a long literal, push_back("...") allocates once for the temporary and then moves the pointer, so allocations are the same; only the small move and destructor are saved. For types where a move equals a copy (large std::array members), the saving is a full copy. Measure before rewriting code for it.

TrickyIs v.emplace_back(v[0]) safe when the vector is full and must reallocate?

Answer

Answer. Yes. The standard library must handle arguments that refer into the container itself, and libstdc++ and libc++ do it by constructing the new element in the new buffer before relocating (and destroying) the old elements.

Why. The library may not assume that an argument is unrelated to the container. push_back(v[0]) has always had to work, and LWG 2164 (resolved in C++20) added the note to the sequence-container requirements that for a.emplace(p, args) "args may directly or indirectly refer to a value in a", so even v.emplace(v.begin(), v.back()), a middle insertion where the referenced element is about to be shifted, must work. Implementations handle that case by constructing the new value into a temporary first. Your own containers must use the same order for appends: allocate, construct the new element, relocate, free. The common wrong answer is "undefined, take a copy first"; a hand-rolled vector that grows first and then reads the argument does read freed memory, but the standard one does not.

ConceptWhat is the difference between m[k] = v and m.insert_or_assign(k, v)?

Answer

Answer. For a new key, m[k] = v default-constructs the value and then assigns v; insert_or_assign constructs the value directly from v. For an existing key, both assign. insert_or_assign also tells you which happened (it returns pair<iterator, bool>) and works for values without a default constructor.

Why. operator[] must return a reference before the assignment runs, so it has to put some value in the node first. That costs a default construction plus an assignment and fails to compile if the value type has no default constructor. insert_or_assign (C++17) was added to fix exactly this.

TrickyDoes v.reserve(100) invalidate iterators? Does a later push_back invalidate references if v.size() was 10?

Answer

Answer. reserve(100) invalidates all iterators, pointers and references if 100 exceeds the current capacity, because it reallocates. After it, push_backs up to size 100 invalidate only the end() iterator.

Why. [vector.capacity]: reallocation invalidates everything, and no reallocation happens during insertions until the size would exceed the reserved capacity. People think reserve is a pure hint that leaves existing references alone. Also, reserve with a smaller value never shrinks, and resize is a different operation that changes size() and constructs elements.

Trickystruct P { int x, y; }; std::vector<P> v; v.emplace_back(1, 2); Does it compile?

Answer

Answer. In C++20, yes. In C++17 and earlier, no.

Why. emplace_back uses ::new (p) P(1, 2), with parentheses. An aggregate has no constructor taking two ints, and before C++20 aggregates could only be initialised with braces. P0960 (C++20) allows parenthesised aggregate initialisation, which differs from braces in two ways: narrowing is allowed and temporaries bound to reference members are not lifetime-extended. In C++17 code use v.push_back({1, 2}) or give P a constructor.

ConceptWhat does emplace_hint do and when is it O(1)?

Answer

Answer. It inserts the element using the iterator as a starting point, placing it as close as possible to just before the hint. If the element belongs immediately before the hint, insertion is amortised constant time; otherwise it falls back to the normal O(log n) search.

Why. For tree-based maps, checking "does the key fit between prev(hint) and hint" takes two comparisons, then the node is linked in and the tree rebalanced (amortised O(1)). Bulk-loading sorted data with emplace_hint(m.end(), ...) is the common use. C++03 specified the fast case as "inserted right after the hint", C++11 (LWG 233) changed it to "just before". Old code that passes prev(end()) for appends is still correct, but the constant-time path is only guaranteed for the C++11 form (libstdc++ happens to check both sides).

Predict the output and find the bug

Drills

OutputThe vector has room for exactly one element. What is printed?

#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

struct T {
    int v;
    T(int x) : v(x) { std::printf("ctor(%d)\n", v); }
    T(const T& o) : v(o.v) { std::printf("copy(%d)\n", v); }
    T(T&& o) noexcept : v(o.v) { std::printf("move(%d)\n", v); }
    ~T() { std::printf("dtor(%d)\n", v); }
};

int main() {
    std::vector<T> v;
    v.reserve(1);
    v.emplace_back(1);
    std::puts("--");
    v.emplace_back(2);
    std::puts("-- end");
    v.pop_back();
    v.pop_back();
}
Answer
ctor(1)
--
ctor(2)
move(1)
dtor(1)
-- end
dtor(2)
dtor(1)

Answer. The first emplace constructs in place. The second needs a bigger buffer: ctor(2) runs first, directly in the new buffer, then element 1 is moved across and the old copy destroyed. The two pop_back calls destroy the last element, then the first.

Why. Constructing the new element before relocation is what makes self-referencing arguments safe. The moved-from element still prints dtor(1) because this type's move copies the int. With a single old element the libstdc++ and libc++ traces agree; with more, their order of moves and destructors differs, which is why the program pops explicitly instead of relying on the vector's destructor order.

OutputA vector of strings, four ways to add an element. For each string the program prints its size and last character. What is the output?

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<std::string> v;
    v.push_back({3, 'a'});
    v.emplace_back(3, 'b');
    v.push_back(std::string(3, 'c'));
    v.emplace_back("dd", 1);
    for (const auto& s : v) std::printf("%zu%c ", s.size(), s.back());
    std::printf("\n");
}
Answer
2a 3b 3c 1d

Answer. push_back({3, 'a'}) makes the two-character string "\x03a"; emplace_back(3, 'b') makes "bbb"; push_back(std::string(3, 'c')) makes "ccc"; emplace_back("dd", 1) makes "d".

Why. The braces in push_back list-initialise a std::string, and list-initialisation picks the initializer_list<char> constructor whenever it is viable, so 3 becomes the character with code 3. Emplace uses parentheses, which selects string(size_type count, char ch). The last call selects string(const char* s, size_type n), which takes the first n characters. Same tokens, different constructors: the brace-vs-paren split is the root of most emplace surprises.

OutputInserting into a map with keys that already exist. What is printed?

#include <cstdio>
#include <map>
#include <string>

int main() {
    std::map<std::string, int> m{{"a", 1}};
    auto [i1, ok1] = m.insert({"a", 2});
    auto [i2, ok2] = m.emplace("a", 3);
    auto [i3, ok3] = m.try_emplace("a", 4);
    auto [i4, ok4] = m.insert_or_assign("a", 5);
    m["b"];
    std::printf("%d%d%d%d a=%d b=%d size=%zu\n", ok1, ok2, ok3, ok4, m["a"], m["b"], m.size());
}
Answer
0000 a=5 b=0 size=2

Answer. All four report "not inserted" (false), but insert_or_assign overwrote the value with 5. m["b"] as a bare statement inserts a value-initialised 0.

Why. insert, emplace and try_emplace never modify an existing element; the bool is the only sign they did nothing. insert_or_assign returns false to mean "assigned rather than inserted". The operator[] side effect is a classic: using m[k] to test for presence silently adds entries; use find, contains (C++20) or at instead.

OutputA non-copyable, non-movable type in three containers. What compiles and what is printed?

#include <cstdio>
#include <deque>
#include <list>
#include <map>
#include <mutex>

struct Pinned {
    int id;
    std::mutex m;
    explicit Pinned(int i) : id(i) {}
};

int main() {
    std::deque<Pinned> d;
    d.emplace_back(1);
    d.emplace_front(0);
    std::list<Pinned> l;
    l.emplace_back(2);
    std::map<int, Pinned> mp;
    mp.try_emplace(7, 3);
    std::printf("%d %d %d %d\n", d[0].id, d[1].id, l.front().id, mp.at(7).id);
}
Answer
0 1 2 3

Answer. All of it compiles and prints 0 1 2 3.

Why. std::mutex makes Pinned neither copyable nor movable. deque, list and maps never relocate existing elements, so emplace into them only needs the constructor. std::vector<Pinned>::emplace_back would not compile, because growing a vector must move or copy elements. push_back(Pinned(1)) would fail in every container: it needs a move constructor to get the temporary into the slot.

OutputWhat does this print, and why might it surprise a reviewer?

#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

struct Price {
    long ticks;
    explicit Price(long t) : ticks(t) {}
};

int main() {
    std::vector<Price> book;
    double mid = 101.75;
    book.emplace_back(mid * 4);      // intended: quarter ticks
    book.emplace_back(-0.9);
    std::printf("%ld %ld\n", book[0].ticks, book[1].ticks);
}
Answer
407 0

Answer. 407 0. Both doubles are converted to long by truncation toward zero, and the explicit constructor is called without complaint.

Why. The double-to-long conversion happens inside the container's ::new (p) Price(std::forward<double>(d)), a parenthesised direct-initialisation, so narrowing is allowed and the explicit is ignored. book.push_back(Price{mid * 4}) is ill-formed (narrowing in braces: Clang rejects it, GCC only emits a -Wnarrowing warning for a non-constant value), and book.push_back(mid * 4) would fail because the constructor is explicit. In trading code, a silent truncation of a price is the kind of bug that costs money, so avoid emplace for types whose constructors take numeric arguments that could be the wrong type.

Find the bugThis program reads the first price after adding a fourth one. ASan reports a heap-use-after-free. Why?

#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<int> prices{100, 101, 102};
    int& best = prices[0];
    prices.emplace_back(103);
    std::printf("best=%d\n", best);
}
Answer

Answer. prices{100, 101, 102} has capacity 3 in both standard libraries, so emplace_back(103) reallocates, and best refers into the freed old buffer.

Why. Every reallocation invalidates all references, pointers and iterators. Fixes: keep an index (std::size_t best = 0;) and read prices[best] later, call reserve with the final size before taking references, or use a container that does not relocate (std::deque for appends). The output is marked undefined behaviour: without ASan this often prints 100 because the freed memory has not been reused yet, which is why such bugs survive testing.

Find the bugThe loop duplicates every even number. It crashes under ASan. What is wrong?

#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<int> v{1, 2, 3, 4};
    for (int& x : v)
        if (x % 2 == 0) v.push_back(x);
    std::printf("size=%zu\n", v.size());
}
Answer

Answer. Inserting into a vector while iterating it with a range-for. The loop's hidden begin and end iterators (and x) are invalidated by the first reallocation, so the next increment reads freed memory.

Why. Range-for caches auto __end = v.end() before the loop. Even with enough capacity it would be wrong, because the cached end would not include the new elements. Fix: iterate by index up to the original size, for (std::size_t i = 0, n = v.size(); i < n; ++i) if (v[i] % 2 == 0) v.push_back(v[i]);, which is safe because push_back(v[i]) handles self-reference. Or collect into a second vector and append afterwards.

Find the bugA session table stores entries with operator[]. Why does it not compile, and what is the fix?

#include <map>
#include <string>

struct Session {
    std::string user;
    explicit Session(std::string u) : user(std::move(u)) {}
};

int main() {
    std::map<int, Session> sessions;
    sessions[42] = Session("ada");
}
Answer

Answer. operator[] must default-construct a Session when the key is missing, and Session has no default constructor. Use sessions.try_emplace(42, "ada") (insert only) or sessions.insert_or_assign(42, Session("ada")) (insert or overwrite).

Why. operator[] is compiled as one function that handles both the "found" and "not found" paths, so the default constructor is required even if the key always exists at run time. Adding a default constructor just to satisfy it weakens the class invariant (a session without a user). try_emplace also avoids the extra assignment.

Find the bugA monitor keeps a list of sensors it tracks. ASan aborts at the end of main. Why does push_back catch this at compile time while emplace_back does not?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <vector>

struct Sensor { int id; };

int main() {
    Sensor primary{1};
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Sensor>> owned;
    owned.emplace_back(&primary);        // compiles: unique_ptr(Sensor*) is explicit
    std::printf("tracking sensor %d\n", owned[0]->id);
}
Answer

Answer. emplace_back(&primary) calls the explicit constructor unique_ptr(Sensor*), so the vector now "owns" a stack object. When owned is destroyed it calls delete on &primary, and ASan reports "attempting free on address which was not malloc()-ed". owned.push_back(&primary) would be rejected, because the implicit conversion from Sensor* to unique_ptr is exactly what explicit forbids. Fix: if the vector should own, write owned.push_back(std::make_unique<Sensor>(primary)); if it only observes, make it std::vector<Sensor*>.

Why. explicit on unique_ptr's pointer constructor exists to make every ownership transfer visible in the source. Emplace's direct-initialisation skips that check, so the leak in this chapter's theory and this bad delete are two faces of the same problem. People say "emplace and push_back are the same except for performance"; for types with explicit constructors they accept different programs. Without ASan the output is undefined: the bad delete may abort, corrupt the heap or appear to work.

Find the bugThe registry is meant to keep the first connection for each host. Sometimes the second connection object is destroyed even though it was never stored. Why?

#include <cstdio>
#include <map>
#include <memory>
#include <string>

struct Conn {
    std::string host;
    explicit Conn(std::string h) : host(std::move(h)) {}
    ~Conn() { std::printf("closing %s\n", host.c_str()); }
};

int main() {
    std::map<std::string, std::unique_ptr<Conn>> registry;
    registry.emplace("db", std::make_unique<Conn>("db#1"));
    auto spare = std::make_unique<Conn>("db#2");
    registry.emplace("db", std::move(spare));       // key already present
    std::printf("spare is %s\n", spare ? "still ours" : "gone");
    std::puts("end of main");
}
Answer
closing db#2
spare is gone
end of main
closing db#1

Answer. The key is passed as const char*, so emplace constructs the node (moving spare into it) before it can compare keys. The key exists, the node is destroyed, and db#2 is closed. Use registry.try_emplace("db", std::move(spare)), which leaves spare untouched when the key exists.

Why. The standard does not promise that a failed emplace leaves its arguments alone. Both standard libraries look the key up first only when the first argument already has the key type (std::string here), so the behaviour even depends on how the caller spells the key. try_emplace was introduced in C++17 for exactly this.

Write the code

Coding

CodeImplement TinyVector<T> with push_back(const T&), push_back(T&&), emplace_back(Args&&...) returning T&, reserve, size, capacity and operator[]. Growth doubles, relocates with std::move_if_noexcept, and must handle v.emplace_back(v[0]) when full. Trace it with a noisy type.

Answer

Approach. Both push_back overloads forward to emplace_back. On growth, allocate the new block, construct the new element at index size in it first (the arguments may refer to old elements), then relocate the old elements, destroy them and free the old block. If constructing the new element throws, free the new block; if relocation throws (only possible when copying), destroy what was built.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>

template <class T>
class TinyVector {
public:
    TinyVector() = default;
    TinyVector(const TinyVector&) = delete;
    TinyVector& operator=(const TinyVector&) = delete;
    ~TinyVector() { std::destroy_n(data_, size_); alloc_.deallocate(data_, cap_); }

    void push_back(const T& v) { emplace_back(v); }
    void push_back(T&& v) { emplace_back(std::move(v)); }

    template <class... Args>
    T& emplace_back(Args&&... args) {
        if (size_ < cap_) {
            T& r = *std::construct_at(data_ + size_, std::forward<Args>(args)...);
            ++size_;                         // only after construction succeeded
            return r;
        }
        return grow_and_emplace(cap_ ? 2 * cap_ : 1, std::forward<Args>(args)...);
    }
    void reserve(std::size_t n) { if (n > cap_) relocate_to(n); }

    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::size_t capacity() const { return cap_; }
    T& operator[](std::size_t i) { return data_[i]; }

private:
    template <class... Args>
    T& grow_and_emplace(std::size_t ncap, Args&&... args) {
        T* nd = alloc_.allocate(ncap);
        try {
            std::construct_at(nd + size_, std::forward<Args>(args)...);   // before relocation
        } catch (...) {
            alloc_.deallocate(nd, ncap);
            throw;
        }
        try {
            move_elements(nd);
        } catch (...) {
            std::destroy_at(nd + size_);
            alloc_.deallocate(nd, ncap);
            throw;
        }
        adopt(nd, ncap);
        return data_[size_++];
    }
    void relocate_to(std::size_t ncap) {
        T* nd = alloc_.allocate(ncap);
        try { move_elements(nd); } catch (...) { alloc_.deallocate(nd, ncap); throw; }
        adopt(nd, ncap);
    }
    void move_elements(T* nd) {          // strong guarantee: on throw, nd holds nothing
        std::size_t i = 0;
        try {
            for (; i < size_; ++i) std::construct_at(nd + i, std::move_if_noexcept(data_[i]));
        } catch (...) {
            std::destroy_n(nd, i);
            throw;
        }
    }
    void adopt(T* nd, std::size_t ncap) {
        std::destroy_n(data_, size_);
        alloc_.deallocate(data_, cap_);
        data_ = nd;
        cap_ = ncap;
    }

    std::allocator<T> alloc_;
    T* data_ = nullptr;
    std::size_t size_ = 0, cap_ = 0;
};

struct Noisy {
    int v;
    Noisy(int x) : v(x) { std::printf("  ctor(%d)\n", v); }
    Noisy(int a, int b) : v(a * 10 + b) { std::printf("  ctor(%d,%d)\n", a, b); }
    Noisy(const Noisy& o) : v(o.v) { std::printf("  copy(%d)\n", v); }
    Noisy(Noisy&& o) noexcept : v(o.v) { std::printf("  move(%d)\n", v); }
    ~Noisy() { std::printf("  dtor(%d)\n", v); }
};

int main() {
    TinyVector<Noisy> v;
    std::puts("emplace_back(1):");      v.emplace_back(1);
    std::puts("emplace_back(v[0]):");   v.emplace_back(v[0]);       // full: grows, reads v[0] first
    std::puts("push_back(Noisy(3)):");  v.push_back(Noisy(3));
    std::puts("emplace_back(4, 2):");   Noisy& r = v.emplace_back(4, 2);
    r.v += 100;
    std::printf("size=%zu cap=%zu last=%d\n", v.size(), v.capacity(), v[3].v);
    std::puts("destroy:");
}

  ctor(1)
emplace_back(v[0]):
  copy(1)
  move(1)
  dtor(1)
push_back(Noisy(3)):
  ctor(3)
  move(3)
  move(1)
  move(1)
  dtor(1)
  dtor(1)
  dtor(3)

  ctor(4,2)
size=4 cap=4 last=142
destroy:
  dtor(1)
  dtor(1)
  dtor(3)
  dtor(142)

Complexity and pitfalls. Amortised O(1) appends. In the second block the copy of v[0] is made into the new buffer before the old element is moved and destroyed, which is what keeps the self-reference valid. The third block shows the full cost of push_back of a temporary during growth: the temporary is built, moved into the new slot, both old elements are relocated and destroyed, and finally the temporary dies. The fourth block shows emplace_back(4, 2) constructing in place and returning a usable reference. Pitfalls: growing first and constructing second (reads freed memory for v.emplace_back(v[0])); using std::move instead of move_if_noexcept for relocation; incrementing size_ before construction succeeds; forgetting that the element destructor order of this class (front to back) is a choice, and libc++ chooses back to front.

Estimated rating: ~1900 · placement construction, exception-safe growth and the self-reference ordering in one class

CodeWrite my_try_emplace(map, key, args...) for a std::map using only lower_bound, key_comp and emplace_hint, with the same guarantee as try_emplace: when the key exists, the value arguments are not touched. Return std::pair<iterator, bool>.

Answer

Approach. lower_bound(key) returns the first element not less than key. If it is not end() and key is not less than its key, the key exists: return it with false without touching the arguments. Otherwise lower_bound is exactly the correct hint (the new key belongs just before it), so emplace_hint with piecewise_construct inserts in amortised O(1) after the O(log n) lookup.

#include <cstdio>
#include <map>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <tuple>
#include <utility>

template <class Map, class K, class... Args>
std::pair<typename Map::iterator, bool> my_try_emplace(Map& m, K&& key, Args&&... args) {
    auto it = m.lower_bound(key);
    if (it != m.end() && !m.key_comp()(key, it->first)) return {it, false};
    it = m.emplace_hint(it, std::piecewise_construct,
                        std::forward_as_tuple(std::forward<K>(key)),
                        std::forward_as_tuple(std::forward<Args>(args)...));
    return {it, true};
}

int main() {
    std::map<std::string, std::unique_ptr<int>> m;
    auto [a, ok1] = my_try_emplace(m, std::string("x"), std::make_unique<int>(1));
    auto p = std::make_unique<int>(2);
    auto [b, ok2] = my_try_emplace(m, std::string("x"), std::move(p));
    auto [c, ok3] = my_try_emplace(m, std::string("w"), std::move(p));
    std::printf("ok=%d%d%d x=%d w=%d p=%s size=%zu\n", ok1, ok2, ok3, *a->second, *c->second,
                p ? "set" : "null", m.size());
    std::printf("first key=%s\n", m.begin()->first.c_str());
}
ok=101 x=1 w=2 p=null size=2
first key=w

Complexity and pitfalls. O(log n) lookup plus amortised O(1) linking. The second call leaves p owning 2, which the third call then moves into the new "w" entry; that is why p is null only at the end. Pitfalls: comparing with == instead of the map's comparator (wrong for custom orderings); calling emplace instead of emplace_hint after the lookup (correct, but it repeats the O(log n) search); passing the key as std::forward<K>(key) to lower_bound and then forwarding it again (forward once, at the last use, Ch 21).

Estimated rating: ~1600 · needs lower_bound equivalence via the comparator and the exact hint semantics

CodeWrite safe_emplace_back(v, args...), which behaves like v.emplace_back(args...) but refuses (at compile time) a single argument that is not implicitly convertible to the element type, and refuses narrowing for single arithmetic arguments. Multi-argument calls stay allowed. Show which calls compile using a requires check.

Answer

Approach. For one argument, require std::is_convertible_v<A, T> (rejects explicit constructors) and that T{std::declval<A>()} is well-formed (brace initialisation rejects narrowing). For zero or several arguments, require std::constructible_from<T, Args...> and forward to emplace_back.

#include <concepts>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

template <class T, class A>
concept SafeSingle = std::is_convertible_v<A, T> && requires(A&& a) { T{std::forward<A>(a)}; };

template <class T, class... Args>
concept SafeArgs = (sizeof...(Args) != 1 && std::constructible_from<T, Args...>) ||
                   (sizeof...(Args) == 1 && (SafeSingle<T, Args> && ...));

template <class T, class Alloc, class... Args>
    requires SafeArgs<T, Args...>
T& safe_emplace_back(std::vector<T, Alloc>& v, Args&&... args) {
    return v.emplace_back(std::forward<Args>(args)...);
}

template <class V, class... Args>
constexpr bool can_emplace = requires(V& v, Args&&... a) { safe_emplace_back(v, std::forward<Args>(a)...); };

int main() {
    using UP = std::vector<std::unique_ptr<int>>;
    using VV = std::vector<std::vector<int>>;
    using VI = std::vector<int>;
    static_assert(!can_emplace<UP, int*>);                 // explicit constructor
    static_assert(can_emplace<UP, std::unique_ptr<int>>);  // an owner is fine
    static_assert(!can_emplace<VV, int>);                  // explicit size constructor
    static_assert(can_emplace<VV, int, int>);              // multi-arg: allowed on purpose
    static_assert(!can_emplace<VI, double>);               // narrowing
    static_assert(can_emplace<VI, short>);                 // widening

    UP up;
    safe_emplace_back(up, std::make_unique<int>(5));
    VV vv;
    safe_emplace_back(vv, 3, 9);
    std::printf("%d %zu %d\n", *up[0], vv[0].size(), vv[0][0]);
}
5 3 9

Complexity and pitfalls. Compile-time only. The brace test also rejects types that are not brace-constructible from themselves in odd ways, and for aggregates T{a} means "first member from a", so the check is a heuristic rather than a proof. Multi-argument calls still go through explicit constructors; that is usually what the caller means (emplace_back(3, 9) for "three nines").

Estimated rating: ~1700 · concept composition with a pack-size switch and a narrowing probe through brace initialisation

CodeBuild a Registry that owns polymorphic plugins by name: template <class T, class... Args> T& create(std::string name, Args&&... args) constructs a T (derived from Plugin) with forwarded arguments, stores it in an unordered_map<std::string, std::unique_ptr<Plugin>> and returns a reference to the concrete type. Creating a duplicate name must throw std::invalid_argument without constructing anything.

Answer

Approach. Look the name up first; if present, throw before building anything. Otherwise std::make_unique<T>(std::forward<Args>(args)...), keep a raw T* to return, and move the owner into the map with try_emplace. The owner exists before the map allocates, so a failing insert cannot leak. The reference stays valid across rehashes because the map stores pointers and node-based maps never move their nodes.

#include <concepts>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <string>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <utility>

struct Plugin {
    virtual ~Plugin() = default;
    virtual const char* kind() const = 0;
};

class Registry {
public:
    template <class T, class... Args>
        requires std::derived_from<T, Plugin>
    T& create(std::string name, Args&&... args) {
        if (items_.contains(name)) throw std::invalid_argument("duplicate plugin: " + name);
        auto obj = std::make_unique<T>(std::forward<Args>(args)...);
        T& ref = *obj;
        items_.try_emplace(std::move(name), std::move(obj));
        return ref;
    }
    Plugin* find(const std::string& name) const {
        auto it = items_.find(name);
        return it == items_.end() ? nullptr : it->second.get();
    }
    std::size_t size() const { return items_.size(); }
private:
    std::unordered_map<std::string, std::unique_ptr<Plugin>> items_;
};

struct Counter : Plugin {
    static inline int made = 0;
    int start;
    explicit Counter(int s) : start(s) { ++made; }
    const char* kind() const override { return "counter"; }
};
struct Echo : Plugin {
    std::string prefix;
    std::unique_ptr<int> level;
    Echo(std::string p, std::unique_ptr<int> l) : prefix(std::move(p)), level(std::move(l)) {}
    const char* kind() const override { return "echo"; }
};

int main() {
    Registry r;
    Counter& c = r.create<Counter>("hits", 10);
    Echo& e = r.create<Echo>("log", "> ", std::make_unique<int>(3));   // move-only argument
    for (int i = 0; i < 100; ++i) r.create<Counter>("c" + std::to_string(i), i);   // rehashes
    c.start += 1;                                                      // still valid
    try { r.create<Counter>("hits", 99); }
    catch (const std::invalid_argument& ex) { std::printf("%s\n", ex.what()); }
    std::printf("hits=%d echo=%s%d kinds=%s,%s made=%d size=%zu\n", c.start, e.prefix.c_str(),
                *e.level, r.find("hits")->kind(), r.find("log")->kind(), Counter::made, r.size());
}
duplicate plugin: hits
hits=11 echo=> 3 kinds=counter,echo made=101 size=102

Complexity and pitfalls. Average O(1) per operation plus the construction. made=101 proves the duplicate call constructed nothing. Pitfalls: checking existence after constructing (wasted work and side effects); items_.emplace(name, new T(...)) (the explicit-constructor leak from this chapter); returning *items_[name] as Plugin& and static_casting later; taking name as const std::string& and then copying it into the map (by value plus move is one copy fewer for rvalue names).

Estimated rating: ~1500 · combines forwarding, make_unique, try_emplace and reference stability of node containers

CodeImplement InplaceVector<T, N>, a fixed-capacity vector with no heap allocation (the shape of C++26's std::inplace_vector), with emplace_back returning T&, push_back overloads, pop_back, size, operator[] and a destructor. When full, emplace_back throws std::bad_alloc without constructing anything. Elements must never move, so non-movable types work.

Answer

Approach. Store alignas(T) std::byte buf_[N * sizeof(T)] and a count. emplace_back checks capacity first, then constructs with std::construct_at at slot size_. Access goes through std::launder(reinterpret_cast<T*>(buf_) + i) because the objects were created in raw storage (see Ch 14). Copying and moving the container itself are deleted to keep the example short.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <mutex>
#include <new>
#include <utility>

template <class T, std::size_t N>
class InplaceVector {
public:
    InplaceVector() = default;
    InplaceVector(const InplaceVector&) = delete;
    InplaceVector& operator=(const InplaceVector&) = delete;
    ~InplaceVector() { while (size_) pop_back(); }

    template <class... Args>
    T& emplace_back(Args&&... args) {
        if (size_ == N) throw std::bad_alloc();
        T* p = std::construct_at(slot(size_), std::forward<Args>(args)...);
        ++size_;                                   // only after construction succeeded
        return *p;
    }
    void push_back(const T& v) { emplace_back(v); }
    void push_back(T&& v) { emplace_back(std::move(v)); }
    void pop_back() { std::destroy_at(&(*this)[--size_]); }

    T& operator[](std::size_t i) { return *std::launder(slot(i)); }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    static constexpr std::size_t capacity() { return N; }

private:
    T* slot(std::size_t i) { return reinterpret_cast<T*>(buf_) + i; }
    alignas(T) std::byte buf_[N * sizeof(T)];
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};

struct Pinned {
    int id;
    std::mutex m;                                  // not copyable, not movable
    explicit Pinned(int i) : id(i) { std::printf("  make %d\n", id); }
    ~Pinned() { std::printf("  drop %d\n", id); }
};

int main() {
    InplaceVector<Pinned, 2> v;
    Pinned& first = v.emplace_back(1);
    v.emplace_back(2);
    try { v.emplace_back(3); }
    catch (const std::bad_alloc&) { std::puts("  full"); }
    std::printf("first=%d size=%zu sizeof ok=%d\n", first.id, v.size(),
                sizeof(v) >= 2 * sizeof(Pinned));
    v.pop_back();
    std::puts("end");
}
  make 1
  make 2
  full
first=1 size=2 sizeof ok=1
  drop 2
end
  drop 1

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) for every operation and zero allocations, which is why low-latency code favours this shape for small bounded collections. References are never invalidated by insertion, since elements never move. Pitfalls: incrementing size_ before construction (a throwing constructor leaves a "live" garbage slot that the destructor will destroy); forgetting alignas(T); using T buf_[N] instead of raw bytes, which default-constructs N objects up front and requires a default constructor; omitting std::launder, which is technically required when reaching objects through a pointer to the byte array.

Estimated rating: ~1700 · raw aligned storage, construct_at, launder and the size-after-construction ordering

Cheat sheet

Theory
  • push_back(x) copies or moves an existing T; emplace_back(args) constructs in the slot via allocator_traits::construct, with parentheses.
  • Only emplace_back(ctor args) avoids work: the temporary, its move and its destructor. With an existing object or a T{...} argument the two are identical.
  • Dangers of emplace: calls explicit constructors (emplace_back(new T) into unique_ptrs leaks on growth failure; vector<vector<int>>::emplace_back(10) is ten zeros), allows narrowing, cannot take braced lists.
  • Aggregates: emplace_back(1, 2) needs C++20 parenthesised aggregate init.
  • emplace_back returns T& since C++17 (void before); emplace_hint returns an iterator; associative emplace returns pair<iterator, bool>.
  • Maps: try_emplace never touches arguments if the key exists; insert_or_assign overwrites; operator[] needs a default constructor; piecewise_construct + forward_as_tuple for multi-argument keys or values.
  • Growth: new element constructed first, then relocation with move_if_noexcept; every reference and iterator dies. reserve once with the final size; deque and node containers never relocate.
