Part F · Move semantics and value passing · Chapter 23

Copy elision

Copy elision is the rule that lets (and since C++17, forces) the compiler to build an object directly where it will finally live, so the copy or move that the source code seems to ask for never runs. Interviewers ask about it because it decides how many constructors a line of code calls, why a factory can return a std::mutex by value in C++17 but not in C++14, and why std::move in the wrong place makes code slower.

TheoryDrillsCoding· about 3 hours· prerequisites: Ch 20 (value categories, move constructors)

What copy elision is

Theory

Mental model. Every object needs storage. When the source code says "make a temporary, then copy it into x", the cheapest implementation is to skip the temporary and construct straight into x. Copy elision is the language rule that permits this: two objects that the abstract machine would create are treated as one, and the copy or move constructor between them (and the matching destructor) is never called.

There are two quite different forms, and most interview confusion comes from mixing them up:

FormExampleStatus in C++17 and laterChapter
Initialising from a prvalue (unnamed temporary), often called RVO when it is a returnreturn T(args);, T x = T();, f(T())Guaranteed. No copy or move exists in the abstract machine, so none can run, and the constructor does not even need to exist.This chapter
Returning a named local (NRVO)T x; ...; return x;Still optional. The move or copy constructor must be usable even when the compiler elides it.Ch 24
throw of a local, catch by valuethrow local;, catch (T e)Optional. GCC and Clang elide neither in practice.This chapter

The rule lives in [class.copy.elision] for the optional cases and in [dcl.init] / [basic.lval] for the guaranteed one. The guaranteed case is not described as "elision" in the C++17 wording at all: it falls out of what a prvalue is, which the next sections explain.

Why it matters in practice

  • Counting. "How many constructor calls does this line make?" is a staple question, and the answer depends on knowing which steps are elided.
  • Types that cannot move. std::mutex, std::atomic, std::lock_guard and any class with deleted copy and move can be returned from a factory by value in C++17. In C++14 that code does not compile.
  • Performance. A move of a std::vector is cheap but not free (copy three pointers, null the source's three, and later run the destructor on the moved-from shell). For types with inline storage (std::array, small-buffer types) a move is as expensive as a copy, so elision is the only way to make returning by value free.
  • Observable behaviour. If a copy constructor prints or counts, elision changes the program's output. That is allowed, which makes elision the main exception to the as-if rule.

The pre-C++17 world: optional elision, required constructors

Theory

In C++11 and C++14, T x = make(); where make does return T(); describes three objects in the abstract machine: the temporary T() inside make, the temporary that is the function's return value, and x. Two moves connect them (copies for a type without a move constructor). The standard then allowed the implementation to merge all three into one.

Two consequences follow from "allowed but not required":

  1. The constructor still had to be accessible and not deleted. The program was checked as if the moves happened, then the compiler was permitted to skip them. A class with a deleted move constructor could not be returned this way even though no move would ever run in the optimised program.
  2. The count was compiler-dependent in principle. In practice every mainstream compiler elided these cases at every optimisation level, because elision is decided in the front end, not by the optimiser.

You can still see the C++14 abstract machine today. GCC and Clang accept -fno-elide-constructors, which turns off the optional elisions. In C++14 mode it shows every step:

// static T make() { return T(); }   T x = make();
$ g++-16 -std=c++14 -fno-elide-constructors   (Clang 22 prints the same)
ctor move dtor move dtor dtor
//  T()   ->ret  ~T()  ->x  ~ret  ~x

Three constructions and three destructions for one line. With elision (the default) the same C++14 program prints ctor dtor.

Interview trap

"C++14 compilers did not elide, C++17 made them start" is wrong. GCC and Clang elided these cases in C++98 already. What C++17 changed is the rule: the elision is no longer an optimisation that needs a usable move constructor, so non-movable types become returnable and -fno-elide-constructors can no longer undo it.

C++17: prvalues and temporary materialisation

Theory

C++17 (paper P0135, "guaranteed copy elision through simplified value categories") redefined what a prvalue is. A prvalue is not an object. It is a recipe for initialising an object: "call T(args) on whatever storage I end up in". The object it initialises is called its result object, and the context decides where that is.

  • T x = T(1);: the result object of T(1) is x.
  • return T(1); in a function returning T: the result object is whatever the caller is initialising with the call, which may be the caller's variable, a by-value parameter, a member, or a temporary.
  • T x = T(T(T()));: the outer T(...) is a prvalue of the same type initialised from a prvalue of the same type, so the rule "a prvalue of the same type initialises the object directly" ([dcl.init]/17.6.1) applies three times. One default construction, into x.

Temporary materialisation

Sometimes a real object is needed: you cannot bind a reference to a recipe or read a member from it. The temporary materialisation conversion ([conv.rval]) turns a prvalue into an xvalue that denotes a fresh temporary object. It happens only when the context needs an object:

  • binding a reference: const T& r = T();, T&& r = make();, passing T() to a const T& or T&& parameter (including push_back(T()), see Ch 22);
  • member access: make().size(), T().v;
  • a discarded-value expression: the statement make(); on its own (the temporary is destroyed at the end of the full-expression);
  • array-to-pointer conversion on a prvalue array, and std::move(T()) (which binds to a reference parameter, so it materialises and then forces a move).

Unevaluated operands never materialise anything: sizeof(make()) and decltype(make()) do not call make.

Key facts

Expression (T has a tracing ctor/copy/move)C++17/20/23 callsC++14, defaultC++14, -fno-elide-constructors
T x = T();ctorctorctor, move
T x = T(T(T()));ctorctorctor, move, move, move
T x = make(); with return T();ctorctorctor, move, move
take(T()); with void take(T)ctorctorctor, move
T x = std::move(T());ctor, movector, movector, move
T x = b ? T(1) : T(2);ctor (one branch)ctorGCC: ctor, move; Clang: ctor, move, move
throw T(); then catch (const T&)ctorctorctor, move
Non-movable T: T x = make();compileserror: deleted moveerror

All rows were checked on GCC 16 and Clang 22. The only disagreement is the conditional row in the last column: Clang materialises the chosen operand and then moves twice (operand into the conditional's result, result into x), while GCC moves once. Both are valid C++14 abstract machines with optional elision switched off. In C++17 mode -fno-elide-constructors leaves every prvalue row at a single ctor; only named returns (NRVO, Ch 24) change.

Where the object is built: the return slot and the calling convention

Theory

How can a callee construct an object inside the caller's variable? The ABI gives it the address. Under the Itanium C++ ABI (Linux, macOS, every non-Windows platform GCC and Clang target), a function that returns a class type "in memory" receives a hidden pointer argument to uninitialised storage, the return slot. LLVM calls this parameter sret (structure return).

  • x86-64 System V: the slot address arrives in rdi (so the visible arguments shift to rsi, rdx, ...). The callee returns the same address in rax.
  • AArch64 (AAPCS64): the slot address arrives in x8, a register reserved for this purpose, so the ordinary arguments keep x0 to x7.

The caller decides what the slot is. For T x = make(); it passes &x. For use(make()) with a by-value parameter it passes the address of the parameter's storage. For make().size() it passes the address of a temporary it allocated on its own frame. The callee does not know or care: it runs T's constructor with this equal to the slot.

When the slot is not used

Small trivially copyable types are returned in registers instead. Compiling for x86-64 Linux with Clang 22 at -O1 gives:

struct Small { long a, b; };            Small small()  -> mov eax, 1 ; mov edx, 2 ; ret
struct Big   { long a[4]; };            Big big()      -> stores through rdi, mov rax, rdi
struct NonTriv { long a; NonTriv();
  NonTriv(const NonTriv&); ~NonTriv(); }; NonTriv nt()  -> call NonTrivC1 with this = rdi, mov rax, rdi

NonTriv is only 8 bytes, yet it goes through the hidden pointer. The Itanium ABI rule is that a class that is non-trivial for the purpose of calls (it has a non-trivial copy constructor, move constructor or destructor, or all of its copy and move constructors are deleted) must be passed and returned in memory, because its address is part of its identity: it may store this, and its destructor must run on the object that was constructed. For a trivially copyable type, a register return does physically copy bytes, but no constructor is called and the program cannot tell, so this is not a copy in the C++ sense.

Know this cold

"Return by value" for a class with a non-trivial constructor or destructor means "the caller lends the callee its storage". Elision is not a trick added on top of the ABI; the ABI was designed for it. The callee that does return T(v); literally runs the constructor on the caller's variable.

Returning non-movable and non-copyable types by value

Theory

Because a C++17 prvalue needs no copy or move constructor, a factory can return types that can never be copied or moved: std::mutex, std::atomic<int>, std::lock_guard, std::condition_variable, or your own class with both deleted. The caller can also initialise members, by-value parameters and aggregate elements from such a factory.

#include <atomic>
#include <cstdio>
#include <mutex>

struct Pinned {
    int id;
    explicit Pinned(int i) : id(i) {}
    Pinned(const Pinned&) = delete;
    Pinned(Pinned&&) = delete;
};

static Pinned make_pinned(int id) { return Pinned(id); }
static std::atomic<int> make_counter() { return std::atomic<int>(5); }
static std::mutex make_mutex() { return std::mutex(); }

struct Holder {
    Pinned p;
    Holder() : p(make_pinned(2)) {}   // member initialised from a prvalue
};

struct Agg { Pinned p; };

int main() {
    Pinned a = make_pinned(1);
    std::atomic<int> c = make_counter();
    std::mutex m = make_mutex();
    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(m);
    Holder h;
    Agg ag{make_pinned(3)};
    std::printf("%d %d %d %d\n", a.id, h.p.id, ag.p.id, c.load());
}

1 2 3 5

The same program in C++14 fails on every line that initialises an object from the factory, because the abstract machine still contains a move from the return value:

#include <cstdio>

struct Pinned {
    int id;
    explicit Pinned(int i) : id(i) {}
    Pinned(const Pinned&) = delete;
    Pinned(Pinned&&) = delete;
};

static Pinned make_pinned(int id) { return Pinned(id); }   // C++14: error, needs Pinned(Pinned&&)

int main() {
    Pinned a = make_pinned(1);                             // C++14: error again
    std::printf("%d\n", a.id);
}

GCC 16 reports use of deleted function 'Pinned::Pinned(Pinned&&)' and Clang 22 reports call to deleted constructor of 'Pinned', both in -std=c++14.

What already worked before C++17

  • return {}; or return {args}; is copy-list-initialisation of the return value directly from the braced list. No temporary of type T exists, so it compiled in C++11 even for std::mutex (as long as the constructor is not explicit). The caller's auto m = make(); still failed in C++14.
  • Binding the result to a reference, auto&& m = make(); or const auto& m = make();, uses lifetime extension instead of a move, so it compiled in C++14.

The exception: base-class subobjects

Guaranteed elision does not reach base-class subobjects. struct D : Pinned { D() : Pinned(make_pinned(3)) {} }; is rejected by both GCC 16 and Clang 22 in C++17 and C++20 with a "deleted move constructor" error. The reason (core issue CWG2403) is that a base subobject is potentially overlapping: the derived class may reuse the base's tail padding for its own members, and a function returning a complete Pinned would write sizeof(Pinned) bytes, clobbering them. Ordinary members are fine, as the Holder example shows. (For a [[no_unique_address]] member, which is also potentially overlapping, the two compilers currently disagree: Clang 22 accepts it and GCC 16 rejects it.)

Putting a factory result into a container

std::optional<Pinned>::emplace(make_pinned(7)) does not compile: emplace takes its arguments by forwarding reference, which materialises the prvalue, and then Pinned would have to be constructed from a Pinned&&. The fix is to pass an object that converts to Pinned by calling the factory. The container constructs Pinned(std::forward<Lazy>(l)), and GCC and Clang let the conversion function's prvalue result initialise the element in place. Strictly, the C++17 and C++20 wording only considers Pinned's constructors here, which would bind the converted prvalue to Pinned(Pinned&&) and fail; core issue CWG2327 asks for the elision that compilers already perform. Coding drill 3 builds this adaptor.

By-value parameters, conditional expressions, throw and catch

Theory

Passing prvalues to by-value parameters

A by-value parameter is an object initialised from the argument, so a prvalue argument of the same type initialises the parameter directly. take(T()) and take(make()) each call exactly one constructor; the parameter is the result object. Passing an lvalue copies, and passing std::move(lvalue) moves. This is why "take by value and move from it" is a good default for sink parameters: callers that pass temporaries pay nothing extra.

One detail that surprises people: who destroys the parameter. Under the Itanium ABI the caller allocates the parameter's storage and the standard leaves it implementation-defined whether the parameter is destroyed when the function returns or at the end of the caller's full-expression. GCC and Clang destroy it at the end of the full-expression in the caller. Do not write output-comparing code that depends on that order; count calls instead.

The conditional operator

b ? T(1) : T(2) is a prvalue when both operands are prvalues of the same class type, so T x = b ? T(1) : T(2); and return b ? T(1) : T(2); build directly into the result object. If both operands are lvalues (b ? x : y), the result is an lvalue, and initialising from it is a copy. That is the classic way to lose elision, discussed in Ch 24.

throw and catch

  • throw T(args); copy-initialises the exception object from a prvalue, so in C++17 the exception object is constructed directly. One constructor.
  • throw local; may elide (optional) if local is a non-volatile automatic object whose scope does not extend beyond the innermost enclosing try block. GCC and Clang do not elide it; they apply the implicit move instead (the object is moved into the exception object, since C++11 for locals).
  • catch (T e) may elide the copy from the exception object into e only if doing so changes nothing but the skipped constructor and destructor. In practice GCC and Clang always copy. Catch by const T&: no copy, no slicing.

-fno-elide-constructors in C++14 and C++17

Theory

-fno-elide-constructors (GCC and Clang) disables the optional elisions. It is a teaching and debugging tool; nobody ships with it. Its effect depends on the language mode, because the set of optional elisions shrank in C++17.

Code-std=c++14 -fno-elide-constructors-std=c++17 -fno-elide-constructors
T x = make(); where return T();ctor move dtor move dtor dtorctor dtor
T x = T(T(T()));ctor move move move, then 4 dtorsctor dtor
T x = nrvo(); where T t; return t;ctor move dtor move dtor dtorctor move dtor dtor
T x = param(T()); where return p;ctor move move move, then 4 dtorsctor move dtor dtor

Read the C++17 column carefully. The prvalue cases do not change: the flag cannot disable guaranteed elision because there is nothing to disable. The NRVO case gains exactly one move, from the local t into the return slot (implicit move, because t is a local being returned). The parameter case is a move in both modes because parameters are never eligible for elision; C++14 adds two more moves for the prvalue argument and the return temporary. Every row above was produced by both GCC 16 and Clang 22.

Tip

To see the C++14 abstract machine of a snippet, compile it with -std=c++14 -fno-elide-constructors. To check whether a type is returnable without a move in your codebase's language mode, delete its move constructor temporarily and compile.

When elision cannot happen

Theory

Elision needs the object being initialised and the source to be the "same object" in a way the compiler can arrange before the source is created. Each case below breaks that, and each was checked on both compilers (calls shown for C++20):

CaseExampleResultWhy
Returning a by-value parameterT f(T p) { return p; }moveThe caller built p in its own storage before the call; it cannot also be the return slot. Implicit move applies.
Returning a data memberreturn h.m;copyA subobject of another object, not an automatic variable; no implicit move either.
Returning a global or staticreturn g;copyIts lifetime is not the function's; it must survive.
Different object per branchif (b) return a; return c;moveBoth locals are alive at once, and only one can occupy the slot (NRVO, Ch 24).
Conditional of lvaluesreturn b ? a : c;copyThe expression is not a plain name, so neither NRVO nor implicit move applies.
Conversion to another typeW f() { T t; return t; }move, then W(T)The slot holds a W, not a T; t needs its own storage.
std::move of the sourcereturn std::move(t);, T x = std::move(T());moveThe expression is an xvalue (a reference), not a prvalue or a name, so the rules no longer match.
Base-class subobjectD() : Base(make_base()) {}move (error if deleted)Potentially overlapping subobject, CWG2403.

Notice the split between "move" and "copy". When elision fails for a local or a parameter, the implicit move on return still saves you from a copy. When the source is a member, a global or a non-name expression, you get a full copy. Ch 24 covers the implicit-move rules and their C++20 and C++23 extensions.

Side effects: an exception to the as-if rule

Theory

The as-if rule ([intro.abstract]) lets a compiler perform any transformation that does not change observable behaviour (I/O, volatile accesses). Copy elision is one of the very few places where the standard explicitly allows a change in observable behaviour; the other commonly cited one is omitting or merging allocations in new expressions ([expr.new]), so a replaced operator new may not be called. If a copy constructor writes to stdout, increments a global counter or registers this in a list, elision skips those effects, and the program is still correct.

Two consequences matter for real code:

  • Copy and move constructors must mean "make an equivalent object" and nothing else. Code that relies on a copy constructor running (reference counting by copy, logging that a value was "passed", assigning IDs on copy) breaks silently when elision kicks in, and behaves differently in C++14 with optional elision disabled.
  • Tests that count operations are fine if they target guaranteed elision (prvalues) or behaviour that GCC and Clang both implement consistently. Tests that depend on NRVO are testing the compiler, not the language.

Elision also changes which object's address you see. With elision, this in the constructor equals &x in the caller. Recording this in the constructor and comparing it with the final address is a portable way to prove that elision happened without printing pointers (reading drill 6).

Interview trap

"The compiler may only skip a copy constructor if it has no side effects" is wrong. Elision is permitted even when the constructor or destructor has side effects. This is the whole point of naming it in the standard instead of leaving it to the as-if rule.

Concept and tricky questions

Drills

ConceptWhat is copy elision, and what are its guaranteed and optional forms in C++17?

Answer

Answer. Copy elision is constructing an object directly in its final location so that a copy or move constructor (and the matching destructor) that the source code implies never runs. Guaranteed: initialising an object from a prvalue of the same type (return T();, T x = T();, passing T() by value, throw T();). Optional: NRVO (return local;), throw local; and catch (T e).

Why. The guaranteed form is a consequence of C++17's definition of a prvalue as an initialiser without its own storage ([basic.lval], [dcl.init]/17.6.1). The optional forms are in [class.copy.elision]/1 and still require an accessible copy or move constructor. A common wrong answer is "RVO and NRVO are both guaranteed since C++17"; only the unnamed case is.

ConceptWhy do some people say "guaranteed copy elision" is a misleading name?

Answer

Answer. Because in C++17 there is no copy to elide. A prvalue is not an object; it is a recipe that initialises its result object. return T(); does not create a temporary and then skip a move: it says "initialise the caller's object with T()".

Why. P0135 changed the value-category model rather than adding a new elision rule. That is why the move constructor need not exist, why -fno-elide-constructors cannot bring the moves back, and why the standard wording for it is in [dcl.init] rather than [class.copy.elision]. Saying "the compiler is now required to optimise" is the misconception; the language simply stopped describing the extra objects.

TrickyHow many constructors does T x = T(T(T())); call in C++17? In C++14? In C++14 with -fno-elide-constructors?

Answer

Answer. C++17: one default constructor, guaranteed. C++14: one default constructor in practice (GCC 16 and Clang 22 both elide), but the move constructor must be accessible. C++14 with -fno-elide-constructors: one default constructor and three moves, then four destructors.

Why. In C++17 each T(prvalue of T) is a prvalue of the same type initialised from a prvalue of the same type, so [dcl.init]/17.6.1 collapses them all into x. In C++14 each functional cast creates a temporary initialised by moving from the inner temporary, then x is moved from the outer one, giving three elidable moves. People often answer "three moves in C++17" (thinking of the casts as copies) or "the compiler might do three moves" (it is not allowed to in C++17).

TrickyIs copy elision an application of the as-if rule?

Answer

Answer. No. Elision is explicitly allowed to change observable behaviour, for example skipping a copy constructor that prints. It is the best-known such exception; the other commonly cited one is allocation elision for new expressions.

Why. The as-if rule only permits transformations that leave I/O and volatile accesses unchanged. A compiler could never prove that skipping a user-defined copy constructor with side effects is unobservable, so the standard grants the permission separately in [class.copy.elision]. The wrong answer "elision only happens when the copy constructor is trivial or side-effect free" confuses it with ordinary optimisation.

ConceptWhat is temporary materialisation, and name four contexts that trigger it.

Answer

Answer. The conversion that turns a prvalue into an xvalue denoting a newly created temporary object ([conv.rval]). Triggers: binding a reference (const T& r = T();, passing to a T&& or const T& parameter), member access on a prvalue (make().v), a discarded-value expression (make(); as a statement), and array-to-pointer conversion of a prvalue array. std::move(T()) is a reference binding too.

Why. A recipe has no address, so anything that needs an object forces one into existence. After materialisation the object is a normal temporary and any copy or move into another object is a real call; that is why v.push_back(T()) costs a move while v.emplace_back() does not (Ch 22). Unevaluated operands (sizeof, decltype) never materialise.

TrickyCan -fno-elide-constructors make a C++17 program call a move constructor for T x = make(); where make does return T();? What about T t; return t;?

Answer

Answer. No for return T();: the output stays ctor dtor on GCC 16 and Clang 22. Yes for return t;: it becomes ctor move dtor dtor, one move from the local into the result.

Why. The flag disables optional elision only. The prvalue case is not elision any more, so there is nothing to turn off. NRVO is still optional, so disabling it exposes the implicit move. Candidates who learned the flag in the C++11 era expect two moves in both cases; in C++14 mode that is what you get.

ConceptAt the machine level, how does a function return a std::string by value on x86-64 Linux?

Answer

Answer. The caller allocates storage for the result and passes its address as a hidden first argument in rdi. The callee constructs the string at that address and returns the same address in rax. On AArch64 the hidden pointer goes in x8.

Why. std::string has a non-trivial copy constructor and destructor, so under the Itanium C++ ABI it is "non-trivial for the purpose of calls" and must be returned in memory. LLVM marks this parameter sret. That hidden pointer is what makes elision possible: the callee's return std::string(...) constructs straight into the caller's variable. Saying "the string is built on the callee's stack and copied back" describes no real implementation.

TrickyAn 8-byte class with a user-defined destructor and a 16-byte plain struct { long a, b; }: which one goes through the hidden return pointer on x86-64?

Answer

Answer. The 8-byte class with the destructor goes through the hidden pointer. The 16-byte plain struct comes back in rax and rdx.

Why. Size alone does not decide it. The Itanium C++ ABI forces any type with a non-trivial copy constructor, move constructor or destructor into memory, because the object's address must stay stable between construction and destruction. Trivially copyable aggregates of up to 16 bytes follow the C rules (System V classifies them into registers). Checked with Clang 22 --target=x86_64-linux-gnu -O1. The common wrong answer is "anything up to 16 bytes is returned in registers".

TrickyA member Pinned p; can be initialised with p(make_pinned(2)) even though Pinned is not movable. Why does struct D : Pinned { D() : Pinned(make_pinned(3)) {} }; fail?

Answer

Answer. Base-class subobjects are potentially overlapping, and guaranteed elision does not apply to them. Both GCC 16 and Clang 22 reject the base initialiser with a deleted-move-constructor error.

Why. A derived class may place its own members in the base's tail padding. The factory writes a complete Pinned of sizeof(Pinned) bytes (and for a polymorphic base would set the wrong vptr), so building it in place could corrupt the derived object. Core issue CWG2403 records this; compilers materialise a temporary and then need the move constructor. A workaround is a Pinned constructor taking the factory's arguments, or holding Pinned as a member.

ConceptHow many objects of type T exist for throw T(); caught by catch (const T& e)? And by catch (T e)?

Answer

Answer. By reference: one, the exception object, constructed directly from the prvalue. By value: two, because e is copied from the exception object (GCC 16 and Clang 22 print ctor copy).

Why. The exception object is copy-initialised from the operand of throw; a prvalue operand initialises it directly in C++17. The copy into a by-value catch parameter is only optionally elidable, and implementations do not elide it because the exception object lives in a runtime-allocated area. Catching by value also slices derived exceptions, which is the stronger reason to catch by const&.

TrickyWhich of these compile in C++14 for std::mutex: (a) std::mutex f() { return {}; } (b) auto m = f(); (c) auto&& m = f(); (d) std::mutex m = std::mutex();

Answer

Answer. (a) and (c) compile in C++14; (b) and (d) do not. All four compile in C++17.

Why. (a) copy-list-initialises the return value from {} directly, with no intermediate std::mutex object, which was legal since C++11. (c) binds a reference to the returned temporary and extends its lifetime, so no move is needed. (b) and (d) copy-initialise from a temporary of the same type, which in C++14 requires a usable move or copy constructor, and std::mutex has both deleted. Verified on GCC 16 and Clang 22. Many people think return {}; needed C++17.

ConceptWhy can the compiler never elide the move in T f(T p) { return p; }?

Answer

Answer. The parameter p and the return slot are two distinct pieces of storage, both chosen by the caller before f starts. The callee cannot make them the same object, so it moves p into the slot. The standard excludes parameters from NRVO explicitly.

Why. Under the Itanium ABI the caller constructs the argument in its own frame and passes its address, and separately passes the return-slot address. Since C++11, return p; treats p as an rvalue first (implicit move), so you get a move rather than a copy. Writing return std::move(p); adds nothing; GCC warns with -Wredundant-move under -Wextra and Clang under -Wall.

TrickySomeone writes T x = std::move(T()); "to make sure it moves instead of copying". What does it cost?

Answer

Answer. It adds a move and a destructor call. Without std::move the line is one constructor; with it, a temporary is materialised, x is move-constructed from it, and the temporary is destroyed at the end of the statement.

Why. std::move takes a reference, so its argument is materialised, and its result is an xvalue, not a prvalue. Guaranteed elision only applies to prvalues, so the rule no longer matches. The prvalue was already the best case; there was never a copy to avoid. For a non-movable type this line fails to compile, while T x = T(); works.

Answer. The prvalue version builds only T(2), directly in x. The lvalue version constructs both locals and then copies a into the result.

Why. b ? T(1) : T(2) is a prvalue of type T, and only the chosen operand is evaluated, so it initialises the return slot. b ? a : c is an lvalue that is neither a prvalue nor a plain name, so there is no elision and no implicit move; copy initialisation from an lvalue calls the copy constructor. Rewrite as if (b) return a; return c; to get moves (Ch 24). Many candidates expect a move because "it is a local being returned".

Find the bugThis compiles in C++17 but the team must also support C++14. Which lines break, and how would you make it compile in C++14 without making Lock movable?

#include <cstdio>
#include <mutex>

class Lock {
public:
    explicit Lock(int id) : id_(id) { std::puts("locked"); }
    Lock(const Lock&) = delete;
    Lock(Lock&&) = delete;
    ~Lock() { std::puts("unlocked"); }
    int id() const { return id_; }
private:
    int id_;
};

static Lock acquire(int id) { return Lock(id); }

int main() {
    Lock l = acquire(7);
    std::printf("holding %d\n", l.id());
}
Answer

Answer. In C++14 both return Lock(id); and Lock l = acquire(7); are errors: each copy-initialises a Lock from a temporary Lock, which requires the deleted move constructor even though the compiler would elide it. A C++14-compatible version returns with a braced list (the constructor must then be non-explicit) and binds the result with auto&&:

#include <cstdio>

class Lock {
public:
    Lock(int id) : id_(id) { std::puts("locked"); }   // not explicit, so return {id} works
    Lock(const Lock&) = delete;
    Lock(Lock&&) = delete;
    ~Lock() { std::puts("unlocked"); }
    int id() const { return id_; }
private:
    int id_;
};

static Lock acquire(int id) { return {id}; }   // list-initialises the return value directly

int main() {
    auto&& l = acquire(7);                     // lifetime extension, no move
    std::printf("holding %d\n", l.id());
}

locked
holding 7
unlocked

Why. Before C++17, elision was an optional optimisation applied to a program that had to be valid with the moves present ([class.copy]/31 in C++14). The braced return has no source object of type Lock, and reference binding uses lifetime extension instead of initialisation from a temporary. In C++17 the original program is valid as written.

Answer. (1) one constructor, the exception object built directly. (2) the local is constructed, moved into the exception object, then destroyed during unwinding before the handler runs. (3) one constructor plus a copy into the by-value catch parameter.

Why. throw T() copy-initialises the exception object from a prvalue, which is guaranteed elision. throw t could optionally be elided but GCC 16 and Clang 22 apply the implicit move instead. The copy into catch (T) is also optional to elide and neither compiler does it. Both copies vanish if you catch by const T&.

OutputThis program proves elision without printing addresses. What does it print?

#include <cstdio>

struct T {
    static const T* built_at;
    T() { built_at = this; }
    T(const T&) { std::puts("copy"); }
    T(T&&) noexcept { std::puts("move"); }
};
const T* T::built_at = nullptr;

static T make() { return T(); }
static T wrap() { return make(); }

struct Box { T member; Box() : member(wrap()) {} };

int main() {
    T x = wrap();
    std::printf("%d\n", T::built_at == &x);
    Box b;
    std::printf("%d\n", T::built_at == &b.member);
    const T& r = make();
    std::printf("%d\n", T::built_at == &r);
}
Answer
1
1
1

Answer. Three 1s and no copy or move lines.

Why. The constructor records this, the address it is building. For x the return slot passed down through wrap and make is &x. For the member, the slot is the member's storage inside b. For const T& r, the prvalue is materialised into a lifetime-extended temporary, and the slot is that temporary, which r refers to. Comparing pointers and printing a boolean keeps the output deterministic.

Find the bugThe author added std::move everywhere "to avoid copies" and the profiler shows more move constructor calls than before. Predict the output and fix it.

#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>

struct T {
    T() { std::puts("ctor"); }
    T(const T&) { std::puts("copy"); }
    T(T&&) noexcept { std::puts("move"); }
    ~T() { std::puts("dtor"); }
};

static T make() { return std::move(T()); }

int main() {
    T x = std::move(make());
    std::puts("done");
}
Answer
ctor
move
dtor
move
dtor
done
dtor

Answer. Two extra moves and two extra destructions. Remove both std::move calls: return T(); and T x = make(); give ctor, done, dtor.

Why. Each std::move binds a prvalue to a reference parameter, which materialises a temporary, and returns an xvalue. Guaranteed elision only matches prvalues, so each step becomes a real move. GCC 16 and Clang 22 both flag each call under -Wall: "moving a temporary object prevents copy elision" (-Wpessimizing-move). The belief that std::move "makes things move" is the root error: it is a cast, and a prvalue was already better than any move.

OutputMaterialisation and unevaluated operands. Which lines construct objects?

#include <cstdio>

struct T {
    int v = 5;
    T() { std::puts("ctor"); }
    T(const T&) { std::puts("copy"); }
    T(T&&) noexcept { std::puts("move"); }
    ~T() { std::puts("dtor"); }
};

static T make() { return T(); }

int main() {
    std::puts("-sizeof");  std::printf("%d\n", static_cast<int>(sizeof(make()) > 0));
    std::puts("-member");  std::printf("%d\n", make().v);
    std::puts("-discard"); make();
    std::puts("-ref");     const T& r = make();
    std::puts("-end");     (void)r;
}
Answer
-sizeof
1
-member
ctor
5
dtor
-discard
ctor
dtor
-ref
ctor
-end
dtor

Answer. sizeof calls nothing. Member access and the discarded call each materialise a temporary that dies at the end of the statement. The reference binding materialises a temporary whose lifetime is extended to r's scope, so its dtor prints after -end.

Why. The operand of sizeof is unevaluated. Member access and discarded-value expressions need an object, so [conv.rval] creates one; temporaries are destroyed at the end of the full-expression ([class.temporary]), which is why 5 prints before dtor. Binding to const T& extends the lifetime. No copies or moves appear anywhere.

Find the bugWhy does this fail on both compilers in C++20, when initialising a member the same way works?

#include <cstdio>

struct Pinned {
    int id;
    explicit Pinned(int i) : id(i) {}
    Pinned(const Pinned&) = delete;
    Pinned(Pinned&&) = delete;
};

static Pinned make_pinned(int id) { return Pinned(id); }

struct Derived : Pinned {
    int extra = 0;
    Derived() : Pinned(make_pinned(3)) {}
};

int main() {
    Derived d;
    std::printf("%d\n", d.id);
}
Answer

Answer. A base-class subobject is potentially overlapping, so it cannot be the result object of a prvalue from a factory. The compiler materialises a temporary and needs Pinned(Pinned&&), which is deleted. Fix: construct the base from the factory's arguments, or hold Pinned as a member.

#include <cstdio>

struct Pinned {
    int id;
    explicit Pinned(int i) : id(i) {}
    Pinned(const Pinned&) = delete;
    Pinned(Pinned&&) = delete;
};

static Pinned make_pinned(int id) { return Pinned(id); }

struct AsBase : Pinned {
    AsBase() : Pinned(3) {}                  // construct the base directly
};

struct AsMember {
    Pinned p;
    AsMember() : p(make_pinned(4)) {}        // members are fine
};

int main() {
    AsBase a;
    AsMember m;
    std::printf("%d %d\n", a.id, m.p.id);
}

3 4

Why. The derived class may store extra in Pinned's tail padding, and a function that returns a Pinned writes a full sizeof(Pinned). Core issue CWG2403 excludes potentially-overlapping subobjects from the in-place rule. GCC 16 and Clang 22 both report the deleted move constructor.

OutputA factory returns a Derived prvalue, and the caller stores it in a Base. Is anything elided?

#include <cstdio>

struct Base {
    Base() { std::puts("Base ctor"); }
    Base(const Base&) { std::puts("Base copy"); }
    Base(Base&&) noexcept { std::puts("Base move"); }
    ~Base() { std::puts("Base dtor"); }
};

struct Derived : Base {
    Derived() { std::puts("Derived ctor"); }
    ~Derived() { std::puts("Derived dtor"); }
};

static Derived make_derived() { return Derived(); }

int main() {
    {
        Base b = make_derived();
        std::puts("using b");
    }
    std::puts("end");
}
Answer
Base ctor
Derived ctor
Base move
Derived dtor
Base dtor
using b
Base dtor
end

Answer. The Derived object is built in place inside a temporary, but b is then move-constructed from that temporary's Base part (slicing), and the whole temporary is destroyed at the end of the statement.

Why. Guaranteed elision needs the prvalue to have the same type as the object it initialises ([dcl.init]/17.6.1). Here Base is initialised from a Derived prvalue, so overload resolution picks Base(Base&&), binding its reference parameter materialises a Derived temporary, and the move is a real call. The common wrong answer is "one construction, because a prvalue is always built in place": the slot passed to make_derived is the temporary, not b, because b is too small to hold a Derived. Return Base from the factory (or store a Derived) to get zero moves.

OutputThe copy constructor has a side effect. What does the counter say?

#include <cstdio>

static int copies = 0;
static int moves = 0;

struct T {
    T() = default;
    T(const T&) { ++copies; }
    T(T&&) noexcept { ++moves; }
};

static T make() { return T(); }
static T pass(T t) { return t; }

int main() {
    T a = T(T(make()));
    T b = pass(make());
    T c = pass(a);
    std::printf("copies=%d moves=%d\n", copies, moves);
}
Answer
copies=1 moves=2

Answer. One copy (the lvalue a into pass's parameter) and two moves (each return t; from a parameter into the return slot).

Why. T a = T(T(make())) is all prvalues: zero operations. pass(make()) builds the parameter in place, then moves it out because parameters cannot be NRVO'd. pass(a) copies into the parameter, then moves it out. The side effects of the skipped constructors simply never happen, which the standard permits. Answering "copies=3" (treating every T(...) as a copy) is the usual mistake.

Write the code

Coding

CodeWrite a factory make_registry(std::string name) that returns, by value, a Registry holding a std::mutex, a std::atomic<long> counter and the name. Registry must be neither copyable nor movable. Show it initialising a local, a class member and an aggregate element, and add a thread-safe add(long) used from two threads.

Answer

Approach. Delete both copy and move. Let std::mutex and std::atomic members make that implicit, and delete explicitly for clarity. The factory returns a prvalue (return Registry(std::move(name));), so C++17 builds it in the caller's storage. Members and aggregate elements are result objects too, so they can be initialised from the factory call. The mutex protects a non-atomic total to show the lock in use.

#include <atomic>
#include <cstdio>
#include <mutex>
#include <string>
#include <thread>
#include <utility>

class Registry {
public:
    explicit Registry(std::string name) : name_(std::move(name)) {}
    Registry(const Registry&) = delete;
    Registry(Registry&&) = delete;
    Registry& operator=(const Registry&) = delete;
    Registry& operator=(Registry&&) = delete;

    void add(long v) {
        hits_.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(m_);
        total_ += v;
    }
    long hits() const { return hits_.load(); }
    long total() { std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(m_); return total_; }
    const std::string& name() const { return name_; }

private:
    std::string name_;
    std::mutex m_;
    std::atomic<long> hits_{0};
    long total_ = 0;
};

static Registry make_registry(std::string name) { return Registry(std::move(name)); }

struct Service {
    Registry reg;
    Service() : reg(make_registry("svc")) {}
};

struct Pair { Registry a; Registry b; };

int main() {
    Registry local = make_registry("local");
    std::thread t1([&] { for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) local.add(1); });
    std::thread t2([&] { for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) local.add(2); });
    t1.join();
    t2.join();
    Service s;
    Pair p{make_registry("a"), make_registry("b")};
    std::printf("%s hits=%ld total=%ld\n", local.name().c_str(), local.hits(), local.total());
    std::printf("%s %s %s\n", s.reg.name().c_str(), p.a.name().c_str(), p.b.name().c_str());
}

local hits=2000 total=3000
svc a b

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) per call. Do not return a named local (Registry r(...); return r;): NRVO is optional, so it needs a move constructor and will not compile. Do not try to put it in a std::vector, which needs moves for reallocation. In C++14 none of the initialisations compile.

Estimated rating: ~1400 · straightforward once you know prvalue returns need no move constructor; the trap is returning a named local

CodeWrite a tracing type Probe that counts default constructions, copies, moves and destructions in a global struct, plus a helper that runs a callable and returns the counts it caused. Use it to assert that a chain of three factories feeding a by-value parameter makes zero copies and zero moves, and that a sink function that does return p; makes exactly one move.

Answer

Approach. Keep counters in a static struct. measure(f) resets the counters, runs f, and returns a snapshot taken after f returns (so destructors of temporaries inside f are included). Assertions use a small check function that prints PASS or FAIL, so the program's output is deterministic and verifiable.

#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>

struct Counts { int ctor = 0, copy = 0, move = 0, dtor = 0; };
static Counts g_counts;

struct Probe {
    int v = 0;
    Probe() { ++g_counts.ctor; }
    explicit Probe(int x) : v(x) { ++g_counts.ctor; }
    Probe(const Probe& o) : v(o.v) { ++g_counts.copy; }
    Probe(Probe&& o) noexcept : v(o.v) { ++g_counts.move; }
    Probe& operator=(const Probe&) = default;
    Probe& operator=(Probe&&) = default;
    ~Probe() { ++g_counts.dtor; }
};

template <class F>
static Counts measure(F f) {
    g_counts = {};
    f();
    return g_counts;
}

static void check(const char* what, bool ok) { std::printf("%s %s\n", ok ? "PASS" : "FAIL", what); }

static Probe make(int v) { return Probe(v); }
static Probe add_one(int v) { return make(v + 1); }
static Probe twice(int v) { return add_one(v * 2); }
static int consume(Probe p) { return p.v; }
static Probe sink(Probe p) { p.v += 100; return p; }

int main() {
    Counts c = measure([] { std::printf("value %d\n", consume(twice(3))); });
    check("factory chain: 1 ctor, 0 copies, 0 moves", c.ctor == 1 && c.copy == 0 && c.move == 0 && c.dtor == 1);

    c = measure([] { Probe r = sink(make(1)); std::printf("value %d\n", r.v); });
    check("sink: exactly one move", c.ctor == 1 && c.copy == 0 && c.move == 1 && c.dtor == 2);

    c = measure([] { Probe a(5); Probe r = sink(a); (void)r; });
    check("sink from lvalue: one copy, one move", c.copy == 1 && c.move == 1);
}

value 7
PASS factory chain: 1 ctor, 0 copies, 0 moves
value 101
PASS sink: exactly one move
PASS sink from lvalue: one copy, one move

Complexity and pitfalls. Constant overhead per operation. Keep the counters non-atomic only for single-threaded tests. Reset before each measurement, and check destructions too: a missing dtor count reveals a leaked or lifetime-extended temporary. Do not assert NRVO-dependent counts in portable tests; this test only relies on guaranteed elision and the parameter rule, which are the same on every conforming compiler.

Estimated rating: ~1300 · simple bookkeeping; the insight is predicting the counts correctly before asserting them

CodeWrite a generic adaptor Lazy (C++17) that wraps a callable returning a non-movable type N, so that std::optional<N>::emplace and std::map<K, N>::try_emplace can store the factory's result in place. Show that emplace(make()) does not compile and that your version does, with no move constructor on N.

Answer

Approach. emplace(args...) constructs N(std::forward<Args>(args)...) in the container's storage. If the single argument is an object with a conversion function operator N(), GCC and Clang use that conversion function and let its prvalue result initialise the element directly. This is compiler behaviour that goes slightly beyond the letter of the standard: the C++17 wording only considers N's constructors, so it would bind the converted prvalue to the deleted N(N&&). Core issue CWG2327 covers this gap, and both compilers already implement the elision. The adaptor holds the callable and calls it inside the conversion. A deduction guide lets callers write Lazy{lambda}.

#include <cstdio>
#include <map>
#include <optional>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

struct Conn {
    int fd;
    explicit Conn(int f) : fd(f) { std::printf("open %d\n", fd); }
    Conn(const Conn&) = delete;
    Conn(Conn&&) = delete;
    ~Conn() { std::printf("close %d\n", fd); }
};

static Conn connect(int fd) { return Conn(fd); }

template <class F>
struct Lazy {
    F f;
    operator decltype(std::declval<F&>()())() { return f(); }
};
template <class F> Lazy(F) -> Lazy<F>;

int main() {
    std::optional<Conn> slot;
    // slot.emplace(connect(3));   // error: Conn(Conn&&) is deleted
    slot.emplace(Lazy{[] { return connect(3); }});

    std::map<std::string, Conn> pool;
    pool.try_emplace("db", Lazy{[] { return connect(4); }});
    pool.try_emplace("cache", Lazy{[] { return connect(5); }});
    std::printf("%d %d %d\n", slot->fd, pool.at("db").fd, pool.at("cache").fd);
    pool.erase("db");
}

open 3
open 4
open 5
3 4 5
close 4
close 5
close 3

The commented-out line fails because emplace takes Args&&...: binding connect(3) to that reference materialises a temporary Conn, and constructing the element from it needs the move constructor.

Complexity and pitfalls. No overhead beyond the factory call. The conversion operator must return exactly N by value; returning a reference would reintroduce a copy. Do not make Conn constructible from arbitrary types through a template constructor, or that constructor may win over the conversion. The program erases "db" explicitly before printing ends, because the order in which a std::map destroys its remaining elements is an implementation detail (libstdc++ and libc++ differ), and output tests must not depend on it.

Estimated rating: ~1900 · needs the materialisation rule for forwarding references plus the conversion-function trick

CodeWrite ScopedTimer start_timer(bool verbose, const char* label) returning a non-copyable, non-movable RAII timer configured in one of two ways depending on verbose, with zero moves. The timer prints its label and mode on construction and on destruction. Do not use heap allocation or std::optional.

Answer

Approach. Returning one of two named locals needs a move. Instead, return a conditional expression whose operands are both prvalues of the same type: return verbose ? ScopedTimer(label, Mode::Verbose) : ScopedTimer(label, Mode::Quiet);. That expression is itself a prvalue, only the chosen operand is evaluated, and it initialises the caller's object directly. Two separate return statements of prvalues work just as well.

#include <cstdio>

enum class Mode { Quiet, Verbose };

class ScopedTimer {
public:
    ScopedTimer(const char* label, Mode m) : label_(label), mode_(m) {
        std::printf("start %s %s\n", label_, mode_ == Mode::Verbose ? "verbose" : "quiet");
    }
    ScopedTimer(const ScopedTimer&) = delete;
    ScopedTimer(ScopedTimer&&) = delete;
    ~ScopedTimer() { std::printf("stop %s\n", label_); }
private:
    const char* label_;
    Mode mode_;
};

static ScopedTimer start_timer(bool verbose, const char* label) {
    return verbose ? ScopedTimer(label, Mode::Verbose) : ScopedTimer(label, Mode::Quiet);
}

static ScopedTimer start_timer2(bool verbose, const char* label) {
    if (verbose) return ScopedTimer(label, Mode::Verbose);
    return ScopedTimer(label, Mode::Quiet);
}

int main() {
    {
        ScopedTimer a = start_timer(true, "parse");
        ScopedTimer b = start_timer2(false, "emit");
        std::puts("working");
    }
    std::puts("done");
}

start parse verbose
start emit quiet
working
stop emit
stop parse
done

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1). ScopedTimer t1(...), t2(...); return verbose ? t1 : t2; would need a copy constructor, and two named locals with two returns would need a move constructor, so both fail to compile. The deleted move constructor is a good guard: it turns any accidental non-elided path into a compile error.

Estimated rating: ~1400 · knowing that a conditional of two prvalues is still a prvalue

CodeWrite a non-copyable, non-movable Node that registers its own address in a global intrusive list on construction and unregisters on destruction, plus a factory make_node(int) returning it by value. Prove (without printing pointers) that the address registered at construction is the final address of the object in the caller, including when the factory result initialises a struct member.

Answer

Approach. Self-registering objects are a classic reason types cannot be moved: the registry stores this. With guaranteed elision the constructor runs on the final storage, so registering this in the constructor is safe even for a factory. The list is a doubly linked intrusive list (head pointer plus prev/next in each node). A contains(const Node*) check proves the final address is registered.

#include <cstdio>

class Node {
public:
    explicit Node(int id) : id_(id), next_(head_) {
        if (head_) head_->prev_ = this;
        head_ = this;
    }
    Node(const Node&) = delete;
    Node(Node&&) = delete;
    ~Node() {
        if (prev_) prev_->next_ = next_; else head_ = next_;
        if (next_) next_->prev_ = prev_;
    }
    static bool contains(const Node* n) {
        for (const Node* p = head_; p; p = p->next_) if (p == n) return true;
        return false;
    }
    static int size() { int k = 0; for (const Node* p = head_; p; p = p->next_) ++k; return k; }
    int id() const { return id_; }
private:
    int id_;
    Node* prev_ = nullptr;
    Node* next_;
    static Node* head_;
};
Node* Node::head_ = nullptr;

static Node make_node(int id) { return Node(id); }

struct Owner {
    int tag;
    Node node;
    Owner() : tag(1), node(make_node(20)) {}
};

int main() {
    Node a = make_node(10);
    Owner o;
    std::printf("%d %d size=%d\n", Node::contains(&a), Node::contains(&o.node), Node::size());
    {
        Node tmp = make_node(30);
        std::printf("inner size=%d id=%d\n", Node::size(), tmp.id());
    }
    std::printf("after size=%d ids=%d,%d\n", Node::size(), a.id(), o.node.id());
}

1 1 size=2
inner size=3 id=30
after size=2 ids=10,20

Complexity and pitfalls. Registration and removal are O(1); contains is O(n). ASan confirms no dangling pointers in the list. In C++14 this design was impossible to return by value; people used std::unique_ptr<Node> or out-parameters. Do not use it as a base subobject initialised from make_node (CWG2403), and add a mutex if nodes are created on several threads.

Estimated rating: ~1600 · intrusive list bookkeeping plus the guarantee that this in the constructor is the final address

Cheat sheet

Theory
  • C++17: a prvalue is an initialiser, not an object. return T();, T x = T(T(T()));, f(T()) and throw T(); construct once, directly in the result object, and need no copy or move constructor.
  • Temporaries appear only through materialisation: reference binding (including std::move and push_back), member access, discarded expressions. After that, copies and moves are real.
  • Non-movable types (std::mutex, std::atomic, your own) can be returned from factories and used to initialise locals, members and aggregate elements in C++17, but not base-class subobjects (CWG2403). In C++14 use return {...}; plus auto&&.
  • ABI: the caller passes the return slot's address (rdi on x86-64, x8 on AArch64, sret in LLVM) for any type that is non-trivial for calls; small trivially copyable types come back in registers.
  • No elision for: by-value parameters (move), members and globals (copy), b ? lvalue : lvalue (copy), conversions to another type, anything wrapped in std::move.
  • -fno-elide-constructors shows the C++14 abstract machine; in C++17 it only affects the optional elisions (in practice NRVO), never prvalue initialisation.
  • Elision may skip constructors with side effects: an explicit exception to the as-if rule. Never put logic in a copy constructor that must run.
  • Named returns (NRVO) are still optional and are covered in Ch 24.

Part F · Move semantics and value passing · Chapter 24

NRVO

Named return value optimisation lets a compiler build a function's named local directly in the caller's storage, so T result; ...; return result; costs nothing. Unlike the unnamed case in Ch 23, NRVO is still optional, and when it does not happen the implicit move on return decides whether you pay a move or a full copy. Interviewers use it to test whether you can predict constructor counts, know when return std::move(x) hurts, and can restructure a function so the optimisation applies.

TheoryDrillsCoding· about 3 hours· prerequisites: Ch 20 (move semantics), Ch 23 (copy elision)

RVO versus NRVO

Theory

Mental model. A function that returns a class by value is handed the address of the caller's storage, the return slot (Ch 23). If the function builds its answer in a local variable, the compiler can decide to place that local in the return slot from the start. Every write to result is then a write to the caller's object, and return result; has nothing left to do.

RVO (unnamed)NRVO (named)
Shapereturn T(args);T r; ...; return r;
C++17 statusGuaranteed (prvalue semantics, not really an optimisation)Optional ([class.copy.elision]/1.1)
Needs a usable copy or move constructor?NoYes, even when elided
Disabled by -fno-elide-constructors in C++17?NoYes
Fallback when not appliedNone neededImplicit move, else copy

The term "RVO" is used loosely. Some people use it for both forms and say "URVO" (unnamed RVO) for the first. In an interview, say which one you mean, and say that only the unnamed one is guaranteed.

The conditions that allow NRVO

Theory

[class.copy.elision]/1.1 permits eliding the copy or move in a return statement when all of these hold:

  1. The returned expression is the name of an object (possibly parenthesised: return (r); also qualifies).
  2. That object has automatic storage duration: a local variable, not a static, global, member or array element.
  3. It is not a function parameter and not a catch-clause parameter.
  4. It is not volatile.
  5. Its type is the same class type as the function's return type, ignoring cv-qualifiers. A const T local returned from a function returning T qualifies.

The standard says nothing about multiple return statements. That part is the compiler's problem: it has to decide, when it allocates the local, whether that local can live in the return slot. It can only do so if every return that executes while the local is alive returns that local. If another path returns a different object while this one is still alive, both cannot occupy the slot.

Know this cold

The portable recipe: declare one local of the return type near the top of the function and return that name on every path. GCC and Clang then apply NRVO at every optimisation level, including -O0. Anything else is compiler-dependent.

Same type, ignoring cv

A local of a different type never qualifies, even if it converts. std::optional<T> f() { T t; return t; } must construct the optional from t, so the best you get is a move (the implicit move on return, next section). The same holds for std::unique_ptr<Base> returned from a std::unique_ptr<Derived> local, and for a base class returned from a derived local (that one also slices).

What GCC and Clang actually do

Theory

Because NRVO is optional, the honest answer to "is it elided?" is "check". The table below was produced by a tracing type (constructor, copy and move print) on GCC 16 and Clang 22 at -O1, C++20 unless stated. The column shows the operations between the local's construction and the caller's object.

Function bodyGCC 16Clang 22Notes
T r; return r;elidedelidedThe canonical case. Also at -O0.
T r; if (b) return r; r.v = 1; return r;elidedelidedSeveral returns of the same name are fine.
T a, c; if (b) return a; return c;movemoveTwo locals alive together: neither can be the slot.
if (b) { T a; return a; } else { T c; return c; }a elided, c movedboth elidedDisjoint scopes. Clang gives each local the slot; GCC gives it to one local per function.
if (b) { T a; return a; } T c; return c;a elided, c movedboth elidedSame as above; a switch with one local per case behaves the same way.
T a; if (b) { T c; return c; } return a;c elided, a movedc elided, a movedThe inner local gets the slot; the outer one cannot.
T a; if (b) return T(); return a;a moveda movedA prvalue return on another path stops NRVO for a.
T f(T p) { return p; }movemoveParameters are excluded by the standard.
auto [a, n] = pair; return a;movecopyA structured binding is not a variable; see below.
return h.member;, return global;, return local_static;copycopyNot automatic objects, so neither NRVO nor implicit move.
T& r = a; return r;, return arr[0];copycopyA reference or a subobject is not the local itself.
return b ? a : c;copycopyNot a name, so no NRVO and no implicit move.
T t; return std::move(t);movemoveNot a name any more: NRVO blocked. Both warn.

Structured bindings

The names introduced by auto [a, n] = ...; are not variables: they are names for parts of a hidden variable. The C++20 and C++23 wording of "implicitly movable entity" talks about variables, so returning a does not qualify, and Clang 22 copies. GCC 16 moves in C++20 and C++23 mode (and copies in C++17 mode). Neither compiler applies NRVO. If you need to return a binding cheaply, write return std::move(a);: here it is the right call, because NRVO was never possible, and neither compiler warns about it.

The implicit move on return: C++11, C++20, C++23

Theory

If NRVO does not happen, the copy is still avoided in most cases by the rule that a returned local is first treated as an rvalue. The rule has grown in three steps.

StandardRuleNew cases that move
C++11 (plus CWG1579 for C++14)If the operand names a local or parameter, overload resolution first treats it as an rvalue. In the original wording, this was used only if the chosen constructor's first parameter was an rvalue reference to the returned object's type.return local;, return param;; CWG1579 added converting constructors taking U&&, such as unique_ptr<Base> from a unique_ptr<Derived> local.
C++20, P1825 ("more implicit moves")Removes the "rvalue reference to the returned object's type" restriction and adds rvalue-reference variables.Returning a T&& local or parameter by name; constructors taking the source by value; slicing to a base (Base f() { Derived d; return d; } moves the base part); throw of a parameter.
C++23, P2266 ("simpler implicit move")A returned implicitly movable entity is simply an xvalue, with no two-phase overload resolution.Functions returning a reference: T&& f(T&& x) { return x; } now compiles; T& f(T&& x) { return x; } now fails.

Compilers treat parts of these changes as defect reports and apply them in older modes. Verified on GCC 16 and Clang 22:

  • Slicing a derived local to a base return type, and a converting constructor that takes its argument by value: both compilers move in every mode from C++14 on.
  • Returning an rvalue-reference parameter or local by name (T f(T&& r) { return r; }): Clang moves in every mode; GCC copies in C++14 and C++17 and moves from C++20. This is a real compiler difference in C++17 code.
  • T&& f(T&& x) { return x; }: rejected by both in C++20, accepted by both in C++23.
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <optional>
#include <string>

struct Base { virtual ~Base() = default; virtual const char* name() const { return "base"; } };
struct Derived : Base { const char* name() const override { return "derived"; } };

static std::unique_ptr<Base> make_base() {
    auto p = std::make_unique<Derived>();
    return p;                       // unique_ptr<Derived> -> unique_ptr<Base>: implicit move
}

static std::optional<std::string> lookup(bool found) {
    std::string s(40, 'x');         // longer than any small-string buffer
    if (!found) return std::nullopt;
    return s;                       // string -> optional<string>: implicit move
}

int main() {
    std::unique_ptr<Base> b = make_base();
    std::optional<std::string> o = lookup(true);
    std::printf("%s %zu %d\n", b->name(), o->size(), lookup(false).has_value());
}

derived 40 0

make_base would not compile if return p; tried to copy, because unique_ptr is move-only. That is the simplest proof that the implicit move happens through a converting constructor.

Why return std::move(local) is a pessimisation

Theory

return std::move(r); changes the operand from a name into an xvalue. NRVO requires a name, so it is now impossible: the local lives in the callee's frame and the caller's object is move-constructed from it. You traded zero operations for one move plus one destructor call, and for a type without a cheap move (a std::array, a struct of scalars, a small-buffer type) that move is a full copy of the bytes.

CodeEffectWarning
T r; return std::move(r);Blocks NRVO; forces a move-Wpessimizing-move (GCC: in -Wall; Clang: in -Wall)
T f(T p) { return std::move(p); }No effect: parameters move implicitly anyway-Wredundant-move (GCC: in -Wextra; Clang: in -Wall)
return std::move(T());Materialises a temporary, forces a move-Wpessimizing-move, "moving a temporary object"
return std::move(member_);Needed: members never move implicitlynone
return std::move(*this); in an &&-qualified memberNeedednone
T f(T&& r) { return std::move(r); }Needed for GCC in C++17 and earlier; redundant from C++20none from either compiler

Interview trap

"return std::move(x) is always safe, at worst redundant." Wrong for locals: it disables NRVO. The rule of thumb is: never std::move a local or a by-value parameter in a return; do std::move members, *this, structured bindings, and things you only hold by lvalue reference but own.

const locals and const return types

Theory

Two different uses of const interact with returns, and they fail in different ways.

A const local

T f() { const T r = build(); return r; } is still eligible for NRVO, because the types match ignoring cv. GCC and Clang elide it. But if NRVO fails (two const locals on different branches, or -fno-elide-constructors), the implicit move finds a const T rvalue, which cannot bind to T&&, so overload resolution picks the copy constructor. Making a local const silently turns the fallback from a move into a copy.

A const return type

const T f(); was once recommended (pre-C++11) to stop f() = x;. Today it is harmful:

  • T x = f(); is still fine: a prvalue of type const T initialises a T directly (same type ignoring cv), so nothing runs.
  • x = f(); calls the copy assignment operator, because a const T rvalue cannot bind to T&&.
  • v.push_back(f()); copies for the same reason, and std::move(f()) yields const T&&, which also copies.

GCC and Clang warn about const on scalar return types (-Wignored-qualifiers, in -Wextra), where it is meaningless, but neither warns for class types, where it does harm. Remove const from by-value return types.

-fno-elide-constructors, -O0 and debug builds

Theory

GCC and Clang decide NRVO in the front end (GCC in its C++ front end; Clang marks the NRVO candidate during semantic analysis and code generation then allocates it in the return slot), not in the optimiser. So the result does not depend on -O: every case in the table above prints the same at -O0 and -O1 on both compilers (checked). A debug build of a GCC or Clang program has the same constructor counts as the release build.

-fno-elide-constructors turns NRVO off. In C++17 and later it leaves prvalue initialisation alone, so its only visible effect on T r; return r; is one extra move:

$ g++-16 -std=c++17 -fno-elide-constructors nrvo.cpp   (Clang 22 identical)
ctor move dtor dtor           // T r; return r;  -> r constructed, moved into x
$ g++-16 -std=c++14 -fno-elide-constructors nrvo.cpp
ctor move dtor move dtor dtor // plus the C++14 move from the return temporary

MSVC behaves differently: it has historically applied NRVO only when optimising, and recent versions changed that behind a conformance switch. This guide's harness does not include MSVC, so treat any MSVC-specific claim as something to check against its current documentation (/Zc:nrvo) and on your own build. The portable conclusion is the same as before: never write code whose correctness depends on NRVO happening, only code whose speed benefits from it.

Tracing programs on both compilers

Theory

Interview answers about NRVO should come with a way to check them. Three techniques, from cheapest to most precise:

  1. A tracing type that prints or counts in its constructor, copy, move and destructor. Run it under both compilers. Count per call, because destructor placement of temporaries varies more than the counts do.
  2. Address identity. Record this in the constructor, then compare it with the caller's &x and print the boolean. If they are equal, the local was the caller's object. This avoids printing pointers.
  3. Delete the move constructor temporarily. If the function still compiles, every return path is a prvalue; if NRVO is what you rely on, it will not compile (NRVO needs a usable constructor). This proves which category you are in, not whether elision happened.
#include <cstdio>

struct T {
    static const T* last;
    int v = 0;
    T() { last = this; }
    T(const T& o) : v(o.v) { last = this; }
    T(T&& o) noexcept : v(o.v) { last = this; }
};
const T* T::last = nullptr;

static const T* inner = nullptr;

static T one_local(int n) {
    T r;
    inner = &r;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) r.v += i;
    return r;
}

static T two_locals(bool b) {
    T a, c;
    inner = b ? &a : &c;
    return b ? T(a) : T(c);    // explicit copies: a prvalue, but never the local
}

int main() {
    T x = one_local(4);
    std::printf("one_local: local is x: %d, v=%d\n", inner == &x, x.v);
    T y = two_locals(true);
    std::printf("two_locals: local is y: %d, y built in place: %d\n", inner == &y, T::last == &y);
}

one_local: local is x: 1, v=6
two_locals: local is y: 0, y built in place: 1

inner == &x is true only because NRVO placed r in x. Printing it is safe here because both GCC and Clang elide this canonical shape; in general such a program has compiler-dependent output, which is exactly the point being tested.

Concept and tricky questions

Drills

ConceptWhat is the difference between RVO and NRVO, and which is guaranteed in C++17?

Answer

Answer. RVO (unnamed) is return T(args);: a prvalue initialises the caller's object, guaranteed since C++17 and needing no copy or move constructor. NRVO is T r; return r;: the compiler may place r in the return slot, but it is still optional and the copy or move constructor must be usable.

Why. P0135 made prvalues initialisers without storage, which covers the unnamed case. A named local is an object with its own lifetime that the compiler would have to prove can share storage with the result, so the standard leaves it as permission in [class.copy.elision]/1.1. "Both are guaranteed since C++17" is the common wrong answer.

ConceptList the conditions under which the standard permits NRVO.

Answer

Answer. The return operand is the (possibly parenthesised) name of a non-volatile object with automatic storage duration, which is not a function or catch parameter, whose type is the same class as the return type ignoring cv-qualifiers.

Why. Each condition guarantees the compiler controls where the object lives: statics and members live elsewhere, parameters are allocated by the caller, and a different type cannot share storage with the result. Nothing in the standard mentions how many returns there are; that limitation is practical, because only one object can occupy the slot at a time.

TrickyT a, c; if (b) return a; return c;: is NRVO applied? Is it a copy? How do you fix it?

Answer

Answer. No NRVO on GCC 16 or Clang 22, but no copy either: each return moves. To get NRVO, restructure so only one object is alive at a return: declare one result and fill it according to b, or give each branch its own scope with its own local.

Why. When a and c are both alive, the compiler must choose their storage before it knows which will be returned, and only one can be the return slot. The implicit move on return still treats each name as an rvalue. Saying "it copies" confuses this with return b ? a : c;, which does copy.

Trickyif (b) { T a; return a; } else { T c; return c; }: the two locals are never alive together. Do GCC and Clang elide both returns?

Answer

Answer. Clang 22 elides both. GCC 16 elides a but moves c. The same split appears with a fall-through (if (b) { T a; return a; } T c; return c;) and with a switch that has one local per case.

Why. NRVO is possible for both locals because their lifetimes do not overlap. Clang's analysis works per scope and lets each local take the slot in turn. GCC's picks a single local per function to place in the return slot (in these tests, the one in the first return statement) and treats the others as ordinary locals, which are then moved by the implicit-move rule. Both outcomes conform because NRVO is optional. If you need NRVO on every compiler, use one result variable for the whole function. Verified at -O0, -O1 and -O2.

ConceptWhat is the implicit move on return, and what did C++20 (P1825) and C++23 (P2266) change?

Answer

Answer. When return x; names an automatic local or parameter, the compiler first tries to initialise the result as if x were an rvalue, so it moves instead of copying. C++20 removed the restriction that the selected constructor take an rvalue reference to x's own type and added rvalue-reference variables (T&& r). C++23 replaced the two-step lookup with "the name is an xvalue", which makes T&& f(T&& x) { return x; } legal and T& f(T&& x) { return x; } ill-formed.

Why. The aim each time was to move from anything that is about to die. The C++11 wording missed converting constructors with by-value parameters, base-class slicing, and rvalue references. Compilers back-port much of this: GCC 16 and Clang 22 move when slicing to a base even in C++14 mode, while for T&& parameters GCC waits for C++20 and Clang does not.

TrickyWhen is return std::move(x); correct, and when is it harmful?

Answer

Answer. Harmful for a local of the return type: it blocks NRVO and forces a move (-Wpessimizing-move). Redundant for a by-value parameter (-Wredundant-move). Correct for a data member, *this in an rvalue-qualified member function, a structured binding, an object held through an lvalue reference that you own, and (before C++20, for GCC) an rvalue-reference parameter.

Why. NRVO and the implicit move both only apply to a plain name of an implicitly movable entity. Members, references and bindings are not such names, so without std::move they are copied. Locals and parameters already move implicitly, so wrapping them gains nothing and for locals loses the elision.

TrickyTo stop accidental moves, a class keeps its copy constructor and declares C(C&&) = delete;. Does C f() { C c; return c; } compile? Does C g() { return C(); }?

Answer

Answer. f does not compile in any standard mode; GCC 16 and Clang 22 both report the deleted move constructor. g compiles from C++17 on (and fails in C++14).

Why. NRVO is optional, so return c; must be valid as if the move happened. The implicit move performs overload resolution with c as an rvalue, and C(C&&) is the best match. A deleted function still takes part in overload resolution, so it is selected, and selecting a deleted function makes the program ill-formed; the compiler does not fall back to the copy constructor, because the fallback only happens when overload resolution fails. return C(); is a prvalue and needs no constructor at all in C++17. The usual wrong answer is "it falls back to the copy". If you want a copyable type that never moves, leave the move constructor undeclared (a user-declared copy constructor already suppresses the implicit one) instead of deleting it: then the rvalue binds to C(const C&).

TrickyWhat do these return, and which one is a bug? decltype(auto) a() { std::string s = "x"; return s; } and decltype(auto) b() { std::string s = "x"; return (s); }

Answer

Answer. a returns std::string by value (eligible for NRVO). b returns a reference to the dead local s, a dangling reference: std::string& in C++20 and std::string&& in C++23. Both compilers warn (-Wreturn-local-addr in GCC, -Wreturn-stack-address in Clang).

Why. decltype(auto) deduces the type with decltype rules. decltype(s) is the declared type, std::string, but decltype((s)) is the type of an expression, which for an lvalue is T&. In C++23, P2266 makes a returned movable name an xvalue, so the parentheses deduce T&& instead, still dangling. With a plain return type std::string or auto, return (s); is harmless and still eligible for NRVO, which is why people think parentheses never matter.

ConceptDoes making the returned local const prevent NRVO?

Answer

Answer. No, NRVO still applies, because the type matches ignoring cv-qualifiers, and GCC and Clang elide it. But the fallback changes: if NRVO is not applied, the const object cannot be moved from, so it is copied.

Why. The implicit move treats the name as an rvalue of type const T; T(T&&) cannot bind to it, so T(const T&) wins. With two const locals returned on different branches, both compilers print a copy (reading drill 5). Make locals const only if they are not returned.

TrickyWhat does declaring a return type const std::vector<int> f(); cost?

Answer

Answer. Nothing for auto v = f(); (still constructed in place), but every assignment v = f(); and every push_back(f()) copies instead of moving.

Why. A const T prvalue initialising a T is still same-type initialisation. Once it is materialised to bind to a reference, it is an xvalue of type const T, which cannot bind to T&& and only binds to const T&, so copy assignment and copy construction are chosen. No warning catches this for class types. The old advice (Scott Meyers, pre-C++11) to return const values is obsolete.

TrickyA function does auto [key, value] = parse(line); return value;. Is value moved?

Answer

Answer. It depends on the compiler. Clang 22 copies it in every mode. GCC 16 moves it in C++20 and C++23 and copies in C++17. Neither applies NRVO. Write return std::move(value); to get a move everywhere.

Why. Structured binding names refer to subobjects of a hidden variable; they are not variables themselves, and the implicit-move rule speaks of variables. GCC chose to treat them as movable. This is one of the few places where std::move in a return is the right fix, and neither compiler warns about it.

ConceptDo GCC and Clang apply NRVO in a -O0 debug build? What switches it off?

Answer

Answer. Yes. Both decide NRVO in the front end, so -O0 and -O2 give the same constructor counts. -fno-elide-constructors switches NRVO off (and in C++14 mode also the prvalue elisions).

Why. Elision changes which object a name refers to, which must be known when the variable's storage is allocated, before any optimisation pass. Verified for every case in this chapter at -O0 and -O1. MSVC has a different history (NRVO tied to optimisation, later a conformance flag) that this guide has not tested.

TrickyWhy does std::unique_ptr<Base> f() { auto p = std::make_unique<Derived>(); return p; } compile, given that p is an lvalue and unique_ptr cannot be copied?

Answer

Answer. Because of the implicit move on return: p is treated as an rvalue, and unique_ptr<Base>'s converting constructor from unique_ptr<Derived>&& is selected.

Why. NRVO is impossible (different type). In the original C++11 wording the implicit move only counted if the constructor took an rvalue reference to the returned object's own type, so this was a copy attempt and failed; CWG1579 (applied to C++14 and by compilers as a fix) allowed converting constructors, and C++20 P1825 generalised it further. Writing return std::move(p); is not needed.

Predict the output and find the bug

Drills

OutputOne local, several returns of it, and a lambda. Count the operations.

#include <cstdio>

struct T {
    int v = 0;
    T() { std::puts("ctor"); }
    T(const T&) { std::puts("copy"); }
    T(T&&) noexcept { std::puts("move"); }
    ~T() { std::puts("dtor"); }
};

static T build(bool early) {
    T r;
    if (early) return r;
    r.v = 42;
    return r;
}

int main() {
    std::puts("-early"); { T x = build(true); }
    std::puts("-late");  { T x = build(false); std::printf("%d\n", x.v); }
    auto lam = [] { T r; r.v = 7; return r; };
    std::puts("-lambda"); { T x = lam(); std::printf("%d\n", x.v); }
}

-early
ctor
dtor
-late
