Answer. One constructor per call, no copies or moves, on both GCC 16 and Clang 22.

Why. Every path returns the same named local, so the compiler places r in the caller's x. Multiple return statements are not a problem as long as they all name the same object. A lambda's body is an ordinary function body, so the same applies.

OutputTwo locals, one returned per branch, and a nested scope.

#include <cstdio>

struct T {
    int v;
    explicit T(int x) : v(x) { std::printf("ctor %d\n", v); }
    T(const T& o) : v(o.v) { std::printf("copy %d\n", v); }
    T(T&& o) noexcept : v(o.v) { std::printf("move %d\n", v); }
    ~T() { std::printf("dtor %d\n", v); }
};

static T either(bool b) {
    T a(1), c(2);
    if (b) return a;
    return c;
}

static T nested(bool b) {
    T outer(3);
    if (b) {
        T inner(4);
        return inner;
    }
    return outer;
}

int main() {
    std::puts("-either"); { T x = either(false); }
    std::puts("-nested true"); { T x = nested(true); }
    std::puts("-nested false"); { T x = nested(false); }
}
Answer
-either
ctor 1
ctor 2
move 2
dtor 2
dtor 1
dtor 2
-nested true
ctor 3
ctor 4
dtor 3
dtor 4
-nested false
ctor 3
move 3
dtor 3
dtor 3

Answer. either: no NRVO, c is moved. nested(true): inner is built directly in x, no move. nested(false): outer is moved.

Why. In either both locals are alive at the returns, so neither gets the slot, and the implicit move applies. In nested, inner's whole lifetime is inside the branch, and while it is alive the only return is return inner;, so both compilers give it the slot. outer cannot have it too, because it is alive while inner is using it. Note that dtor 3 prints before dtor 4 in the second block: outer dies when nested returns, while inner is x.

OutputDisjoint scopes written two ways, each called so that the second local is returned. This output is for GCC 16; what does Clang 22 print?

#include <cstdio>

struct T {
    T() { std::puts("ctor"); }
    T(const T&) { std::puts("copy"); }
    T(T&&) noexcept { std::puts("move"); }
    ~T() { std::puts("dtor"); }
};

static T if_else(bool b) {
    if (b) { T a; return a; }
    else   { T c; return c; }
}

static T fall_through(bool b) {
    if (b) { T a; return a; }
    T c;
    return c;
}

int main() {
    std::puts("-if_else");      { T x = if_else(false); }
    std::puts("-fall_through"); { T x = fall_through(false); }

-if_else

Answer. GCC 16 moves c in both functions. Clang 22 elides both, printing only ctor and dtor for each block. Called with true, both compilers elide a.

Why. In both functions a and c are never alive at the same time, so NRVO is possible for each. Clang assigns the return slot per scope. GCC places only one local per function in the slot, the one in the first return statement, so c lives in the callee's frame and is moved out by the implicit move. Because NRVO is optional, both results conform. A single result variable gets NRVO on both compilers.

Find the bugThe author wanted to "help the compiler". Predict the output and fix it.

#include <array>
#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>

struct Frame {
    std::array<double, 512> samples{};
    Frame() { std::puts("ctor"); }
    Frame(const Frame&) { std::puts("copy"); }
    Frame(Frame&&) noexcept { std::puts("move (4 KB memcpy)"); }
    ~Frame() { std::puts("dtor"); }
};

static Frame capture() {
    Frame f;
    f.samples[0] = 1.5;
    return std::move(f);
}

int main() {
    Frame f = capture();
    std::puts("done");
}
Answer
ctor
move (4 KB memcpy)
dtor
done
dtor

Answer. std::move(f) blocks NRVO, so a 4 KB move (which for a std::array is a copy of every element) and an extra destructor run. Fix: return f;, which prints ctor, done, dtor.

Why. NRVO requires the operand to be the name of the local; std::move(f) is an xvalue expression. Both GCC 16 and Clang 22 warn at -Wall: "moving a local object in a return statement prevents copy elision" (-Wpessimizing-move). For types with inline storage, "move" is not cheaper than copy, so the only way to make returning free is elision.

OutputTwo const locals and a single const local. Watch the fallback.

    return c;
}

Answer. Member, global and reference: copies. By-value parameter: a move. The first ctor is the global g, and the last dtor is g at program exit.

Why. NRVO and the implicit move both need the name of an automatic object (local or, for the move, parameter). h.member is a subobject, g has static storage, and r is a reference, so each is an lvalue and is copied. Use return std::move(h.member); when the holder is about to die. The parameter is moved implicitly but never elided.

Find the bugThis forwarding helper compiles in C++23 but the project builds with -std=c++20. Why does it fail there, and what is the portable fix?

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

static std::string&& pass_through(std::string&& s) {
    s += "!";
    return s;          // C++20: s is an lvalue here
}

int main() {
    std::string a = "hi";
    std::string b = pass_through(std::move(a));
    std::printf("%s\n", b.c_str());
}
Answer

Answer. In C++20 the name s is an lvalue, and an rvalue reference return type cannot bind to an lvalue. The implicit move only applied to initialising a returned object, not a returned reference. C++23 (P2266) makes a returned implicitly movable entity an xvalue, so the code compiles there. The portable fix is return std::move(s);.

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

static std::string&& pass_through(std::string&& s) {
    s += "!";
    return s;          // C++23: s is an xvalue in a return statement
}

int main() {
    std::string a = "hi";
    std::string b = pass_through(std::move(a));
    std::printf("%s\n", b.c_str());
}

hi!

Why. GCC 16 says "cannot bind rvalue reference of type 'std::string&&' to lvalue" and Clang 22 says "rvalue reference to type ... cannot bind to lvalue" in C++20 mode; both accept it in C++23. The flip side of P2266: std::string& f(std::string&& s) { return s; } compiles in C++20 and fails in C++23, because an xvalue cannot bind to a non-const lvalue reference.

OutputReturning a structured binding. This output is for Clang 22; what does GCC 16 print in C++20 mode, and how do you make them agree?

#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>

struct T {
    T() { std::puts("ctor"); }
    T(const T&) { std::puts("copy"); }
    T(T&&) noexcept { std::puts("move"); }
    ~T() { std::puts("dtor"); }
};

static std::pair<T, int> parse() { return {}; }

static T first() {
    auto [value, code] = parse();
    (void)code;
    return value;
}

int main() {
    T x = first();
    std::puts("done");
}
Answer
ctor
copy
dtor
done
dtor

Answer. Clang 22 copies. GCC 16 prints move instead of copy in C++20 and C++23 (and copy in C++17). Writing return std::move(value); gives a move on both, with no warning.

Why. value names a member of the hidden pair object, not a variable, so it is not an implicitly movable entity under the standard wording that Clang follows. NRVO is impossible either way, since the returned object is a subobject. The dtor after copy is the hidden pair being destroyed when first returns.

OutputA const return type, used for initialisation and for assignment.

#include <cstdio>

struct T {
    T() { std::puts("ctor"); }
    T(const T&) { std::puts("copy"); }
    T(T&&) noexcept { std::puts("move"); }
    T& operator=(const T&) { std::puts("copy="); return *this; }
    T& operator=(T&&) noexcept { std::puts("move="); return *this; }
    ~T() { std::puts("dtor"); }
};

static const T make() { T t; return t; }

int main() {
    std::puts("-init");   T x = make();
    std::puts("-assign"); x = make();
    std::puts("-end");
}
Answer
-init
ctor
-assign
ctor
copy=
dtor
-end
dtor

Answer. Initialisation is free (NRVO into x). The assignment calls copy=, not move=.

Why. make() is a prvalue of type const T. Initialising a T from it is same-type initialisation, and inside make NRVO places t in the slot. For the assignment, the prvalue is materialised as a const T temporary, which cannot bind to T&&, so copy assignment is selected. Drop the const from the return type to get move=.

OutputAn rvalue-reference parameter and an rvalue-reference local, returned by name in C++20.

#include <cstdio>

struct T {
    T() { std::puts("ctor"); }
    T(const T&) { std::puts("copy"); }
    T(T&&) noexcept { std::puts("move"); }
    ~T() { std::puts("dtor"); }
};

static T make() { return T(); }
static T from_param(T&& r) { return r; }
static T from_local() { T&& r = make(); return r; }

int main() {
    std::puts("-param"); { T x = from_param(T()); }
    std::puts("-local"); { T x = from_local(); }
}
Answer
-param
ctor
move
dtor
dtor
-local
ctor
move
dtor
dtor

Answer. Both move in C++20 on GCC 16 and Clang 22.

Why. C++20 (P1825) made rvalue-reference variables implicitly movable. In -std=c++17 the compilers disagree: GCC 16 prints copy for both functions, while Clang 22 already moves, applying the change as a fix to older modes. If your code must be portable to C++17, write return std::move(r); for rvalue references; it is not a pessimisation, because a reference is never eligible for NRVO.

Write the code

Coding

CodeThe function below returns one of two locals and is called in a hot loop. Rewrite it so NRVO applies on both GCC and Clang, and prove it with a counting type that asserts zero copies and zero moves for both values of the flag.

Report summarise(const std::vector<int>& xs, bool detailed) {
    Report brief;  brief.title = "brief";  brief.total = sum(xs);
    Report full;   full.title = "full";    full.total = sum(xs);  full.rows = xs;
    if (detailed) return full;
    return brief;
}
Answer

Approach. Two live locals rule out NRVO. Declare a single Report r, fill the common parts, branch only on what differs, and return r on every path. That also stops computing work for the branch you throw away. The test type counts copies and moves in static counters, and the test checks both flag values.

#include <cstdio>
#include <numeric>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

static int copies = 0, moves = 0;

struct Report {
    std::string title;
    long total = 0;
    std::vector<int> rows;
    Report() = default;
    Report(const Report& o) : title(o.title), total(o.total), rows(o.rows) { ++copies; }
    Report(Report&& o) noexcept : title(std::move(o.title)), total(o.total), rows(std::move(o.rows)) { ++moves; }
};

static Report summarise(const std::vector<int>& xs, bool detailed) {
    Report r;
    r.total = std::accumulate(xs.begin(), xs.end(), 0L);
    if (detailed) {
        r.title = "full";
        r.rows = xs;
        return r;
    }
    r.title = "brief";
    return r;
}

int main() {
    std::vector<int> xs{1, 2, 3, 4};
    for (bool detailed : {false, true}) {
        copies = moves = 0;
        Report r = summarise(xs, detailed);
        std::printf("%s total=%ld rows=%zu copies=%d moves=%d %s\n", r.title.c_str(), r.total,
                    r.rows.size(), copies, moves, copies == 0 && moves == 0 ? "PASS" : "FAIL");
    }
}

brief total=10 rows=0 copies=0 moves=0 PASS
full total=10 rows=4 copies=0 moves=0 PASS

Complexity and pitfalls. O(n) for the sum and the optional row copy (that copy is of the vector, not of the Report, so it is not counted). Keep exactly one Report object in the function; a return Report{} on an error path would block NRVO for r on GCC and Clang (both move r then), so return r in a cleared state instead.

Estimated rating: ~1300 · simple refactor once you know that one live local is the condition compilers check

CodeWrite a header-only tracing type Traced and an RAII checker ExpectOps that records the copy and move counts at construction and, at destruction, prints PASS or FAIL against expected numbers. Use it to document, as executable tests, five return patterns: single local, two locals, by-value parameter, data member, and return std::move(local).

Answer

Approach. Static counters in Traced; ExpectOps snapshots them in its constructor and compares the difference in its destructor. Each test is a block that creates an ExpectOps and then calls the function, so the check happens at the closing brace after all temporaries are gone. Only patterns that GCC and Clang handle identically are asserted.

#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>

struct Traced {
    static inline int copies = 0, moves = 0;
    Traced() = default;
    Traced(const Traced&) { ++copies; }
    Traced(Traced&&) noexcept { ++moves; }
};

class ExpectOps {
public:
    ExpectOps(const char* what, int c, int m)
        : what_(what), want_c_(c), want_m_(m), c0_(Traced::copies), m0_(Traced::moves) {}
    ~ExpectOps() {
        int c = Traced::copies - c0_, m = Traced::moves - m0_;
        std::printf("%s %-14s copies=%d moves=%d\n", c == want_c_ && m == want_m_ ? "PASS" : "FAIL", what_, c, m);
    }
private:
    const char* what_;
    int want_c_, want_m_, c0_, m0_;
};

struct Box { Traced t; };

static Traced single()               { Traced r; return r; }
static Traced two(bool b)            { Traced a, c; if (b) return a; return c; }
static Traced param(Traced p)        { return p; }
static Traced member()               { Box b; return b.t; }
#pragma GCC diagnostic ignored "-Wpessimizing-move"
static Traced moved()                { Traced r; return std::move(r); }

int main() {
    { ExpectOps e("single", 0, 0);       Traced x = single(); }
    { ExpectOps e("two locals", 0, 1);   Traced x = two(true); }
    { ExpectOps e("param", 0, 1);        Traced x = param(Traced()); }
    { ExpectOps e("member", 1, 0);       Traced x = member(); }
    { ExpectOps e("std::move(local)", 0, 1); Traced x = moved(); }
}

PASS single         copies=0 moves=0
PASS two locals     copies=0 moves=1
PASS param          copies=0 moves=1
PASS member         copies=1 moves=0
PASS std::move(local) copies=0 moves=1

Complexity and pitfalls. Constant overhead. Declare ExpectOps before the call in each block so that its destructor runs last (locals die in reverse order). The #pragma silences the deliberate pessimising move on both compilers (Clang honours GCC diagnostic pragmas). Do not add the disjoint-scope fall-through or structured-binding patterns to a portable suite: GCC and Clang differ there.

Estimated rating: ~1400 · small RAII test fixture; the hard part is predicting each count correctly

CodeWrite a fluent RequestBuilder that supports both RequestBuilder b; b.url(...).header(...); Request r = b.build(); (builder reusable, so build copies) and Request r = RequestBuilder().url(...).header(...).build(); (temporary builder, zero copies of the request). Prove the second chain does not copy the Request.

Answer

Approach. Overload on the builder's value category with ref-qualifiers. Setters on an lvalue builder return RequestBuilder&; setters on an rvalue builder return RequestBuilder&& so the chain stays an rvalue. build() const & returns a copy of the stored request; build() && returns std::move(req_), which is necessary because req_ is a member and would otherwise be copied. A counter in Request checks the result.

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

static int req_copies = 0, req_moves = 0;

struct Request {
    std::string url;
    std::vector<std::string> headers;
    Request() = default;
    Request(const Request& o) : url(o.url), headers(o.headers) { ++req_copies; }
    Request(Request&& o) noexcept : url(std::move(o.url)), headers(std::move(o.headers)) { ++req_moves; }
};

class RequestBuilder {
public:
    RequestBuilder& url(std::string u) & { req_.url = std::move(u); return *this; }
    RequestBuilder&& url(std::string u) && { req_.url = std::move(u); return std::move(*this); }
    RequestBuilder& header(std::string h) & { req_.headers.push_back(std::move(h)); return *this; }
    RequestBuilder&& header(std::string h) && { req_.headers.push_back(std::move(h)); return std::move(*this); }

    Request build() const & { return req_; }              // copy: the builder stays usable
    Request build() && { return std::move(req_); }        // member: std::move is required
private:
    Request req_;
};

int main() {
    Request a = RequestBuilder().url("https://x.test").header("A: 1").header("B: 2").build();
    std::printf("temp builder: %s headers=%zu copies=%d moves=%d\n",
                a.url.c_str(), a.headers.size(), req_copies, req_moves);

    req_copies = req_moves = 0;
    RequestBuilder b;
    b.url("https://y.test").header("C: 3");
    Request r1 = b.build();
    Request r2 = b.header("D: 4").build();
    std::printf("reused builder: %zu %zu copies=%d moves=%d\n",
                r1.headers.size(), r2.headers.size(), req_copies, req_moves);
}

temp builder: https://x.test headers=2 copies=0 moves=1
reused builder: 1 2 copies=2 moves=0

Complexity and pitfalls. The temporary chain costs one Request move (a few pointer writes) and no copies; the move cannot be elided because the source is a member, not a local. Returning RequestBuilder&& from setters means auto&& b = RequestBuilder().url(...); dangles after the statement; document that the temporary chain must end in build(). Returning RequestBuilder by value instead is safer but moves the whole builder at each step.

Estimated rating: ~1700 · ref-qualified overloads and knowing that members need an explicit std::move

CodeWrite partition_by_sign(const std::vector<Item>&) that returns two lists, the negatives and the non-negatives, as one object, with zero copies of the result object and no copies of Item beyond the one per input element. Compare it with a version that builds two locals and returns {neg, pos}, and show the counts.

Answer

Approach. return {neg, pos}; list-initialises the result from two lvalues, which copies both vectors (and every Item in them). The implicit move does not apply because the operand is a braced list, not a name. Two good fixes: return {std::move(neg), std::move(pos)};, or (better) declare the result struct as the single local, fill its members directly, and return it by name so NRVO applies.

#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

static int item_copies = 0;

struct Item {
    int v;
    explicit Item(int x) : v(x) {}
    Item(const Item& o) : v(o.v) { ++item_copies; }
    Item(Item&&) noexcept = default;
    Item& operator=(const Item&) = default;
    Item& operator=(Item&&) noexcept = default;
};

struct Split {
    std::vector<Item> neg, pos;
};

static Split split_copying(const std::vector<Item>& in) {
    std::vector<Item> neg, pos;
    for (const Item& i : in) (i.v < 0 ? neg : pos).push_back(i);
    return {neg, pos};                         // copies both vectors
}

static Split split_nrvo(const std::vector<Item>& in) {
    Split out;
    for (const Item& i : in) (i.v < 0 ? out.neg : out.pos).push_back(i);
    return out;                                // single local: NRVO
}

int main() {
    std::vector<Item> in;
    for (int x : {-3, 5, -1, 0, 7}) in.emplace_back(x);

    item_copies = 0;
    Split a = split_copying(in);
    std::printf("copying: neg=%zu pos=%zu item copies=%d\n", a.neg.size(), a.pos.size(), item_copies);

    item_copies = 0;
    Split b = split_nrvo(in);
    std::printf("nrvo:    neg=%zu pos=%zu item copies=%d\n", b.neg.size(), b.pos.size(), item_copies);
}

copying: neg=2 pos=3 item copies=10
nrvo:    neg=2 pos=3 item copies=5

Complexity and pitfalls. O(n) both ways, but the copying version doubles the element copies (5 to fill the locals plus 5 to copy them into the result). Vector growth inside push_back moves items rather than copying them because the move constructor is noexcept; without noexcept, reallocation would copy and the counts would rise (Ch 20). Call reserve if you know the sizes.

Estimated rating: ~1500 · spotting that a braced return of lvalues copies, and fixing it with a single named result

CodeWrite choose(bool prefer_fast, ...) that computes two candidate plans of a move-only type Plan (it owns a std::unique_ptr) and returns the better one without copying. Then write a variant that returns std::unique_ptr<PlanBase> from a local std::unique_ptr<FastPlan>, with no std::move in any return statement.

Answer

Approach. Both candidates must exist before choosing, so NRVO is out. Because Plan is move-only, any copy would be a compile error, which proves there are none; the implicit move on return a; / return b; moves the winner. The second variant relies on the converting move constructor of unique_ptr being picked by the implicit move. A counter records the moves.

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

static int plan_moves = 0;

class Plan {
public:
    Plan(std::string name, int cost) : name_(std::move(name)), cost_(std::make_unique<int>(cost)) {}
    Plan(Plan&& o) noexcept : name_(std::move(o.name_)), cost_(std::move(o.cost_)) { ++plan_moves; }
    Plan(const Plan&) = delete;
    int cost() const { return *cost_; }
    const std::string& name() const { return name_; }
private:
    std::string name_;
    std::unique_ptr<int> cost_;
};

static Plan choose(bool prefer_fast, int n) {
    Plan fast("fast", n * 2);
    Plan cheap("cheap", n + 10);
    if (prefer_fast || fast.cost() <= cheap.cost()) return fast;   // implicit move
    return cheap;                                                  // implicit move
}

struct PlanBase { virtual ~PlanBase() = default; virtual const char* kind() const = 0; };
struct FastPlan : PlanBase { const char* kind() const override { return "FastPlan"; } };

static std::unique_ptr<PlanBase> make_plan() {
    auto p = std::make_unique<FastPlan>();
    return p;                                                      // unique_ptr<FastPlan> -> unique_ptr<PlanBase>
}

int main() {
    Plan a = choose(false, 20);
    Plan b = choose(true, 20);
    std::printf("%s %d, %s %d, moves=%d\n", a.name().c_str(), a.cost(), b.name().c_str(), b.cost(), plan_moves);
    std::unique_ptr<PlanBase> p = make_plan();
    std::printf("%s\n", p->kind());
}

cheap 30, fast 40, moves=2
FastPlan

Complexity and pitfalls. One move per call, which for Plan is two pointer-sized moves. Writing return prefer_fast ? fast : cheap; would not compile: the conditional is an lvalue, so it needs the deleted copy constructor. Do not make the candidates const, or the implicit move cannot bind and the code again needs a copy.

Estimated rating: ~1300 · using a move-only type as a compile-time proof that the return path never copies

Cheat sheet

Theory
  • RVO (return T(...);) is guaranteed in C++17; NRVO (T r; return r;) is optional and needs a usable copy or move constructor.
  • NRVO needs the plain name of a non-parameter, non-volatile automatic local of the return type (cv ignored). Portable recipe: one result local, returned by name on every path.
  • Compilers differ: two live locals give a move on both; with locals in disjoint scopes Clang elides every one, GCC only the first returned; structured bindings are copied by Clang and moved by GCC (C++20 and later).
  • If NRVO fails, a returned local, parameter, or (C++20) rvalue-reference variable is moved, including through conversions (unique_ptr<Derived> to unique_ptr<Base>, T to optional<T>). Members, globals, references and ?: expressions are copied.
  • Never return std::move(local) (-Wpessimizing-move) or std::move(param) (-Wredundant-move). Do std::move members, *this and structured bindings.
  • const locals keep NRVO but turn the fallback into a copy; const return types make assignments copy. Avoid both for returned values.
  • C++23 (P2266): a returned movable name is an xvalue, so T&& f(T&& x) { return x; } compiles and T& f(T&& x) { return x; } breaks.
  • GCC and Clang apply NRVO at -O0; -fno-elide-constructors disables it. Check claims with a tracing type on both compilers.

Part G · Mixed practice · Chapter 25

Miscellaneous tricky questions

Real interviews rarely stay inside one topic. A question about a lambda turns into a question about thread lifetime, a framing bug turns into one about struct padding, and a constructor reads a parameter it has already moved from. This chapter is a bank of those cross-topic traps, grouped by theme, with every program compiled on GCC and Clang and every bug proven by a sanitizer where one can see it.

DrillsCoding· about 5 hours· prerequisites: chapters 1 to 24, or the confidence to be caught out

OOP and object model traps

Drills

These questions look like inheritance trivia, but each one hides a rule about object layout, construction phases or name lookup. Background is in Ch 1, Ch 2 and Ch 3.

Find the bugEach feed registers a tick callback in its constructor. After the second emplace_back, the first feed's callback misbehaves. Why?

#include <cstdio>
#include <functional>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class Feed {
public:
    explicit Feed(std::string name) : name_(std::move(name)) {
        on_tick = [this](double px) { std::printf("tick %.2f for a %zu-char feed\n", px, name_.size()); };
    }
    std::function<void(double)> on_tick;

private:
    std::string name_;
};

int main() {
    std::vector<Feed> feeds;
    feeds.emplace_back("XNAS-primary-equities-feed");
    feeds.emplace_back("XLON-primary-equities-feed");  // grows: feeds[0] is moved
    feeds[0].on_tick(101.25);
}
Answer

Answer. The lambda captures this, the address of the object under construction. When the vector grows from capacity 1 to 2, it move-constructs feeds[0] into the new buffer and frees the old one. The implicit move constructor moves on_tick as a value, so the new object's callback still holds the old address, and calling it reads name_ from freed memory. ASan reports heap-use-after-free. Without ASan it prints a plausible line, here a 0-character name, purely by luck.

Why. Implicit copy and move copy member values, and a value that points back into the object itself (a captured this, a self-pointer, an iterator into one of its own members) is stale in the copy. The same happens on any relocation: std::sort, std::swap, or returning the object without elision. The usual wrong answer blames std::function, which copied the lambda correctly. Fixes: pass the object to the callback instead of capturing it (std::function<void(Feed&, double)>); or make the class non-copyable and non-movable and keep it in a container that never relocates (std::deque, std::list, std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Feed>>); or rebind the callback in hand-written copy and move constructors. Capturing this in a thread or timer callback has the same lifetime problem (Ch 4).

OutputA non-virtual helper calls a virtual function. What does each phase print?

#include <cstdio>

struct Base {
    Base() { hello("ctor"); }
    virtual ~Base() { hello("dtor"); }
    void hello(const char* when) const { std::printf("%s: %s\n", when, name()); }
    virtual const char* name() const { return "Base"; }
};

struct Derived : Base {
    Derived() { hello("Derived ctor"); }
    ~Derived() override { hello("Derived dtor"); }
    const char* name() const override { return "Derived"; }
};

int main() {
    Derived d;
    d.hello("main");
}
Answer
ctor: Base
Derived ctor: Derived
main: Derived
Derived dtor: Derived
dtor: Base

Why. During Base's constructor and destructor the object's dynamic type is Base ([class.cdtor]). The implementation makes this real by storing Base's vptr while the base constructor runs, switching to Derived's vptr once Derived's constructor starts, and switching back when ~Derived finishes. Calling through a helper does not get around it, because the helper reads the same vptr.

The common wrong answer is "ctor: Derived", from candidates who know Java or C#, where the override runs before the derived fields are initialised. C++ refuses to call into a derived part that does not exist yet (or no longer exists). If a base needs derived-specific setup, pass the data to the base constructor or use a two-phase factory.

OutputPredict all four sizes on a 64-bit Linux or macOS target. Two of them surprise most candidates.

#include <cstdio>

struct Plain  { long long x; char a; };
struct PlainD : Plain { char c; };

struct Poly  { virtual void f() {} char a; };
struct PolyD : Poly { char c; };

int main() {
    std::printf("Plain=%zu PlainD=%zu Poly=%zu PolyD=%zu\n",
                sizeof(Plain), sizeof(PlainD), sizeof(Poly), sizeof(PolyD));
}
Answer
Plain=16 PlainD=24 Poly=16 PolyD=16

Why. Plain is 8 + 1 bytes padded to 16, and Poly is an 8-byte vptr plus one char, also padded to 16. Both have 7 bytes of tail padding. The difference is what a derived class may do with those bytes. The Itanium C++ ABI (used by GCC and Clang on Linux and macOS) never reuses the tail padding of a base that is a POD in the C++03 sense, so PlainD::c goes at offset 16 and the class grows to 24. Poly is polymorphic and therefore not a POD, so its tail padding is fair game: PolyD::c sits at offset 9 and the size stays 16.

The rule exists because C code may memcpy a whole POD, padding included, which would overwrite a derived member living in that padding. The practical lesson: never memcpy or memset a base subobject with sizeof(Base), because for non-POD bases the derived class may own those bytes. MSVC uses a different ABI and gives different numbers, so say "on Itanium" when you answer. See Ch 1 for basic padding rules.

OutputA C library takes a callback and a void* context, and the strategy registers itself. What do the first two lines print on a 64-bit GCC or Clang target, and why would the callback crash without the second c_register?

#include <cstdio>

struct Logger {
    virtual ~Logger() = default;
    int level = 1;
};

struct Listener {
    virtual ~Listener() = default;
    virtual void on_event(int e) = 0;
};

struct Strategy : Logger, Listener {
    void on_event(int e) override { std::printf("event %d\n", e); }
};

// A C library stores a callback and an opaque context pointer.
static void (*g_cb)(void*, int);
static void* g_ctx;
static void c_register(void (*cb)(void*, int), void* ctx) { g_cb = cb; g_ctx = ctx; }

static void trampoline(void* ctx, int e) { static_cast<Listener*>(ctx)->on_event(e); }

int main() {
    Strategy s;
    c_register(trampoline, &s);  // Strategy* converted straight to void*
    Listener* good = &s;
    Listener* bad = static_cast<Listener*>(g_ctx);
    std::printf("offset of Listener: %td\n", reinterpret_cast<char*>(good) - reinterpret_cast<char*>(&s));
    std::printf("round trip correct: %d\n", bad == good);
    c_register(trampoline, static_cast<Listener*>(&s));  // the fix
    g_cb(g_ctx, 7);
}
Answer
offset of Listener: 16
round trip correct: 0
event 7

Why. Converting Strategy* to Listener* adjusts the address to the Listener subobject, which follows the Logger part (a vptr plus an int, padded to 16 bytes). Converting to void* does no adjustment: it is the address of the whole object, which is also the address of its Logger part. static_cast<Listener*>(void*) cannot know where the pointer came from, so bad points at the Logger subobject. Calling on_event through it loads Logger's vptr and calls whatever sits in that slot of Logger's vtable: undefined behaviour, in practice a crash or a call to the wrong function.

The rule: a round trip through void* is valid only when you cast back to exactly the type you converted from. So convert to the type the callback expects before erasing it, as the last c_register does. The wrong answer is "static_cast fixes up base offsets": it does so only between related class types, never from void*. With single inheritance the offset is 0 and the bug is invisible, so it appears the day someone adds a base class. The same applies to the arg of pthread_create, epoll_event.data.ptr and every C "user data" pointer.

TrickyTwo processes map the same shared memory region. The writer constructs a Quote there with placement new. Quote has a virtual price() and a std::string venue. The reader casts the region to Quote* and calls price(). What happens?

Answer

Answer. Undefined behaviour, and in practice a crash or garbage. The object contains pointers that only mean something in the writer: the vptr (the address of Quote's vtable in the writer's mapping of the executable) and the string's data pointer (into the writer's heap, or with SSO into the object at the writer's mapping address). With ASLR, the reader maps the executable and the shared region at different addresses, so the virtual call jumps through a wrong address and reading venue dereferences someone else's heap. It "works" when the reader is a forked child of the writer, or ASLR is off, which is exactly how such code passes its tests.

Why. std::is_trivially_copyable_v<Quote> is false: a class with virtual functions never has a trivial copy constructor, and that is the language telling you its bytes are not a self-contained value. Shared memory, files and network buffers need trivially copyable types without pointers: integers, fixed-size char arrays, offsets instead of pointers (as Boost.Interprocess's offset_ptr does), and an enum tag instead of a vptr, with each process dispatching on the tag itself. The reader also never created an object: for implicit-lifetime types, C++23's std::start_lifetime_as is the sanctioned way to say "treat these bytes as a T". A mutex or atomic placed in shared memory has its own rules (PTHREAD_PROCESS_SHARED, lock-free atomics only, Ch 5).

OutputA dispatch table stores pointers to member functions. Is a call through &Venue::name virtual? And how big is the pointer?

#include <cstdio>

struct Venue {
    virtual ~Venue() = default;
    virtual const char* name() const { return "venue"; }
};

struct Nasdaq : Venue {
    const char* name() const override { return "nasdaq"; }
};

int main() {
    Nasdaq n;
    const Venue& v = n;
    const char* (Venue::*pick)() const = &Venue::name;
    std::printf("%s\n", (v.*pick)());
    std::printf("%s\n", v.Venue::name());
    std::printf("%zu\n", sizeof(pick));
}
Answer
nasdaq
venue
16

Why. A pointer to a virtual member function does not store an address of Venue::name. It stores "call vtable slot k", so calling it through any object dispatches virtually and reaches Nasdaq::name. The qualified call v.Venue::name() is the one way to suppress virtual dispatch, and it is how an override calls the base version. On the Itanium ABI a member function pointer is two words: a function address or vtable offset, and a this adjustment needed for multiple inheritance. On x86-64 the low bit of the first word marks the virtual case; ARM64 cannot use that bit, so it moves the flag into the adjustment word. That is why it is 16 bytes, cannot be cast to void*, and why std::function or a lambda is usually a simpler table entry. MSVC uses sizes from 8 to 24 bytes depending on the inheritance model.

Find the bugThe program uses a smart pointer, so it must be safe. What does it print, and is it correct?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <string>

struct Message {
    ~Message() { std::puts("~Message"); }
};

struct Quote : Message {
    std::string symbol = "a symbol long enough to live on the heap";
    ~Quote() { std::puts("~Quote"); }
};

int main() {
    std::unique_ptr<Message> m = std::make_unique<Quote>();
}
Answer

Answer. It typically prints only ~Message, and the behaviour is undefined. unique_ptr<Message> uses default_delete<Message>, which runs delete on a Message*. Deleting a derived object through a base pointer whose destructor is not virtual is undefined ([expr.delete]). In practice ~Quote never runs and the heap buffer of symbol leaks.

Fix. Give Message a virtual destructor, or a protected non-virtual one so that deletion through the base does not compile. Two traps live here: the converting constructor from unique_ptr<Quote> compiles without complaint, and GCC's -Wdelete-non-virtual-dtor stays quiet because Message has no virtual functions at all. shared_ptr behaves differently, because it captures the deleter when the first owner is created (Ch 11).

Find the bugWhy does this clone() override fail to compile, and what is the idiomatic fix?

#include <memory>

struct Shape {
    virtual ~Shape() = default;
    virtual std::unique_ptr<Shape> clone() const = 0;
};

struct Circle : Shape {
    std::unique_ptr<Circle> clone() const override { return std::make_unique<Circle>(*this); }
};

int main() {
    Circle c;
    auto p = c.clone();
    return p ? 0 : 1;
}
Answer

Answer. Covariant return types only work for raw pointers and references to classes ([class.virtual]). unique_ptr<Circle> and unique_ptr<Shape> are unrelated class types, even though one converts to the other, so the override's return type is invalid.

Fix. Return std::unique_ptr<Shape> from every override, which is enough in most code. If callers need the precise type, keep a private virtual Circle* clone_impl() const (raw pointers are covariant) and give each class a public non-virtual clone() that wraps it in the right unique_ptr. Many candidates think templates or auto can make the override work. They cannot, because virtual functions cannot be templates and an override cannot have a deduced return type.

Memory and allocation traps

Drills

Lifetime, ownership and the gap between "allocated" and "constructed". Background is in Ch 9, Ch 11 and Ch 14.

OutputHow big is each closure on a 64-bit GCC or Clang target? What does the size of by_ref tell you?

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>

int main() {
    int qty = 100, side = 1;
    double px = 101.25;
    std::string venue = "XNAS";
    auto none = [] { return 0; };
    auto by_ref = [&qty, &side] { return qty * side; };
    auto by_val = [qty, side] { return qty * side; };
    auto mixed = [side, px] { return side * px; };
    auto owns = [venue] { return venue.size(); };
    std::printf("none=%zu by_ref=%zu by_val=%zu mixed=%zu owns_string=%d\n", sizeof none, sizeof by_ref,
                sizeof by_val, sizeof mixed, sizeof owns == sizeof(std::string));
    return none() + by_ref() + by_val() + static_cast<int>(mixed() + owns()) > 0 ? 0 : 1;
}
Answer
none=1 by_ref=16 by_val=8 mixed=16 owns_string=1

Why. A lambda is an unnamed class with one data member per captured entity ([expr.prim.lambda.capture]). With no captures it is an empty class of size 1, because every object needs a distinct address. Two ints take 8 bytes, and int plus double is padded to 16 by alignment. A by-value std::string capture holds a whole std::string (32 bytes in libstdc++ and 24 in libc++, which is why the program compares instead of printing). The layout of reference captures is unspecified, but GCC and Clang store one pointer per reference, so by_ref is two pointers. The wrong answers are "0, references are free" and "8, the size of two ints".

Two consequences. A by-reference closure is a bundle of pointers into the current stack frame, so storing it beyond the frame (in a std::function, a thread or a callback list) is the returned-pointer-to-a-local bug in disguise. And size decides allocation: libstdc++'s std::function stores a closure inline only if it is trivially copyable and at most 16 bytes, and libc++ allows somewhat larger nothrow-movable closures. Anything bigger is heap-allocated on construction and on every copy (Ch 18).

Find the bugA hot path duplicates quotes with memcpy "because it is faster than the copy constructor". It prints the right line. What happens next?

#include <cstdio>
#include <cstring>
#include <string>

struct Quote {
    std::string symbol;
    double px = 0;
};

int main() {
    Quote a{"a symbol name long enough to need the heap", 101.25};
    Quote b;
    std::memcpy(&b, &a, sizeof a);
    std::printf("%s %.2f\n", b.symbol.c_str(), b.px);
}
Answer

Answer. A double free when main returns. memcpy copied the string object's bytes, including the pointer to its heap buffer, so a.symbol and b.symbol both own the same buffer and both destructors free it. ASan reports attempting double-free. The print is correct, which is why the bug survives code review.

Why. memcpy and memset are valid only for trivially copyable types ([basic.types.general]). Quote has a std::string member, so its copy is a real function that allocates. With a short symbol the bug changes shape: libstdc++ strings in SSO mode point at their own inline buffer, so b.symbol would point into a and break as soon as a changes or dies. GCC warns with -Wclass-memaccess, and the warning is right. If the copy is genuinely hot, make the type trivially copyable: store the symbol as a fixed char[8] or a small integer id, then static_assert(std::is_trivially_copyable_v<Quote>), and plain assignment compiles to the same memcpy anyway.

OutputThe same three lines are written for vector<bool> and for vector<int>. What prints?

#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<bool> flags{true, true};
    auto f = flags[0];
    flags[0] = false;

    std::vector<int> nums{1, 1};
    auto n = nums[0];
    nums[0] = 0;

    std::printf("%d %d\n", static_cast<int>(f), n);
}
Answer
0 1

Why. vector<bool> is a specialisation that packs bits, so operator[] cannot return bool&. It returns a proxy object, vector<bool>::reference, that holds a word pointer and a bit mask. auto f deduces that proxy type, so f still refers to bit 0 and sees the later write. For vector<int>, auto n is a plain int copy.

Other consequences: bool* p = &flags[0]; does not compile, flags.data() does not exist, and two threads writing different elements race because they share a word (unlike every other vector<T>). Write bool f = flags[0]; to get a value. If you need real bools, use std::vector<char>, std::deque<bool> or std::unique_ptr<bool[]>.

OutputA buffer is passed to a function that "takes an array of 16 ints". What are the three sizes?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>

static void fill(int buf[16]) { std::printf("inside %zu\n", sizeof(buf)); }

template <std::size_t N>
static void fill_ref(int (&buf)[N]) { std::printf("ref %zu\n", sizeof(buf)); }

int main() {
    int data[16] = {};
    std::printf("outside %zu\n", sizeof(data));
    fill(data);
    fill_ref(data);
}
Answer
outside 64
inside 8
ref 64

Why. A function parameter declared as an array is adjusted to a pointer ([dcl.fct]), and the 16 is ignored completely. Inside fill, buf is an int*, so sizeof gives the pointer size. Passing a reference to an array keeps the type and lets a template deduce N. In networking code this bug looks like recv(fd, buf, sizeof buf, 0) inside a helper, which silently reads 8 bytes at a time. Both compilers warn (-Wsizeof-array-argument). Pass std::span<int> to carry the size explicitly.

TrickyA host loads a pricing plugin with dlopen, gets a std::unique_ptr<Pricer> from its factory, and unloads the plugin with dlclose during reconfiguration. The process crashes later, when the unique_ptr goes out of scope. Why there?

Answer

Answer. The object outlives the code that defines it. Its vptr points at a vtable inside the plugin, and its virtual destructor is code inside the plugin. Once dlclose unmaps the library, deleting the object jumps into unmapped memory (a SIGSEGV) or into whatever was mapped there since. Any function pointer, std::function target, string literal or type_info that came from the plugin dangles in the same way. dlclose has also run the plugin's static destructors, so plugin globals the object relies on are gone.

Why. Code must outlive every object that uses it, so the library handle needs an owner too. Fixes: return std::shared_ptr<Pricer> whose deleter captures a shared_ptr to the library handle (the library is closed by the last object's deleter); destroy every plugin object before calling dlclose; or never unload (RTLD_NODELETE, which many production systems choose). The crash can depend on the build, because glibc may decline to unmap a library at all, for example when it defines STB_GNU_UNIQUE symbols, which GCC emits for some inline and template statics. The wrong answer blames unique_ptr: any owner would crash, because the bug is the order of two lifetimes.

OutputOrder has a class-specific operator new that counts pool allocations. Which of the three factories go through it?

#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <new>

struct Order {
    static inline int pool_allocs = 0;
    long id = 0;
    static void* operator new(std::size_t n) {
        ++pool_allocs;
        return ::operator new(n);
    }
    static void operator delete(void* p) { ::operator delete(p); }
};

int main() {
    std::unique_ptr<Order> a(new Order);
    std::printf("new: %d\n", Order::pool_allocs);
    auto b = std::make_unique<Order>();
    std::printf("make_unique: %d\n", Order::pool_allocs);
    auto c = std::make_shared<Order>();
    std::printf("make_shared: %d\n", Order::pool_allocs);
}
Answer
new: 1
make_unique: 2
make_shared: 2

Why. make_unique<Order>() is defined as unique_ptr<Order>(new Order()), so the class-specific operator new is found by the new-expression. make_shared needs one block that holds the control block and the object, so it allocates that block through std::allocator (which calls ::operator new) and constructs Order inside it with placement new. The class's allocator is bypassed completely. In a trading system that relies on class-level pools to avoid the global heap on the hot path, a single make_shared quietly reintroduces malloc.

Fixes: use std::allocate_shared with an allocator that draws from the same pool (it must allocate the combined block, so its size is larger than sizeof(Order)), or use std::shared_ptr<Order>(new Order) and accept the separate control block allocation, which still goes to the global heap. Pool design is covered in Ch 15.

TrickyLegacy code does auto* p = static_cast<Order*>(std::malloc(sizeof(Order))); p->symbol = "AAPL"; where Order has a std::string member. It "works" in testing. What is actually happening?

Answer

Answer. Undefined behaviour. malloc returns raw bytes, and no Order or std::string object exists there. p->symbol = "AAPL" calls string::operator= on garbage: it reads an uninitialised data pointer and size, and may free or write through a random address. It seems to work when the bytes happen to look like an empty short string.

Why. Allocation and construction are separate steps. new does both, malloc does only the first. The fix is placement new, Order* p = new (mem) Order;, and later p->~Order(); std::free(mem); (Ch 14). C++20 lets malloc implicitly create objects of implicit-lifetime types (trivial types such as int arrays or plain structs, P0593), which is why the same code is fine for a struct of ints. A class with a std::string member is not implicit-lifetime.

Move semantics, forwarding and elision traps

Drills

Most of these programs compile cleanly and silently copy. Background is in Ch 20 to Ch 24.

Find the bugThe constructor moves the symbol into the member and records its width for column alignment. Every width prints as 0. Why, and why does swapping the two initialisers in the list not help?

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

class Instrument {
public:
    explicit Instrument(std::string symbol)
        : symbol_(std::move(symbol)), width_(symbol.size()) {}
    void show() const { std::printf("symbol=%s width=%zu\n", symbol_.c_str(), width_); }

private:
    std::string symbol_;
    std::size_t width_;
};

int main() {
    Instrument("VOD.L").show();
    Instrument("BRK.A-long-composite-symbol-name").show();
}
Answer
symbol=VOD.L width=0
symbol=BRK.A-long-composite-symbol-name width=0

Answer. Members are initialised in declaration order, so symbol_ comes first, and its initialiser moves from the parameter. When width_(symbol.size()) runs, symbol is a moved-from string. That is "valid but unspecified", and both libstdc++ and libc++ leave it empty, for short (SSO) and long strings alike. Reordering the mem-initialisers in the source changes nothing, because the order is fixed by the member declarations ([class.base.init]). GCC and Clang warn with -Wreorder when the two orders differ, which is the only hint you get.

Fix. Read from the member, which already exists: width_(symbol_.size()), correct only because symbol_ is declared first. Or compute from the parameter before any move, or move in the constructor body. The rule: once a parameter appears inside std::move in an initialiser list, it must not appear again later in that list. clang-tidy's bugprone-use-after-move catches it. The same declaration-order rule decides when a std::thread member starts running relative to the members it uses.

Trickystd::vector<std::atomic<int>> slots(8); compiles and works as a table of per-venue counters. Someone adds slots.resize(16) and the build breaks. Why does one compile and not the other, and what are the options?

#include <atomic>
#include <deque>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<std::atomic<int>> slots(8);  // fine: elements built in place
    std::deque<std::atomic<int>> more;
    more.emplace_back(1);                     // fine: a deque never relocates
    slots.resize(16);                         // error: needs to move elements
    return slots[0] + more[0];
}
Answer

Answer. std::atomic can be neither copied nor moved. The size constructor only value-initialises elements in place, which atomic supports. resize, reserve, push_back, emplace_back and insert may reallocate, and reallocation relocates the existing elements by moving or copying them, so these members require the element type to be MoveInsertable. The check is at compile time, so the build fails even if the capacity would have sufficed. std::mutex, std::condition_variable and any class holding one behave the same way.

Why. It is also the right outcome for threads: relocating an atomic while other threads use it can never be made safe. Options: size the table once and never grow it; use std::deque<std::atomic<int>> with emplace_back, which only constructs in place because a deque never relocates existing elements; use std::unique_ptr<std::atomic<int>[]>; or wrap each atomic in a struct with a copy constructor that loads and stores, which is safe only while no other thread is touching the table. For per-thread counters, also pad each slot to a cache line (Ch 19). The wrong answer is "atomic has no default constructor": it has one, and since C++20 it value-initialises the value (P0883).

OutputWhich overload does each call pick?

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

static void take(const std::string&) { std::puts("lvalue"); }
static void take(std::string&&) { std::puts("rvalue"); }

int main() {
    std::string&& r = std::string("tmp");
    take(r);
    take(std::move(r));
    take(static_cast<decltype(r)>(r));
    auto&& fwd = r;
    take(std::forward<decltype(fwd)>(fwd));
}
Answer
lvalue
rvalue
rvalue
lvalue

Why. A named variable is an lvalue whatever its declared type, so take(r) picks the const& overload even though r is an rvalue reference. decltype(r) is std::string&&, so the cast produces an xvalue, which is all std::move does. auto&& fwd = r binds a forwarding reference to the lvalue r, so fwd's type is std::string& and std::forward returns an lvalue. The answer "rvalue" for the last line comes from forgetting that forwarding preserves the category of the initialiser, and r as an expression is an lvalue.

OutputOrders move from a pending std::set to a send queue, first with std::move on the element and then through extract. Count the copies and moves.

#include <cstdio>
#include <iterator>
#include <set>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Order {
    static inline int copies = 0, moves = 0;
    std::string id;
    explicit Order(const char* s) : id(s) {}
    Order(const Order& o) : id(o.id) { ++copies; }
    Order(Order&& o) noexcept : id(std::move(o.id)) { ++moves; }
    bool operator<(const Order& o) const { return id < o.id; }
};

int main() {
    std::set<Order> pending;
    pending.emplace("ord-0001-with-a-long-client-tag");
    pending.emplace("ord-0002-with-a-long-client-tag");
    std::vector<Order> sent;
    sent.reserve(2);

    sent.push_back(std::move(*pending.begin()));
    std::printf("move from set element: copies=%d moves=%d\n", Order::copies, Order::moves);

    auto node = pending.extract(std::next(pending.begin()));
    sent.push_back(std::move(node.value()));
    std::printf("move from extracted node: copies=%d moves=%d\n", Order::copies, Order::moves);
    std::printf("set size=%zu\n", pending.size());
}
Answer
move from set element: copies=1 moves=0
move from extracted node: copies=1 moves=1
set size=1

Why. Elements of a std::set (and keys of a std::map) are const, because changing one in place would break the tree's ordering. *pending.begin() is a const Order&, std::move turns it into const Order&&, and that binds only to the copy constructor. So the first "move" is a silent copy, and the element also stays in the set. C++17's extract unlinks the node and returns a node handle that owns it, and node.value() gives non-const access, so the second move really moves. The common wrong answer is "copies=0 moves=2": std::move never casts away const.

Node handles have two more uses interviewers like: other.insert(std::move(node)) transfers an element between sets or maps without allocating, and auto nh = m.extract(k); nh.key() = k2; m.insert(std::move(nh)); changes a map key in place. The same trap appears in for (auto& [k, v] : m) out.push_back(std::move(k));, which copies every key while really moving every value.

Find the bugThe lambda owns the order through an init-capture and should hand it back. Why does it not compile?

#include <memory>
#include <utility>

int main() {
    auto order = std::make_unique<int>(42);
    auto task = [o = std::move(order)]() { return std::move(o); };
    auto back = task();
    return *back == 42 ? 0 : 1;
}
Answer

Answer. A lambda's operator() is const unless the lambda is mutable, so inside the body o is a const std::unique_ptr<int>. std::move(o) yields const unique_ptr&&, which can only bind to the deleted copy constructor. Both compilers report a call to a deleted function.

Fix. Write [o = std::move(order)]() mutable { return std::move(o); }. This is the lambda version of the const-member trap, where a move silently becomes a copy (Ch 20). With a copyable type such as std::string it would compile and silently copy instead of failing, which is worse. A lambda holding a unique_ptr is move-only, so it cannot be stored in std::function. Use C++23 std::move_only_function or a template parameter.

ConceptWhat does std::swap(a, b) cost for a type with a copy constructor and no move constructor, and why do libraries provide a member swap or a hidden friend?

Answer

Answer. The generic std::swap is T tmp = std::move(a); a = std::move(b); b = std::move(tmp);. With no move operations, all three steps copy, so swapping two large buffers costs three deep copies and two allocations. A type-specific swap exchanges the internal pointers in O(1) and cannot throw.

Why. Generic code calls using std::swap; swap(a, b); so argument-dependent lookup finds a better overload in the type's namespace (a hidden friend is found only that way, which keeps overload sets small). A noexcept swap is the building block for copy-and-swap assignment and for the strong exception guarantee. With a proper noexcept move constructor and move assignment, the generic version is already cheap, and a custom swap only saves a few pointer writes.

Threads and locks traps

Drills

Ownership questions turn into concurrency questions as soon as a second thread can see the object. Background is in Ch 4, Ch 5 and Ch 6.

Find the bugEvery access to status_ holds the mutex, yet ThreadSanitizer reports a race. Where is the unprotected access?

#include <cstdio>
#include <mutex>
#include <string>
#include <thread>

class Session {
public:
    const std::string& status() const {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(m_);
        return status_;
    }
    void set_status(std::string s) {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(m_);
        status_ = std::move(s);
    }

private:
    mutable std::mutex m_;
    std::string status_ = "connecting";
};

int main() {
    Session s;
    std::thread writer([&] {
        for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) s.set_status(i % 2 ? "logged-in-and-streaming-quotes" : "heartbeat-overdue-reconnecting");
    });
    std::size_t total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) total += s.status().size();
    writer.join();
    std::printf("%d\n", total > 0);
}
Answer

Answer. status() returns a reference, and its lock_guard is released when the function returns. The caller reads the string (here size(), in real code a copy or a log line) after the unlock, while the writer may be move-assigning a new value into it and freeing the old buffer. The read is unprotected: a data race, and with long strings a possible use after free. TSan reports the race between the move assignment and the read.

Fix. Return by value (std::string status() const copies under the lock), or offer with_status(f) that runs f under the lock, or publish immutable snapshots as std::shared_ptr<const std::string>. A lock protects the accesses made inside its scope, and references, pointers, iterators and string_views that escape the scope escape the protection with them. The wrong answer blames the mutable mutex, which is correct and necessary for a const getter. The Synchronized exercise below has the same pitfall.

TrickyThis function crashes rarely, and only in production. The shared_ptr is supposed to keep feed alive. What is wrong?

void start(std::shared_ptr<Feed> feed) {
    std::thread([&feed] { feed->run(); }).detach();
}
Answer

Answer. The lambda captures the parameter feed by reference. No copy of the shared_ptr is made, so the reference count never goes up. start returns, the parameter is destroyed, and the detached thread later reads a dangling reference to a dead shared_ptr object on a stack frame that has been reused. If that was the last owner, the Feed is gone as well.

Why. It works most of the time because the new thread usually reads feed before start returns. Capture by value, [feed] or [feed = std::move(feed)], so the thread owns a reference. The member-function version of this bug is [this] in a lambda given to a thread or a timer: capture self = shared_from_this() instead. Also question the detach(): a detached thread that touches globals can still be running while static destructors run after main returns.

Find the bugDouble-checked locking: the fast path avoids the lock and the slow path checks again under it. What is wrong?

#include <cstdio>
#include <mutex>
#include <thread>

struct Registry { int ready = 42; };

static Registry* instance = nullptr;
static std::mutex mtx;

static Registry* get() {
    if (!instance) {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mtx);
        if (!instance) instance = new Registry;
    }
    return instance;
}

int main() {
    int a = 0, b = 0;
    std::thread t1([&] { a = get()->ready; });
    std::thread t2([&] { b = get()->ready; });
    t1.join();
    t2.join();
    std::printf("%d %d\n", a, b);
}
Answer

Answer. The unlocked read of instance races with the locked write. A reader that sees a non-null pointer on the fast path never takes the mutex, so nothing orders its reads of *instance after the writer's construction of the Registry. The compiler or CPU may publish the pointer before the ready = 42 store, and on ARM or POWER the reader can see the pointer and still read a stale ready. TSan reports the race on instance.

Fix. The simplest correct singleton is a function-local static: static Registry r; return &r;. Since C++11 its initialisation is thread-safe, and compilers implement it with exactly this double-check, done correctly with an acquire load of a guard byte. If you need the pointer form, make instance a std::atomic<Registry*>, load it with memory_order_acquire and store it with memory_order_release, or use std::call_once. The coding section has the atomic version. Saying "x86 is strongly ordered, so it is fine" is wrong twice: the compiler may reorder the stores, and the race is undefined behaviour on every architecture.

TrickyA server keeps per-request state (the client id and a scratch buffer) in thread_local variables. It worked with one thread per connection. After a move to a fixed thread pool, logs sometimes show the wrong client id and memory keeps growing. What changed?

Answer

Answer. A thread_local lives as long as its thread, not as long as the task. With a thread per connection, the thread's exit reset everything. In a pool, each thread runs many unrelated requests, so a task that does not overwrite the id (an error path, an early return, an exception before the assignment) logs the previous client's id. Scratch buffers keep their peak capacity forever, in every pool thread, so one 100 MB request pins 100 MB per thread that ever served one.

Why. The variable is perfectly thread-safe, which is why the wrong answer "thread_local is not thread-safe" misses. The bug is scope. Tie request state to the request: pass a context object explicitly, or set it with an RAII guard at task start that restores it in its destructor, exceptions included. Shrink or cap scratch buffers after large requests. C++20 coroutines make thread_local request state actively wrong, because a coroutine may resume on a different thread after co_await. Pool threads usually live until shutdown, so their thread_local destructors run then, and leak checkers report the memory as still reachable rather than leaked.

TrickyA read-mostly cache uses std::shared_mutex. On a miss, the reader, still holding its std::shared_lock, calls lock() on the same mutex to insert the value. Under load the service hangs. Why, and what is the correct pattern?

Answer

Answer. std::shared_mutex has no upgrade operation. lock() waits until every shared owner has released, including the calling thread itself, which never will: a self-deadlock. The standard makes locking a mutex you already own undefined behaviour, and in practice it hangs. Even a real upgrade would deadlock two readers upgrading at the same time, each waiting for the other's shared hold, which is why Boost's upgrade_mutex allows only one upgradable owner at a time.

Why. The correct pattern: release the shared lock, take a std::unique_lock, check again (another thread may have inserted the value in the gap), then insert. Better still, compute the value with no lock held and insert it with try_emplace under the exclusive lock, keeping whichever copy arrived first. The wrong answer is "writer starvation": this hang has nothing to do with fairness and happens with a single thread. For very hot reads, remember that every lock_shared still writes the mutex's cache line, so snapshot publication (the Published<T> exercise in Ch 26) or RCU scales better.

OutputOrders are published to three venues "in parallel" with std::async, and the futures are discarded. Venue 0 is the slowest. In what order do the lines appear, and how long does the loop take?

#include <chrono>
#include <cstdio>
#include <future>
#include <thread>

static void publish(int venue) {
    std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(20 * (3 - venue)));
    std::printf("published to venue %d\n", venue);
}

int main() {
    for (int v = 0; v < 3; ++v)
        (void)std::async(std::launch::async, publish, v);  // "fire and forget"
    std::puts("all sent");
}
Answer
published to venue 0
published to venue 1
published to venue 2
all sent

Why. The future returned by std::async with launch::async blocks in its destructor until the task has finished ([futures.async]). The discarded temporary dies at the end of each full expression, so every iteration waits for its own task and the loop is sequential: 60 + 40 + 20 = 120 ms. If the tasks really ran in parallel, venue 2 (20 ms) would print first and the loop would take about 60 ms. The (void) cast silences the [[nodiscard]] warning that recent standard libraries attach to std::async, but not the blocking.

Fix: keep the futures in a vector and wait for them after the loop, or submit to a thread pool. Two more traps: with the default policy (launch::async | launch::deferred) the library may defer the task, which then runs only if someone calls get or wait; and only futures from std::async block in the destructor, while those from std::promise or std::packaged_task do not, so the same-looking code behaves differently.

OutputFour threads each do 100000 increments with memory_order_relaxed. Can increments be lost?

#include <atomic>
#include <cstdio>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::atomic<long> hits{0};
    std::vector<std::thread> ts;
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i)
        ts.emplace_back([&hits] {
            for (int k = 0; k < 100000; ++k) hits.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
        });
    for (auto& t : ts) t.join();
    std::printf("%ld\n", hits.load());
}
Answer
400000

Why. Atomicity and ordering are separate properties. Every atomic read-modify-write is indivisible and sees the latest value in the variable's modification order, whatever memory order you pass ([atomics.order]). relaxed only drops the guarantees about other memory locations, so it is the right choice for statistics counters. The final load() after join() is ordered by the joins. What relaxed cannot do is publish data: if a thread writes a buffer and then sets a relaxed flag, another thread can see the flag and stale buffer contents.

Networking traps

Drills

Socket bugs hide because loopback tests deliver everything at once. Background is in Ch 7 and Ch 8.

Find the bugFrames are a 4-byte big-endian length followed by the payload. The reader works on every local test. Here the sender's second segment is still in flight. What does the reader return?

#include <arpa/inet.h>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <unistd.h>

static std::string naive_read_frame(int fd) {
    uint32_t len_be = 0;
    recv(fd, &len_be, sizeof len_be, 0);
    uint32_t len = ntohl(len_be);
    std::string payload(len, '\0');
    ssize_t n = recv(fd, payload.data(), len, 0);
    std::printf("asked %u, got %zd\n", len, n);
    return payload;
}

int main() {
    int sv[2];
    if (socketpair(AF_UNIX, SOCK_STREAM, 0, sv) != 0) return 1;
    const char msg[] = "NEW AAPL 100@189.25";
    uint32_t len_be = htonl(sizeof msg - 1);
    send(sv[0], &len_be, sizeof len_be, 0);
    send(sv[0], msg, 8, 0);  // the rest has not arrived yet
    std::string got = naive_read_frame(sv[1]);
    std::printf("payload \"%.8s\", last byte %d\n", got.c_str(), got.back());
    close(sv[0]);
    close(sv[1]);
}
Answer
asked 19, got 8
payload "NEW AAPL", last byte 0

Answer. A blocking recv returns as soon as some data is available, up to the size you asked for. It got 8 of 19 bytes, the code ignored the count, and the frame was handed on with 11 zero bytes at the end. The next call would then parse " 100@189" as a length header, and the stream is desynchronised for good. The first recv of the header has the same bug: a 4-byte header can arrive as 1 + 3.

Why. TCP is a byte stream. Segment boundaries, the sender's send calls and the receiver's recv calls are unrelated, and loopback hides this because small writes arrive in one piece. Fix it with a read_exact loop that keeps calling recv until the requested count arrives, returns failure on 0 (peer closed mid-frame) and retries on EINTR. Ch 8 builds the full send_all/recv_exact pair and a framer on top of it. Also check len against a maximum before allocating, or a hostile peer can send 0xFFFFFFFF.

TrickyA gateway uses select and has run for months. A configuration change raises the number of client connections past about a thousand, and it starts crashing in unrelated code, or aborting with *** buffer overflow detected ***. Why?

Answer

Answer. An fd_set is a fixed bitmap of FD_SETSIZE bits, 1024 on glibc. FD_SET(fd, &set) with fd of 1024 or more writes past the end of the object, usually on the stack, and corrupts whatever lives next to it: an OS limit turning into memory corruption. When the program is built with _FORTIFY_SOURCE, glibc checks the descriptor inside FD_SET and FD_ISSET and aborts with that message, which is the kind outcome. Because descriptors are allocated lowest-free first, the first connection to get number 1024 triggers it, even if few of the others are still active.

Why. select cannot wait on a descriptor numbered 1024 or above at all, so the fix is poll or epoll, which take arrays or registrations with no limit on descriptor values (Ch 8). Raising ulimit -n is what exposes the bug, and redefining FD_SETSIZE is not supported by glibc. "select is slow with many descriptors" is true but does not explain a crash.

TrickyA client connects to a primary gateway whose address is firewalled, so packets are silently dropped. connect blocks for about two minutes and then fails with ETIMEDOUT. Connecting to a reachable host with nothing listening fails at once with ECONNREFUSED. Explain both, and how you bound the wait.

Answer

Answer. A reachable host with a closed port answers the SYN with RST, so connect fails within one round trip. A black-holed address answers nothing, so Linux retransmits the SYN with exponential backoff: an initial timeout of 1 s and net.ipv4.tcp_syn_retries = 6 retries give 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 + 32 + 64 = 127 s before ETIMEDOUT. An ICMP unreachable from a router produces EHOSTUNREACH or ENETUNREACH quickly instead.

Why. To bound the wait, use a non-blocking connect: set O_NONBLOCK, expect EINPROGRESS, poll for POLLOUT with your own timeout, then read getsockopt(SO_ERROR), because writability alone does not mean success. On Linux, TCP_SYNCNT lowers the retry count per socket, and SO_SNDTIMEO also limits a blocking connect. For failover, start the backup attempt after a short delay instead of waiting for the first to fail, which is what Happy Eyeballs (RFC 8305) does for IPv6 and IPv4. Wrong answers: "SO_RCVTIMEO limits it" (it does not apply to connect) and "connect times out after 75 s" (an old BSD figure).

OutputA connection log line prints the source and destination addresses. What do the two lines print?

#include <arpa/inet.h>
#include <cstdio>

int main() {
    in_addr a{}, b{};
    inet_pton(AF_INET, "10.0.0.1", &a);
    inet_pton(AF_INET, "192.168.1.20", &b);

    const char* src = inet_ntoa(a);
    const char* dst = inet_ntoa(b);
    std::printf("%s -> %s\n", src, dst);

    char s1[INET_ADDRSTRLEN], s2[INET_ADDRSTRLEN];
    inet_ntop(AF_INET, &a, s1, sizeof s1);
    inet_ntop(AF_INET, &b, s2, sizeof s2);
    std::printf("%s -> %s\n", s1, s2);
}
Answer
192.168.1.20 -> 192.168.1.20
10.0.0.1 -> 192.168.1.20

Why. inet_ntoa returns a pointer to a static buffer inside the C library, and every call overwrites it. src and dst are the same pointer, so both print the last address converted. Written as printf("%s -> %s", inet_ntoa(a), inet_ntoa(b)) it is even worse: both arguments still alias, and which address wins depends on the unspecified argument evaluation order. glibc makes the buffer thread-local, so threads do not corrupt each other, but POSIX does not require that. Use inet_ntop with your own buffer, which also supports IPv6. strerror, localtime, gethostbyname and strtok share the same static-buffer design, and each has a reentrant replacement (strerror_r, localtime_r, getaddrinfo, strtok_r).

TrickyA load-test client opens and closes 30000 short connections per minute to one server. After a while connect fails with EADDRNOTAVAIL, and ss shows thousands of sockets in TIME_WAIT on the client. Why the client, and what are the fixes?

Answer

Answer. TIME_WAIT is held by whichever side closes first (the active closer), and here that is the client. Each TIME_WAIT entry keeps its 4-tuple reserved for 2·MSL (60 seconds on Linux), and with a single server address and port the only free part of the tuple is the client's ephemeral port. Linux's default range is 32768 to 60999, about 28000 ports, so 30000 closes a minute exhausts it.

Why. TIME_WAIT exists so that a late duplicate segment from an old connection is not accepted by a new one, and so the final ACK can be resent if it is lost (RFC 9293). Fixes, best first: reuse connections (keep-alive, pooling); let the server close first so it holds TIME_WAIT (cheap for a server with one listening port); widen net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range; enable net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse, which lets new outgoing connections reuse TIME_WAIT ports safely using timestamps. SO_REUSEADDR is the server-side answer to "bind fails after restart" and does not help here. Never use SO_LINGER with a zero timeout to skip TIME_WAIT, because it sends RST and can drop data.

OutputA binary market data frame contains a zero byte. The handler turns the received buffer into a std::string in two ways. What are the sizes?

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <unistd.h>

int main() {
    int sv[2];
    if (socketpair(AF_UNIX, SOCK_STREAM, 0, sv) != 0) return 1;
    const char frame[] = {'H', 'B', '\0', '4', '2', '\n'};  // binary protocol: a 0 byte is data
    send(sv[0], frame, sizeof frame, 0);

    char buf[64];
    ssize_t n = recv(sv[1], buf, sizeof buf, 0);
    std::string as_cstr(buf);      // stops at the first 0 byte (and needs one to exist)
    std::string exact(buf, static_cast<std::size_t>(n));
    std::printf("recv=%zd as_cstr=%zu exact=%zu\n", n, as_cstr.size(), exact.size());
    close(sv[0]);
    close(sv[1]);
}
Answer
recv=6 as_cstr=2 exact=6

Why. std::string(const char*) treats its argument as a C string and stops at the first '\0', so it keeps "HB" and silently drops the rest. If the received bytes happen to contain no zero, the same constructor reads past the data and possibly past the buffer, which is undefined behaviour (ASan reports a stack-buffer-overflow). The (pointer, length) constructor copies exactly n bytes, embedded zeros included. A std::string holds zeros without trouble, and only APIs built on c_str() (printf("%s"), strlen, C libraries) stop at them.

Always carry the count that recv returned: std::string(buf, n), std::string_view(buf, n) or std::span. Related traps: std::string s = "a\0b"; has size 1, while "a\0b"s has size 3 because the literal operator receives the length; and strcpy or strlen in a framer truncate binary payloads. The wrong answer is "6 6".

OutputA protocol header is sent with send(fd, &hdr, sizeof hdr, 0). The spec says it is 7 bytes. What does the program print?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>

struct Header {
    uint8_t type;
    uint32_t length;
    uint16_t seq;
};

struct [[gnu::packed]] PackedHeader {
    uint8_t type;
    uint32_t length;
    uint16_t seq;
};

int main() {
    std::printf("%zu %zu %zu %zu\n", sizeof(Header), offsetof(Header, length),
                sizeof(PackedHeader), offsetof(PackedHeader, length));
}
Answer
12 4 7 1

Why. length needs 4-byte alignment, so 3 padding bytes follow type, seq sits at offset 8, and the struct is padded to 12. Sending the struct sends 12 bytes, including padding with indeterminate contents (an information leak), in host byte order. [[gnu::packed]] removes the padding, but every access to length is now misaligned, taking a reference or pointer to it is dangerous (GCC warns with -Waddress-of-packed-member), and the byte order is still wrong. The portable way is to serialise field by field into a byte buffer: write type, then htonl(length) with memcpy, then htons(seq), and parse the same way. HFT feed handlers often do use packed structs for speed, but only on a known architecture and with explicit endian conversion of each field.

TrickyA server accepts a connection, forks a child to run a helper program, and then the parent closes the connection. The client never sees EOF and hangs. Why?

Answer

Answer. fork duplicates the file descriptor table, so the child holds its own descriptor for the same socket. The kernel only sends FIN when the last descriptor referring to the socket is closed. The parent's close just drops a reference, and the helper keeps the connection open for as long as it runs.

Why. Descriptors refer to shared open file descriptions with a reference count (Ch 4). Fixes: open sockets with SOCK_CLOEXEC (or accept4(..., SOCK_CLOEXEC)) so they close automatically on exec, close unneeded descriptors in the child, or call shutdown(fd, SHUT_WR) in the parent, which sends FIN regardless of how many descriptors exist. The same mechanism causes "port still in use" after a server restarts, when a forked child still holds the listening socket.

ConceptWhat do the return values of recv on a TCP socket mean: a positive count, 0, and -1 with errno set to EAGAIN, EINTR or ECONNRESET?

Answer

Answer. A positive value is the number of bytes copied, possibly fewer than requested. 0 means orderly shutdown: the peer sent FIN and no more data will arrive in that direction (it is not "no data right now"). -1 with EAGAIN/EWOULDBLOCK means a non-blocking socket has nothing to read yet, so go back to poll/epoll. EINTR means a signal interrupted the call before any data arrived, so retry. ECONNRESET means the peer sent RST (it crashed, or closed with unread data), so the connection is dead.

Why. A loop that treats 0 as "try again" spins at 100% CPU after the peer leaves, and a loop that treats EAGAIN as fatal drops healthy connections. Note that recv with a length of 0 also returns 0, so do not call it with an empty buffer and then mistake that for EOF.

OutputTimeouts are configured in milliseconds and passed to an API that takes whole seconds. What does each conversion produce?

#include <chrono>
#include <cstdio>

int main() {
    using namespace std::chrono;
    auto timeout = milliseconds(1999);
    seconds s = duration_cast<seconds>(timeout);
    microseconds us = timeout;                // widening: implicit and exact
    std::printf("cast=%lld floor=%lld ceil=%lld round=%lld us=%lld\n",
                static_cast<long long>(s.count()), static_cast<long long>(floor<seconds>(timeout).count()),
                static_cast<long long>(ceil<seconds>(timeout).count()), static_cast<long long>(round<seconds>(timeout).count()),
                static_cast<long long>(us.count()));
    auto ratio = milliseconds(1500) / seconds(1);
    std::printf("ratio=%lld neg=%lld\n", static_cast<long long>(ratio),
                static_cast<long long>(duration_cast<seconds>(milliseconds(-1500)).count()));
}
Answer
cast=1 floor=1 ceil=2 round=2 us=1999000
ratio=1 neg=-1

Why. duration_cast truncates toward zero, like integer division, so 1999 ms becomes 1 s and -1500 ms becomes -1 s (where floor would give -2). A conversion that can lose precision must be written explicitly, while a widening one (milliseconds to microseconds) is implicit and exact. C++17 adds floor, ceil and round (ties to even) so you can choose. Dividing two durations gives a plain count, also truncated: 1500 ms / 1 s is 1. The wrong answer is "it rounds to the nearest second".

For timeouts, round up. A 1999 ms deadline truncated to 1 s fires early, and a sub-millisecond timeout truncated to 0 makes poll (which takes an int of milliseconds) return immediately, so the event loop busy-spins at 100% CPU.

What the standard says vs what the compiler does

Drills

Here "it printed X on my machine" and "the language guarantees X" are different answers. Know which category each result falls into: defined, unspecified, implementation-defined or undefined.

OutputWhat does show(next(), next()) print?

#include <cstdio>

static int counter = 0;
static int next() { return ++counter; }
static void show(int a, int b) { std::printf("%d %d\n", a, b); }

int main() {
    show(next(), next());
}
Answer
