Answer. Either 1 2 or 2 1, and both are correct. The order in which function arguments are evaluated is unspecified ([expr.call]). On this guide's ARM64 test machine both GCC and Clang print 1 2, but GCC on x86-64 has historically evaluated many argument lists right to left, and the order may change with the optimisation level, the argument types or the compiler version. The output is not compared for that reason.

Why. Unspecified is not undefined: since C++17 each argument is evaluated completely before the next one starts (they are indeterminately sequenced), so the program is valid and prints one of the two results. Before C++17 the sub-expressions of different arguments could interleave, which made f(std::unique_ptr<T>(new T), g()) leak if g() threw between the new and the unique_ptr constructor. That leak is gone in C++17. If the order matters, evaluate into named locals first.

OutputSame counter, now with stream insertion and with a map assignment. What does C++20 guarantee?

#include <iostream>
#include <map>

static int counter = 0;
static int next() { return ++counter; }

int main() {
    std::cout << next() << ' ' << next() << ' ' << next() << '\n';
    std::map<int, int> m;
    m[next()] = next();
    std::cout << m.begin()->first << ' ' << m.begin()->second << '\n';
}
Answer
1 2 3
5 4

Why. C++17 (P0145) added sequencing rules for a few operators. In E1 << E2 and E1 >> E2, E1 is sequenced before E2, so chained stream output now runs left to right even though each << is a function call. In assignment E1 = E2 (and compound assignment), the right operand is sequenced before the left, so the value next() runs first and returns 4, then the key next() returns 5. In C++14 both lines were unspecified, so a compiler could legally print 3 2 1 for the first one, and older compilers sometimes did. The same rule makes v[i] = i++; well defined since C++17, and explains why m[k] = m.size(); stores the size before the insertion.

OutputAn overflow guard: will_grow(INT_MAX) should return false. What does an optimising compiler make of it?

#include <climits>
#include <cstdio>

static bool will_grow(int x) { return x + 1 > x; }

int main(int argc, char**) {
    int big = INT_MAX - 1 + argc;  // INT_MAX when run with no arguments
    std::printf("%d\n", will_grow(big));
}
Answer

Answer. With optimisation, both GCC and Clang compile will_grow to return true and print 1. Without optimisation you may see 0, because the addition wraps on the hardware. The output is not compared here because the program has undefined behaviour.

Why. Signed overflow is undefined ([expr.pre]), so the compiler may assume it never happens, and then x + 1 > x is always true. This is how loops like for (int i = 0; i >= 0; ++i) become infinite and how overflow checks written after the fact disappear. Correct guards test before the operation: x < INT_MAX, or __builtin_add_overflow(x, 1, &out), or C++26 std::add_sat. Unsigned arithmetic wraps by definition, and -fwrapv makes signed wrap too, at some cost to loop optimisation. UBSan (-fsanitize=signed-integer-overflow) catches it at run time.

OutputAre these two lines undefined behaviour in C++20? If not, what do they print?

#include <cstdio>

int main() {
    int i = 5;
    i = i++ + 1;
    int k = 1;
    k += k++;
    std::printf("%d %d\n", i, k);
}
Answer
6 3

Why. Both were undefined before C++11 and still undefined in C++14, because the side effect of i++ and the assignment to i were unsequenced. Since C++17 the right operand of every assignment, including compound assignment, is sequenced before the left operand and before the assignment itself. So i++ + 1 is fully evaluated (value 6, and i becomes 6), then 6 is stored. For k += k++, the right side yields 1 and sets k to 2, then k = k + 1 gives 3. i++ + i++ and f(i++, i++) are still not defined the way people hope: the first is undefined, the second unspecified. Never write this in real code, but know why it is legal now.

Trickychar c = '\xFF'; if (c < 0) ... takes the branch on an x86-64 Linux box and not on an ARM64 Linux box. Which compiler is wrong?

Answer

Answer. Neither. Whether plain char is signed is implementation-defined, and the ABI decides. x86-64 Linux, Windows and Apple's ARM64 ABI use signed char. The standard ARM64 Linux (AAPCS64), 32-bit ARM Linux and POWER ABIs use unsigned char. char, signed char and unsigned char are three distinct types in every case.

Why. This bites parsers that index tables with a char (a negative index on x86, fine on ARM) and checksum code that adds bytes. Use unsigned char or std::uint8_t for raw bytes, or std::byte, and convert explicitly. -funsigned-char and -fsigned-char change the default and break ABI compatibility with other libraries. Other implementation-defined favourites: sizeof(long) (8 on Linux, 4 on Windows) and right shift of a negative number (arithmetic on every mainstream compiler, and defined that way since C++20).

OutputTwo ways to look at the bits of a float. What prints, and which commonly used third way is undefined?

#include <bit>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstring>

int main() {
    float f = 1.0f;
    auto viaBitCast = std::bit_cast<std::uint32_t>(f);
    std::uint32_t viaMemcpy;
    std::memcpy(&viaMemcpy, &f, sizeof f);
    std::printf("%08x %08x\n", viaBitCast, viaMemcpy);
}
Answer
3f800000 3f800000

Why. IEEE 754 single precision stores 1.0 as sign 0, biased exponent 127 (0x7f) and fraction 0, which is 0x3f800000. Both ways copy the object representation, which is well defined. The undefined way is *reinterpret_cast<std::uint32_t*>(&f): it reads a float object through a uint32_t glvalue, which breaks the strict aliasing rule ([basic.lval]). The optimiser assumes that an int* and a float* never refer to the same object, and may reorder or delete the accesses. Union type punning is allowed in C but is undefined in C++, although GCC documents it as an extension. memcpy of 4 bytes compiles to a single register move, so the safe versions cost nothing. std::bit_cast (C++20) is also constexpr.

OutputA feed parser stores small fields as std::int8_t and std::uint8_t. What do the stream insertions print?

#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

int main() {
    std::int8_t side = 66;
    std::uint8_t qty = 50;
    std::cout << side << ' ' << qty << '\n';
    std::cout << +side << ' ' << +qty << ' ' << static_cast<int>(qty) << '\n';
    std::cout << std::to_string(qty) << '\n';
}
Answer
B 2
66 50 50
50

Why. On every mainstream platform std::int8_t and std::uint8_t are typedefs for signed char and unsigned char, and iostreams have character overloads for both. So 66 prints as B and 50 as 2. Unary + applies integral promotion to int, as does the explicit cast, and std::to_string has no character overloads, so it prints the number. The standard would allow these typedefs to name distinct extended integer types, but no mainstream implementation does that. The wrong answer is "66 50".

Extraction is worse: std::cin >> qty reads one character, so the input 50 stores 53 (the code of '5'). std::format("{}", qty) prints 50, because std::format formats only char as a character and treats signed char and unsigned char as integers.

ConceptWhat does the inline keyword actually guarantee in modern C++? Does it make a function get inlined?

Answer

Answer. inline is about the one-definition rule, not about inlining. An inline function or (since C++17) inline variable may be defined in several translation units, as long as every definition is token-for-token identical, and the linker keeps one copy. Whether a call is expanded in place is the optimiser's choice, and it inlines non-inline functions and ignores the keyword freely.

Why. It is what lets you define functions in headers. Member functions defined inside a class body, constexpr functions and function templates are implicitly inline. The trap is the "identical" requirement: two TUs that see different definitions (different #defines, or two unrelated classes both called Node in the global namespace) cause an ODR violation, which is undefined behaviour with no diagnostic required. The linker silently keeps one version. Put file-local helpers in an anonymous namespace or mark them static. To force or block inlining, use [[gnu::always_inline]] or [[gnu::noinline]].

Find the bugThe destructor reports flush failures by throwing, and it is explicitly marked noexcept(false). What happens when an order fails?

#include <cstdio>
#include <stdexcept>

struct Flusher {
    ~Flusher() noexcept(false) {
        std::puts("flush failed, throwing");
        throw std::runtime_error("disk full");
    }
};

int main() {
    try {
        Flusher f;
        throw std::runtime_error("bad order");
    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        std::printf("caught %s\n", e.what());
    }
}
Answer

Answer. std::terminate is called and the program aborts. The catch never runs. Even the puts line may not appear when stdout is a pipe, because abort does not flush stdio buffers.

Why. Throwing bad order starts stack unwinding, which destroys f. If a destructor called during unwinding exits with an exception, there would be two exceptions in flight, and C++ handles that by calling std::terminate ([except.terminate]). Without the noexcept(false) it is even worse: destructors are implicitly noexcept, so any throw out of them terminates, unwinding or not (GCC warns with -Wterminate). Fix: never let exceptions escape a destructor. Provide an explicit flush() or close() that can throw, and have the destructor call it inside try { } catch (...) { } as a best-effort fallback. std::uncaught_exceptions() lets a destructor know whether it is running because of unwinding, which the Transaction exercise below uses.

Rapid-fire one-liners

Drills

Screening rounds often open with a burst of these. Aim to answer each in one sentence and then give the reason in a second sentence if asked.

ConceptCan you overload a function on its return type alone?

Answer

Answer. No. Overloads must differ in their parameter lists (including const/ref qualifiers on member functions).

Why. A call expression has to be resolved without knowing what the result is used for, and the result may be discarded. Return types only enter the signature of function templates, and a conversion operator template can fake "overload on return type" when that is really needed.

TrickyWhat does delete p; do when p is null, and what does free(nullptr) do?

Answer

Answer. Nothing in both cases. They are defined no-ops, so if (p) delete p; is redundant.

Why. The real danger is the opposite case, a non-null pointer that was already deleted. Setting a pointer to null after delete turns a later double delete into a harmless no-op, but it also hides the logic error. Smart pointers remove the question entirely.

ConceptWhy is std::endl slower than '\n' in a loop that writes a million lines to a file?

Answer

Answer. std::endl writes a newline and flushes the stream, so each line becomes a separate write system call. '\n' just appends to the buffer.

Why. A million syscalls cost far more than the formatting. For a terminal, std::cout is often line buffered anyway, which hides the difference in tests. Use '\n' and flush explicitly where you need durability or interactivity.

ConceptWhat is the largest payload of a single UDP datagram over IPv4, and what actually limits it in practice?

Answer

Answer. 65507 bytes: the 16-bit IP total length (65535) minus the 20-byte IP header and the 8-byte UDP header. In practice anything above the path MTU (about 1472 bytes of payload on Ethernet) is fragmented, and losing one fragment loses the whole datagram.

Why. Market data protocols keep datagrams under the MTU for this reason. If the receive buffer is smaller than the datagram, recv truncates it and the rest is discarded (MSG_TRUNC tells you).

TrickyCan you re-seat a reference, for example inside a class's copy assignment operator?

Answer

Answer. No. Assigning to a reference assigns to the object it refers to. That is why a class with a reference member gets a deleted copy assignment operator.

Why. If you need a rebindable reference, store a pointer or std::reference_wrapper<T>, which is also what lets containers hold "references".

ConceptWhich ephemeral port range does Linux use for outgoing connections by default?

Answer

Answer. 32768 to 60999, set by net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range. IANA recommends 49152 to 65535, which Windows and macOS use.

Why. The range limits how many concurrent connections one client address can open to one server address and port, together with TIME_WAIT. See the TIME_WAIT drill in the networking section.

TrickyIs sizeof('a') the same in C and C++?

Answer

Answer. No. In C++ a character literal has type char, so the size is 1. In C it has type int, so the size is usually 4.

Why. C++ changed the type so that overloads such as print(char) and print(int) pick the right one for print('a'). It is a classic question about why C++ is not a superset of C, along with void* needing a cast and auto meaning something else.

Write the code: cross-topic exercises

Coding

Each exercise fixes one of the traps above properly. Interviewers grade the edge cases as much as the happy path, so each answer lists the pitfalls they look for.

CodeWrite BitVector, a packed bit array with a proxy reference, and get the proxy's assignment right.

Store bits in std::uint64_t words. Support push_back(bool), size(), count(), a const operator[] returning bool, and a non-const operator[] returning a proxy that supports b[i] = true, b[i] = b[j], conversion to bool and flip(). Explain what auto r = b[i]; means for your users.

Answer

Approach. The proxy holds a pointer to one word and a single-bit mask. Assigning a bool sets or clears the bit. The proxy's copy assignment is the subtle part: b[i] = b[j] must copy the bit value, so it is written as "convert the source to bool, then assign", whereas the defaulted version would re-point the proxy and leave the vector unchanged. count() uses std::popcount per word, which works because unused high bits of the last word are kept at zero.

#include <bit>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

class BitVector {
public:
    class reference {
    public:
        reference(std::uint64_t& word, std::uint64_t mask) : w_(&word), m_(mask) {}
        reference(const reference&) = default;
        reference& operator=(bool b) {
            if (b) *w_ |= m_; else *w_ &= ~m_;
            return *this;
        }
        reference& operator=(const reference& other) { return *this = static_cast<bool>(other); }
        operator bool() const { return (*w_ & m_) != 0; }
        void flip() { *w_ ^= m_; }

    private:
        std::uint64_t* w_;
        std::uint64_t m_;
    };

    explicit BitVector(std::size_t n = 0) : words_((n + 63) / 64), size_(n) {}

    void push_back(bool b) {
        if (size_ % 64 == 0) words_.push_back(0);
        ++size_;
        (*this)[size_ - 1] = b;
    }
    reference operator[](std::size_t i) { return reference(words_[i / 64], std::uint64_t{1} << (i % 64)); }
    bool operator[](std::size_t i) const { return (words_[i / 64] >> (i % 64)) & 1u; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::size_t count() const {
        std::size_t c = 0;
        for (std::uint64_t w : words_) c += static_cast<std::size_t>(std::popcount(w));
        return c;
    }

private:
    std::vector<std::uint64_t> words_;
    std::size_t size_;
};

int main() {
    BitVector b(70);
    b[3] = true;
    b[69] = true;
    b[64] = b[3];   // copies the bit, not the proxy
    auto r = b[5];  // r is a proxy: writing through it changes b
    r = true;
    b[69].flip();
    b.push_back(true);
    const BitVector& cb = b;
    std::printf("size=%zu count=%zu b5=%d b64=%d b69=%d b70=%d\n",
                cb.size(), cb.count(), cb[5], cb[64], cb[69], cb[70]);
}
size=71 count=4 b5=1 b64=1 b69=0 b70=1

Complexity and pitfalls. Element access is O(1) with a shift and a mask, and count() is O(n/64). Pitfalls that interviewers probe: the defaulted proxy assignment (silently does nothing to the vector), auto r = b[i] holding a proxy that dangles once push_back reallocates words_, generic code that expects T& (bool& x = b[i] fails to compile), and concurrency: two threads writing different bits of the same word race, which is never true for distinct elements of an ordinary vector. These are exactly the reasons std::vector<bool> is considered a design mistake. A resize that shrinks must also clear the bits above the new size, or count() breaks.

Estimated rating: ~1600 · easy bit arithmetic, but the proxy's copy assignment and lifetime are a real test.

CodeImplement Lazy<T>: a correct double-checked lazy initialiser.

T& get(F make) builds the value with make() on first use and returns it. It must be safe when many threads call it at once, make must run exactly once, and the fast path after initialisation must take no lock. The destructor frees the value.

Answer

Approach. Store the pointer in a std::atomic<T*>. The fast path is an acquire load: if it sees the pointer, it also sees everything the constructor wrote, because the writer published the pointer with a release store after construction. The slow path takes a mutex and checks again, so only one thread builds the value. Inside the lock the re-check can be relaxed, since the mutex already orders it after any earlier publisher.

#include <atomic>
#include <cstdio>
#include <mutex>
#include <string>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

template <class T>
class Lazy {
public:
    Lazy() = default;
    Lazy(const Lazy&) = delete;
    Lazy& operator=(const Lazy&) = delete;
    ~Lazy() { delete ptr_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed); }

    template <class F>
    T& get(F&& make) {
        if (T* p = ptr_.load(std::memory_order_acquire)) return *p;
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mtx_);
        T* p = ptr_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        if (!p) {
            p = new T(make());
            ptr_.store(p, std::memory_order_release);
        }
        return *p;
    }

private:
    std::atomic<T*> ptr_{nullptr};
    std::mutex mtx_;
};

int main() {
    Lazy<std::string> config;
    std::atomic<int> builds{0};
    std::atomic<std::size_t> total{0};
    std::vector<std::thread> ts;
    for (int i = 0; i < 8; ++i)
        ts.emplace_back([&] {
            const std::string& c = config.get([&] {
                builds.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
                return std::string("venue=XNAS depth=10");
            });
            total.fetch_add(c.size(), std::memory_order_relaxed);
        });
    for (auto& t : ts) t.join();
    std::printf("builds=%d total=%zu\n", builds.load(), total.load());
}
builds=1 total=152

Complexity and pitfalls. After initialisation each call is one acquire load (a plain load on x86, ldar on ARM64). Pitfalls: a plain T* (the original bug), relaxed on the fast path (no visibility of the constructed object), publishing the pointer before construction finishes, and an exception from make(): here it propagates, the lock is released by RAII and the next caller retries, which is the same behaviour as a function-local static. In real code a function-local static or std::call_once is simpler. Write this version when the object must be per instance or destroyed at a chosen time.

Estimated rating: ~1700 · short, but needs a precise explanation of acquire/release and of the re-check.

CodeWrite an AsyncLogger that moves log I/O off the hot threads and shuts down safely.

log(std::string) may be called from any thread and must only enqueue. One background thread writes lines to a sink, here a std::vector<std::string>& standing in for a file. The destructor must flush every line logged before it started, join the thread, and never throw or deadlock. Lines from one thread must keep their order.

Answer

Approach. A mutex-protected vector is the queue and a condition variable wakes the worker. The worker swaps the whole queue into a local batch under the lock and writes the batch after unlocking, so slow I/O never blocks producers. The destructor sets stop_ under the lock, notifies and joins, and the worker exits only once it has seen stop_ and found the queue empty, which guarantees the final flush. The thread is declared as the last member, so everything it touches is constructed before it starts and is still alive until it is joined.

#include <condition_variable>
#include <cstdio>
#include <mutex>
#include <string>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

class AsyncLogger {
public:
    explicit AsyncLogger(std::vector<std::string>& sink) : sink_(sink), worker_([this] { run(); }) {}
    AsyncLogger(const AsyncLogger&) = delete;
    AsyncLogger& operator=(const AsyncLogger&) = delete;
    ~AsyncLogger() {
        {
            std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(m_);
            stop_ = true;
        }
        cv_.notify_one();
        worker_.join();
    }

    void log(std::string line) {
        {
            std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(m_);
            q_.push_back(std::move(line));
        }
        cv_.notify_one();
    }

private:
    void run() {
        std::vector<std::string> batch;
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(m_);
        for (;;) {
            cv_.wait(lk, [this] { return stop_ || !q_.empty(); });
            batch.swap(q_);
            const bool stopping = stop_;
            lk.unlock();
            for (auto& s : batch) sink_.push_back(std::move(s));  // the slow part, unlocked
            batch.clear();
            lk.lock();
            if (stopping && q_.empty()) return;
        }
    }

    std::vector<std::string>& sink_;
    std::mutex m_;
    std::condition_variable cv_;
    std::vector<std::string> q_;
    bool stop_ = false;
    std::thread worker_;  // last: starts after, and is joined before, everything it uses
};

int main() {
    std::vector<std::string> sink;
    {
        AsyncLogger logger(sink);
        std::vector<std::thread> ts;
        for (int t = 0; t < 4; ++t)
            ts.emplace_back([&logger, t] {
                for (int i = 0; i < 250; ++i)
                    logger.log(std::to_string(t) + ":" + std::to_string(i));
            });
        for (auto& th : ts) th.join();
    }  // destructor flushes and joins
    int last[4] = {-1, -1, -1, -1};
    bool ordered = true;
    for (const auto& line : sink) {
        int t = line[0] - '0';
        int i = std::stoi(line.substr(2));
        ordered = ordered && i == last[t] + 1;
        last[t] = i;
    }
    std::printf("lines=%zu per-thread order kept=%d\n", sink.size(), ordered);
}
lines=1000 per-thread order kept=1

Complexity and pitfalls. Each log is one short critical section, and the worker takes the lock once per batch rather than once per line. Pitfalls: writing to the sink while holding the lock (every producer then waits for the disk), checking stop_ before draining (lines are lost at shutdown), waiting without a predicate (lost and spurious wakeups), declaring the thread before the queue or mutex (members are initialised in declaration order, as the width bug in the move section shows), and calling log from a destructor of a static object after the logger is gone. A low-latency version replaces the mutex with a per-thread SPSC ring, formats lazily, and bounds the queue, choosing between blocking and dropping when it is full.

Estimated rating: ~1600 · standard producer and consumer code, judged on the shutdown path and on doing I/O outside the lock.

CodeWrite Synchronized<T>, a value that can only be reached while its mutex is held.

Provide lock(), which returns a proxy that holds the lock and gives -> and * access, and with(f), which calls f(value) under the lock and returns its result. There must be no way to reach the value without locking. Test with four threads appending to a Synchronized<std::vector<int>>.

Answer

Approach. The value and its mutex are private members of the same object, so the only doors are the two accessors. The proxy owns a std::unique_lock and a reference to the value, and it is returned by value, which C++17 guaranteed elision constructs directly in the caller. with takes a scoped_lock and forwards f, and decltype(auto) preserves a returned reference or value exactly.

#include <cstdio>
#include <mutex>
#include <thread>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

template <class T>
class Synchronized {
public:
    template <class... Args>
    explicit Synchronized(Args&&... args) : value_(std::forward<Args>(args)...) {}

    class Locked {
    public:
        Locked(std::mutex& m, T& v) : lock_(m), v_(v) {}
        T* operator->() const { return &v_; }
        T& operator*() const { return v_; }

    private:
        std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lock_;
        T& v_;
    };

    [[nodiscard]] Locked lock() { return Locked(m_, value_); }

    template <class F>
    decltype(auto) with(F&& f) {
        std::scoped_lock guard(m_);
        return std::forward<F>(f)(value_);
    }

private:
    std::mutex m_;
    T value_;
};

int main() {
    Synchronized<std::vector<int>> fills;
    std::vector<std::thread> ts;
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i)
        ts.emplace_back([&fills, i] {
            for (int k = 0; k < 1000; ++k) fills.lock()->push_back(i);
        });
    for (auto& t : ts) t.join();
    std::size_t n = fills.with([](const std::vector<int>& v) { return v.size(); });
    {
        auto locked = fills.lock();
        locked->push_back(-1);
        std::printf("size=%zu last=%d\n", n, locked->back());
    }
}
size=4000 last=-1

Complexity and pitfalls. One lock per access, so batch work inside one lock() or with rather than locking per element in hot paths. Pitfalls: auto& v = *fills.lock(); compiles and leaves v unprotected, because the proxy (and its lock) dies at the end of the full expression. Returning a reference out of with leaks the value past the lock in the same way. Calling lock() twice on one thread deadlocks, since std::mutex is not recursive. Folly's Synchronized and Boost's synchronized_value are production versions, with shared locks for readers.

Estimated rating: ~1600 · a small template whose value is in the lifetime reasoning about the proxy.

CodeSerialise an order message to a portable wire format and parse it back safely.

The wire format is big-endian and packed: type (1 byte, 'N'), order_id (8), price in units of 1/10000 (signed, 8), qty (4) and side (1 byte, 'B' or 'S'), 22 bytes in all. Write encode(order, buf, len) returning the bytes written (0 if the buffer is too small) and decode(buf, len) returning std::optional<Order>, rejecting short buffers and invalid fields. No packed structs, no casts of the buffer to a struct pointer.

Answer

Approach. Two small templates do every field: put_be writes an unsigned integer most significant byte first with shifts, and get_be reads it back. Shifts work on values, not memory, so the code is correct on any host byte order and needs no htonl (which has no portable 64-bit form). Signed fields go through their unsigned type, a conversion that is well defined both ways since C++20. Decoding checks the length before reading and validates the type and side bytes.

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <optional>
#include <type_traits>

struct Order {
    std::uint64_t id;
    std::int64_t price;  // 1/10000 units
    std::uint32_t qty;
    char side;
};

constexpr std::size_t kWireSize = 1 + 8 + 8 + 4 + 1;

template <class U>
static unsigned char* put_be(unsigned char* p, U v) {
    static_assert(std::is_unsigned_v<U>);
    for (int i = sizeof(U) - 1; i >= 0; --i) *p++ = static_cast<unsigned char>(v >> (8 * i));
    return p;
}

template <class U>
static const unsigned char* get_be(const unsigned char* p, U& v) {
    v = 0;
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < sizeof(U); ++i) v = static_cast<U>((v << 8) | *p++);
    return p;
}

static std::size_t encode(const Order& o, unsigned char* buf, std::size_t len) {
    if (len < kWireSize) return 0;
    unsigned char* p = buf;
    *p++ = 'N';
    p = put_be(p, o.id);
    p = put_be(p, static_cast<std::uint64_t>(o.price));
    p = put_be(p, o.qty);
    *p++ = static_cast<unsigned char>(o.side);
    return static_cast<std::size_t>(p - buf);
}

static std::optional<Order> decode(const unsigned char* buf, std::size_t len) {
    if (len < kWireSize || buf[0] != 'N') return std::nullopt;
    Order o{};
    std::uint64_t price = 0;
    const unsigned char* p = buf + 1;
    p = get_be(p, o.id);
    p = get_be(p, price);
    p = get_be(p, o.qty);
    o.price = static_cast<std::int64_t>(price);
    o.side = static_cast<char>(*p);
    if (o.side != 'B' && o.side != 'S') return std::nullopt;
    return o;
}

int main() {
    unsigned char buf[64];
    std::size_t n = encode(Order{12345, 1892500, 100, 'B'}, buf, sizeof buf);
    std::printf("wire size %zu\nbytes:", n);
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < 9; ++i) std::printf(" %02x", buf[i]);
    std::printf("\n");
    if (auto o = decode(buf, n))
        std::printf("id=%llu px=%lld.%04lld qty=%u side=%c\n",
                    static_cast<unsigned long long>(o->id), static_cast<long long>(o->price / 10000),
                    static_cast<long long>(o->price % 10000), o->qty, o->side);
    std::printf("truncated: %s\n", decode(buf, n - 1) ? "accepted" : "rejected");
    buf[0] = 'X';
    std::printf("bad type: %s\n", decode(buf, n) ? "accepted" : "rejected");
    std::printf("negative price round trip: %s\n",
                decode(buf + 32, encode(Order{1, -5, 1, 'S'}, buf + 32, 32))->price == -5 ? "ok" : "broken");
}
wire size 22
bytes: 4e 00 00 00 00 00 00 30 39
id=12345 px=189.2500 qty=100 side=B
truncated: rejected
bad type: rejected
negative price round trip: ok

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) per message, and compilers turn the shift loops into a single load or store plus a byte-swap instruction. Pitfalls: send(fd, &order, sizeof order, 0) (padding, host byte order and an information leak, as in the struct drill above), reinterpret_cast of the receive buffer to a struct pointer (strict aliasing and misalignment), reading fields before checking the length, and shifting a signed value. Sequence numbers and a version byte belong in a real header so that a parser can reject messages it does not understand. Exchange protocols such as ITCH and SBE use exactly this kind of fixed layout.

Estimated rating: ~1300 · simple byte handling, judged on endianness, bounds checks and avoiding aliasing tricks.

CodeWrite a Transaction guard that rolls back on failure and never throws from its destructor.

It records operations into a shared log. commit() makes them permanent. If the guard is destroyed without a commit, it removes its operations and reports whether the cause was an exception or a forgotten commit. The destructor must be safe to run during stack unwinding.

Answer

Approach. Remember the log size at construction, and on rollback erase everything after it. To tell "unwinding" from "forgot to commit", compare std::uncaught_exceptions() in the destructor with the value saved in the constructor. Comparing counts (rather than calling the removed std::uncaught_exception()) gives the right answer even when the guard is created inside another object's destructor during unwinding. Nothing in the destructor can throw: erasing strings from the end of a vector never allocates.

#include <cstdio>
#include <exception>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class Transaction {
public:
    explicit Transaction(std::vector<std::string>& log)
        : log_(log), mark_(log.size()), uncaught_(std::uncaught_exceptions()) {}
    Transaction(const Transaction&) = delete;
    Transaction& operator=(const Transaction&) = delete;

    void add(std::string op) { log_.push_back(std::move(op)); }
    void commit() {
        committed_ = true;
        std::printf("committed: %zu ops\n", log_.size() - mark_);
    }
    ~Transaction() {
        if (committed_) return;
        const char* why = std::uncaught_exceptions() > uncaught_ ? "exception" : "no commit";
        std::size_t n = log_.size() - mark_;
        log_.erase(log_.begin() + static_cast<std::ptrdiff_t>(mark_), log_.end());
        std::printf("rolled back %zu ops (%s)\n", n, why);
    }

private:
    std::vector<std::string>& log_;
    std::size_t mark_;
    int uncaught_;
    bool committed_ = false;
};

int main() {
    std::vector<std::string> log;
    {
        Transaction t(log);
        t.add("A1");
        t.add("A2");
        t.commit();
    }
    try {
        Transaction t(log);
        t.add("B1");
        throw std::runtime_error("risk check failed");
    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        std::printf("caught: %s\n", e.what());
    }
    {
        Transaction t(log);
        t.add("C1");
    }
    std::printf("log:");
    for (const auto& op : log) std::printf(" %s", op.c_str());
    std::printf("\n");
}
committed: 2 ops
rolled back 1 ops (exception)
caught: risk check failed
rolled back 1 ops (no commit)
log: A1 A2

Complexity and pitfalls. Rollback is O(k) in the operations added. The destructor runs before the catch handler, which is why "rolled back" prints first. Pitfalls: doing fallible work (I/O, allocation) in the destructor, using the boolean std::uncaught_exception() (deprecated in C++17 and removed in C++20) which is wrong for nested guards, and letting commit() set the flag before a step that can throw. In a real system commit() is where errors surface and may throw. The destructor's job is only the cleanup that cannot fail. The Library Fundamentals TS calls these scope_success and scope_fail.

Estimated rating: ~1400 · simple bookkeeping, tested on unwinding order and on the no-throw destructor rule.
