Part G · Mixed practice · Chapter 26

Timed mock rounds

Five interview rounds, each a fixed set of questions in the order a real interviewer would ask them: a warm-up concept, then tricky follow-ups, then code reading, then a problem to write. Work each round under its time limit before opening any answer, then mark yourself with the scoring line. Round 5 is pitched at HFT and low-latency systems interviews.

DrillsCoding· about 5 hours including review· prerequisites: chapters 1 to 25

How to run a round

Drills

Set a timer, read every question first, and answer on paper or in a blank editor without compiling. Speak your answers aloud for the concept and tricky questions, because that is what an interviewer hears. For output questions, write the exact output. For bug questions, name the bug, say how you would prove it (which sanitizer or test) and give the fix. Leave the code problem for last and budget about a third of the round for it.

Know this cold

Scoring for rounds 1 to 4: concept questions 1 point, tricky, output and bug questions 2 points each, and the code problem 4 points (2 for a correct solution, 1 for stating the complexity, 1 for handling the edge cases listed in the answer). Give yourself half marks for an answer that is right but whose reason is wrong or missing, because interviewers mark the reason.

Round 1: generalist warm-up

DrillsCoding

Time limit: 30 minutes. Scoring: 18 points (2 concept × 1, 2 tricky × 2, 2 output × 2, 2 bug × 2, code 4). 15 or more is a strong pass, 11 to 14 a pass, and below 11 means revisiting Ch 1, Ch 4 and Ch 8. This is the round a product company runs for a general C++ role.

Conceptwrite(fd, buf, 4096) on a regular file returned 4096. Is the data on disk? Walk through what happened, and say what fsync adds.

Answer

Answer. Not necessarily. write is a system call: the CPU enters the kernel, which copies the bytes from your buffer into the page cache (kernel memory that caches file pages), marks those pages dirty and returns. Every other reader of the file sees the new data at once, because they read the same cached pages. The data reaches the device later, when writeback flushes dirty pages (by default once they are about 30 seconds old, vm.dirty_expire_centisecs = 3000, or earlier under memory pressure). A crash of the process loses nothing, while a power cut before writeback loses the write. fsync(fd) blocks until the file's data and metadata are on stable storage, including a flush of the device's cache. fdatasync skips metadata that is not needed to read the data back, and a newly created file also needs an fsync on its directory before its name is durable.

Why. The interviewer is testing the gap between "the call returned" and "the effect is durable", the same gap as with send, which only copies into the socket buffer. Bonus points: fwrite and std::ofstream add a user-space buffer on top, so the data may not even have reached write yet (fflush moves it to the kernel, fsync to the disk). O_DIRECT bypasses the page cache and O_DSYNC makes each write durable. On Linux a failed fsync may drop the dirty pages and clear the error, so a retry can falsely succeed (PostgreSQL's 2018 "fsyncgate"): treat a failed fsync as fatal. Journals and order logs fsync before acknowledging.

ConceptBesides "the connection is now open", what do the two sides learn or agree on during the TCP three-way handshake?

Answer

Answer. Each side picks a random initial sequence number (ISN) and learns the other's, since each SYN consumes one sequence number and must be acknowledged. The SYN and SYN-ACK also carry options that are only valid there: the maximum segment size (MSS, 1460 on Ethernet with IPv4), the window scale factor (so windows can exceed 64 KiB), SACK-permitted, and timestamps. Each side also advertises its initial receive window.

Why. Random ISNs protect against segments from an old connection with the same 4-tuple and make blind injection attacks harder. Options that are missing from the SYN cannot be turned on later, which is why a middlebox that strips window scaling caps throughput for the whole connection. The handshake costs one RTT before any data, which is what TCP Fast Open and TLS 1.3 0-RTT try to shave off (Ch 8).

TrickyA colleague sorts orders with std::sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](const Order& a, const Order& b) { return a.price <= b.price; });. It usually works, and occasionally crashes inside std::sort when many prices are equal. Why?

Answer

Answer. <= is not a strict weak ordering, because comp(a, a) returns true. std::sort requires one ([alg.sorting]), and violating it is undefined behaviour. libstdc++'s introsort uses an "unguarded" insertion sort that relies on the comparator stopping at a sentinel element. With <= and runs of equal keys, the inner loop walks past the beginning of the range and reads (and writes) memory outside the vector.

Why. The requirement is irreflexive, transitive and with transitive equivalence. < on prices satisfies it, <= does not, and a comparator over floating-point values containing NaN does not either. Newer libstdc++ debug modes (-D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG) and libc++'s hardening mode detect some violations. Use a.price < b.price, and if equal prices must keep arrival order, use std::stable_sort or compare (price, seq) pairs with std::tie.

TrickyA profile shows malloc on every call to symbols.find("AAPL"), where symbols is a std::map<std::string, int>. Why, and how do you remove it without changing the key type?

Answer

Answer. map::find takes a const key_type&, so the string literal is converted to a temporary std::string on every call. "AAPL" fits in the small string buffer, so that allocation is free in practice, but longer keys (or std::string_view arguments) really allocate. Declare the map with a transparent comparator, std::map<std::string, int, std::less<>>, and find gains a template overload that compares the const char* or string_view with the stored keys directly.

Why. std::less<> declares the member type is_transparent, which enables heterogeneous lookup (C++14 for ordered containers). Unordered containers support it since C++20, but they need both a transparent hash and a transparent equality. The wrong fix is to cache std::string keys at every call site, which only moves the allocation.

OutputA logging helper has three overloads. Which one does each call pick?

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>

static void emit(bool) { std::puts("bool"); }
static void emit(int) { std::puts("int"); }
static void emit(const std::string&) { std::puts("string"); }

int main() {
    using namespace std::string_literals;
    emit("ready");
    emit(std::string("ready"));
    emit('a');
    emit("ready"s);
}
Answer
bool
string
int
string

Why. A string literal is a const char[6], which decays to const char*. Converting a pointer to bool is a standard conversion, while reaching const std::string& needs a user-defined conversion (the std::string constructor), and any standard conversion sequence beats a user-defined one ([over.ics.rank]). So emit("ready") logs a boolean. 'a' is a char, and promotion to int beats the conversion to bool. With an actual std::string argument, or the "ready"s literal, the string overload is an exact match.

The same trap exists with std::variant<bool, std::string> v = "x";, which held the bool until C++20 changed the converting constructor (P0608). Fixes: add an emit(const char*) or emit(std::string_view) overload, or delete the dangerous one: void emit(const char*) = delete; forces callers to choose.

OutputSizes and signed values meet. What are the four lines?

#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<int> v;
    std::printf("a %d\n", v.size() - 1 > 0);
    std::printf("b %d\n", -1 < 1u);
    std::printf("c %d\n", static_cast<int>(v.size()) - 1 < 0);
    std::printf("d %d\n", std::ssize(v) - 1 < 0);
}
Answer
a 1
b 0
c 1
d 1

Why. v.size() is a size_t, and 0 - 1 in unsigned arithmetic wraps to SIZE_MAX, which is greater than 0. In -1 < 1u the usual arithmetic conversions turn -1 into unsigned, giving UINT_MAX < 1, which is false. Converting to a signed type first gives the intuitive answer, and C++20's std::ssize returns a signed ptrdiff_t for exactly this purpose. The classic bug is for (size_t i = v.size() - 1; i >= 0; --i), which never terminates (and crashes on an empty vector). -Wall -Wextra warns about line b (-Wsign-compare). C++20's std::cmp_less(-1, 1u) compares mixed signs correctly.

Find the bugThe fill sizes are right, but the total and the average come out wrong. What is the bug?

#include <cstdio>
#include <numeric>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<double> fills{0.5, 0.25, 0.75, 1.5};
    auto total = std::accumulate(fills.begin(), fills.end(), 0);
    std::printf("total=%g average=%g\n", static_cast<double>(total),
                static_cast<double>(total) / static_cast<double>(fills.size()));
    std::vector<int> volumes{2'000'000'000, 2'000'000'000};
    std::printf("volume=%lld\n", std::accumulate(volumes.begin(), volumes.end(), 0LL));
}
Answer
total=1 average=0.25
volume=4000000000

Answer. std::accumulate keeps its running sum in the type of the initial value, and 0 is an int. Each step computes acc = acc + x in double and converts the result back to int, truncating: 0.5, 0.25 and 0.75 each truncate back to 0, and the last step gives 1. The true total is 3.

Fix. Pass an initial value of the right type: 0.0, or 0LL for large integer sums as on the second line, where an int initial value would overflow, which is undefined behaviour. Compilers stay quiet because the narrowing happens inside a standard header. std::reduce has the same rule. C++23's std::ranges::fold_left computes in the type of op(init, element), which would be double here.

Find the bugA helper returns a string_view to avoid copying the name. What is wrong?

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

static std::string_view venue_name(int id) {
    std::string name = "venue-" + std::to_string(id) + "-primary-matching-engine";
    return name;
}

int main() {
    std::string_view v = venue_name(7);
    unsigned sum = 0;
    for (char c : v) sum += static_cast<unsigned char>(c);  // reads the characters
    std::printf("%zu chars, checksum %u\n", v.size(), sum);
}
Answer

Answer. The view points into the local name, which is destroyed when the function returns, so main reads freed heap memory. ASan reports heap-use-after-free. The implicit conversion from std::string to std::string_view makes this compile without a cast. Clang warns with -Wreturn-stack-address, because it knows that string_view borrows from std::string. GCC usually stays quiet.

Fix. Return std::string. NRVO or a move makes that cheap, and there is nothing to save by returning a view of something the function itself owns. A string_view return is right only when the characters live elsewhere and outlive the call: a string literal, a member of a long-lived object, or a slice of the caller's input.

CodeImplement an LRU cache of int keys and values with O(1) get and put.

LruCache(capacity); std::optional<int> get(int key) returns the value and marks the key most recently used; put(int key, int value) inserts or updates, and when the cache is full it evicts the least recently used key first. Capacity 0 stores nothing.

Answer

Approach. Keep the entries in a std::list ordered from most to least recently used, and an unordered_map from key to list iterator. List iterators stay valid when other nodes are inserted, erased or moved, so the map never needs fixing up. A hit moves its node to the front with splice, which relinks the node without copying or allocating. Eviction removes the back node and its map entry.

#include <cstdio>
#include <list>
#include <optional>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <utility>

class LruCache {
public:
    explicit LruCache(std::size_t capacity) : cap_(capacity) {}

    std::optional<int> get(int key) {
        auto it = index_.find(key);
        if (it == index_.end()) return std::nullopt;
        items_.splice(items_.begin(), items_, it->second);
        return it->second->second;
    }

    void put(int key, int value) {
        if (cap_ == 0) return;
        if (auto it = index_.find(key); it != index_.end()) {
            it->second->second = value;
            items_.splice(items_.begin(), items_, it->second);
            return;
        }
        if (items_.size() == cap_) {
            index_.erase(items_.back().first);
            items_.pop_back();
        }
        items_.emplace_front(key, value);
        index_[key] = items_.begin();
    }

private:
    using Item = std::pair<int, int>;
    std::size_t cap_;
    std::list<Item> items_;
    std::unordered_map<int, std::list<Item>::iterator> index_;
};

static void show(const char* label, std::optional<int> v) {
    if (v) std::printf("%s=%d ", label, *v);
    else std::printf("%s=miss ", label);
}

int main() {
    LruCache c(2);
    c.put(1, 10);
    c.put(2, 20);
    show("get1", c.get(1));
    c.put(3, 30);           // evicts 2, the least recently used
    show("get2", c.get(2));
    c.put(1, 11);           // update moves 1 to the front
    c.put(4, 40);           // evicts 3
    show("get1", c.get(1));
    show("get3", c.get(3));
    show("get4", c.get(4));
    LruCache none(0);
    none.put(1, 1);
    show("zero", none.get(1));
    std::printf("\n");
}
get1=10 get2=miss get1=11 get3=miss get4=40 zero=miss

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) average per operation (hash lookup plus constant list relinking), O(capacity) memory. Pitfalls: storing list indices or using a vector, whose iterators are invalidated by erasure; forgetting to refresh recency on an update; erasing the map entry after pop_back (the key is gone by then, so read it first); and capacity 0. A thread-safe version needs a mutex even for get, because a hit modifies the list. For a hot cache, a node-based list allocates on every insert, so production versions use an intrusive list over a preallocated node pool.

Estimated rating: ~1500 · a standard design question, judged on iterator stability and the eviction order.

Round 2: systems team screen

DrillsCoding

Time limit: 30 minutes. Scoring: 18 points (2 concept × 1, 2 tricky × 2, 2 output × 2, 2 bug × 2, code 4). 15 or more is a strong pass. This round leans on the OS, process lifetime and locking, as a backend or infrastructure team would. Review material: Ch 4, Ch 6 and Ch 8.

ConceptWhat is the difference between a minor and a major page fault? What happens the first time a program writes to a 1 GiB buffer it just got from malloc?

Answer

Answer. A page fault happens when the CPU touches a virtual page with no valid mapping in the page table. A minor fault is resolved without I/O: the kernel allocates a zeroed page, or maps a page already in the page cache, or breaks a copy-on-write share. A major fault needs disk I/O, for example reading a page of a memory-mapped file or swapping a page back in, and costs milliseconds instead of about a microsecond. A large malloc is served by mmap, which only reserves address space. Each first write to a 4 KiB page then triggers a minor fault that allocates and zeroes one physical page, so the first pass over 1 GiB takes about 262000 faults.

Why. This is why latency-sensitive programs "pre-fault" buffers at startup (touch every page, or use MAP_POPULATE and mlock), and why RSS grows only as memory is touched. Huge pages (2 MiB) cut the number of faults and TLB misses by a factor of 512. Linux overcommit means the malloc succeeds even when the memory might not exist, and the failure shows up later as the OOM killer.

ConceptA 20 GiB in-memory risk server calls fork() so that the child can write a snapshot to disk, as Redis does. Why does fork return quickly, what does it still cost, and why can the parent's latency spike afterwards?

Answer

Answer. fork copies no data pages. It duplicates the page tables and marks every private writable page read-only in both processes, so the child sees a frozen snapshot through copy-on-write. What it does copy is the page tables themselves: with 4 KiB pages, 20 GiB is about 5.2 million entries, roughly 40 MiB of tables, and the parent is stopped while they are copied, on the order of 10 ms per GiB. Afterwards, the first write by either process to a shared page takes a page fault that copies that page, so a write-heavy parent sees latency spikes and its memory use can grow towards double.

Why. With transparent huge pages each copy-on-write fault copies 2 MiB instead of 4 KiB, which is why Redis recommends disabling THP. With strict overcommit (vm.overcommit_memory = 2), fork of a large process can fail outright, because the kernel must reserve memory for a full copy. Only the calling thread exists in the child (Ch 4). To run another program, posix_spawn or vfork avoids copying page tables at all.

TrickyFour threads each write std::cout << "id="ch26- << id << " px=" << px << '\n';. Is this a data race? What does the log look like?

Answer

Answer. It is not a data race: the standard guarantees that concurrent use of the standard stream objects does not cause a data race as long as they are synchronised with stdio (the default, sync_with_stdio(true)) ([iostream.objects.overview]). But each << is a separate call, so pieces of different lines interleave: id=1 px=id=2 px=10.5.

Why. Thread safety per call does not make a sequence of calls atomic. Fixes: format the whole line into a string first and write it with one call, or use C++20 std::osyncstream(std::cout) << ..., which buffers the line and emits it atomically when the temporary is destroyed. After std::ios::sync_with_stdio(false) (a common speed trick) the guarantee is gone, and concurrent writes become a real data race. In a low-latency system, threads should push log records to a queue and one thread should do the I/O.

TrickyThe main thread detects a fatal configuration error and calls std::exit(1) while worker threads are still running. Occasionally the process crashes on the way out instead of exiting cleanly. Why?

Answer

Answer. exit runs the destructors of objects with static storage duration (and atexit handlers) while the other threads keep running. A worker that is still using a global logger, a global std::map or a static allocator pool can touch an object that has just been destroyed. The crash then happens in a worker, far from the exit call.

Why. Process exit does not stop threads first: they are killed only when the process finally terminates after the destructors. Options: stop and join the workers before exiting (the clean answer), use std::quick_exit with at_quick_exit handlers, which skips static destructors, or _exit, which skips everything including stdio flushing. Returning from main behaves like exit, so the same crash appears if main returns with detached threads. A destroyed std::thread that is still joinable calls std::terminate instead, which at least fails loudly.

OutputA risk check looks up per-symbol limits. How many symbols does the map hold afterwards?

#include <cstdio>
#include <map>
#include <string>

int main() {
    std::map<std::string, int> limits{{"AAPL", 500}};
    int over = 0;
    for (const char* s : {"AAPL", "MSFT", "TSLA"})
        if (limits[s] > 100) ++over;
    std::printf("over=%d size=%zu MSFT=%d\n", over, limits.size(), limits["MSFT"]);
    std::printf("has GOOG=%d size=%zu\n", limits.contains("GOOG"), limits.size());
}
Answer
over=1 size=3 MSFT=0
has GOOG=0 size=3

Why. operator[] means "find or insert": for a missing key it inserts a value-initialised int (0) and returns a reference to it. So reading limits["MSFT"] silently adds MSFT and TSLA with a limit of 0. That is why operator[] is not available on a const map, and why it fails to compile for value types without a default constructor. Use find, contains (C++20) or at (throws std::out_of_range) to read. In a risk system this bug is worse than a crash, because a missing limit becomes a limit of zero (or, with a different check, no limit at all). With several threads, operator[] is also a write, so readers sharing a lock in read mode race.

OutputGlobals, a function-local static and a static local in main. In what order are they built and destroyed?

#include <cstdio>

struct Tracer {
    const char* n;
    explicit Tracer(const char* s) : n(s) { std::printf("+%s ", n); }
    ~Tracer() { std::printf("-%s ", n); }
};

Tracer g1("g1");

static Tracer& logger() {
    static Tracer t("logger");
    return t;
}

Tracer g2("g2");

int main() {
    std::printf("main ");
    logger();
    static Tracer local("local");
    std::printf("end\n");
}
Answer
+g1 +g2 main +logger +local end
-local -logger -g2 -g1

Why. Globals in one translation unit are constructed before main in definition order, so g1 then g2; defining logger() between them changes nothing, because a function-local static is built only when control first passes its declaration. Every object with static storage is destroyed after main returns in the reverse order of the completion of their constructors ([basic.start.term]), mixing globals and locals in one sequence. The trap: if ~g2 called logger() to log its own shutdown, it would use a destroyed object, because the logger was built after g2 and is therefore destroyed before it. The usual fix for a logger used during shutdown is a deliberately leaked singleton: static Tracer& t = *new Tracer("logger");.

Find the bugRemove all even order ids from a std::list. What is wrong?

#include <cstdio>
#include <list>

int main() {
    std::list<int> orders{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6};
    for (auto it = orders.begin(); it != orders.end(); ++it)
        if (*it % 2 == 0) orders.erase(it);
    std::printf("%zu\n", orders.size());
}
Answer

Answer. erase(it) frees the node that it points to, and the loop then executes ++it, which reads the freed node's next pointer. ASan reports heap-use-after-free. Without ASan it often appears to work, because the freed node's memory still holds the old links.

Fix. Use the iterator that erase returns: for (auto it = l.begin(); it != l.end();) it = (*it % 2 == 0) ? l.erase(it) : std::next(it);. Better, use orders.remove_if(pred) or C++20 std::erase_if(orders, pred), which work for every standard container. For a list, erasing invalidates only iterators to the erased node, unlike a vector, where every iterator after the erased element is invalidated.

Find the bugEach class locks its own mutex, and each method is correct on its own. The system hangs a few times a day. Find the cycle.

#include <mutex>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

struct Risk;

struct Book {
    std::mutex m;
    std::vector<int> orders{1, 2, 3};
    Risk* risk = nullptr;
    void on_fill(int qty);
    void cancel_all() {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(m);
        orders.clear();
    }
};

struct Risk {
    std::mutex m;
    long exposure = 0;
    Book* book = nullptr;
    void update(int qty) {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(m);
        exposure += qty;
    }
    void breach() {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(m);
        exposure = 0;
        book->cancel_all();
    }
};

void Book::on_fill(int qty) {
    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(m);
    orders.push_back(qty);
    risk->update(qty);
}

int main() {
    Book b;
    Risk r;
    b.risk = &r;
    r.book = &b;
    std::thread t1([&] { for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) b.on_fill(1); });
    std::thread t2([&] { for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) r.breach(); });
    t1.join();
    t2.join();
}
Answer

Answer. A lock-order inversion. on_fill holds Book::m and then takes Risk::m inside update. breach holds Risk::m and then takes Book::m inside cancel_all. If thread 1 holds the book lock while thread 2 holds the risk lock, each waits for the other forever. The harness only compiles this program, because running it can hang.

Fix. Never call into another component while holding your own lock. on_fill should update its orders under the lock, release it, then call risk->update. breach should reset exposure under its lock and call cancel_all after releasing it. When two locks really must be held together, take them in one step with std::scoped_lock lock(book.m, risk.m);, which uses a deadlock-avoidance algorithm. Tools: TSan reports "lock-order-inversion (potential deadlock)" from a single run, even when the hang does not happen, and so does Helgrind.

CodeWrite Published<T>: configuration that many reader threads read constantly and one writer occasionally replaces.

get() returns a snapshot that stays valid and unchanged for as long as the reader holds it, even while a new version is published. update(f) applies f to a copy of the current version and publishes the result. Readers must never see a half-updated object, and the old version must be destroyed only when its last reader lets go.

Answer

Approach. Store the current version as std::shared_ptr<const T>. A reader copies the pointer under a short lock, which bumps the reference count, and then uses the immutable snapshot without any lock. The writer copies the current version, modifies the copy outside the read lock, and swaps the pointer in under the lock. Readers holding the old snapshot keep it alive, and it is freed when the last one drops it. A second mutex serialises writers so that two concurrent updates cannot lose each other's changes.

#include <atomic>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <mutex>
#include <thread>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

template <class T>
class Published {
public:
    explicit Published(T initial) : cur_(std::make_shared<const T>(std::move(initial))) {}

    std::shared_ptr<const T> get() const {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(m_);
        return cur_;
    }

    template <class F>
    void update(F f) {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> w(writer_);
        auto next = std::make_shared<T>(*get());
        f(*next);
        std::shared_ptr<const T> old;
        {
            std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(m_);
            old = std::exchange(cur_, std::move(next));
        }
    }  // old is released here, outside the read lock

private:
    mutable std::mutex m_;
    std::mutex writer_;
    std::shared_ptr<const T> cur_;
};

struct Limits {
    int max_qty;
    long max_notional;  // invariant: max_notional == max_qty * 200
};

int main() {
    Published<Limits> cfg(Limits{100, 20000});
    std::atomic<int> violations{0};
    std::vector<std::thread> readers;
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i)
        readers.emplace_back([&] {
            for (int k = 0; k < 2000; ++k) {
                auto snap = cfg.get();
                if (snap->max_notional != snap->max_qty * 200L) ++violations;
            }
        });
    std::thread writer([&] {
        for (int k = 0; k < 1000; ++k)
            cfg.update([](Limits& l) {
                l.max_qty += 1;
                l.max_notional = l.max_qty * 200L;
            });
    });
    for (auto& t : readers) t.join();
    writer.join();
    std::printf("violations=%d max_qty=%d\n", violations.load(), cfg.get()->max_qty);
}
violations=0 max_qty=1100

Complexity and pitfalls. A read is one short critical section plus two atomic count updates. An update copies T. Pitfalls: returning const T& instead of a shared_ptr (the object may be replaced and freed while in use), modifying the published object in place (readers see half an update), destroying the old version while holding the read lock (its destructor might be slow), and writers without their own lock (two read-modify-write updates race and one is lost). C++20 std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<const T>> removes the read mutex where the library supports it, and production systems use RCU or hazard pointers to make reads free of shared writes altogether.

Estimated rating: ~1600 · a short design whose correctness rests on immutability and on shared_ptr lifetime.

Round 3: memory and move semantics

DrillsCoding

Time limit: 30 minutes. Scoring: 18 points (2 concept × 1, 2 tricky × 2, 2 output × 2, 2 bug × 2, code 4). 15 or more is a strong pass. This is the round a C++ library or engine team runs to check ownership reasoning. Review material: Ch 11, Ch 20 and Ch 22.

ConceptWhy does std::optional<int&> not compile in C++23, and what do people use instead?

Answer

Answer. The C++17 optional forbids reference types because assignment would be ambiguous: opt = x; could either rebind the optional to refer to x or assign through to the referred object, and the two choices behave differently depending on whether the optional was engaged. The committee left it out rather than pick. The usual replacements are a plain T* (null means empty, and the pointer is non-owning by convention) or std::optional<std::reference_wrapper<T>>.

Why. A function like find_order(id) that may return "no order" is exactly where people reach for it. Returning T* is clear and cheap. C++26 adds std::optional<T&> (P2988, voted into the working draft in June 2025) with rebinding assignment, matching what Boost has done for years. Never return std::optional<T> by value when the caller needs to modify the original, since that silently copies.

ConceptName three reasons why std::vector<T> growth might copy every element instead of moving it.

Answer

Answer. First, the move constructor is not noexcept while a copy constructor exists, so move_if_noexcept picks the copy to keep the strong guarantee. Second, T has no move constructor at all, typically because a user-declared destructor or copy operation suppressed the implicit one. Third, the move constructor exists but copies anyway, for example because a member is const or because it was written as m(o.m) instead of m(std::move(o.m)).

Why. All three compile silently. A fourth, rarer cause is a member whose own move is not noexcept: a defaulted move constructor is noexcept only if every member's move is, so one such member (some older std::function or third-party types) makes the whole class copy. Check with static_assert(std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<T>) next to the class.

TrickyA task queue is std::queue<std::function<void()>>. Pushing [conn = std::move(conn)] { conn->flush(); }, where conn is a std::unique_ptr, fails to compile. Why, and what are the fixes?

Answer

Answer. std::function requires its target to be copy constructible, because std::function itself is copyable and must be able to copy whatever it holds. A lambda that captures a unique_ptr by move is move-only, so it cannot be stored.

Why. Fixes: use C++23 std::move_only_function<void()>, which drops the copy requirement (and adds const and noexcept qualifiers in its signature); write a small type-erased move-only callable yourself; or convert the resource to std::shared_ptr so the lambda becomes copyable, at the cost of an atomic count and shared ownership you did not want. Do not "fix" it by capturing a raw pointer and releasing the unique_ptr, which leaks if the task is never run.

TrickyTo avoid reallocations, code calls v.reserve(1000); on an empty std::vector<double> and then fills it with for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) v[i] = price(i);. It runs, and the values read back correctly. Is it correct?

Answer

Answer. No, it is undefined behaviour. reserve changes the capacity only. The size is still 0, so no elements exist, and operator[] with an index not less than size() is undefined. It appears to work because the memory is allocated and double needs no construction. Then v.size() is still 0, so any loop over the vector, any copy and any push_back ignores or overwrites the "stored" values.

Why. Use resize(1000) (or the size constructor) and then assign, or keep reserve and use push_back/emplace_back. For a class type the bug is worse, because assignment then runs on objects that were never constructed. Hardened library modes catch it at run time: -D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS for libstdc++ and -D_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE=_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE_FAST for libc++ both turn an out-of-range operator[] into an abort, which is cheap enough to leave on in many production builds. v.at(i) throws std::out_of_range instead.

OutputCount the copies and moves for brace initialisation and for emplace_back.

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Tracked {
    static inline int copies = 0, moves = 0;
    std::string s;
    Tracked(const char* p) : s(p) {}
    Tracked(const Tracked& o) : s(o.s) { ++copies; }
    Tracked(Tracked&& o) noexcept : s(std::move(o.s)) { ++moves; }
};

int main() {
    std::vector<Tracked> a{"x", "y", "z"};
    std::printf("braces: copies=%d moves=%d\n", Tracked::copies, Tracked::moves);
    Tracked::copies = Tracked::moves = 0;
    std::vector<Tracked> b;
    b.reserve(3);
    b.emplace_back("x");
    b.emplace_back("y");
    b.emplace_back("z");
    std::printf("emplace: copies=%d moves=%d\n", Tracked::copies, Tracked::moves);
}
Answer
braces: copies=3 moves=0
emplace: copies=0 moves=0

Why. A braced list first builds a hidden const Tracked[3] array (three converting constructions), and std::initializer_list gives only const access to it. The vector cannot move from const elements, so it copies all three. emplace_back constructs each element in place from the const char*, and reserve prevents any relocation. Consequences: std::vector<std::unique_ptr<int>> v{std::make_unique<int>(1)}; does not compile, and initialising a vector of large strings from a braced list allocates every string twice. C++26 does not change this, so for move-only or expensive types use reserve plus emplace_back.

OutputA stateful callback counts its calls. It is copied into a std::function, which is then copied and moved. What prints?

#include <cstdio>
#include <functional>
#include <utility>

int main() {
    auto counter = [n = 0]() mutable { return ++n; };
    std::function<int()> f = counter;
    f();
    f();
    int from_f = f();
    int from_counter = counter();
    std::printf("f=%d counter=%d\n", from_f, from_counter);
    std::function<int()> g = f;
    std::function<int()> h = std::move(f);
    int from_g = g();
    int from_h = h();
    std::printf("g=%d h=%d\n", from_g, from_h);
}
Answer
f=3 counter=1
g=4 h=4

Why. std::function stores its own copy of the callable, so the mutable lambda's counter n is duplicated: three calls through f leave the original counter untouched, and its first call returns 1. Copying f copies the state (so g continues from 3), and moving f transfers it (so h also continues from 3). A moved-from std::function is valid but unspecified. Both libraries leave it empty, so calling it would throw std::bad_function_call, but code must not rely on either outcome.

To share one state, capture a pointer or a shared_ptr, or store std::ref(counter), which puts a reference_wrapper inside the std::function. The same copying hides in std::thread, which copies its callable, and in algorithms such as std::for_each, which take function objects by value. The common wrong answer is "f=3 counter=3".

Find the bugA move-only packet buffer. The program prints 1500 and then dies. Why?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstring>
#include <vector>

class Packet {
public:
    explicit Packet(std::size_t n) : size_(n), data_(new char[n]) { std::memset(data_, 0, n); }
    Packet(Packet&& o) noexcept : size_(o.size_), data_(o.data_) {}
    Packet(const Packet&) = delete;
    Packet& operator=(const Packet&) = delete;
    ~Packet() { delete[] data_; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }

private:
    std::size_t size_;
    char* data_;
};

int main() {
    std::vector<Packet> q;
    q.push_back(Packet(1500));
    std::printf("%zu\n", q[0].size());
}
Answer

Answer. The move constructor copies the pointer but does not clear it in the source. The temporary Packet(1500) is destroyed at the end of the push_back statement and frees the buffer, so the element in the vector holds a dangling pointer, and its destructor frees the same buffer again at the end of main. ASan reports attempting double-free.

Fix. Leave the source empty: data_(std::exchange(o.data_, nullptr)) and size_(std::exchange(o.size_, 0)). A move must leave the source in a state its destructor can handle. Better still, hold the buffer as std::unique_ptr<char[]> and let the compiler generate the moves (rule of zero). This bug hides in tests that never destroy the moved-from object before the program ends, and it is a favourite because the code looks complete.

Find the bugA recorder starts its background thread in the constructor. TSan reports a race in a program with no visible sharing. Where?

#include <cstdio>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

class Recorder {
public:
    Recorder() : worker_([this] { samples_.push_back(42); }) {}
    ~Recorder() { worker_.join(); }
    std::size_t count() const { return samples_.size(); }

private:
    std::thread worker_;
    std::vector<int> samples_;
};

int main() {
    static Recorder r;
    std::printf("%zu\n", r.count());
}
Answer

Answer. Members are initialised in declaration order, and worker_ is declared before samples_. The thread starts while samples_ has not been constructed yet, so the new thread's push_back races with the main thread's construction of the vector, which may also overwrite the element the thread just added. count() then races with the thread too, since nothing waits for it. TSan reports the race on the vector's members.

Fix. Declare the thread last so every member it uses exists before it starts, and treat starting a thread as the final step of construction. Here the object is also published to the thread before its constructor finishes, so if the class had derived classes or virtual functions, the thread could see a half-built object. Reading results requires synchronisation as well: join (or wait on a condition) before calling count(). With std::jthread declared last, the destructor also gets the order right: it stops and joins the thread before the other members are destroyed.

CodeWrite a string interner that maps symbol names to dense ids and back, with views that never dangle.

std::uint32_t intern(std::string_view s) returns the existing id for a known string or assigns the next id. std::string_view name(id) returns the stored text, and every view or id handed out must stay valid for the interner's lifetime, however many strings are added later. Lookups of known strings must not allocate.

Answer

Approach. Store each string once in a std::deque<std::string>: pushing at the end of a deque never moves existing elements, so references to them stay valid. The hash map is keyed by std::string_views that point at those stored strings, so a lookup with the caller's string_view hashes the characters without building a std::string. A vector of views gives O(1) id-to-name.

#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <deque>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <vector>

class Interner {
public:
    std::uint32_t intern(std::string_view s) {
        if (auto it = ids_.find(s); it != ids_.end()) return it->second;
        const std::string& stored = store_.emplace_back(s);
        auto id = static_cast<std::uint32_t>(views_.size());
        views_.push_back(stored);
        ids_.emplace(views_.back(), id);
        return id;
    }
    std::string_view name(std::uint32_t id) const { return views_.at(id); }
    std::size_t size() const { return views_.size(); }

private:
    std::deque<std::string> store_;  // never relocates existing strings
    std::vector<std::string_view> views_;
    std::unordered_map<std::string_view, std::uint32_t> ids_;
};

int main() {
    Interner in;
    std::uint32_t a = in.intern("AAPL");
    std::uint32_t m = in.intern("MSFT");
    std::string key = "AAPL";
    std::uint32_t again = in.intern(key);
    std::string_view early = in.name(m);
    for (int i = 0; i < 10000; ++i) in.intern("SYM" + std::to_string(i));
    std::printf("AAPL=%u MSFT=%u again=%u size=%zu\n", a, m, again, in.size());
    std::printf("early view=%.*s name0=%.*s\n", static_cast<int>(early.size()), early.data(),
                static_cast<int>(in.name(0).size()), in.name(0).data());
}
AAPL=0 MSFT=1 again=0 size=10002
early view=MSFT name0=AAPL

Complexity and pitfalls. O(length) per intern (one hash), O(1) per name. The tempting std::vector<std::string> store is the trap: on growth it moves the strings, and a short string's characters live inside the std::string object (SSO), so every string_view to it dangles. Long strings would survive by accident, which makes the bug data-dependent. Keying the map by std::string would work but costs a second copy of every name, and lookups with a string_view would need C++20 heterogeneous lookup (a transparent hash and equality). An arena of characters with views into it is the faster production layout (Ch 17).

Estimated rating: ~1500 · short code, judged on reference stability and on not allocating for lookups.

Round 4: networking and the OS boundary

DrillsCoding

Time limit: 30 minutes. Scoring: 18 points (2 concept × 1, 2 tricky × 2, 2 output × 2, 2 bug × 2, code 4). 15 or more is a strong pass. Expect this round for networking, backend and exchange-connectivity roles. Review material: Ch 7, Ch 8 and Ch 4.

ConceptYou type https://example.com/ into a browser on a fresh laptop. List the network steps until the first byte of the page arrives, in order.

Answer

Answer. (1) DHCP has already given the laptop an IP address, a default gateway and a DNS server. (2) The browser resolves example.com: it checks its own and the OS caches, then sends a UDP query to the resolver. Because the resolver is on another network, the packet goes to the gateway, whose MAC address the laptop learns with ARP. The resolver walks root, .com and the authoritative server if it has no cached answer. (3) A TCP three-way handshake to port 443 (one RTT). (4) A TLS 1.3 handshake (one more RTT): ClientHello with a key share and SNI, ServerHello, certificate and Finished, then keys are derived. (5) An encrypted HTTP request (HTTP/2 negotiated through ALPN), and the server's response.

Why. The interviewer listens for layering (ARP below IP, DNS over UDP, TLS over TCP) and for where round trips go: DNS, TCP and TLS each cost at least one RTT before the request. Bonus points: NAT rewrites the source address at the home router, HTTP/3 replaces TCP and TLS with QUIC to merge those handshakes, and connection reuse skips everything after step 2 for later requests.

ConceptWhat does a socket's receive buffer (SO_RCVBUF) do, and what happens to a UDP market data feed when the application falls behind and the buffer fills?

Answer

Answer. The receive buffer is the kernel memory where packets wait between arriving from the NIC and being read by the application. For TCP, a full buffer shrinks the advertised window to zero and the sender is told to wait, so no data is lost. UDP has no flow control, so once the buffer is full the kernel silently drops every new datagram. The application only notices through sequence-number gaps, and the kernel counts the drops (RcvbufErrors in netstat -su or /proc/net/snmp).

Why. Bursts at the market open can be many times the average rate, so feed handlers set a large SO_RCVBUF (Linux caps it at net.core.rmem_max, and reports back double the value you asked for, because it reserves room for bookkeeping) and, more importantly, keep the reading thread from ever blocking. A big buffer only absorbs bursts. It does not help if the consumer is slower on average, and it adds queueing delay to every packet behind the backlog.

TrickyYour client is blocked in recv on a TCP connection. What does it see if the server process crashes, and what if the server machine loses power?

Answer

Answer. If the process crashes, the server's kernel closes its sockets: it sends FIN (or RST if unread data was pending), and the client's recv returns 0 or fails with ECONNRESET almost immediately. If the machine loses power, nothing is sent at all. The client's recv keeps blocking indefinitely, because an idle TCP connection exchanges no packets and so cannot notice that the peer is gone.

Why. TCP detects a dead peer only when it tries to send: retransmissions of unacknowledged data eventually time out (with the Linux default tcp_retries2 = 15, after about 924.6 seconds, roughly 15 minutes), or TCP_USER_TIMEOUT sets a shorter limit. For idle connections, enable keepalive and shorten it (TCP_KEEPIDLE, TCP_KEEPINTVL, TCP_KEEPCNT), since keepalive is off unless you set SO_KEEPALIVE, and even then the first probe comes only after 2 hours of silence (tcp_keepalive_time = 7200), followed by 9 probes 75 seconds apart. Trading protocols such as FIX add application-level heartbeats for exactly this reason: a missed heartbeat interval is the reliable signal. When the machine reboots and the client then sends, the fresh kernel answers with RST.

TrickyExchanges publish market data over UDP multicast, not TCP. Why, and what does a feed handler do when it sees sequence number 1005 right after 1003?

Answer

Answer. Multicast lets the network replicate one stream to every subscriber, so the exchange sends each packet once and all participants receive it at nearly the same time. TCP would need one connection per client, and one slow client's retransmissions and flow control would never be allowed to delay the others. A gap from 1003 to 1005 means 1004 was lost or reordered. The handler buffers 1005 onward, waits briefly in case 1004 arrives late or on the second feed, and otherwise requests a retransmission or rebuilds its state from a snapshot channel.

Why. Exchanges usually publish two identical feeds (A and B) over separate network paths, and the handler takes whichever copy of each sequence number arrives first (line arbitration), which hides most single-path losses. Recovery uses a separate TCP or unicast retransmission service and periodic snapshots. The order book must not be updated past a gap, since applying 1005 without 1004 can leave a phantom order. Every packet carries a sequence number precisely because UDP itself gives no ordering or delivery guarantee.

OutputA thread blocks in read on an empty pipe, and a timer signal arrives after 50 ms. What does read return?

#include <cerrno>
#include <csignal>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstring>
#include <sys/time.h>
#include <unistd.h>

static void on_alarm(int) {}

int main() {
    int p[2];
    if (pipe(p) != 0) return 1;
    struct sigaction sa {};
    sa.sa_handler = on_alarm;
    sigemptyset(&sa.sa_mask);
    sa.sa_flags = 0;  // no SA_RESTART
    sigaction(SIGALRM, &sa, nullptr);

    itimerval t{};
    t.it_value.tv_usec = 50000;
    setitimer(ITIMER_REAL, &t, nullptr);

    char c;
    ssize_t n = read(p[0], &c, 1);
    int err = errno;
    std::printf("read=%zd errno=%s\n", n, err == EINTR ? "EINTR" : std::strerror(err));
}
Answer
read=-1 errno=EINTR

Why. When a signal handler runs while a thread is blocked in a "slow" system call (reads from pipes, sockets and terminals, accept, connect, waits), the call is interrupted. Without SA_RESTART it returns -1 with errno == EINTR, and no data has been lost. With SA_RESTART the kernel restarts most such calls transparently, and this program would block forever. Some calls never restart, whatever the flag (on Linux epoll_wait, poll, select and calls with a timeout such as nanosleep), so robust I/O code always retries on EINTR. Signals installed with the old signal() function get SA_RESTART semantics on glibc and BSD, which is why the bug often hides until someone switches to sigaction.

OutputWhich numbers does the kernel hand out? The program prints them relative to the first descriptor.

#include <cstdio>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <unistd.h>

int main() {
    int a = open("/dev/null", O_RDONLY);
    int b = open("/dev/null", O_RDONLY);
    close(a);
    int c = open("/dev/null", O_RDONLY);
    int d = dup(b);
    std::printf("a=+%d b=+%d c=+%d d=+%d\n", a - a, b - a, c - a, d - a);
    close(b);
    close(c);
    close(d);
}
Answer
a=+0 b=+1 c=+0 d=+2

Why. POSIX requires open, socket, accept, dup and friends to return the lowest-numbered descriptor not currently open. After close(a), the next open immediately reuses a's number. dup(b) gets the lowest free number, which is now after b. In a normal process 0, 1 and 2 are taken, so a is 3. This rule is how shells redirect output (close 1, then open a file, and it becomes stdout), and it is what makes the next bug dangerous.

Find the bugThe receive helper failed with a reset connection, yet the code went on to parse a header. Why?

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <sys/types.h>

struct Header { unsigned char bytes[8]; };

static ssize_t fake_recv(void*, std::size_t) { return -1; }  // as if errno == ECONNRESET

int main() {
    Header h;
    ssize_t n = fake_recv(&h, sizeof h);
    if (n < sizeof h) {
        std::puts("short read or error, handle it");
        return 0;
    }
    std::puts("header complete, parsing");
}
Answer
header complete, parsing

Answer. n < sizeof h compares a signed ssize_t with an unsigned size_t. The usual arithmetic conversions convert n to size_t, so -1 becomes SIZE_MAX, the comparison is false, and the error path is skipped. The code then parses an uninitialised header. -Wall -Wextra warns about it (-Wsign-compare), which is the cheapest bug fix in this chapter.

Fix. Check for errors first and separately: if (n < 0) { handle errno } if (static_cast<std::size_t>(n) < sizeof h) { short read }, or use std::cmp_less(n, sizeof h) from C++20, which compares mixed signs by value. Better, put the loop and both checks inside one recv_exact helper (Ch 8), so call sites never see a raw return value.

Find the bugAn error path closes a connection early, and later the audit log stops working. Connect the two.

#include <cerrno>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstring>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <unistd.h>

struct Conn {
    int fd;
    ~Conn() { close(fd); }
};

int main() {
    int log = -1;
    {
        Conn c{open("/dev/null", O_RDONLY)};
        close(c.fd);                        // error path closes early
        log = open("/dev/zero", O_RDONLY);  // gets the lowest free number
        std::printf("same number: %s\n", log == c.fd ? "yes" : "no");
    }                                       // ~Conn closes c.fd again
    char buf[4];
    ssize_t n = read(log, buf, sizeof buf);
    std::printf("read from log: %zd (%s)\n", n, n < 0 ? std::strerror(errno) : "ok");
}
Answer
same number: yes
read from log: -1 (Bad file descriptor)

Answer. A double close. The error path closes c.fd but leaves the number in the object, the log file is opened and receives the same number (lowest free descriptor), and then ~Conn closes that number again, which closes the log. Every later write to the log fails with EBADF, or worse, a third open reuses the number and log lines go into some other file or socket.

Fix. Make one owner responsible for closing: a move-only RAII handle whose reset() closes and sets the stored value to -1, and never call close on a descriptor you do not own. In multi-threaded programs the same bug is a race: another thread's accept can grab the number between the two closes. No sanitizer catches it, but strace -e trace=close shows two closes of one number, and a failed close returning EBADF is a sign of it. Also note that on Linux you must not retry close after EINTR, since the descriptor is already released.

CodeWrite LineReader, which turns arbitrary chunks from a stream socket into complete lines.

feed(chunk, on_line) appends the bytes and calls on_line(std::string_view) once per complete line, without the trailing \n or \r\n. A partial line must be kept until the rest arrives, possibly several chunks later. Lines (complete or partial) longer than max_line bytes must make feed return false so the caller can drop the connection. Scanning must stay linear even when a long line arrives one byte at a time.

Answer

Approach. Keep a buffer of unconsumed bytes and the position up to which it has already been searched for a newline, so that bytes are scanned only once. Each feed appends, then repeatedly finds the next \n from the scan position, strips an optional \r, and hands out a view of the line. After the loop, the consumed prefix is erased in one step and the length limit is checked on whatever partial line is left.

#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

class LineReader {
public:
    explicit LineReader(std::size_t max_line) : max_(max_line) {}

    template <class F>
    bool feed(std::string_view chunk, F&& on_line) {
        buf_.append(chunk);
        std::size_t start = 0;
        for (std::size_t nl; (nl = buf_.find('\n', scan_)) != std::string::npos;) {
            std::size_t end = (nl > start && buf_[nl - 1] == '\r') ? nl - 1 : nl;
            if (end - start > max_) return false;
            on_line(std::string_view(buf_).substr(start, end - start));
            start = nl + 1;
            scan_ = start;
        }
        buf_.erase(0, start);
        scan_ = buf_.size();
        return buf_.size() <= max_;
    }

private:
    std::size_t max_;
    std::string buf_;
    std::size_t scan_ = 0;
};

int main() {
    LineReader r(64);
    auto print = [](std::string_view line) {
        std::printf("[%.*s]\n", static_cast<int>(line.size()), line.data());
    };
    r.feed("GET /a HT", print);
    r.feed("TP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\n\r\npart", print);
    r.feed("ial", print);
    r.feed("\n", print);
    LineReader small(8);
    std::printf("oversize rejected: %s\n", small.feed("0123456789", print) ? "no" : "yes");
}
[GET /a HTTP/1.1]
[Host: x]
[]
[partial]
oversize rejected: yes

Complexity and pitfalls. Amortised O(n) in the bytes received: each byte is scanned once and the erase moves only the leftover partial line. Pitfalls: searching from the start of the buffer on every chunk (quadratic for a slow sender), forgetting the partial line at the end of a chunk, assuming a \r\n pair never splits across two chunks (it can, which is why the \r is stripped only once the \n is seen), and no length limit, which lets a peer that never sends a newline exhaust memory. Views passed to on_line are valid only during the call, since the next feed modifies the buffer.

Estimated rating: ~1300 · simple parsing, judged on partial input, the length limit and linear scanning.

Round 5: the hard round (HFT and low-latency systems)

DrillsCoding

Time limit: 45 minutes. Scoring: 22 points (2 concept × 1, 3 tricky × 2, 2 output × 2, 2 bug × 2, code 6: 3 for a correct solution, 1 for the memory orders explained, 1 for the cache layout, 1 for complexity and edge cases). 18 or more is the bar for a trading-firm onsite, and 14 to 17 is a pass for most systems roles. Interviewers here push every answer one level deeper, so practise the "why" sentences aloud. Review material: Ch 5, Ch 19 and Ch 25.

ConceptWhy do trading systems pin their hot threads to dedicated cores, and what else must be configured for the pinning to remove jitter?

Answer

Answer. Pinning (pthread_setaffinity_np or taskset) stops the scheduler from migrating a thread, which would cost it its warm L1/L2 caches and TLB, and lets a busy-polling thread own a core without being preempted. For that to work, the core must also be kept free of other work: remove it from the general scheduler (isolcpus or cpusets), stop the periodic timer tick on it (nohz_full), move device interrupts elsewhere (/proc/irq/*/smp_affinity), move kernel threads and RCU callbacks off it (rcu_nocbs), and disable deep C-states and frequency scaling so the core never sleeps or slows down.

Why. Each of these is a source of microsecond-scale interruptions that pinning alone does not prevent: a timer interrupt, a network IRQ, a kernel worker or a wake-up from a deep sleep state. Also keep the hot threads on the NIC's NUMA node and avoid putting two hot threads on hyperthread siblings, which share a core's execution units and L1 cache. The cost is cores that sit spinning at 100%, which is accepted in exchange for predictable latency.

ConceptWhat does kernel-bypass networking (for example Solarflare Onload, ef_vi or DPDK) remove from the receive path of a UDP packet?

Answer

Answer. In the normal path, the NIC writes the packet into a kernel ring buffer and raises an interrupt (or the kernel polls it via NAPI), the kernel's network stack processes it (IP, UDP, socket lookup), queues it on the socket, wakes the waiting thread, and recvfrom copies it into user memory across a system call. Kernel bypass maps the NIC's receive rings directly into the process, and a dedicated thread busy-polls them. That removes the interrupt, the context switch and wake-up, the system call and the copy, and the kernel stack itself.

Why. The kernel path costs several microseconds with significant jitter, while bypass brings the wire-to-application time down to around a microsecond or less. The costs: a core spinning at 100%, a user-space network stack (Onload keeps the sockets API, ef_vi and DPDK give raw frames), and losing kernel tools such as tcpdump on that traffic. It is usually combined with core isolation (isolcpus, nohz_full), IRQ affinity and huge pages.

TrickyA seqlock protects a 64-byte quote: the writer increments a sequence counter to odd, writes the fields, and increments it back to even. A reader copies the fields and retries if the counter was odd or changed. Why can the reader see a torn quote, why is that acceptable, and what is the C++ memory-model problem?

Answer

Answer. The reader takes no lock, so it can copy some fields from the old quote and some from the new one while the writer is in the middle of an update. That is acceptable because it then sees a changed sequence number and discards the copy, so a torn value is never used. The memory-model problem is that the reader's plain reads of the fields race with the writer's plain writes, which is a data race and therefore undefined behaviour in C++, even though the result is thrown away.

Why. Correct C++ versions make every payload field a std::atomic accessed with memory_order_relaxed (or copy it with relaxed atomic word loads), and they order the accesses with fences: the reader does an acquire load of the sequence, reads the payload, then atomic_thread_fence(memory_order_acquire) before re-reading the sequence. The writer does a release fence after making the counter odd and a release store to make it even. Without the fences, the CPU or compiler may move payload reads outside the two sequence reads. Seqlocks suit one writer and many readers of small data that changes often, because readers never write to shared memory and so never bounce the cache line. The writer can starve readers if it updates continuously.

TrickyWhat machine code does x.store(1) (default seq_cst) on a std::atomic<int> compile to on x86-64 and on ARM64? And x.load()?

Answer

Answer. On x86-64 a seq_cst store is an xchg (a locked instruction that acts as a full barrier), or a mov followed by mfence. A seq_cst load is a plain mov. On ARM64 the store is stlr (store-release) and the load is ldar (load-acquire), and that pair alone gives sequential consistency.

Why. x86 is TSO: the only reordering it allows is a later load passing an earlier store sitting in the store buffer, so the store side must drain the buffer, and that is the expensive operation: very roughly 10 to 30 cycles uncontended depending on the core, and far more when the line is contended. Release stores and acquire loads are plain movs on x86, which is why memory_order_release on a publish flag is free there while seq_cst is not. ARM's stlr/ldar were designed to implement exactly the C++ model, so seq_cst costs little more than release/acquire there. Relaxed operations are plain loads and stores on both. A fetch_add is lock xadd on x86 whatever the order, and ldaddal (with LSE atomics) or an ldaxr/stlxr loop on ARM64.

TrickyYou need nanosecond timestamps for every packet. How expensive is clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) on Linux, why is it not a real system call, and when would you read the TSC directly?

Answer

Answer. Typically some tens of nanoseconds (often quoted as 15 to 30 ns on a modern x86 server) when the kernel's clocksource is the TSC. glibc implements it in the vDSO, a small shared library the kernel maps into every process together with a data page holding the current clock parameters. The call reads the TSC with rdtsc and converts it using that data, with no switch into the kernel. If the clocksource is hpet or acpi_pm (some virtual machines, or after the kernel has marked the TSC unstable), the vDSO falls back to a real system call. A real system call costs roughly 100 ns or more, plus mitigations for speculative-execution attacks. Reading the TSC directly (__rdtsc(), or rdtscp to stop it executing early) costs a few nanoseconds (some tens of cycles) and gives raw tick counts that you convert to time later, off the hot path.

Why. Raw TSC is safe on modern CPUs with an invariant TSC (constant rate across frequency changes and synchronised across cores), which you should check in /proc/cpuinfo (constant_tsc, nonstop_tsc). rdtsc is not serialising, so measuring a short region needs rdtscp or fences. Never measure latency with CLOCK_REALTIME/system_clock, which NTP can step backwards. For wire timestamps, NICs offer hardware timestamping (SO_TIMESTAMPING), which is more accurate than anything done in software after the fact.

OutputA price-level bitmap marks which of 64 ticks have resting liquidity. What do the bit operations print?

#include <bit>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <initializer_list>

int main() {
    std::uint64_t levels = 0;  // bit i set: there is liquidity at tick i
    for (int tick : {3, 17, 40}) levels |= std::uint64_t{1} << tick;
    std::printf("lowest=%d highest=%d count=%d\n", std::countr_zero(levels),
                63 - std::countl_zero(levels), std::popcount(levels));
    std::printf("ceil=%u single=%d ctz0=%d\n", std::bit_ceil(1000u), std::has_single_bit(1024u),
                std::countr_zero(std::uint64_t{0}));
    levels &= levels - 1;  // clear the lowest set bit
    std::printf("after pop lowest=%d\n", std::countr_zero(levels));
}
Answer
lowest=3 highest=40 count=3
ceil=1024 single=1 ctz0=64
after pop lowest=17

Why. std::countr_zero counts trailing zero bits, which is the index of the lowest set bit, and 63 - std::countl_zero is the index of the highest. std::popcount counts set bits. std::bit_ceil rounds up to a power of two (ring buffer sizes) and std::has_single_bit tests for one. x &= x - 1 clears the lowest set bit, so the next level appears. The C++20 <bit> functions are defined for zero (countr_zero(0) is the bit width, 64), unlike __builtin_ctz(0), which is undefined because x86's bsf leaves its result undefined for a zero input. The wrong answer for the second number is countl_zero(levels) itself, which is 23.

Each call compiles to one or two instructions (tzcnt, lzcnt and popcnt on x86-64 with BMI, rbit plus clz on ARM64). One word covers 64 price levels, and a summary word over 64 words covers 4096 levels with two lookups, which is how some order books find the best bid or ask without scanning.

OutputByte arithmetic in a feed parser. What are the four lines?

#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>

int main() {
    std::uint8_t a = 200, b = 100;
    auto sum = a + b;
    std::uint8_t wrapped = a + b;
    std::uint8_t flags = 0x0F;
    std::printf("sum=%d size=%zu\n", sum, sizeof(sum));
    std::printf("wrapped=%d\n", wrapped);
    std::printf("~flags==0xF0: %d\n", ~flags == 0xF0);
    std::printf("uint8(~flags)==0xF0: %d\n", static_cast<std::uint8_t>(~flags) == 0xF0);
}
Answer
sum=300 size=4
wrapped=44
~flags==0xF0: 0
uint8(~flags)==0xF0: 1

Why. Integer promotion converts operands narrower than int to int before any arithmetic ([conv.prom]). a + b is an int with value 300, so auto deduces int. Storing it into a uint8_t reduces it modulo 256, giving 44. ~flags flips all 32 bits of the promoted int, giving 0xFFFFFFF0 (-16), which is not 0xF0. The dangerous relative: std::uint16_t x = 0xFFFF; x * x promotes both operands to signed int, and 65535 · 65535 overflows it, which is undefined behaviour although every type in the source is unsigned. Write 1u * x * x or cast to std::uint32_t first. Checksums and bitmask parsing in feed handlers are where this shows up.

Find the bugA single-producer single-consumer ring uses atomic indices, all relaxed "because there is only one writer per index". The sums usually match. What is wrong?

#include <atomic>
#include <cstdio>
#include <thread>

constexpr unsigned N = 1024;
static long data[N];
static std::atomic<unsigned> head{0}, tail{0};

int main() {
    constexpr int items = 20000;
    std::thread producer([] {
        for (int i = 1; i <= items; ++i) {
            unsigned h = head.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
            while (h - tail.load(std::memory_order_relaxed) == N) {}
            data[h % N] = i;
            head.store(h + 1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
        }
    });
    long long sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < items; ++i) {
        unsigned t = tail.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        while (head.load(std::memory_order_relaxed) == t) {}
        sum += data[t % N];
        tail.store(t + 1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
    }
    producer.join();
    std::printf("%lld\n", sum);
}
Answer

Answer. The index stores do not publish the data. A relaxed store of head creates no happens-before edge, so the consumer may see the new head and still read the old contents of data[h % N], and the plain accesses to data are a data race (TSan reports it). The same problem runs the other way: a relaxed tail store lets the producer overwrite a slot the consumer is still reading. On x86 the hardware happens not to reorder these particular stores, so the sums match there unless the compiler reorders them, while ARM really can.

Fix. The producer's head.store must be release and the consumer's head.load in the wait loop acquire, and symmetrically tail.store release with the producer's tail.load acquire. Each side's load of its own index can stay relaxed, since only that thread writes it. "One writer per variable" removes the need for read-modify-write operations, not the need for ordering. The coding question below builds the full version.

Find the bugA latency monitor timestamps orders with std::chrono::high_resolution_clock. Once a day it reports negative latencies. The program prints each clock's is_steady. Explain the output and the bug.

#include <chrono>
#include <cstdio>

template <class C>
static void show(const char* name) {
    std::printf("%s steady=%d\n", name, static_cast<int>(C::is_steady));
}

int main() {
    show<std::chrono::system_clock>("system_clock");
    show<std::chrono::steady_clock>("steady_clock");
    show<std::chrono::high_resolution_clock>("high_resolution_clock");
}
Answer
system_clock steady=0
steady_clock steady=1
high_resolution_clock steady=0

Answer. This output is for GCC with libstdc++, where high_resolution_clock is an alias of system_clock: wall-clock time, which NTP or an operator can step backwards (or forwards). A latency computed across such a step comes out negative or hugely positive. With Clang and libc++ the third line prints steady=1, because libc++ aliases it to steady_clock, so the same code is correct on one toolchain and broken on the other.

Why. The standard only says high_resolution_clock has the shortest tick period available, and it may be an alias of either clock. On Linux both system_clock and steady_clock already tick in nanoseconds, so it buys nothing. Measure intervals with steady_clock (CLOCK_MONOTONIC) or a raw TSC, use system_clock only for timestamps that must match wall time (logs, exchange reports), and record both if you need both. Adding static_assert(Clock::is_steady) next to latency code turns this into a compile error.

CodeImplement a lock-free single-producer single-consumer ring buffer, SpscRing<T, N>.

bool push(const T&) returns false when full and bool pop(T&) returns false when empty. Exactly one thread calls push and exactly one other thread calls pop. N is a power of two. Use the weakest correct memory orders, avoid false sharing between the producer's and the consumer's data, and keep the shared cache-line traffic per operation as low as possible. Explain each memory order.

Answer

Approach. Use two monotonically increasing indices, head (written only by the producer) and tail (written only by the consumer), and map them to slots with & (N - 1), so "full" is head - tail == N with no wasted slot and unsigned wraparound is harmless. The producer writes the slot and then publishes it with a release store of head, and the consumer's acquire load of head makes the slot contents visible. The same pairing on tail tells the producer that a slot has been fully read and may be reused. Each side also keeps a private cached copy of the other side's index and reloads it only when the cache says full or empty, which removes most cross-core cache-line transfers.

#include <array>
#include <atomic>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory>
#include <thread>

template <class T, std::size_t N>
class SpscRing {
    static_assert(N >= 2 && (N & (N - 1)) == 0, "N must be a power of two");

public:
    bool push(const T& v) {
        const std::size_t h = head_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);  // only we write head_
        if (h - tail_cache_ == N) {
            tail_cache_ = tail_.load(std::memory_order_acquire);       // slot reads are done
            if (h - tail_cache_ == N) return false;
        }
        buf_[h & (N - 1)] = v;
        head_.store(h + 1, std::memory_order_release);                 // publish the slot
        return true;
    }

    bool pop(T& out) {
        const std::size_t t = tail_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);  // only we write tail_
        if (t == head_cache_) {
            head_cache_ = head_.load(std::memory_order_acquire);       // see the slot contents
            if (t == head_cache_) return false;
        }
        out = buf_[t & (N - 1)];
        tail_.store(t + 1, std::memory_order_release);                 // hand the slot back
        return true;
    }

private:
    alignas(64) std::atomic<std::size_t> head_{0};  // producer line
    std::size_t tail_cache_ = 0;
    alignas(64) std::atomic<std::size_t> tail_{0};  // consumer line
    std::size_t head_cache_ = 0;
    alignas(64) std::array<T, N> buf_{};
};

int main() {
    constexpr long items = 100000;
    auto ring = std::make_unique<SpscRing<long, 1024>>();
    std::thread producer([&] {
        for (long i = 1; i <= items; ++i)
            while (!ring->push(i)) {}
    });
    long long sum = 0;
    long expected = 1;
    bool in_order = true;
    for (long got = 0; got < items;) {
        long v;
        if (!ring->pop(v)) continue;
        in_order = in_order && v == expected++;
        sum += v;
        ++got;
    }
    producer.join();
    std::printf("received=%ld sum=%lld in_order=%d\n", items, sum, in_order);
}
received=100000 sum=5000050000 in_order=1

Complexity and pitfalls. O(1) per operation and wait-free for each side (a failed push or pop returns at once). Pitfalls: relaxed publication (the previous bug), using % with a non-power-of-two N together with free-running indices (correct only if N divides the index range, so a power of two), leaving one slot empty to tell full from empty (wasteful when indices are free-running), putting head_ and tail_ on one cache line, and calling push from two threads (two producers need a CAS on head, which is a different, MPSC design). A 64-byte-aligned object on the heap needs C++17 aligned new, which make_unique uses. Real HFT queues also pad T to a cache line or batch the index stores, and some replace the index check with a per-slot sequence number so the consumer reads only the slot's own line.

Estimated rating: ~1900 · short code, but every memory order and the cache layout must be justified under questioning.
